# The Legendarium of Dia-thìr — The Age of Sundering (An Aois Scaraidh)

# Chapter One: Of the Three Crews

*LE 1*

> *Cha chuir mi duine thairis, agus cha chùm mi duine air ais.*
> I will send no one over, and I will keep no one back.
>
> — the queen's word, as the harbour songs of Seann Skell give it

## I. Of the House as It Stood

In those days the island was a settled house, and it thought of itself so. The kings and queens of Dia-thìr kept their hall at Cathair dhearg on An Cnoc Ruadh, above the place where the mining roads came down to the Abhainn dhomhain. The custodians kept the vein under the mountain from Taigh na Fèithe above the diggings at Muileann dhearg, which was the heir of Talla na Lasrach, and they kept Leabhar a' Chùraim there, in which every hearth that held the right to the coal was written. At Dùn ìseal itself Brìde's flame still burned in Talla na Lasrach, and the stone cup stood on the threshold where the lords of the shares had sworn their peace, and Coimheadaichean na Lasrach came and went about it as their mothers had. Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measured out an gual dathach hearth by hearth, a handful at a time, and it had not changed by a word since Fionnlagh Dall first filled the cup.

The orders of An Creideamh Sean sat apart from one another at their own fires, and each thought itself the only true keeper. The dawn-hawk was flown at Cnoc bheag. An Fhianna kept their stone at Caol leathan. At Seann Skell in the west the harbour court swore its oaths over Manannan's cup with the scorpion on it, which breaks at a lie. Scoiltean nan Draoidhean argued over the question of the stag, and Òrd Mhacha read the omens of the two horses in the trees. The ancestors were fed at the hearths of the east in the old way, as they always had been. Of na h-Earrannan Mòra into which the first king's kingdom had been parted there was little left but the stones on the bounds of the provinces, and the names of a few that the shires still answered to when the clerks were not listening.

And there was the sea. The sea was at the island's back, and nobody looked at it except to fish. The boats of Dia-thìr were sewn-plank coasters, their strakes stitched together with root and gut and caulked with moss and tallow, and they never slept a night out of sight of land. There was nothing out there that anyone wanted. An Saoghal Thall lay west over the open water, the tellers said, Tìr nan Òg and Magh Meall, with Donn's house on its rock on the way; but the living did not go there, and it did not come to them.

In that settled house there was a queen, Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, who had been crowned in An Talla Dearg at fifteen, eight years before, when her mother Mòr nic Coinnich died. She was twenty-three. She had a husband, Uilleam mac Iain, who was kind and liked hounds, and as yet no child, and a younger sister, Mòrag, who was married to a steady man of the western shore and had come up to the capital that winter to be near her. And she had a scribe, Murchadh mac Eòghainn, who had served her mother and wrote a close square hand that the clerks of Leabhar a' Chùraim envied.

Into that house there came a rumour.

## II. Of a Word on the Quays

The word came first to the western quays in the deep of winter, in the moon of Faolach, when the storms walk up and down the coast and the boats lie drawn up above the tide-line. It came on 6 am Faoilleach, LE 1. Where it came from, the tellers at the hearth do not know, and they have never much minded. No one could point to the boat that brought it. It was simply there one morning on the quay at Cuan shean, as a smell of smoke is there, and by evening everyone on the waterfront had heard it: that out over the open sea, farther than any coaster had ever gone, there was a coast, and no one lived on it who was like the Dia-thìrich.

The fishers of Cuan shean said it to one another as they mended nets in the lee of the rope-sheds. They said it at the fire in the long house where the crews ate. By the end of the moon they were saying it at Ros bheag, and at Inis àrsaidh, and up the coast at Ceann mhòr, where the north-west headlands run out into weather. Nobody said he had seen the coast. Everybody knew a man who knew a man.

Eachann mac Lachlainn was the skipper of a boat of six oars out of Cuan shean, a broad slow man with a grey beard cut square, who had fished the same water for thirty years and did not believe anything until he had it in his hands. He heard the tale three times in one day and laughed at it three times. Then his own sister's son, who crewed for him, said that he had been told it by a woman who had been told it by a pilot of Ros bheag, who had been blown off the land in the autumn gales and had come back after nine days with his water gone and his eyes strange; and that the pilot had said he saw the coast before the wind turned. Eachann went to find the pilot. The pilot, when he was found, said that he had seen nothing but grey water and his own death, and that anyone who said otherwise was a liar. But he said it too loudly, and he would not look at Eachann while he said it.

That was the way of it all winter. Every telling led back to another telling. Every man who might have been first said that it was not he.

## III. Of the Three Crews in the Red Hall

By the moon of Samhnas it had reached the capital. The crews came up the river road from the west, as crews did when the fishing was done, to sell salt fish and seal-oil at the autumn market below An Cnoc Ruadh and drink the proceeds; and they brought the tale with them, and it got into the town and up the hill and through the door of An Talla Dearg, and on 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1, the queen sent for them.

Three crews came, one after another, over the course of that moon. The first was Eachann mac Lachlainn's of Cuan shean. The second was a crew of Ros bheag, whose skipper was a woman, Oighrig nic Raghnaill, lean and quick, with a scar along her jaw where a line had once parted. The third came late, from Ceann mhòr in the far north-west, three days on the road: a crew of hard, silent men under Tòmas mac Uilleim, who looked at An Talla Dearg as though it might sink.

The queen had them in at the board after the day's pleas, one crew each night, with the fire built up and bread and ale set out, as if they were guests and not witnesses. She sat at the head of the board in her chair of black oak. Her husband sat on her right, and on her left Murchadh mac Eòghainn with his board and his pen and a leaf of good skin. The lesser household ate at the lower board and listened. Mòrag was among them, with her husband, Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh, beside her.

Eachann told it first, standing, with his cap crushed in his two hands. He told it plainly, as he would have told the price of fish. A coast lay out over the open water, he said, west and north of west, many days off. It was low and dark, with a white edge where the sea broke. There was smoke on it in places but no hall and no boat. The water there was colder than ours, and the fish were bigger. He had not seen it. He knew a man who had.

"Were you the first to hear it?" the queen said.

Eachann thought about that honestly, turning his cap. "No, lady," he said. "I was about the last."

Murchadh wrote it all, in his close square hand, and at the end of the telling he read it back aloud. Eachann listened with his head on one side, like a dog listening for a whistle, and then said, "Aye. That's it," and sat down and drank his ale, and was very much relieved.

The second night Oighrig nic Raghnaill told it otherwise. The coast lay north, she said, a long way north, past the north cape and beyond Uilebheist na Mara's water, and it was high: cliffs, and a great river coming down white out of them, and forests running to the edge of the cliffs, taller than any oaks on the island. There was no smoke on it at all. The pilot who had seen it was her mother's cousin, and he had sworn to it on the cup at Seann Skell, and the cup had not broken. Would a man lie on the cup?

"Men have," said Uilleam mac Iain from the queen's right hand, mildly. He was fond of the harbour court's stories.

"Not that one," said Oighrig, and looked at him until he looked away.

"Were you the first to hear it?" said the queen.

"No, lady. Half of Ros bheag had it before me."

The third night Tòmas mac Uilleim of Ceann mhòr told it hardly at all. He stood with his men behind him like a wall and said, in the thick speech of the north-west, that the coast was east, over the grey water where the mist lies, and that you could smell it on certain mornings when the wind came round, a smell of pine and wet ash; and that the old men of Ceann mhòr had always said there was land there, and had said so to their sons since before there was a queen in Cathair dhearg or a hall on An Cnoc Ruadh or a cup at Dùn ìseal. The rest of the island had only now caught up with them.

"Have you seen it?" the queen said.

"Nobody sees it. It's behind the mist."

"Were you the first to hear it?"

Tòmas looked at her for a while. "Lady," he said, "we never heard anything else."

When the three crews had gone and the fire was low, Murchadh sat at the end of the board and read over what he had written on the three nights. The queen sat and watched him. He was an old man and had written down a great deal in his life, and he did not often frown at his own work; but he frowned now. At last he dipped his pen and wrote a line at the foot of the leaf, below the third telling, and sanded it, and turned the leaf round on the board so that she could read it.

*They agree on the coast, and on nothing else.*

Beathag read it twice, and then smiled for the first time in three nights. "That's the truest thing on the leaf," she said.

"It is the only thing on the leaf I am sure of, lady," said Murchadh.

## IV. Of the Question at the Lower Board

There was one other thing said in the hall in those three nights, and Murchadh did not write it, because it was not a telling. The queen remembered it.

It was on the first night, when Eachann had finished and sat down and was drinking his ale with the sweat drying on him. The questions went round the board as they did after any plea. The queen's husband asked whether the fish were really bigger. A custodian who happened to be at court asked whether there were any coal on the far coast, and whether anyone had broken it to see what colour it was, and Eachann said he had no idea and that the man who had seen it was not the kind to go breaking stones. A lady of the household asked if the people were tall.

"There are no people, lady," said Eachann. "That's the whole of it. There's nobody there."

"There's smoke," someone said.

"Smoke is not people," said Eachann, and that was felt to be a good answer, and people laughed.

Then from the lower board Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill said, not loudly: "How many days' water would a boat need?"

Eachann turned round on his bench to see who had asked. He did not know her. "Days' water?"

"To get there. If a boat went. How much water would she carry, and for how many days, and how many would she carry, to get there and have some over."

There was a small silence at the upper board. It was not a question anyone had thought to ask. It belonged to a different kind of talk.

"No boat of ours could get there, lady," said Eachann. "A boat of ours would come apart in a night out of sight of land. She's sewn, you see. She works in a sea, all her seams working, and she wants to be pulled up on a beach every night and let dry. You couldn't get a boat of ours there."

"Then what kind of boat could?"

He opened his mouth and shut it. He was an honest man. "I don't know," he said. "Nobody's ever built one."

"No," said Mòrag. "Nobody has." And she let the talk go on to other things, and ate her bread, and did not speak again that night.

Beathag watched her sister over the rim of her cup. Mòrag was nineteen. She had been married two years, to a man of the western shore whom she had chosen herself and who adored her quietly and without fuss; she had a house at Inis àrsaidh, near Seann Skell, and no child yet; and she had the same face their mother had had, long and steady, which people called calm. Beathag had known her all her life, and knew better. She had seen that face at eight years old, looking at the ice on the mill-pond at Cathair dhearg in the moon of Faolach, the day before Mòrag walked out on it to see if it would bear her.

It had borne her. That was the trouble with Mòrag. Things mostly did.

## V. Of the Choosing Begun

After the three crews went home, the tale did not go home with them.

It went down the river road into the west, and up the coal-roads into the mountain country, and along the coast in every boat that put in anywhere. By the moon of Dubhlas, the black moon at the dark of the year, it was being told at hearths from Baile chrom in the north-west to Seann Vell in the south-east. At most hearths it was told as one tells of a wonder, and then the talk turned to the price of barley. At some it was not.

An Roghnachadh began then, though nobody called it that, and it began without anyone beginning it. The chronicles call it a vote, and so it is written on 8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1; but there was no day in that winter on which anyone stood up and called for hands, and no roll yet, and no rule. There was only a question that began to be asked at certain hearths, quietly, after the children were asleep: *Would we go?* And the question, once asked at a hearth, did not go away from it again.

It was asked first, and most, on the west coast, where the tale had come in and where the people knew boats. At Inis àrsaidh, the fishing town at the mouth of the river below Seann Skell, two households said aloud in the drying-shed, before the whole town, that if a boat were ever made that could get there, they would be on it. The town laughed at them. The two households did not laugh, and after a while the town stopped. At Ros bheag they argued about it in the long house till the fire went out. At Cuan shean the rope-makers, who had nothing to do with the sea except to sell it rope, said the whole thing was fishermen's nonsense and that nobody would ever build such a boat. But they said it every night.

It was asked, too, in places nobody expected. The custodians of the vein, who held the right to the coal by apprenticeship and by the long training of the hands, turned out to have more in them of the wish to see a new thing than anyone had supposed. Perhaps it was because the coal had taught them that the world had more colours in it than most people could see. Perhaps it was only that they were bored. But when the tale came to Taigh na Fèithe, some of the young custodians sat up half the night over it; and one of them, a man of the western diggings called Fearchar mac Ruairidh, went down to the capital in the moon of Dubhlas on some errand of Taigh na Fèithe's and asked, while he was there, to be told the three tellings from Murchadh's leaf.

There was no rule in it, and that is the thing the tellers find hardest to believe. Nobody drew lots. No lord told his people to go, and no priest told them to stay. Those who wished to, went on wishing; those who did not, did not. They have tried every way to find a cause in it: a dearth, a quarrel, a prophecy, a sickness in the coal. There was none. The harvest had been good. The island was at peace. It was only that a door had been opened in a wall that everyone had thought was solid, and some people found they wanted to go through it.

## VI. Of Mòrag and the Skipper

Mòrag went down to Cuan shean before the moon was out.

She told her sister she was going to see to the house at Inis àrsaidh before the worst of the winter, which was true. With Aonghas and two servants she went down the river road, three short days in the rain, and saw to the house. And then she borrowed a pony and rode on down the coast the dozen miles to Cuan shean, alone, and found Eachann mac Lachlainn mending a net in the lee of a rope-shed, and sat down on an upturned tub beside him, and asked him the whole thing again.

He was surprised to see her, and then less surprised. He told it again. She asked him questions that nobody in An Talla Dearg had asked: how long the pilot of Ros bheag had been out; which way the wind had been; what the stars had been doing, if he had seen them; how a coaster's seams worked in a sea, and how long before they started, and whether a thicker plank would help, and what wood the planks were, and whether there was any wood on the island big enough for a boat that did not need sewing.

"Oak," said Eachann at last, after a long time. "If you wanted a boat that didn't need sewing. You'd want oak. Big oak, and a keel to her, like the old tellings say Rìghrean na Cloiche' boats had, and you'd want a man who knew how to set a keel. There's nobody alive that knows that."

"Somebody might learn."

"Somebody might." He tied off his knot and bit the twine. "Lady, is the queen going to send ships?"

"The queen," said Mòrag, "has said nothing at all."

That was true too. Beathag had said nothing at all, all winter. She had heard the three tellings and had Murchadh write them, and then she had gone back to pleas of boundary ditches and grain dues and a quarrel between two millers of Muileann bhàn over a stream, and if anyone raised the far coast at her board she listened politely and changed the subject. The court had decided that she thought it nonsense. Mòrag knew that she did not.

"She'll have to say something," said Eachann. "Sooner or later. If folk start meaning it."

"Yes," said Mòrag. "She will." She stood up and thanked him and gave him a silver ring off her finger for his trouble, which he tried not to take and then took, and rode back to Inis àrsaidh in the dark with the rain behind her.

Aonghas was waiting up for her by the fire. He looked at her face when she came in, and did not ask where she had been.

"There's nobody alive that knows how to set a keel," she said, sitting down and holding out her wet hands to the fire.

"No," said Aonghas.

"But there's oak."

"There's oak," he agreed. He got up and fetched her a dry shawl and put it round her, and sat down again, and after a while he said: "Doire fhionn. Up the north road. The grove there has the biggest oaks on the island. My grandfather used to say you couldn't see the tops from the ground."

Mòrag turned and looked at him. He was looking at the fire.

"I've been thinking about it too," he said.

## VII. Of the Queen at Her Window

Beathag found out, of course. She had the reports of every reeve in the west, and a sister's movements are not a secret in a country where the queen's sister is known by sight in every harbour. A rider brought word to An Talla Dearg that the lady Mòrag had been at Cuan shean, and had sat an afternoon with the skipper Eachann mac Lachlainn, and had given him a ring.

She said nothing about it. When Mòrag came back up the river road at the turn of the year, before the moon of Faolach, the sisters ate together as they always did, and talked of the house at Inis àrsaidh and the damp in its north wall, and of Uilleam's hounds, one of which had had pups under the queen's own bed. Mòrag did not speak of the coast and Beathag did not ask.

But on the morning Mòrag and Aonghas were to go back west for good, Beathag stood at the window of her bower, which looked down over the yard of An Talla Dearg to the gate and the river road beyond it, and watched them go.

It was a clear cold morning with the frost still on the cobbles. Aonghas saw to the ponies. Mòrag stood in the middle of the yard in her grey travelling cloak and talked to someone. Beathag did not know him at first; then she did. It was Eachann mac Lachlainn, the skipper of Cuan shean, who had come up the river road again with some errand of his own, or with none, and had stopped at the hall to pay his respects.

They were not talking about anything. Beathag could see that from the window. Mòrag was asking something and Eachann was answering and drawing a shape in the air with his hand, long and pointed at both ends, and Mòrag was nodding. Then she laughed, and put her hand on the skipper's arm, and walked with him to the gate as a lady walks a friend to the gate. At the gate she stopped and looked out along the river road, west, toward the sea, as though she could see down it all the way to the coast; and stood so for a long moment, not moving, with the skipper beside her waiting to be dismissed.

Beathag had seen her sister look at a great many things. She had never seen her look at anything like that.

She stood at the window until the ponies had gone out through the gate and down the road and round the shoulder of the hill. Then she went down to the hall, where the day's pleas were waiting, and Murchadh with his board.

"Lady," said the old man, "the millers of Muileann bhàn are here again about the stream."

"Let them wait a little," said Beathag. She sat down in the black oak chair and looked at the empty board for a while. "Murchadh. The leaf of the three crews. You have it safe?"

"In the chest, lady."

"Good. Leave it there." She was silent again. Then she said: "Write nothing of the lady Mòrag's journey to Cuan shean. Nor of the skipper at the gate this morning. None of it is a matter for the roll."

Murchadh looked at her. He had served her mother, and he had known both sisters since they were in the cradle, and he was not a fool. "Lady," he said, "it is not a matter for the roll yet."

"No," said Beathag. "Yet." And she sent for the millers.

## VIII. Of What Stood at the End of the Year

So ended the first year of the age, though nobody on the island knew that an age had begun. The kings of Dia-thìr had always counted their years by their own reigns and by the harvests, and that year was written in the rolls of An Talla Dearg as the ninth year of Queen Beathag, a good year for barley and a middling one for fish, and in Leabhar a' Chùraim at Taigh na Fèithe as a year in which the handful was measured and burned at every lawful hearth and the galleries gave as they always gave.

Nothing had been built. No boat had been laid down, no oak felled, no roll opened, no word given. The queen had said nothing. The custodians had said nothing. The three crews had gone back to their fishing, and in the spring Oighrig nic Raghnaill's boat of Ros bheag took the best catch of herring on the west coast in ten years and she forgot, for a whole moon, to talk about anything else.

But there was a question at certain hearths now, and it would not go away. At Inis àrsaidh two households had said aloud that they would go. Up at Taigh na Fèithe a young custodian had asked to hear the three tellings. On the beach at Cuan shean a skipper who had never believed anything until he held it had begun to draw, in the air and on the sand of the beach and on the planks of his own boat with a burnt stick, the shape of a hull that did not yet exist, long and pointed at both ends, and to stare at what he had drawn. And at Inis àrsaidh, near Seann Skell, the queen's sister and her husband sat up at night by the fire and talked about oak.

# Chapter Two: Of the Boards in the Harbour-House

*LE 2*

## I. Of Taigh a' Chalaidh

Taigh a' Chalaidh stood at the head of the west quay, where the Abhainn naomh widens into its river pool before it goes down to the sea. It was a long low house of grey stone with a turf roof, older than anyone could say, and it had a single door facing the water and a single window facing the town, so that whoever sat inside could see both the boats and the people who owned them. The town called it Taigh a' Chalaidh, the harbour-house, and nothing else, as though there were no other harbour in the world.

In it sat the harbour scribe, and in the second year of the age the harbour scribe was Calum mac Nèill.

He was a spare, stooped man of thirty-odd with ink in the cracks of his fingers and a habit of humming through his nose while he worked, which his wife said would drive her into the river. His father had been harbour scribe before him, and his father's mother before that. The office was not a great one. He kept the rolls of the harbour: which boat lay at which berth, who owed dues and who had paid them, what came in and what went out, fish and salt and seal-oil, hides from up the river, barley down it. He wrote on boards. Leabhar a' Chùraim at Taigh na Fèithe was kept on good skin, and the queen's scribe at Cathair dhearg wrote on skin; but the harbour of Seann Skell had never had so much money that it could write its daily business on anything better than planed boards of alder, which could be scraped and written again, and hung on pegs along the walls in rows.

Calum liked the boards. He liked the sound of the knife cutting the letters, a small dry sound, and the curl of the shaving, and the way a board held what was cut into it. A skin could be scraped clean and no one the wiser. A cut in a board showed.

He was not a man who thought much about the sea. The sea was where the boats went, and he wrote down when they came back.

## II. Of the Opening of the Roll

The talk of the far coast had been going on in Seann Skell for a year and a half, as it had been going on everywhere in the west, when the first household came into the harbour-house and asked to be written down.

It was in the moon of Pailteach, the moon of plenty, at the end of harvest. The barley was in and the herring had not yet come, and the town was idle and restless. A fisher of Inis àrsaidh came in off the quay with his wife behind him, and stood before Calum's board with his cap in his hand, and said that he wished his household entered.

"Entered for what?" said Calum. He had a board of harbour dues on his knee and was adding it up.

"For going," said the fisher. "When the ships go."

Calum put the dues board down. "There are no ships," he said.

"There will be," said the fisher's wife. She was a sturdy woman with forearms like a baker's, and she looked at Calum as though he were being slow on purpose. "Everybody says. And when they go, there'll be a hundred wanting to go on them, and they'll want to know who asked first. So we want it written. Now. Who asked first. You write the harbour, don't you? This is harbour."

Calum looked at them for a long moment. He thought of telling them to go home. He thought of the queen at Cathair dhearg, who had said nothing all this while, and of the custodians at Taigh na Fèithe, who had said nothing either; and it occurred to him that if he sent these two away, they would go to some other scribe, or to no scribe, and the thing would be written badly or not at all. And a harbour scribe of Seann Skell did not like a thing to be written badly.

So he got up and took down a new board of alder from the rack, and planed it smooth, and cut at the head of it, in his best letters:

*Those who mean to go.*

Then he sat down again and asked the fisher his name.

He wrote it on 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2. That board was the first of the roll, which Leabhar a' Chùraim afterward called Rolla nan Deònach, and it hung on the wall of the harbour-house at Seann Skell for longer than anyone then living would live.

## III. Of the Rule of the Whole Household

He wrote more than the fisher's name. That was the first thing he decided, and he decided it before he had thought about it, with his knife already in the wood.

"Who is your household?" he said.

The fisher looked puzzled. "Me. Her. The two boys. My mother, that lives with us."

"Does your mother mean to go?"

The fisher and his wife looked at each other. "We've not asked her," said the wife.

"Then go and ask her," said Calum, "and come back, and I'll write you all, or none of you."

They stared at him. The fisher said, a little hotly, that he did not see what his mother had to do with it. Calum put down his knife and explained it, slowly, as he would have explained a harbour due, and in the explaining he found out what he thought.

The coal was the reason. Every hearth on the island that held the right to the coal was entered by Taigh na Fèithe in Leabhar a' Chùraim, and every season the handful was measured out to the hearth, the whole house that sat round one fire, and never to a single man or woman. A hearth was one thing in Leabhar a' Chùraim's eyes. If half of a household went and half stayed, what then? Two hearths where there had been one, each with half a right? Or one cold half-hearth and the handful measured to nobody? The custodians would not stand for it. And a household, Calum said, was a hearth to more than the custodians. A boy did not go over the sea and leave his grandmother by the fire. Or if he did, he should have to stand in the harbour-house and say so, before the whole town, with his grandmother beside him.

"So you'll write us whole," said the fisher's wife slowly, "or not at all."

"I'll write you whole," said Calum, "or not at all."

She thought about that. Then she nodded, once, as if she had been haggling over fish and had got a fair price. "That's right," she said. "That's how it should be." And she took her husband by the arm and went to ask his mother.

They came back the next morning, all five of them, the old woman on a stick at the rear, and stood in a row before the board while Calum cut their names, one under another, joined by a line down the left side that he cut last to show they were one household. The old woman watched the knife the whole time. When he had finished she said, "Is that us, then?" and he said it was, and she touched the board with one finger, very lightly, where her name was, and went out without another word.

That was how the roll came to be written by household and never by single name. The tellers have made a great deal of it since, and said that going was a thing a family did together or not at all. So it was. But it began with a scribe who did not wish to argue with Taigh na Fèithe over half a hearth.

## IV. Of Those Who Came

After the first household, the harbour-house was never empty.

They came in off the quay all through the autumn: fishers with tar on their hands and salt in the creases of their faces, who had been out past the headlands in weather and thought they knew what the sea was; boat-wrights from the strand below the town; net-makers, rope-makers, a cooper. They came down the Abhainn naomh from the farms up the river in carts, the farm wives with a child on the hip and another at the skirt, and stood in the doorway blinking at the dark after the bright river. A shepherd came from the hills behind the town with his dog, and the dog lay down under the board and would not be moved. A young woman came alone, with no household but herself, and Calum had to decide whether one was a household; he decided that it was.

They asked him questions he could not answer. Where would they go? When? In what? Who would lead them? How many would there be? Would the queen send them, or forbid them? Would the coal go with them? He said, over and over, that he did not know, that he was only the harbour scribe, that he wrote down the harbour. They looked at him as if he were keeping something back. Some of them brought him gifts, a string of fish, a pot of honey, as if a gift would get them a better place on the board. He gave the gifts back, which offended them more than keeping them would have done.

By the moon of Damhrach there were four boards on the wall.

And they went away again. That was the part nobody had expected, and it was the part that stayed with Calum longest.

## V. Of the First Striking-Out

The first to strike out was a net-maker of the town, a man of forty called Iain, whom Calum had known all his life. He had entered his household in the first week, himself and his wife and three children, in a loud cheerful voice, and stood talking in the doorway afterward about the fish they would take off the far coast, as big as calves.

He came back before the moon was out.

Late in the day, when the harbour-house was empty, he came in and stood before the board with his face grey. He did not say anything for a while. Then he said, "Strike us out."

Calum looked up at him. "What's happened?"

"Nothing's happened." Iain rubbed his face with both hands. "Nothing. I woke up in the night and lay there, and I thought: the sea. That's all. I thought of the sea at night, with no land. And I couldn't breathe, Calum. I couldn't get my breath. My wife held me like a child. Strike us out."

Calum took down the board, and found the name, and took his knife and cut it through: one long stroke through the middle of each letter, from the first letter of Iain's name to the last of his youngest child's, and then the line down the left side that joined them, cut across at the top and the bottom.

Iain watched him do it. When it was done he said, low: "Can't you scrape it off? So nobody knows?"

Calum turned the board so that the net-maker could see it. The names were still there, every letter, with the stroke through them.

"No," he said. "I can't."

"You scrape the dues boards. I've seen you."

"When a due is paid, I scrape it, because it's done and no one needs it. This isn't done." Calum hung the board back on its peg. He did not know, until he said it, that he believed it. "You meant to go, Iain. That was true. And now you don't, and that's true too. The board will say both. If I scrape it off, it'll only say the second, and that's half a lie."

Iain stood there a moment longer. Then he laughed, not happily, and said, "You're a hard man for a scribe," and went out.

He came back the next spring and entered his household again. By midsummer he had struck it out again. Calum cut the second stroke through the second entry without a word, and the net-maker did not ask him to scrape it.

## VI. Of the Widow of the Strand

There were others. There was the young couple from up the river who entered, and struck out when the wife found she was with child, and entered again when the child was born, and struck out again when it sickened. A pair of brothers, rope-makers, who entered together and then quarrelled and came in separately on the same day, one to strike and one to stay, and had to be told that they were one household and must agree or be struck together; they went out shouting at each other, and came back together at dusk, and struck. There was the shepherd, whose dog died that winter, who came in and struck out and said it would not be right to go without the dog.

And there was the widow of the strand, whose coming and going ran through the whole of that first year and beyond it.

Her name is not on any board that survives, so she will not be named here. She was a boat-wright's widow, a thin woman with white hair who lived in a hut on the strand below the town among the sawpits and the half-built coasters, and who came up to the harbour-house in the moon of Samhnas, in the first rain, to be entered, alone. Calum wrote her. She came back in the moon of Dubhlas, in the dark of the year, and asked to be struck. He struck her. She came back in the moon of Faolach, in the wolf-storms, and asked to be entered again. He looked at her a long while, and then wrote her again, on a new line, below the first entry with its stroke through it.

In the moon of Gearras, after Là Fhèill Brìde, she came again.

"Strike me," she said.

He took the knife. Before he cut, he said, "May I ask why?"

She looked at the board, at her own name written twice and struck once. "My husband's in the ground behind the strand," she said. "Every time I think of going, I think of him there and nobody to cut the grass on him. And every time I think of staying, I think of him there and me on the strand looking at the water all the rest of my days, and I think, he'd have gone. He'd have gone the first day. He'd have been in here before the fisher." She was quiet. "So I go back and forth. Strike me."

He struck her. And she did not come back, that spring or ever; and when the harbour scribe of a later year took down the boards to count them, he found the widow's name written three times and struck three times, one under another, like a ladder.

## VII. Of the Harbour-House at Night

The roll changed the harbour-house, and it changed the town's use of it.

It had been a place where people came to pay their dues and quarrel about berths. Now it was a place where people came to say the most important thing they had ever said, in front of the harbour scribe and whoever else happened to be standing in the doorway. It became something between a court and a shrine. People came in who had no business with the roll at all, only to look at the boards, to read the names, to see who was going and who had changed his mind. Old men sat on the bench by the door all day and watched. Children dared each other to touch the boards. Once a woman came in and read the whole roll through, board by board, very slowly, and then went and sat on the quay and wept for an hour, and no one ever found out whose name she had been looking for.

People came at night, too. The ones who could not say it by day came after dark, when the quay was empty. So Calum began to keep a lamp burning in the harbour-house late, long after the harbour's own business was done, and to sit up by it with a board on his knee, in case anyone came. His wife complained of the cost of the oil. He paid for it out of his own pocket, and went on doing it.

And they came. A man who had fought his father for a month over it, and won, and could not bear to see his father's face while he said it. A girl who was not supposed to be out of her mother's house. A custodian's servant, sent secretly by his master to read what the roll held and count it for Taigh na Fèithe, who confessed as much at once, and whom Calum let read, because the roll was not a secret.

## VIII. Of the Waiting for a Word

All that autumn the town waited for the queen to speak, and she did not.

It was the first thing anyone asked a rider off the river road: had the queen said anything? And the rider always said no, and the asker always looked as though he had been cheated of something he was owed. A great many people in Seann Skell, it turned out, had been sure that the crown would decide it for them one way or the other. Some hoped she would forbid it, so that they could be angry with her and stay. Some hoped she would command it, so that they could go and blame her. Most, Calum thought, hoped she would do something, anything, so that the thing would be taken out of their own hands and they could sleep.

The talk on the bench by the door ran every way. The queen was against it and waiting for it to die down. The queen was for it and waiting for the custodians. The queen's sister had been seen at Cuan shean asking about boats, so the queen must mean to send her. The queen had quarrelled with her sister over it and they no longer spoke. An old man who had once carried a message to An Talla Dearg and had never since let anyone forget it said that the queen was a deep one, like her mother, and would say nothing until the last moment and then say exactly the right thing; and everyone on the bench agreed with him, and none of them could say what the right thing would be.

The custodian's servant who had come to read the roll by night came again in the moon of Damhrach, and this time he brought a question from his master. How many households on the boards held the right to the coal? Calum did not know. He had not asked. The harbour roll was not Leabhar a' Chùraim, and a fisher did not tell the harbour scribe whether his hearth took the handful. The servant went away with his question unanswered, and Calum sat a long while afterward looking at the boards, and understood for the first time that somewhere up in the mountain country, sixty miles off, men who had never set foot on the quay were counting his roll against their own, and that what they found in it would matter to them far more than it mattered to him.

It frightened him a little. He had cut the first board because a fisher's wife had told him it was harbour business, and she had been right. Now it was Taigh na Fèithe's business too, and An Talla Dearg's; and he had the uneasy sense of a man who has laid a plank across a ditch for his own use and turns round to find a cart coming over it.

He did not close the boards. But he began to write more carefully, and to ask of each household, before he cut, whether its hearth took the handful; and he put a small mark beside those that did, a notch like a flame, so that when the question came again he could answer it.

## IX. Of Dòmhnall mac Chaluim and the Closing of the Boards

Calum's son Dòmhnall was his clerk that year, a quiet, serious boy of fourteen who was learning the knife. He watched the roll grow and shrink and grow again through that first autumn, and one night in the moon of Damhrach, by the late lamp he said what he had been thinking.

"You should close it."

Calum looked up.

"The roll," said Dòmhnall. "Close the boards. Nobody's asked you to keep them. The queen hasn't. Taigh na Fèithe hasn't. You started it yourself, because a fisher came in, and now it's eating the harbour-house. You can't get the dues done for people in the doorway. Half the town's in here every day crying. It isn't harbour business. Close it and tell them to go to the queen."

Calum thought about it honestly. His son was right on every count but one.

"The queen hasn't said close it," he said. "Nor has she said open it. She's said nothing at all. And while she says nothing, who is to say whether a man may go or not? Not me. I'm the harbour scribe. I write the harbour." He laid his hand flat on the board on his knee. "These people have a right to have it written, what they mean. If I shut the boards, I've said no for them. And I'm not the one to say no."

"Then who is?"

"Nobody, maybe." Calum was quiet for a while. "Maybe that's the answer. Maybe there's no one who can say no."

Dòmhnall did not argue. But when he went to bed he looked back from the door, and saw his father still sitting by the lamp, not writing anything, looking at the boards on the wall.

## X. Of the Question His Wife Asked

Calum's wife was a practical woman named Seonag, who kept geese and sold their eggs on the quay, and she had watched the roll all winter with a face that told him nothing. She did not ask him about it and he did not tell her. They talked about the geese and the price of oil and Dòmhnall's knife-hand, which was coming along.

Then, the same night, lying in the dark in the box-bed with the wind going over the roof, she said: "Would you go?"

He lay still. He could hear the river running past the end of the quay, and a loose board somewhere on the harbour-house knocking.

"The boards need a keeper," he said.

She did not answer that. After a while she turned over, away from him, toward the wall. He thought she had gone to sleep. Then she said, into the dark, quite quietly: "That's not what I asked. And that's the answer anyway, isn't it. You want to."

He did not say anything. There was nothing he could say that would not be a lie, and he had spent the whole winter refusing to scrape a lie onto a board.

In the morning he went down to the harbour-house as usual, and lit the lamp, though it was daylight, and sat down by it. And the first to come in that day was a boat-wright of the strand, a lean dark man called Alasdair mac Iain, who did not come to be entered. He came to read the roll. He read every board on the wall, slowly, moving his lips, and then he stood in the middle of the floor and said to no one in particular, "There's not a boat on this island that could carry the half of them."

"No," said Calum.

"Then somebody had better build one," said Alasdair, and went out.

# Chapter Three: Of the Queen's Word and the Queen's Sister

*LE 2 – 3*

## I. Of the Bower in the Red Hall

Mòrag came up the river road to Cathair dhearg in the moon of Damhrach, when the stags were roaring on the hills above the Abhainn dhomhain and the first gales were stripping the rowans. She came alone but for one servant, and she did not go to the hall. She went straight up the back stair to her sister's bower, as she had done since they were girls, and knocked once and went in.

Beathag was at the window with one of her husband's shirts in her lap, sewing a patch on the elbow. She did not look surprised.

"You've come about the roll," she said.

"I've come about you," said Mòrag. She took off her wet cloak and hung it on the peg by the door, where their mother's cloak had hung, and sat down on the chest under the window without being asked. "Half the west is waiting on you. The harbour-house at Seann Skell has five boards full, and it's full of people every day asking whether the queen will send them or forbid them. Nobody knows what to do. They say the crown will decide."

"And what do you say?"

"I say decide." Mòrag leaned forward. "Beathag. Either tell them to go, and put the crown behind it, and they'll build the ships in a year; or tell them it's folly, and forbid it, and it'll die away by Bealltainn. But say something. You can't leave them hanging on a board in a harbour-house, cutting their names in and out."

Beathag bit off her thread and looked at the patch, and smoothed it with her thumb.

"Do you know what the crown has done, in all the years since Goraidh Mòr?" she said at last. "It has kept the roads. It has kept the granaries. It has judged the boundary ditches and the millers' quarrels and the dues. It has never once sent anyone anywhere. It has never told a fisher where he might fish or a farmer where he might plough. And it has never kept a free man or woman where they did not wish to stay." She looked up. "You want me to begin now? With this? With the sea?"

"I want you to lead."

"I am leading. I am leading them to make up their own minds." Beathag set the shirt aside. "If I command it, every household that goes, goes because the queen said so. And when the sea takes them, and it will take some of them, Mòrag, you know that, their mothers will curse An Talla Dearg, and they'll be right to. And if I forbid it, every household that wanted to go and didn't will hate the crown for the rest of their lives, and teach their children to. And the ones who'd go anyway will go in the dark, in whatever they can find, and drown. No. The crown won't send, and it won't forbid."

Mòrag sat very still on the chest. "Then you'll let me go," she said.

It was the first time either of them had said it. Beathag looked at her sister for a long moment, and Mòrag saw her face change: not much, a tightening at the corners of the mouth, the look their mother used to get when a plea went against someone she liked.

"I'll let anyone go," Beathag said. "That's what I've just told you."

"That isn't what I asked."

"It's what I'm answering." Beathag stood up and went to the window and stood with her back to the room, looking down at the yard where the grooms were bringing in the horses. "I'm the queen, Mòrag. If I say one thing for the whole island and another for my sister, there's no word at all. It's just a queen with favourites. You're free. You're as free as the fisher of Inis àrsaidh who went in first. No freer. No less free."

"And if I go?"

Beathag did not turn round. "Then you'll go," she said. "And I'll be the queen who let her."

## II. Of the Word That Went Down the Road

The word went down the river road three days later, with a rider of the queen's household on a grey horse, in the autumn of LE 2. It was written by Murchadh mac Eòghainn on a leaf of skin and sealed with the queen's seal, and copies of it went to Cuan shean and Ros bheag and Ceann mhòr and Baile chrom and every other harbour of the west, and to Taigh na Fèithe above Muileann dhearg.

It was not long. Leabhar a' Chùraim gives it only in substance: that the crown would send no one across the water, and would keep no one back; that any household of Dia-thìr might go that wished to, and stay that wished to; that the crown would neither help nor hinder the building of ships, but would judge any quarrel that arose from it by the old law, as it judged all quarrels; and that the queen asked the people to think long and choose with their eyes open.

Mòrag rode down behind the rider. She had not meant to. She had meant to go home to Inis àrsaidh in a day or two, by easy stages, and let the word get there before her. But she stood at the gate of An Talla Dearg in the grey morning and watched the grey horse go down the road with the leaf in its rider's satchel, and she found she could not bear to be behind it. She called for her pony and went.

She rode the whole twenty-four miles in one day, in rain. The road went down out of the hills along the river and through the wet fields of the lowland, past farms where the barley stubble stood grey and drowned and the cattle stood with their backs to the weather, and then along the edge of the marshes toward the coast; and all the way the rider was ahead of her, a grey shape in the grey rain, never more than a mile off and never less. She did not try to catch him up. At dusk she came down the last hill with the pony blowing, and saw the lamps of Seann Skell below her, and the river pool, and the long dark line of the west quay, and the one lit window of the harbour-house at its head.

## III. Of the Reading at the Door

The rider had reached the harbour-house before her and the reading had begun. Half the town was on the quay. They stood in the rain in a crowd round the door, with their hoods up and their shoulders hunched, and the harbour scribe Calum mac Nèill stood in the doorway with the lamp behind him and the queen's leaf in his hands, and read it aloud.

He read it twice, because the people at the back had not heard. Mòrag sat on the pony at the back of the crowd and heard it the second time, the plain words in the scribe's dry voice, and watched the faces.

She had thought they would cheer. Some of them did, a few young men near the front who had been on the boards from the first week. But most of the crowd did not. They stood in the rain and listened, and when Calum finished and lowered the leaf there was a long silence, and then a low sound that went through the crowd like wind through barley, and she understood that it was not joy. They had wanted the queen to decide for them. And she had handed it back to them, every household of them, to decide for themselves.

A woman near Mòrag said, to nobody, "Well, that's no help," and went home.

But the crowd did not go home, most of it. It stayed on the quay in the rain, talking in knots, well after Calum had taken the leaf in and hung it on a peg beside the roll. And someone in one of the knots began to say the word over, in a sing-song, as the fishers of the west turn anything into a song if they say it often enough; and someone else took it up; and by the time Mòrag had led her pony down to the water's edge to drink, there were a dozen voices on the quay saying it together, not quite in tune:

> *Cha chuir mi duine thairis, agus cha chùm mi duine air ais.*
> I will send no one over, and I will keep no one back.

The queen had never said it in those words. The harbour songs of Seann Skell have said it so ever since, and they are younger than Leabhar a' Chùraim and less careful, and nobody on the west coast has ever wished to hear it any other way.

## IV. Of Aonghas at Inis àrsaidh

She did not go into the harbour-house that night. She rode on the three miles to Inis àrsaidh in the dark and came into her own house soaked to the skin, and Aonghas was up, sitting by the fire, as he always was when she was away.

He had heard. Everybody had heard by then; the word had run down the three miles of the shore road faster than a pony. He looked at her as she stood dripping in the doorway, and got up and took her cloak, and put her in the chair by the fire and put a cup of hot ale in her hands and knelt and pulled her boots off, and only then said, "Well?"

"She won't send and she won't forbid," Mòrag said.

"I heard."

"She won't say anything to me that she doesn't say to the fisher." Mòrag drank. Her hands were shaking with cold. "I asked her straight. I asked her, if I go. And she said, then you'll go."

Aonghas sat back on his heels and looked up at her in the firelight. He was a big fair man, slow-spoken, a farmer of the good land up the river behind the town, who had married the queen's sister to the astonishment of the whole west and had never once, in three years, behaved as if it were anything remarkable.

"So," he said. "Do we go?"

She looked at him. She had lain awake over this for a year and a half. She had rehearsed every argument, every way of saying it, how she would put it to him and what he would say and what she would answer. She had been ready for a fight.

"I haven't finished," she said. "I was going to ask you. It was all ready. The oak, and the keel, and how nobody knows, and how somebody will have to learn, and that the queen won't stop us, and that we'd go together or not at all, because the harbour scribe writes a household whole or not..."

"Yes," said Aonghas.

"...and that I know it's your father's land, and your mother's grave behind the house, and..."

"Mòrag," said Aonghas. "Yes."

She stopped. He was still kneeling on the hearth with her wet boots in his hands, looking up at her with his slow patient face, and she saw that he had decided long before, perhaps on the night by this same fire when he had told her about the oaks of Doire fhionn, and had been waiting, as he always waited, for her to catch up.

She put the cup down and began to laugh, and then to cry, and he got up off the hearth and held her.

## V. Of the Knife

She went into the harbour-house the next afternoon, alone. Aonghas had offered to come. She had said that the scribe would know him, and that the household was the household whether one of them stood there or both, and that she wanted to do this herself. He had understood.

It was raining again. The harbour-house was full, as it was every day now, and the bench by the door was full of old men, and the floor was full of people reading the boards, and at the far end under the window Calum mac Nèill sat at his board with his knife. She came in out of the rain with her hood up, and some of the old men on the bench looked at her and did not know her, and then one did, and nudged the next.

She stood in front of the board. Calum looked up. She saw him know her, before she had lowered her hood; she saw the knowing go through his face and out again, and his face go smooth and careful.

"Lady," he said.

"I wish my household entered," said Mòrag. "The household of Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh, of Inis àrsaidh. Two of us. Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh, and Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill."

The harbour-house had gone quiet behind her. Without looking round, and without sitting, though there was a stool, she stood and watched Calum take a fresh board from the rack, and plane it, and set the knife to it. He cut slowly, and very well.

She spelled it out for him. She knew he did not need it. Every scribe in the west knew how to spell the name of the queen's sister; it was on half the leaves that came down from An Talla Dearg. But she spelled it all the same, letter by letter, in a clear voice that carried to the back of the house, *M, ò, r, a, g*, and watched every letter go into the wood, and then *nic Dhòmhnaill*, all of it; and then her husband's name above it, because he was the head of the household on the board; and then the line down the left side that joined them. It seemed to her that the knife was a long time about it. When the last stroke was cut and the shaving had curled away and dropped to the floor, she let out a breath she had not known she was holding.

"Thank you," she said.

Calum looked up at her. He did not say anything. Whatever he thought, he kept it behind his careful face.

She pulled her hood up again and went out into the rain. Behind her, as the door shut, she heard the harbour-house begin to talk.

He wrote nothing beside the entry. There was no rule that said he should, and he was not a man to make one. The chroniclers have written a great deal about it since, and none of them was in the room.

## VI. Of the Vein-House above Muileann dhearg

Sixty miles east, up in the mountain country, the copy of the queen's word came to Taigh na Fèithe by the coal-road, three days after it was read at Seann Skell, and the custodians sat down to think what it meant for them.

Taigh na Fèithe stood on a shoulder of the hills above the diggings at Muileann dhearg, where the galleries went into the mountain. It was a long hall of dark stone, older than the queen's line, with store-houses round a yard and the carriers' gate on the downhill side. In its inner room, in a niche lit by a lamp that was never let go out, stood Crom's stone, the slab that had lain on the first break of the vein. In the room beyond it, on a table of black oak, lay Leabhar a' Chùraim, which had been kept since An Aois Naomh, and in which every hearth on the island that held the right to the coal was written. Taigh na Fèithe was heir to Talla na Lasrach, where Brìde's flame had first been bound; Coimheadaichean na Lasrach still kept the flame there, and the stone cup on the threshold, but it was here, above the galleries, that the handful was measured and the book was kept, and it was here that the custodians met.

The master of Taigh na Fèithe in those years was Eòghann mac Mhuirich, an old man of Coimheadaichean na Lasrach' blood, dry and thin and very patient, who had spent sixty years in the service of the vein and had never once, the custodians said, been seen to hurry. He read the queen's word through at the table, twice, by the light of the lamp before Crom's stone, and then he folded it and said:

"We had better count."

## VII. Of the Question of the Coal

They did not count at once. First they argued, through the whole of that winter and into the spring, over a question that the queen's word did not touch and that no one at Seann Skell had thought to ask.

The right to the coal was earned. That was Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig as it had stood since An Aois Naomh. A custodian served his apprenticeship at the vein, seven years under a master, learning the galleries and the colours and the measure; and a hearth that held the right to the handful held it because its people had kept the coal and Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, generation after generation. The right lived in the hands that had learned it. It was written in Leabhar a' Chùraim against the hearth, and Taigh na Fèithe measured to it.

Then what happened to the right when the hearth went over the sea?

Some of the custodians said it went with them. The right was in the hands, and the hands would be the same hands on the far coast as on this one. Others said that the right was to the vein, and the vein was here; a right to a thing on the far side of the sea was no right at all, and the hearth should be struck from the book on the day it sailed. And some, the old ones mostly, said nothing, but looked at each other; because there was a third question under the other two, and none of them wished to be the first to ask it. If the right lived in the hands, and the hands went away, did the vein lose something? Did it answer fewer?

Fearchar mac Ruairidh was the loudest of those who said the right went with the hearth. He was a custodian of the western diggings, a big, black-browed man of thirty with a laugh that carried through stone walls, who had been apprenticed at twelve and had spent eighteen years in the galleries and could name every colour of broken coal by feel in the dark. He had heard the three tellings from Murchadh's own leaf, the winter before last, and had been talking about them ever since.

"The coal knows the hands," he said, at the long table in the hall, in the moon of Gearras, with the wind hammering on the shutters. "You all know it. You've all felt it. You put your hand on a broken face and it's warm to you and cold to the lad beside you. That's not in the book. That's not in the vein. That's in us. Wherever we go, it goes."

"Then take your hands over the sea, Fearchar," said an old custodian of the southern galleries, "and see if the far coast has a vein in it for them to warm."

There was laughter. Fearchar laughed too. But Eòghann mac Mhuirich, at the head of the table, did not laugh, and after a while the others noticed, and stopped.

"We'll count," said Eòghann. "We'll count first. Then we'll know what we're arguing about."

## VIII. Of the Count Made Twice

They sent to Seann Skell for a copy of the roll. The harbour scribe sent it willingly, board by board, copied onto skin by his son, with a small mark like a flame beside each household whose hearth took the handful. It came up the coal-road in the spring, and more boards after it, for the roll went on growing all that year, and in the high summer, in the moon of Lùghnas, the custodians sat down at the long table with the copy of the roll on one side and Leabhar a' Chùraim on the other, and counted.

It took them nine days. They went hearth by hearth, household by household, the roll's name against the book's name, reading aloud and ticking. Eòghann sat at the head of the table and did not count; he listened. Fearchar read the roll aloud, because he had the loudest voice. A young custodian of the capital's diggings read the book. Two clerks ticked.

On the ninth day, in the evening, the clerks added their ticks and looked at each other, and added them again, and gave the figure to Eòghann on a slip of skin.

He read it, and read it again, and looked up at the custodians round the table, who were watching him.

"Nearly one in five," he said.

Nobody spoke. One hearth in five of all the hearths on the island that held the right to the coal was on Rolla nan Deònach. Not one in fifty, which was what most of them had expected; not one in twenty, which was what the pessimists had said. Nearly one in five. Fishers, farmers, weavers, boat-wrights; and custodians, many custodians, whose hands the vein had answered, whose apprenticeship had been seven years at these same galleries; and the queen's own sister.

"That's wrong," said someone.

"Count it again," said Eòghann.

They counted it again. It took them seven more days, because they were faster now and angrier. They changed the readers round, so that no one could say a tired voice had skipped a name. Fearchar read the book this time, and the young custodian from the capital read the roll. The clerks ticked.

On the sixteenth day, on 14 an Lùnastal, LE 3, they gave Eòghann the second slip. It was the same figure, within a hearth or two.

He sat and looked at it for a long time. Then he took his pen and wrote it in Leabhar a' Chùraim, in his own old careful hand, under the day; and beside it he wrote that the count had been made twice, because the first figure had not been believed. By whom, he did not say; there was no need.

## IX. Of Fearchar's Own Name

When he had finished writing, Eòghann laid down the pen and said, without looking up: "Is there anything else?"

There was a silence. Then Fearchar mac Ruairidh stood up from the long table.

He had not said anything for sixteen days that was not a name read aloud. He stood with his big hands flat on the table and his black brows drawn down, and he looked, for once, like a man who did not know how loud to be.

"My household is on the roll," he said. "Fearchar mac Ruairidh, of the western diggings, and his wife and his two daughters. It's on the fourth board. I went down to Seann Skell in the moon of Samhnas and had it cut. I counted my own name twice, reading it, and ticked it, and said nothing." He swallowed. "I should have said before we began, and didn't. The figure was what I wanted first. I wanted to know whether I was one of a handful of fools or one of a great many." He looked round the table. "Now I know."

Nobody said anything. The young custodian from the capital was staring at him. The old custodian of the southern galleries, who had laughed at him in Gearras, had put his face in his hands.

Eòghann mac Mhuirich did not look up from the book. He sat with the pen laid down beside it and his old dry hands folded on the table in front of him, and he looked at the figure he had just written as though it were a stranger.

"Sit down, Fearchar," he said at last, quite gently.

Fearchar sat.

The master of Taigh na Fèithe turned the leaf of Leabhar a' Chùraim, very carefully, so as not to smudge the ink, and wrote the date at the head of the next leaf, and the words *the handful for the season*, in the same hand as before; and began to read the names of the hearths aloud, one after another, as he had read them every season for sixty years, for the measuring. And the custodians round the table, one by one, took up their pens and followed him, and none of them looked at Fearchar, and none of them looked at each other, and the lamp before Crom's stone in the next room burned steady and small, as it always had.

# Chapter Four: Of the Oaks of Doire fhionn

*LE 3 – 5*

## I. Of a Wright Who Sewed Planks

Alasdair mac Iain was a boat-wright of the strand below Seann Skell, and in the fourth year of the age he had never built anything that could not be carried up a beach by six men.

That was what a boat was, on Dia-thìr. The wrights of the strand built coasters and fishing boats as their grandmothers had: they split their planks from oak and ash with wedges, and shaped them with the adze, and laid them edge to edge on a frame of bent ribs, and sewed them together with split root and twisted gut through holes bored along the edges, and stopped the seams with moss and tallow. A good sewn boat was light and supple; she gave in a sea, every seam working, like a basket in a stream. She wanted to be pulled up every night and let dry, and her stitching looked to, and her moss renewed. She would take a crew of six along the coast from headland to headland in a day and bring them home loaded with fish. Three nights on the open sea would have killed her.

Alasdair had built perhaps forty such boats. He was a lean dark man, not tall, with a long jaw and a way of looking at a piece of timber that made the other wrights of the strand fall silent, as though he were listening to it. He was known on the strand as the best of them at a hull's lines. The strand knew him too as a man who asked too many questions, who would stand for half a morning looking at a sea running up the beach and not say what he was thinking.

What he was thinking, from the day he read the roll in the harbour-house, was a keel.

## II. Of the Keel in the Tellings

There was no keel on the island. There were keels in the tellings.

The old tellers of the west said that the boats of Rìghrean na Cloiche, in An Aois Ailein, had been built on a spine of oak: a single long timber down the middle of the bottom, and the ribs rising out of it on either side like the ribs of a beast from its backbone, and the planks fastened to the ribs with wooden pegs, not sewn. Such a boat, the tellers said, stood stiff in a sea and cut the water where a sewn boat rode it, and she could stay out for days. Rìghrean na Cloiche had sailed round the whole island in such boats, the tellers said, and to the islands off the coast; and then, as the tellers always said of everything in An Aois Ailein, the making of them had been forgotten.

Alasdair did not know whether to believe it. But he had noticed, as a boy, that the old coasters on the strand, the ones built by the grandfathers of the men who built them now, had a thicker plank down the middle of the bottom than the others, a plank that was more than a plank, shaped out of a single long timber with a ridge along its underside; and that the wrights who built them now left it out, because it was heavy and hard to make and nobody could say what it was for. He had thought, then, that it was what was left of something.

So through the winter after the queen's word, and all the next year, he built small hulls on the strand, no longer than his arm, on spines of oak. He built them with pegs, and with nails of hardwood, and with his own sewing, one way and another. He floated them in the river pool and pushed them over with a stick to see how they came up. Then he took them down to the mouth of the river where the sea came in and let them go on the ebb and walked along the shore to see where they came ashore, and how. The other wrights laughed at him, and then stopped laughing, and then began to come and stand beside him on the shore with their hands under their arms and watch.

By the end of the fourth year he knew four things. A keel would make a hull stiff. A stiff hull could be bigger. A bigger hull could carry water and stores for many days. And the keel would have to be made of a single timber longer than any oak he had ever seen.

## III. Of the Lady at Inis àrsaidh

He went to the queen's sister, because there was no one else to go to.

The queen had said she would neither help nor hinder. The custodians had said nothing, and were said to be quarrelling among themselves. The harbour-house kept the roll, but it had no money and no timber. The households on the roll were fishers and farmers and wrights, and none of them had anything to give but their own hands. But the lady Mòrag of Inis àrsaidh had been on the roll since the autumn of the queen's word, and she had asked the Cuan shean skipper about oak, and she had silver of her own.

She received him in the house at Inis àrsaidh, by the fire, with her husband. She had a child now, a boy of a few moons, who lay in a basket by the hearth and watched the flames. Alasdair stood awkwardly with his cap in his hand and told them about the keel.

He told it badly, he thought. He was not a talker. But Mòrag listened without interrupting, and when he had finished she asked him three questions: how long the keel must be, how many such timbers the fleet would want, and whether he knew where to find them. He answered the first two. To the third he said that he did not.

"Doire fhionn," said Aonghas, from the other side of the fire.

Alasdair looked at him.

"Up the north road," said the big farmer. "Forty-odd miles. There's a grove there, on the hill above the village, older than any of the Doires. My grandfather took me to see it when I was a boy. He said the oaks had been standing since before Rìghrean na Cloiche. You couldn't see the tops from the ground." He was quiet a moment. "It's the grove the village is named for. They won't like it."

"They'll like it less if we don't ask," said Mòrag. She looked at Alasdair. "Go and look at them. If they're what you need, come back and tell me, and I'll pay for the felling and the hauling, and the households of the roll will give their labour. If they're not, come back and tell me that, and we'll look somewhere else."

"And if the village won't give them, lady?"

"Then we'll ask the village what it wants," said Mòrag, "and see whether we can give it."

## IV. Of the Road North

He set out at the turn of the fifth year, in the moon of Gearras, after Là Fhèill Brìde, when the hearths had been swept and relit and the days were beginning to lengthen. On foot and alone he went, with a pack and a staff and a coil of line with knots in it every arm's length, for measuring.

The north road went up out of the Seann Skell country along the river, and then over the long low hills toward the north coast, through a country of small farms and peat-moss and scrub birch, with the wind always in his face. He made fifteen miles the first day and slept in a byre. The second day it rained, and he made less. On the third day, in the afternoon, he came over a rise and saw below him a village of grey houses in a fold of the hills, with a stream running through it and smoke going up; and on the hill above the village, on its eastern side, a darkness against the sky that he took at first for a cloud.

It was the grove.

He stood on the rise and looked at it for a long time. He had seen oaks all his life. The strand below Seann Skell was built of oak, and every boat he had ever made was oak. These were something else. They stood on the crown of the hill in a ring, perhaps sixty of them, with a few lesser trees about their feet, and they were so high and so broad that the hill itself looked small beneath them, and their bare winter crowns made a black net against the grey sky that shifted as the wind went through it. He could hear the wind in them from where he stood, a mile off: a low roar, like surf.

He went down into the village as the light was going, and asked at the first door for the keeper of the grove.

## V. Of Eilidh nic Ruairidh

The keeper of the grove was an old woman called Eilidh nic Ruairidh, who lived in the last house of the village at the foot of the grove hill, with a cow and a great many cats. She was small and bent and brown as a nut, and her eyes were very clear. She had kept the grove for fifty years, she told him, as her mother had before her. It was not a hard office. The grove kept itself. The keeper walked round it at Na Ceithir Fèilltean, and saw that no one cut the living wood, and gathered the fallen boughs for the village hearths, and told the children not to climb.

She listened to him with her hands folded on her stick. When he had told her what he wanted, and why, she did not say anything for a long while.

"Come up in the morning," she said at last. "I'll show you."

In the morning they went up the hill together, slowly, because she was slow. The grove was bigger close to than it had looked from the rise. The trunks were so thick that three men could not have joined hands round the smallest of them, and they went up straight and grey and furrowed for sixty feet before they branched. The ground under them was deep in old leaves and mast, and very quiet. Even the wind, which roared in the crowns, did not come down to the floor of the grove. A few birds moved in the high branches. Nothing else.

Alasdair walked from tree to tree with his knotted line, measuring. He put his hands on the bark. He looked up each trunk, along its length, the way he looked along a plank for a warp. Eilidh walked beside him and said nothing.

When he had been round the whole ring he came back to her and said, "These are what I need."

"I know," said Eilidh.

"I need a score of them, or near it, for the keels. And the frames from the others, and the planks. I'd need most of the grove."

"I know that too." She stood leaning on her stick, looking up into the crowns. "Well. You'd better tell me which."

He did not understand her. She turned and looked at him with her clear eyes.

"You'll not take them as a crowd," she said. "Not in my grove. If they're going, you'll choose them, one by one, and you'll tell me why that one and not the next, and I'll tell you its name. They've all got names. My mother gave me the names and her mother gave them to her. And when you've chosen, you'll know what you've taken. That's my price."

## VI. Of the Naming of the Trees

It took them two days. He had thought it would take an hour.

He went from tree to tree again, with the old woman beside him, and at each one he stopped and said whether he wanted it and why. This one, because it was straight for seventy feet, and would make a keel with no scarf in it. This one, because it had a great branch coming off low down at the right angle to make the stem-post of a hull, the timber that rises from the fore end of the keel. Not that one; it was hollow at the heart, he could hear it when he knocked. This one, for frames, because it was crooked, and its crooks were the shapes of ribs.

And at each one Eilidh told him its name. The Grey Mare. The Old Man's Knee. The Two Sisters, which were two trunks grown out of one root, and which he took both of. Crom's Finger. The Bent Back. The Eyrie, because a hawk had nested in it every spring for longer than anyone remembered. The Drowned Woman, for a reason Eilidh would not tell him. The Queen, which was the biggest in the grove, and which he stood under for a long time, and at last said he would take for the first keel.

He had not meant to feel anything about it. He was a wright; he felled oaks every year. But by the end of the second day he had a list of names in his head that he could not get out of it, and when he came to the last tree of the ring, a young one, no more than two hundred years old, standing a little apart, and said that he did not need it, he found that his hands were shaking.

"That's the Child," said Eilidh. "You'll leave it?"

"I'll leave it."

"And the others?"

He looked round the ring. Of sixty-odd trees he had chosen fifty-four.

"The others go," he said.

Eilidh nodded. She did not seem angry. She looked, if anything, relieved, as though a thing she had been waiting a long time to hear had been said at last, and it was worse than she had feared and not as bad as she had dreamed.

"It won't grow again," she said. "You know that. You can cut an ash and it comes up from the stool. An oak like these, you cut it, it's gone. There'll be nothing on this hill but the Child and the stumps, and the Child will never be what these are, not in my time nor yours nor anyone's we'll know." She was quiet. "And the village will still be Doire fhionn. The fair grove. It'll keep the name. It won't have any reason to."

He had no answer. He stood in the silent grove with the knotted line in his hands and could not think of one.

"Well," said Eilidh at last. "Go and tell your lady. And tell her to send men who know how to fell a tree so that it doesn't smash itself. I'll not have the Queen broken for want of care."

## VII. Of the Felling

They came in the moon of Sìolach, the seed-time: eighty men from the households of the roll, fishers and farmers and wrights, with axes and saws and wedges and ropes, and a dozen yoke of oxen from the farms up the Abhainn naomh, and Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh at their head, because he knew oxen. Mòrag's silver paid for their bread and the village's barley and the fodder for the oxen. The village of Doire fhionn stood in its doorways and watched them come up the road, and did not speak to them.

The felling took most of the summer. Each tree was felled toward the downhill side, onto a bed of cut brush to break its fall, with ropes on its crown and men on the ropes to guide it. Alasdair was there for every one. The Queen went last. It took two days to bring down, and when it fell, in the evening, with a long tearing groan and then a crash that shook the ground under the village and brought the cows lowing out of the byres, the men on the ropes stood still and did not cheer, and some of them took off their caps.

Eilidh nic Ruairidh did not come up the hill while the felling went on. But at the end of each day, when the men came down to the village to eat, she was sitting in her doorway with her cats round her, and Alasdair would stop and tell her which tree had gone that day, by its name. She would nod, and say nothing, and he would go on.

After the Queen fell, he stopped at her door as usual. She was not in the doorway. He looked in, and saw her sitting by her cold hearth in the dark with her hands folded on her stick, and did not go in.

## VIII. Of the Ox-Sleds on the North Road

A keel-timber seventy feet long cannot be carried. It must be dragged.
