They built sleds of lesser oak, low and broad, with runners shod in ash, and rolled the great trunks onto them with levers and ropes, and yoked the oxen six pair to a sled, and dragged them south down the north road toward the sea. It was forty-two miles. With a keel-timber on the sled, the oxen made three miles in a good day and one in a bad one. They broke two sleds on the first hill. They had to widen the road at every bend, cutting back the banks and the birch scrub, and at the stream below the village they had to build a causeway of stone before the sleds would cross it. The farmers along the road came out and stood at their gates to watch the trunks go by, and some of them cursed, because the road was ruined for their carts, and some of them brought out ale.

It went on all that summer and into the autumn. The sleds went down one after another, strung out along the road for twenty miles, with the drovers walking beside the oxen and the wrights walking beside the trunks, and the sound of it could be heard, the farmers said, a mile off on a still day: the groan of the runners on the stones, and the drovers' cries, and the oxen blowing.

Nearer the sea, on the shore of Loch chrom below the capital, there was a wood of wild oak, rough and crooked, that had never been anyone's grove; and in the same summer a party of woodcutters from the roll went there and built themselves huts at the wood's edge, to fell crooked oak for frames and knees that the fleet would need in hundreds. The huts did not outlast the felling; the woodcutters went home to the roll when the last knee was hauled out, and the bracken came up through the floors. The wood kept its name, Doire fhiadhaich, the wild grove, and the tellers of that shore say still that timber for the fleet was felled there.

## IX. Of the First Keel

The first keel came down to the strand below Seann Skell in the moon of Teasach, the hot moon, in high summer. It was the Queen.

Alasdair had cleared a length of the strand above the high-water line, and dug a saw-pit beside it, and laid a bed of heavy oak blocks in a long straight line on the shingle, level to a hair, which he had spent a week getting right with a line and a trough of water. The oxen dragged the sled down onto the strand and along beside the blocks, and fifty men with levers rolled the great trunk off the sled and onto the blocks, and it lay there, grey and furrowed and enormous, seventy feet from end to end.

Then they began to shape it.

It took them the rest of that moon and half the next. They split the trunk down its length with wedges, and hewed away the sapwood with axes and adzes, and squared it, and shaped it: flat on top where the frames would sit, and deeper at the middle than at the ends, and with a ridge along its underside, like the ridge on the thick bottom plank of the old coasters that Alasdair had wondered at as a boy. He shaped the ridge himself. He did it by eye and by the feel of the adze in his hands, walking up and down the length of the timber a hundred times a day, sighting along it, stooping, laying his palm on it, and cutting a little more. No one on the island had ever done this before, and there was no one he could ask.

On 14 an Lùnastal, LE 5, it was done, and he stood at the fore end of it and looked along it to the after end, and saw that it was straight and true; and the men of the strand stood round it in a ring and looked at him, and at it.

"Well," said one of them. "What's it want now?"

"Ribs," said Alasdair. "Then planks. Then as many more of it as there are oaks on the sleds."

## X. Of the Fellowship of the Strand

He could not do it alone, and he could not do it with a crowd. He needed wrights who would learn it as he had learned it, and keep it, and not wander off to their fishing when the herring came.

So in the moon of Lùghnas, at the feast of Lugh, he called the wrights of the Seann Skell strand together on the shingle beside the first keel, all of them, masters and journeymen, some forty men, and asked them to bind themselves to the fleet: to work at it and nothing else until it was built, and to take apprentices, and to share what each of them learned with all the others. He asked it badly. He was no talker. But they had all stood on the shore with their hands under their arms and watched his little hulls come up out of the water, and most of them said yes.

They made it a fellowship. Leabhar a' Chùraim gives its name as Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights. They took the custodians of the vein for their pattern, because the custodians were the only fellowship on the island that anyone respected: every apprentice was to be bound for seven years, as a custodian's apprentice was bound to the galleries, and was to learn the whole craft and swear to keep it and teach it. A custodian came down from Taigh na Fèithe to swear the apprentices, a grave young man in undyed wool who did not know one end of a boat from the other and said so, and heard their oaths all the same over a coal from the vein in a clay dish, as Taigh na Fèithe heard its own.

The first apprentice sworn was a boy of the strand called Coinneach mac Fhearghais, fourteen years old, the son of a coaster-wright, with big hands and a stammer, who had been hanging about Alasdair's little hulls for a year. He knelt on the shingle with his hands on the coal and swore to the fellowship in a voice that cracked on every other word. When he stood up he looked at the keel, and then at Alasdair, and grinned, and Alasdair found that he was grinning too.

## XI. Of the Frames Standing on the Strand

By the end of the moon of Pailteach they had the first frames up.

They rose out of the keel on either side in pairs, one pair for each arm's length of its seventy feet, curved crooks of oak from the Bent Back and the Old Man's Knee and the wild wood by Loch chrom, pegged into the keel with treenails of heart-oak and joined across at the top by beams. From the harbour-house at the head of the west quay, the town could see them over the roofs of the strand: two long rows of curved grey timbers standing against the sky, bare and pale, with the light coming through between them.

The town came down to look. People stood on the shingle in the evening and stared at the thing on the blocks. It was bigger than any boat they had ever seen, and it did not look like a boat. It looked, the harbour scribe Calum mac Nèill wrote on a board that night, like the ribs of a great beast lying dead on the shore, picked clean by the birds. He meant it kindly. He did not know how else to say it.

Alasdair heard none of it, walking up and down the length of the keel inside the frames, as he walked it every evening, with his palm running along the top of each rib as he passed, feeling for the fair curve.

He thought of the old woman at Doire fhionn, sitting in the dark by her cold hearth with her hands on her stick. And he thought of the Queen, the biggest oak in the grove, lying under his feet now, shaped and squared and pegged, with the ribs rising out of her. He thought that he had never made anything in his life that had cost so much, and that he did not yet know whether it would float.

The Child was still standing on the hill above Doire fhionn, alone among the stumps. Word of that came down to the strand later in the year with a drover, who said the village had built a low wall of stones round it, and that the old keeper went up every evening and sat beside it until dark.

# Chapter Five: Of the Hull that Lay Down

*LE 6 – 9*

## I. Of the Launching of An Fhaoileag

Through the rest of that fifth year, and into the sixth, the frames on the strand below Seann Skell filled in. The town that had come down to stare at the bare ribs came down again to watch the planks go on, one strake and then the next, pegged to the frames with treenails of heart-oak and caulked with tow and pitch in the old way, though nothing else about her was old. Alasdair mac Iain walked her length every evening still, his palm on the wood, and by the moon of Gearras she had a deck, and a mast stepped through it into the keel he had laid with his own hands, and rigging that the rope-walks of Cuan shean had sent west by cart, coil on coil.

They called her An Fhaoileag, the gull, because she rode high and pale on the water when she was floated off the blocks, and because a boy on the strand said she looked like a bird about to go up. Alasdair had wanted no name at all, or a plainer one, but the wrights had built her and the wrights named her, and he did not argue it.

The mast went in on a cold, still morning with the whole fellowship standing round the step and Coinneach mac Fhearghais, oldest now of the first apprentices though he was not yet twenty, holding the foot of it steady while four men walked it up on sheer-legs of borrowed spruce. It went home clean, no binding, no easing with a maul, and the wrights took that for a good sign, the way wrights on the strand had always taken such things for signs, though none of them could have said what god or luck they meant by it. Rigging came down from Cuan shean in coils on a cart that took two days on the road, hemp still smelling of the fields it had grown in, and the strand spent a fortnight reeving it through blocks that had never held a rope so heavy, learning as they went which of their old coaster's knots would bear the strain and which would not.

On the morning of her launch the whole strand and half the town stood along the harbour-house wall to see her go down. A custodian of the vein came, at Mòrag's asking, and set a coal from Taigh na Fèithe in a clay dish at her step, as was done for a house's first hearth, because a ship going out onto open water for the first time was thought to want the same blessing as a house standing up for the first time. Calum mac Nèill wrote in his roll that day that the harbour-house had never held so many people at once, not even for the reading of the queen's word.

She took the water clean, without a shudder, and rode the wash of her own launching like a thing that had done it a hundred times. Alasdair stood at the harbour wall with his hands under his arms, as he had stood since he was a boy watching other men's boats, and for the length of that morning he let himself believe the thing was finished.

It was not finished. It had not yet begun.

## II. Of the Following Sea

A trial crew of fourteen took her down the Abhainn naomh three days later, to try her in open water before ever a household's goods went aboard her. Alasdair would not sail in her himself; he never went to sea in any hull he had built, and no one on the strand thought to ask him why. He walked instead along the north bank of the river with the tide, and came out at last on the headland above Ros àrsaidh, the point where the boats of Inis àrsaidh had always put out to the open sea, and stood there with his hands jammed under his arms in the wind off the water.

His sister's boy Tormod Beag was aboard her. He was fifteen that year, all wrist and elbow, and he had begged a place on the trial crew for a month before Alasdair gave it to him, more to be rid of the begging than for any other reason. Alasdair had told him to keep low and hold on and do nothing that was not asked of him. Tormod had grinned and said he would.

She came down out of the river mouth with the ebb under her and turned her head into open water, and for a while she went as well as any hull Alasdair had ever watched, better. The wind was out of the south-west, no more than the sea took every day of that season, and she carried it easily, heeling a little and coming up again. Two coasters out of Inis àrsaidh stood off to watch her pass, their crews idle on the oars, and one of the men called across the water that she went like something that had done it before, and the trial crew laughed and called back that she had not, not once, and the laughing carried clear to the headland where Alasdair stood. Alasdair began, against every rule he set himself, to be glad of her.

Then a sea came up astern of her, bigger than the ones before it, the kind that gathers itself out of nothing on a coast that has been building weather all week without quite letting it fall. He saw her stern lift to it. He had seen a hundred small boats lift to a following sea and come down again, and he waited for her to come down.

She did not come down soon enough. Her stern rose and her bow went under, and the water that should have run off her deck did not run off fast enough, because she was deeper and heavier and slower to shed a sea than any boat the island had ever built, and no one, not even Alasdair, had known that until that morning. She hung a moment with her bow buried and her stern high, and then she went over on her side as a tired animal lies down, not fighting it, folding into the water she had ridden so well an hour before.

There were fourteen heads in the sea and then there were fewer. Alasdair went down off the headland at a run, over ground he did not remember afterward crossing, shouting to the strand before he was near enough for shouting to do any good. Men came off the headland and off the strand at Inis àrsaidh in every boat that could be got into the water in time, oarsmen still buttoning their coats as they ran the boats down the shingle, and they brought back three living and the bodies of eight of the drowned; three more were never found at all, and the sea gave up nothing more of them that year or any year after. Tormod Beag was among the eight brought back. Alasdair carried him up the beach himself, though the boy weighed nothing at all by then, nothing a man his age should have been able to feel as light, and he did not let anyone else take the weight from him the whole way up to the boat-shed.

## III. Of the Names Cut at Inis àrsaidh

Inis àrsaidh kept no roll of its own like the harbour-house at Seann Skell; it had no need of one before that week. But it kept a board, as every fishing town on that coast kept a board, for the names of those the sea did not give back whole, and the old woman who kept it, whom the village called the roll-keeper though the office had no other name, brought it out and set it against the wall of the boat-shed and cut eleven names into it that night by the light of two lamps, working slowly because her hand was not steady and because there had never before been eleven names cut on one night.

The village sat up with her while she cut them. That was the custom, though no one could have said when it began: the cutting was not to be done alone, in case the knife slipped, or in case grief slipped, and there was no telling the two apart in the dark. Alasdair sat with the rest, on an upturned creel, and watched his nephew's name go into the wood letter by letter, and said nothing, because there was nothing he had any right to say that would not have sounded like an excuse.

They keened the eight that were found in the old way, the women's voices going up together and falling together, on the shingle where the boats were drawn up, with the bodies laid out under sailcloth and a lamp at each head. Alasdair's sister could not keen for her own son; she sat by him dry-eyed and silent while the other women's voices rose around her, and it was an aunt of the boy's father, come over from Ros bheag, who keened in her place, because the custom held that the loudest grief in a house is not always the one closest to the loss, and someone must carry it who still has a voice to carry it with. For the three that were not found there was no body to keen over, and the village did what was done in such a case: it lit a lamp on the shore all the same and let it burn down alone, and no one sat with that one, because there was no one to sit with.

Alasdair's sister did not come near him that night, and he did not go near her. He learned afterward, from his sister's husband, that she had said only one thing when the word reached her, which was that the boy had never once, in fifteen years, been given anything he had to ask for twice; she had thought, she said, that the asking might have been a kind of protection, and it was not. Alasdair carried that sentence a long way, and it did not get lighter with carrying.

He stayed at Inis àrsaidh three days, doing whatever was asked of him and nothing that was not, mending a net, hauling water, standing where he was told to stand. On the third day the roll-keeper found him sitting by the board in the daylight, reading the eleven names as though he had not already read them a hundred times in the dark, and she said to him, not unkindly, that a board could be read by a man once and remembered, and that reading it again and again was a way of staying somewhere a person had already left.

He went back to Seann Skell that evening, by the inland path rather than the road along the strand, where the second frame stood waiting for him under its canvas, so as not to see it until he was ready.

## IV. Of the Fire on the Strand

Eleven days passed before he was ready. On the twelfth, at night, with no one told he was going, he walked down to the tide-line below the blocks and built a driftwood fire, and sat by it with a stick, and began to draw a keel in the wet sand.

He drew the first one as he had built it: straight, deep, true along its whole length, a spine with the ribs rising square off it on either side, drawn on the day he laid it as the only honest line a keel could carry. He looked at it a long while. Then he rubbed it out with the flat of his hand and drew it again, and this time he took the straightness out of the forward third of her, where she met the sea first, and let it curve up and in, hollowing what had been full and filling what had been hollow toward her middle, so that the water coming at her from ahead would be turned aside along her sides instead of gathered up under her counter and carried aft to break her stern down as it had broken An Fhaoileag's.

He could not have said, that night, in words another wright could have taken away without watching him do it, what exactly he had changed. No single measurement carried it. The whole run of her forward body carried it, an inch here and half an inch there, multiplied along thirty feet of timber until the sum of it was a different animal. He rubbed it out a third time and drew it once more to be sure his hand had not lied to him the first two times, and it had not.

He sat by the fire until it burned down to nothing and the tide came up and took the sand smooth again, and by the time it did that he no longer needed the drawing. It was in his hands the way a tune is in a fiddler's hands after he has played it enough times to stop thinking about the notes, and it would stay there, and he would teach it to no one by writing it down, because there was no way he knew to write it down, only to show it, plank by plank, to the men who worked beside him until it was in their hands too.

## V. Of the Second Keel

The second keel was laid before the spring turned, on the same bed of oak blocks above the tide-line where the first had lain, cut from a timber of the Doire fhionn oaks that had been kept back, against Alasdair's own advice at the time, as too short for a deep keel and fit only for framing. It was not too short for what he needed of it now. The new run forward took less length to cut than the old, because the fault he was correcting lay in her lines and not in her size.

He would not let the wrights call her anything until she was planked. Some on the strand wanted to call her for Tormod Beag; Alasdair heard of it and said, through Coinneach mac Fhearghais, that the boy's name was not going onto a hull until a hull had been built that would not need to earn forgiveness for it. No one argued with him. Coinneach, who was seventeen that year and the steadiest of the young wrights, took over much of the day-to-day setting of frames that season, because Alasdair was often at the shed with the drawing rather than on the blocks, going over the new run again and again with a batten and a straightedge before he would trust his own hands a second time.

Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill sent silver down from Inis àrsaidh again that spring, as she had for the felling of the oaks, though no one had asked her a second time. Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh carried it himself, and stood a while on the strand watching the new frames go up before he said anything of why he had come. He told Alasdair, plainly, that his wife had heard of the drowning within the week and had slept badly since, her own household being one that meant to sail aboard some hull of this same fleet, and that the silver came as a bargain rather than a charity: build her right, and build her sound, and Mòrag would answer for the timber and the cordage for as long as the fellowship needed either. Alasdair took the silver and said less than he was asked, which the strand had come to know as his way of saying yes.

There were wrights who doubted the new run before they had planked a foot of her, men who had built sewn boats all their lives and trusted a keel that lay straight the way a man trusts a rule he was taught as a boy. Alasdair did not argue with them either. He set two of the doubters to plank her forward sections, where the change ran deepest, and let the wood make the argument for him; by the time the garboard strake was hung and fair along her new run, fitting the frames without the wedging and forcing that a poor line always asks for, the doubt had gone quiet, though it had not, in every man, gone away.

By midsummer An Dara Fhaoileag stood in frame on the strand, lower in the bow than her sister had stood, fuller amidships, narrower where she met the water first. The town, which had come down twice before to stare at the ribs of a beast, came a third time and said less about it. They had learned, in the space of one season, that a hull on the strand was not a promise.

## VI. Of Those Who Struck Themselves Out, and Those Who Entered

Word of the drowning reached the harbour-house at Seann Skell before the bodies had finished coming ashore, carried by a man of Inis àrsaidh who had run most of the way. Calum mac Nèill wrote it into his roll that night in four lines, dated, and under it, because he did not know what else to do with a thing that size, he ruled a line across the whole leaf.

In the weeks after, eleven households struck themselves from the roll. None of these were the households of the fourteen who had sailed, most of whom had never been on the roll at all, being crew hired for the trial and no more than half-committed to the crossing; these were households from up and down the coast who had heard the telling and found that what had been a season's talk was now a thing that could happen to a son sent out to try a boat that was not even the ship that would carry him across the water. Calum cut the strokes through their names himself, as the rule required, and left the names standing to be read, as the rule also required, because the net-maker Iain's household had struck itself twice and been read, and the rule did not bend for grief any more than it had bent for anything else.

But in those same weeks eleven other households entered, the number was remarked on at the time and is remarked on still, though no one has ever found a reason for it beyond the coincidence of the count. Among them was a fishing household of Inis àrsaidh itself, kin of one of the three men brought back alive, who came to the harbour-house and gave their names and said, when Calum asked them why now of all times, that they had watched the sea take what it wanted once already and saw no more reason to fear it for waiting. A widow of Ros bheag entered too, a woman with no husband left to lose and two grown daughters who had asked to go before the drowning and been refused; she told Calum only that a mother who forbade the sea one week and could not answer for it the next had no business forbidding anything, and gave the names of all three.

Calum wrote both counts, the eleven struck and the eleven entered, on facing pages, and drew no line connecting them, and no comment under either. It is the one page in the whole roll where a later reader can see the shape of the thing without being told what to think of it.

## VII. Of the Rope-Walks of Cuan shean

At Cuan shean, a dozen miles down the coast, the news reached the harbour front within the day, and when it did it changed nothing that Iain Ròpaire could see in the work of his rope-walks, which had been going on from first light to last since the queen's word first came down.

Cuan shean had given over its hemp fields to the fleet the year the keel was laid, and by the sixth year of the age its harbour front was three long rope-walks end to end, each the length of a good cable, where the spinners paid out hemp from bundles at their waists and the walkers went backward down the walk with it, twisting the strands together at a steady pace that a man could keep up from dawn to dark if he did not think too hard about it. The walks ran from first light because hemp twisted best with the morning damp still in it, and by noon the whole harbour front smelt of it, green and sharp, a smell the older fishermen of the town said they would carry to their graves and be glad of. Iain had walked a rope-walk himself since he was younger than Tormod Beag had been, and he was master of all three now, a broad, slow-spoken man who counted his own steps under his breath without knowing he did it, and whose hands, from thirty years of the hemp, were harder across the palm than the sole of a boot.

The trouble, when it came, had nothing to do with the hemp; it was a trouble of ignorance. A rope-maker at Cuan shean knew his cordage the way Alasdair knew his timber, by hand and by eye, but he had never seen a keel or a frame or a mast-step, and he made his rope to lengths and weights that a written order gave him, without knowing what the rope was for or where the strain would fall on it. Two shroud-lines sent west that spring parted at the deadeye within a season, and the wrights sent word back up the coast, not a complaint exactly, more a puzzlement, asking why rope that had held on a coaster for ten years should fail on a hull that had not yet crossed open water once.

Alasdair sent two of his wrights north to Cuan shean that summer to answer it, Coinneach among them, and they did what neither side had thought to do before: they walked the rope-walks themselves, end to end, and named the parts of a hull to the spinners and the walkers as they went, stem and sternpost, garboard and futtock, the standing parts and the running, what took the ship's whole weight and what took only the wind's. Iain Ròpaire, who had never in thirty years thought of his trade as needing another man's trade explained to him, found that once he knew what a shroud held up he made a different rope for it without being told a different measure, and that the walkers, who had always kept their pace by nothing but habit, began without anyone teaching it to them to set the hull's own words into the rhythm of their feet, stem, stern, garboard, keel, over and over down the length of the walk, so that the work went no faster but somehow sat easier in the hand.

Iain never wrote any of it down. He had no cause to. But he took to walking the middle rope-walk himself again that summer, though he had not walked one in years, master's work being mostly standing and watching by then, because he wanted the words in his own feet before he trusted them to anyone else's. His wife asked him why, at his age, he was coming home with rope-burn on his palms like a boy's, and he told her only that a man who gave an order ought to know what it cost to carry it out. The households of Cuan shean, when they told each other years afterward how the town had come to make the fleet's best cordage, told it as the year the rope-walks learned the names of a ship.

## VIII. Of the Sail-Cloth of Baile àrsaidh

A little north of Cuan shean, in the shire of Baile àrsaidh, the levy on woven cloth had been running since the year the second household struck itself from the roll at Seann Skell, though it had no name yet beyond what the shire seat's tally-keeper called it in his own book: a length, close-woven, from every household that wove, owed once and reckoned against nothing, neither rent nor tithe.

He kept it on tally-sticks in the old way, a notch for a length delivered and a second cut for a length short, and by the ninth year of the age he had cut more notches than he had thought the shire held households that wove at all, because women who had never sent so much as a hank of thread to the shire seat before sent their close-woven lengths that year, some of them households with no one on the roll and no thought of ever being on it. He asked one such woman, an old weaver of a hill farm a long day's cart-ride inland who had not seen the sea since she was a girl, why she troubled to send cloth for ships she would never sail in and never see. She told him that her granddaughter had married into a household that had gone, and that a sail was the one part of a ship a weaver's hands could put something of herself into, and that she would rather her granddaughter went dry than went in a boat with a stranger's thread in her sail.

He cut her notch and said nothing to that, because there was nothing in his book for it, only a length and a date. He kept the sticks in a chest at the shire seat, one for each year of the levy, bundled with a thong and a wooden tag scratched with the year, and by the ninth year the chest wanted a second lid to close over the first. The tallies survive; how many households paid, and how many like the hill weaver paid for reasons the notch does not carry, is not now to be known, and the tally-keeper never thought to ask a second time, having learned from the first that the answer would not fit on his stick.

## IX. Of the Hull that Stood Beside Her Sister

By the ninth year of the age An Dara Fhaoileag was planked from keel to sheer and stepping her mast, and Alasdair, who had not let the wrights name her, at last let them, and they called her An Dara Fhaoileag, the second gull, because no better name came to hand and because the strand had grown used, by then, to naming its hulls for what they were rather than for what was hoped of them.

She stood on the strand where the first had stood, lower forward, fuller in the belly, narrower at the bow than any hull the island had built before her, and every wright who worked her hull now worked to the pattern that had been drawn once in wet sand and rubbed out twice before it was trusted. Alasdair walked her length in the evenings as he had walked the first, his palm on the wood, and if he still would not sail in any hull himself, no one asked him why any longer.

The rope for her rigging came down from Cuan shean already knowing, in the walkers' hands if nowhere else, what strain it would be asked to bear. Her sailcloth had come, close-woven, from households up and down a shire whose weavers had never seen a mast go up. Eleven names stood cut into a board at Inis àrsaidh that the tide never reached and the weather was already beginning to soften at the edges, and would go on softening for as long as anyone thought to keep the board upright. On the harbour-house rolls at Seann Skell, eleven strokes lay across eleven names on one page and eleven fresh names stood uncrossed on the facing one, and Calum mac Nèill had still found no comment that belonged under either.

Alasdair stood at the harbour wall in the last light of that ninth year and looked at the hull standing there, lower and fuller and, he believed, honest in a way the first had not been, and did not let himself be glad of her, not yet, not the way he had let himself be glad once before. He only trusted her, which was a smaller thing and, he had learned, a safer one, and it would have to do until the sea had had the chance to prove him right or wrong a second time.

Coinneach mac Fhearghais found him there after the light had gone and the strand had emptied, and asked him, since he had never once been answered the first time he asked it, three years before, whether the fleet would truly be finished within his own lifetime, or whether it was a thing being built for other men's sons to sail. Alasdair looked a long while at An Dara Fhaoileag, and past her at the black shape of the shed where the third already stood framed under its canvas, and said only that he did not know, and that not knowing was the one honest answer he had given anyone about any of it since the day he first read the roll in the harbour-house. Coinneach asked nothing further, and the two of them stood together at the wall a while in the dark, listening to the tide work at the stones below the new quay, until the cold sent them both in.

# Chapter Six: Of the Star-Steersmen of Cuan ruadh

*LE 11 – 18*

## I. Of the Six Who Went East

Catrìona nic Iain was eleven years old the first night she went out with her father's boat past the Ros àrsaidh bar and did not know, coming home, which way the harbour lay until the smell of the smoke told her.

She never forgot it. She was a pilot of Ros bheag by the time she was sixteen, one of a handful of young ones who could bring a boat home along the coast in fog by the fall of the swell alone, and she thought herself good at her trade. Then the roll opened at Seann Skell, and the wrights began to lay down hulls no coaster's pilot had ever been asked to steer, and it came out, in the talk on the quays, that none of them, not the oldest, not the best, had ever held a course out of sight of land after dark. A coaster hugged the shore and put in before dusk. A hull bound for a coast three weeks off the mist could do neither.

The custodian Fearchar mac Ruairidh, who by then went about the west coast on the households' business more than he sat at Taigh na Fèithe, put the question to the harbour-masters of four ports in one season: who, on this coast, has ever steered by the stars alone? The answer came back the same from all four. No one now living. But there were tellings, thin and half-believed, of steersmen away on the eastern shore, at a town called Cuan ruadh, who still did.

It was a hundred miles off, by the map that hung in the harbour-house at Seann Skell, drawn crooked from an older one and marked in Alasdair Saor's own hand where the roads ran; and no road ran straight to it. A man would go up the coal-roads into the mountain country, and down again on the far side, and a week on foot was thought a fast crossing.

Six were chosen to go: two from Ros bheag, two from Ceann mhòr, one from Cuan shean, and Catrìona, because she had asked to be sent before anyone had thought to ask her. She was the youngest of the six and the only woman, and the master of the Ros bheag boats, an old man who had taught her the coast himself, told her plainly to her face that a season away from her own harbour would lose her half her custom.

"Then I'll get it back," she said, "and something with it."

The other four she came to know on the road better than she had known them at their own quays, the way a fortnight's walking will do. The two Ceann mhòr men were brothers, broad and slow-spoken, who had never in their lives been more than a day's sail from Faire a' Chinn; the Cuan shean man was a rope-maker's son who had gone to sea only twice and admitted it, on the third day, without shame; and of the second Ros bheag pilot, a lean, silent woman named for a grandmother nobody living remembered, Catrìona learned only that she had lost a brother at sea and had asked to go east for reasons she never once spoke of the whole journey.

They went out in the moon of Bealltach, when the roads were driest, with staffs and packs and a little silver among them from Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill's own purse, sent by a rider with word that the lady of Inis àrsaidh wished them well and asked to be told, when they came home, what they had learned. They went up the coal-road past Muileann dhearg, where Taigh na Fèithe stood black on its hill and the custodians looked out at them from the gate and said nothing; and over the shoulder of the mountain country the road gave out into a track between screes, where the wind never stopped and the going was a mile in an hour over broken stone. On the fourth night the weather turned on them above the last of the lochs, a cold rain driving level off the moor with no shelter in it anywhere, and they spent the dark hours crowded under an overhang of rock with their backs to each other for warmth, and in the morning the Cuan shean man's feet were so cut about with the stones that the Ceann mhòr brothers had to carry his pack the rest of that day between them.

They went down again by a country none of them knew, of heather and small lochs and cairns whose names they did not have, and on the seventh evening they came over a last rise and saw the sea again, grey and enormous, with a town at the water's edge and boats drawn up along a strand that faced, for the first time in any of their lives, east, out over open water with no far shore in the telling of it at all.

Cuan ruadh smelled different from any harbour on the west coast. Catrìona noticed it before she noticed anything else: no weed-smell of low tide flats, but a clean cold reek of open water, as though the town stood at the very edge of something with nothing beyond it but distance. The boats drawn up were narrow and deep for their length, built, she saw at once, on a different rule than any coaster she knew, sewn like the rest but with a thick shaped plank down the middle of the bottom, of the kind the old men of the west said their grandfathers' boats had carried.

"They go out of sight of land here," said one of the Ceann mhòr brothers, low, as they stood looking down at the strand. "They always did."

Nobody at Cuan ruadh made much of them. A boy took them to a byre where they might sleep and a woman brought them fish and barley bread without asking who had sent them, as though six strangers off the mountain road were a thing that happened often enough not to need remarking on; and it was only the next morning, when Catrìona asked at the well where the steersman lived, that the woman drawing water looked at her a long moment before she answered, in the way of someone deciding how much a stranger deserved to be told.

## II. Of the Steersman of Cuan ruadh

The man they were sent to was called Seumas Reultach. It was a by-name the town had settled on him so long ago that no one now living had heard the name his mother gave him. He was old, older than any of them had reckoned an old man could be and still climb a cliff path without a staff, and he received them at his own door with no surprise at all, as though six strangers from the far side of the island turned up asking to be taught the stars once in every generation, which, it came out over the following days, was very nearly true: his own grandmother had taught two men from the north coast, long before any of them were born, who had gone home and, so far as Seumas knew, taught no one.

"You'll have to come at night," he told them, "for the stars aren't out by day, whatever else you may have heard," and it was the only joke Catrìona ever heard him make in all the months that followed.

They came at night, every clear one, up a path above the town to a headland where the wind stripped every sound but its own, and Seumas Reultach, wrapped in a sealskin that had been his father's, taught them to stand still and look up until the sky stopped being a scatter of light and became a shape.

The first night he taught them nothing at all. He walked them up the path in the last of the dusk, sat them down in a half-ring on the cold grass with their backs to the lights of the town, and told them to be silent and to look up, and for the better part of two hours nobody spoke and nothing was named. The rope-maker's son grew restless and was told, once, without heat, to be still; the lean woman from Ros bheag did not move at all. When at last Seumas rose and said that was enough for one night and led them back down, the Cuan shean man asked him, aggrieved, what they had learned.

"You have learned that it takes a while," said Seumas, "before a man stops seeing points of light and starts seeing a sky. Come back tomorrow if it's clear."

He began, on the second night, with what he called the wheel: how the whole sky turned, slow as a millstone, about a fixed point low over the northern sea that never moved though everything else did, and how a man who found that point and kept it always at his shoulder, whichever way the boat's head lay, need never be lost in the dark. The star that stood nearest it, low and steady above the water on a clear night, he named to them: Reul na Stiùire. From three others set in a line he showed them how to find it, so that on a cloudy night, if even one showed through a gap, a man who knew the shapes could still find his star by where the others would have stood.

Catrìona had thought, before that first night, that she already knew the sky a little, from six years of putting to sea before dawn. She learned, on the headland above Cuan ruadh, that she had known nothing: not one true name, not one bearing, not the difference between a star that held its place the whole night through and one that only seemed to, low near the water, and set within the hour.

Seumas taught them the whole turning year of the sky as a farmer taught a son the turning year of the fields: which stars stood over the stern at Samhnas and which at Teasach, how the wheel itself shifted its whole aspect between the black months and the bright, so that a man steering the same course by the same star in winter and in summer must know to look for it in a different quarter of the sky or lose his heading entirely. He taught them to read the smell of the dark, the particular cold that came before a change of wind, the look of the water under starlight when a swell was building that the eye alone, in daylight, would have missed. Most of it he gave them only as it was given him, mouth to ear, night after night, with nothing written, because there was nothing to write it on that would survive a sea crossing and because, he said once, a thing carried in the hand is more easily lost than a thing carried in the head.

The lessons did not always go easily. There were nights of cloud when nothing could be taught at all and the six sat idle in the byre while the rope-maker's son grumbled that they had come a hundred miles to learn nothing; there was a week in the first winter when the lean woman from Ros bheag fell sick of a fever off the crossing and Seumas himself came down from his house each evening to sit by her, not to teach, only to sit, until she was well; and there was a night, deep in that same winter, when one of the Ceann mhòr brothers, cold and homesick and tired of being corrected, said aloud on the headland that a man could learn to fish by starlight for twenty years on the west coast and never need a word of any of this, and that they had been sent on a fool's errand by a custodian with too much silver and not enough sense. Seumas let him finish. Then he asked him, quietly, how he meant to find his way home across open water once the last headland of Dia-thìr had sunk below the sea behind him, and the man had no answer, and came back to the headland every clear night after that without being asked again.

Catrìona asked more questions than the rest of them together, and it was to her, more than to any of the others, that Seumas began after the first winter to speak of things beyond what he set out each night to teach: the names his own teacher had given the stars, some of them older, he thought, than the town; a telling of steersmen from an age before Rìghrean na Cloiche who were said to have gone west of the sunset and not come back, which he would neither say he believed nor quite say he did not; and once, on a night of no cloud when the wheel stood very clear, the plain admission that no one now at Cuan ruadh, himself least of all, any longer sailed by night as their grandfathers had, because there was nowhere left on that coast that the daylight coasting trade could not reach before dark, and the knowledge had gone on being taught, generation after generation, to fewer and fewer, for the sake of the teaching and not because anyone still needed it. "Until now," he said, and looked at her, and said nothing more that night.

In the second winter Fearchar's rider came again, with word that the ships were being laid down in earnest now and asking whether any part of the teaching might be set down, that it should not all ride on six heads and the chance of the sea. Seumas thought about it three days. Then he sent for a scraped hide and an awl, and set his own granddaughter, whose hand was steadier than his own had ever been, to cutting the marks as he named them to her by the fire: the wheel, Reul na Stiùire and the three that found it, and the four turning marks of the year. Catrìona watched the girl's awl go into the hide, stroke by careful stroke, and thought it the strangest thing she had yet seen at Cuan ruadh, stranger than the deep-keeled boats or the wheel of the sky, that a thing which had lived only in old men's mouths for as long as anyone could tell should be made, in one winter evening, to hold still.

When it was done, and no more, the Cuan shean man asked why not the rest of it, the swell-reading and the wind-smell and the hundred small signs that had taken two winters to teach. Seumas Reultach looked at him a long while and said that some things a hide could hold and some things only a life could, and that he had given them the first kind and meant to go on giving them the second kind as long as he had breath, and after that it would go the way such things went.

He had less breath than any of them knew. In the third spring, in the moon of Faolach, in the wolf-storms, he took to his bed with a cough that would not leave him, and for a fortnight the six of them took it in turn to sit with him, for there was little else by then to teach and much, Catrìona thought, that they still owed him. He rallied enough, on the first clear night after the fortnight's rain broke, to insist on the cliff path once more, leaning on two of them going up and refusing, at the top, to be helped to sit. He named the wheel to them one last time, as though they might have forgotten it, and fell silent, and they thought he had only gone quiet the way he sometimes did. When the others thought at last that he had gone in out of the cold as he always did, he had not. They found him at the top of the cliff path in the morning, sitting with his back against the stone he always leaned on, his sealskin drawn close, his face turned up to where the wheel had gone round while he sat there and left Reul na Stiùire exactly where it always was.

They buried him at Cuan ruadh, among his own people, with the whole town come down to the graveside though none of the six had ever seen more than a handful of its people at once before; and his granddaughter gave the hide with its marks into Catrìona's keeping, saying only that her grandfather had meant it to go west, and that she herself could read it as well as any of them and had no need to keep it. Catrìona said afterward that of all the things she had been taught that winter the truest was the one nobody had set out to teach her: that a man could hold a whole sky in his head and pass almost none of it on, and that whatever they carried west out of Cuan ruadh, hide and memory both, it would always be less than what he had known.

## III. Of the First Trial and the Star Named on the Quay

They went home in the moon of Faolach still, still six, for Seumas had never been one of them to lose; over the mountain country by the same track, with the same wind, carrying nothing on the outward road that they had not carried in, and everything that mattered on the road back in their own heads, and the hide, wrapped against the wet in a fold of the lean woman's cloak because she alone among them thought to ask for the driest place to carry it.

At Ros àrsaidh, where the coast lay open enough for a night's sailing without much risk of the rocks, they held the first trial that summer, and half the town came down to the strand to see it fail. Two boats went out after dark: one steered the old way, close along the shore with a man forward calling the water at every length, lanterns swinging at bow and stern so the watchers on the cliff could follow her the whole night; and one by Catrìona alone, with two of the Ros àrsaidh men to work the sail and say nothing, out past the headland into open water and every lantern doused, with nothing to go by but Reul na Stiùire held at her shoulder as Seumas had taught her, and the smell of the wind, and the set of the swell under the keel. For the first hour, she said afterward, she was as frightened as either of the men with her, listening for the sound of a wave breaking on rock that she could not see and trusting, against everything her years on that coast had taught her, that the star at her shoulder and not the black loom of the land was the thing to steer by. Then the fear went, the way it had gone on the headland above Cuan ruadh once she had stopped listening to what she thought she knew and started listening to what she had been taught, and the rest of the night she held her course as easily as she had ever held one along a shore she could see.

She brought her boat back before the other one, and put it exactly where she had said she would the evening before, at first light, on the tide she had named; and the two men who had gone with her, sick with fear the whole night through by their own later admission, would not say a word against it afterward, though one of them would not go out with her by night again for a year.

Word of the trial went along the coast faster than Catrìona could follow it herself, and by the next year she had more asking to learn from her than she and the other five together could teach, and no time to teach them, for the harbour-house was calling in the households of the roll that spring, and every one of the six pilots had entered long since, and was wanted.

She reached Seann Skell in the moon of Sìolach, late, having stopped a fortnight at Ros bheag to see her mother, who was old and would not be going, and to leave with her what little silver she had, and to say the kind of goodbye that neither of them named for what it was. The harbour road into Seann Skell was busier than she had ever known it, carts and barrows and whole families afoot with what they could carry, and the town itself, when she came down into it at last, smelled of pitch and sawdust and woodsmoke in a way it never had in her girlhood, so that for a moment, tired from the road, she hardly knew it. When she came down at last to the harbour front she found the boards already crowded and the town talking of nothing else: the households of the roll had met, it was said, and chosen who should lead them, and it was done, though nobody she asked could say quite how, only that it was Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's own sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh of Taigh na Fèithe, and that the two of them were even now down at the new stones of the west quay looking over the first hulls.

She found them there in the evening light, the queen's sister in a plain grey cloak with the wind pulling at it, and the custodian beside her with his hands behind his back, the two of them standing where the stonework was still raw and pale and the tide had not yet worn it, looking at a hull that stood half-ribbed on its frame like the bones of something not yet grown its skin. Along the strand behind them the town went on with its evening as though nothing had changed in it at all, boats coming in, nets spread to dry, a woman calling a child in to supper; and Catrìona thought, standing a little apart with her pack still on her shoulder and the hide from Cuan ruadh wrapped inside it, how strange it was that a choosing which the whole harbour was talking of should have left the harbour looking exactly as it always had.

"You're the one who went east," said Mòrag, before Catrìona had said who she was.

"I am."

"And you came back knowing the stars."

"I came back knowing some of them. There was more to know than any six of us could carry."

Mòrag looked at her a moment, the way, Catrìona thought afterward, a woman looks at a thing she has been waiting to be given without knowing its shape beforehand. "I have a hull," she said. "An Ròn Glas. She'll carry my own household and I don't yet know how many more, and she'll need someone at the steering oar who can hold a course the night the coast goes out of sight for good, because after that there'll be nothing else to hold it by. Will you be her pilot?"

Fearchar said nothing, but he was watching Catrìona's face as if the answer mattered to him nearly as much as it did to Mòrag, and afterward, when it was too late to ask him, she wondered whether it was because he already knew, better than anyone else on that quay, how few of them there would ever be who could do what she could do. He had, she remembered later, counted households on a copied roll and found them fewer than he wished; he was a man used to finding that a thing the venture needed came in short measure, and used to taking what there was of it without complaint.

"I will," said Catrìona, and found, saying it, that she had known her own answer since the headland above Cuan ruadh and had only been waiting, without knowing it, for someone to ask her the question in words.

Mòrag nodded, once, as though a thing long uncertain had at last been set down in its right place, and turned back to the hull. But before she did, Catrìona, not quite knowing why she said it, lifted a hand toward the darkening sky over the river mouth, where the first stars were beginning to show through the last of the light, and found the one she wanted without having to search for it, as she no longer had to search for anything in that part of the sky.

"That one," she said. "Low, over the water. That's the one I'll be steering by, my lady, the night the coast goes."

Mòrag looked where she pointed, and said nothing for a while, and the light went on failing over the river, and the star Catrìona had named stood where it always stood, the one point in the whole turning sky that never moved.

# Chapter Seven: Of the Handful for the New Hearth

*LE 19 – 31*

> *Dòrlach airson an teallaich ùir,*
> *is an seann teallach fhathast blàth.*
> A handful for the new hearth,
> and the old hearth still warm.
>
> — a couplet written beside the ruling in Leabhar a' Chùraim

## I. Of the Boy Given to the Vein-House

Donnchadh mac Thormoid was nine years old when his father walked him up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe and left him there, the way a man leaves a lamb with a shepherd he trusts and does not look back at, for looking back is thought to unsettle the lamb. It was the custom, by then, to swear a boy or a girl to the vein's service for seven years if the household could spare the hands and Taigh na Fèithe would have them, the same manner in which the wrights of the strand at Seann Skell had begun to swear their own apprentices; and Tormod, who cut turf for three households on the moor above Muileann dhearg and had five children and not much land, thought his youngest son's hands better spent at a desk than on a spade. He said as much to the boy on the road up, not unkindly. Donnchadh remembered the words for the rest of his life, though he came in time to doubt his father had meant them as a kindness at all, only as the truth, plainly given, the way a poor man gives a true thing to a child because he has nothing softer to give.

Taigh na Fèithe stood black on its hill above the diggings, built of the same dark stone the galleries were cut from, so that from a distance it seemed less built than grown, a knuckle of the mountain that had learned to keep a roof. Within, it smelled of tallow and cold stone and, faintly, always, of the coal underneath, a smell Donnchadh never afterward could smell anywhere else without seeing the low black door of the custody-room and the shelf where the book was kept. He was set to sweeping at first, and to carrying water for the elder clerks, and only after the better part of a year to holding a stylus at all, and then only to copy, letter after letter, the names already written by better hands, until his own hand no longer shook doing it.

The master of Taigh na Fèithe in those years was Eòghann mac Mhuirich, an old man even then, stooped from sixty years bent over Leabhar a' Chùraim, who had written the figure of the counted households in the third year after the word of the far shore and, as the tale went among the clerks, had not looked up from the page for the length of a hundred breaths after he wrote it. He kept Donnchadh at his own elbow more than the other boys, not, Donnchadh came to think, because he showed any particular gift, but because Eòghann liked a quiet hand nearby and Donnchadh had learned early not to talk while a man was thinking.

It was in his first winter at Taigh na Fèithe, before he had held the stylus at all, that Donnchadh saw Fearchar mac Ruairidh come up the hill on a grey horse with mud to its hocks, and heard, crouched by the door with an armful of kindling he had no reason to be slow about carrying in, the middle of a trouble that had already run four years and would take two more to settle and that he would, in the end, be given the pen to close.

## II. Of the Petition

Fearchar mac Ruairidh had gone, by then, from a custodian who sat at Taigh na Fèithe board twice a season to a man who was hardly ever off the road: down to Seann Skell to see the boards, out to the shire seats to hear how the levy of sail-cloth was going, up again to Taigh na Fèithe with word of what the harbour needed and what the households of the roll had asked of him, though none of them, strictly, had any right to ask him anything at all, the roll being a thing of household and hearth and not of office. He had taken the asking on himself, the clerks said, the way a man takes on a debt nobody has billed him for, because somebody had to carry it and he found himself standing nearest when it fell.

What he wanted, that first day and for six years after, was simple to say and hard, it turned out, to grant. The departing would go with what they could carry on their backs and in their hulls: tools, seed, cloth, the small worth of a household uprooted. They would not go with fire already in their hands, unless the island gave it to them, and there was only one fire on the island that was not any man's own to give: the coal of the vein, which Leabhar a' Chùraim measured out hearth by hearth under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig and had never, in all the years since Fionnlagh Dall filled the cup, measured out to anything that was not a hearth standing still on Dia-thìr.

"Let each hull that is fit to sail carry a measure," Fearchar said, the first time Donnchadh heard him say it, standing in the yard with his hat still in his hand and rain running off his shoulders, to Eòghann and two of the elder custodians who had come out to hear him because it was raining too hard to make him wait outside. "One measure. Sealed, counted, entered in the book like any other hearth's. I ask for no more than Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig already gives a household that stays."

"Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measures a hearth," said one of the custodians, a heavy man named Cailean whom Donnchadh came later to know as a hard voice at every board and a soft one at every sickbed, "not a keel. A hearth stands where it stood. It does not go anywhere. What you are asking, Fearchar, though you dress it kindly, is that the vein answer for a fire it will never see burn and never see go cold, on the far side of I know not what water, for I know not how long. This is a new law, and none of us here has the right to make one."

"Then I ask you to make one," said Fearchar, "or else to tell the households of the roll plainly, before they go, that the coal they have held the right to since their grandmothers' grandmothers will end, for them, the day they step aboard. I would rather they heard it now, from you, than found it out cold, three weeks past the mist."

Nobody answered him that day. Eòghann sent him down the hill with a cup of broth against the rain and a promise that the matter would be put to the board at the next burning, which was Taigh na Fèithe's way, Donnchadh learned, of saying that a thing was too large to be settled standing up in a wet yard.

## III. Of the Winter Burning

It was not settled at the next burning, nor the one after. Donnchadh grew a hand's width and lost two milk teeth and buried his mother's brother, who died of a fever that went round the coal-breakers' cots below the hill, in the years Taigh na Fèithe argued Fearchar's petition back and forth across its own board without coming any nearer an answer than it had been the day he stood dripping in the yard. He came to know the shape of the argument the way he knew the shape of the hill from his window: Cailean and two or three others holding that the coal had never crossed water and never should, that a measure sealed and sent out of sight of Taigh na Fèithe was a measure Leabhar a' Chùraim could no longer answer for, gone from Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's keeping into nobody's; and Fearchar, with a smaller knot of custodians who had come round to him one by one, holding that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measured hearths because hearths were what the island had ever had need of measuring, and that a hearth crossing open water was still a hearth, only a stranger one, and deserved no less than any other.

The winter burning of the year Donnchadh turned eleven was the one Taigh na Fèithe remembered afterward, because it was the one at which the argument, having worn itself thin over six years, finally wore through. Donnchadh was eleven that winter, old enough to be let sit at the back of the hall with the other clerks' boys while the custodians spoke, though not old enough to be asked his own mind on anything, and he remembered the hall by its cold more than by anything said in it for the first hour: a long low room cut into the hill, lit by rush-lights that guttered whenever the door opened, with the custodians ranged along both sides of the board and Leabhar a' Chùraim lying closed at its head, as it always lay when a matter touched what was written in it.

Cailean spoke longest, and hardest. "We are not asked to give a handful of coal," he said, near the end of it, when his voice had gone rough with two hours of being answered. "We are asked to say that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig follows a household wherever a household chooses to go, though it go past the edge of everything Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was ever made to answer for. If we say it once, for a ship, we may be asked to say it again, for I do not know what, and I would have us think three times before we hand away the one thing on this island that has never once been given past its own bounds."

"And if we do not say it," Fearchar answered him, quiet now himself, all the road-weary force gone out of his voice and something flatter and more tired left in its place, "then I will stand on the west quay the day the fleet goes out, and I will watch fires kindled on those decks with wood alone, and I will know, better than any man in this hall, which households among them held the right to the coal their whole lives and go without it now for the first time, because we would not answer a small thing simply because it frightened us to answer it. I have counted those households, Cailean, with my own hand. Better to answer for a measure of coal gone where none of us can follow it than answer to them, one day, for why we let them go cold out of pride in Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, that was never made to be proud of anything."

There was a silence after that which Donnchadh remembered as longer than it can truly have been, the kind of silence in which a room decides something without any one voice being heard to decide it. Eòghann, who had said almost nothing the whole evening, put both hands flat on the board at last and said that he would have Leabhar a' Chùraim opened, and the question put to writing, and that they would vote it as they voted any other matter that had been talked enough. They voted before the rush-lights burned out. Donnchadh did not, at eleven, understand every word of the ruling as it was first spoken aloud, but he understood, from the way the hall emptied afterward, quiet and a little spent, like a house after a birth that has gone on too long and come out well at the last, that something had been decided that would outlast the argument that made it.

## IV. Of the Clean Copy

The ruling was simple enough, once it was written plain, though it had taken six winters and one long night to arrive at: each hull that should be found fit to sail might carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household might burn in a season under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, entered in Leabhar a' Chùraim as any hearth's measure was entered, and sealed by Taigh na Fèithe's own mark so that no man could say, after, that it had been taken rather than given. It answered for no hearth once it was gone past the mist, and promised no more fire after that one measure than the household would have found in its own grate at home in a single ordinary winter: exactly the size of thing Leabhar a' Chùraim had always measured, Donnchadh thought later, and no bigger. Fearchar had asked for a hearth's worth and been given, in the end, precisely that, dressed up in six years of argument to make it look larger than it was.

He was fifteen, and six years at the desk, when Eòghann called him at last to make the fair copy; the ruling had lain four years in rough marks, for the master would let no entry into Leabhar a' Chùraim in a hand he did not trust. His hand was not the finest in Taigh na Fèithe; the ruling had been argued and voted and set down in rough marks by an old scribe's cramped fingers, and somebody young enough to sit a whole day without his back giving out was wanted to render it clean for the book that would stand, unaltered, for as long as Taigh na Fèithe kept records at all. It was his first entry in Leabhar a' Chùraim proper, and he remembered every line of it afterward the way another man remembers his first field ploughed alone.

He copied it letter for letter, the sealed measure, the single household's season, Taigh na Fèithe's mark; and when he had finished, and sanded the page, and sat back to let the ink set, he noticed a thing that nobody in the hall, arguing six winters over whether the coal might go at all, had thought to argue over: that the ruling, in giving the coal, gave nothing else with it. Every other entry he had copied that year, weddings recorded for the dowry-right, deaths recorded for the inheritance of a hearth, opened or closed with some small word of Taigh na Fèithe's own, a blessing on the hearth, a wish for its long burning, the kind of thing a scribe wrote as much from habit as from instruction. This entry had none of it. It measured the coal and said nothing over it. Donnchadh sat a long while with his sanded page before him, deciding whether that was an oversight to be mended or a thing the custodians had meant, without saying so aloud, and in the end he copied it exactly as it had been given him, with no blessing added, because it was not his place to add one, and because, he thought, turning it over afterward on the walk back to his own cot, perhaps a hall that could not agree for six winters whether to give the coal at all had simply had no blessing left in it to spare.

## V. Of the Measures Sealed

The measures themselves were made the year after: not counted out against any tally of hulls, for nobody at Taigh na Fèithe yet knew, or claimed to know, how many hulls the strand at Seann Skell would in the end put in the water, but sealed as they were asked for, each one against the words *for each hull that shall be ready*, a phrase Donnchadh had copied into the ruling himself and had not, until he watched the first measures made, understood the weight of. It meant that Taigh na Fèithe had bound itself to a number it could not know in advance, open-ended as a debt with no term set on it, and that every measure sealed that year and the years after would go down the coal-road to Seann Skell without any man at Taigh na Fèithe ever adding up how many had gone, because the ruling had never asked for a count, only for readiness.

He watched the first of them sealed on a grey morning in the moon of Dubhlas, in the low room off the custody-hall where Taigh na Fèithe kept its scales: a store-clerk weighing out the coal against the same stone weights used for any household's handful, no more careful and no less, and Eòghann himself pressing the mark into the wax while Fearchar stood by, hat again in hand, saying nothing at all, as though he had used up every word he had on the matter in six years of asking and had only silence left to spend on seeing it done.

## VI. Of the Masons Sent West

The queen sent no household of her own to the roll, then or ever, but some years after the first measures were sealed, when the hulls on the strand had grown too deep for the old staging, she lent the harbour's trade something Taigh na Fèithe could not give it: hands. A gang of masons out of the capital, under a man named Ailean mac Nèill, a broad, sun-browned mason not yet thirty who had cut his teeth dressing stone for An Cnoc Ruadh's own walls, came down the river road to Seann Skell that spring with wagons of squared stone and the queen's word that they were sent for the harbour's trade and for no other reason the rider would name. It was said afterward, at Taigh na Fèithe as everywhere else, that Beathag had sent them for the fleet and called it trade because trade was a thing a queen might send masons for without anyone asking whom she had sent them to help; but it was also said, by those who had watched her rule since her mother's day, that she had never once, in more than thirty years on An Talla Dearg's high seat, called a thing by any name but the truest one she could give it without breaking her own word, and that if she called it trade, then trade, in some fashion known best to herself, was what she believed it to be.

Ailean's gang lengthened the west quay through that summer and the next, dressed stone laid course on course where the old timber staging had done duty since before anyone living could remember, so that the deep hulls building on the strand above might one day lie alongside at low water without grounding their new keels on the mud the old quay had never needed to clear. It was hard, wet work, the tide taking back at every ebb what the masons had set at every flood, and Ailean, the harbour-house's own scribe Calum wrote that year in a note that came up with the coal-tallies and that Donnchadh, still a boy at his desk, read twice for the pleasure of a line written plain, "curses the sea in three tongues and lays stone against it anyway, which is more than most men do against anything."

## VII. Of the Queen on the New Stones

It is told that Beathag herself rode down to Seann Skell in the second summer of the quay's building, the only time in all the years of the fleet's making that she is known to have gone to see it with her own eyes, though her sister's household had been on the roll more than twenty years by then and the hulls as long abuilding on the same strand. She rode the twenty-four miles in a day, with a small following and no herald sent ahead to have the town made ready for her, and stood a while on the new-laid stone in the evening light, watching the tide come in against courses that had not yet worn smooth, while Ailean's men, who had not been told a queen was coming and would not have known her by sight if a rider had not named her quietly among them, went on laying stone within a few yards of her as though she were any woman come down to watch the work.

Mòrag came to her there, on the stones, the two sisters standing together where the masonry was still raw and pale and the tide had not yet worn it, and it is told that they spoke a while of nothing that mattered: of a horse Mòrag had lately sold, of a leak in a roof at Inis àrsaidh that had taken three tries to mend, of the queen's son, grown too tall for the low doors of An Talla Dearg. Neither sister spoke, that evening, of the coal, or the roll, or the half-built hulls standing along the strand behind them; it was, the harbour-house's own note of that day says, as though each had decided, without a word passing between them to decide it, that an evening might be spent as an evening and not as a leave-taking, though it is also told that when the queen rode home the next morning she looked back once, from the top of the harbour road, at the stones and the half-built hulls and her sister standing among them, and did not look back a second time.

Donnchadh never saw that evening; Taigh na Fèithe's business kept him on the hill that whole summer, sealing measures against tallies that came up from Seann Skell in a hand he did not know. But the note of it came to him with the coal-figures, as most news of the coast did, folded into the same rider's pouch as a tally of barrels and a line about the weather, and he copied the line about the queen's visit into Leabhar a' Chùraim's own margin, where such things were sometimes kept though they answered to no ruling and no law, because it seemed to him, turning fifteen that year and beginning to understand that not every true thing needed a ruling to be worth the keeping, a fact Taigh na Fèithe ought not to let go unwritten.

## VIII. Of the Death of Uilleam mac Iain

In the last days of that same year, in the moon of Damhrach, word came up the coal-road that the queen's consort, Uilleam mac Iain, was dead: a man who had never sat at Taigh na Fèithe's board nor asked it for anything in his life, kind, it was said, and fond of hounds, who had given Beathag her son and had stood, by every account Donnchadh ever heard, quietly behind her through more than thirty years of a crown that was never his own to wear. He had been ill through the summer, the rider said, and had not mended.

The queen kept the funeral small: no great muster of the shires, no feast that would have cost the granaries a season's worth of grain in a year the harvest had been thin, only An Talla Dearg's own household and the few custodian heads whose presence courtesy required, gathered a single day at Cathair dhearg and gone home again before the week was out. It was remarked on, at Taigh na Fèithe as everywhere the tidings travelled, that a queen who had refused to send her own sister anywhere and refused, with the same breath, to keep her back, should bury her own husband as quietly as a crofter buries a wife: no more show made of her grief than Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig made of a hearth's handful. Eòghann, who was by then very old and had himself less than a year left to him, said only, when the tidings reached Taigh na Fèithe's board, that a queen who measured everything else in her kingdom by what it truly was and not by what it might be dressed to look, would hardly begin dressing up her own sorrow at the one moment in her life least suited to the dressing.

## IX. Of the Last Stone and the Sealing by Lamplight

Ailean mac Nèill's gang set the last stone of the lengthened quay in the following spring, a plain block no larger than any other in the whole course, laid at the seaward end where the new masonry met the old timber staging and the two were bound together with an iron cramp that Ailean himself drove home, the harbour-house's note says, with three blows and no more, as though he grudged the stone a fourth. There was no ceremony made of it that the tellings remember: the tide came in over it that evening exactly as it had come in over every stone before it, and a boy of the strand, running the new-laid course end to end because a boy will always run the length of a new thing before an adult thinks to stop him, was the only soul on the whole quay who marked, aloud, that it was finished.

On the same evening, though neither of them ever knew the other's hour, Donnchadh sealed a measure of coal by lamplight in the low room off the custody-hall at Taigh na Fèithe, alone but for the store-clerk who weighed the coal against the stone weights, pressing Taigh na Fèithe's mark into the wax with a hand that no longer shook at all, sixteen years old and seven years come from a nine-year-old led up a hill by a father who had not looked back. He had by then sealed a good many measures and copied a good many entries, and this one, so far as he knew, differed from the last only in the number written against it in the book; but he found himself, that evening, holding the lamp a moment longer than the sealing needed, over a page that gave, as every page like it had given since his own fair copy first set the words down plain, a handful of coal and no blessing, to a hearth not yet built, on a shore no one at Taigh na Fèithe had ever seen and no one there, by then, much expected to.

# Chapter Eight: Of the Grain Strife and the Forty-One Barges

*LE 37 – 39*

## I. Of the Lean Harvest

Tormod mac Coinnich had kept the granaries at Àth shean for eleven years before the harvest failed under him, and in all that time he had let no petitioner leave the store-house door without a plain answer, yes or no, said to his face. It was the only pride he owned to. He was not a clever man, by his own reckoning, and he had never once been asked to sit at An Talla Dearg's board; but he could tell to the bushel what a granary held, and he had buried, as a boy, two brothers and a sister in a year when the barley failed and the reeve of that day had answered every petitioner with a smile and no grain, and he had never in his life forgotten the smell of the empty store-house in that spring, which was of nothing at all, of swept stone and mouse-droppings and cold.

He kept the memory of that spring the way another man might keep a scar: not spoken of, not forgotten, touched now and again in the dark to be sure it was still there. He had been seven years old that year. The store-house at Àth shean, he remembered, stood open and swept and empty, while the reeve of that day, a smiling man named Uisdean whom the shire had trusted for twenty years and trusted no more after, told petitioner after petitioner that there would be grain enough by the new moon, and the new moon came and went with no grain in it. He remembered his mother boiling the last of the seed-barley rather than let it go to the following year's planting, because a planting a family does not live to see does a family no good; and he remembered, most of all, the particular nothing-smell of an empty granary in a hungry season, swept stone and old dust and a cold that seemed to come up out of the bare floor, which he had gone back to smell, deliberately, more than once in the years since, on ordinary days when the stores stood full, as a man touches an old wound to be certain it has healed and to remember, at the same time, exactly how it had felt when it had not.
