In the autumn of LE 37 the barley came in thin across the shires south of the mountain, the fourth-poorest harvest of Tormod's eleven years by his own tally-sticks. The granaries at Àth shean, well kept, would carry the country through to the green without much pinching, so long as nothing else was asked of them. Something else was asked of them.

The word came down from Cathair dhearg in the moon of Damhrach, carried by a rider who had ridden two days and slept badly: the fleet at Seann Skell must be fed for its crossing, and the grain for it would come, in whatever measure the council settled on, out of the south shires' stores, because the south shires' stores were the fullest on the island and the nearest to the rivers that ran to the coast. Tormod heard it read out at his own door and said nothing to the rider beyond thanking him for his trouble. That night he sat a long while at his own table with the tally-sticks laid out in their rows, running his thumb along the notches as though he might read something in them beyond what was cut there, and his wife watched him and did not ask what he was thinking, because she had been married to him twenty years and knew.

## II. Of the Barred Doors

The council at An Talla Dearg divided on the question through that whole dark season, and divided, by every account that ever reached Àth shean, along no line a plain man could follow. Some of the queen's own councillors held that a household could not be sent out onto open water without bread enough to see it through the crossing, whatever that crossing cost the island behind it; others held that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measured a hearth and had never measured a granary, and that grain given to the departed was grain the island's own children would not eat the following spring. The queen herself, it was said, sat through the sessions with her hands folded and gave no opinion that any rider carried south, which was, by then, well known to be her custom in matters she had not yet decided to settle by her own word alone.

What was decided, and by whom, and on what day, Tormod mac Coinnich never learned, then or after. He only knew that no ruling came, week on week, while the rivers ran high with the autumn rain and the barges that would have carried grain to the coast sat idle at their moorings, and the petitioners for the fleet's stores began to come to his own door at Àth shean asking for grain on the strength of a council that had, so far as he could tell, not yet spoken.

He turned the first of them away with a plain no, as was his custom, and thought that would be the end of it. It was not. Within the week a second petitioner came, with a sealed leaf from a captain of one of the hulls that Tormod could not read and did not trust, and after him a third, and by the turn of the moon there were men at his gate most mornings, some civil and some not, asking for measures of barley on no authority he could name. He remembered the reeve who had smiled at his mother with an empty store-house behind him, and on a morning in early Samhnas, with no ruling yet come from the capital and the granaries at Àth shean the last full ones south of the mountain, Tormod mac Coinnich barred the store-house doors himself, set a watch of four men on them day and night, and told the next petitioner, and every one after, that the grain would move when the council's own seal came down and not a day before.

It was not a popular thing to have done. A captain's steward, a broad man with a fleet's own urgency in him and none of a shire's patience, climbed the granary steps on the third day of the bar and asked Tormod straight out whether he meant to let households starve at sea for the sake of his own tallies.

"I mean to let no one starve, here or at sea," Tormod told him, "which is why the grain stays counted and under a roof until I am told, by someone whose word I can write down, how much of it is to go and where. I have watched a granary opened on a smiling man's word before. I will not watch it again."

"You'll answer for this at An Talla Dearg."

"I have answered for worse to worse men than sit there," Tormod said, which was not, strictly, true, but the steward did not know that, and went away down the steps red in the face, to the plain satisfaction of the watch, who told the tale in the town that evening with more relish than the moment had held.

Worse than the steward, by far, were the quiet ones. A woman of the south shires came one grey morning with a basket over her arm as though she meant only an ordinary errand, and asked Tormod, in a voice that never once rose, whether her own son's household, entered on the roll and waiting at Seann Skell with two small children, would go hungry on the crossing for Tormod mac Coinnich's stubbornness. He gave her the same answer he gave every petitioner, that the grain would move when the council's seal came and not before, and she heard him out, and thanked him with more courtesy than the steward had shown, and went away down the road with her empty basket still on her arm; and it was she, and not the steward, whom Tormod thought of on the cold watches of that winter, turning her quiet voice over in his mind at an hour when there was no one to answer it and nothing to be done but stand by a barred door and wait for a word that did not come.

The watch stood through Samhnas and Dubhlas and on through the black months after, four men at the granary doors in every weather, relieved every third day, eating from the same stores they guarded because Tormod would not have it said that his own watch went hungry while it kept a full store shut. He walked the round with them himself most nights, more from restlessness than from any doubt of the men he had set there, and came to know the sound the wind made off the river against the granary's north gable better than he knew, by then, his own wife's step on the stair.

Riders came from the capital twice that he counted, once with a leaf that named no figure and satisfied no one, once with nothing written at all, only a spoken word that the matter was still before the council. He read the leaf by lamplight at his own table and set it aside and did not sleep well that night. His own doing gave him no trouble; what kept him awake was a slower doubt, that no one above him at all knew what should be done, and a granary reeve who has begun to think that has nothing left to stand on but his own tally-sticks and his own memory of an empty store-house, which is a narrow thing to build a winter's stand on.

He was not a man given to speech, and he made none to the watch beyond the ordinary business of the round; but on one bitter night near the turn of the year, with the four of them huddled under the granary eave out of a sleet that had not let up since dusk, the youngest of them, a lad not yet twenty who had taken the watch mostly for the extra measure of barley it earned his own mother's house, asked him outright whether he thought the grain would ever move at all, or whether they would stand there the rest of their lives guarding a door nobody meant to open.

"It will move," Tormod said, "when someone above me stops being afraid of his own decision and puts his name to one." And then, because the boy looked so cold and so young standing there in the sleet, he added, more gently than he had said anything to anyone that whole hard season, "It is not your fear to carry, lad. Stand your watch and go home to your mother when it's done, and leave the rest to older backs than yours."

The boy said nothing more that night, but he told it afterward, many years on, as the truest thing he had ever heard said of that whole strange winter, and the only comfort anyone had offered him in the whole of it.

## III. Of the Doors Reopened

One morning in early Sìolach, with the frost still on the ground and the year's first green not yet showing along the ditches, a single rider came down to Àth shean with no leaf at all, only a word for Tormod's own ear: that the grain might move, at such a measure as the council had fixed, and that the reeve of the granaries was thanked for his care of them. Nothing was said of how the matter had been settled, nor by whom, nor why that morning and not another; the rider, when Tormod asked him plainly, said only that he had been sent to say what he had said, and no more, and Tormod, who had asked harder men harder questions all that winter and got no better answer from any of them, let it go.

He took the bar down from the store-house doors with his own hands, though it was work for two men, and stood in the open doorway a while in the cold with the granary dark and full behind him, before he called the watch off and told the waiting carters they might load. The rider who had brought the word lingered long enough to take a cup of small ale against the cold of the road ahead of him, and Tormod, pouring it himself, asked once more, plainly, whether the rider truly knew no more of the matter than he had said.

"I know less than you think, reeve," the rider told him, not unkindly. "I was given a word to carry and a road to carry it on. What was said at An Talla Dearg to make that word, I was not in the room to hear, and if I had been, I doubt I'd have understood the half of it. They argue there the way rivers argue with their own banks, all winter, and then one morning the ice goes out and no one can say which thaw broke it." He finished the ale, thanked the reeve for it, and rode on north before the light failed, and Tormod never afterward learned so much as his name.

He felt, standing in the doorway once the rider had gone, less like a man vindicated than like a man who has held his breath a long time and is only now allowed to let it out, with no one troubling to say whether he had held it for anything at all.

No one asked him back to his office that spring. A new reeve was named to the granaries at Àth shean before the barley was in the ground again, a younger man with better friends at the capital, and Tormod mac Coinnich, who had kept the stores of the south shires for eleven years and shut them for the better part of one hard winter on his own reckoning and no one else's, packed what was his own out of the reeve's house and walked home to the farm his father had left him, a morning's walk south of the town. He worked it the rest of his life without complaint, and without once, so far as anyone who knew him ever heard, saying a word against the council that had left him to stand a winter's watch alone and never told him why.

## IV. Of the Forty-One Barges

The barges went down that spring the way grain had always gone from the south shires to the capital, on the broad slow water of Abhainn dhomhain, low in the water and heavy, poled and towed by turns where the current ran against them, each one carrying what forty households might not eat in a season laid up against the crossing of households that would eat none of it on the island again.

On Drochaid Cathair dhearg a woman named Mairead nic Iain kept the tally that spring, as she had kept it most springs of her working life, cutting a notch in a fresh hazel stick for every laden hull that passed beneath the bridge going down toward the sea. It was not thought a hard office, nor a great one; she sat on the parapet with her legs over the water in fine weather and under the lee of the bridge-house in foul, and she had counted salmon boats and wool barges and the ordinary traffic of the river for so long that the counting had long since become a kind of restfulness to her, a thing her hands did while the rest of her watched the water and the gulls and, that spring, the strange low broad-bellied barges that she had never counted before and would, she suspected, though no one had told her so outright, never count again.

She began her tally on the day the first barge came down, low and slow under the bridge's middle arch with two men poling and a third asleep in the bow, and she kept it faithfully as the days went on and the barges followed one another down, sometimes three in a morning and sometimes none for two days together, until the season's grain had all passed under her and gone on, by the coast road of the water, past Ros àrsaidh and up the Abhainn naomh to the waiting quay at Seann Skell.

The bridge-keeper, an old man who had held the toll there longer than Mairead had been alive, came out to lean on the parapet beside her most mornings that the barges ran, and between them they made a kind of game of guessing, before each one came under the arch, whether it would ride high or low, empty going up or full going down; and it was he who first remarked, watching a barge pass with its gunwales scarcely a hand's breadth above the water, that he had never in all his years on that bridge seen so much grain moved south to north in a single season, not even in the famine years when the capital had gone hungry and the shires had sent everything they could spare. Mairead said nothing to that, only cut her notch and watched the water settle again behind the barge's wake, because it was not her place to have an opinion on what the grain was for, only to count it as it passed.

When the last of them had gone by, a week and more after the first, she cut her final notch and counted the sticks in her lap, and made the whole of that spring's grain, from the shires south of the mountain to the fleet's own stores, forty-one barges, and told the bridge-keeper so, and he wrote it in his own book, and neither of them thought there was anything more to be done with the number than to write it down.

She never learned, then or after, what had been argued over the grain at An Talla Dearg that winter, nor why the doors at Àth shean had stood barred so long, nor what word had opened them again; she only knew, from where she sat on the bridge parapet with her sticks in her lap, that the river had carried what it was asked to carry, and that forty-one was the number of times it had done so that spring, and she set that down as the whole of her own part in the matter, which, in her own reckoning, it was.

## V. Of the Roll at Seann Skell

At Seann Skell, that same season, in the moon of Pailteach when the barley was in and the last of the barges from the south had not yet reached the quay, Calum mac Nèill cut a household onto Rolla nan Deònach that he had feared, since the day the boards were first opened, to see standing before his own board, and had put off imagining, in his own heart, for as long as he could manage it.

It was his own daughter's household: Mairead nic Chaluim, a grown woman of five-and-twenty, born ten years after the boards were first hung on their pegs, and her husband Dùghall mac Iain, a fisher of Inis àrsaidh whom she had married against no one's wishes and with everyone's blessing, six years gone. They came to the harbour-house together on an ordinary morning, no different in their dress or their manner from any of the hundreds of households that had stood before Calum's board in the years since the roll was opened, and Mairead gave her own name and her husband's and the names of their two children in the same clear voice she had used, as a small girl, to recite her letters for him at their own hearth, and watched his knife the whole time it was in the wood, the way every one of them watched it, as though the cutting were the thing that made the going real and not the choosing that had come before it.

She had brought the two children with her, a boy of four holding fast to his father's hand and a girl not yet two on Dùghall's hip, and it was the boy, more than the parents, who watched the whole business with the frank interest of a child who has been told a thing is important and means to see for himself what makes it so; he asked, in the small silence after his mother had given the last of the names, whether the boat they would sail on had a name of its own, and Dùghall told him, low, that it did, though he did not yet know which of the hulls at the quay would be theirs, and the boy seemed satisfied with that, as children often are with the promise of a thing rather than the having of it.

Calum's son Dòmhnall, who kept the boards with him still and had grown from the quiet boy who had once asked his father to close them into a quieter man who no longer asked, stood at his father's shoulder that morning and said nothing at all, and it was Dòmhnall, not Calum, who reached first for the cup of ale that was kept, by then, for every household's first entering, and set it in his sister's hands. He held her a moment by the shoulders after, the way a brother will who does not trust himself to say anything worth the saying, and let her go again, and it was the only part of that whole ordinary morning that anyone standing in the harbour-house doorway thought worth remembering afterward.

Calum wrote the household in the same hand he had used for every entry before it, steady, without a tremor that any watcher could have named, and it was only after his daughter and her husband had gone back out onto the quay, and the harbour-house stood empty a moment in the ordinary business of the morning, that his own hand, laid flat on the board where the ink was drying, was seen by no one but himself to be shaking, and he stood a while with it so, and then went on to the next entry waiting in the doorway, because the boards, as he had told his wife long before, needed their keeper, whatever the keeper himself might be feeling that morning, and the queue at the door did not know, and had no cause to know, whose name had just gone onto the wood.

## VI. Of the Hulls at the Quay

By the spring of LE 38 the fleet lay complete at Seann Skell, the whole length of the new stone quay taken up with hulls that had not existed, any of them, when the first crew of Cuan shean had walked up the river road with its tale of a far shore. Leabhar a' Chùraim at Taigh na Fèithe, when its clerk came down that season to make the reckoning, wrote the number as nineteen; a later hand, in the margin of the same leaf, made it twenty-one; and no one, then or since, has ever been able to say with any certainty which of the two counts was the truer, or why they should have differed at all over a fleet lying, the whole of it, in plain sight against one short stretch of stone.

Calum's grandson Niall, Dòmhnall's boy, was nine years old that spring and had grown up entirely within sight of the roll and the boards and the quay his grandfather kept, so that the fleet, to him, was less a wonder than a fact of the world he had been born into, the way the river was a fact, or the harbour-house. He had a habit, that spring, of running the whole new length of the quay after his lessons were done, from the old stones at the east end where the fish-boats still lay to the new dressed stone at the west where the deep hulls rode, touching each hull's timbers with his hand as he passed as though he were counting them the way his grandfather counted households onto a board, though no one had asked him to count anything at all.

He never once, that spring or the next, brought the count out even. It would begin well enough at the east end, one, two, three, murmuring the numbers under his breath the way Dòmhnall had taught him his letters, and somewhere past the tenth hull, or the twelfth, a gull would go up off a mast, or a rope-maker would call across to a wright he knew, or the light on the water would catch his eye and hold it a moment longer than he meant, and when he came to himself again he no longer knew whether he stood at the fourteenth hull or the fifteenth, and had, every time, to choose whether to go back to the beginning and start the whole count fresh, or to let it go and simply finish his run to the western stones and stand there a while, breathing hard, looking out at the whole fleet riding together against the new quay in the spring light, with the losing of the count already forgotten in the plain pleasure of having run the length of it.

Once, near the end of that spring, one of the older wrights caught him at it, hand flat on a strake, lips moving, and asked him, not unkindly, what number he had reached. Niall told him honestly that he did not know, that he had lost it somewhere past the pitch-sheds, and the wright laughed, a short surprised bark of a laugh, and said that he himself, who had helped lay four of the hulls with his own hands, could not have told the boy the true count either, not to save his life, and that Niall was in good company in his not knowing. The boy turned that over a good while afterward, walking home along the quay in the last of the light, and found, somewhat to his own surprise, that it pleased him more than a straight answer would have done, though he could not then, and never later, have said quite why.

His grandfather, watching him from the harbour-house door on one such evening, said nothing of it to the boy, then or later; but it is told that Calum remarked once, to his wife Seonag, that there might yet come a year when no one on the island could say for certain how many hulls had lain at that quay, and that he did not know, himself, whether that was a thing to be sorry for.

# Chapter Nine: Of the Night of Lamps and the Sunwise Turn

*LE 39 – 40*

> *Dòrlach airson an teallaich ùir,*
> *is an seann teallach fhathast blàth.*
> A handful for the new hearth,
> and the old hearth still warm.

## I. Of the Queen on the New Stones

Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill came down to Seann Skell in the moon of Sìolach, when the barley stood green and short in the strips above the river and the last of the fleet's rigging was going up on hulls that had, the year before, been only frames on the strand. She came with a small household, six riders and a groom and no more, and she had told no one at the harbour-house to expect her; the first word Niall mac Dhòmhnaill's father had of the queen's coming was the queen herself, standing in the door of Taigh a' Chalaidh out of the rain with her hood still up, asking whether the harbour scribe was within.

He was. Calum mac Nèill had kept the boards of Seann Skell for thirty-nine years by then and had stood before three kings and one queen at An Talla Dearg in that time, and he still, his son said afterward, went white to the lips when he saw who stood in his own doorway. He gave her the chair kept for the reeve when the reeve came to check the rolls, and stood himself, and she let him stand, because there are things a queen does not trouble to change in another man's house.

She did not ask to see the boards. She had had copies of the roll sent to Cathair dhearg every season since the boards were first hung, and she knew, better than most men at An Talla Dearg, how many households had gone onto them and how many had come off again; there was nothing in the wood that the copies had not already told her. What she asked for, when Calum had got his voice back enough to ask what she wanted of him, was to walk the quay.

He walked with her himself, a half-step behind and to the side as the custom of the harbour-house had it, past the fish-boats at the old stones and out along the new dressed work the masons had laid nine years before, and the hulls of the fleet lay against it the whole length of the walk, nineteen or one-and-twenty of them, riding a little high yet for want of their full stores, their new-cut timbers pale against the darker, salted wood of the coasters moored further down. Beathag stopped at no one hull longer than another. She walked the length of the quay once, from the fish-stones to the western end where the water ran deep enough at low tide for the largest of the keels, and stood there a while with the wind off the sea working at the edge of her hood, and said, to no one in particular, that she had not thought, when the first crew came up the river road with its tale of a far shore, that she would live to see so many hulls built on an island that had never built one.

Calum said nothing to that. It did not seem a thing that wanted an answer.

She found her sister on the way back, though whether she had come down to Seann Skell to find her, or had only known she would, Calum could not afterward have said, and did not ask. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill was on the strand below the new quay with a coil of rope over one shoulder, helping a rope-maker's boy stow gear against the weather that was coming in off the water, her sleeves rolled and her hands as roughened, by then, as any fisherwoman's on that shore; and when she straightened and saw who stood above her on the stones, she came up the slip at her own pace, neither hurried nor slowed, wiping her hands on her skirt as she came, the way she might have come up to greet any traveller who had asked for her at the harbour-house door.

The two sisters stood together on the new stones a little apart from Calum and from the queen's household, and what passed between them there, no one who stood by ever told, not Calum, who did not go close enough to hear, and not the two riders who stood at the queen's back with their eyes on the weather and not on the queen. It was not a long conversation. Leabhar a' Chùraim, when it comes at last to speak of that day at all, gives it in one line: that the queen came to Seann Skell in Sìolach and was seen upon the quay with her sister, and went home again before the sailing, as her word of long before had bound her to do.

It is told, though not in Leabhar a' Chùraim, that Beathag put her hand once to the back of Mòrag's head, the way an elder sister will to a younger one who has not stopped being the younger one no matter how many years or how many miles come between them, and that Mòrag let her, and that neither of them wept where Calum or the riders could see it, whatever was done with the weeping once the queen's household had ridden back up the river road and Mòrag had gone down again to the rope-maker's boy and the gear that wanted stowing before the weather came in.

Beathag did not stay the night. She had told Calum, on the walk out to the western stones, that she would not be at Seann Skell for the sailing, whenever it came, because a queen who has sworn to send no one over and keep no one back has no business standing on a quay to watch her own sister taken from her by a promise she made herself; and Calum, who had thought a great many things about the queen's word in the thirty-seven years he had kept it written above his own door, thought that the truest thing he had yet heard said of it. She rode north before dusk, in the rain that had held off all day and came down at last as her household cleared the last houses of the town, and Niall, who was ten that spring and had watched the whole of the queen's visit from the harbour-house step with his grandfather's hand on his shoulder to keep him from getting underfoot, remembered afterward chiefly the sound of the horses going away up the river road in the wet, and his grandfather standing a long while in the doorway after the sound had gone, looking at nothing that Niall could see.

## II. Of the Lamps on the Sills

The fleet's full stores went aboard through the whole of Bearnach, the gap-moon between the last of the winter's keep and the first green of the year, when the granaries stand at their lowest and every household on the island counts what is left in the barrel and reckons how far it will stretch. Niall was eleven that Bearnach, and had grown, in the two years since he had run the quay counting hulls and losing the count, into the age at which a harbour scribe's grandson is given work rather than only allowed to watch it; and the work his grandfather gave him, on the last evening before the sailing, was a hazel stick shaved clean along one face and a small knife with a worn horn handle, and the instruction, given once and not repeated, that he was to sit on the wall of the west quay when the fleet went out in the morning and cut one notch for each hull as she passed, and no talking.

He had heard, by then, every telling there was to hear of why the count mattered and why no one trusted a single teller's word for it alone; the harbour-house kept three tallies of everything that passed its boards, his grandfather had told him more than once, because two men's memories never agreed and a third was needed to settle which of the first two lied, though neither, as often as not, had lied at all, only remembered differently. Niall took the stick and the knife with both hands, the way he had been shown to take anything his grandfather gave him that was not a toy, and did not ask what would be done with his tally once it was cut, because a boy of eleven who has grown up in a harbour-house learns early that some questions get no answer and are better not asked twice.

That evening, as the light went, every house along the Seann Skell waterfront set a lamp on its sill, and kept it burning. No one had told them to. It began, so far as anyone could afterward say, at the fish-stones end of the quay, where a widow whose only son was going out with the fleet lit her own lamp early against the dusk and left it burning past her own bedtime because she had nothing else that evening to do with her hands; and it went on from house to house along the strand the way a rumour goes, without any one person carrying it, until the whole curve of the harbour was pricked with light from the fish-stones to the new western stones where the fleet lay. Niall's grandmother Seonag lit their own lamp at the harbour-house window without being asked, and when Niall asked her why, she said only that a lit window was a thing a body understood without being told what it meant, and that some things were better left at that.

Niall went down to the quay before the lamps had all been lit, because he could not sit still in the house that evening and his grandfather, for once, did not tell him to. The hulls lay close against the new stones, so close in places that a boy could have dropped a pebble onto a deck without much trying, and the whole length of the quay smelled of pitch and wet hemp and, under both, the tallowy reek of the sheep's fat the crews had been rubbing into the blocks and running-gear all that week against the salt to come. Somewhere aboard one of the nearer hulls a woman was singing under her breath, some working song with no words Niall could catch, and a man's voice told her, not unkindly, to hush, and she did, and started again a little later when he had gone forward.

He found his aunt Mairead's household aboard the third hull from the western end, a low broad-waisted ship named, so far as anyone had told him, for nothing he had heard, her deck crowded with barrels lashed down under oiled hide and her people moving about the business of a last evening with the particular quiet haste of those who mean to be done with the loading before dark. Mairead saw him on the quay wall and came to the rail, her sleeves rolled to the elbow and a smear of pitch on one wrist, and asked him, in the ordinary voice she had always used to him, whether his grandfather had given him a proper task for the morning or meant to leave him idle on the wall like any other spectator.

He showed her the stick and the knife. She looked at them a moment longer than the showing needed, and then she said that he was to cut a good deep notch for her hull when it came, whichever number it fell at, so that whatever else the tally lost or kept, hers would be cut clean; and she reached down over the rail and put her hand once, briefly, on the top of his head, the same gesture, though he had no way of knowing it, that the queen had used on her sister on the new stones two moons before. Then her husband Dùghall called her back to the lashings, and she went, and Niall sat on the wall a while longer with the stick across his knees, watching the lamps come out along the whole curve of the strand behind him, one and then another, until there was no dark house left between the fish-stones and the western end.

His grandfather found him there past full dark and did not send him home. Calum stood beside him a long while without speaking, his eyes on the lit windows behind the hulls rather than on the hulls themselves, and it was Calum, in the end, who spoke first, saying only that he had kept the boards of that harbour for near forty years and had thought, when the first name went onto them, that he understood what the roll would cost the town; and that he had been wrong about the size of it, though not, he thought, about the shape. Niall did not understand all of what his grandfather meant by that, and did not ask him to explain it, because the night did not seem to want explaining. They sat together on the wall until the cold drove them in, and behind them, the whole length of the waterfront, the lamps burned on into a night that no one along that shore, by every later telling, slept much through at all.

## III. Of Mòrag's Last Walk

Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill walked the waterfront of Seann Skell alone that same night, from the fish-stones to the western stones and back again, twice over, though no one had asked her to and she told no one she meant to do it.

She had spent the whole of that Bearnach at the harbour, seeing her own household's gear stowed and her husband Aonghas's and, in the last days, the gear of her grown daughter Beathag Òg's household besides, for Beathag Òg had married into a Ros bheag family two years before and had brought her own name onto the roll within the year, mother following daughter as often, by then, as daughter followed mother; and Mòrag had not, in all that season's labour, found an hour to walk the quay simply to look at it, the way a person looks at a room she means to leave the following morning and will not see again.

She did it that night instead. The lamps were lit along every sill by the time she started out, and she walked past them slowly, naming the households to herself as she passed each house. She needed no reminding who lived where; it seemed to her, she told her husband afterward, a thing worth doing once before she could no longer do it: to walk a street she had known the whole of her life and put a name to every lit window on it, as though the naming were itself a kind of leave-taking that the sailing in the morning would not have room for.

She found Catrìona nic Iain on the deck of An Ròn Glas, the hull that would carry Mòrag's own household and Aonghas's and a dozen more of Cuan shean's people besides, coiling a line at the foot of the steering oar with the particular unhurried care of a pilot who has done the same work a hundred times and means to do it once more, correctly, before it matters. Catrìona had been made pilot of that hull at Seann Skell the year before, on the quay, the same evening she had first named Reul na Stiùire to Mòrag by its Dia-thìris name, and the two women had not, in the year since, had much cause to speak beyond the ordinary business of a hull being fitted for sea; but Catrìona straightened when she saw who stood at the rail, and said, without being asked, that the oar answered well and the ship rode true in the little chop of the harbour, and that whatever else the morning brought, it would not bring a fault in the steering.

Mòrag thanked her for it, and stood a while at the rail looking down the length of the deck where her own people's gear lay lashed among Cuan shean's, and asked Catrìona, once, whether she was afraid. Catrìona thought about it before she answered, which Mòrag afterward said she had liked in her more than any answer the girl might have given straight off, and said at last that she was less afraid of the sea than of the not-knowing what lay past it, and that she supposed those were, in the end, close to the same fear worn two different ways. Mòrag said she thought that was true of most of them on the roll, and left it there, because there did not seem, that night, to be a better thing to say about it than the plain truth already said.

It was on her second pass along the strand, going back toward the fish-stones in the last of the evening light, that she saw the man standing by his cart at the head of the slip below the harbour-house, a tall man in a carter's coat with a horse still in the traces beside him, neither loading the cart nor unloading it, only standing, the way a man stands who has come to a place to decide something and has not yet decided it. She knew him, a little, the way a household of the roll comes to know the carters who bring goods down to the quay for those still packing; his name, she had heard once and did not forget, was Fionnlagh, and he had brought loads down to the western stones three times that season without, so far as she had ever seen, putting his own name to the boards.

She did not go to him, and he did not come to her, only passed within a stone's throw of where he stood, close enough to see that his cart was empty, and that he watched the lamps along the strand with the same stillness with which she had, herself, watched Catrìona's hands on the coiled line. Something in the set of him, she said to her husband that same night, told her plainly enough that here was a man who had already made his choice and stood at his cart only to be certain of it one more night before the boards closed for good. It did not seem, then, a thing a stranger should interrupt, so she walked on without speaking to him; and in the morning, when the fleet went out, his cart stood in the same place, and he stood beside it still, and did not go aboard any hull that passed.

Mòrag went back to the house she had taken near the fish-stones as the last of the light went, and sat up late with Aonghas over a fire that neither of them let go out, and said little of what she had seen or felt on her two walks along the strand, because there did not seem, between two people who had already said everything that could be said about the morning to come, to be much profit in saying it twice.

## IV. Of the Sunwise Turn

On 19 an Giblean, LE 40, in the grey before sunrise, with the lamps along the waterfront burned low but none of them yet gone entirely out, the fleet of the willing went out from Seann Skell.

Niall was on the wall of the west quay by the time the first grey showed over the eastern hills, the stick and the knife in his lap and his knees drawn up under his chin against the cold that comes off water before the sun is properly up. The town had gathered along the whole length of the strand behind him, more people than he had ever seen crowded onto that stretch of stone at once, and yet, he remembered afterward, it was a quiet crowd, quieter than a market day or a feast day, as though everyone on the waterfront had agreed, without a word passed between them, that there was nothing that morning that wanted shouting about.

The first hull came off the quay a little before the sun cleared the hills, warped out from the stones on lines that a dozen hands ashore paid out together, and swung her bow round, away from the straight run down the river toward the open water, toward the head of the pool where the Abhainn naomh widened below the town before narrowing again to the sea. Niall had heard his grandfather say, more than once in that last week, that the fleet meant to go out sunwise round the pool for the luck of it, the way a man walks sunwise round a well he means to drink from, or round a house new-built before he sleeps his first night in it; but seeing it done was another thing from hearing it told, and he watched the first hull swing wide and slow with something closer to wonder than to the grief he had half expected of himself.

He cut his first notch as she passed him, close enough along the quay wall that he could have named half her crew by sight, and did not look long at any one face among them, because his grandfather had told him, the one instruction given twice that whole week, that a counter who looks too long at faces loses his count, and Niall meant, that morning above every other, not to lose it.

An Dara Fhaoileag came after her before the first had gone half round the pool, and the third close on the second, until the whole fleet was strung out across the water in a long curving line, nineteen hulls or one-and-twenty, going round the pool sunwise in the grey light with the town silent along the strand behind them. Niall cut his notches steadily, one, two, three, murmuring the count under his breath the way his grandfather murmured a leaf's entries while he wrote them, and did not let a gull's cry or a call across the water turn his eyes from the stick and the passing hulls the way it had turned them, two years before, when he had tried the same count for no better reason than his own idleness. He knew An Ròn Glas when she came, by the grey seal cut into her stem-post, and cut her notch no deeper and no shallower than any other's, though he looked, for the length of one breath only, at the woman standing at the steering oar with her hand steady on the loom, and thought that he had never before seen anyone look so entirely at ease doing a thing he himself could not have begun to do.

His aunt Mairead's hull went by third from the last, low in the water with her full stores aboard, and Mairead stood at the rail with Dùghall and their two children and lifted a hand to the quay, not waving exactly, only holding it up a moment the way a person does to be seen rather than to signal anything in particular, and Niall, remembering what she had told him the evening before, cut her notch deep, deeper than his grandfather's instruction strictly wanted, and did not think, that morning, that anyone would ever come to check the depth of one notch against another on a stick kept, in the end, for no purpose he was ever told.

At the foot of the pool the fleet straightened out of its long curve and turned down the Abhainn naomh toward the sea, hull after hull falling into the line, and it was there, his grandfather told him afterward, that the harbour-house's own written account of the sailing came to its end, because a scribe can write only what passes before his door, and the river beyond the pool's foot passed beyond any door Seann Skell had. Niall kept his count a while longer, watching the sterns go small down the river between the willows, and could not, in the end, have said with any certainty whether his own stick agreed with his grandfather's or with the tallies any other counter along that strand was cutting that same morning; only that he had cut one notch for every hull he had seen pass, and had not once, that morning, let his eyes wander long enough to lose the number.

When the last hull had gone from sight round the first bend below the pool, the crowd along the strand stood a while longer looking at the empty water before it began to disperse, and it was some little time before anyone on that whole long strand moved to go home. The harbour songs, sung on later anniversaries of that morning by people who had not themselves stood on the quay to see it, tell that a mist came down on the water behind the last hull as she cleared the river's mouth, and did not lift again until she was gone from any watcher's sight; whether that mist stood there in truth, or only in the songs that were made afterward to close the telling properly, no one who was on the quay that morning ever afterward could say for certain, Niall least of all, who had kept his eyes on his stick and not on the weather.

He put the stick inside his shirt, against his skin, before he climbed down off the wall, though no one had told him to keep it rather than hand it over, and no one, that day or afterward, ever asked him for it back.

## V. Of the Boundary Ditch

At Cathair dhearg that same morning, in An Talla Dearg above the river, Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill sat the ordinary court of the day and heard, among the first matters brought before her, a dispute between two farmers of the shire nearest the capital over a ditch that marked the boundary of their two holdings, which one of them held had shifted its course in the spring floods and the other held had not shifted at all, only been dug a little wider by a neighbour with more land than sense.

It was not a great matter, and the court did not treat it as one. The queen heard both farmers out in turn, asked the elder of the two clerks present what the boundary stones of that parish showed, and gave her ruling before noon, that the ditch should be walked and marked again by the parish reeve within the month and the stones set where the walking found them, whatever either farmer might say of floods or neighbours; and the two men, neither wholly satisfied nor wholly aggrieved, thanked her in the manner the court required and went back out to the yard to find their horses.

No rider had yet come up the river road from Seann Skell that morning, nor would one come for two days more, for the distance was four-and-twenty miles and no rider rode it faster than a long day's going even with the best of horses under him; and so the queen who had stood on the new stones at Seann Skell in Sìolach and taken her leave of her own sister without ceremony, as her own word had bound her to do, sat that morning in her own hall and heard a boundary dispute between two farmers she had never met and was not likely to meet again, and gave it the same weight and the same care she had given every such dispute brought before her in all the years of her reign, because a queen who has sworn to send no one over and keep no one back has, on the morning her own sister goes over, no other work to do that the day will let her leave undone.

It is told that she asked, once, near the end of that day's court, whether any word had come up from the coast, and that the clerk at her elbow, who knew as well as she did that no word could yet have come, told her only that none had, and that she said nothing further about it, and turned to the next matter on the roll.

That evening the harbour scribe of Seann Skell walked the length of the west quay alone, from the fish-stones to the new western stones where the fleet had lain the night before, and found the berths standing empty along their whole length for the first time since the masons finished them, the water lapping at stones that had known nothing but hulls; and it is Calum's own words, given to his son Dòmhnall that same night and kept afterward in no book but the family's own memory, that a harbour is a strange thing to walk empty, being built for nothing else but to be full, and that he did not think, walking it that evening, that he would ever again see it as anything but a place where something was missing, whatever ships came afterward to lie against those same stones.

# Chapter Ten: Of the Count from the Turn

*LE 40 – 46*

## I. Of the Entry a Day Too Late

Leabhar a' Chùraim of Taigh na Fèithe above Muileann dhearg was kept in a hand steadier than most, and the hand that kept it in the autumn after An Diosal belonged to a clerk of six-and-twenty named Donnchadh mac Thormoid, who had been given the leaf and the ink-horn ten winters before by a master who was dead within the year of the giving, and who had gone on keeping them since because no one above him had troubled to say he should stop.

He was not the man who had counted the hulls; that had been a boy on a harbour wall sixty miles off, with a hazel stick and a knife, and Donnchadh had never met him and never would. What came to Donnchadh, in the ordinary course of Taigh na Fèithe's business, was a leaf carried up from Seann Skell by a rider who did not know, or did not say, why the leaf had been so long on the road, and it was Donnchadh's office, not his curiosity, to enter what the leaf told him into the great book of the custody and ask no more of it than the book required.

The leaf told him that the fleet of the willing had gone once round the river pool at Seann Skell sunwise, as a man walks round a well for luck, and had gone down the river after and out past the north cape, and that this had happened, by the harbour scribe's own hand, on a day the leaf gave plainly enough. What troubled Donnchadh, turning the leaf over by the light of Taigh na Fèithe's lamp with his master's old rule laid open beside it, the rule by which every entry in Leabhar a' Chùraim was dated against the feasts of the turning year, was that the day the leaf gave fell after Samhain, and by every account he had ever had of the sailing, of the last stores laid in and the last measures sealed and the three tellings that had first brought word of a far shore to the queen's own board, the fleet had gone out long before that, in the spring, in the gap-moon of Bearnach, with the barley scarcely green.

He was a careful clerk, and carefulness in a clerk is a kind of honesty that asks no questions it cannot answer. Turning the leaf a second time and a third, holding it near enough the lamp that the pitch-smoke stung his eyes, he found in it nothing that explained the gap between the day the fleet had gone and the day Taigh na Fèithe was told of the going: no word of a delay on the road, no note that the first leaf had been lost and this one written after in its place, no apology from the harbour scribe for a silence of half a year that no one at Seann Skell, so far as the leaf showed, had thought worth accounting for. A rider might have been sent back down to Seann Skell to ask. None was. It was, he told himself, setting the ink-horn to the page, a clerk's business only to copy the leaf faithfully into the great book, gap and all, and let the book stand as the book had been given to him.

So he wrote it: the turn of the fleet, entered under the day a full turning of the moon and more after the feast of Samhain, though every other account he had of the matter set the sailing in the spring. He signed the entry with his own mark, as his master had taught him, closed the book, and banked Taigh na Fèithe's night fire himself, because the boy whose office that was had gone home early with a fever, and thought no more of the gap that night than a man thinks of a stone he has stepped around a hundred times on a familiar road.

## II. Of the Years of the Diosal

Four years passed at Taigh na Fèithe much as the four before them had, in the reckoning of hearths and the sealing of measures and the slow correspondence, letter and counter-letter, between the custodians of Muileann dhearg and An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg over matters that the histories of great houses call small and the households they touch call everything: a gallery's roof timbered too thin, a widow's right to her dead husband's handful, a boundary stone moved a foot by a neighbour's ox-sled and moved back by night.

Donnchadh kept Leabhar a' Chùraim through all of it, and kept also, by then, a second book that was his own and answered to no one, a plain thing of scraped hide bound with cord, in which he set down, for his own convenience and no other man's, the sums and the debts and the running totals that the great book's formal hand had no room for. It was in this private book, in the fourth year after the turn, that he first found himself wanting a single fixed point from which to count forward, because the island's own way of dating things, by the reign of a queen or the year of a feast or the season a gallery was opened, served Leabhar a' Chùraim well enough but served his own sums badly, requiring him each time to look up how many years a given reign or a given gallery had already run before he could set two figures against each other at all.

He chose the turn. It was, of all the fixed points he had to hand, the nearest and the strangest, a day already written into the great book under a date that fit no other account of it, and it had at least the merit, in a clerk's eye, of being an ending rather than a beginning, a single day after which nothing further needed to be asked of the fleet, whatever might yet be asked of everything else. He began to write, in the margins of his own book only, the year of An Diosal beside the year of the reign, first for the year then running, which he called the fourth of An Diosal, and then, working backward with a patience that cost him the better part of an evening, for every year in his own book since the turn, so that the private ledger of a clerk of thirty came, without ceremony and without anyone above him ever asking that it should, to be the first place on the island where the years were counted from an absence rather than a reign.

He told no one. It did not occur to him that the habit was worth telling, being no more, in his own reckoning, than a clerk's shortcut for his own sums, and if any other hand at Taigh na Fèithe noticed the odd figures in the margin of his private book, no one troubled to ask him what they meant, and he was not a man who offered explanations that were not asked for.

There was, besides, a plainer reason he kept the habit to his own book and no further, one he would not himself have put into words if asked, though it sat behind the choosing all the same: a reckoning that began from the turn was a reckoning that began from a loss, and Donnchadh, who measured hearths and galleries for his trade and had learned early that a measure is only as good as the men willing to trust it, did not know whether the custodians above him, who had lost sons and daughters and whole households to that same turn, would thank a junior clerk for fixing their years to it in a book that anyone might read. His own book no one read but himself. He kept the count there, and there it stayed, a private arithmetic run alongside Taigh na Fèithe's public one, the two agreeing in every figure that mattered and differing only in the one thing that, to Donnchadh's mind, mattered to no one but him: from what day the years were said to run.

He found, working the count backward and then forward again through that fourth year, a small and useless satisfaction in the plainness of it, that a thing so large as the going of a fifth of the coal-right's households could be made to sit, in a clerk's own ledger, beside the price of a barrel of sealed measures or the wages owed a mason for a season's work on Taigh na Fèithe wall, one figure among many, asking no more of the page than any other figure did. It was not, he would have said if pressed, that the going meant no more to him than a barrel's price; only that a ledger has no way of saying which of its figures broke a household and which merely counted one, and he had long since made his peace with a trade that could not tell the difference.

## III. Of the Tidings that Reached Seann Skell

That same year, word came to Seann Skell of the fleet, though by what road it came, or in whose mouth, or aboard what small boat put in at the old stones below the harbour-house, no one who was there that autumn ever afterward agreed well enough to say.

It fell to Calum mac Nèill to receive it, as it fell to him to receive most things that came to the harbour-house wearing the shape of news, and he was an older man by then than he had been when the boards were first hung on their pegs, grey through the beard and slower in the hand, though his hand, when it came to the actual forming of letters, had not yet begun to fail him. His wife Seonag had taken to saying, of late, that he sat too long over the boards for a man his age, and he had taken to answering, when he answered at all, that the boards had had a keeper his whole life and would want one after him, and that there was no sense training a new keeper's hand while the old one still held its line.

The word, when it came, came as broken speech rather than as a leaf already written, a telling passed from a boat that did not stay to be questioned to a fisherman of the strand who could not himself say afterward which of the boat's crew had spoken or in what tongue, and it fell then to Calum to set that broken speech down in the harbour-house's own hand before it broke further in the passing. He did it that same evening, by lamplight, with his hand, his wife noted afterward, less steady over that leaf than she had seen it over any other in forty years of watching him write, so that the letters toward the leaf's foot ran smaller and closer together than at its head, as a man's hand will when he is hurrying to set down what he fears he may otherwise lose before he has it whole.

What the telling gave him, so far as his shaking hand caught it, was this: that the fleet, or some good part of it, had come at last to a shore across the open water, and that it had come to two shores and not to one, two separate landfalls reached by hulls that had not, it seemed, all held together the whole of the crossing, though whether storm had parted them, or purpose, or some quarrel among the crews that the telling did not touch, Calum's leaf did not say and Calum did not pretend to know. The telling ran on a little further, naming, or seeming to name, some particular of the second shore that might have settled the matter one way or another, and it was there, at the leaf's very foot, in the smallest and most hurried of all the hand's letters, that it simply stopped, with no mark of an ending, as though the teller had been called away, or the listener's patience had failed, or the leaf had been torn and the torn part lost before ever it reached the boards.

Calum read it over three times before he judged it fit to send on, and found, each time, that it told him no more at the third reading than it had at the first, and that the not-knowing sat worse with him than a plain bad tiding would have done, because a plain bad tiding, however hard, is a thing a man can grieve and be done with, and this was a thing that asked to be carried unfinished a good while longer, by him and by whoever received it after him.

He did not sleep well that night, and Seonag, waking once to find him sitting up with the lamp still lit and the leaf still before him though he had long since finished the copying of it, asked him plainly what more there was in it that he had not yet set down. There was nothing more in it, he told her; that was the whole trouble with the thing, that it had stopped where it had stopped and left him with no more right than any fisherman on the strand to guess at what lay beyond its torn foot, and yet he was the one whose hand had carried it, and a hand that carries a tale unfinished, he said, feels the weight of the unfinished part as much as of the part it actually holds. Seonag, who had kept house with a harbour scribe long enough to know when an answer was the whole of what she would get, blew out the lamp herself when he would not, and left him to sit a while longer in the dark with the leaf under his hand, which he did, by his own account afterward, until the sky over the water had begun to grey.

In the morning he read the leaf once more before he sealed it for the rider, and it was then, turning it over a last time by the grey early light, that he noticed what he had been too tired the night before to mark: that the hand which had first spoken the broken tale to the fisherman on the strand had used, in the one clear phrase Calum's own leaf preserved whole, a word for the second shore that the island's own tongue did not commonly use of any coast it had seen with its own eyes, a word more often kept for a shore known only by report. He set that observation nowhere in the copy he sent on, judging it, on reflection, too slight a thread to hang a further guess from, and it went with him, unwritten, to his grave some fourteen years after, one more thing the harbour-house's own boards would never show.

## IV. Of the Hearths of Inis àrsaidh

The telling did not stay long behind the harbour-house door. It went out, as such things do in a fishing town smaller than its harbour, along the strand and up the lanes before the ink on Calum's leaf was fully dry, carried by the fisherman who had first heard it and by every mouth that heard it from him after, each mouth losing a little of the whole and adding a little of its own, until the tale that reached the hearths of Inis àrsaidh, an hour's walk down the river, bore only a family likeness to the leaf Calum had written.

It was heard hardest at Inis àrsaidh because it was from Inis àrsaidh, more households than from any other single place on the roll, that the fleet had carried its people, and there was scarcely a hearth in the fishing town that autumn without some cousin or son-in-law or a whole young family gone in one of the nineteen hulls or one-and-twenty, the number no one there had ever settled either. An old net-mender of the strand, who had given two grandsons to the roll and kept, since, a lamp of her own on her sill though the custom had not yet spread beyond Seann Skell's own waterfront, was heard to say, when the tale of two shores reached her, that two shores were better than none, and was heard also, not an hour later, by the same neighbour who carried her the tale, to say that two shores were worse than one, since a man does not know, now, which of the two to grieve toward or which to hope toward, and must do both at once with a heart no bigger than it was before.

Nothing in the tale, as it reached Inis àrsaidh, told anyone which of the two coasts held which household, and the town did what towns do with a tale too broken to answer the one question every hearth in it wanted answered: it kept both halves of the tale alive at once, telling it one way at one hearth and another way at the next, until the not-knowing became, in a manner Calum would have understood better than most, the whole of what there was to know.

## V. Of the Copy that Went by Two Roads

Calum's leaf, once it was judged fit, did not stay at Seann Skell. A fair copy of it went by rider up the river road to Cathair dhearg, where the queen's own scribes kept the roll of what the crown was told, and a second copy, made from the first by Calum's own son Dòmhnall in a hand less hurried than his father's, went the sixty miles east to Taigh na Fèithe, where it came, in the course of things, to the same board at which Donnchadh mac Thormoid had four years before entered the turn under its unaccountable date.

He read it standing, Leabhar a' Chùraim still open on the board before him from an earlier entry, and set the two leaves side by side without quite meaning to, the old entry of the turn and the new copy of the tidings, and saw between them a silence of four years that neither leaf so much as gestured toward, the fleet gone out one grey morning and nothing more heard of it, so far as Taigh na Fèithe's own book showed, until this. He entered the tidings as he had entered the turn, faithfully and without comment, copying Calum's broken telling into Leabhar a' Chùraim's formal hand exactly as it stood, torn end and all, resisting, as he had resisted before, any temptation a lesser clerk might have felt to smooth the gap where the leaf gave out or to guess, in the book's own voice, at what the missing end might have said.

At Cathair dhearg the other copy went, as such things did, before the queen's own council in An Talla Dearg, and there it fared rather less quietly than it had at Taigh na Fèithe's plain board. The council of Dia-thìr had never yet had to weigh a piece of news it could neither confirm nor disprove, and it did with this one what councils do with such things: it argued. One custodian of the old houses held that two shores meant the fleet had prospered, having found land enough for all its hulls though not all in the one place; another held the opposite, that two shores meant the fleet had failed to hold together at all, and that a fleet scattered on a strange sea was a fleet in worse case than one that had never sailed together to begin with. A third asked, and was not answered, which of the nineteen or one-and-twenty hulls the tale meant by its second shore, and whether the queen's own sister's hull, Mòrag's own Ròn Glas with the pilot of Ros bheag at its steering oar, had held to the first landfall or been carried to the second, and it was at this question, more than at any other put that day, that the whole board turned, as one body, to look at the queen.

Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill sat at the head of the board through the whole of the argument with her hands folded on the wood before her and said, by every account of that day that came down afterward, nothing at all. She had the leaf brought to her once more when the council's voices had run themselves out, and read it over herself, alone, by the light from the hall's high windows, and set it down again exactly where it had lain, and gave no order that it be answered, denied, or sent further, so that the council, having nothing else to do with a silence from its own queen, let the matter drop where it lay and turned to the business the day had actually brought it: a dispute over a ditch between two farms on the river, no different in its particulars from a hundred such disputes the hall had settled before and would settle again.

She kept the leaf by her a good while after the council had gone on to its ditch, longer than the ditch took to settle, and it is told that she had it copied once more in her own hand that same evening, a thing she did for no other piece of business that year, and that the copy she made agreed word for word with the one Calum had sent, down to the place where the telling stopped, so that whatever she had hoped to find by setting the words down again herself, in her own letters, she did not find it, and put the copy away with the rest of the year's leaves where it lay, so far as anyone at An Talla Dearg ever afterward saw, unread again. In the council's hearing she had asked nothing of which shore her sister's hull had reached, though it was known to every custodian at that board that the third man's question was the one that concerned her before all the rest, and it was said of her by those who served her closest that a queen who forbids herself a question in front of her own council does not therefore stop asking it once the council has gone.

## VI. Of the Grain Ruling and the Bridge

The two years that followed brought An Talla Dearg the ordinary weather of a kingdom's business, the kind that fills the greater part of any council's year and the smaller part of any chronicle that troubles to be honest about it. A dispute over the grain owed by the upland shires to the crown's own granaries, long argued and longer delayed, was at last settled in the second of those years in the queen's own favour, the upland reeves agreeing to a measure they had refused for three seasons running once it was put to them, as it had not been put before, in the queen's own hand rather than a steward's. In the same season the bridge at Àth shean, whose middle pier had stood cracked and shored with timber since a flood two winters before, was at last mended in stone by masons sent down from the capital, the last of the timber props pulled clear on a morning cold enough that the masons broke the ice on the river to set their final course.

Between the grain ruling and the mending of the bridge, in the ordinary order of the council's business, with no greater weight given to it than to either, the queen made one further entry in the roll of the house of Dia-thìr, an entry that her own scribes wrote, when the day came, in the same plain hand they had used for the grain and would use for the bridge, no larger, no darker, set apart by no mark that a reader turning the leaf idly would have paused at.

## VII. Of the Name Written the Ordinary Way

It was Murchadh mac Eòghainn who held the pen that day, as he had held it since before the three crews first walked up the river road with their tale of a far shore, an old man now, older than any other hand still serving at An Talla Dearg, whose eyes had begun to want more light than the hall's high windows gave even at noon and whose fingers, in the cold months, had to be worked a while by the fire before they would close properly round a quill.

The queen gave him the words herself, standing at his shoulder rather than sitting, as she did for no other entry he had written that year, and the words, when he had them whole, struck him, though he gave no sign of it and asked no question, as being fewer than the matter seemed to want and plainer than any matter he had ever set down at that board before: that Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, and the children of Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, were struck from the order of succession to the crown of Dia-thìr, as persons no longer on Dia-thìr.

He wrote it as he had been given it, in the ordinary hand, and it was only in the forming of the name itself, Mòrag's own name, that his pen slowed by the smallest degree a watcher might have caught, not faltering, not blotting, only slowing, the way an old man's step will slow over ground he has walked a thousand times before without ever once, until that day, having cause to feel its particular shape beneath his foot. He wrote the name in the same letters he had given it every time he had written it before, in the roll of the first tellings, in the entry of Mòrag's own household onto the harbour boards, in a dozen ordinary mentions of the queen's sister across four decades of a scribe's ordinary business, and it was, in the end, exactly that, the name written the ordinary way, that seemed to trouble him longest after the ink had dried.

The queen did not stand over him again once the entry was made. She read it once where it lay, gave him no word of thanks and no word of anything else, and went out of the hall by the same door she had come in by, and it was left to Murchadh, as it was left to no one else in that hall or any other, to close the book on a name he had written a hundred times before and would, so far as the roll of the house of Dia-thìr was ever afterward concerned, never write again.

## VIII. Of the Leaf Sanded

He sat a while after she had gone, the pen still in his hand though there was nothing further that day for it to write, and did at last what he did at the end of every entry he had ever made in that book, no more and no less: he took the fine sand from the box that had stood at his elbow at that board for forty years and more, and shook it evenly across the wet ink, and let it lie a moment, and tipped it off again into the box for the next leaf's use, an old man's hands moving through a motion so long practised that they needed, by then, no more of his mind's attention than his own breathing did.

The hall was near empty around him by then, the day's business done and the light going long and low through the high windows, and if any of the few who remained thought to watch him at it, they saw only what they had seen him do at the close of a thousand ordinary days: an old scribe closing his book, sanding his last leaf, and setting both aside for the morning, in a hand that gave away, to any eye that did not already know what the leaf held, nothing at all of what had just been written under it.

# Chapter Eleven: Of the White Sorrow

*LE 50 – 55*

## I. Of What Was Said at Seann Skell

Nothing was known of the fleet after the tale that stopped at Calum's torn leaf, and a thing not known does not stay empty long in a harbour town. By the fiftieth year of the count men who had never crossed water further than the fishing grounds off Cuan ruadh spoke of the crossing as though they had stood at the rail of it themselves, and the harbour-house at Seann Skell, which kept the only leaf anyone could point to and call a record, was asked so often what it knew that Niall mac Dhòmhnaill's father took, in the end, to answering every asker the same way, tired of hearing his own silence mistaken for a secret: that the boards held what the boards held, and a man who wanted more than that should go and ask the sea.

The tale that took hold hardest, and outlasted every other, was told first, so far as anyone could afterward say, by a coal-carrier's widow who had never in her life set foot on a hull, and it ran that the children born to the departed on the far shore came into the world with less in their hands than their parents had carried away, and the children born to those children less again, until by the third generation over the water there would be nothing left in a family that Dia-thìr would know for its own. No one could say how the carrier had come by it, and she herself, pressed on it at the fair the next spring, only shrugged and said that a thing does not have to be seen to be felt, and that a mother knows when her milk is thinner than her own mother's was, whether or not a physician can explain to her why. It was not a tale that could be tried against anything Seann Skell held. There was no letter from the far shore to set beside it, no child of the crossing to measure, only the shape of the tale passed mouth to mouth along the strand and up the lanes, gathering, as such tales do, a little more certainty with each telling than the last mouth had given it.

A custodian of the coal, down from Taigh na Fèithe on the shire's business that same year, heard the carrier's tale told over a jug in the harbour-house taproom and gave it an answer of his own that the taproom liked better, or at least argued over longer. The coal, he said, plainly enough that a man three tables off could hear him, was not a thing carried in the blood the way a chin or a temper was carried; it answered to the hand that had learned the galleries and kept Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, and a hand once away from the vein for a lifetime, let alone two, would forget the galleries the way any hand forgets a trade it does not practise, whatever blood ran in it. The strength was not thinning in the departed's children, on his reckoning. It had simply been left behind at Muileann dhearg, the way a man leaves a tool in a shed he no longer visits, and a tool left long enough in a shed is a tool a man's own son will not know how to use: no one has put it in his hand and shown him.

The two tales did not agree, and nobody at Seann Skell troubled overmuch to make them agree, for both said, in their different ways, the one thing the harbour town most wanted said: that something in the departed, or their children, was growing less than it had been. A third telling, heard less often and never in the taproom but sometimes from an old woman at a hearth, held that nothing was lessening at all, that the far shore had simply never had the coal to answer to in the first place, so that the children born there were exactly what any child would be, no thinner and no lesser, only unremarked because there was nothing on that shore to remark them against; and this telling, though it troubled fewer households to argue over, was, for reasons no one who told it could have named, the one that most often silenced a room rather than filled it, and was therefore told least. Of the three, or the dozen half-tales that stood between them, nothing was proved and nothing disproved, for there was no one aboard any hull who could be asked, and Taigh na Fèithe, which alone might have spoken with authority on what the coal answered to and what it did not, said for some years nothing at all in public, keeping its own reckoning, as it kept everything, inside its own walls.

## II. Of the Second Count

It was Taigh na Fèithe's own reckoning, made once more thirteen years after the sailing and set down without a word of what the harbour towns were saying, that in the end carried more weight than any tale told over a jug, though it travelled less far and to fewer households, for a custody-book is not a thing that passes mouth to mouth. Eòghann mac Mhuirich, who had counted the households of the coal-right once before the fleet sailed and once again the autumn Rolla nan Deònach closed, was dead these many years by the fiftieth season of the count, and the counting fell, as most things at Taigh na Fèithe now fell, to younger hands under an older name; but the custom of the count had not changed, and in the thirteenth year past the turn the custodians sat down once more with the roll and Leabhar a' Chùraim open side by side, as they had sat down twice before, to see what stood and what did not.

Donnchadh mac Thormoid was thirty-nine that year, no longer the boy who had written his first fair copy by a winter fire, and it was his hand, steadier now than any other at the table, that carried the greater share of the tallying, column against column, hearth against hearth, Rolla nan Deònach checked off one name at a time against the households that remained on the coal-right. It was slow work and dull work, the kind that asks nothing of a man's judgement and everything of his patience, and it took the better part of a season before the figure stood plain before them: one hearth in five of all the hearths that had held the right to the coal at the turn was gone from the coal-right now, neither more nor fewer than the fifth that had gone aboard the fleet, so that the going, whatever else it had done, had at least done nothing further to the number left behind. It was the figure the older custodians round the table had half expected and had none of them, Donnchadh noticed, troubled to say aloud before the count was finished, as though naming it early might somehow alter what the counting found.

He wrote the figure into Leabhar a' Chùraim in his own plain hand, one hearth in five, and beneath it, where a lesser clerk might have let the matter rest, he set down a second line that no one at the table had asked him for and that he had thought a long while, by his own account afterward, before he let himself write. He had gone back, in the slow weeks of the counting, over every measuring Taigh na Fèithe had made since the turn, and had found in them nothing that answered to the tale carried about the taproom at Seann Skell or to the custodian's tale of a tool left in a shed. The vein, he wrote, answered no differently now, to the hands of those who had stayed, than it had answered before the turn; the handful measured true against every hearth that held the right, exactly as it had always measured, and if some thinning was at work upon the children of the departed on whatever shore they had reached, it was at work there, on that shore, and not here, upon the coal or the hands that remained to serve it. It was a small line in a large book, four sentences among ten thousand others, and it settled nothing that the taproom at Seann Skell had been arguing over for a decade, since it spoke only of what stood on this side of the water and said nothing at all of the other. But it was carried up to Cathair dhearg with the rest of that season's reckoning, as every reckoning was, and it came, in the ordinary course of An Talla Dearg's business, before the queen.

Beathag read the figure once, standing at the window of the small room off the hall where she kept the season's leaves before they went to the council, one hand in five, a figure she had carried in her own reckoning, unwritten, since the roll had closed thirteen years before and had never once, in all that time, let herself say aloud to anyone. She read Donnchadh's second line beneath it, the note that the vein answered no differently for those who had stayed, and stood a while with the leaf in her hand before she read it again, more slowly the second time than the first, as though the sentence might give up something on a second reading that it had withheld on the first. It gave up nothing more.
