It was, she saw when she had read it twice, exactly what it had seemed at the first reading, a clerk's plain observation, offered without comfort and without cruelty, that whatever was becoming of her sister's children on their far shore, it was becoming of them there and not here, and that the coal itself, the thing every custodian at Taigh na Fèithe had spent his life learning to serve, held no opinion at all on who had gone and who had stayed. She set the leaf down on the pile with the rest of that season's business, in its place, neither above the grain figures nor below them, and told her scribe, when he came in, that the council might have the whole of it at its next sitting, and said no more of it to him or to anyone else that day.

## III. Of the White Sorrow

It was in the same year, or the one after, that the queen first wore the undyed wool, and the court, which had grown used by then to reading its mood in Beathag's dress the way a farmer reads weather in the sky, marked the change before any word was given for it.

She had worn colour at Cathair dhearg all her reigning life, the deep blue the house of Dòmhnall had kept since before her mother's time, and on the morning she first came into the hall in wool taken plain from the fleece, undyed and uncarded fine, the whole board fell silent before she had crossed half the floor, for a queen does not change the colour she has worn for sixty years without a household somewhere reading it for grief. She gave the court no announcement, taking up the day's first petition as she always took it, a boundary dispute between two farms on the river no different from a hundred such disputes the hall had settled before, and saying nothing at all about the wool, so that for the length of that first morning the hall was left to guess, in the low voices men use when the person they are guessing about sits ten feet from them, whether the queen mourned a death not yet announced, or a death long past that had only now found its proper dress.

It was her own steward, in the end, who gave the court what word there was to give, and he gave it plainly, having asked the queen directly, as few others at that board would have dared to. She mourned, she told him, her sister, who was ten years and more beyond any word reaching Cathair dhearg and would, by every reckoning a sensible woman could make, remain beyond it now; and she had chosen, since there was no grave to stand at and no body to wash, to mourn as she could, in the only cloth that seemed to her to hold no lie in it, since undyed wool asks no dye-master's skill and tells no story about the house that wears it beyond the bare fact of the wearing.

She set, besides the wool, one place at her own table that no one sat at: a cup, a trencher and a straight knife, laid at the board's foot every evening the queen dined in hall, whether she dined alone or with the whole council about her, and left untouched through the meal and cleared away after with the rest, as though the person for whom it was laid might yet, on any given evening, come late to the hall and take the seat. No one at court asked who the place was laid for. There was no need to ask. It was laid, plainly enough for every eye in the hall to read, for Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, who had gone from the same hall fourteen years before with a promise between the sisters that neither had spoken of since, and who would not, by any road the hall could imagine, ever come late to a meal at Cathair dhearg again.

The court did not at first know what face to keep before it. A death it could have mourned in the old way, with black and a wake and an ending that let grief run its course and be done; but this was a grief with no ending fixed to it, a sister neither known to be dead nor known to be living, mourned in a rite that asked the whole hall to sit each evening beside an emptiness that gave back no word either way, and more than one at that board found, in the weeks after the queen first sat down to it, that they did not know whether to speak of the empty place at all, or to pass it in silence as they might pass any other piece of the hall's furniture, and settled, most of them, on the second course, since it asked less of a man than the first.

It did not stay only at Cathair dhearg. The court called it, before the year was out, an Tùrsa Geal, the name settling on it the way names settle on a thing that answers to no better one, and within a generation, so it came to be told afterward at more hearths than An Talla Dearg's own, a household anywhere on the island that had given someone to the fleet might keep the same rite in its own small way, undyed wool for the season of the mourning and a place laid empty at the table, cup and trencher and a knife laid straight, for whoever of theirs had gone and not been heard from since. It asked no priest to keep it and no vein-house to license it. A household that had never sat within a hundred miles of Cathair dhearg and had never heard the queen's own name spoken twice in a year kept it all the same, in whatever manner its own hearth could manage, because the emptiness it answered to was the same emptiness in every house that kept it, high or low, and a rite that answers a true emptiness spreads on its own account, needing no crown behind it and no law.

## IV. Of the Seven Houses

The fifteenth year past the turn brought Taigh na Fèithe a piece of business that had been coming toward it, by every custodian's own reckoning, since the year the roll first closed, though no one had troubled to name it plainly until that year was upon them.

A fifth of the coal-right's households were gone, and the coal-right, whatever else it might be, was above all a thing that had to be served: galleries walked, the handful measured, Leabhar a' Chùraim kept true against every hearth still standing on it, and a fifth fewer hands to serve it than had served it at the turn. The custodians who remained had spent the years since the turn stretching the old apprenticeship thinner than it had ever been stretched, a master taking two pupils where he had once taken one, a gallery walked by a single custodian where two had walked it before, and it had held, after its fashion, for fifteen years; but it was Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now Taigh na Fèithe's senior clerk and no longer its youngest hand at any table, who said first, at a sitting called for another matter entirely, that a rule built for the numbers of the old apprenticeship had gone as far as the older custodians' own stretching could carry it, and that Taigh na Fèithe owed itself, if it owed nothing else, an honest look at what remained rather than a continued pretence that nothing had changed.

What Taigh na Fèithe found, when it looked honestly, was seven kindreds among the remaining custodian households large enough, and old enough in the coal's service, to answer for a share of the galleries between them without waiting on a new apprentice's seven years to grow into the work: the households that had stood, at the turn, under the names of Muirich, Fearchar, Ìomhar, Raghnall, Tormod, Coinneach and Lachlann, each with enough hands left to it, counted across its whole kindred and not household by household, to keep a gallery's measure true on its own account. It was not, the older custodians were careful to say among themselves before the matter ever came to a full sitting, a thing done lightly or done because seven was a number the island's tellings favoured; it was done because seven kindreds, and no more nor fewer, were found, on the plain evidence of the roll, to hold between them hands enough for the work that fifteen custodians the year before the turn had needed to hold.

The sitting that set it in order ran the better part of two days, the longest Taigh na Fèithe had held in Donnchadh's own memory, and it was not without its arguing, for a custodian whose household stood outside all seven kindreds, of an old name that had kept a single gallery honourably for three generations but stood too small, after the turn, to answer for a share on its own account, spoke long and with some bitterness against a rule that would fold his household's right into a neighbour's kindred rather than let it stand, however narrowly, on its own feet as it always had. He was heard out to the end, as the custom of the sitting required, and answered by an old woman of Clann Thormoid who said only that she had buried a brother and two nephews to the same roll that had thinned his own household, and that she would sooner see her own right folded into a larger house that could still walk every gallery it answered for, than see it stand alone and proud over galleries it could no longer properly serve; and it was her answer, more than any argument the master of Taigh na Fèithe himself made, that the sitting was afterward said to have turned on.

The right passed, from that year, by house and no longer by the apprenticeship alone: a custodian born into one of the seven, Muirich, Fearchar, Ìomhar, Raghnall, Tormod, Coinneach or Lachlann, held a claim upon the coal's service that an outsider still had to earn by the seven years' apprenticeship as before, but held it now as a birthright of the kindred rather than as a thing each hand had to prove afresh from nothing. The seven heads, chosen by their own kindreds and sworn at Taigh na Fèithe before Crom's stone in the same week the sitting closed, took an oath none of them had taken before, since none of the island's older Laws had ever asked a custodian to answer for a whole kindred's hands rather than his own two, and Donnchadh, who wrote the oath into Leabhar a' Chùraim in the same plain hand he had used for every entry of his working life, found himself, when the seven had sworn and the book lay open to dry, thinking less of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig than of the fifth of hands the sitting had never once, in two days of arguing, troubled to name aloud: the hands that were not there to be stretched or folded or sworn to anything, because they were fifteen years and a whole sea away, on a shore Taigh na Fèithe's own book had no line to enter them against any longer.

## V. Of the Crowning at Cathair dhearg

Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill was seventy and six years old in the summer Taigh na Fèithe swore its seven heads, older by a decade and more than any ruler of her line had lived to be at Cathair dhearg within living memory, and had sat An Talla Dearg for one-and-sixty years, since a girl of fifteen had been crowned in a hall too large for her, before the fleet was so much as spoken of on the western quays. She had outlived the consort who had stood beside her at that first crowning and the sister who had sailed from beneath her own promise, and she had governed, through all of it, in the plain manner the court had come, over six decades, to call simply the queen's way: neither sending nor keeping back, neither swearing to a grief nor forbidding the swearing of it, a hand that measured a boundary ditch on the same morning it measured a fleet's departure and gave neither more of itself than the other seemed to want.

She died at Cathair dhearg that same summer, in the season when the barley stood green and short in the strips above the river, much as it had stood the year she came down to Seann Skell to walk the new quay; and the court, which had watched her grow slow and then slower over the two years before it, was told afterward that she had held the boundary petition of that very morning to its usual end, hearing both farmers out and giving her ruling in the plain voice she had always used for such matters, before she went to her own rooms and did not rise from them again. Seventy and six years old, she was the oldest of her line to sit An Talla Dearg since the years when a ruler's age had meant something other than what any other man's or woman's age meant, and no one at that court thought to remark upon the number, for by then a long life was simply a long life, and a queen who died at seventy-six after one-and-sixty years upon the hall's stone floor had lived and reigned exactly as long, and no longer, than any woman of good health and hard use might reasonably hope to.

Her son was crowned in the same hall within the month, Raghnall mac Uilleim, son of Beathag and of Uilleam mac Iain who had died at the hall six-and-twenty years before, a man of seven-and-forty himself by the year of his crowning, grey already at the temple and no stranger to An Talla Dearg's business, having sat at his mother's board through the greater part of two decades and heard more of the coal-right's disputes and the shires' grain reckonings than most men twice crowned elsewhere on the island ever heard in a lifetime. He was crowned, as his mother had been and her mother before her, in the plain rite of the house of Dòmhnall, no more and no less than the setting of the old circlet upon his head by the eldest custodian present and the reading of his name into the roll of the house; and it was noted, by more than one at that crowning, that he wore, beneath his own crowning colours, a strip of undyed wool at the wrist, worn quietly and without remark, as a man might wear a thing he had grown up watching his mother wear and had never once, in seven-and-forty years, thought to ask her leave to wear himself.

## VI. Of the Empty Place Laid Once More

They kept the wake for Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill three nights at Cathair dhearg, as the house of Dòmhnall had always kept its wakes, the hall lit end to end and the court coming and going through the small hours as custom asked of it, and it was on the second of those nights that the queen's own steward, grown old himself in her service and near the last of those who had served her from her own youth, did the thing that afterward the whole court spoke of longest, though he did it quietly and without any word of ceremony to mark it.

He had the cup, the trencher and the straight knife brought out once more and laid at the board's foot, exactly as they had been laid every evening the queen dined in that hall since she first put on the undyed wool, and left there through the whole of the wake's second night, untouched, as the place had always been left, while the court passed it going to and from the queen's own bier at the hall's head, and few among them, that night, could have said with any certainty which of the two sisters the place was laid for.

It might have been laid, as it had always been laid before, for Mòrag, gone these fifteen years and further from any word reaching Cathair dhearg than she had ever been; the steward himself, asked afterward, would say only that he had laid it as he always laid it, in the manner the queen herself had kept, and that he had not thought, doing it, to lay it for any different reason than the one that had first set it there. But it stood that second night at the foot of a board where the queen herself now lay cold at the hall's other end, and more than one who passed it going to the bier found their eye caught by the small emptiness at the board's foot before it was caught by the greater emptiness at the board's head, and could not, standing between the two, have said honestly which absence weighed the heavier on them, the sister fifteen years across an unanswering sea, or the queen not yet a full day gone from the hall she had sat for one-and-sixty years, both alike unreachable now by any road the living court could travel, and both, that one night, kept in the same plain wool and the same untouched place, as though the hall, having mourned one so long in this fashion, had found in the end that it knew no other way to mourn the second.

# Chapter Twelve: Of the Empty Harbour

*LE 56 – 67*

## I. Of the Boards Given Over

Calum mac Nèill kept the boards of Taigh a' Chalaidh for fifty-six years, and in the last two of them his eyes wanted so much light to read a leaf by that his son Dòmhnall took to holding the lamp close over his shoulder whenever an entry was made, so close that the old man complained, more than once, that his own son meant to set his hair alight before his years did the rest of the work themselves. He died in the between-moon of the fifty-eighth year of the count, at Seann Skell, in the room above the harbour-house where he had slept every night of his keeping, and it is told that the last thing his hand reached for, before it stopped reaching for anything, was the corner of the board nearest his bed, the one on which the earliest names of the roll still stood, cut through where they had been struck and plain where they had not.

He had kept a promise that no one had asked him to keep twice: the boards would not be closed while the queen had not closed them, and they were not closed at his death either, though there was no roll left open on them by then for any household to enter or strike its name from, the fleet eighteen years gone and no new leaving to be counted. What Calum's boards had become, in the years since An Diosal, was less a roll than a wall that the town looked to and did not read closely, the names on it grown as familiar and as little regarded as the harbour-house's own stones, until a stranger asked after one of them and the whole town remembered, for the length of the asking, what the boards were for.

The harbour-house did not go to Dòmhnall, who had held the lamp for his father and had expected, without ever quite saying so aloud, that the office was his by the same right it had been his father's, passed from a scribe before Calum in its turn. It went instead to Niall mac Dhòmhnaill, Dòmhnall's own son, a man of nine-and-twenty who had been eleven years old on the night of An Diosal and had stood on the west quay wall with a hazel stick and a knife, cutting a notch for every hull that went round the pool. Calum had never told the town, in so many words, which of the two men he meant to follow him, but he had begun, in the year before his death, to send for Niall rather than for Dòmhnall whenever a difficult entry wanted a second hand, and the town of Seann Skell, which watched such things closely because it had little else that season to watch, had drawn its own conclusions some while before Calum's will was read aloud at the harbour-house door.

Dòmhnall took it as well as a man takes such a thing when he has had a year to see it coming and no year at all to make his peace with it. He stood at his father's shoulder through the reading of the will, said nothing while it was read, and afterward, alone with Niall on the harbour strand, said only that the boards were the queerest inheritance a man could be passed over for, since no one living had ever grown rich or great from keeping them, and that his father, whatever else he had been, had never once in fifty-six years asked whether the work he gave his whole life to was worth the giving. Niall answered that he did not know either, and that he meant to keep them all the same, and father and son, who had lived in the same house under the same lamp, worked the harbour-house together civilly enough for the rest of that year and every year after, Dòmhnall keeping the trade rolls and the harbour dues, Niall keeping the boards that no household entered any longer and the knife that no hull now needed counting.

He took the stick down from the shelf where it had stood since the night of the turn, the hazel stick with its row of notches cut too fast and too many to be read again for any true count, and he did not put it back. It stood from that day at his own elbow when he sat to write, in the same place his grandfather's ink-horn had always stood, though he used it for nothing and could have told no one, asked, exactly why he kept it there rather than on the shelf with the rest of what Calum had left behind him.

His grandmother Seonag, the goose-keeper Calum had married before Niall's own father was born, outlived her husband by less than a year, and in the months between the two deaths she came down most mornings to the harbour-house to sit by the fire while Niall worked, saying little, watching him form the letters at the board her husband had sat at for fifty-six years. She told him once, in one of those quiet mornings, that Calum had never once in all his keeping told her whether he thought the boards worth the life he had given them, and that she had stopped asking him after the first few years of their marriage, having come to believe that a man who kept such a question to himself that long meant to keep it there for good. Niall did not ask himself, aloud or otherwise, whether his own answer would differ from the one his grandfather had never given, but he noticed, in the years that followed, that he had stopped expecting anyone to ask him.

## II. Of the Lamps Grown about the Berth

No one had ordered a rite kept at the quay the ships had sailed from, and no one, so far as Niall's own boards or his grandfather's before them ever showed, could name the year it began, only that by the time Niall took up the pen it had already the settled shape of a thing long kept rather than newly made. On the eve nearest the day of An Diosal, as near as the harbour-house's own dating let anyone reckon it after so many years without a fixed count, the households of Seann Skell that had given someone to the roll, and a good number that had not, brought down to the west quay whatever small light they could carry, a rushlight, a fish-oil lamp, a coal from the hearth wrapped close in a clay pot against the wind off the water, and set it along the stones where the fleet had lain, and stood a while, and went home again without a word said over it that anyone thought worth remembering.

Niall had gone down himself, the first autumn of his keeping, more from a scribe's habit of wanting to see for himself what he might one day be asked to write of than from any devotion of his own, and had stood at the edge of it with his grandfather's stick, which he had brought without quite meaning to, held loose in one hand. The rite was not large by then, a few dozen lamps along stones that had once held the whole west quay's worth of light on a single night, and half those who kept it were old enough to remember the sailing themselves, or old enough at least to have been told of it young by someone who did. He watched an old woman he did not know set her lamp down at the very edge of the stone where the ships had lain, closest of any that were set that night, and stand over it a long while with her lips moving and no sound coming from them that he could make out, and when she had gone he asked a boy nearby, one of the harbour-house's own runners, whose lamp it had been, and the boy said only that it was old Mairead's, that she came every year, and that no one now living knew for certain which of her kin the lamp was kept for, since she herself, asked, gave a different name most years.

He wrote it into his own leaf that night, not because any board required an entry of a rite the crown had never ordered and Taigh na Fèithe had never asked after, but because it seemed to him, turning the matter over by his own late lamp, that a harbour scribe who wrote down every dispute over a cracked hull and every barrel landed at the quay and said nothing of the one night in the year when half the town came down to the water with a light in its hand, was keeping a stranger kind of silence than any his grandfather had ever kept before him. The entry he made was short, and it named no one, and it has outlasted every longer thing he wrote that year.

## III. Of the Harbour at Half Trade

Murchadh mac Raghnaill, harbour-master of Seann Skell, was of an age with Niall and had held his own office a year longer, having been given the berths and the dues of the harbour by a predecessor who retired to his daughter's house up the Abhainn naomh rather than die at his post as Calum had. It was Murchadh's business, not Niall's, to count what trade the harbour carried, and in the sixth year of Niall's keeping he brought his own count to the harbour-house door and set it beside the boards for anyone to read, a plain reckoning of the berths that stood empty against the berths that stood full on an ordinary market morning, and it showed, without any softening he cared to give it, that the harbour of Seann Skell carried, that year, not much more than half the trade it had carried before An Diosal.

It was not a mystery to either man why this should be so, and Murchadh did not write it as though it were one. The fishing households that had crewed the greater part of the fleet's boats before the turn, and had gone in no small number aboard the fleet itself, had left both fewer hands to work the harbour's boats and fewer mouths at Seann Skell to buy what those boats brought in, and the rope-walks along Cuan shean's stretch of the waterfront, which had once kept every hand they could hire twisting hemp against the fleet's endless want of cordage, found themselves that same year with more rope made than the harbour's remaining trade could use, and let hands go for the first time in the memory of anyone still walking the walks, old men who had twisted rope there since before the sailing and had never once, in all those years, seen the walk's own master turn a willing hand away.

Murchadh's reckoning was matter-of-fact where a lesser clerk's might have reached for grief, and Niall, reading it over at the harbour-house board, found himself wondering, not for the first time, whether the harbour-master's plainness came from a harder heart than his own or only from a kind of mercy that wore the shape of bookkeeping. He copied the figures into his own boards without comment, as his grandfather would have done, and set Murchadh's leaf beside Rolla nan Deònach on the same wall, the names of those who had gone and the count of what their going had cost the harbour they left behind, side by side on stones that had room enough, by then, for both.

## IV. Of the Word that Came and Was Not Written

In the seventh year of his keeping a boat put in at Seann Skell from up the coast with a hand aboard, a man Niall did not know and never learned the name of, who told it in the taproom of a house near the strand, over the second cup rather than the first, that he had heard from a cousin who had heard it from a trader out of Ceann mhòr that a second fleet, smaller than the first and gone by a different season, had put out from somewhere on the island's own shore in the years just after An Diosal, and had likewise never been heard from since.

It reached Niall the following morning, brought to him by the same runner who had told him whose lamp burned closest to the quay-stone, the boy repeating it with the particular relish of someone passing on a thing he has been told twice already and half believes for the telling's own sake, and Niall listened to the whole of it standing at his board with his pen already in his hand, as he had a hundred other pieces of harbour gossip in his years of keeping. He asked the boy who the man was and where his boat had gone, and got no clear answer to either, and asked whether anyone else in the taproom had heard the same tale from any other mouth before that night, and got, again, nothing he could set his hand to.

He did not write it. In seven years at the boards he had written a great many things a stranger might have judged smaller and stranger than this: a dispute over a landed catch's true weight, a fight between two carters over a berth neither had paid for, the exact hour a lost child was found asleep under an upturned coble. A tale with no name behind it and no second mouth to confirm it, he judged, was not a harbour matter at all, whatever else it might be, and the boards, his grandfather had taught him before he could properly hold the pen, were not the place for a thing a scribe could not stand behind. He thought of it again, once or twice, in the weeks after, turning it over the way a man turns over a ring he is not sure is good silver, and each time set it aside unwritten, until the thinking of it, too, grew less frequent, and at last stopped.

Dòmhnall, told of it over the trade rolls one evening, asked his son outright why he would not set down even so much as the hearing of it, a rumour being a fact of a kind in its own right, whatever the truth or falsehood of what it rumoured, and Niall answered that a boat's dues were a fact of that kind and a rumour was not, and that he did not mean to spend the rest of his life discovering where the difference between the two ran thin. Dòmhnall let the matter drop, as he had let a good many matters drop between them since the will was read, but it is told that he repeated the tale once or twice after, in the ordinary way of a man passing on harbour gossip, careful each time to say that the harbour-house's own scribe had heard it too and set it aside, as though Niall's silence carried a kind of authority the tale could be hung on.

## V. Of the Watch at Ceann mhòr

Twenty miles up the coast at Ceann mhòr, in the same year the rope-walks let their first hands go, a fisher's daughter named Seonag nic Dhùghaill climbed the headland above the town at first light on a morning no different, so far as anyone could afterward say, from any other morning, and stood there through the whole of the day's turning, looking out over open water, and came down again at dusk having seen nothing but gulls and a change of weather coming in from the west.

She had lost no one to the fleet herself, her own family being newer to Ceann mhòr than the sailing was old, but she had grown up on tellings of it from older fishing folk of the town who had, and she said afterward, when asked why she had gone up, only that it seemed to her a thing someone ought to be doing, and that she did not see why it should not be her. Other households of Ceann mhòr, hearing what she had done, began within the season to take a turn of their own on the headland, a day at a time, household by household, so that by the year's end there was scarcely a week the headland stood unwatched from first light to dusk, and the custom, which had no name at its beginning beyond "Seonag's watch", came in time to be called simply Faire a' Chinn, by fisher-folk up and down that stretch of coast who had never met Seonag herself and knew her only as the woman who had started it.

No sail was ever seen from that headland in Seonag's own lifetime, nor, so far as the harbour-house at Seann Skell ever had report of, in the lifetime of anyone who kept the watch after her, and it is told that she herself, asked late in her years whether she still believed a sail might come, said only that a watch kept for a sure thing was no watch at all, and that she had climbed the headland the first morning expecting nothing, and had found, in the not-finding, reason enough to climb it again.

## VI. Of the New Name and the Old

By the eighth year of Niall's keeping the old name of the west quay, the plain harbour name it had carried since before the roll was ever opened, had begun to fall out of common mouths at Seann Skell in favour of a newer one that no one could point to a single day of coining, Cidhe an Diosail, spoken now by carters and fish-wives and children too young to have known anyone who sailed from it, as though the stones had never been called anything else. The harbour-house's own boards had kept the old name a while longer than the town's own mouths had, out of a scribe's habitual caution about changing what stood written, but in the ninth year, with the old name gone so thoroughly from ordinary speech that a stranger asking after it by its old form was as likely as not to be misunderstood, Niall entered the new name into Rolla a' Chalaidh himself, in his own hand, Cidhe an Diosail, and let the old name stand beside it once, crossed through but not scraped, in the manner his grandfather had taught every apprentice of that board: a struck name stays visible.

The name that passed out of use at the west quay found a use elsewhere. Cidhe an Iar, the west quay's own old name, was taken up that same year by the fishers of the new wharf built at the strand's north end to handle the catch that no longer had the old quay's room to land at, and within a season or two the fishers who worked it used the name for their own wharf without, so far as Niall could tell, any sense that they had inherited it from anywhere, or any thought at all for where it had come from.

It was in the same years, and in no entry Niall could point to as the first, that he began to notice Rolla a' Chalaidh using a word he had grown up hearing spoken only with an object, roghnaich, to choose this or that, now standing alone in a clerk's hand, a household roghnaich, chose, with nothing following it that any reader needed told, since every reader by then knew well enough what a household that had chosen, unqualified, had chosen to do. He used the word so himself, once or twice, before he noticed he had done it, and when he did notice, he let the usage stand in his own leaf rather than correct it to the fuller, older form, judging, as his grandfather might have judged before him, that a scribe's business was to write the tongue his town actually spoke rather than the tongue it had once spoken and no longer troubled to.

## VII. Of the Children Who Never Saw It

Niall had, by the ninth year of his keeping, three children of his own grown near enough to grown that they helped about the harbour-house on a market day, and none of the three, nor any child born at Seann Skell in a dozen years and more before them, had ever seen the west quay with a fleet of nineteen hulls, or one-and-twenty, lying at it, waiting on a tide. To them the sailing was a thing told rather than a thing remembered, a story their own father kept the boards of and could point to the stones of, no different in its bones from any other tale an old woman might tell a child at a winter hearth, save that this one had a harbour-house full of leaves to back it and a wall of names a child could run a finger along and ask, of any one of them, who that had been.

His eldest daughter, a girl of ten that year, asked him once, watching him enter an ordinary day's dues, whether he himself had seen the ships go, and he told her that he had, that he had stood on the very wall she was leaning against with a stick in his hand cutting notches for the counting of them, and she looked at the wall a long while after he had told her, as though trying to see upon it something her own eyes could not find there, and asked no more that day. He did not correct whatever she had imagined in the looking, and did not know, himself, what it was she had hoped to see.

## VIII. Of the Last Coaster and the Last Entry

Alasdair mac Iain, Alasdair Saor, who had laid the first deep keel any hand on the island had ever laid, and had redrawn it in sand by a driftwood fire after the first hull lay down and drowned eleven souls off the headland, and had bound the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into one fellowship and seen a boy of that fellowship sworn before a custodian in the manner of the vein, was by the sixty-seventh year of the count an old man bent nearly double over the same strand he had first walked to Doire fhionn from as a young one, and still, to the last season of his life, unwilling to let a hull leave his yard that he had not laid a hand to himself.

His last work was a small thing beside the deep-keeled hulls of the fleet, a sewn-plank coaster of the old kind built for a fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh who wanted nothing grander than a boat that would carry his catch to market and bring him home again dry, and Alasdair built it that spring as he had built every boat before it, going down himself to check the set of every plank though his hands by then shook too much to hold an adze steady for more than a few strokes at a time, leaving the finer work to the journeymen he had trained and trusting, as he had trusted the fellowship's oath for sixty years, that a hand he had taught would not betray the eye that had taught it.

The coaster was launched at Inis àrsaidh in the last days of the moon of Teasach, and Alasdair died at Seann Skell before the week was out, at the end of that same summer, in the yard where he had laid the first frames of the fleet's first hull like the ribs of a beast on the open strand. Niall entered his death the same day the word of it reached the harbour-house, in the ordinary hand he kept for every death the town brought to his boards, and set beside it, on the same leaf, in the same sitting, the entry he had been putting off making for the better part of a year: that the west quay, called of old by a plainer name, stood now and would stand hereafter in Rolla a' Chalaidh as Cidhe an Diosail, and that the name it had given up passed, by the town's own usage rather than any order of his, to the wharf at the strand's north end.

He sat with the two entries a while after the ink of both had dried, the old shipwright's death and the quay's new name, set down one above the other on a leaf no different in its ruling from any other leaf in the harbour-house's long keeping, and it is told that he said to no one in particular, closing the book, a line the harbour folk of Seann Skell were already saying of their own accord by then, of one thing and another, though he may have been the first to set it down: is fhada an cuan, is goirid a' chuimhne. Long is the sea, and short is memory. He banked the harbour-house's night fire himself, the boy whose office it was having gone home early, and set his grandfather's stick back in its place at his elbow for the next day's writing, exactly where it had stood every night since the boards were given over to him.

# Chapter Thirteen: Of the Moulds in the Fire

*LE 68 – 109*

> *Beathaich an seabhag, ach na sàsaich e.*
> Feed the hawk, but do not glut him.
>
> — the first saying in Leabhar an t-Seabhaig

## I. Of the Fellowship After Alasdair

Coinneach mac Fhearghais had been the first apprentice Alasdair Saor ever swore, a boy of fourteen with a stammer and hands too big for the rest of him, and he was the last of that first swearing left alive when the old man's yard passed to him. He kept the stammer into old age, worse when he was angered and gone almost entirely when he was easy, and the wrights of the fellowship had long since stopped remarking on it, the way a household stops remarking on a low door once every member of it has learned to duck. He took the mastership of the fellowship of the strand as Alasdair had held it, by the plain fact that no one else living had built so many hulls under the old man's own eye, and he kept the fellowship's oath and its coal exactly as it had been kept before him, swearing no fewer apprentices than the yard could rightly feed and turning away, more than once, a father who came with a willing son and no craft in the boy's hands to show for it.

There was less for the fellowship to build by then than there had been in Alasdair's day, no one on the island wanting a hull that meant to lose sight of land, and the yard at Seann Skell that had once laid three keels at a time to the fleet's own hunger kept, in Coinneach's years, to one coaster at a season and sometimes none, the wrights filling the slack months with the mending of fish-boats and the cutting of oars for households that had never owned a boat worth the name. Coinneach never complained of it where any apprentice could hear him. Niall, who came down to the strand most autumns to enter the yard's launches in his boards, noticed that the old man had taken to standing longer than the work wanted over each new keel laid, running a flat hand along the wood the way another man might run a hand along a horse he did not expect to keep much longer.

Niall asked him once, the autumn he came down to enter a coaster no grander than any of the season's before it, whether a small boat built to carry a fish merchant's catch to market gave a wright the same satisfaction a deep-keeled hull once had, and Coinneach was a long while answering, turning the question over the way he turned over a plank before he trusted an adze to it. He said at last, the stammer catching only on the first word, that a boat was a boat whatever water it was built to cross, and that a man who could not find his satisfaction in a coaster well built had likely never had much satisfaction in a hull's building at all, only in the size of the thing he had built, which was a different pride and a smaller one. Niall wrote none of that down, judging it a wright's own business rather than the harbour-house's. He remembered it all the same, and in the years that followed set the same question to more than one man who complained to him of smaller work than he had once been given.

In his seven-and-seventieth year he told his eldest journeyman, a quiet man named Griogair who had been with him since before his own beard came in grey, that he did not think he would see another spring's launching from the strand himself, and he said it without any weight in his voice that Griogair could afterward point to as grief, only as a fact set down the way Coinneach set down every fact, plainly and once. He died the following winter, in the between-moon that comes some years to true out the count with the sun, in the same house on the strand where he had lived since his marriage, and it is told that his last words, got out whole and without the old stammer for the first time in years his family could remember, were that the fellowship's coal was to go to Griogair and to no one else, whatever any elder journeyman might claim by right of years alone. Niall entered the death the day word of it reached the harbour-house, and set beside it, from old habit rather than any instruction from the boy himself, the note that Coinneach mac Fhearghais had been the last man living who remembered kneeling on the shingle with Alasdair Saor's own hand over his.

## II. Of the Last Journeymen and the Moulds Burned

Griogair kept the fellowship sixteen years more, and it is told of those sixteen years only that they were quiet ones, the yard laying its one coaster a season as before and losing, each year, an apprentice or two to households that had work nearer home and no patience left for an oath that fed a man no faster than the sea did. In the eighty-fourth year of the count Griogair called what journeymen the fellowship still had to the strand at the season's turning and told them, without ceremony, that there was not craft enough left in the ordering of the island's own boats to keep an oath sworn for the building of a fleet, and that he meant to release every man there from it and close the fellowship's coal himself, being the last to hold it and having no wife's son to pass it to. The journeymen took the release as men take a thing they have half expected for years and half hoped would not come in their own time: some went to the rope-walks at Cuan shean, some to farm the strips their fathers had left them, and one, a young man called Tòmas who had sworn only two years before, walked the whole way to Doire fhionn to learn the woodward's craft among the stumps of the old grove, saying to anyone who asked that a trade with a future in it, however small, was worth more than the memory of one that had none. Griogair kept for himself only his own tools and the last coaster laid before the release, a boat he finished alone over the following winter with no journeyman left to hand him a plank, and sold it at spring to the same fish merchant of Inis àrsaidh whose father had bought Alasdair's own last hull, saying nothing of the fellowship's ending to the merchant beyond that the price would be a little higher, there being no apprentice's wage to spread the cost across any longer.

Niall entered the fellowship's closing in the boards the day Griogair brought him word of it, and found, setting down the entry, that he did not know what heading to give it under, Rolla a' Chalaidh having no place kept for the ending of an oath that no one had thought to enter as a beginning, Alasdair having sworn his first apprentices on the open shingle with no scribe there to write it down. He set it, in the end, under the same heading he had used for the launching of every hull the fellowship had ever built, judging that an ending belonged with its beginnings whatever the boards' own ruling said, and let the matter stand.

The following winter came in hard and early, the worst any living at Seann Skell could remember, and in the depth of Faolach, the storm-moon, with the town's own store of driftwood and cut peat running thinner than any household cared to own to its neighbours, someone went into the shed on the strand where the fellowship's old patterns and keel-moulds had stood since the fleet's own building, untouched by anyone in years, and carried the whole of it out board by board to be burned. No name was ever set to whose hand did the carrying, and none of the households that burned that wood in their own hearths that winter thought, so far as anyone afterward owned, that they were burning anything more than seasoned oak cut to no purpose any man living still had use for. Murchadh mac Raghnaill, the harbour-master, noted in his own reckoning that the fellowship's shed on the strand had come down that winter and its ground stood empty, and wrote nothing of what the shed had held, the moulds and patterns by which every hull of the fleet had been laid true having by then passed so far out of any use that their going seemed to him no more a loss than the pulling-down of an old fence. Niall, reading Murchadh's leaf at the harbour-house board, thought of asking after it, and did not, telling himself that a scribe who chased down every burned plank in a hard winter would have no ink left for anything else the town wanted written.

## III. Of a King's Death and a Line in the Custody-Book

Word came to Seann Skell some weeks late, as word from Cathair dhearg generally did, that Raghnall mac Uilleim, who had held An Talla Dearg since Niall was a young man, had died in his eighty-fifth year, and that the heads of the shires had crowned his son Raghnall mac Raghnaill in his place without dispute, the new king seven-and-forty years old and already grey at the temples when the crown was set on him. Niall entered the death and the crowning on the same leaf, as Leabhar a' Chùraim at Cathair dhearg was said to have done before him, one line for the reign that had just closed and one for the reign beginning, and found, turning the matter over afterward, that he could not himself recall a single thing the old king had done in the whole of his seven-and-thirty years on the hall that a harbour scribe at Seann Skell would have had cause to write down. It was not, he thought, that Raghnall mac Uilleim's reign had wanted for length; it was that it had wanted, so far as the west coast ever heard of it, for anything happening in it at all, the vein measured out as it had always been measured, the shires kept as they had always been kept, and Rolla a' Chalaidh of Seann Skell no fuller nor emptier for a change of crown than they would have been for a change of season.

The town kept no rite for the old king's death beyond what any household kept for its own dead, a light set out and a word said, and the taprooms along the strand talked more, in the weeks the news was fresh, of the hard winter just past and the fellowship's burned shed than of the man who had worn the crown for seven-and-thirty years and left it, by every account that reached the west coast, exactly as he had found it. Niall wrote the new king's name into the boards under the old one and did not, this once, add anything of his own beside it, judging that a scribe who had nothing to say of a reign owed that reign at least the honesty of his silence.

Dòmhnall, keeping the trade rolls at the same board, said once, reading the two lines over his son's shoulder, that a king who left nothing behind him for a harbour scribe to write was perhaps the kindest king a coast so far from An Talla Dearg could hope for, since every king the west coast's own tellings remembered with any weight had cost it a war, a levy, or a fleet, and Niall allowed that this might be so, though he added that he would not himself care to be remembered, when his own boards were closed, by two bare lines and nothing beside them. Dòmhnall answered that a harbour scribe's own boards were a different matter entirely from a king's reign, being read by fewer eyes and closer ones, and the two men let the question drop there, as they let most questions drop by then, having worked the same board together long enough to know which ones were worth pressing and which were not.

## IV. Of the Death of Niall mac Dhòmhnaill

Niall kept the harbour-house boards six-and-forty years in all, ten fewer than his grandfather Calum had kept them, and in his last years his own hand grew as unsteady over a leaf as Calum's had been, though it was his sight that held and his fingers that failed him, the opposite trouble from the one he had watched close in on the old man in the room above the harbour-house when he himself was a boy holding the lamp. He worked to the very end of his strength, entering a small dispute over a landed catch's weight in the same careful hand he had used for every dispute of forty years before it, and it is told that the entry stands unfinished in the boards to this day, the last stroke of the last letter trailing off where his hand stopped rather than where the sense of the sentence did.

He died in the season of Bealltach of the hundred-and-fourth year of the count, at Seann Skell, five-and-seventy years old, in the harbour-house rather than in any bed, having been carried there by his own wish when it grew plain to those about him that he would not see the next morning out. In the last hours anyone sat with him he asked for his grandfather's hazel stick to be brought and set in his hand, the same stick he had carried down as a boy of eleven to the west quay wall on the night of An Diosal, and he held it a long while without speaking, running his thumb along the row of notches cut too fast and too many to be read again for any true count. Those who sat with him afterward could not agree, comparing what they remembered of that night, whether he had said anything at all in the hours before the end, or whether the working of his lips they took for speech had been no more than the working of an old man's breath. What is agreed is that he never once, in six-and-forty years at the boards nor in the hour of his death, told any living soul the number he had come to, privately, in all the years since that night, for the hulls that went round the pool at the turn; and the stick passed, at his own asking, into the ground with him rather than to the shelf, so that whatever count it had held for him, cut too fast on a boy's knee in the dark, went with it.

His eldest daughter, grown by then to a woman with children of her own about the harbour-house, asked him once, in the last year of his life, whether he had ever settled the count for himself, having heard him spoken of all her childhood as the boy who counted the hulls. He told her, she said afterward, that a man who had spent forty years keeping other men's counts honest owed his own the same honesty, and that an honest count, once cut in haste on a dark quay by a boy of eleven with cold hands and a bad light, could not be mended by an old man's wishing at his own fireside forty years on, whatever number the wishing might land on. She did not ask him again, and the boards of Seann Skell passed, in the season after his death, to hands the harbour-house had already chosen against the day, the office running on as offices at Seann Skell had always run on, one keeper's leaf taken up where the last one's had stopped.

## V. Of the Coal-Breakers Below the Hill

At Muileann dhearg, below Taigh na Fèithe where the coal-road came down off the hill, a man named Eachann Briseadair had for some years kept a shed of his own, of a different kind from the fellowship's, where the raw coal brought down from the galleries was broken and sorted before it went out to the shires under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's own measure. He had learned the breaking from his father, who had learned it from a custodian of Taigh na Fèithe two generations before either of them, and he was, by the seventieth year of the count, the only man on the hill whose own household did the whole of the work rather than hiring it out season by season to whoever's hands were free.

It is told at Muileann dhearg that Eachann built his first house of stone below Taigh na Fèithe's own gate in the two-and-seventieth year, his sons and their wives building three more beside it within the decade, so that what had been a scatter of turf shielings at the foot of the hill became, before Eachann himself was an old man, a settled row of houses with its own well and its own smith, known at first only as the coal-breakers' row and in time, once it had grown past what any one word for a scatter of houses could properly hold, by the name Taigh na Fèithe had long given the whole of that ground: Muileann dhearg, the red mill, for the colour the dust of the breaking left on every stone and every hand that worked there. Eachann lived to see it a town in more than name, with its own reeve answering to Taigh na Fèithe rather than to any shire, and died in it at sixty, in the same shed where he had broken his first load of coal as a boy at his father's side, his own sons by then old enough to keep the work without him and his grandsons already learning it at their fathers' hands, the way the breaking had come down to Eachann himself.

He was buried, at his own asking, on the rise above the shed rather than within it, where a man standing at his grave could see the whole of the row he had raised and the coal-road climbing past it to Taigh na Fèithe gate, and it is told that his eldest son set no stone over him beyond a lump of the coal itself, unbroken, judging that his father would rather be marked by the thing his hands had spent a life breaking than by anything a mason could cut for him. The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe, hearing of it, sent down no objection, the coal being Eachann's by Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's own measure to burn or to keep as any household chose, and the stone-that-was-not-a-stone stood on the rise above Muileann dhearg for longer than any household there could afterward say, weathering no differently than Taigh na Fèithe's own walls did.

Donnchadh mac Thormoid, who had kept Taigh na Fèithe's own boards since he was fifteen years old and had by the seventieth year of the count grown into the office as fully as any man grows into a coat cut for him young, entered Eachann's first house in his own leaves the season it was raised, and it was in that same season, or near enough to it that Donnchadh himself could never afterward be certain which had come first, that word reached Taigh na Fèithe from Cathair dhearg that the crown's own scribes at An Talla Dearg had begun to date their rolls by the count he himself had kept alone at Muileann dhearg for near thirty years, setting aside the reckoning by any king's reign for the turning he had first set his own hand to as a clerk of thirty with no one asking him to. He said nothing of it to anyone about him when the word reached him, only sat a while at his own board with the leaf before him unmarked, and it is told that he wrote, at the foot of that day's ordinary entry, a single line that named no pride and claimed no credit, only that An Talla Dearg now counted its years as Muileann dhearg had long counted its own, and let the matter stand at that.

## VI. Of the Lots Drawn Among the Seven Houses

Na Seachd Taighean that held the right to the coal under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig had each, since the houses were made, kept a claim on this gallery or that within the vein without any settled order to which house's claim ran deepest, and disputes over a gallery's true bounds had grown, in Donnchadh's own years at the boards, frequent enough that the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe judged the matter could not be left to grow any older before it was settled once for all. In the hundred-and-ninth year of the count, a generation after the fellowship at Seann Skell had released its last journeymen, the heads of Na Seachd Taighean were called to Muileann dhearg and set, each in turn, to draw a stone from a covered bag before the custodians and the whole household of Taigh na Fèithe looking on, each stone marked in a hand none of the houses' own heads could read, so that no house might afterward claim its gallery had been given rather than drawn.

Donnchadh kept the boards that day as he kept every day, but he wrote afterward, in his own private hand rather than in Taigh na Fèithe's formal rolls, that he had never in all his years at Muileann dhearg seen seven grown heads of houses stand so still nor speak so little as they stood and spoke while the bag went from hand to hand, each drawing his stone and reading its mark aloud to the custodian before any other man in the hall was let see it. The galleries fell as the stones fell, some houses drawing deep and rich ground and others drawing thin, and it is told that not one head among the seven, in all the years that followed, was ever heard to say aloud that his own house's stone had wronged it, whatever might have been said of it in private at his own hearth. The stones themselves, once every gallery was claimed and entered, went back into the same bag they had been drawn from, and the bag was hung on a peg in Taigh na Fèithe's own hall rather than broken up or put away, so that any man who doubted the drawing might come and see the very stones that had made it.

## VII. Of the Stones Shown to a Visitor

That same year Donnchadh was an old man in his own right, the youngest apprentice at Taigh na Fèithe calling him, without any unkindness meant by it, the oldest thing on the hill after the coal, and it fell to him more often than to any custodian to show a visitor about the hall when one came, Taigh na Fèithe's affairs by then running largely on the memory of a scribe who had kept them longer than anyone else living. A grandson of Eachann Briseadair's, a boy of ten sent up from the coal-breakers' row on some errand of his father's, found himself waiting a while in Taigh na Fèithe's hall for the custodian he had been sent to, and Donnchadh, seeing him stand alone and plainly curious rather than put a task in front of him, took the bag down from its peg and let him hold it.

The boy asked what the stones were for, and Donnchadh told him, in fewer words than the telling had ever taken him before, of the day the seven heads had stood in that same hall and drawn them, and of how no house since had ever been heard to say the drawing had wronged it. He did not tell the boy which stone had fallen to which house, judging that the boy's own family, being coal-breakers and not among the seven, had no more claim on that knowledge than any other visitor might, and the boy, turning the stones over in the bag with the plain interest of a child handling a thing older than his own grandfather, asked only whether the stones were magic, and Donnchadh told him, honestly, that he did not know, having never asked a custodian the question and not meaning to begin asking it now, in his own last years, when the not-knowing had served him well enough for fifty. He hung the bag back on its peg before the custodian came, and the boy went off to his errand having learned, so far as Donnchadh could tell, only that Taigh na Fèithe kept old stones in a bag and an old man who would talk of them if a boy stood still long enough to be talked to.

## VIII. Of the Last Entry

Donnchadh wrote, in the same season the boy had come and gone, the last entry Taigh na Fèithe's own boards ever received from his hand: the season's burning of coal, household by household, in the measure Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig had held since Fionnlagh Dall, set down in the same careful order he had set it down every season since he first took up the boards at fifteen, beginning with Na Seachd Taighean in the order their galleries had fallen at the drawing and ending, as it had always ended, with the coal-breakers' row that answered to Taigh na Fèithe rather than to any house's claim. He died that same season, at Muileann dhearg, in the room above the hall where he had slept since his father first walked him up the coal-road as a boy, and it is told that a custodian, comparing the last leaf of his hand against the first he had entered at fifteen, could find no difference between them that any stranger to both would have thought worth remarking, the same careful order and the same plain hand at five-and-ninety that had been set down at fifteen.

No one at Muileann dhearg troubled to say, over his grave, anything grander than that the boards had lost the only hand that had ever kept them, since none living could remember another, and Taigh na Fèithe went on, in the season that followed, exactly as it had gone on through every season of his keeping, the coal broken and measured and carried down the road below the hill to the row of houses that bore his own count in their gate as surely as the crown itself now bore it in An Talla Dearg's rolls. The bag of Clachan a' Chrannchuir hung where it had hung since the drawing, on its peg in Taigh na Fèithe's hall, and no hand troubled to take it down again for some while after, the boy from the coal-breakers' row being the last, for a long season, to have held it and turned it over and set it, unread, back in its place.

# Chapter Fourteen: Of the King the Houses Made

*LE 125 – 211*

## I. Of Two Lines in One Book

At Cathair dhearg in LE 125 King Raghnall mac Raghnaill died in his eightieth year, and Leabhar a' Chùraim gave him, as it had given his father before him, a single line: the name, the year, and no more. His son Ìomhar mac Raghnaill was crowned in the same hall the same season, three-and-thirty years old and already the father of a boy of his own, and it is told that the old men of the court, remembering the father's crowning three-and-thirty years before, said there was little to choose between the two days beyond the faces, the same silver cup passed from hand to hand and the same oath said in the same words over it. The reign that followed was long and it was quiet, and a quiet reign, as the harbour scribes of the west coast had already learned to say of Raghnall mac Uilleim's, is the kind that leaves the least for any book to hold.

Yet the years were not empty, only unhurried, and a teller who wishes to be honest with them must find room for what filled them, small as it was beside a crowning or a death. At Muileann chiar, where a seam of silver had been worked since An Aois Naomh within four families who called themselves the smiths of the seam, LE 149 saw the fellowship's oldest craft turned at last to a use beyond its own trade: rings of the pale metal, broad enough to sit close about the throat, beaten out for the heads of Na Seachd Taighean to wear at Taigh na Fèithe and at An Talla Dearg alike, so that a stranger new to the court might know a custodian from any other lord by the collar at his neck before a word was said. Inis mhòr in the north, in those same years, put barges on the Abhainn ghorm to carry its grain down to Caol bheag and along the coast to Cnoc bheag, sewn-plank boats of the old pattern that never lay a night out of sight of land, for no one on the island since the fleet had wished to be out of sight of it; and it is told that a boy of Inis mhòr, watching the first barge loaded, asked his father why a boat so laden should not simply go the shorter way across open water, and got for his answer only a look, and no word at all.

In LE 156 a coughing sickness ran through Caol fhiadhaich on the south-west coast and killed some ten of its people before it burned itself out, fewer than a hard winter alone might have taken, and the reeve of that shore held, afterward, that it was the shared meal kept through the whole of the sickness, every household eating at the one board rather than shutting its door against its neighbours, that had kept the number so small. It is told that the reeve's own wife was the first to fall sick, and that she herself would not let her own door be barred against the board, saying that a household that ate apart out of fear would go on eating apart long after the fear had any cause, and that a shore so small could not afford the habit. She lived, and the custom lived after her: the board was still shared at Caol fhiadhaich, sickness in the shore or none, when the cough was remembered by no one but the reeve's own book, and it is told there, in a hand grown old, that the meal had by then outlived the memory of why it was ever begun.

Whether the meal or the mercy of the season deserved the credit for how few the cough took, no one at Caol fhiadhaich troubled to settle, holding that a shore glad of its own dead being few had better things to spend its arguing on than the reason for it.

It is in the leaves of Taigh na Fèithe, not An Talla Dearg's, that the fullest word of those years is kept, for Ìomhar's own reign left the crown's scribes little to enter beyond the ordinary turning of the shires, while the custodians of Muileann dhearg went on measuring the handful, hearth by hearth, exactly as Fionnlagh Dall had first measured it, Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig untouched by a change of king any more than the tide is touched by one. The scribe who kept those leaves after old Donnchadh mac Thormoid — a younger cousin of his own line, trained at Donnchadh's own elbow in his last years and given the boards on his death — wrote of King Ìomhar chiefly that he came up to the mountain twice in every year to see the galleries walked and the measures sealed, as the kings of his line had done since Beathag's day, and asked, each time he came, after the health of whichever house's head happened to be standing nearest him, a small courtesy that cost him nothing and that more than one house remembered of him long after they had forgotten anything else he had ever said or done.

He is remembered at Muileann dhearg, too, for one habit no king before or after him is recorded as keeping: he would stand at the mouth of whichever gallery was being walked that day and ask the youngest hand present, whether a bound child of seven years or a journeyman of twenty, to name for him the parts of the working he could see from where he stood, the prop, the cut, the tally-mark on the wall showing how far that season's measure had already gone. Some of the custodians thought it a king's idle amusement and no more; Taigh na Fèithe's own scribe, who watched him do it a dozen times across as many years, wrote once that it seemed to him less amusement than a kind of counting of his own, a king who had no child to leave the hall to making certain, gallery by gallery, that the hands who would go on working it after him at least knew what they held in them. He never said as much himself, and no one thought, while he lived, to ask him.

## II. Of a Boy at Baile Mòr dhomhain

Fearchar mac Lachlainn was born in the house of Clann Fhearchair at Baile Mòr dhomhain, the elder son, and yet the one who, by every reckoning his own family made in his boyhood, was least likely ever to be asked to carry anything heavier than his own name. His younger brother Iain was the one their father set, from the time either of them could walk, to keep the house's hall when he should be gone; Fearchar was given instead to Taigh na Fèithe's own custom, a boy's seven years bound to a custodian's household to learn the galleries and the measures as every child of Na Seachd Taighean was meant to learn them, whether or not he was ever to sit at the head of his own table. He came home from that binding at fourteen knowing the weight of a sealed measure by its heft alone and the sound a gallery makes when its timbering has begun, quietly, to fail, knowledge that served him, in the years that followed, rather better than anyone in his own house had thought to expect it would.

He kept, into his own old age, one memory of those seven years that he told often enough to his own children that it passed down in the house of Clann Fhearchair as a small story of its own: a night in his eleventh year when the custodian he was bound to woke every hand in the gallery, the boy among them, because a timber had begun to sing, a low steady note none of the older men could place until the custodian herself set her ear against the wood and named it, and had the whole gallery cleared before the prop gave way an hour later with no one beneath it. Fearchar remembered standing outside in the cold with the other bound children, none of them told plainly what the noise had meant, and understanding all the same, from the set of the grown faces around him, that the vein answered to more than a measure and a season, and that a house's right to the coal was worth exactly as much as the care the house put into listening for what the coal had to say. It was a lesson, he used to tell his own sons afterward, that no crown he ever wore taught him any better than a mountain gallery had taught a boy of eleven standing in the dark.

He was seven years old, by his own later telling, when word came to Baile Mòr dhomhain that Am Buabhall Fortanach, the old road-house on the mountain road, had burned to its footings in LE 164, and that its keeper Eilidh nic Chaluim meant to raise it again in stone rather than in the timber it had always stood in before. He remembered, or believed he remembered, riding out with his father to see the new walls going up, and being given, by Eilidh herself, a bowl of the jugged buffalo the house was already known for before its own roof was finished, and thinking, as a boy of seven thinks of such things, that a house built to outlast fire was a fine thing for a man to leave behind him, better than a crown, which he had not then any reason to think about at all.

Thirteen years old, Fearchar heard his father's letters tell the house of Clann Fhearchair that King Ìomhar's only son, Raghnall Beag, had died of a fever at Cathair dhearg, a boy not much older than himself, and he remembered his father saying, low, over the letter, that a king with no other child was a house with one wall standing, and that the wind would find it sooner or later whatever anyone did. Fearchar did not understand, at thirteen, what his father meant by it, and did not ask, judging correctly enough that a boy who asked too many questions of a letter that troubled his elders was likely to be sent from the room before he got an answer.

The spirit-house the keepers of Na Seann Spioradan raised at Dùn ìseal in LE 179, where the dead of the eastern shires had their names cut new on wooden posts each generation as the old posts rotted away, was a thing Fearchar came to know only at second hand, for Baile Mòr dhomhain kept its own dead by its own older custom and sent no names east to be cut on another shire's posts; but it is told that he visited it once as a young man, on a journey with his father to the eastern coast, and stood a long while before the posts reading names he knew nothing of, and said afterward only that a shire that cut its dead's names in wood rather than stone must trust its own memory further than he would care to trust his.

He was three-and-twenty, newly married and settled to what he believed would be the whole of his life, keeping his own small share of his house's galleries and answering to his brother Iain in every matter that touched the hall, when word reached Baile Mòr dhomhain in LE 180 that King Ìomhar mac Raghnaill had died at Cathair dhearg with no living child, the line that ran back through Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill and the queen who had neither sent her sister nor kept her ended in a single sentence in Leabhar a' Chùraim, and that the heads of Na Seachd Taighean were summoned to the capital to choose, for the first time since An Diosal, a king the crown's own blood had not simply handed down to them.

## III. Of the Silences in the Yard

Iain went up to Cathair dhearg as the head of Clann Fhearchair's own house, for their father was three years dead by then and had named him to the headship, and Fearchar went with him only as an elder brother who kept the galleries and had no more claim on the meeting than any other custodian. He remembered the yard of An Talla Dearg as smaller than he had pictured it from his father's tellings, and colder, the seven neck-rings of Muileann chiar catching what little sun there was as the heads stood in a loose ring about the well and said, for the better part of a morning, nothing at all that any of them could afterward be brought to repeat in full.

It was the head of Clann Ìomhair who broke the silence first, saying only that the line of Beathag had held the hall a hundred years and more and that no house among the seven had any better claim to it than another, which was less an argument for any one name than a plain statement that the argument, once begun, would not end quickly; and it was the head of Clann Mhuirich, the oldest of the seven present and the one whose own house had given most of Coimheadaichean na Lasrach in An Aois Naomh, who said, after a further silence, that a hall so long kept by inheritance might do better kept, this once, by choosing, since a house chosen rather than born to the crown would know from its first day what it owed the six that had chosen it. No one answered her directly, but the silence that followed her words was of a different kind than the one before it, and Iain, standing at his brother's shoulder, felt the meeting turn, though he could not afterward have said on what hinge.

They spoke Iain's own name before the day was out, as head of a house whose galleries ran deep and whose dealings with the other six had never once, in living memory, come to open quarrel, and it was Iain himself who turned it aside, saying plainly that a man who kept one house's hall well enough might yet keep a kingdom's poorly, and that he for one would rather be remembered as a fair head of Clann Fhearchair than a middling king of Dia-thìr. A murmur went round the ring at that, less agreement than the sound seven tired people make when a hard morning has at last produced one sentence plain enough to hold onto, and it was into that murmur that Iain named his own brother, standing beside him in the yard with nothing to say for himself, a custodian of no particular note who had spent his own seven years among the galleries and knew, better than any man born to a hall, what Taigh na Fèithe asked of the houses that answered to it.

Fearchar felt every face in the ring turn to him at once, and remembered afterward that his first thought, before fear or refusal or any grander feeling had time to reach him, was a plain wish that he had worn a better coat, having ridden up from Baile Mòr dhomhain expecting nothing of the day beyond standing at his brother's shoulder and going home again unremarked. The head of Clann Raghnaill, a broad man with a scar across one brow who had said nothing at all until then, asked him outright, in the flat way of a custodian asking after a season's measure, whether he could read a gallery's timbering by ear, and Fearchar, too startled to judge whether the question was mockery or something else, answered honestly that he could, or had been able to once, as a bound child, and had had no cause since to test whether the ear for it stayed with a man once his seven years were done. It is told that the head of Clann Raghnaill said nothing further to that, only nodded once, as a custodian nods when an answer has satisfied a question he did not trouble to explain the reason for asking.

Fearchar's own account of what followed, given years later to his son and kept in the family's own memory rather than in any leaf of Taigh na Fèithe, was that he tried three times to refuse before the heads would hear him refused, saying first that he was a younger son with no training for a hall, then that his own house had a better claim in his brother, and last, when neither answer moved them, that he did not want the thing, which he judged, and rightly, to be the one argument likeliest to move seven heads who had spent a whole morning weighing a crown too heavy for any one house to want alone. It was the head of Clann Mhuirich who answered that last refusal, saying that a man who did not want the crown was, of the men in that yard, the only kind she would trust to wear it, and it is told that no one spoke again after she had said it, the seven neck-rings catching the last of the light as the heads, one after another, bent their own heads to a man who had not asked to be chosen and could give them no better reason to choose him than that he had not asked.

He was crowned at Cathair dhearg in 19 an Gearran, LE 182, five-and-twenty years old, the first king in Leabhar a' Chùraim's own memory set on the hall by Na Seachd Taighean standing in a cold yard until their silence turned, of its own weight, into a name, rather than by the blood of the hall before him. No silver cup was found ready for the rite, the last having been put away at Ìomhar's death with no clear order for its keeping, and it is told that the head of Clann Mhuirich sent a servant running to her own lodging for the cup her own house kept, a plainer vessel than the crown's own would have been, so that Fearchar mac Lachlainn drank his first oath as king from a cup that belonged, strictly, to none of Na Seachd Taighean and to one of them alone, a small confusion no one thought worth correcting once the oath was said.

## IV. Of the Double Court

He kept the crown nine-and-twenty years, and it is told at Baile Mòr dhomhain, though seldom at An Talla Dearg, that he never once in all those years stopped thinking of himself as a custodian who happened to sit a throne rather than a king who happened to know the galleries. He divided his court from the second year of his reign, keeping the greater part of each year at Cathair dhearg as every crowned ruler before him had done, and a lesser part at Baile Mòr dhomhain among his own house and within an easy ride of Taigh na Fèithe, so that no matter that touched the coal need wait on a rider's journey to reach him. The double court settled, by LE 194, into a custom his own house kept for as long as it held the crown, and it was Iain who kept Clann Fhearchair's hall at Baile Mòr dhomhain whenever the court was away at the capital, a headship within a headship that suited him, by his own account, a great deal better than a crown ever would have.
