The two brothers wrote to one another through every season of the division, letters that a later hand at Baile Mòr dhomhain gathered and kept as one leaf-book rather than let scatter through the house's leaves, and it is from those letters, more than from anything An Talla Dearg's own scribes set down, that the plainer texture of the reign is known: a dispute over a boundary stone between two shires settled by Fearchar in three lines and referred back to Iain to see enforced; a petition from a widow of Muileann dhearg for a second season's measure after a bad year, granted; a complaint, more than once repeated in Iain's own hand, that the capital's cooks put too much salt in a dish that had never wanted it at Baile Mòr dhomhain, over which the two brothers seem to have corresponded at greater length than over any single matter of the coal in the whole of the reign.

Fishers of Àth fhiadhaich, on the eastern coast, joined in one fellowship in LE 209 after a season of losses no single household could carry alone, three boats lost in one autumn's weather and two households left with neither boat nor the timber to build another, sharing boats and nets thereafter among families who had fished the same waters apart from one another for longer than any of them could say why. A fisherman of that shore, sent up to Baile Mòr dhomhain the following spring on some ordinary errand of tribute, was brought before the old king almost by accident, the household he lodged with having mentioned, in passing, that he came from the coast where the new fellowship had lately been made, and Fearchar kept him a full hour asking after the manner of it: how the boats were shared, whose name a catch was entered under, what was done when one household's boat failed and another's held. The fisherman, by his own account given, years afterward, to his own grandchildren, had expected a king's questions to be grander than a fellowship's own accounting, and found himself instead answering much the same questions any custodian might have asked of a gallery's sharing among Na Seachd Taighean, and it was only riding home that it came to him what the old king had truly been asking after all along: the fellowship, and whether a thing built from loss could be trusted to hold once the loss was forgotten.

The founding was read out, when word of it first reached Baile Mòr dhomhain, as a small thing beside the coal and the crown, though Fearchar himself is said to have remarked, after that hour with the fisherman, that a fellowship made from loss rather than plenty was likely to outlast one made the easier way, having already proved, before it was a year old, that its members would stand by one another when standing by one another cost something. It was a saying his own house kept after him, said sometimes of the coal-right when Na Seachd Taighean' own dealings grew strained, though never, so far as the leaf-book records, in his own hearing.

He grew old at the work slowly and without complaint, riding between his two halls until the riding grew hard, and in his last years he kept, more than any other habit of his reign, the one he had carried up from his own boyhood among the galleries: he went on asking the youngest hand at any working he visited to name what stood before him, prop and cut and tally-mark, though by then his own knees would no longer let him crouch at a gallery's mouth to hear the answer, and a custodian would crouch for him and repeat the child's words up into the light. His own son Fearchar Donn, brought to the mountain young as his father had been, was asked the same question at seven years old as every other bound child was asked it, and gave, by the account kept at Muileann dhearg, an answer no better and no worse than any other child's, which the old king is said to have called, laughing, the first honestly ordinary thing his own house had produced in two reigns.

He died, in the end, at Baile Mòr dhomhain in LE 211, among his own house rather than at An Talla Dearg, four-and-fifty years old, his brother Iain at his bedside and his own son, called Fearchar Donn for the colour of his hair, already a grown man ready to take the hall without dispute from any of the seven. He asked, in his last days, that no coal be burned beyond the ordinary handful for any rite made over him, saying that a custodian who had spent a lifetime measuring the vein for other households had no wish to be measured out of it more generously than any tenant of his own galleries would be, and Taigh na Fèithe kept the asking to the letter, so that the fire lit for the old king's own rite was, by every account, no larger than the fire any house of the seven lit for its own dead that same season. They buried him, as his own father had been buried, in the ground of Clann Fhearchair rather than in any royal tomb at the capital, and it is told that Na Seachd Taighean sent their heads to stand at the grave, each still wearing the neck-ring of Muileann chiar his own house had worn since before Fearchar was crowned, and that not one of them, in the whole of the burying, was heard to say that the choosing made in that cold yard nine-and-twenty years before had been anything other than the right one. Fearchar Donn was crowned at Cathair dhearg within the season, without dispute from any house, the first son to follow a father the houses themselves had made, and so the crown, having once been chosen rather than inherited, went back, as if it had never left it, to the plainer road of a son following a father into the hall.

# Chapter Fifteen: Of the Hawk of Acaill

*LE 215 – 251*

## I. Of the Glove at Cnoc bheag

At Cnoc bheag, up the river from the coast where the dawn-hawk rite of An Aois Naomh had been kept without a break since before the fleet, the mews stood on the shoulder of the hill above the shrine, and the keeping of it had passed, as far back as anyone at Cnoc bheag could say, from father to child and never once to a stranger. Artair had kept it since before his own daughter was born, and by the time this telling opens he was five-and-sixty years old and had kept it the better part of his life, his hands grown too stiff in the cold mornings to knot a jess without help and his knees no longer equal to the climb from the shrine to the mews block before first light. His daughter Gormshuil climbed it for him now, most mornings, and had done since she was a girl old enough to carry a hawk on her own wrist without her arm shaking, though it was still Artair, sitting on the bench below with a blanket over his knees, who called up which bird was to fly and in what order, as his own father had called it up to him.

The shrine below the mews was a plain thing, a ring of standing stones no higher than a man's shoulder about a bare patch of turf worn down to the earth by feet, with a single stone taller than the rest set at the eastern edge for the sun to clear before the flying began. It drew, in the ordinary way of things, the households of the hill and the river-bend below it, coal-cutters and their wives come up before the day's work to stand in the cold and watch a bird cross the grey sky and come back to a glove, and go down again to their fires no wiser for it than they had come, save that a morning begun at the shrine was reckoned, by long custom, a morning less likely to end badly. Gormshuil had known most of those faces her whole life, and could have named, without troubling to think, which households sent their eldest daughter to watch and which sent a servant in their place, and what each family's coal-right at Taigh na Fèithe came to that season, for the talk on the shrine's ledge before the flying ran as often to the size of the next handful as to the bird.

It was a young bird, not yet a full year in the mews, that gave them the lesson Gormshuil would carry the rest of her life, though neither of them thought it more than a bad morning at the time. A novice keeper new to the mews that season, eager to see the bird fly well before the rite's watchers, had fed it heavy the evening before, thinking a full crop would make for a calm bird and a steady flight. It made instead a bird that sat on the block at first light with its feathers loose and its eye half shut, and when Gormshuil raised her glove and called it, it looked at her, and looked away, and would not come. She called it twice more. The third time Artair, without being asked, said from the bench below that there was no use calling a bird that had already eaten its fill of the day before it began, and that she might as well save her wrist and let it sit.

"It will not fly hungry either," said the novice, red in the face, thinking he was being corrected for a fault rather than told a fact. "I have seen a starved one snap at the glove."

"You have seen right," Artair said, "and wrong in the same breath, which is the whole trouble with hawks and most other things besides. Feed it too little and it turns on the hand that starves it. Feed it too much and it will not leave the hand at all. There is one measure between the two, and it is not a wide one, and it is not the same for every bird or every morning, which is why the keeping of it is a craft and not a rule a man could write once and be done with." He looked up at his daughter, who still stood with her arm out and the sullen bird ignoring her. "Bring it down and don't fly it today. Let the novice sit with it and learn its crop by his own eye instead of by his fear of being wrong in front of the shrine."

Gormshuil brought the bird down, and said nothing at the time of what her father had said, turning it over instead in the weeks that followed the way a person turns over any true thing said carelessly, testing it against other true things until it either breaks or holds. It held. She had grown up hearing the shrine's telling that the hawk of the dawn rite was no common bird of the mews but stood for one far older, one the keepers before her father's father's father had called Mòd, and said to be as old as Fionntan mac Bòchra, eldest of men, who remembered all things with him from before there was a shrine to keep or a mews to keep it in; she had heard that telling so often it had worn as smooth in her mind as a step worn hollow by feet, a thing repeated rather than thought. It was her father's plain word about a young bird's crop, not the old telling, that first made her think hard about the measure rather than the bird that carried it.

Three years on, Artair's knees had failed him for the climb entirely, and it was Gormshuil, not the novice nor any other keeper of the mews, who went up alone in the grey before dawn and called Mòd down from the block for the first time with no one but herself to answer for the flight. She was three-and-thirty years old that morning, by her own later count, and she would say afterward, to the few who asked her directly, that she had gone up frightened of the bird and come down frightened of something else, though she was slow for a long while to say what. Her father, watching from the bench with his blanket over his knees, said only, when she came down to him, that Mòd had flown as well for her as for any keeper he had watched in a long life, and that a bird cared nothing at all for whose wrist it left so long as the wrist knew the measure, which was the last thing of any weight he told her before his own strength failed him further and his talk turned, as an old man's talk will, to smaller things: the weather, the state of the mews roof, whether the novice keeper had learned yet to judge a crop by his own eye instead of by fright.

## II. Of the Empty Perch

Artair died at Cnoc bheag five years after the morning of the overfed bird, in his own bed above the shrine with his daughter beside him, three-score and ten years old, and the mews he had kept the better part of his life passed to Gormshuil without dispute, as it had passed to him and to his father before that. They buried him on the hillside above the mews, in the plain way the hill's own households buried their dead, wrapped in undyed cloth and laid with his face to the shrine rather than to any house of the departed the coast might have kept for him, since a keeper of the mews was reckoned, on that hill, to belong to the birds and the standing stones before he belonged to any other rite. The coal-cutters and their wives who had stood so many mornings on the shrine's ledge came up in numbers greater than the ledge had ever held for a living rite, and it was noted afterward, by those who noted such things, that not one household of the hill sent a servant in its own stead that day.

The shrine kept its rite the morning after his burying as it kept it every morning, because a rite that stops for a death is a rite that will stop again for the next one, and Gormshuil went up to the block in the grey light with her father not two days in the ground and called Mòd down herself, dry-eyed at the flying and not dry-eyed after it, alone on the hillside where no one from the shrine below could see her face.

It was in the weeks of her mourning, when the watchers who came to the shrine asked her, as was the custom, to say a few words over her father's empty place on the bench, that she first put into open speech what she had turned over quietly since the overfed bird. She told them her father's plain word about the measure, and then, because the watchers waited for more and she found she had more to give them, she told them that the hawk of the rite was Mòd himself, old as Fionntan mac Bòchra and remembering with him all that the island had forgotten of its own beginning, and that the vein under Muileann dhearg, which fed every hearth on the island its handful and no more, was a hawk of that same kind: a hungry hawk, to be fed the measured handful and starved of nothing it truly needed, but never once glutted past what the giving hand could spare. A hawk overfed will not hunt, she told them, and a hawk starved will turn on the hand that starves it, and the keeping of the measure between the two was not a rule written once at Taigh na Fèithe and left to stand, any more than a bird's crop could be judged once and trusted for every morning after. It wanted watching, the way her father had watched it, all his life and to the day his knees gave out under him.

The watchers who heard her that first time were mostly her father's own people, keepers and their households who had come to the shrine for years and would have listened to Gormshuil nic Artair out of long habit whatever she had said over the empty bench. But she said the same thing again the next season, and the one after, shaping it a little further each time without changing what stood at the centre of it, and it began, in the slow way such things begin, to be spoken of beyond the shrine's own households, still nameless as a teaching, only a thing the hawk-keeper's daughter at Cnoc bheag said over the bird, worth a morning's walk to hear for oneself.

## III. Of Those Who Came to Hear

Word of it reached the north coast before it reached the capital, carried, as such things were carried on the island, by the ordinary business of trade rather than by any messenger sent for the purpose: a wool-buyer of Bàgh an t-Seabhaig who had business at Cnoc bheag over a debt of hides heard Gormshuil speak one dawn while he waited for the shrine's steward to finish the shrine's own accounts, and carried the telling home with the hides, embroidering it a little in the carrying as such tellings are embroidered, so that by the time it reached the hawk-keepers of the coast it had already begun to sound less like a woman's plain word over her father's empty seat and more like a teaching worth sending someone to hear at first hand. Three keepers of the coastal shrines came inland that same year to judge it for themselves, and stayed a week, sleeping in the mews steward's own house and rising each dawn to stand at the back of the shrine's ledge among the coal-cutters' wives, saying little until the week was nearly out. The eldest of the three, a woman near Gormshuil's own age who had kept a shrine on Bàgh an t-Seabhaig since before Gormshuil was a hawk-keeper's daughter at all, asked her on the last morning whether she had ever herself gone hungry enough to know the second half of what she taught, or only ever watched a bird do it for her. Gormshuil answered that she had gone hungry twice in her life that she counted, once as a child in a hard winter and once the week her father died, and that she had disliked the lesson both times and kept it both times besides, which the elder judged, after turning it over a moment, answer enough. The three went home saying the teaching had lost nothing in the carrying after all, which was unusual enough to be remembered on its own account.

Within a few years more, and without Taigh na Fèithe's own scribes troubling themselves over what was said at a hillside shrine two days' walk from the capital, the watchers who climbed to Cnoc bheag for the dawn rite had grown from the handful of her father's own households to a congregation the shrine's ledge could no longer easily hold, and Gormshuil, who had never asked to be more than her father's daughter keeping her father's mews, found herself asked, more mornings than not, to say the teaching whole rather than in the pieces it had first come out in. She gathered it, in the end, into the shape it would keep for the rest of her life and after it: that Mòd, Seabhag Acaill, was old as Fionntan mac Bòchra and remembered with him what the island no longer remembered of its own first years; that every hearth's coal was a feeding of An Seabhag Acrach beneath the mountain, owed the measured handful and no more; and that the craft of keeping the measure, in a mews or at a vein-house both, was a watching that wanted doing fresh each time, never a law fixed once for every morning after, just as her father had watched a young bird's crop rather than trust a rule written the year before.

Those who heard the teaching whole, gathered under one roof rather than caught in pieces on the shrine's ledge, called themselves before long a house rather than a congregation, and in LE 229 they set about raising one: a low hall of timber and dry stone below the mews block, roofed before the following winter, that took the name Taigh an t-Seabhaig, the house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig, and gave the old dawn-hawk rite of Cnoc bheag, for the first time in its long keeping, a hall of its own rather than an open hillside and a shrine ledge worn hollow by generations of standing feet. Gormshuil kept the mews as she always had, and kept the house besides, though she said, more than once to those close enough to hear her say it, that she would rather have gone on calling Mòd down to an empty hillside than to a hall full of watchers waiting for her to speak, and was believed by those who knew her, and not quite believed by those who did not.

## IV. Of the House at Ros gheal and the Flood at Seann Vell

The teaching did not stay at Cnoc bheag. Among the watchers who had climbed the hill in the years the house was building were two of Gormshuil's own pupils, a brother and sister of a coastal household at Ros gheal, who asked her leave to carry the dawn rite down to the shore rather than make every fisher's family of that coast walk two days inland to hear it. She gave them the leave, and something more besides: she went down to Ros gheal herself in LE 239, the season the second house was raised, to see the first rite kept there and to judge, as her father had once judged a young bird's crop by his own eye, whether the teaching had travelled whole or had thinned on the road the way a telling carried by a wool-buyer will thin. The rite at Ros gheal was kept on a spit of rock above the tide-line rather than a hillside turf, its ring of stones half salt-eaten already, and a wind off the sea made the hawk's flight a shorter, harder thing than the still air of Cnoc bheag's morning; the fishers who stood at the ledge there smelled of net-tar and brine rather than of coal-smoke, and asked the pupils, when the flying was done, after the size of the season's catch rather than the size of any hearth's handful. Gormshuil judged the teaching had travelled whole enough for all that, though the sea air and the salt-caked stone of the coast gave it a harder edge than the hillside's had, and she came home content to let the house at Ros gheal keep its own measure of it rather than ask it back to Cnoc bheag word for word. Between the two houses, her pupils took on the country that lay between the coast and the hill, so that a shire that had once sent every dying hearth's household two days inland for the rite could now walk half a day to the shore instead.

It was a pupil of the Ros gheal house who brought her, some years after, the report she remembered longest of any that reached her at Cnoc bheag, though she had no part in the flood and never travelled far enough south-east to see it with her own eyes. In LE 244, a wet spring, the river at Seann Vell, far off on the south-east coast, rose in a night past every bank the mill-wrights had trusted, and carried the lower mills of that town away whole, wheel and stone and all, so that the millers of Seann Vell had to build again on the higher ground the following season, cursing, as millers everywhere curse, a river that had kept its banks faithfully for longer than any living miller could remember and chose that one wet spring to break them. The pupil who brought the report to Cnoc bheag had gone to Seann Vell on other business and stood on the higher bank himself, watching the new mills go up, and he told Gormshuil, half in earnest and half hoping to please her, that the flood was a kind of overfed hawk: a river fed too full too fast, turning on the hand that had trusted it. She heard him out, and told him plainly, in front of the others who had gathered to hear the report, that a river was a river and not a hawk, and that a teaching stretched to cover every misfortune under the sky stopped, before long, covering anything at all; a keeper who saw the measure in a hawk's crop and nowhere else had understood it better than one who saw it everywhere and had therefore, in the end, seen it nowhere. It was remembered afterward, among her own pupils, as one of the harder things she ever said to a young man trying to flatter her, and one of the truer. She sent him back to Seann Vell before the season turned, not with any correction to carry to the millers, who wanted none, but with a plain instruction to stand a while longer on the higher bank and watch how the new mills were set before he judged a whole river by one wet spring; he went, and came back the following year saying only that the wheels turned as well on the higher ground as they ever had on the lower, which she thought, though she did not say so to him, the better report of the two.

## V. Of the Marked Sayings

Gormshuil kept the mews and the house both into her own old age, calling Mòd down from the block most mornings until her hands, like her father's before her, grew too stiff for the climb, and after that sitting on the bench below where her father had once sat, watching a younger keeper fly the bird and saying, when she was asked, no more and no less than the measure wanted. She grew, in those last years, sparer of speech than she had been as a younger woman gathering the teaching into its shape, as though she had come to trust that the shape once given would hold its own weight without her standing over it every dawn to prop it up, and those who sat with her on the bench in the cold remembered her as often silent as speaking, watching the flight with the same close, unhurried eye her father had once turned on a young bird's crop.

She died at Cnoc bheag, two-and-sixty years old, in the same season the house at Ros gheal marked its own eighth year, and was buried, at her own asking made long before, on the open hillside above it, beside her father, rather than within the new hall she had raised, where the dawn rite had been kept before there was any roof over it at all.

Among those who had sat longest at her teaching was a young man of the house named Ùisdean mac Pàdraig, who had come to Cnoc bheag as a boy to be apprenticed to the mews and stayed to be apprenticed, in the end, more to the teaching than to the birds. It fell to him, in the years after her death, to gather what she had said into a single book, so that a teaching that had travelled by wool-buyers and pupils and half-remembered reports for thirty years might be kept in one hand rather than scattered across every household that had ever heard her speak. He set himself, before he wrote a word of it down, one rule he never afterward broke: that every saying he set on the leaf without having heard it from her own mouth would be marked as such, plainly, so that no reader coming after him would mistake another keeper's memory of her for his own. To fill the book at all he had to travel further than he had ever travelled in her lifetime, down to the salt-eaten shrine at Ros gheal and along the country between it and the hill, sitting with pupils grown old themselves now and asking them, patiently, to give him back word for word what they remembered her saying, and marking, more often than not, that two households a day's walk apart remembered the same saying in two different shapes, so that he was left to choose which shape to set down and mark the choice as his own rather than hers. He kept the rule to the letter for all that, and when the book was finished the marked sayings, gathered from every house and shire the teaching had reached in her lifetime, far outnumbered the few he had heard for himself, standing at the bench below the mews block on mornings when he was too young to know he was hearing anything worth marking at all.

He finished the book in LE 251 and called it Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, and set at its head, before any of the sayings he had gathered from other hands, the one he had heard himself, standing below the block on an ordinary morning with the mews still smelling of the night's straw and Gormshuil's voice carrying down to him no louder than she needed it to carry, the whole of the teaching folded, as she had once folded her father's plain word about a young bird's crop, into a single line short enough for a child to carry home unbroken:

> *Beathaich an seabhag, ach na sàsaich e.*
> Feed the hawk, but do not glut him.

# Chapter Sixteen: Of the Firlot of Cathair dhearg

*LE 254 – 289*

## I. Of the Girl Who Counted the Baskets

Sìleas nic Fhearchair was eleven years old when she first understood that a king's word was only as good as the thing it was measured against. She stood that day at her father's elbow in the market below An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg, where two women had come near to blows over a basket of barley. One swore it held its full weight; the other swore it did not, and that she had been cheated by the same basket twice before at the same stall. King Fearchar Donn, grown heavy and slow with age by then and disliking to be drawn from his hall for such things, sent a steward to weigh the grain against the palace's own measure and settle it. The steward came back and said the baskets did not agree: the market's was smaller than the hall's by the width of two fingers across the rim, and had been for longer than anyone selling there could remember.

"Then whose is the true one?" Sìleas asked, before anyone had thought to ask it of her.

Her father laughed, not unkindly, and said that was a question for men older than either of them, and led her away by the hand. She did not forget it. That night at supper she asked him again, in front of the steward, whether the market's basket or the hall's was the true one, and the steward answered that the hall's was, being the elder measure, and her father said only that it hardly mattered which was elder so long as folk agreed on one, and went back to his meat. She turned the two answers over in her head for days, the steward's and her father's, and could not make them into a single thought, and kept trying anyway, for she was a child who did not like leaving a thing half understood.

She was a quiet child, given to watching rather than speaking, and the court took her silences for shyness until it learned better. Her mother had died birthing her; the one brother she had been born after had died a child, and she had no sister, only her father's slow decline and the hall full of men who spoke over her head as though she were a stool set in the wrong place. She learned early to sit very still at the edge of a council and be forgotten, and to carry away afterward more of what had been said than any of the men who had said it would have credited a girl of her years with keeping.

Fearchar Donn had reigned since he was a young man, son of the first king the custodian houses ever chose, and he wore his last years like a coat too heavy for the season. His last ride north to Muileann dhearg, to see Taigh na Fèithe's winter burning as every king before him had gone at least once, fell in his fifty-ninth year, and he never made the ride again. He sat in An Talla Dearg and let the shires send their disputes to him on skins and boards, and answered them slower each year, until the answers came so slow that the shires had generally settled the matter themselves before the king's word reached them.

In the spring of LE 256 he took to his bed with a cough that would not leave his chest, and did not rise from it again. Sìleas sat with him through the worst of it, thirteen years old, dry-eyed because she had already grieved him in pieces over the preceding years and had none left to spend on the last of him. He died in the month of Bealltach, sixty-eight years old, and was carried up to be laid among the kings at the burying-ground behind the hall.

She was not crowned that year, nor the next. The custom the houses kept, and had kept since the choosing that made her grandfather's line, held that no one too young to be answered for their own oath should be crowned to make one, and thirteen was reckoned too young. The heads of the seven custodian houses, who had sworn to keep the vein and the right to it in the year of an Tùrsa Geal, took it in turn to sit the hall in her name, a month at a time, and quarrelled among themselves over which of their number should have her ear. She learned in those two years to tell a man's true business from the business he gave as his reason for coming, and she learned it well, for she had nothing else to do but listen.

## II. Of the Crowning at Fifteen

She was crowned in the moon of Damhrach, LE 258, fifteen years old, in the same hall where her father had died and his father before him. The cup that was passed hand to hand at a crowning was old beyond any teller's naming of it, worn thin at the lip where generations of royal mouths had touched it, and the oath said over it was the same oath, word for word, that had been said over Fearchar mac Lachlainn when the houses chose him. Sìleas said it in a clear voice that carried to the back of the hall, and an old woman near the door, who had heard four crownings in her life, said afterward that the girl's voice had not shaken at all, which the old woman took for a good sign and was not wrong to.

She did not weep, and she did not smile. She took the cup, drank from it, and handed it on, and the heads of Na Seachd Taighean came forward one by one and put their hands between hers and swore to hold the vein and its right as it had always been held. Their faces she watched as they did it, the way she had learned to watch faces in the two years of the regency, and marked which of them meant it and which of them were only saying words that custom required, though she said nothing of what she marked, then or for years after.

That night, alone in the chamber that had been her father's, she found the old market steward's tally of the two baskets, still among his leaves where no one had thought to clear it. She kept it. It was a small thing to keep, a scrap that answered nothing by itself, but she was a girl who kept small things until they came useful, and this one came useful sooner than she expected.

## III. Of Am Fuath Mòr and the Hooked Wall

In the autumn of her second year crowned, a storm out of the north broke over the harbour of Seann Toll, on the island's north coast, that the fishers there came to call Am Fuath Mòr. It came in the black of night with no warning the watch could give, and it took the old harbour wall down in one working of the sea, stone from stone, and with the wall went forty boats at their moorings and eighteen men and women who had gone down in the dark to try to save them. The town buried its dead on the headland above the ruined wall, in a row so long that the reeve who kept the count lost his place twice and had to begin it again.

The reeve was a young man named Raghnall mac Nèill, thirty-four years old that winter, who had held the office only four years and had never buried so many at once. He had gone down to the strand himself in the worst of the storm, roused by a boy pounding on his door, and had stood in water to his knees hauling on a rope with three other men to bring in a boat with two children still lashed inside it, and had not been quick enough with two more ropes that broke before they were ever thrown. He carried that failure with him the rest of his life and never once, in any letter or telling that survives of him, laid the blame anywhere but on the wall.

That spring he wrote to the capital, not asking for grain or silver, which the crown could ill spare after a hard season, but asking leave to send to the masons who had built the queen's own bridge and ask them what a wall might be built to, that the sea could not take down twice.

Sìleas granted it without a council, which some of the older heads thought unqueenly of her, a girl of seventeen deciding a matter of stone and mortar on her own word. She had read Raghnall's letter twice and noted that it asked for nothing but knowledge, and thought that a request worth granting on its own account. The masons went north and stood a long while on the ruined headland with Raghnall, turning stones over with their boots and arguing among themselves in a tongue of angles and courses that the fishers standing about could not follow. What they gave him in the end was a plan for a wall built higher than the old one and turned at its outer end in a hook, so that the worst of the sea's push broke against the curve of it and spent itself before it could reach the harbour behind.

It took three years to raise, stone hauled from a quarry two days inland by cart and sled, and every able hand in the town given over to it in the slack months between one catch and the next. There were those in the town who grumbled that a hook at the wall's end was a strange shape for honest stone, more suited, they said, to a fish-trap than a harbour, and would not believe it until they saw the first winter gale come on and watched the sea's whole strength break against the curve of it and slide away spent, no higher at the harbour's throat than on a calm evening. Raghnall stood on the finished wall the day the last course was set and put his palm flat against the stone, the way a man tests a beast's flank before he trusts it, and it stood through every storm that came after, in his lifetime and long past it.

## IV. Of the Walls of Dùn dhearg and a Supper Kept Cold

The same year the mason's plan went north to Seann Toll, Sìleas took a consort of her own choosing: Dùghall mac Ìomhair, a young man of the eastern hill-house Clann Ìomhair, whom she had known since the two years of her regency, when his father had sat the hall in her name for one of the twelve months and brought his son along to the capital because there was no one else to leave him with. Dùghall was quiet in a way she found she liked, slow to speak and slower to promise, and where the other heads' sons had courted her with gifts and verses she had never asked for, he had once, in her sixteenth year, simply told her which of the men speaking to her in the hall that day meant what they said and which were only speaking to be seen speaking, and been right about all six. They were married at Cathair dhearg in the month of Faolach, with Na Seachd Taighean' heads in attendance and Raghnall mac Nèill's letter about the wall arriving, by chance, the same week, so that the wedding feast and the granting of the masons were spoken of together for a season after, as though one had somehow caused the other. At the feast Dùghall's father rose and made the kind of speech a father makes at such a thing, full of the honour done his house and the long friendship between it and the crown, and Sìleas, watching him say it, thought she heard under the honour a note of a man reckoning what the marriage had bought him, though she could not then have said what she thought he meant to spend it on.

It was not a full year later that word came from the east that Clann Ìomhair had begun to wall their own seat at Dùn dhearg in stone, without asking the crown's leave to do it. No custodian house had raised walls of its own before; the crown had always been asked, if only as a form, and the form had always been granted, but this time no one had asked. Sìleas heard it first from a rider and said nothing for the length of a held breath, then asked only how far along the work stood, which told the rider she meant to let it stand rather than to send men to pull it down, though she gave no word either way that day.

She summoned Dùghall's father to An Talla Dearg that season, on some other business that both of them understood to be a pretext, and had a supper laid for him in the hall's smaller chamber, the one kept for guests who were neither strangers nor quite family. It was a good supper, by every account that survives of it: fowl and barley bread and the last of the summer's fruit, laid out with proper care, and good candles burned rather than the tallow the chamber usually made do with. No one who was in the room that evening ever called it a warm one. Dùghall sat between his wife and his father and said almost nothing through the whole of it, turning his cup on the board without drinking from it, and his father, for his part, ate well and spoke of the roads and the harvest and never once mentioned the stone going up around his own hall, and neither did the queen. Twice the old man asked after her health with a warmth that fooled no one at the table, and twice she answered him with the same warmth, in the same measure, and both of them understood exactly what was being said by everything that was left unsaid.

When the meat was cleared the old man made as if to speak of the roads a third time, and Sìleas set down her own cup with enough plainness that he heard it, and asked him instead how the quarrying went at Dùn dhearg, since she had heard the stone there cut cleaner than the stone at Cathair dhearg's own quarries. He allowed that it did. She said she was glad to hear a custodian house so well provided in its own hills that it need trouble the crown for nothing, not even leave, and let the silence that followed sit as long as it wished to. When the old man rose to go, she walked him to the door herself, which was more courtesy than the evening had otherwise shown him, and told him only that a house wise enough to wall itself was wise enough to remember whose land it stood on. He bowed and said nothing to that either, and the walls of Dùn dhearg went up all the same, and stood, and no crown's men were ever sent against them.

## V. Of the Quarrel over a Basket

It was in that same year, riding to the market below the hall on some ordinary business she no longer troubled to remember afterward, that Sìleas came on a quarrel over a basket that put her in mind of the one she had watched as a child of eleven. She did not get down from the cart. She sat above the crowd and watched a woman selling oats and a farmer buying them come near to open blows over whether the basket between them held what it was sworn to hold, and heard, under the shouting, the same complaint she had heard as a girl: that the baskets of the market were not the baskets of the shire seat, nor the shire seat's the same as the next shire's, and a man might be cheated or might cheat without either party quite meaning it, simply because no two measures on the island agreed.

That same evening she sent for the old steward's tally, the scrap she had kept since her crowning night, and set it beside her on the table while she wrote out, in her own hand, what she meant to do. There would be one measure, and one only, cut to a fixed size and bound in iron so that no season's swelling or shrinking of the wood could cheat it, and copies of it, exact to the width of a finger, sent to every shire seat on the island, so that a basket weighed true at Cathair dhearg would weigh true anywhere a Dia-thìrich stood to sell or buy. She had the first of them made by the capital's own coopers, oak staves bound with three iron hoops, and had her own mark burned into the base of it before it left her hands, so that no one could ever claim a later copy was truer than the standard it was copied from. It went out from Cathair dhearg by cart, one to each shire seat, through the summer and autumn of that year, and the shires came to call it, simply, the firlot of Cathair dhearg, for they had no other name to give it and needed none.

It did not end every quarrel over a basket; nothing so simple ever does. But within a handful of years a man buying grain a hundred miles from the capital could set his own basket against the shire seat's firlot and know, without argument, whether he had been cheated or had cheated, and where before the answer to that question had depended on which of the two disputants shouted longer, it now depended on nothing but the iron-bound oak, which shouted at no one.

The first quarrel it settled outright, and the first that was ever written down as settled by it and nothing else, was at Àth shean, the granary town, some nine years after the firlots went out. A carter and a miller had fallen out over a load of oats, each swearing the other had shorted him, and had gone on swearing it in the open street until the reeve, tired of the noise, sent for the town's firlot and measured the load out in front of both of them and the crowd their shouting had drawn. It came out exact to the mark. The carter, who had been the louder of the two, said nothing further and went home; the miller, more graciously, offered to stand the reeve a cup for his trouble, which the reeve accepted, and the reeve's own account of the day, which survives among the granary's older boards, ends by noting that the whole matter had taken less time to settle than the quarrel itself had taken to shout.

## VI. Of the Tally-Houses and the Long City's Market

Her son Uisdean was born in the twelfth year of her reign, a quiet, watchful child who watched the court the way she had watched it herself as a girl, and she found she could not decide whether that pleased her or unsettled her, and did not try very hard to decide.

The firlot solved the size of a basket, but it did not solve what a man was owed for what the basket held, and by the twenty-sixth year of her reign she had turned her mind to that harder question. A weaver of the capital might bring cloth to the granary and take grain for it, and swear afterward that the grain given was less than the cloth was worth, and there was nothing but memory and temper to prove either side of it once the goods had changed hands and both parties had gone their ways. She set a tally-house in each of the crown's own granaries, a plain room with a table and a box of hazel sticks, where a clerk sat through the market days and cut a notch for every measure of grain given over for cloth, or salt, or a day's labour on the roads, splitting the stick lengthwise so that each party to the trade kept half and neither half could be altered without it showing against its match. It was the first reckoning of trade that ran the length of the island in one hand, and no coin passed through any of it, for the island had none and did not yet know it wanted any. A trader from the long city in the south, watching the first sticks cut at the granary of Cathair dhearg, remarked to the clerk that he had never in his life seen a bargain that could not be argued about afterward, and the clerk answered, without looking up from his cutting, that this was rather the point of it. The trader asked what was to stop a man simply cutting a false notch on his own half after the fact; the clerk held up the two halves of a finished stick, showing how the grain of the wood ran unbroken from one to the other only when they were laid together true, and said that a man was welcome to try, and welcome to explain the false cut to whoever held the other half.

The long city was Cathair fhada, on its ridge in the south, and it was there, three years on, that Sìleas granted the charter the merchants of that country had been asking for since before her father's day: a market on the ridge at every full moon, with its own tally-house for the trade of the south, so that the honey and hemp and wax and pottery that had gone north by ones and twos, whenever a single trader found the road worth the walking, might now go up together, a company at a time, timed to the moon so that no one need travel the road alone. The first full-moon market was held in the month of Ògach, and drew traders from three days' walk in every direction; the reeve of Cathair fhada, an old woman who had petitioned for the charter longer than anyone else living, stood at the ridge's edge that whole first day and would not be persuaded to sit down, though her family begged her to, saying she had waited twenty years to see it and meant to see all of it standing up.

## VII. Of the Bridge

In the one-and-thirtieth year of her reign the old stone bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain at Cathair dhearg, which had stood since before her grandfather's grandfather and had never in living memory been wide enough for two loaded carts to pass each other without one backing to the bank, was widened at last, the masons cutting new stone in against the old so that the join could hardly be told from the road above it. It was, by then, an ordinary kind of work for her to order; she had ordered walls and wharves and granary floors in every shire on the island by that year, and thought little more of a bridge than she thought of any of them.

She rode down to see it finished on a grey morning in Bearnach, with Uisdean, nineteen now and already carrying himself like a man who expected one day to be asked for his own judgment on such things, riding beside her. The masons had cut her name into the downstream parapet, low down where a woman leaning over the rail to watch the water might find it without looking for it, in letters plain enough that a child learning them could read them without help. She had not asked for this, and stood a long moment looking at it, the water going by beneath, brown and quick with the spring rain, before she got down from her horse and put her hand flat on the stone and ran her thumb along the cut of her own name, feeling the edges of the letters the way a blind woman might read a thing by touch rather than by sight.

She said nothing to Uisdean about what she was thinking, and he, watching her, asked nothing, having learned that much from her already. Behind them the carts that had waited on the near bank began to cross, two abreast for the first time in the bridge's long life, and neither of them turned to watch them go.

# Chapter Seventeen: Of Carson an Làmh Seo

*LE 300 – 324*

## I. Of the Carters' Roads

Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn had walked the roads of the middle shires for the better part of forty years before he ever thought to stop walking them, and by his own account he might have gone another forty had a question not caught up with him on the way and refused, at last, to be carried any further on foot.

He was a druid of the schools of Flidais, lady of the deer, one of a scattered handful who kept no fixed hearth but went from house to house and hall to hall teaching what the schools called Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, the stag's teaching: that the vein answered a hand for some measure in it, a measure the schools themselves had never agreed how to name. It was old work, older than any house he taught in, and it suited a man who liked roads better than roofs. He carried little: a stick worn smooth at the grip, a satchel of hide with his writing-boards in it, and the coat he had worn so many winters that it had come to feel, to him, like a second skin he could not have shed even had he wished to.

In the summer of LE 304 the roads brought him south to the high passes above Imrich nam Pantar, where the herders of that country kept the days of the panthers' crossing as carefully as any feast of the crown or Taigh na Fèithe. He came down off the hill road on the second of those days and found the whole valley emptied of flocks: no sheep on the slopes, no goats on the rock, every gate along the panthers' path standing open and every herder's dog shut up indoors, so that a man walking the valley that morning might have thought some plague had taken every beast on it at once. An old herdswoman he shared a fire with that night told him the great cats had crossed the mountains at the same season for longer than her grandmother's grandmother could number, coming down from the high passes and going on to the southern fens, and that the valley's dead who had ever tried to keep a flock on the path that week were remembered by name still, though none of them by more than a line. "We do not ask why they cross where they cross," she said, working a knot from a length of cord as she said it. "We only know that they do, and we get out of the way." Coinneach thought about that a long while after the fire had burned down, turning her plain sentence over the way he turned most things over, and found in it, though she had not meant it so, something close to the schools' own oldest teaching: that a thing might be true and useful without any man alive being able to say why it was so.

He came north again by the carters' road above Inis mhòr, and stopped, as he had stopped a dozen times before on that stretch of road, at the road-house called An Leòmhann Buidhe, in LE 304 as in every year before it, where the coal-carters of the northern mining road broke their journey for oatcakes fried in linseed oil and the barley spirit they called fire water. The keeper that year was a broad, red-faced man who watered his fire water more than his custom deserved and had been fined for it twice, and said so himself, cheerfully, to anyone who asked, as though the fining were a kind of fame. The carters who drank there talked, as carters everywhere talked, of the roads and the weather and the loads on their carts, but Coinneach, sitting apart with his own cup and listening more than he drank, heard something under the talk that year that he had not heard so plainly before: an old carter complaining that the coal came slower off the northern galleries than it once had. The ground held coal enough, the man swore; what it lacked was hands the vein would answer quickly, so that Taigh na Fèithe had taken to setting two men to a face where one had sufficed in his father's day. Coinneach said nothing to this. He had heard its like at a dozen road-houses over a dozen years, always in passing, never dwelt on, a grumble among grumbles about weather and loads. But he had begun, without quite deciding to, to keep a private count of how often he heard it.

He kept that count the way another man might have kept a tally-stick, cutting no notch that any eye but his own would ever read, only a private mark on the inside of his own memory each time the complaint came round again: a vein-house steward at a naming feast saying the same of the western galleries; a woman selling combs at a market fair who told him, unasked, that her own grandfather had worked a face alone that it now took two men to answer at all; a boy of no more than ten who asked him outright, at a hearth where Coinneach had stopped for the night, why the vein loved some hands and hated others, and whether it might simply be running short of the hands it loved best. He answered the boy as he answered every such question on the road, with the schools' old careful phrases about measure and merit that satisfied no one, least of all himself, and walked on the next morning turning the boy's plain word, hated, over in his mind for the better part of a week.

## II. Of the Grove at Muileann chiar

From An Leòmhann Buidhe the road ran on to Dùn thais and, a little beyond it, to the sacred wood the schools kept at Muileann chiar, Coille Naomh Muileann chiar, where Flidais's white stag was said still to be seen on quiet evenings by those patient enough to stand still for one. Coinneach had been coming to that grove since he was a boy sent to learn his letters from the schools' own teachers, and he came to it now, in the autumn of that year, an old man by the reckoning of most trades though the schools counted their own differently, to sit among the oaks with three or four of the older teachers and speak of what he had heard on the roads.

They were not surprised by it. One of them, a stooped woman named Beathag nic Ruairidh who had taught in that grove longer than Coinneach had been alive, said only that the schools had always known the question was there, under the teaching, waiting to be asked whole rather than caught in pieces the way Coinneach had been catching it for years: whether the fleet that went out in the days of the Roll had carried away, along with a fifth of every household's right to the coal, something of the very measure the schools claimed to teach. "You have been asking half a question your whole life," she told him, not unkindly, "on every road you have ever walked, one carter at a time. A half question asked a thousand times is still a half question." She was the one who first said to him what he did not, in the end, forget: that the schools had always taught by scattering their teaching one hearth at a time, as a sower scatters seed, and that a question of that size and that danger wanted a different ground to grow in, a fixed hall where it could be turned over by rule rather than by chance, among pupils who had come to argue and not merely to be fed and housed for a night.

Coinneach walked the bounds of the sacred wood alone the following spring, the way the schools' teachers walked it once in a lifetime to mark it in their own memory before they died, tracing the old boundary stones through bracken and standing stands of birch, and came out at the far side with his mind made up, though he could not afterward have said the exact hour it had been made. The question would not be carried hearth to hearth any longer. It would have a house, and a rule, and be argued properly by those who came to argue it, rather than go on leaking out sideways in a road-house over cups of fire water, half heard and half denied before the words were even finished.

## III. Of the House Raised at Dùn thais

He chose Dùn thais for the house, a walled town on its hill a day's walk from the grove and near enough the carters' road that pupils would not have to leave the road far to find it, and near enough Caol bheag and the coast towns beyond it that word of a fixed hall, once it had a fixed hall to carry word of, might travel without a druid's own feet to carry it. In LE 314 the house went up: a long hall of grey stone with a turf roof and one door, built by masons of the town in trade for a season's teaching of their own sons, with benches down both walls and a hearth at the far end and, before the hearth, a table where the master of the house would sit. Coinneach had the old question of the schools cut into the lintel over the one door before the roof was even finished over it, Carson an làmh seo?, why this hand, in letters deep enough, the mason promised him, to outlast three generations of thumbs tracing them. Taigh na Deasbaid, he called it, and when the mason asked what a house needed such a hard question over its door for, he told him only that a door was as good a place as any to keep a question where every soul who came in or went out would have to pass beneath it.

The first pupils were few: two boys of Dùn thais itself, a girl from a farm within a morning's walk, and an old shepherd who had heard Coinneach teach once at a hearth twenty years before and had never stopped turning the memory over since. Coinneach set them a rule that first winter that the house kept ever after: that a question, once set, would be argued on the benches through the turning of a full year, by whoever chose to sit them, with no answer given from the master's own chair until the year was out, and sometimes not then. It was slow going. The old shepherd complained, more than once, that a man of his years had not much year left to spend arguing one question at a time, and Coinneach told him that this was precisely why the rule stood: that a question worth a year's arguing was worth more than an answer swallowed whole in an afternoon and never tasted again.

Word travelled slower than Coinneach had hoped, and faster than he had feared. Within a few years pupils were coming from as far as Caol bheag, three days' walk along the coast road and the carters' track that joined it, sent by parents who had heard, from a trader or a carter or a fisher who had heard it from someone else again, that there was a hall at Dùn thais where a hard question was argued properly and not merely swallowed. One of them, a fisherman's son of no more than sixteen, walked the whole distance with nothing but a sack of oatcakes and a borrowed cloak, and told Coinneach, when he was asked why he had come so far for one question among the schools' many, that his own village priest had set the question once at a naming feast and then refused, when pressed, to say any more about it, which the boy had taken, rightly enough, for a sign that there was more to be got at Dùn thais than at home. Coinneach kept him, as he kept every pupil who arrived hungry enough to walk that far for an argument rather than an answer, and the house grew a bench's width at a time through those years, never crowded, never empty, the register of questions kept in a plain board book that lay open on the master's table for any pupil to read back through. The fisherman's boy, whose name was Aonghas mac Nèill, stayed on past the year of his own first question and became, in time, the pupil Coinneach trusted to keep the register straight when his own eyes tired of the board in poor light, and it was Aonghas mac Nèill who once remarked that a stranger reading through those first years of questions set and argued would have found nothing in the book to trouble a single one of Na Seachd Taighean: whether a hall raised without a hearth-fire kept was truly a house; whether a debt owed to a dead man could be owed still to his line; whether a question, once answered wrongly for a generation, was better mended slowly or torn up and asked again from nothing. Good, solid questions, argued a full year each on the benches, and set down in the register with no more danger in them than a fair.

Beathag nic Ruairidh came down from the grove once in those years to see what he had built, walked the length of the hall with her hand trailing along the cold stone the way she might have tested a wall's mortar, and sat through a full evening's arguing without speaking a word of her own. She told him afterward, on the road back toward the grove, that he had built exactly the ground she had told him a question of that size wanted, fixed and ruled and patient, and that she had not doubted he would, only wondered how long he meant to let the house grow comfortable arguing safe things before he set it the one question it had truly been raised for. He told her, honestly, that he did not know, and she said that this, too, she had expected of him, and left it there.

## IV. Of the Open Disputation

Ten years the house stood before Coinneach set, at last, the question he had been carrying since the valley where the panthers cross and the fire at the herdswoman's hearth. He had turned it over on every road he had walked since, to the knock of his own stick, and it had grown no safer for the turning; if anything it had grown harder, for he was an old man now, two-and-sixty that winter, master of a house with a growing register and a growing name, and a man with a name to lose thinks longer before he risks it than a young man with nothing yet built to risk.

He spoke of it once, and only once, to Aonghas mac Nèill, the night before he set it, the two of them alone in the hall after the benches had emptied and the last candle had been let burn down rather than snuffed, for neither of them wanted to sit in the dark while they spoke of it. Aonghas asked him plainly whether he meant to ask it the next night, having guessed as much from the way his master had gone quiet over supper, and Coinneach told him he did, and that he had put it off eleven years past the year he had first meant to ask it, and could not honestly say the eleven years had made him any braver, only older. Aonghas asked him what he feared would come of the asking. Coinneach said that he did not know, which was true, and that this not-knowing was itself the whole reason the house existed, to hold a question open in a room built for nothing else until whatever came of it came. Aonghas said nothing further, banked the fire himself so his master would not have to rise and do it, and went to his own bed leaving Coinneach alone at the table with the register, where he sat a long while before he, too, went to sleep.

He stood up in his own hall to ask it in the winter of LE 324, on a night when the benches were as full as he had ever seen them and the air inside the door had gone thick with wet wool drying at the hearth and the smoke of tallow candles burned low. The night itself he had chosen without telling anyone so, waiting only until the hall was full enough that the asking, once made, could not be quietly forgotten by the few who happened to be present. He stood by the table with the register closed beneath his hand and let the hall settle before he spoke, the way he had taught every pupil who ever sat those benches to let a silence settle before an answer, and found, when the room was as still as it would get, that his own voice came out steadier than he had expected it to.

"We ask why the vein answers this hand and not that one," he said. "Then let us ask it of the hands that went. Were they the hands it answered best? And if they were, does it answer fewer now?"

No one spoke. A bench creaked as someone shifted on it. Somewhere at the back of the hall a young man laughed, once, a short startled sound with no mirth in it, and then thought better of it and went quiet, and two or three heads turned to find him and did not. Coinneach waited, as the rule of his own house bade every master wait, for someone on the benches to take the question up. When no one did, when the silence had stretched long enough that even the old shepherd, three years dead by then in the register's memory of him but still spoken of on those benches, would have called it answer enough, Coinneach sat down, opened the register, and wrote the question into it in his own hand, dated, unanswered, exactly as every other question the house had ever argued was written.

He had expected argument. He had not, in truth, expected the answer that came instead, which was silence of a different kind, carried out of the hall by whichever of the pupils that night had kin among the seven custodian houses and repeated, shire by shire, until it reached every one of the seven halls before the winter was out. The houses did not send anyone to Dùn thais to dispute the question, and did not send anyone to close the house, and raised, so far as the record of that year shows, no voice against Coinneach himself. What they did, each in its own hall and in its own time, was forbid the question at their own tables: told their households, plainly, that it was not to be asked at a meal where a head of the house sat, nor answered if some fool asked it despite the telling. It was remarked afterward, by more than one clerk who kept a house's accounts of such things, that the seven had forbidden deeds before, walls raised without leave and oaths sworn without witness and grain hoarded against a lean season, but never before a question, and that a forbidding of this new kind unsettled more than one house that had thought itself settled.

## V. Of the Queen's Death and the Road Home

The same year that Na Seachd Taighean carried their ban to their own tables, word reached Dùn thais, by the same slow chain of carters and traders that had once carried Coinneach's own fame there, that the shires of the northern plain around Baile Mòr mhòr had, in the last of LE 324, taken in so many families from the failing upland farms in the run of poor seasons just past that the town there had all but doubled within the memory of pupils not yet grown, and that its reeve had been forced to divide the common grazing anew to make room for flocks that had never grazed it before. Coinneach heard the report the way he heard most things that reached him at the house those years, sitting at his own table with the register open before him, and thought, though he set nothing of the thought down, that a country losing its upland farms one poor season at a time and a schools' house losing its old certainty one question at a time were perhaps not so far apart as the two reports, arriving on the same cart, made them sound. The carter who brought the news of Baile Mòr mhòr had walked the road himself that spring, on other business, and told Coinneach that the reeve there had stood in the mud of the newly divided grazing with a stick of his own, much like Coinneach's, and marked off shares with it for households that had never held a share of common land in their lives. The reeve had said to no one in particular, loud enough for the carter to hear it, that a shire could take in every family the hills sent down to it and still, in the end, run short of grass. Coinneach thought that a plainer way of saying what he himself had spent ten years working up the courage to say in one hard sentence, and told the carter so, and the carter, who had no idea what his master meant by it, agreed pleasantly and asked whether the house had any oatcakes to spare a hungry man before he took the road on north.

It was in the same season, before the year was fully out, that the harder news came: in LE 324 Queen Sìleas nic Fhearchair had died at Cathair dhearg, in An Talla Dearg where she had reigned longer than any ruler the record kept before her, one-and-eighty years old and more than fifty of them spent on the crown her father had left her too young, by the houses' own custom, to take at once. Her son Uisdean, himself no young man by then, was crowned in her place before the season turned again, and the crown's scribes, in the way of scribes everywhere, wrote his crowning and his mother's death on the same board, one line after the other, as though the two were a single piece of news rather than a life's whole ending and a life's whole beginning set side by side. Coinneach had never sat in An Talla Dearg nor spoken a word to the queen in the whole of her long reign, but he had cut the firlot's mark once, idly, into the corner of his own writing-board years before, the way half the island had, and found, reading her death off a passing cart's board at the foot of his own hall's steps, that the news struck him harder than he would have expected news of a stranger to strike a man his age. A reign that had run the whole length of his own walking life, road-house to road-house, grove to grove, had ended in a single line on a board, and would be argued over by clerks for a season and then, like most such lines, be carried by the next thing worth carrying.

He walked out from Dùn thais alone that evening, along the carters' road he had walked a hundred times before the house was ever built, past An Leòmhann Buidhe's low lamp and on into the dark beyond it, an old man now with a stick worn smoother at the grip than it had been forty years before and a house behind him with his own question written into its register in his own hand, unanswered, and forbidden, by his own reckoning, at every table on the island but the one bench he had raised for it himself. Walking, he thought that he had wanted the question argued, not silenced, and had got instead a silence larger and better organised than any he had broken by asking it: a silence with Na Seachd Taighean behind it now instead of one old habit of not asking. A long while passed before he turned back toward the house and its one lit window, and he told no pupil, that night or any night after, what he had thought on the road, though more than one of them noticed, in the years that followed, that their master had grown a shade quieter than he had been before that winter, and put it down, as pupils will, to the plain count of years, and were only half right to.

# Chapter Eighteen: Of Salt and the Listing Hull

*LE 344 – 394*

## I. Of the Hull that Would Not Ride True

Ruairidh mac Artair had been a merchant of Inis àrsaidh four-and-forty years old and prosperous in a small, steady way, buying wool in the western shires and selling it on down the coast, when he first began to say to anyone who would listen that a deep hull, built as the fleet's own hulls had once been built, would carry twice the wool of any sewn-plank coaster and outrun the weather besides, and that a man willing to pay for the building of one stood to make back its cost inside three seasons. He had never himself seen a deep-keeled hull afloat, the last of them long since broken up or rotted at their moorings, but he had heard the old tellings of the fleet from his grandmother as a boy, and he had a merchant's confidence that a thing once done could be done again by any man willing to pay what the doing cost.

He found wrights enough willing to try it, the coast still keeping a handful of men who called themselves shipwrights though none now living had built anything deeper than a coaster, and he laid out silver and salt and a season's patience on a keel set down on the strand below the town in the manner, as near as the wrights could reconstruct it from the shapes of old broken timbers still lying half sunk in the shallows, of the hulls Alasdair Saor had once laid there himself. What none of them had, and what none of them thought to ask after until the hull stood built and ready for the water, was the particular scarfing of the keel's long timbers end to end that had let Alasdair's own hulls flex a little in a following sea rather than fight it; that lore had gone into the ground with the last of his fellowship's journeymen, unwritten, a thing carried in the hand rather than on hide, and no one now living had the hand it had been carried in.

The hull went down the strand on a morning in LE 344 with half the town come to watch, Ruairidh himself standing at the water's edge with his arms folded and his chin up, and it took the water well enough for the length of ten heartbeats before it began, very slowly, to lean. It did not lie down as An Fhaoileag had once lain down off Ros àrsaidh, with men drowning under it; it only leaned, and kept leaning, past what any hull under sail could be trusted to right itself from, until the wrights standing knee-deep beside it called out that she would not ride true loaded nor light, and that was the whole of it. No one died. Ruairidh stood a long while looking at his hull canted over in the shallows like a beast that had lain down to die on its own ground, and then he told the wrights, in a voice that surprised those who heard it by its steadiness, to break her up for the timber, since good oak was good oak whatever shape it had been cut to and he did not mean to lose the whole of what he had spent on her.

One of the wrights, an old man named Coll who had spent forty years building nothing deeper than coasters and had taken the work on Ruairidh's silver more from curiosity than from any confidence in his own hand, stood a long while beside the leaning hull before the breaking-up began, running his palm along the keel's underside where it lay bared to the air, and said, to no one in particular, that the wood was as good as any he had ever cut, and that the fault lay somewhere he could not put a name to, a way of setting one timber against the next that his own master had never had to teach him because no one in his own lifetime had ever asked a keel to do more than a coaster's keel needed to do. He said it again, differently, to Ruairidh himself, when the merchant came to settle the wrights' wages: that a man could see a joint had failed without being able to see, in the failed joint, the shape of the joint that would not have failed, and that this not-seeing was a harder thing to carry away from a season's work than any silver lost. Ruairidh paid him in full and said nothing to that, judging, as he judged most things by then, that there was no profit in an old wright's grief over a craft that had gone out of any living hand before either of them was born.

She came apart over the following fortnight, plank by plank, and the oak of her went into byres and cart-frames and, in the end, a good deal of it into the strengthening of a granary roof at Inis àrsaidh that stood the better for it for years after. Children of the town came down for a season afterward to play among the ribs of her before the last of the timber was carted off, running the length of what had been her spine and counting her frames aloud for the game of it, losing the count each time and starting again, meaning nothing by it beyond the game itself. Ruairidh never spoke of building another. He went back to buying wool and selling it on by coaster as he had before, a little poorer and, those who knew him said, a little quieter than the man who had stood at the water's edge that morning with his chin up, and it was some years before anyone else on the coast thought to try a deep hull again, and longer still before anyone succeeded.

## II. Of the Bridge-Keeper's Boyhood and the Springs on the Flats

Some eighty miles to the north-east, on the river above Ros fhionn, a boy named Iain mac Ùisdein kept his father's toll at the stone crossing the district called Drochaid Ros fhionn, whose mason, generations dead, was remembered only by the hearth-sign cut sharp into its keystone. Iain was nine years old the first year he was set to sit at the bridge's north end with the tally-stick and watch the carts go over, and he grew up on that bridge the way another boy grows up on a farm or at a forge, knowing the sound of every cart's wheels before he saw them and the particular groan the third plank from the south end gave under a laden ox-cart that it never gave under an empty one.

The district he watched over was a poor one in those years, a scatter of farms and turf-cutters' holdings on the flats above the river, and the bridge itself carried little enough traffic that his father had time, most days, to teach him his letters between carts, holding the tally-book open on his knee and making the boy copy out the day's crossings twice, once for practice and once for the true record. The bridge itself Iain came to know the way another boy knows a field he has walked every day of his life: the particular lean of the north parapet where a flood two generations back had shifted a single course of stone and no mason since had thought it worth the cost of setting right; the swallows that nested each spring under the third arch and would not be driven off however many carts crossed above them; the deep pool below the second pier where the district's boys swam in Teasach and where his own father had taught him, holding him under the arms in water that never quite lost its chill even at the height of summer. He learned to read a carter's face before the cart came into sight, whether the man was one who paid his toll without argument or one who would try, as two or three along that stretch of road always tried, to talk the toll down by a claim that his load was lighter than it looked, and his father taught him to answer such men by walking round the cart once, slowly, and naming its weight within a stone or two by eye alone, a trick that shamed more than one careless dealer into paying what he owed without further words wasted on either side.

It was on the flats below the bridge, in the summer Iain turned fifteen, that a farmer digging a new drainage ditch struck water that came up warm to the hand and tasted, when a curious neighbour dipped a finger in it, unmistakably of salt.

Word of it went first to Ros fhionn's own reeve and from him, within the season, to men who understood such things better than a farmer digging a ditch, and by the following spring, in LE 354, the flats above the town held a dozen shallow pans laid out to catch the brine and let the sun and wind do the rest, tended by the same farmers and turf-cutters who had dug for nothing better than dry ground for their oats. Iain, still sitting his father's bridge most days, watched the first carts of white salt go over southward that same year, and it did not occur to him then, a boy of fifteen with a tally-stick and no thought beyond the next laden ox-cart, that he was watching the beginning of the one thing that would, before he was an old man himself, make the bridge under his feet worth more than any bridge on that stretch of river had ever been worth before.

## III. Of a King's Death Far to the South and a Cloth Worn Nearer Home

The tidings that had reached the bridge not long before, carried by a rider bound for the shire seat who stopped only long enough to water his horse and pass on what he carried, concerned nothing nearer than Cathair dhearg: that Uisdean mac Dhùghaill, who had held An Talla Dearg since he was a man of four-and-fifty and was himself the son of Sìleas nic Fhearchair who had reigned sixty-six years before him, had died in his two-and-eightieth year, and that his own son, Uisdean mac Uisdein, a man already thirty years old and long past needing any regency to hold the hall for him, had been crowned in his place without dispute. Iain's father set the tidings down in the margin of the tally-book, as he set down anything worth remembering that the bridge had no better place to keep, and the two of them talked of it, father and son, for the length of one evening's supper, and then talked of it no more, An Talla Dearg and its business being to a bridge-keeper's household on the northern flats a thing that happened, as the seasons happened, somewhere too far off to be altered by any word either of them might have had about it.
