Nearer home, and to Iain's own family a thing of more weight, the weavers of Baile gharbh had by then been some years at a heavy cloth, undyed, woven close enough to shed a season's rain without oiling, that had begun to spread out from Baile gharbh across the whole of the north-east as the common cloak of anyone who worked out of doors in the wet months. Iain's mother had one herself, bought at the Ros fhionn market from a Baile gharbh carter for less than a dyed cloak would have cost and worth twice the price for the rain it turned. It was in that same undyed grey, 18 an t-Sultain, LE 361, tells, that the district first began to mark its mourning, a household that had lost someone wearing the plain wool rather than any dyed thing until the season turned, in the manner, the old women of the flats said, of an Tùrsa Geal the whole island had once worn together for the fleet, though none of them now living had seen that mourning themselves and knew of it only as their own mothers had told it to them. Iain's grandmother died that winter, and his mother wore the grey cloak a full season after, and it was the first mourning the boy himself remembered closely enough to carry with him, the particular grey of an ordinary rain-cloak turned, by nothing more than a household's own silence in it, into something else.

## IV. Of the Handful from Each Load

By the time Iain had his father's own place at the bridge, the salt of Ros fhionn had become, as the flats' own saying had it, worth more than its weight in argument, for there was scarcely a load crossed south over Drochaid Ros fhionn in those years that was not salt or bound for the salting of something, and the district's shire seat, casting about for some due it might fairly lay on a trade that had made the flats rich almost overnight, settled at last, LE 369, on granting the bridge's own keeper a handful from every load that crossed, to be kept and sold on the bridge-keeper's own account in place of any toll in kind, salt being worth more on that stretch of river than anything else a farmer was likely to carry.

Iain kept the handful honestly, by his own strict reckoning of what a handful was, never grasping a second time at a sack that had already given up its share, and it became known along the whole road that Ros fhionn's bridge-keeper took no more than his due and no less, which was, among carters who had dealt with less scrupulous men at other crossings, a kind of fame. One carter, a heavy-set woman named Beitris who ran salt down to the shire seat twice a season and had once had a whole extra fistful taken from her at a crossing farther south by a keeper who closed his hand quick and opened it slow, took to stopping at Iain's bridge a full quarter-hour longer than her business required, simply, she told him once, to watch him take his handful in the open, in full view of her and anyone else on the road, and count it back into his own box before her eyes, because it did a body good, after the other crossing, to be robbed honestly for once, in plain daylight, by a man who wanted nothing from her but what the shire seat had granted him. He built, in the second year of the toll, a stout box of oak beside his stool at the bridge's north end, iron-bound against damp, and it filled faster than he had thought any box could fill, so that within a handful of years the carters along the road had begun to say, half in jest and half not, that Iain's salt-box held more against a hard winter than some whole villages of the flats could claim to have laid by, and the saying outlived the man who first made it and passed, as such sayings do, into the common speech of the district.

## V. Of the Wells that Cracked at Cill ghlas

In LE 379 the earth moved, one night in early autumn, under the hills about Cill ghlas, a small village far to the south-west of the bridge, in Taigh na Fèithe's own country, and the shaking, brief as it was, brought down a byre and cracked three of the village's wells so that their water ran brown for a season after and had to be carried in from farther off until the ground settled and the springs found their own course again. The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe, hearing of it within days, as any tremor near their own hill was a thing they made it their business to hear of quickly, sent men down into the galleries below Cill ghlas to see what the shaking had done there, and found, to the relief of everyone from the master of Taigh na Fèithe down to the least of the diggers, that the galleries stood exactly as they had stood before, not a prop shifted nor a wall so much as scored, the whole force of the tremor having spent itself on the village's own wells and roofs and left the deep workings, driven true and shored well by generations of custodian craft, untouched.

Word of it reached Drochaid Ros fhionn within the week, as word of anything touching the vein reached every corner of the shire sooner or later, and Iain, hearing it from a carter bound for Cill ghlas with a load of the very salt that had made his own box so heavy, thought little of it beyond a passing wonder at how a village's wells could crack while the ground far beneath it, hollowed out by generations of digging, held fast; and it was some years before he heard, from the same carter returning the other way, that the diggers who had gone down that autumn had said among themselves, though never where the master of the store could hear it, that they had felt the shaking reach them even below, a long slow groan through the rock that none of them cared to speak of twice.

The carter, a broad, slow-spoken man who had made the Cill ghlas run for the better part of twenty years, told it to Iain over the second telling much as he had told it the first time, standing his ox at the north parapet while the toll was reckoned and taking his time about the story the way a man takes his time about anything he does not often get to tell to a fresh ear. The village, he said, had lost nothing worse than the byre and the three wells and a season's worry over brown water, and had rebuilt the byre by the following spring with stone hauled, at the custodians' own offer, from Taigh na Fèithe's surplus, a small kindness that the village had not looked for and did not soon forget, Taigh na Fèithe's custodians being known along that stretch of the shire for counting a coal-right more carefully than they counted a debt of neighbourliness. Iain took his handful from the carter's own load, as he took it from every load, and thought, watching the man drive on south with his ox leaning into the yoke, that a shaking felt through solid rock by men working half a mile under a hill was a stranger thing to carry home to a wife than any bridge toll he had ever had to reckon.

## VI. Of the Hollow Man, a King's End, and the Fish of Àth fhiadhaich

The shepherds who ran their flocks on the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills, far off in the mountain country, had kept, for as long as anyone on the flats could remember, one custom that no reeve had ever managed to argue them out of: they lit no fire on those pastures after dark, whatever the cold, for the old carvings cut into the rock there told of a thing called Marbh-bheò, that walked the hills without breath and fell upon any who lit a light within its sight. A reeve had been sent up from Muileann chiar once, 26 an Giblean, LE 394, a sensible man who thought the shepherds' custom a foolishness that cost them dear in cold nights, and had gone up to argue them out of it in person; he came down again before dark the same day, and no one who asked him why ever got a clear answer, only that he had seen enough of the hills by daylight to have no wish to test them by night, and the shepherds went on lighting no fires, as they had before, and as they would after. Iain heard the whole of it from the reeve's own mouth, some years on, the man having taken to stopping at the bridge on his rounds and being, by then, willing enough to talk of it to a bridge-keeper he had known long enough to trust with the telling, though not to any stranger who might carry it back to Muileann chiar as a tale against his own good sense. He had gone up, he said, meaning only to walk the pastures by daylight and judge for himself whether the carvings were worth the fear the shepherds spent on them, and had found the carvings plain enough, old work, weathered past any clear reading of what they had first meant to show; what had turned him back before dark, he said, was nothing in the stone at all, but a stillness in the whole of that high ground that he had not met on any other hillside he had walked in thirty years of riding the shire, a stillness with no birds in it, and he had judged, standing in the middle of it with the light beginning to fail, that a man's own good sense was worth less on that particular ground than the shepherds' fear was, and had come down. He never went back to argue the point again, and the shepherds, hearing of his single visit and his single retreat, took it for a confirmation of their custom rather than any defeat of it, and lit no fires the more firmly for it ever after.

It was in that same season, the district's own count agreeing near enough with the count kept at An Talla Dearg, that word came south along the road that Uisdean mac Uisdein, who had held the hall two-and-forty years since his father's death, had himself died at two-and-seventy, and that his son Aonghas, a young man of two-and-twenty, had been crowned in his place at Cathair dhearg with less dispute than any crowning the district's own memory held, being the first king, so the rider who carried the tidings said, taught his letters as a child by a tutor set over him for the purpose, a woman named Mòr nic Nèill, LE 394, rather than left, as kings before him had mostly been left, to pick up his letters as he could between other business. Iain, by then a grown man with sons of his own old enough to sit the bridge in his place on the days his knees would not carry him down to the stool, thought of his own father teaching him his letters between carts on that same bridge, and found something in the tidings of the young king's tutor that pleased him more than the crowning itself, a plain thing he understood better than he understood the business of crowns.

That same year, or near enough to it that the district's own tellers never troubled to separate the two, word reached the bridge that Àth fhiadhaich, a fishing town some way south that had salted its catch poorly and lost more of it to spoiling in a bad season than any town ought to lose, had begun sending carts north for Ros fhionn salt rather than trust its own poorer workings any longer, 23 an t-Ògmhios, LE 394, and from that year the mining shires further south, which took their fish salted from Àth fhiadhaich as they had for generations, ate it cured with salt that had first crossed Iain's own bridge, a handful of it left behind in his box each time, though neither the fishers of Àth fhiadhaich nor the diggers who ate their catch ever thought to wonder, buying or selling it, how many hands and how many bridges a sack of salt had passed through before it reached a miner's own board.

Iain kept his father's toll at Drochaid Ros fhionn the whole of his working life, and the box beside his stool, iron-bound and never quite empty, held by the end more salt than any single winter of his own household could use, so that he gave the surplus away each spring to whichever of the flats' families had come off worst in the hungry months, judging, as his father had judged before him, that a handful honestly taken owed something back to the road it was taken from. He never built a deep hull, nor wished to; he had heard, once, as a boy, the tale of Ruairidh mac Artair's hull that would not ride true, carried up the road by some carter or other the way all such tales were carried, and it had struck him even then, sitting his stool with the tally-stick in his lap, that a keel laid without the hand that once knew how to lay it was no better than a bridge built without a mason's true eye for the stone, and that a man did better, on the whole, to keep what his own hands had actually been taught than to reach after what his grandmother's tellings alone could give him. He kept that thought, along with the salt, and passed both down, in the end, to his own sons at the same stool, with the same box between them.

# Chapter Nineteen: Of the Stone that Cries Out and the Two Horses

*LE 400 – 446*

## I. Of the Net-Maker of Inis thais

Dòmhnall mac Ailein mended nets for a living at Inis thais, on the strand below the citadel where the boats came up at low water, and he had done so since he was a boy at his father's knee, and would have gone on doing so, by his own account given late in life, if he had not one morning found himself with more idle hours than herring to mend and a mind that would not let a plain thing lie plain.

The plain thing was the stone that stood a little back from the tide-line, grey and long as a man lying down, which the town had always called Clach and left alone, and around which a handful of old families still kept a watch by turns, as their fathers had kept it before them, road-guards once, in some telling now half forgotten, who had sworn themselves wolf-sworn on a carved stone at another town's gate and had brought the name south with them, or had it already, no one now living could say which. Dòmhnall was thirty-five years old, a spare man with a net-maker's hands, thickened and scarred across the palms from years of twine, and he had never in his life been taken for anyone the town would gather to hear. He began by talking to the men who mended nets beside him, because they were there and would not walk off while his hands were still moving.

He told them the stone was watching, and that it would cry out one day beneath the man or woman who by right should sit An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg, as a hound knows its own master's step among a crowd of strangers' steps; and that the families who watched it kept a household still under oath, wolf-sworn still, whatever the wolf they had first sworn against, no mere custom grown stale with age. Their proper name, the name their oath deserved, was an Fhianna, who keep the whole island as a wolf keeps its range, walking the bounds of it though no one has asked them to and none but themselves remembers why. Some of the net-menders laughed at him the first day, not unkindly. By the second day fewer laughed. By 28 am Màrt, LE 409, there were men and women come down from the upper town as well, standing at the edge of the net-menders' work to hear a man they did not know for a teacher say plainly what half of them, it turned out, had half believed since childhood and never once said aloud.

One of the old watching families, hearing a net-maker put words on a duty they had kept without words for three generations, sent their eldest down to the strand to ask him plainly what right he had to name a thing he had not sworn to. Dòmhnall answered, by the account still told of it at Inis thais, that he had sworn nothing and claimed no watch of his own, and that the naming was not his to give or withhold; he had only said aloud what the stone had already been doing under their own hands for longer than any of them could count, and if the name displeased them they were free to keep the older silence and let him talk to the empty air instead. The old man went back to his family and reported, so it is told, that the net-maker was either a fool or telling the truth, and that he could not himself tell which, though he came back down to the strand the following morning to hear him again, and brought his own sons with him the morning after that.

He never claimed to have made anything new. He said only that he had put a true name on an old thing, the way a man finds the right word for a smell he has known all his life and never named, and from that day the ones who stood to hear him, growing by ones and threes through that year and the next, called themselves the first gathering of Òrd na Cloiche at Inis thais, though the order, as the older men among them were careful to say, was no younger than the hall built about the wolf-stone at another town's gate, generations before any of them were born. Dòmhnall did not correct them when they called him a founder, and did not claim the word for himself either. He went on mending nets. He only did it now with people standing near.

## II. Of the Wolf-House Roofed with Slate

What his hearers wanted, once they were past the first summer of standing on the strand in whatever weather came, was a roof, and Dòmhnall, who understood twine and rope and very little of timber or stone, let the ones among them who understood such things see to it. A shipmaster of the town, a woman named Beathag nic Raoghnaill who had carried wool and hides along the southern coast for twenty years and had never once thought herself religious, offered to fetch the roofing herself rather than trust it to a stranger's hold, and sailed north and came back a season later with a hull low in the water under the weight of northern slate, blue-grey and heavier by far than the thatch the town was used to laying.

They raised the hall about the stone through that year and the next, a plain building of undressed stone with the slate laid close above it, and it stood, when it was finished, 16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 419, the first roof on the whole coast built to outlast the man who built it, or so the town said of it afterward, half in wonder and half in complaint at what the slate had cost to bring. Dòmhnall stood under it the day the last course was laid and put his hand flat against the wall beside the stone, and said to Beathag, who had brought the slate and stayed to see it laid, that a roof built to last past its builder was a kind of oath, though a duller one than a man swore with his own mouth, and she said back to him, being a plain woman and no teacher, that a roof built to last was mostly a roof that did not leak, and that she would leave the oaths to him.

The families who had watched the stone before Dòmhnall ever spoke of it took their old watch under the new roof and called themselves, from that year on and without argument among themselves, an Fhianna, and kept a horn there that was blown at the turn of every tide, morning and evening, the way the boats themselves were called and released. Children of the lower town, who had grown up half afraid of the grey stone and its silent watchers, began instead to set their morning's business by the horn without a thought for what it sounded for, the way any horn, once it has sounded long enough, is heard before it is remembered.

The horn fell, by lot among an Fhianna's own households, to whoever's turn it was that season to keep the tide-watch, and the blowing of it became, within a few years, a small honour that passed from house to house the way the old road-watch had once passed, so that a child of Inis thais might grow from a boy who feared the stone to a young man who blew its horn and back to an old man again without the town ever once needing to write down whose turn came next. Dòmhnall's own hearers, once they had a roof to gather under, began to travel: a fisherman of the town who had heard him twice went inland one winter to sell hides and came back having told the naming to three villages he passed through, none of which he ever visited again, so that the stone's true name went out from Inis thais the way water goes out from a spring, in threads too small and too many for anyone to trace back afterward to their single source.

## III. Of the Harbour Shrine at Caol leathan

Not every town took the naming so easily. At Caol leathan, where the wolf-stone's own hall had stood since before any of Dòmhnall's hearers were born, there was a shrine down by the harbour that the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig had also long claimed, a low stone house above the tide where offerings of both faiths had been laid, uneasily, side by side, for longer than either order cared to reckon.

It came to a head, as such things do, over a feast day that fell the same year for both: the hawk's own reckoning marking it a day for flying the young birds down to the water for the first time, Òrd na Cloiche's marking it a night an Fhianna kept vigil against no enemy either could name. Both orders arrived at the shrine door on the same morning to find it wanted for the same hours, and neither would give way, Òrd an t-Seabhaig's priests saying their reckoning was the older, an Fhianna saying the stone did not reckon by the hawk's moons and never had.

The king's reeve at Caol leathan, a level-headed man named Murchadh mac Ailpein who had settled land disputes along that coast for a dozen years and had no patience left over for the disputes of gods, walked down to the shrine himself and stood between the two crowds until they consented, more from weariness than agreement, to hear him. He proposed nothing new: only that the shrine's days be halved between the two orders as the sacred woods of an older age had once been halved between rival claimants, each order keeping what hours were its own and neither trespassing on the other's, 29 am Faoilleach, LE 429. Both sides took it sourly at first, Òrd an t-Seabhaig's priests muttering that half a shrine was no shrine at all, an Fhianna saying much the same in different words, but the division held, through that year and every year after. Neither order ever came to love it; they only found, in all the years that followed, no better quarrel to replace it with.

Murchadh himself, asked by his own clerk why he had troubled to walk down to a shrine dispute at all when the crown's business at Caol leathan ran to harbour tolls and fish-weirs and rarely to gods, answered that a harbour town with two faiths quarrelling over one roof was a harbour town that would soon enough be quarrelling over its weirs and tolls as well, whatever the first quarrel had been about, and that a reeve who let the small fire burn unwatched had no business complaining of the larger one later. He wrote the division down on a single strip of hide, one side for Òrd an t-Seabhaig's hours and one for an Fhianna's, and nailed it to the shrine door himself, and it hung there, replaced twice as the hide wore through, for as long as the division held.

## IV. Of Seann Skell Walled and the Market at the New Gate

In those same years the northern town of Seann Skell, on the bay the hawk-keepers called their own, put up a wall around its own streets for the first time, the old open harbour town having grown past what an unwalled shore could keep safe of its own goods, and the crown granted a market inside the new landward gate where the amber of that coast was sold alongside whale-oil, honey, and the wool of the northern moors, 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 435.

The amber-workers of the bay, who had for two generations sold whatever rough stone washed up along their own shingle to whichever trader offered first, whether inside a wall or out, swore among themselves, as the price of the gate's protection, to sell no rough amber outside the walls from that year forward, so that the crown's own toll-takers might see every piece pass and take their due of it. One of them, a young man named Ailig an Òir who had never in his life paid a toll on anything and saw no reason to begin, was caught within the year selling a season's gathering to a passing trader on the open shingle a mile short of the gate, and was made, by his own guild before the crown's reeve ever heard of it, to forfeit the whole of that season's take to the market fund inside the walls; and he paid it, by every account that reached the town after, without argument, judging that a guild's own anger was a costlier thing to cross than any single season's amber.

The market, once it was a season or two old, kept its own small order of business without much help from the crown's toll-takers at all: honey-sellers set up nearest the gate, where the smell of it might draw a buyer in off the road before he had thought to look for anything else, and the whale-oil men kept to the far corner by the wall, downwind, where the lamps that burned it through the winter dark could be filled without the whole square smelling of the trade. Sheep from the northern moors came down twice a year, at the two turning feasts, driven in by drovers who slept the nights before and after in the lee of the new wall and grumbled, as drovers everywhere grumbled, that a walled town charged more for a night's shelter than an open shore ever had, and paid it anyway, because the wall kept the wind off as well as it kept the amber counted.

## V. Of Dòmhnall's Death

Dòmhnall mac Ailein taught on the strand at Inis thais for five-and-thirty years past the day he first opened his mouth to the men beside him, and never once, in all that time, took up any office the order might have given him, saying that a net-maker who called himself a priest was worth less to the stone than a net-maker who went on mending nets. In his last years his hands grew too stiff for the finer twine-work, and he sat instead on an upturned creel at the edge of the strand while younger hands mended what he could no longer mend himself, and talked, when anyone stopped to listen, of nothing more than the tide and the weather and, now and again, of the stone, in much the same tone he used for the tide and the weather, as though the three had never seemed to him three separate subjects at all.

He died in his seventieth year, not long before the fire that would take the roofs of a village he had never seen, quietly, in the small house he had kept his whole life within sound of the tide-horn he had never asked anyone to blow, and an Fhianna carried him to the shrine themselves and set him down before it, not within it, judging, as he would himself have judged, that the stone's own watch belonged to those still living to keep it. It is told at Inis thais that Beathag nic Raoghnaill, by then an old woman herself, stood longest at the grave of anyone in the town, and said to no one in particular that she had brought a roof to shelter a man who wanted no roof of his own kept over him, and did not know, to her own dying day, whether that had been a kindness or a joke the tide alone understood.

The old man who had once sent his eldest son down to question Dòmhnall's right to name the stone came to the shrine that day too, bent now with age past what his own sons had been on the morning of that first asking, and stood a long while before the grey stone with his hand on it, saying nothing that anyone thought worth carrying home afterward. He had blown the tide-horn himself, in his own turn, more mornings than he could any longer count, and it was noticed, though not remarked on at the time, that he was the last to leave the shrine that evening, after even the dead man's own household had gone home to their supper.

## VI. Of the Two Horses

At Cathair dhearg King Aonghas mac Uisdein, seven-and-forty years crowned and come nine-and-sixty years old himself by then, had watched the quarrels of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and Òrd na Cloiche from An Talla Dearg with the wariness of a man who owed his own crown to neither order and meant to keep it that way. He had grown, in his father's house and his own, alongside a third rite altogether, older on the northern moors than either the hawk's flight or the stone's watch: Òrd Mhacha' rite of Macha, kept by families who tended two horses foaled of one mare on one night, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black, yoked from their first spring to a single chariot pole so that neither ran without the other.

It was said among Òrd Mhacha, and Aonghas had heard it said at his own father's table before he had any crown to weigh it by, that the two horses were two powers kept always in balance, one light and one dark, neither swallowing the other, and that the vein under the hill at Muileann dhearg belonged to both alike, fed by dark labor and bringing up bright fire, and that a house or a crown that forgot to keep the two yoked together would find, sooner or later, one horse running loose and the chariot broken behind it. He remembered, from a boy's own memory and no clearer than a boy's memories usually are, being lifted onto his father's shoulder once at such a rite to see over the heads of the grown worshippers of Òrd Mhacha, and asking why there were two horses and not one, and his father telling him that one horse pulling alone always pulls a chariot in a circle, and that it takes two, pulling together and never quite agreeing, to pull it straight.

Aonghas had no love of quarrels; he had watched, these forty years and more, the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna divide a single shrine's hours between them and count it a victory, and he had begun to think, as an old man thinks slowly toward a decision he cannot quite date the start of, that a crown ought to keep something that did not need dividing. When he first told his own household he meant to ride out to Òrd Mhacha' rite himself, one of his older councillors, a man who had served his father before him and had buried two wives and outlived most of his own objections to anything, said only that a crown was free to keep whatever custom pleased it, but that a crown seen kneeling to a moor-custom might find Na Seachd Taighean asking, before the year was out, why a crown could not be seen kneeling to their own custom instead. Aonghas answered that he did not mean to kneel to anything, only to put his hand where the rite asked every hand to go, and that a house wanting the same honour need only send its own hands to stand at a yoke-pole, since Òrd Mhacha, so far as he had ever heard, turned no one away who came to pull.

He rode out to Òrd Mhacha' own rite the spring he turned nine-and-sixty, 31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 441, a man come to stand at a yoke-pole among the families who had kept the rite since before his own house held the hall, rather than a king come merely to be shown a wonder, and he took the near pole in his own two hands when the horses were brought up together at dawn, one hand to the grey side and one to the black, the way the rite asked of anyone who meant to stand in it and do more than watch. The court that had ridden out with him, seeing their king at a yoke-pole in the wet grass like any wood-watcher's son, did as courts do, and within the year half An Talla Dearg's own household had taken up the rite alongside him. So Òrd Mhacha, which had kept to its own moors and its own quiet families for longer than any crowned house had troubled to notice it, became from that year the order of Cathair dhearg and of the crown, without a single quarrel fought over it, the way a stream that has run quietly along a field's edge for years becomes the field's only water once a dry summer comes.

## VII. Of the Fire at Tobar dhearg

That same year, in the season Òrd Mhacha call the between-moon, a fire ran through the thatch of Tobar dhearg, a small place among the southern quarries where the roofs had always been thatch because the quarries near it cut building stone and had never troubled to cut slate, and it took most of the village before the last of it was beaten out with wet sacking and river water carried up in whatever would hold it, 28 am Màrt, LE 446. No one died in it, though three families lost the whole of what stood over their heads, and the village's own headman, walking the black ground the next morning with his boots already through to the ash beneath, said only that a roof was easier lost than a life and that the village would build again before the winter found them without one.

They built again in slate, this time, the quarries near Tobar dhearg holding, as it turned out, stone fit for roofing as well as for building, once a man troubled to look for it there, and word of it went as far as Seann Skell within the year: that a village burned to the ground in the spring had roofed its houses again in stone before the first frost, and had never once gone back to thatch. Tobar dhearg was known, from that year on, along the whole of the southern road, for its slate roofs, the way another town was known for its wool or its market, a plain fact that outlived, as plain facts do, the fire that had made it true.

One of the three burned-out families, a quarryman's household that had lost a byre and half a season's stored grain along with its roof, took the new slate first of any house in the village, judging, as the quarryman himself put it to whoever would listen, that a man who cut the stone for a living had less excuse than any neighbour to go on sleeping under straw. His own children slept that first slate-roofed winter, so the family told it afterward, more soundly than they had slept since before the fire: less for any particular warmth the stone gave that thatch had not, than for the plain unfrightening weight of it overhead in a bad wind, a weight thatch had never had and had never been missed for until the night it was gone.

Aonghas heard the tidings of the fire at An Talla Dearg and sent what the crown's own granaries could spare south before the winter closed the roads, and then, the following spring, rode out again to Òrd Mhacha' rite as he had the year before. A thing done once by a king and never repeated is no rite, only a single day's fancy, and he meant this one to hold. He came to the yoke at dawn as the horses were brought up, Liath Macha pale as the mist off the northern sea and Dubh Sainglenn dark as the coal Taigh na Fèithe sent up by the basket-load, and he set his hand to the pole again, one side and then the other, an old man now by any village's reckoning though not yet by his own house's long custom, and stood there a while in the wet grass with a hand on each yoke-pole, the grey horse and the black quiet under his two hands together.

# Chapter Twenty: Of the Burned Tracts

*LE 450 – 509*

> *Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine.*
> We did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire.
>
> — a verse of the cold shires

## I. Of the Woman Who Taught at Doire chiar

Eilidh nic Iain was born at Doire chiar, a village of turf and grey stone set among birch and low hazel where Taigh na Fèithe's own writ ran thin and the coal had never been found worth the digging, and she was called Eilidh Dhubh from girlhood for hair black as a crow's wing rather than for anything darker in her, though those who did not love what she taught said it, before she was old, with more than one meaning. Her father kept bees and a scatter of goats on the hill above the village and had no more learning than his letters, but her mother's mother had been one of the last to sit under a teacher of the rival school, the school of An Aois Naomh that held the vein answered labour and not birth, and the old woman had kept the teaching in her own head the way a house keeps a coal banked under ash, needing only breath to wake it, and had given it whole to her granddaughter before she died.

Eilidh was thirty years old, unmarried and settled to nothing anyone in the village could name, when she began to say the teaching aloud at the well and afterward under the gable of her own house, to whoever of the village came to stand and listen: that the vein under the hill belonged to no house by right of blood, that a custodian's son was no more owed a gallery than a collier's, and that Na Seachd Taighean who now wore the neck-rings of Muileann chiar had kept, over four generations, a measure meant for all of them alone, calling it custom and calling custom law. She did not shout it and did not dress it in threat. She said it the way a woman says a thing she has turned over long enough to trust, plainly, at whatever hour the listening came to her, and within a year she had written down, in a hand her mother had taught her, the whole of what she said, so that those who could not come every evening might have it read to them by whoever among them had letters.

The tracts, as they came to be called, were no more than a double handful of sheets by the second year, copied and copied again by whoever in the village or beyond it wanted a set of their own, on whatever scraped hide or planed board could be found, so that no two copies in the whole country agreed exactly in their wording though none, by every account, disagreed in their sense. Eilidh herself never wrote a fair copy twice the same, saying that a teaching kept too carefully to one form of words was already halfway to a law, and a law was the last thing she meant it to become.

## II. Of the Reading at Harvest

It was at the harvest gatherings that the tracts travelled furthest, carried by pupils who went from Doire chiar to whatever gathering their own kin kept that season, in the north-east where the grain came thin off stony ground and every household's harvest was a shared labour before it was ever a shared feast. A gathering at Muileann chiar, LE 484, heard the tracts read for the first time by one of Eilidh's own pupils, a young man named Coinneach Odhar who had learned his letters from her expressly so that he might read where she herself would not travel, and it is told that the head of the household hosting the gathering, a woman of no love for Taigh na Fèithe's seven, let him stand on her own threshing floor to do it, the grain still unwinnowed at his feet, and gave him besides a bowl of the harvest's own new ale when he had finished, which he took as thanks enough for the walking.

Not every household took to it so easily. At a gathering nearer Muileann dhearg a farmer's wife, hearing the tracts read out over her own supper, said aloud that a teaching which told a collier he was owed a custodian's gallery was a teaching that would get colliers killed for believing it, and that Eilidh Dhubh, whatever the truth of her words, might have kept them for wiser company than a harvest table with children at it. Coinneach Odhar, by his own later telling, had no answer ready for her and gave none, and walked the two days home turning the woman's words over as carefully as he had ever turned Eilidh's own.

Eilidh heard of the exchange within the season, harvest news travelling as fast as harvest grain along the same roads, and said to Coinneach, when he told her of it, only that the woman was not wrong to fear for her sons, and that a teaching a body could not afford to believe out loud was not therefore a teaching that had stopped being true; the fear and the truth were two different debts, and a teacher's business was with the second, though she never claimed the first was small. She went on reading it herself wherever she was asked, and let her pupils carry it further than her own legs would go, and in this way, by LE 484, the tracts of Doire chiar were known, by name if not by the whole text, from the eastern hills to Cnoc bheag itself, though not one copy had yet been shown to anyone at Taigh na Fèithe.

## III. Of the Order from Muileann dhearg

It could not stay unshown forever. A journeyman of the seam who had heard the tracts read at a gathering carried word of them, meaning no particular harm by it, to a cousin who kept Taigh na Fèithe's own store at Muileann dhearg, and the store-keeper, being a cautious man in a cautious office, passed the word up the gallery to those whose business it was to be troubled by such things. The order that came down within the month was plain and, by Taigh na Fèithe's own lights, moderate: every copy of the tracts of Doire chiar was to be brought to Muileann dhearg and given up, and no penalty would fall on any household that gave one up freely; only a household found still holding one after the season's end would answer for it.

The carriers who went from house to house collecting them, two custodians' clerks and a reeve's man riding with them for the look of the crown's own authority, found the giving up easier than any of the three had expected, and afterward not one of them could say for certain whether that ease came of fear or of indifference, since a copied sheet, however dear the teaching on it, cost little to write again once it had been read aloud in a hundred households and carried in as many memories. Some hundred sheets were brought to Muileann dhearg that season, more than the store-keeper's own reckoning had guessed the whole country held, and they were burned in Taigh na Fèithe's own yard on a still morning with the smoke going up straight before the gathered custodians and, at the edge of the crowd, Eilidh Dhubh herself, who had walked the day and a half from Doire chiar to see it done rather than have it done and told to her after.

She said nothing while the sheets burned, and nothing was asked of her, and when the fire had burned down to a black smear on the yard's own stone she turned and walked the day and a half home again, and within the fortnight was teaching at her own gable as she had every evening for eleven years, a fresh sheet of the tracts already begun in her own hand before the ash at Muileann dhearg had properly cooled. No custodian of the seven ever gave an order against her person, then or after; whether that mercy came of Taigh na Fèithe judging her too old, too poor, or too plainly harmless to trouble with a heavier hand, or of some custodian among the seven who had heard her once and could not afterward bring himself to move against her, is not told, and Eilidh herself, asked once by a pupil why she thought she went unpunished when her own words had gone to the fire, said only that a teaching burned once and taught again the next morning had already answered the question better than she could.

## IV. Of the Wood and the Road

The country beyond Doire chiar's own gable was, in those same years, quietly settling a handful of older claims that had nothing to do with a woman's teaching, and a teller who follows only the tracts would miss how much else, that generation, was being handed from one keeping to another without a blow struck over any of it. At Cnoc bheag Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, held in common since An Aois Naomh by more claimants than any one custody-book had ever troubled to name in full, passed by royal grant to the priests of Macha alone, LE 471, and the other claimants withdrew from the wood within the season, without protest that any scribe of An Talla Dearg thought worth setting down; why they went so quietly, whether from a weariness of sharing a single grove among too many hands or from some understanding struck away from any hall's hearing, is not told, and no teller since has been able to say more of it than that.

Scoiltean nan Draoidhean, who had held no ground of their own since An Aois Naomh's own quarrels scattered the last of the great teaching-houses, took up in those same years the keeping of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar at Muileann chiar, walking its bounds once in every year in a procession that began as no more than a handful of the schools' own masters and grew, within a decade, into the one rite the schools still kept open to any who cared to walk with them, LE 479. It was a smaller thing by far than the schools had once been, in the tellings that still reached Doire chiar from older men who remembered older tellings still, but it held, year on year, without any house of custody troubling to forbid it or any priest of Òrd an t-Seabhaig or Òrd na Cloiche troubling to claim the wood for a rival rite, and a schoolman who walked it in his old age was heard to say that a single rite kept faithfully a hundred years running was worth more, in the end, than a hundred rites let lapse in the first hard season.

On the drovers' road east of Muileann dhearg, where cattle had been walked over the hills to the mining towns for longer than any single family could claim to have begun the practice, the drovers of Àth chiar took, in the same span of years, to marking their own road with cairns, a stone set at every day's stage so that a beast lost in mist or a driver new to the trade might find the way again without asking, LE 484, the first roads on the whole island so marked, and within a generation every drover from the eastern hills to the mining towns knew the cairns of Àth chiar by name and by number, though not one of them, asked, could have said which drover had set the first stone or in what year.

None of these three things touched Taigh na Fèithe's own quarrel with Doire chiar, and none of the three, set down together, made so much as a single line in Leabhar a' Chùraim; but a country that grants a wood, opens a rite and marks a road, all in the span of a single generation and none of it fought over, is a country quietly rearranging what it keeps and how, and it was the same generation, and very often the same few years, that watched the tracts burned at Muileann dhearg and a fourth copy already begun before the ash had cooled.

## V. Of the Copy Kept at Doire chiar

One copy the carriers never found, kept whole from that year on in a hollow beam of Eilidh's own house, in her mother's own hand rather than her own, the single sheet the old woman had set down before her own death and given to no household but her granddaughter's, LE 484. Eilidh showed it to no one outside her own kin for the whole of her life afterward, saying that a teaching needed a living voice more than it needed a written one, and that the sheet in the beam was kept less for the country's sake than for her mother's, a thing to be shown, if it was ever shown at all, only when the living voice at last fell silent.

The years after the burning brought no second order and no second search, Taigh na Fèithe's own attention turning, as a household's attention will, to nearer and louder troubles: a bad season on the eastern seam that same year, and beyond it the crown's own house shaking under three deaths inside a single generation, of which more is told below. Eilidh taught on at Doire chiar for twenty years more, growing old in the same house she had grown up in, her pupils growing old alongside her and their own children coming in turn to sit under the gable in the evenings, so that by the last years of her teaching she had buried more than one of the first who had ever stood to hear her as young men and women, and had grown, without ever asking for it, into the kind of teacher whose pupils no longer troubled to write down every word she said, trusting, as a village trusts a well it has drawn from all its life, that the water would go on rising however little thought anyone gave to where it came from.

She died at Doire chiar in her seventy-fifth year, LE 505, in the house where she had been born, with three pupils at her bed and a fourth sheet, unfinished, on the board beside her; she had been teaching, by every account of that last evening, within the hour of her death, a young woman of the village a point of the old argument she had made a thousand times before and never once, her pupils said afterward, in quite the same words twice. She was buried in the ground behind her own house rather than in any consecrated plot of Òrd an t-Seabhaig or Òrd na Cloiche or Macha's own priests, none of the three orders having ever claimed her nor she them, and her pupils raised over her no stone at all, judging, as she would herself have judged, that a teaching kept alive in the mouths of the living needed no monument the weather might in time wear blank. Coinneach Odhar, by then an old man himself, read the tracts at her own graveside from the copy he had carried these thirty years, and it is told that more of the village came to hear it read that one time than had ever come to hear Eilidh read it living, a thing he remarked on afterward with no bitterness that anyone could find in him, only a kind of tired wonder that a country waited so often until a well ran dry to learn how deep it had been.

## VI. Of Three Kings in a Single Generation

While Doire chiar kept its own quiet quarrel with Taigh na Fèithe, An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg was losing, in the same span of years, three kings where an ordinary generation loses one. King Aonghas mac Uisdein, who had taken up Òrd Mhacha' rite of Macha in his own old age and set it, before he died, as the crown's own custom, died at seventy-eight years old, LE 450, and Leabhar a' Chùraim gave him, as it gave every crowned head before him, a single line: the name, the year, and no more, though the harbour scribes of the west coast were heard to say among themselves that a reign which had joined Macha's rite to the crown's own household without a blow struck over it deserved a longer line than the book allowed it.

His son Aonghas, called Aonghas Òg though he came to the hall no young man, was crowned the same season at fifty years old, already grey and already, by his own admission to the men who crowned him, no longer certain his own knees would carry him through a rite so long as his father's had been. He kept the crown thirty-four years, a reign remembered afterward for little beyond its own length and its own quiet, Òrd an t-Seabhaig and Òrd na Cloiche having settled, in his father's day, into a peace neither order troubled to disturb again, and Taigh na Fèithe's own quarrel with a woman of Doire chiar being, in An Talla Dearg's own reckoning, too small a thing to trouble a king's attention at all. He died in the winter of his eighty-fourth year, LE 484, the first king of the line to be carried to his grave by the rite of Macha rather than by any older custom of the hall, his own household standing at the yoke-poles of two horses he himself had ridden out to see brought up together every spring of his reign, and it is told that Òrd Mhacha who led that first royal burying under their own rite were themselves uncertain, until the day was nearly done, whether a king's body wanted the same ordering as any wood-watcher's own dead, and settled it, in the end, by giving him exactly that ordering and no more, judging that a rite which bent itself new for every man it buried was no rite worth keeping.

His son Iain mac Aonghais came to the hall at forty-nine years old, already a man with two sons of his own, the eldest a young man grown, and reigned twelve years only, a reign Leabhar a' Chùraim called short even while it was being lived, dying in his sixty-first year, LE 496, of no sickness any teller afterward could put a name to beyond the ordinary wearing-out of a man who had come late to a crown and found little joy in the wearing of it. The houses swore, within the same season, to his eldest son Tormod mac Iain, called Tormod Bàn for hair gone white before he was forty, crowned at thirty-six years old without a single house of the seven raising a question over the succession, a plainness An Talla Dearg's own scribes noted with something close to relief after a generation that had buried three kings in the time an ordinary house buried one.

## VII. Of the Second Son

The second of Iain mac Aonghais's three sons, a boy named Aonghas after his grandfather, was seven years old when his father was crowned and nineteen when his father died, old enough by then to stand at the yoke-poles himself at his brother Tormod's own crowning, though he stood, as a second son stands, a pace back from the hall's own centre and said nothing that any scribe thought worth the setting down. He had grown up, by his own later account given to his own daughter, in the half-attention a second son learns to expect and to make peace with: taught his letters alongside his elder brother but never quite so carefully, given a horse of his own but never the pick of the stable, loved well enough by a father grown old and tired in the office but never once mistaken, by that father or by anyone else in the hall, for the son the crown would fall to.

It was in the thirteenth year of his own life, LE 490, that his father took a second wife, his first having died some years before, and gave the household a third son, a boy called Dùghall for no uncle or grandfather that any of the household could afterward agree on, born at An Talla Dearg rather than at any lesser house, the first of the three brothers to be born under a crown his father already wore. Aonghas, by his own telling, held the child once in the first week of his life and thought little of him beyond the ordinary wonder any young man feels holding an infant too small yet to hold anything back, and could not have said, holding him, what the boy would grow into.

Aonghas mac Iain took no office at his brother's crowning beyond the ordinary place of a king's own kin at An Talla Dearg, and within a few years had settled to the life of a younger son of the crown's own house: a modest hold some way from the capital, a wife of a lesser house of custody, and a house at Inis thais that his wife's kin had kept for three generations.

## VIII. Of the Byre at the Halfway Stage

In those same years the central mining road, which carried the ore and the coal of the eastern hills down toward the capital and carried, in the other direction, the grain and salt the mines themselves could not grow or draw, had long depended for its winter traffic on a single road-house at its halfway stage, a place the ox-drivers had for two generations simply called the great house, kept since before living memory by whichever family held the ground it stood on. In LE 509 its keeper, a careful man named Iain mac Mhurchaidh who had held the house from his own father and meant, by every sign he gave, to hold it a good deal longer yet, judged that a single byre no longer answered the traffic the road now carried, the ox-teams of the mountain having grown, over his own father's lifetime and his, from a handful of wagons in a hard season to a train that some winters filled the yard to its gate before the first snow had properly settled.

He raised a second byre that same year against the far wall of the yard, of the same undressed stone as the first, and began, the winter it was finished, a book of his own: which team lodged which night, whose ox went lame and was nursed back on the house's own fodder, whose driver owed a debt of lodging still unpaid come spring, kept in a hand that grew steadily surer through that first winter as he found the shape the keeping wanted. It was no grand thing, the book, no larger a matter to the country than any careful man's private ledger, and no scribe of An Talla Dearg ever asked to see it nor any custodian of Na Seachd Taighean troubled to learn it existed; but the ox-drivers who passed that way, winter on winter, came to trust the book's own memory better than their own, a driver more than once settling an argument over whose ox had lodged where the previous season by asking the keeper to look it up rather than trusting either man's own account, and in this small way the great house at the halfway stage became, without any of the crown's own notice, the one place on the whole central road where a plain fact, once written down, was believed over a plain man's word.

The worst of that winter's snow closed the road for the better part of three weeks, and the yard held, at the height of it, eleven teams and their drivers crowded into the two byres and whatever floor space the house could spare, fed on stores Iain mac Mhurchaidh had laid in against exactly such a season and had, by his own admission afterward, never quite believed he would need in full. He kept them fed, and kept his book through every night of it besides, by the same fire the drivers themselves sat around telling whatever news the road still carried before the snow had closed it: of a woman at Doire chiar not four years dead whose sayings a driver's own cousin still kept by heart; of a king thirteen years crowned without dispute; of a second son of the crown's own house said to be settling, quietly and without complaint, into a life no history would trouble to write down. The fire burned low before the last of them slept, and Iain mac Mhurchaidh, closing his book for the night, judged, as he judged every winter after, that a country's true weight was carried less by what An Talla Dearg's own scribes thought fit to set in Leabhar a' Chùraim than by the small, careful, unwitnessed keeping of a hundred houses like his own, each holding its own little ledger against the loss the years would otherwise make of it.

# Chapter Twenty-one: Of the Ferry on the Abhainn fhionn

*LE 510 – 552*

## I. Of the Bell at Muileann naomh

Tormod mac Iain had been eighteen years crowned when the bell-founders of Muileann naomh asked him to stand at the casting of the first bronze bell ever made on Dia-thìr for a hawk-house, and he went south to see it, partly because a king who is asked ought to go, and partly because he had heard the founders' own account of the mould and wanted, before he grew too old to care about such things, to watch metal take the shape of sound.

He was four-and-fifty that year, and had been called Tormod Bàn since before he was crowned, for hair gone the colour of good wool while he was still a young man; his father's line ran to early grey, and he had made his peace with it the way a man makes peace with weather. He stood at the founders' pit at 6 an t-Sultain, LE 514, with the vein's own custodians beside him, the households of Clann Fhearchair, Clann Raghnaill and the rest come down to see a thing none of them had seen before, and watched the bronze poured and cooled and the bell hoisted and hung and rung for the first time under a clear sky, a sound none of the hawk-keepers present had ever heard from anything but a human throat or a struck stave. It cracked in its first hard frost that same winter, a fault low in the lip that no one had thought to test for, and the founders cast a second the following spring, thicker at the waist, and that one held, and rang for the burning that year and every year after.

Tormod said little at either casting. He was a king who had learned, watching his own father and grandfather's short reigns pass one after another through a house that had buried three kings in the span of his own youth, that a crown which spoke seldom and watched closely outlasted one that spoke often; and Muileann naomh, in the years that followed, became known the length of the south coast as the house where Òrd an t-Seabhaig had first put its call into bronze, and rang its bell at every measured burning long after the manner of casting it had passed out of anyone's living memory but the founders' own sons.

It became something more than that within a dozen years. Hawk-houses further north, on the coasts where Òrd na Cloiche or the sting-oath of Manannan pressed close against Òrd an t-Seabhaig's own ground, had begun by then to let their teaching thin from one generation of keepers to the next, a rite kept out of habit more than conviction in towns where half the young no longer troubled to learn the old questions; but at Muileann naomh the teaching held as firmly as the bell held its note, 13 an t-Sultain, LE 526, so that the house came to be counted, by common report up and down the coast, the southernmost place where Òrd an t-Seabhaig's own word was still said in full and believed in full, and pilgrims who wanted the old teaching plainly given, without a northern town's newer softenings, began to come to Muileann naomh from towns a week's walk further south than any hawk-house had drawn from before.

His household by then was a small one for a king's: a queen, Oighrig nic Dhùghaill, of a western house that had given the crown no trouble in three generations, and two sons born in the early years of his reign, both alive and grown by then into the ordinary business of being a king's sons, which was mostly waiting. He had, besides them, a brother nearer his own age than either boy, Aonghas mac Iain, settled at Inis thais on the south-west coast with a household of his own, and a half-brother younger than both of them, Dùghall, whom their father had got on a second wife of Baile Mòr dhomhain and who kept, by his own choice more than anyone's decree, to that house and its country rather than to An Talla Dearg. Tormod had never quarrelled with either of them. He had watched enough of his own line's short reigns to know that a house which quarrelled among its own brothers before it needed to was a house asking to be quarrelled with later, and he meant, so far as any king could mean such a thing, not to be that kind of fool.

## II. Of An Gàire Dubh

Five years on, in the moon Òrd Mhacha call Sìolach, a storm the south-coast rolls name An Gàire Dubh, came up out of the west in a single night and drove the sea clean over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg, the other Cuan dhearg, on the red cliffs of the south, and spoiled the whole season's salt fish where it hung drying on the racks below the town.

The tidings reached Cathair dhearg nine days later by a rider who had ridden two horses to death getting there, and Tormod heard them in the hall at 5 am Màrt, LE 519, standing rather than seated, which his own scribes remarked on afterward as a thing he did only when a report troubled him past sitting still for it. He sent grain south before the roads closed for the winter, not because Cuan dhearg's reeve had asked for it — no rider had come with any such asking, only the bare report of the wave — but because he judged, as he told his household plainly enough that a scribe wrote it down, that a town which had just lost a season's food had better things to spend its breath on than begging for what any king with eyes could see it needed.

Cuan dhearg rebuilt that winter and the spring after, a full street back from the old waterfront this time, on ground the sea had never yet reached in any telling the town's oldest households could call to mind, and it held. Tormod rode down himself the following summer to see the new street laid, the only time in three-and-twenty years of kingship, his scribes noted, that he had gone anywhere on the strength of a storm alone rather than a war, a crowning, or a rite the crown was bound to keep.

He walked the new street with the town's reeve, an old salter named Pàdraig Odhar who had lost his own drying racks to the wave and rebuilt them with the rest, and asked him, as they came to the end of the street where the ground began to fall back toward the old waterfront, whether the town had thought of building further back still, out of the wave's reach entirely rather than merely out of this one wave's reach. Pàdraig Odhar said that a fisher who builds too far from the water spends his life walking to it and back, and that a street a street further back was as far as any salter of Cuan dhearg meant to walk for the rest of his days, wave or no wave. Tormod said nothing more of it, judging, as he judged most things by then, that a king who had never salted a fish in his life had less business telling a fisher how far from the sea to live than a fisher had telling a king how far from the vein to dig.

## III. Of the Naming at Tobar dhìreach

It was the custom of Tormod's house to have every child born into the king's own household named at Tobar dhìreach, among the wells that claim the mason's crack, rather than in An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg, a custom his mother had brought into the family and that none of her sons had troubled to break; and in the moon of Bealltach, nine-and-twenty years crowned, he rode south again, this time for the naming of a steward's son, the child of Ailean mac Lachlainn, who had kept the king's own horses and hounds since before Tormod was crowned and asked, as was his right, for his newest boy to be named under the same slab as the king's own children had been.

A reciter of Clann na Ceiste came down from the keepers' house to say the boy's line over him, as their order had done for every child named there since before Tormod's grandfather was crowned, and the reciters of that kindred kept, among the lines they knew, more than one thread a listener might be given: most often, for a child of the king's own household, the line of Rìghrean na Cloiche, whose names the hearths of the east still knew in part. This reciter, an old man named Muireach mac Ailein who had said the naming over Tormod's own children and thought himself long past being asked to choose anything new, stood over the boy a long moment with his hand not yet raised to begin, and then said, to the mild surprise of the household gathered and the plain unsurprise of no one at all, the line of An Clachair instead: Neachdan and those who came after him, back to Teine a' Chlachair taken from the burnt vein.

Nobody asked him why. It was not the custom to ask a reciter why one line came to his mouth before another; the lines were held, Clann na Ceiste's own teaching ran, not chosen, and a reciter who felt one line rise in him over another said what rose. Tormod, standing at the back of the household with his own two sons beside him grown men now and both a head taller than their father, thought little of it beyond the ordinary pleasure a king takes in a well-said naming for a servant who had earned one. Muireach mac Ailein himself, asked once by a younger keeper of the house why Clann a' Chlachair and not Rìghrean na Cloiche' had come to him that day, said only that a reciter does not choose his own mouth's business any more than a river chooses which bank it wears away, and that the boy's own line, whatever it carried, was his to grow into and no one else's to read ahead of him.

## IV. Of the Child at Inis thais

The next year, in Faolach, word came from Inis thais that Aonghas mac Iain's wife, Mairead nic Ailein, had borne a daughter, the first child of that marriage to live past her own naming, and Tormod, who loved his brother more plainly than he had ever managed to say to him outright, rode the sixteen miles down to the coast himself rather than send a rider with the crown's ordinary good wishes.

He found his brother's household in the small stir any first living child brings to a house that has waited for one, Aonghas himself more pleased than Tormod had seen him in years and no less awkward for it, holding the girl as a man holds something he is half afraid of dropping and wholly unwilling to hand to anyone else. They named her Catrìona, for no reason either brother could afterward remember clearly enough to write down, and Tormod stood at the naming with his own two grown sons beside him, come south with their father as they had come to Tobar dhìreach the year before, both a little restless at a rite that was, to their eyes, no more than a cousin's ordinary naming and no business of theirs to stand still for.

Aonghas asked his brother, that evening, over the kind of talk two brothers have when the day's business is done and neither is yet ready to sleep, whether a girl born to a king's brother carried any weight in the world beyond her own father's house. Tormod said he did not know, and did not think it mattered much either way, since the crown sat well enough on his own two sons and would sit on their sons after them, the gods and the ford willing; and Aonghas, hearing that, said nothing more of it, and the two of them sat a while longer by the fire talking of lesser things, a good catch that season and a dispute over a boundary ditch that Tormod would have to settle before the moon was out.

## V. Of Aonghas mac Iain's Death

Aonghas mac Iain died four years later, at Inis thais, in his fifty-fourth year, of a wasting that took him slowly enough that his household had time to send word to Cathair dhearg and Tormod time to ride down and sit with him three days before the end, though not long enough for either brother to say all that two brothers who have never quarrelled might still wish they had said.

Tormod buried him at Inis thais rather than bringing the body north, judging, as he told Mairead nic Ailein when she asked whether the crown would want its own brother laid at An Talla Dearg, that a man who had chosen to live his whole life on that coast had earned the right to lie in its ground rather than in soil his own feet had rarely troubled to stand on. He rode home slower than he had ridden down, by his own scribes' account, and was heard to say once on the road, to no one in particular, that a king buries his father and his brothers and learns nothing from either burying that a farmer does not learn from his own, save that a king's grief has a great many more people standing about to watch him carry it.

Catrìona, four years old that spring, was too young to be told plainly what had happened to her father and was told instead, in the way households tell such things to the very young, that he had gone on ahead of them to wait, and she asked, for some years after, when the household might be going to join him, until she grew old enough to stop asking and to understand the answer she had already half worked out for herself.

Her mother kept the household at Inis thais rather than take her daughter north to An Talla Dearg, though Tormod offered more than once to have them both come and live under his own roof, judging, as she told him plainly enough on the one occasion he pressed it, that a fatherless girl raised in a king's own household would grow up thinking herself owed something no one had yet agreed she was owed, and that she would rather Catrìona grew up a shipwright's neighbour and a fisher's neighbour than a king's ward with a claim nobody had named aloud. Tormod did not press it again, though he rode down to see them twice every year for as long as his own legs and the roads allowed it, and it was noticed, by those of his household who rode with him, that he never once, on any of those visits, spoke to the girl about her father in any way she could later have called an answer.

## VI. Of the Ferry on the Abhainn fhionn

Four years after that, in the wet end of Damhrach when the Abhainn fhionn ran high with the season's rains, Tormod's two sons, well into their thirties by then and neither yet married to a house that suited every custodian's liking, rode north together on the crown's business, a dispute between two shires over a fishing weir that neither elder brother nor younger had much taste for settling but that their father had sent them to settle together, judging it past time the two of them learned to carry the crown's small business between them before either was asked to carry anything larger.

The ferry that crossed the Abhainn fhionn at the ford-keepers' crossing had carried carts and cattle and kings' messengers across that water for longer than any ferryman then living could say, a broad flat hull worked by a rope strung bank to bank, and the ferryman that day, a man named Iain Odhar who had worked the rope himself for eleven years and lost neither man nor beast off it in all that time, judged the water high but not past crossing, as he had judged it a hundred times before in a hundred wet ends of Damhrach, and brought the hull out into the current with the two king's sons, their four horses, and a farmer's cart of wool besides.

The elder of the two, by every account gathered after, had stood near the rope himself for most of the crossing, asking Iain Odhar the ordinary questions a man asks a ferryman he does not often ride with, how deep the channel ran at this height of water and how the rope held against a current that strong, more from the plain habit of a man who liked to understand a thing than from any fear of the water; the younger stood further back with the horses, keeping them quiet, for the elder was always the one who talked to strangers and the younger the one who minded the beasts, a division of the work between them that had held since they were boys and that neither had ever troubled to question.

What came down the river that morning, from higher ground than any of them could see, was a spate the water above had not shown any sign of an hour before, a wall of brown water carrying broken timber and the wrack of some upstream bank, and it took the ferry broadside before the rope could be run in, tipped the flat hull on its beam, and put every soul and beast aboard into water running too fast and too cold for swimming to matter much either way. Iain Odhar came ashore a quarter mile below the crossing, half drowned and clinging to a length of his own rope, and lived another thirty years telling, when anyone asked and a good many times when no one had, that he had reached for the elder of the two boys and had the young man's sleeve in his own hand for the length of three strokes before the current took it from him.

The bodies were found two days apart, the younger downstream on a gravel bar within the day, the elder not until the second morning, caught in driftwood a mile further down where the river widened before Loch chrom. Tormod was at Cathair dhearg when the first rider came, and it is told there that he heard the man out standing, as he had stood to hear the tidings of Cuan dhearg's storm years before, and said nothing at all until the rider had finished, and then asked only which son, and was told it was not yet known which, since only one body had yet come ashore, and stood a while longer with that not-knowing before he asked anything else. 18 an t-Ògmhios, LE 534, is the day Leabhar a' Chùraim sets against it, though the finding of the second body came two days later, and Leabhar a' Chùraim, for once, notes both dates rather than choosing between them.

He had the ferry rope cut and burned that same week, and ordered a second ferry built a mile upstream where the ford-keepers judged the crossing safer in spate, though he never crossed the water again by either rope, in all the years he had left to him, without a rider going ahead first to test how the current ran.

Iain Odhar came to Cathair dhearg himself that winter, on foot, to say before the king what he had already said before the ford-keepers and the shire's own reeve: that he had judged the water as he had judged it a hundred times, that no spate of that height had ever come down without warning in his eleven years on the rope, and that he asked no pardon, since he did not hold himself guilty of anything a hundred crossings before it had not already proven safe to do. Tormod heard him out standing, in the same way he had heard the first rider out, and told him at the end of it that a king does not pardon a man for a river's business, since the river had asked no leave of either of them; and he gave the ferryman a small holding of land above the new crossing, not as payment for the two lives the old crossing had taken, which no holding could pay for, but as a keeper's fee for a man who would watch the new rope the rest of his days more closely than any king's order could make him. Iain Odhar took the land and the office both, and watched the new rope, by every account, more closely than any king's order could have made him for the thirty years he had left to keep it.

## VII. Of the Thirteen Years

He had no other child, and no brother living now but Dùghall, whom he had never distrusted and never quite loved either, the two of them being too far apart in their mothers and their years to have grown close as boys, and too settled in their separate lives as men to grow close afterward. The houses did not press him to name an heir in the first year, out of what plain kindness a court can manage toward a man burying two sons within a week of each other, but by the second year the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe had begun, quietly and among themselves at first, to reckon who stood nearest the crown should the king die without naming one, and by the fourth year the reckoning was no longer quiet.

Three names came to stand nearer than any others. Dùghall, the king's own half-brother, had a following at Baile Mòr dhomhain that owed him rather than the crown its first loyalty, built up over years of holding that country's own small disputes without troubling An Talla Dearg to settle them. Catrìona, Aonghas's daughter, grew up at Inis thais under her mother's roof, the last of the old king's own blood by his brother's line, and though no one had yet said the word claimant to her face, she had begun, by the time she was fifteen, to notice how the households of that coast spoke to her with a weight they did not spend on other girls of her age, and to wonder, without yet asking anyone plainly, what that weight was for. And Raghnall Ruadh, head of Clann Raghnaill, was made master of Taigh na Fèithe at Muileann dhearg in the year Catrìona turned fourteen, the custodians choosing him over two older men of longer service because, as one of them put it to a colleague afterward, a vein-house that might soon answer to no clear crown at all had better answer, in the meantime, to the steadiest hand available; and Raghnall took the office and Leabhar a' Chùraim both, and said nothing at all, in the years that followed, about any claim beyond the one he already held.

A councillor who had served him since before the ferry asked him plainly, in the seventh year, whether he meant to name one of the three before age chose for him, and Tormod answered that he had buried two sons who had done nothing to deserve the water that took them, and that he was not minded to hand a crown to a niece, a half-brother or a vein-master while there was still breath in him to hold it himself a while longer, whatever the custodians whispered among their own counting. The councillor did not raise the question again, and neither, in the years that followed, did any other man of An Talla Dearg, though the counting went on regardless of what was or was not said to the king's own face.

Tormod watched the three of them grow into whatever they were growing into, from An Talla Dearg, grown quieter each year, and did what a childless old king does who cannot bring himself to choose among three claims he has not yet been asked to choose among: he ruled the small business in front of him, a boundary here, a grain dispute there, the yearly burning kept as it had always been kept, and let the larger question stand unanswered, telling himself, in the years he still had strength to tell himself anything, that there was time yet, and that a crown decided in haste was worse than a crown left, for one more season, undecided.

## VIII. Of the King's Death and the Houses Divided

Tormod Bàn died at Cathair dhearg at seven-and-eighty years old, 8 an t-Sultain, LE 547, in his own bed and by no hand but age's, having named no heir in all the years he had left after the ferry, and it is told at An Talla Dearg that his last clear words, said to the scribe sitting with him, were an order that the boundary dispute at Àth chiar, still unsettled after three seasons, should be given to the custodians to finish rather than left for whoever came after him to inherit along with the crown.

He was one-and-fifty years crowned, among the longest reigns his house had seen, and the scribe who wrote his death into Leabhar a' Chùraim noted, in a line no one had asked him to write and that he might as easily have left out, that the king had outlived his brother and both his sons, and had ruled the small business of a kingdom faithfully to the very end of a life that had given him, by any household's ordinary reckoning, more to grieve than to rule.
