Na Seachd Taighean met within the month, as the custom of a vacant hall required, and found that no house among them could bring itself to name one of the three claimants over the other two, Dùghall having the loyalty of the country about Baile Mòr dhomhain, Catrìona the old blood and a growing following of her own along the south-west coast, and Raghnall Taigh na Fèithe and Leabhar a' Chùraim both in his keeping. So the houses held the hall in common: the custodians sitting together in An Talla Dearg in the crown's stead, keeping the small business of the kingdom moving, the grain rulings made and the yearly burning kept, while the larger question sat over all of it unanswered, the way a debt sits over a household that has agreed among itself only that it must, eventually, be paid.

It could not hold. In the fifth year of the common council, within the same season, messengers came from Baile Mòr dhomhain, from Inis thais, and from Muileann dhearg, each naming the same crown for a different head, and the custodians, who had held the hall in common as long as holding it in common was possible, found that it no longer was. 21 an Giblean, LE 552: three claims stood laid before the houses at once where one crown had stood a generation before, and Na Seachd Taighean, which had kept a common council for five careful years rather than choose among the three, chose at last, each house for itself, and found themselves divided.

# Chapter Twenty-two: Of the Ford and the Fouled Wells

*LE 552 – 557*

## I. Of the Gates Shut Against All Three

When the three claims were laid at once before the houses, in the year Leabhar a' Chùraim calls the year of the three crowns, there was one town on the capital shore that did neither. Seann Warr stood on the western water with its salt-pans steaming in the cold and its citadel above the harbour, and when the heralds of Catrìona nic Aonghais, of Dùghall Garbh and of Raghnall Ruadh came one after another to its western gate, each was met by the same woman, and given the same answer.

Mairead nic Ruairidh had held the reeve's staff of Seann Warr for eleven years, mostly for settling disputes over the flax fields and the price of salt, and had never expected to hold it for anything harder. The town she governed was a small one as the capital shore counted towns, its wall built in An Aois Naomh against raiders who had not come in generations, its citadel more often used for storing salt-fish than for standing a watch; but it sat on the one road that ran the whole length of the western shore, and every cart that went from the salt-pans to the capital's own market passed under its gate, so that a claimant who wished to move grain or men along that shore had first to reckon with whoever held the bar across Seann Warr's road.

She heard the first herald out in the gate-house, standing, with her arms folded in her shawl against the wind off the loch, and when he had finished naming his claimant's right she said only that Seann Warr answered to no house until the houses could agree among themselves which one it answered to, and that the gate would open to trade and shut to hosts. The herald, a young man of Cathair dhearg with a good horse and a better opinion of his own errand, told her that this was no answer a reeve of a town so small had any right to give three claimants to a crown. She told him that a town so small had exactly the right its wall could hold, and that his own claimant was welcome to come and find out how much that was.

She said the same to the second herald that afternoon and the same to the third the day after, word for word, so that afterwards men said she had learned it by rote before the first ever came, though she had not; she had simply found, each time, that it was still true, and had seen no reason to trouble herself with new words for an old fact.

20 an Cèitean, LE 553, is the day Leabhar a' Chùraim sets down her answer, though it came, in truth, three times over three days, and was the same answer each time. The bar went up across the western gate that evening, and the men of the town's own watch, farmers and salters who had never carried more than a fowling spear, stood it in turn through that winter and every winter after. Few of them loved one claimant over another; they stood the gate because Mairead nic Ruairidh had told them plainly what would happen to Seann Warr if it chose wrong, and none of them could tell her she was mistaken.

## II. Of the First Siege

Dùghall Garbh came first, in the moon of Faolach the following year, with a host of some four hundred, and sat down before the walls a fortnight, cutting the road east and turning back the carts of salt that were the town's whole trade. He did not want the town badly enough to burn it; what he wanted was for it to open for him rather than starve, and he waited to see which it would do.

It did neither. The salt-pans went on steaming inside the walls, for a town with the sea at its gate does not go hungry as a landward one does, and the brine springs behind the reed marsh gave up more salt than four hundred idle men could eat fish to trade for. Mairead nic Ruairidh sent word out on the ninth night, by a boy who swam the loch shallows below the wall, that the town would give Dùghall's host bread for silver at the market rate and nothing else, and that his men were welcome to buy it standing in the road like any other traders. Some of them did. By the fortnight's end his own carters were grumbling louder than her townsfolk, and he took his host east again, having spent more silver feeding it before Seann Warr's wall than the town's whole autumn trade was worth.

"You have made a fool of him," said her steward, watching the last of Dùghall's spears go up the road.

"I have made nothing of him," Mairead nic Ruairidh said. "He made a fool of himself, coming to sit before a town that keeps its own salt. I only told him the price of bread."

## III. Of the Ford at Àth shean

It is told at Cathair dhearg, from Leabhar a' Chùraim and from the men who carried the tale home, how Dùghall Garbh and Raghnall Ruadh met at the northern ford of Àth shean in the spring of the third year of the war, each having heard that the other meant to cross there, and neither willing to let the other hold the crossing first.

Raghnall Ruadh came to the ford by the straight road, in good order, and made his camp on the near bank in the last light, meaning to force the crossing at first light before Dùghall's host, coming by the longer eastern way, could reach the far side in strength. What he did not know, and what the ford-keepers of Àth shean, who owed him no love after two winters of Taigh na Fèithe's silence toward their town, did not trouble to tell him, was that the river ran a mile of shallows above the town where a man could wade it dry-shod at low water, and that Dùghall's guides, drawn from among the drovers who had used that shallows for forty years to move cattle without paying the ford toll, had told him of it three days before.

Dùghall crossed there in the last watch of the night, in silence, in a column two men wide, the water at the shallows no higher than a man's waist and running cold enough that the drovers who led the crossing had told his men beforehand to bind their weapon-belts high and their breath low, for a man who gasped at the cold could be heard across still water a long bowshot off. It took the better part of two hours to bring four hundred men over dry enough to fight, and Dùghall stood on the far bank the whole while, counting them across in the dark by touch as much as sight, because he had given his word to no man that the shallows would hold and meant to be the last one over if they did not.

They came down on Raghnall's camp from the landward side an hour before dawn, while Raghnall's own watch stood facing the ford and the empty road beyond it, looking for a crossing that was not going to be made where they were looking for it. What followed at the ford was not a battle so much as a breaking. Raghnall's host, caught between the river and a host it had not seen come, went for the water in the dark, some to swim, most simply to be away from the spears, and the ford took more of them than Dùghall's men did. Men who had crossed that ford on market days their whole lives, who knew its stones by their bare feet, went into it in the dark not knowing which bank they were swimming for, and Leabhar a' Chùraim's own account, taken from survivors on both sides in the weeks after, says that more than one man drowned within a spear's throw of solid ground because he had turned himself about in the water and could no longer tell which way the current ran.

Leabhar a' Chùraim counts three hundred dead the next morning when the bodies had come down onto the gravel bars below the town, and says plainly that it could not count how many more the river carried on to the sea uncounted. Raghnall Ruadh himself got away with perhaps a third of his host, riding, they say, without a cloak, having left it and much else on the near bank in the dark, and did not stop riding, by his own men's account, until he had put two days between himself and the ford.

22 an Gearran, LE 554, names the day. Àth shean buried what came ashore in its own ground that spring, in a long grave above the water-meadow, and for two generations after, the town would not sell fish taken above the ford.

Word of it reached Catrìona nic Aonghais at Cathair dhomhain nine days later, where she lay before the walls with her own host, and she heard it standing in the door of her tent with the morning's report of the siege lines still in her other hand, and said nothing for the length of time it takes a man to walk twice round a small fire, and then asked only whether Dùghall meant to press east after Raghnall or turn south. The messenger did not know. She sent him back with an answer for Dùghall that named no ally and asked for none, only that if he came south of the ford he should come knowing that Cathair dhomhain held for him, not for her, and that she would not thank him for taking it out from under her while her lines were dug.

## IV. Of Doire mhin, and of the Child Seònaid

Raghnall Ruadh's men, going south from the ford in the days after, three hundred short of the host they had been and with no silver, no grain and no standing anywhere on the road home, came in the evening to the granary village of Doire mhin, which had given carts and coal both to Taigh na Fèithe without complaint for as long as anyone there could remember, and had done nothing at all to deserve what it got that night, save stand on the road they had to pass.

They took what grain the granary held, which was less than they needed, and fired the granary and a dozen houses about it before they went on. Leabhar a' Chùraim gives them small credit for hatred; they burned the place, it says, so that whoever followed them south, whether Dùghall's men or Catrìona's, should find nothing there to feed on. 24 an t-Sultain, LE 555, is set against it, the second burning Leabhar a' Chùraim records in that war and, as it turned out, the last.

Doire mhin had never been a large village, forty-one households at the fire-count Taigh na Fèithe kept of it, set in a fold of good barley land with a granary at its centre built of stone against fire and flood both, and had given its grain and its coal-carts to the crown's stores for longer than any household there could trace in its own memory. Coinneach mac Ailein farmed eleven acres of it, barley and a strip of flax by the stream, and had two things he was known for on the village green: a temper slow enough that men said you could walk to the granary and back before it rose, and a daughter who asked more questions in a day than the priest asked in a season.

Seònaid nic Coinnich was six years old and asleep when the first of it came through the wall of the house. She remembered afterward, when she was old enough to write it down herself, very little of the fire and a great deal of her father's hands: how Coinneach mac Ailein had her under one arm and a sack of the year's seed-corn under the other before she was properly awake, and ran with her out through the smoke into the yard, where her mother already stood with the two younger children and nothing else, the byre door standing open behind her and the cow already loose and gone into the dark, because a beast, her father said afterward, has better sense in a fire than most men.

They stood at the edge of the near field and watched the granary go, and Seònaid, who did not yet understand what a granary going meant to a household that lived by it, asked her father why the men with the spears let it burn. Coinneach mac Ailein gave her no answer that night. He answered her years later, when she asked him again as a grown woman with a clerk's stylus in her hand, and by then he could say it plainly: those men had come to burn, and a man who has come to burn does not stop for a bucket.

They walked south for six days, with what neighbours had lost the same and no more, forty households or near it, carrying children and seed-corn and very little else, sleeping the first two nights in a byre a farmer three miles off let them share with his own cattle, and the rest under whatever hedge or wall the road offered, because word of the burning had run ahead of them and few doors opened easily to forty households with nothing to trade for a night's floor. Seònaid's mother carried the youngest the whole way and would not be carried herself, though she had been on her feet since before the fire and her own feet, by the fourth day, had begun to bleed through her shoes; Coinneach mac Ailein carried the seed-corn on his back the whole distance and would not set it down even to sleep, because it was, he said, the only thing that stood between the household and a second winter as bad as this one, whatever a first winter without a granary was going to be.

They came at last to Cathair mhòr, where the temple of Macha stood open on the market square and its priests, who had fed the burnt-out and the plague-struck of that shore for longer than the temple's own records ran, took them in without asking whose claimant they had voted for, because the temple had never asked that of anyone and was not going to begin for a war it had not made. The temple's own roll, set apart from Leabhar a' Chùraim's numbered days, records forty-one households sheltered at Cathair mhòr that winter on the temple's grain, Coinneach mac Ailein's among them, and gives their names in a hand that runs on for the better part of a page.

Seònaid remembered the temple floor as warmer than the house had been, which puzzled her all her life, since the house had had its own hearth-coal and the temple floor had none to speak of; she came to think, later, that it was only that so many bodies lay close together on it, and that this was itself a kind of answer to the question her father would not answer, though it took her another twenty years to see it as one.

## V. Of the Second Siege

Dùghall Garbh, having broken Raghnall at the ford, spent the two years after in the slow, grinding work of holding what the ford had won him, and came to Seann Warr a second time, better provisioned and in no mood to buy his own bread at the market rate, and sat before it a full month.

Mairead nic Ruairidh did what she had done before, save that this time the town had less salt trade to spare and the winter came on hard behind the siege, so that by the month's end there were nights when the watch on the western wall stood without dry boots and the town's own children went without the second meal. What broke the siege, in the end, was a rider from the east, three days from Cathair dhearg at speed, who brought Dùghall word that Catrìona had sat down at last before Cathair dhomhain's own walls in earnest, closing its water gate as well as its land gate, and that if he meant to have any voice in the fate of a city that had held for him five years, he could not spend the winter sitting before a town that had never once opened a gate to him and plainly never would.

He took his host east a second time, and Seann Warr did not open its gates to any of the three claimants in the whole ten years of the war that followed, though it buried, by the war's end, more of its own townsfolk to cold and short rations than it ever lost to a spear. The salt-pans never stopped steaming through either siege, winter or summer, because Mairead nic Ruairidh held that a town which let its own trade go idle for another man's war had already lost something no gate could keep out; and it is told that on the worst nights of the second siege, with the watch standing the wall in wet boots and half the town's children crying with hunger, she walked the wall herself before dawn each morning with a lantern. There was little to see by it in the dark; the watch stood easier only for watching her carry it.

Mairead nic Ruairidh held the reeve's staff another twenty years after the war's end, through the crowning and the quiet that followed it, and when she died the town buried her, by her own asking, standing in the gate-house doorway, facing the road, so that she should go on watching it, her steward said, whether or not there was anything left on it worth the watching.

## VI. Of Cathair dhomhain, and the Wells

Cathair dhomhain had declared for Dùghall Garbh in the second year of the war, chiefly because its harbour-master had once carried grain for him as a young man and thought well of him, and Catrìona nic Aonghais came against it in the autumn of the sixth year with a host she had held together, through two lean winters, on little more than her own word that she would not disband it while a rival crown stood claimed against her own.

The city stood well for a siege: walled in An Aois Naomh, its citadel above the river mouth, its granaries deep enough to hold two winters' grain against one summer's siege, and its harbour open behind it to the loch, so that at first Catrìona's lines along the landward wall did nothing at all but let the city go on feeding itself by water, while her own men grew thin on requisitioned oats and the households of her own following began, quietly at first and then less quietly, to ask her captains how much longer a siege that fed the besieged better than the besiegers was worth keeping.

She called her captains to her tent on the seventieth night of it and asked them, one by one, what they would do in her place, and had from most of them the same counsel: raise the siege, or storm the wall while the host still had the strength to storm it, for a siege that starved no one was no siege at all. Only her harbour-master, a fisher's son of Inis thais who had come to her following for no better reason than that his own boat had been burned in the war's first year, said that the wall could be starved as easily as the granaries, for a wall's real weakness lay less in its stone than in its water; and it was from him, a man bred to boats and never to sieges, that she took the notion that broke it. She broke it in the eleventh week by sending her own boats, sewn coasters borrowed and begged from every fishing household on the near shore, out onto the loch by night to close the water gate as her lines closed the land gate, and after that the siege began to be a siege in earnest.

It ran forty days from the water being shut. Leabhar a' Chùraim gives the figure plainly and gives no other: forty days, and no battle in them worth a name of its own, only the slow grinding-down that a siege is, worse for those inside a wall than for those camped before it, because those camped before it can at least walk away from their own dead. Cathair dhomhain buried its dead of the siege, at first, in the ground beyond its own walls where custom set the burying-ground; but a city under close siege cannot always spare the men, the daylight, or the ground beyond the wall for burying, and toward the end the dead of the siege lines, its own soldiers fallen at the wall and those Catrìona's engines had reached within it, were laid nearer the well-heads than any custom would have allowed in a season of peace, because there was nowhere else near enough to lay them.

The wells fouled in the fifth week of the closer siege. It began, as such things do, quietly: a taste in the water that the brewers noticed before anyone else, and then a sickness of the gut that ran first through the youngest and the oldest in the crowded inner streets, and then through the garrison itself, so that men who had held the wall a month against Catrìona's engines began to fall to something no engine had thrown. The garrison's captain, Niall Mòr mac Leòid, held the wall another nine days after the sickness took hold among his own men, because he had sworn to hold it and did not, in his own account of it afterward, know how a man unswears an oath once it is given; but by the thirty-ninth day he had buried more of his garrison to the water than to Catrìona's spears, and on the fortieth he sent to her lines under a branch, asking terms.

## VII. Of the Oath, and the Garrison Walking Out

Catrìona nic Aonghais received his herald standing in the door of her own tent, as she had stood to hear the news of the ford three years before, and this time she did not send the man away with a short answer. She asked him, first, how many of the garrison still stood, and he told her, and she was quiet over the number longer than the length of time it takes to walk round a small fire.

"Tell your captain," she said at last, "that I will take the city, because it has held five years for a claim I do not mean to let stand. But I will not take it over the drowned wells of forty days, and add his men's names to the stone the priests will raise for the well-sickness. Let him march his garrison out under arms, with their own wounded carried and their own dead named, and swear before my whole line that they will not take the field against me again while this war runs, and I will let them go to their own homes, wherever those stand."

The herald asked what surety she would take for the oath, since Niall Mòr mac Leòid had, after all, held the city five years for her rival.

"His word, given before my whole host with his own wounded watching him give it," Catrìona said. "A man does not swear falsely with his own dying men at his back to hear him. If I am wrong in that, I will have learned something worth the learning, and it will not be the first city I have to take twice."

Niall Mòr mac Leòid marched his garrison out of Cathair dhomhain on the forty-first day, some three hundred left of the six hundred that had held it, between two lines of Catrìona's host drawn up silent on either side of the road, and swore the oath standing with his own carried wounded set down behind him where the whole line could see them, in a voice, those who heard it said, that did not shake though the man himself, by then, could barely stand from nine days without proper food or sleep. Catrìona rode the length of both lines afterward, alone, and said nothing to any man in them until she came to where Niall Mòr stood, and there she got down from her horse and took his hand in both of hers before the whole host, garrison and besiegers together, and told him he had held the city better than most kings hold a kingdom, and that she hoped, when this war was done, to have the use of a man who kept his oaths that well.

He did not take service with her then; he went home first, to whatever was left of a household five years' siege had not seen, and it was two years more before he came to her at Cathair dhearg and offered his sword for what remained of the war. But it is told at Cathair dhomhain still, and was told to Seònaid nic Coinnich herself when she gathered the old men's memories of that war for her book, that the garrison walked out between the two silent lines with the wells still fouled behind the wall they left, and that not one spear was raised against them the whole length of the road, though there were men in Catrìona's own lines who had buried brothers to arrows shot from that same wall not a fortnight before.

# Chapter Twenty-three: Of the Hearths Refused

*LE 558 – 560*

## I. Of the List in the Yard

Eòghann mac Dhùghaill had kept the store of Muileann dhearg for eleven years, and in all that time he had done one thing only: he had measured out the handful. A household came up the white road with its sealed stick, and he weighed the coal against the notches on the beam, and he wrote the weight in the book, and the carrier went down again with the basket on his back. That was the whole of his work, and his father's before him, and it had not changed since the law was old.

He was standing in the yard before first light, stamping to keep the blood in his feet, when Raghnall Ruadh came out of the hall with a board under his arm.

The carriers were already gathering at the gate, breath standing white above them, the baskets stacked and the measures laid out on the trestle as they were laid out every morning of the world. Beyond the gate the road went down grey and empty into the grey shires, and somewhere below the mist a cock was crowing at a fire that had not yet been lit.

Raghnall's clerk had drawn the board up by lamplight; Eòghann could see, even across the yard, that the man had barely slept, his hand shaking a little as he held it out to his lord for a last look. Raghnall took it, and read it through once in the thin light, his breath going out slow through his nose, and then he crossed the yard and put it into Eòghann's hands.

It was a list of shires. Eòghann knew most of the names on it: the granges above Doire mhin, the temple of Macha at Cathair mhòr, three market towns that had never done him any wrong, half the households along the Abhainn fhionn. Every hearth and every temple hearth in the shires that had held for Catrìona or for Dùghall, in one column, in the clerk's small cramped hand, with the amount each had drawn last winter written beside it, as though the winter before had been an ordinary winter, and could be totted up like any other.

"None of these," said Raghnall Ruadh.

Eòghann looked at the list, then at him. Nine sons of the store had held this yard before him, back past his father's father to a man whose name was only a mark in Leabhar a' Chùraim, and none of them, so far as the book showed, had ever measured a lie into the beam, and none of them had ever measured nothing. Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was older than any king who claimed the crown of it. It did not know how to withhold.

"Lord," he said, and did not know how to go on.

"None of these," Raghnall said again, in the same voice, as if the first time had not been heard, and he turned and went in out of the wind, and the door of the hall shut behind him with the ordinary small sound a door makes, which seemed to Eòghann, standing there with the board cold in his hands, a very great deal too small a sound for what had just been done.

He stood a while with the list. Then he went to the trestle and told the first carrier in the line, a girl from one of the near granges he had weighed for since she was old enough to carry, that there was nothing for her house this week, nor for the temple at the crossroads, nor for her aunt's hearth at the mill. She did not understand him at first; she thought he was making some kind of joke that store-masters did not make, and asked him twice, and the second time he heard his own voice come out flatter than he meant it, reciting the names off the board the way he had been taught to recite the weights, because it was easier to say a list than to say a reason.

By noon the yard was three-quarters empty of baskets. The store still had coal in it, heaped black under the roof, more than enough; that was the thing Eòghann could not get past, all that day and for a long time after. Nothing had failed. Nothing had run short. A man in a hall had looked at a board and said a word, and the wealth of the mountain sat exactly where it had sat the day before, only now it belonged to no one who needed it.

He weighed the handful for the households still on the board until the light went, because that at least the law still let him do, and then he banked the store's own fire for the night, and stood a moment at the gate looking down the white road with its churned tracks going nowhere in particular, half of them turned back on themselves where a carrier had come up hopeful and gone down again with an empty basket. Somewhere down there, in shires he had never seen and mostly never would, some several hundred hearths that had burned every winter of his life, and his father's, and further back than the book troubled to say, were about to go without.

He did not sleep well that night, nor for many after, though the store went on exactly as before: the beam, the notches, the book, the weighing of what was allowed to be weighed. He kept the list. Why he kept it he could not have said, except that it seemed to him a wicked thing to throw away, as if the names on it deserved at least to be kept somewhere, since they could not be kept warm.

A month into the refusal he broke a habit of eleven years and left the yard himself, on the pretence of counting a grange's stock in person, though the store had never once in his time needed his hands to count what the notches already told him. He walked down the white road past the turn-back tracks to the mill at the edge of the nearest cold shire, and found the girl from the trestle there, the one he had told first, sitting with her mother by a hearth built of nothing but hedge-cuttings and a little dried dung, smoke going up thin and bitter and not much warmth in it that he could feel from the doorway. He had meant to say something to her, some word of the kind a man carries down a road for a month rehearsing, and found when he stood in the doorway that there was nothing in it that would not sound like an excuse.

"You'll tell your notches I came," the girl's mother said to him, not unkindly, only tired past the point of anger, "and they'll not warm us any the more for it."

He went back up the white road with nothing said that he had meant to say, and weighed the handful the rest of that day for the households still allowed it, and found that his hands, at least, still knew the beam even when the rest of him did not know what to do with a law that had stopped, for a season, being a law at all.

## II. Of the Cold Shires

Seònaid nic Coinnich was nine that winter, and she had already learned, at Cathair mhòr, that a fire has more than one kind of life in it.

There was the hearth-fire, which her mother tended in the byre-house where they had lodged since Doire mhin burned, banked low at night and built up at dawn with whatever the priests of Macha allowed a family that owned nothing and had brought nothing away but its names and its grief. There was the temple fire in Macha's low stone house by the market, which the priests kept for the rites of planting and the rites of the dead, and which every family of the burned granges had come to think of, without quite saying so, as the true fire of the town, the one that could not go out because it had never gone out, not in anyone's telling.

It went out that winter, in Dubhlas, on a morning so still that the smoke from the last coals stood up straight before it thinned and was gone.

She was in the market when word went round. It went the way such word does, from one mouth to the next faster than a runner could carry it, and by the time it reached her it had already grown a shape: Taigh na Fèithe had shut its gate on the coal, all of it, to every hearth in every shire that had not declared for Raghnall Ruadh, and Cathair mhòr had declared for Dùghall in the second year of the war and so Cathair mhòr's fires were among the first refused.

Her mother did not weep, which frightened Seònaid more than weeping would have. She only stood in the doorway of the byre-house with her arms folded into her shawl and looked toward the temple, where a thin crowd was already gathering around a cold hearth as if looking at it hard enough might light it, and said, "We had a fire once too, and lost it once too," meaning Doire mhin, and went in to see how long the wood they had gathered from the hedges would last them, since wood was a thing no one's law could measure out or take back.

It was a hard winter for that alone, without the coal; the moss-cutters said afterward that it was no colder than other winters, only that a house without the black stone felt every ordinary cold twice over, because it had grown used, in a generation, to not needing to feel it at all. Children coughed who had not coughed before. An old woman two doors from them, who had come out of Doire mhin on the same day as Seònaid's family and had never really warmed since, was found dead in her bed on a morning when the frost had drawn flowers on the inside of the shutter. No one said the cold had killed her; that is a thing left unsaid of an old woman in a hard winter. But everyone who carried her out knew it, and said nothing, which came to the same end.

The priests of Macha did what they could with wood alone, and it was not little; they sent boys out along the hedgerows with billhooks from first light, and kept a common pot going at the temple door for any household whose own hearth had failed, and one grey-headed priest whose name Seònaid never learned told her mother, more than once, that Macha's own rites did not need the black stone, only the fire itself, of whatever the fire was made. But a common pot feeds a family; it does not warm a house through a night, and Seònaid came to know the particular sound a door made when someone went out before dawn to walk the hedgerows for themselves rather than wait on the priests' boys, a sound she heard from her own family's door more mornings than she liked to count.

It was in that season that the verse went about the cold shires, sung low over the mended hearths and the unmended ones alike, by no one whose name was kept:

> *Cha do chaill sinn blàr, ach chaill sinn an teine.*
> We did not lose a battle, but we lost the fire.

Seònaid heard it first from a carter's boy in the market, who did not know where he had learned it either, only that everyone seemed to know it by the second telling, the way a tune is known before it is thought about. She never afterward heard anyone claim to have made it. It seemed, she thought later, to have come up out of the cold shires themselves, the way water comes up out of ground that has held enough of it.

Her own family's hearth went grey twice that winter and was built up again on borrowed wood both times, once by a granary man who had known her father, once by strangers who asked no thanks and gave none of their names. She watched her mother measure out the last of the good turf on the coldest night, dividing it by eye into portions no bigger than a fist, the way, she thought without yet having the word for it, the store at the mountain measured its own handful, except that her mother's measure was made out of love and the mountain's, that winter, was made out of something else.

Being nine, she did not yet understand that she would spend the rest of her life explaining that winter to people who had not lived it. What she understood, standing at the temple with the crowd that would not disperse from the cold hearth even after the priests had gone in, was only this: that a fire withheld does more work in a shire than a fire burning ever does. A burning fire is only warmth. A withheld one is a lesson, said over and over to everyone who stands and watches it not be lit, about who may give and who may not, and who has decided that they, and not the law, will be the ones to decide it.

## III. Of the White Road

Catrìona nic Aonghais heard the verse of the cold shires before she heard the full account of what had made it, and she understood at once, hearing only the first line sung by a woman selling barley at Cathair dhomhain's gate, that the war had changed its shape under her without her leave.

Six years she had fought for a claim she still, in her own mind on quiet nights, was not wholly sure was better than her cousins' claims. No one had been broken at the ford who had not first broken at her; Cathair dhomhain had been taken only because it would not open, and its garrison let go free because there seemed to her no honour in doing otherwise to men who had only held a gate they were told to hold. She had told herself, through all of it, that she fought for a right that was hers by blood and no worse than her cousins' rights, and no better either, and that the houses would decide it in the end the way the houses decided everything, slowly, and with much talk, and eventually.

Raghnall Ruadh had put an end to that manner of thinking for her, and, she came to believe, for every house on the island, on the morning he handed a list to his store-master.

The word reached her at Cathair dhomhain within the month: Taigh na Fèithe shut. It was shut to no enemy's host, only to an enemy's hearths, granaries she had never besieged going cold because their reeve had once declared the wrong way, temples that had held the same coal-rite since before there were kings, now cold on the same law's authority that had lit them. She had grown up on Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig the way she had grown up on the tide; it had simply always been there, a thing that measured and did not choose. To see it turned into a weapon in one man's hand frightened her more than any field had.

Her clerk read her the tally of shires that had gone cold, town by town, and she made him stop before he had finished. She did not doubt the count. It had only begun to feel, hearing it read out in a level clerk's voice as though it were any other tally, like another siege, laid on her behalf, in her name, by a man she had never once met on a field. She had sat forty days at Cathair dhomhain's wells and told herself the dead there were the war's ordinary cost; she found she could not tell herself the same of hearths going grey in towns she had never marched near, in shires whose only fault, so far as she could learn, was to have once sent word that they held for her, or for Dùghall, or simply had not troubled to send word that they held for Raghnall.

Dùghall Garbh came to her camp himself, in Faolach, with six men and no herald, which she took, rightly, as a kind of oath before he had said a word. He was near the age her father would have been, grey through the beard, and he had lost the enthusiasm for the crown that she remembered in him from the first year of the war; what was left in his face, she thought, looking at him across her own hearth-fire, was something plainer and harder to argue with.

"He has made it so that none of us can have it now," Dùghall said, without preamble, meaning Taigh na Fèithe, meaning perhaps the crown itself. "Whichever of us wins it after this, we win a right that can be shut like a door. I would sooner lose to you than let that stand."

She did not answer him at once. She thought of the wells at Cathair dhomhain, fouled with her own dead and his allies' dead together, and of forty days she did not enjoy remembering; she thought that a woman who had done that for a claim of blood had no great room to be shocked that another claimant had done worse for the same claim. But she thought too of the verse the barley-seller had sung, unbidden, to no one in particular, and understood that a claim which had to be enforced by cold hearths was no longer only a quarrel among three houses; it had become everyone's quarrel, in every shire that burned coal, which was every shire on the island.

They joined their hosts in the same season, without ceremony beyond the joining itself: two war-bands that had spent six years in rival camps now making one camp, uneasily, old wounds still being counted on both sides. A man of Dùghall's who had lost a brother at the ford stood a long while the first night looking across the fires at the men who had broken it, and it was Catrìona herself who went and stood beside him and said nothing, only stood, until he went in to his own fire without doing whatever it was he had been minded to do.

The march north was slower than either host would have made alone, hampered by its own mistrust as much as by the snow, and it went through shires that had gone cold themselves, where the marching men, whichever banner they had followed into the war, found themselves giving up rations at doors they passed rather than be seen by their own captains eating well before people with nothing in the pot. No order was given for it. It happened all along the line of march, in ones and twos, and by the time the host came in sight of the mountain it had fed, by Catrìona's own later reckoning, more mouths than it had killed men to get there, which she thought, when she had leisure to think of it, was as strange an arithmetic as she had ever kept.

They came on Raghnall below Muileann chrom on 14 am Faoilleach, LE 560, snow lying thick enough on the ground that the hosts could be tracked by it afterward for a mile in either direction, black lines through white where men and horses had gone down. Catrìona remembered little of the fighting with any order; she remembered the noise of it going strangely flat in the cold, as though the winter swallowed half of it before it could reach her; she remembered Dùghall's standard going down and coming up again in another man's hand within the same breath, and not knowing, in the moment, whether that meant he lived or had only been carried off to die somewhere she could not see. He had lived, that day; the wound that would carry him off within the year was taken on that field, though no one there judged it more than a hard cut at the time, one among many.

Raghnall Ruadh was killed before the light failed. She did not see it done, and was glad, afterward, that she had not; she heard only that it was quick, and that his own men, when they knew it, did not press on for him. By dark the field was theirs, and she stood on it a long while in the last of the light with the cold coming up through her boots, looking at the shape of a battle already going still and ordinary under the snow, the way any field looks the day after, whatever was fought over it.

The next morning, before she had sent any order of her own to Taigh na Fèithe, its gates opened from within. Raghnall's own custodians, the men who had measured and weighed and written in Leabhar a' Chùraim all through the winter of the refusal, came out and struck off the seal Raghnall had put on the store, without waiting to be told which claimant now held the mountain, because, as one of them said plainly to her clerk, the law had never asked them to wait for that; it had only ever asked them to measure the handful, and they had gone a season without doing the one thing the law had ever asked of them, and were glad, that morning, of an excuse to do it again.

Eòghann mac Dhùghaill was among them at the gate that morning, the board still kept in the store where he had set it that first day, face to the wall, unwilling to scrape the names from it and unwilling to hang it up. He did not show it to the custodians, nor to Catrìona when she came up to the yard some days after and thanked the store for its work as though the refusal had been a hardship visited on the store as much as on the shires, which in its way it had been. He kept the board a long time after, years past the point when anyone but himself remembered what had been written on it, and never scraped it clean; he found, to his own surprise, that he never forgot a single name on it either, whether the board was clean or not.

The carriers who had turned back at the gate two winters running went up the white road once more, and this time came down it loaded, baskets on their backs, breath white in the cold morning the same as every ordinary morning of the world, going down toward shires that had learned, that winter, exactly how much they depended on a road they had never before had cause to think about.

Word of the first hearth relit reached Catrìona at the mountain, brought by a rider who had ridden through the night to bring it, as though it were news of a battle rather than the small quiet thing it was: a temple fire at Cathair mhòr, built up again from a carrier's basket by hands that had built it up from borrowed turf and hedge-wood all that winter, catching at last on coal that was, once more, simply coal, and not a lesson.

She thought of the verse then, the one line of it she had by heart, and thought that whoever had made it unmade, without knowing they were doing it, had left out the other half of the telling: that a fire can be lost without a battle, but it can also, as this one was, be won back without one, by men who had only ever wanted to go on weighing the handful the way their fathers had, and by two claimants who had learned, at last, on the same field, what it cost to let the mountain be turned against the shires it was meant to warm.

# Chapter Twenty-four: Of Catrìona Bhuadhach

*LE 561 – 604*

## I. Of the Wound That Would Not Close

Word came to Catrìona nic Aonghais in Faolach, twelve days after the field below Muileann chrom, that Dùghall Garbh was dying at Baile Mòr dhomhain of a cut he had taken in the fighting and had told no one, that day or for a week after, was more than a graze.

She had not seen the wound herself. She had seen him ride from the field with his standard up again in another man's hand, and had taken that, as everyone in her own camp had taken it, for a sign of nothing worse than a hard day; men lost standards and found them again in a battle without losing much else. It was only afterward, from the mouth of a rider sent ahead of the litter, that she learned the cut had gone in under the arm where the mail gapped, and that Dùghall had bound it himself with a strip of his own shirt and said nothing of it to his own physicians until the fever was already three days old.

"He would not send for you," the rider told her, standing in the doorway of the house she had taken for her lodging, snow melting off his shoulders onto the floor. "He said there was nothing to send for."

She went anyway, and was three days on the road behind him, and arrived at Baile Mòr dhomhain to find the thing already over. Dùghall Garbh had died in the night, in the same low stone hall where his father and his father's father had held their own court apart from the crown for three generations, with his own physician asleep in a chair beside him and no one else in the room. They told her, those who had been in the house, that he had asked once, near the end, whether Taigh na Fèithe gates were open, and been told they were, and said nothing further that anyone had thought to write down.

She stood a long while over him before they closed the hall to strangers, a man she had fought six years to beat and then one season to save, grey through the beard as she remembered him from the camp-fire where he had first come to her with six men and no herald, older now only by the stillness. She had not loved him, and had not, she thought, even wholly trusted him, not in the season they marched together, watching each night to see which of his captains still eyed her own with the old war's suspicion. Yet she had believed him, in the one thing he had said to her that had mattered, that a crown enforced by cold hearths was a crown that belonged to no house at all, and looking down at him she understood that he had believed it to the very end, past the point where believing it cost him anything but his own life.

She sat with him a night before the hall was closed, though there was no longer anyone to sit with, only a body laid out in the manner his own house kept, feet to the door, a cup and a straight knife set beside him that no one had thought to take away though he had no more use for either. A servant of the house brought her a bowl of broth she did not eat and a blanket she did not use, and stood in the doorway a while as though waiting to be dismissed before she understood that the queen meant to sit the whole night through and left her to it. Catrìona found, sitting there, that she could not settle her mind on grief exactly, nor on triumph, though either would have been a simpler thing to carry out of that room than what she did carry, which was closer to a kind of exhausted gratitude, that the war had found an ending that did not require her to be the one who ended it by killing the last man who might have carried it on.

His captains came to her camp within the fortnight, not as men surrendering — there was no field left to surrender on — but as men arriving somewhere they had already decided to be. Their spokesman was an old man named Artair mac Lachlainn who had fought at the ford against Raghnall's host and lost a son there, and he laid no terms before her at all, only said that Dùghall Garbh had told them, before Muileann chrom, what he meant to do if the battle went their way, and that he saw no reason a dead man's word should bind them less than a living one's. In the weeks after the field she had expected to spend a season yet gathering in a house whose lord had died without naming who should have his men, not to spend it, instead, sitting in a borrowed hall listening to captains who had killed men of hers not two winters before tell her, plainly and without much ceremony, that the war they had all three been fighting was over, and had been over since the morning Taigh na Fèithe gates opened from within.

She rode to Cathair dhearg in LE 562, to An Talla Dearg her uncle's line had held since before her birth, and was crowned there in a ceremony she remembered afterward, when she thought of it at all, chiefly for how little of it there was. No old king sat in the hall to hand her the crown as his own had been handed to him; the crown itself had lain fifteen years in a strongbox in Taigh na Fèithe's custody, no one quite sure whose to keep it was until the custodians themselves sent it down under guard with a note, in a clerk's hand, that the crown of Dia-thìr was the crown of Dia-thìr whoever wore it, and Taigh na Fèithe claimed no more of it than that. The heads of Na Seachd Taighean swore to her one after another, in the order the old rolls gave them, and she watched their faces as they knelt and understood, better than she let herself say aloud that day, that not one of them knelt to her because they believed her the rightful queen. They knelt because the war had gone on ten years and killed enough of their own sons that none of them, not even the houses that had held for Raghnall to the last, could find in themselves the appetite to ask whether a fourth claimant might do better.

She was called Catrìona Bhuadhach from that year, Catrìona the Victorious, and she came, in time, to find the name harder to carry than the crown. A victory won because the losing side had exhausted itself first was not, she thought more than once in the quiet of the years that followed, a thing a person ought to be praised for as though it were a feat of arms; and yet the name stuck to her the way names do, said so often by so many mouths that in the end even she began to answer to it as though it were simply hers, the way a scar becomes simply part of a face.

At Muileann dhearg that same winter, Eòghann mac Dhùghaill kept the store as he had kept it through the whole of the refusal, and did not scrape clean the board on which Raghnall Ruadh's list still stood, face to the wall in the storeroom where no visitor saw it. When word of the coronation reached the mountain he sent down, with the season's ordinary account, a single line that the new queen's household never saw and that he never explained to anyone who asked: that the store had gone one whole season without doing the one thing the law had ever asked of it, and would not do so again while he held the beam.

## II. Of the Sentence in the Yard

Three years a queen taught her more of the shape of her own kingdom than ten years a claimant had. She rode the shires that had gone cold in the refusal and found some of them slow to trust a coal that had once been taken from them by a man wearing the same office she now wore; she rode the shires that had stood by Raghnall and found some of them slower still to trust a queen who had beaten their lord in the field. What she came to understand, riding between the two, was that the war had not truly ended at Muileann chrom. It had only stopped being fought with hosts. It went on being fought, in a smaller and more patient way, every time a reeve in a formerly hostile shire wondered aloud whether the new queen might, in a hard winter, do to his hearth what the old master of Taigh na Fèithe had done to another's.

She went up to Muileann dhearg in LE 565 to put a stop to the wondering, and found the seven heads of the houses less willing than she had hoped to have their own power bound in the same stroke that bound the crown's.

They met in the same yard where Eòghann had stood seven years before with the list in his hands, because Catrìona had asked for it to be the same yard, and had said, when one of the heads suggested the hall would be warmer, that the law they meant to write belonged to the place where it had been broken, not to a fire and a bench. It was a cold morning even for the mountain, the beam and the trestle still standing where they always stood, the measures hung on their pegs, and Eòghann himself sent for and set to stand at her shoulder, not to speak unless spoken to, only to be seen standing there while the houses argued over words.

The argument went three days. Every head agreed, in the first hour, that no crown ought to be able to do again what Raghnall Ruadh had done; agreement on that much cost nothing, since Raghnall was dead and none of the seven wished to be thought his heir in spirit. It was the second half of the sentence that cost something, and Catrìona had known, before she rode up the mountain, that it would. A law that bound only the crown left every house free to do, within its own galleries, exactly what Raghnall had done from Taigh na Fèithe's own store; and three of the seven, when she said so plainly, went quiet in a way she had learned by then to read as houses doing arithmetic about their own galleries rather than about the law.

"You ask us to bind our own hands," said the head of Clann Ìomhair, an old woman named Beathag nic Uisdein who had held for Raghnall to the last field and lost two sons doing it, "for a wrong none of us has done."

"None of you has done it yet," Catrìona said. "Raghnall had not done it either, the morning before he did it. He had kept the store honestly for years before that morning. I do not ask you to swear you would never become him. I ask you to write it down so that if any of you ever does, the writing itself will already be older than the wrong, and no one will be able to say the law only learned to forbid it after the fact."

They wrote, and struck out, and wrote again, through the better part of three days, a clerk of Taigh na Fèithe setting each draft on a fresh board and the seven heads picking at it word by word the way Catrìona had once seen carpenters pick at a joint that would not sit true, testing every phrase for the gap a future Raghnall might slip through. Eòghann was asked, on the second day, to say plainly what Raghnall had said to him in the yard, and did, in the same flat voice he might have used to read out a season's weights, and something in the flatness of it did more to settle the argument than any of the queen's own words had. A man who had stood where he stood, and could still say only "he gave me a list, and I measured no lie into the beam before that morning, and none after," was harder for any house to argue against than a queen with a claim to press.

What they set down at the end of the third day was one sentence, no longer than the one Raghnall had spoken in the yard seven years before, and Catrìona thought, hearing Taigh na Fèithe's clerk read the final draft aloud in the cold, that there was a kind of justice in that, a wrong undone in exactly as many words as it had taken to do it: that no claimant, house or king might withhold the measured handful from any lawful hearth. The seven heads set their marks to it one after another, Beathag nic Uisdein last and longest, her hand steady enough on the board but her face, Catrìona thought, that of a woman signing away something she had not fully decided she wished to give up. It was Riaghailt an Teallaich, Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig the record kept that bound the custodians themselves and not only the households that came to them, and it went into Leabhar a' Chùraim beside Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig it was written to guard, in the same hand, on the same page, as though the two had always belonged together.

Eòghann kept his own copy of it, in his small cramped store-hand, and hung it on the peg beside the board that still faced the wall, and told no one, then or later, which board he meant a visitor to read first if ever he showed them the room.

Catrìona rode down from the mountain that third evening in a snow that had begun again in the afternoon and did not let up before she reached the low country, and found herself turning the sentence over in her own mind the whole way, testing it the way the houses had tested it, for the gap she might herself have left in it without meaning to. She had wanted, going up, a wall no future Raghnall could climb; what she had instead, she understood by the time the lights of the first shire town showed through the snow, was a fence with seven gates in it, one for each house, each gate held shut for now by seven heads who had watched what the withholding did to a mountain full of men no better and no worse than their own tenants. A fence was not a wall. She thought, riding through the dark, that it would have to serve, since no queen who had spent ten years learning what a crown could and could not compel was fool enough to believe a wall could ever truly be built at all; the most any law could do, she had come to think, was to make the breaking of it loud enough that the next generation would hear the noise before it happened again, not merely read of it after.

## III. Of the Clerk and the Road

A girl of seventeen came to An Talla Dearg the following year, sent up from Cathair mhòr by a Macha priest who had taught her her letters on the strength of nothing but her own asking, and stood in the yard a whole morning before anyone thought to ask her business. Her name was Seònaid nic Coinnich, and her father, Coinneach mac Ailein, a farmer of Doire mhin, had come through the two winters of the refusal with a cough he never afterward lost; she did not tell the queen this outright, that first morning, only that she could read and write in a fair hand and had walked from Cathair mhòr on the strength of a rumour that the household of a queen who had fought for the cold shires might have use for a clerk who remembered what the cold shires were.

Catrìona took her in without much ceremony, partly because the household's old clerk was failing and partly, she admitted to herself only once the girl was already settled in the scribes' room, because there was something in being served by a daughter of Doire mhin that felt to her like a debt being paid rather than a favour being given. Seònaid proved quick with a pen and quicker with a question, and within a year had made herself useful enough at the ordinary business of the household — tallies, petitions, the endless small grain of a court's paperwork — that no one thought any longer to remark she had come up from a burned granary with nothing but her letters.

The queen's own household, in those years, held its griefs quietly and in order, the way a well-run house holds everything. Her husband, Iain mac Eachainn, whom she had married in the second year of the war more for the alliance his house brought than for any great warmth between them, and had come in the years after to be genuinely fond of, in the unhurried way two people grow fond of each other across a shared table over enough winters, died in LE 594 of a wasting in the chest that no physician in the hall could name or slow. He had never much liked to be spoken of as a king; he had kept, all his years in An Talla Dearg, to the smaller business of the household, the granaries, the stables, the endless small disputes among the servants, and left the larger business of the crown entirely to her, and she found, in the months after his death, that she missed most precisely that smallness, the sound of him settling some trifling quarrel between two grooms in the next room while she sat with a petition she could not settle at all.

Seònaid was not the only one of the cold shires' children the household took in during those years, though she was the one who stayed longest and rose highest; two others, a boy from Cathair mhòr and a girl from a burned granary near the ford, were given places among the household's servants and left again within a few years for households of their own, and Catrìona, who kept a rough tally in her own head of how many such places she had filled since her crowning, thought of it less as charity than as a kind of quiet accounting, a debt the crown owed the shires whose hearths a claimant's war had once cost, paid out a place at a time rather than all at once. Seònaid herself never spoke of the debt in those terms, not to the queen and not, so far as anyone in the scribes' room ever heard, to herself; she asked, in her first winter at the hall, only to be shown Leabhar a' Chùraim's oldest entries, and spent whatever hours the ordinary work of the household left her copying out, in her own fair hand, the tallies of the refusal from the winters her own family went cold, a labour no one had asked of her and that she never fully explained, though the queen, coming on her at it once by lamplight, asked no questions either, only let her be.

She threw herself, that year and the years after, into the one piece of work that felt to her like it might outlast her own reign in a way no ruling of a court ever quite did: a road. Her own town, Inis thais, lay a hard two days from the capital by the old cart-track, a road that turned to a mire from Bealltach to Lùghnas and stranded carts to the axle every wet spring, and she had grown up hearing her own kin at Inis thais complain of it the way people complain of weather, as a fact of the world rather than a thing that might be mended. She had the stone laid herself, in the years between LE 565 and LE 584, south from the capital by a market town on the old track and past Am Buabhall Fortanach at Doire shean, the old hostel Eilidh nic Chaluim had rebuilt in stone four centuries before, all the way down to her own gate at Inis thais; and she rode the whole length of it herself twice while it was building, in a cart with iron-shod wheels she had had made for no other purpose than to feel, under her own body, whether the stone held.

It came to be called Rathad na Banrighinn, though she had never asked for the name and could not, when a courtier first used it to her face, remember having given anyone leave to use it. The first carters to run the whole length of it did so within the year the last stone was laid, salt-carts and grain-carts that had once taken three days where the road now let them do it in two, and one of them, an old man who had driven the mire road for forty years before the stone came, told a rider of the household, in words that were carried back to her and that she kept, in her own way, longer than she kept most compliments, that he had driven the new road with his eyes shut half a mile at a stretch, only to feel the cart go steady under him the whole way, a thing he had never once been able to do on the old track without losing a wheel to it.

The building of the road cost her more of the treasury than any single work of her reign, and more than one head of house asked her plainly, in council, why a queen should spend so much stone on a track to her own town when the mire road had carried grain and salt well enough for three generations before her. She answered them, the one time the question was put to her outright, that she had not built it for her own town at all, though she did not trouble to hide that she was glad it reached her own gate; she had built it because a kingdom bound together by a law written in a cold yard on a mountain ought to be bound together, too, by roads that did not fail every spring, and that a house which could not be reached in the wet season by anything heavier than a laden mule was, in every way that mattered to a hearth in winter, as far from the crown as the far coast the fleet had gone looking for. Whether the council believed her reasons or only tired of arguing against a queen who had already begun laying the stone before the question was put to her, the road went on being built, mile by mile, through the years Taigh na Fèithe's ruling was still settling into Leabhar a' Chùraim's habit.

To Seann Warr, that had shut its own gates against all three claimants and been besieged twice for the shutting and taken by neither, she granted, in LE 594, the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls, a thing no other town on the island held of the crown; and when the grant was cut over the landward gate in stone letters a mason's apprentice had spent a season shaping, she rode down to see it done and stood a while reading her own name in a hand not her own, thinking, as she had thought at her own coronation, that there was a kind of victory in a town's stubbornness that deserved more honour than her own had ever quite earned, since Seann Warr had held to nothing but its own gates, and never once had to be forgiven for choosing wrongly.

## IV. Of the Single Day

She grew old at An Talla Dearg the way her uncle Tormod Bàn's line had grown old before her, without the long unnatural years the first children of the island's oldest houses had once been given and had, one by one, been made to give up; she counted six-and-thirty years at her crowning and eight-and-seventy at her death, and never once, in all the years between, heard anyone remark on the length of her reign as though it were a wonder, only as though it were simply what a long life looked like, now, on Dia-thìr.

She died at Cathair dhearg in LE 604, in the same hall where she had been crowned with so little ceremony, and left behind her a son, Lachlann mac Iain, not yet forty, who had spent the better part of his own life at the edges of her court learning a trade he had never much sought and could not now refuse. He had been, by his mother's own choosing, kept away from Taigh na Fèithe's business until he was old enough to understand what it had cost his mother's generation to bind it, and he came to the crown, in the weeks after her death, with a caution Catrìona herself had never had the leisure to learn slowly; he had learned it, instead, all at once, from watching what the writing of one sentence in a cold yard had taken out of his mother.

She had told him once, the only time he ever asked her outright what it had cost to write Riaghailt an Teallaich, that the hardest part of the three days on the mountain had been the waiting afterward far more than the arguing, the years spent not knowing whether seven marks on a board would hold when the next hard winter came and tested them; and that a king who inherited the ruling already made would never know that particular waiting, which she counted, in her own way, as a mercy she had bought him at some cost and was glad to have bought. He remembered the saying, standing at her grave in a cold that reminded more than one of the older mourners of the yard at Taigh na Fèithe forty years before, and thought that he understood it a little better now than he had when she first said it, though he would go on, in the quiet way of a man newly come into an office too large for him, understanding it better still for years afterward.

The seven heads swore to him within a single day of her burial, a thing the household's clerks remarked on at the time and Leabhar a' Chùraim set down afterward as worth remarking, since no crown in living memory had passed so quickly or so quietly from one hand to the next. Beathag nic Uisdein, grown very old herself by then, was the first to kneel, and was heard by more than one witness to say, low, as she rose, that she knelt this time to the son of the woman who had made her put her own mark to a law she had once thought bound only her enemies, and had come, in the years since, to be glad of the binding.

Seònaid nic Coinnich stood at the back of the hall that day, no longer the girl who had walked up from Cathair mhòr with nothing but her letters but a woman near sixty herself, grey and steady, kept on through three changes of clerk beneath her because no one in the household could be found who knew the old rolls half so well. She had spent the two years before the queen's death gathering, at Catrìona's own asking, the memories of everyone still living who had fought in the war of the three claims — an old man who had stood at the ford, a store-master's son, a woman of Doire mhin who still remembered the cold with a plainness that made even Seònaid, who had lived it too, wince to hear it set down; and she stood in the hall that day of the swearing with the beginning of that work already half written in a chest in the scribes' room, and thought, watching the seven heads kneel one after another in the space of a single afternoon, that she was watching the last event her book would need before she could call it finished, though she did not yet have the last of its words.

It is told that she counted the swearings as they happened, without meaning to, the way a clerk counts anything set before her in order; that she reached seven and found herself still standing, listening to the new king's voice give its first answer in a hall that had heard four changes of ruler go far less smoothly than this one had; and that she went back to the scribes' room that same evening, before the feast that marked the day was even lit, and wrote at the top of a fresh leaf the opening words of the history of the war, in a hand she meant to be steady enough that no one who read it after her would doubt a single line of it.

# Chapter Twenty-five: Of the Book of the Three Claimants

*LE 605 – 650*

## I. Of the Old Boards

Seònaid nic Coinnich had counted the hours of the swearing at Cathair dhearg the way a woman counts a fever, waiting for it to break into something she could name, and when it broke into nothing more than a new king sitting where an old queen had sat, she found she did not know what to do with the counting afterward. She had been Catrìona's clerk for thirty-eight years. She did not know how to be anyone's clerk who was not Catrìona's.

Lachlann mac Iain kept her on, as his mother had told him to before she died, though he did it, Seònaid thought, the way a man keeps a piece of furniture whose use he has not yet worked out: with respect, and no particular purpose. She had a chest in the scribes' room already, and in the chest the beginning of a work the old queen had set her to two years before her death: an old man's account of the ford, a store-master's son's account of his father's board, a woman of Doire mhin's account of the cold. She had taken them down quickly, in the odd hours a court leaves a clerk, and had known even as she wrote them that they were only a beginning, three voices where a war had had thousands, and that a thing set down quickly is not the same as a thing set down whole.

For the better part of a year after the swearing she did nothing about the chest at all, copying grants and witnessing seals and sitting at the foot of a council table where the talk went on around her as if she were the table itself. Petitions came up from every corner of the shires that summer, a broken weir here, a boundary quarrel there, the small unending grain of a kingdom that has just settled a crown and finds it still has to be fed and watered like any other year; and Seònaid, copying them into the record hour after hour in a hand grown steadier than her own thoughts, began to feel the three leaves in the chest at her back the way a person feels a door left open in a cold room, a draught she could not place until she finally turned and looked at where it came from. It was in that year, doing work that did not much matter, that she understood the three accounts she already held were only a doorway, and that most of the men and women who had lived through the war she had lived through as a girl were dying, one by one, without anyone having gone back to ask them anything further.

She went down to Seann Skell in Bealltach on business that was not, in truth, business: a grant of the harbour dues that could as easily have gone by rider, and did not need a clerk to carry it in her own hand. The harbour-house stood where it had always stood, low and long above the strand, its lamp lit though it was midday, out of a habit no one now living could account for.

The scribe who kept the boards that year was a spare, careful man named Ailean mac Mhurchaidh, the fourth or fifth to hold the office since the roll was first opened, though he could not himself have said which; the line of scribes before him had not troubled to number themselves, only to keep the boards. He received her grant, read it, and set it aside without excitement, and when she lingered he seemed to understand, without being told, that she had not come for the grant at all.

"You'll want to see the old boards," he said. It was not a question.

He brought them out from the back room where they were kept, wrapped in oiled hide against the damp off the strand: a dozen of them, the wood gone dark with age and handling, the writing on the nearer ones still sharp, the writing on the far ones softened almost to shadow. He laid them on the counting-table one by one and let her look without saying anything more, which she thought afterward was the kindest thing anyone had done for her in that whole grey year.

She had heard Rolla nan Deònach spoken of all her life, the way one hears of a flood or a fire that happened before one was born: as a fact, worn smooth by telling, with no particular weight to it. She had not understood, until she stood over the boards with her own hands not touching them, that it was a list of names, ordinary names, struck through in some places with a single decisive line and left standing in others, and that every stroke and every name left standing had once been a household deciding something in a room she would never see.

"That one," said Ailean, laying a finger an inch above a name near the board's edge, not touching the wood itself, "is the first that was struck. A net-maker, it's said, who asked the scribe of that day to scrape his name out so no one would know it had ever stood there. He wouldn't do it. Struck through, he told her, so a man may know a decision was made and unmade, but not scraped clean, as if it had never been made at all. Every board since has kept the rule."

Seònaid looked at the line through the name for a long while. She thought of her own father, who had never once, in the whole of his life, told her whether he had thought of going, in the days before she was born when a fifth of the island still could; he had come through the refusal with a cough that never left him and died of it before the old queen, and she had never asked him, and now there was no one left to ask.

"Who keeps the count of what's on these," she said at last, "against what's lost?"

"No one," said Ailean. "The boards are the count. When they're gone, so's the roll."

She rode back to Cathair dhearg with the grant delivered and forgotten, and a different errand taking its place in her without her having chosen it.

## II. Of the Witnesses

She went back, in the winter of that year, to the men and women whose voices already sat in her chest, and found that a second asking drew more out of each of them than the first hurried asking, made in the margins of a busy court, had ever done.

The first was a man named Fearchar Ciar, who had fought at the ford under Raghnall Ruadh's banner in the year Leabhar a' Chùraim counted some three hundred dead, and who was, by his own account, one of perhaps a dozen still living who had stood in the water that day and come out the other side of it. What he had given her two years before, hurried, had been little more than that the water was cold and the noise had gone on longer than he expected and that he had lost a brother he did not care to speak of. Now, with no queen's business waiting on either of them, Seònaid sat with him three afternoons running, asking nothing, only listening, before he told her, on the fourth, of the moment the line broke and which way the men had run and how he had known, from the sound alone before he saw it, that the ford had turned against his side.

She wrote it down that night by her own lamp, and read it back the next day, and found that half of what he had told her did not match Leabhar a' Chùraim's account of the battle at all: the book gave the numbers and the day and the outcome, but nothing of which way a man had run, or what the water had sounded like, or that the fighting had gone on, by Fearchar's memory, well past the hour the book gave for its ending. Both accounts she kept. Setting them side by side on the same leaf, she did not think either was a lie.

The second witness she went back to with more purpose than the first. Dòmhnall mac Eòghainn was the son of Eòghann mac Dhùghaill, who had been master of the store at Taigh na Fèithe in the year of Na Teallaichean Fuara and had kept, until his own death, a board with the names of the shut-out shires written on it, face to the wall, never scraped clean. He had told her of the board once already, briefly, in the last year of the old queen's life; this time, asked to bring it out again, he did so with the same unwillingness his father had shown in showing it to anyone, though he did, in the end, turn it to the light and stand while she copied it in full, where before she had only been let glance at it.

"He never told me why he kept it," Dòmhnall said. "I asked him once, when I was young enough to ask things plainly, and he said only that a man who has done a thing owes it to the doing to remember it, whether the thing was done to him or by him or only in front of him. He wasn't sure, by the end, which of the three it had been, for him."

She copied the names from the board, all of them, though she never learned what use, if any, she would make of a list of shires that the war itself had already listed elsewhere, in its own harder ledger of the dead. She copied it, she told herself, because Eòghann mac Dhùghaill had thought it worth keeping unscraped for the whole of his life, and she did not think it was her place to be the one who finally let it go.

The third witness was the one whose first telling, two years before, had cost Seònaid the most to hear and the least to write.
