Mairead nic Aonghais was a woman of Doire mhin near enough Seònaid's own age that the two of them had been girls in the same winter, in the same charity at the same temple, though neither had known the other then; and what she had given the old queen's clerk the first time, hurried and half against her own will, had been three sentences and a look Seònaid still remembered better than the sentences. Seònaid sent word to Doire mhin, and in LE 618 rode down herself to Cathair mhòr rather than ask the woman to make the journey a second time, and sat with her the better part of a day at the temple whose fire had gone grey and been relit in Seònaid's own childhood.

"I don't remember you," Mairead said, looking at her plainly across the table, "and you don't remember me, and I think that's as it should be. We were none of us paying much attention to each other, that winter. We were paying attention to the fire."

She told it as Seònaid herself would have told it, had anyone thought, at the time, to ask a child: the undyed wool cut down for a girl too big for last year's cloak and too small for a grown woman's; the particular hunger of a cold hearth's second week, food enough in the store and none of it fit to eat, because nothing among it would properly cook; the exact sound, which Seònaid had forgotten until Mairead named it, of ice forming overnight in a water-jar left too near a wall with nothing behind it to warm. Seònaid wrote almost nothing while Mairead spoke; she found, for the length of that afternoon, that she did not need to, because she already had it, had always had it, and had only needed someone else's voice to give her leave to write it down as more than her own single memory.

## III. Of the Custody-Book at the Mountain

She went up to Muileann dhearg in LE 619, a journey she had not made since she was a girl too young to remember it, carried up the white road once, so her mother had told her, on a matter of the family's own right to the coal that had been settled and forgotten long before the refusal ever touched them. She went now on a different errand: to set the leaves she had gathered against Leabhar a' Chùraim itself, the record the crown and every house trusted above any single voice, and to find, where she could, the places where a witness's memory and the book's plain word did not agree.

She found more such places than she had expected, and fewer than she had feared. The book gave the day the ford broke as one day; Fearchar Ciar had sworn to her it was two, the fighting resuming at first light after a night neither side had thought worth entering in any ledger. The book gave the dead at the ford as some three hundred; it did not say, because no clerk of that year had thought to ask, how many of the three hundred had drowned before a blow was struck at them at all, carried under by their own mail in water that had, by every witness's telling, been running high with the spring melt. No book alone could settle such a question. She set both figures down side by side in her own leaves, Leabhar a' Chùraim's count and the water's, and let a reader who came after choose between them, or hold both, as she herself had come to do.

The clerk who kept the book that season was a careful young man, new enough to the office that he still checked his own entries against an older clerk's before he trusted them, and he watched Seònaid work with an interest she found, at first, faintly unsettling, until she understood that he had never before seen anyone treat Leabhar a' Chùraim as a thing to be questioned rather than simply copied. "It's not wrong," he said to her once, defensively, when she pointed out a date that could not be squared with another entry three pages on. "It's only what the clerk of that year was told, and wrote down as he was told it."

"I know it," Seònaid said. "I don't think it's wrong. I think it's a book kept by one man in one room, the same as mine will be, and I'd rather say so plainly than let the next clerk after me believe it fell from the sky whole."

He let her sit three days in the room where the book was kept, under the same low roof cut into the hill that Catrìona had once stood beneath with the seven heads arguing a single sentence into existence, and she found, working there, that the yard outside still kept the beam and the trestle much as it must have stood on the morning Raghnall Ruadh brought his list out into the cold; the carriers still came up the white road with their sealed sticks, stamped their feet against the same cold, went down again with baskets that were never, now, sent back empty. No one in the yard remarked on the history of the place to her, or seemed to think it needed remarking on; a thing that has become ordinary again, she thought, watching them, is very often the truest sign that it was once terrible, since only the terrible ever needs so thorough a forgetting.

She asked, before she left, to see the board Eòghann mac Dhùghaill had kept, thinking it might still hang somewhere in the store, and was told it had gone south with his son years before and was hers to ask after there, which she had, of course, already done. She rode down from the mountain with her leaves no more numerous than when she had climbed it, but surer, in a way she found hard to put into words even to herself, of which of the numbers she carried were the war's and which were only the book's; and she thought, on the road, that this difference was very nearly the whole of the work she had set herself, though she would not have known how to say so plainly to anyone who asked her outright what her book was for.

## IV. Of the Book Made One Tale

By Ògach of the year Leabhar a' Chùraim, copied at Cathair dhearg, gave as LE 624, Seònaid had more leaves of testimony than she had months left, by her own private reckoning, to make anything of them, and she understood, sitting one evening with the boards from Seann Skell, the store-master's tally, the old soldier's account and the temple-girl's memory all spread before her on the same table, that she had a choice to make that no one before her had had to make in quite the same way.

Leabhar a' Chùraim told the war as Leabhar a' Chùraim told everything: an entry for each year, a name, a number, a date, no year touching the year before or after it except by the plain fact of coming after. It was the record the crown trusted, and it was, she thought, turning its pages against her own gathered leaves, no more the war than a tally of a hearth's coal was the fire it had fed. She had read it a hundred times and could not, from it alone, have said which way Fearchar Ciar had run at the ford, or what a cold hearth had sounded like to a girl too young to be told why it was cold.

She resolved, in that year, to write it whole, as one telling and not as the book had always kept it, entry by entry with each year a stranger to the year before it: from the drowning of the two princes in the river's spate through the swearing of the houses to Catrìona's son in a single day, with every witness's voice let into it where she had one, and Leabhar a' Chùraim's plain word standing in where she had none. She did not know, beginning it, that no one on the island had ever done such a thing before; she found that out only afterward, when others told her so, and she was never sure, to the end of her life, whether it was a thing to be proud of or only a thing that happened to fall to her because she was the one still living who had both the leaves and the leisure.

She wrote through the spring and into the summer, at a table in a room off An Talla Dearg that had been Catrìona's own study, working by the queen's old inkstand because it was there and no one had thought to give it to anyone else. Lachlann came in on her once, unannounced, and stood reading over her shoulder longer than she was comfortable with before he said anything.

"My mother is in here," he said at last, meaning the pages, not the room.

"She is," said Seònaid. "So is your uncle Dùghall, and Raghnall Ruadh, and a good many people neither of us ever met."

"Will it say what she was like? Not the queen. The woman."

Seònaid considered the question longer than its length deserved. "It will say what she did," she said, "and what was done because of what she did, and what people who stood near her at the time believed she meant by it. I don't know that any book can do more than that for anyone, king or clerk."

Lachlann looked at the page a while longer, and then went out without answering, and she never learned whether he had found the answer wanting or had only had nothing further to ask.

It was in that same summer, while she worked, that word came down from Inis chrom on the south-west coast of a spotted fever that had begun among the fisher households and was killing, by the time the word reached Cathair dhearg, some forty of the town's people. An Fhianna of an Fhianna stone, whose house stood nearest the sickness, went in among the dying where the town's own folk would not, and buried as many as they nursed, and lost, before the fever burned itself out, a number of their own that the messenger who brought the news could not say with any certainty, only that it was more than a few. Seònaid set down her pen for that fortnight and wrote nothing. The fever had no part in her book. It seemed to her, hearing of it, an ill thing to go on writing an old war's dead while a new town's dead were still being carried out, and she judged, rightly or not, that the two griefs should not share an ink-well.

She took the pen up again after, and finished the last of the war's telling — the ford, the burned granary at Doire mhin, the forty days at the fouled wells, the list at the yard gate, the field below Muileann chrom, the swearing in a single day — on 8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 624, and sat a long while afterward with the finished leaves in front of her, not reading them, only looking at the height of the pile, which seemed to her a strange measure for the whole of a war and yet was the only measure she had.

## V. Of the Reading at the Red Hall

No hand but her own ever copied the book while she lived. Seven years after the last leaf was written she died at Cathair dhearg, in LE 631, of no illness anyone named as remarkable, only the ordinary failing of a body that had gone eighty-two years without once, so far as anyone could tell, resting from its work; and the last thing she is recorded to have said, to the clerk who sat with her, was that the boards at Seann Skell wanted a better roof over the back room, because the damp would have the far ones illegible within a generation if no one saw to it. It was, her sister said afterward, exactly the kind of thing she would say, and exactly the kind of thing no one else would have thought to say, and between the two the sister was not sure which she found harder to bear.

The book she left behind was read into the record at An Talla Dearg the following spring, at Lachlann's own order, by a clerk with a clearer hand than hers had become in her last years, while the king sat and listened without once, those present said, interrupting to correct a fact or soften a memory, though there were passages, concerning his own mother and his uncle and the man his grandfather's rivals had been, that another king might have wished told differently. When it was done he said only that it should be copied again, and kept, and that no copy of it was ever to be made shorter than the one before it, a ruling Taigh na Fèithe's own clerks found strange at first, until it was pointed out to them plainly that a shortened history is a history with someone's choosing already baked into it, and that Lachlann, whatever else might be said of him, had wanted the choosing to stay visible, the way a struck name stays visible on a board, rather than be scraped away in the name of tidiness.

Of the smaller things that had gone on around her in those same years her own book, a history of the war alone, says nothing at all; but Leabhar a' Chùraim and Rolla a' Chalaidh kept them, as they kept everything. At Doire shean on the southern shore, in the year the crown's scribes counted as LE 634, a village that had until then lived by its nets alone laid out beds for oysters in the shallow water of its own bay and found, within a few seasons, that the trade made it rich enough to sit as a shire seat, a thing its own elders would not at first believe of a food that had always before been gathered free off the rocks for anyone who cared to wade for it. And at Seann Tarr in the north-east, where the crowds that gathered for the great feasts at the ancestor shrine had always gone home again with nothing more than what they had brought, the crowds of LE 644 began instead to hold a market on the three feast days, chiefly of honey and of the beeswax that fed the shrine's own lights, so that within a few years more wax was burned at ancestor shrines the length of the north-eastern coast than had ever been burned there before, and no one troubled to remember that a market had not always stood where the feasts stood.

Seònaid nic Coinnich never saw either. She had not gone to Doire shean since she was carried past it as a child on the road east from the burned granary at Doire mhin, and she had never in her life gone to Seann Tarr at all. What she had seen, in the last year given to her, was a book finished, and a king who did not flinch from it, and a scribe at a harbour-house a day's ride off who had shown her, without being asked twice, boards that no one before her had thought worth asking to see.

It is told at Cathair dhearg that when her book was read a second time, some years after the first reading, an old man at the back of the hall who had fought at the ford under a banner that lost said, when it was finished, that it was the truest account of the war he had heard, though it had made his own side out no better and no worse than the winning one, which he had not expected of a history written by the winning queen's own clerk. He was asked what he meant by truest. He said only that he had been there, and it sounded like being there, and that no one had thought to ask him that of any telling before.

# Chapter Twenty-six: Of Manannan's Cup

*LE 650 – 699*

> *Is fhada an cuan, is goirid a' chuimhne.*
> Long is the sea, and short is memory.
>
> — a saying of the western shore

## I. Of the Preaching on the Quay

Mànas mac Ruairidh had grown up under the shadow of the harbour-court at Seann Skell, in a house so near the water that his mother used to say the tide kept better time than his father did, coming and going by a reckoning she never once had to keep and never once caught lying, which was more, she said, than could be said of most husbands. His father Ruairidh had sworn the old oath of the quay in his own youth, the sting-oath the western merchants kept among themselves to bind their word in a trade where a man's whole living might ride on another man's honesty and no scale or measure could weigh that; and he kept, all the years Mànas knew him, a strip of tarred rope hung by the door in token of it, though he never once told his son plainly what the oath bound a man to, saying only that it was enough that it bound, the way the tide was enough without a boy needing to know why it rose.

Mànas asked him once, at twelve, sitting on the sill while his father mended a creel by lamplight, what he had sworn on, exactly, to make the mark that never faded from his palm. His father set the creel down, held up his hand so the lamp caught the old scar full on, a mark gone the colour of weathered wood and shaped, if a boy looked at it long enough, something like a fork of lightning striking down into the wrist, and said only that the mark answered better than his mouth ever could, and that a boy who wanted to know what a sting-oath cost a man would do better to watch how carefully his elders spoke, all his life, than to be told it once and think the telling was the same as the knowing. He let that be the end of it, and went back to the creel, and Mànas, watching him work by the small light, understood without being told again that there were questions in that house that a father answered with his hands and never with his tongue.

He grew to a young man who could splice a rope and gut a fish as well as any on the strand, and had, besides, a voice that carried further over open water than most men's carried over dry land, a gift he discovered by accident one wet morning hailing a boat in from a squall that had half the harbour shouting itself hoarse and unheard, and put, for some years after, to no grander use than calling men in from the rocks to their dinner. By thirty, having buried his mother two winters before and watched his father grow slow and stooped over the same creels, he stood up one still morning on the harbour stones at Seann Skell and said aloud the thing that had been gathering in him, he told those who asked him afterward, since he was a boy on a sill watching a scarred hand answer for a mouth that would not.

He chose, whether by his own design or only because it was the ground he had always stood on, the same stretch of quay where the old sting-creed of An Aois Naomh had first stood up, longer ago than any living memory reached, and called itself, before any other order on the island, the one true faith; and it was there, on 1 an t-Sultain, LE 654, with the tide going out and a handful of fishermen mending net within easy earshot, more from idleness that morning than from any intent to listen, that Mànas named the power he had come, at last, to preach. He named Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, raising his voice only a little, for it carried without needing to be raised: not the stone at Inis thais, not the hawk at Cnoc bheag, not the ancestors under their posts at Dùn ìseal. Cupa na Fìrinne of Truth would not hold a lie spoken over it, he said, and broke, so the old telling had it, in the very hand of the man who tried; and it bore, worked into its rim, the yellow scorpion for its sign, sting and truth being, he said, closer kin than most men supposed. It was Manannan, and no other power under any name the island kept, who had drawn his mist across the eastern sea behind the fleet that had once gone out from this same quay; and what that fleet had done, the going out past every sight of land and star and known shore, must never, while the mist held, be tried again by anyone who called himself faithful to the god whose sea it was.

The net-menders did not stop mending net while he spoke, not at first, and he had sense enough, even new to speaking, not to ask it of them. But before he had finished, one of them had stopped, and it was his own father, who rose from his creel and crossed the wet stones with the rope-mark still plain on his upturned palm and knelt, an old sworn-man on wet stone in front of his own son, and said only, low enough that few beyond Mànas himself ever swore they had heard it, that a mark on a hand was one kind of oath and a thing spoken plain in daylight was another, and that he had waited the whole of his life, without knowing he was waiting, to hear which kind his son would choose to make. Six others knelt after him before the tide had gone out much further, fishermen and net-menders who had known Ruairidh's son since he was a boy hailing boats off the rocks, and it was those seven, the old sworn-man and the six who came behind him, that the harbour afterward remembered as the first of Òrd Mhanannain, though Mànas himself, asked afterward who had truly been first, would only say that a father owes his son that much attention and leave the rest of the honour unclaimed.

Word of it did not travel fast in that first season, no faster than any other quay-talk carried on a wet wind, and Mànas kept mostly to preaching where he had always stood, growing neither rich nor grand on it, sleeping still under his father's roof and eating what his father's nets, and increasingly his own, brought in. It was five years on that the first boats were brought up for blessing at the berth the harbour scribes had begun, a generation before, to call Cidhe an Diosail: a dozen coasters brought in one after another on a still morning, their skippers standing bareheaded on the stones while Mànas, no longer so young himself, passed a cup of harbour water over each hull in turn and spoke the words that would, within his own lifetime, harden into the fixed form of the rite. He used no vessel finer that first year than a plain wooden bowl, having no silver and wanting none, and when one of the skippers, a man better off than most, offered to have a proper cup made and gilded for the purpose, Mànas told him that Cupa na Fìrinne had never needed a smith's hand to make it true, and that a bowl which had held nothing but harbour water and honest words was nearer Cupa na Fìrinne than any gilded thing a smith could raise.

The harbour-court, whose own sworn-men had kept the sting-oath at Seann Skell since long before Mànas's father wore the mark, did not welcome the new teaching as readily as the net-menders had, and for some years after the first kneeling the court's own scribe, a careful man named Donnchadh mac Ailein who had no particular quarrel with Manannan but a settled one with any change to the harbour's old order, refused to enter the order's blessings in Rolla a' Chalaidh alongside the tallies of hulls and cargoes, saying that a rite was not a hull and had no business on a board kept for hulls. Mànas never pressed the matter, and told his own congregation, when one of them grumbled at the scribe's refusal, that a rite recorded on a board and a rite kept true in a man's own dealings were not the same thing, and that he would rather have the second without the first than the first without the second. It was not until some years after Mànas's own death that the harbour-house began, of its own accord and without any order from the court, to note in its margins when a hull had been blessed at Cidhe an Diosail, a small mark beside the entry that later harbour scribes kept without ever troubling to ask why it had begun.

In the month after that first preaching on the quay, word came up the coast road that Lachlann mac Iain had died at Cathair dhearg, eighty-nine years old and quiet to the last, fifty years on the throne his mother had left him without, so far as the harbour ever heard, doing anything a quay would trouble to remember; and that his daughter Anna, fifty-four years old and long past any waiting for it, had been crowned in the same hall. Mànas heard the tidings the way the town heard most tidings, from a rider who stopped at the horse-trough by the harbour-court to water his horse and talked while it drank, and he is not recorded to have said anything about it at all, which the harbour took, rightly or not, for a kind of answer of its own: that the sea's governance and the crown's were, to his mind, two different powers entirely, and that the death of one king, however long his quiet reign, was the crown's business to mark and not the tide's.

## II. Of the Cup Carried Down the Coast

The teaching went where the fishing went, which was down the coast before it went anywhere else, carried less by Mànas's own feet, which stayed mostly within a day's walk of Seann Skell to the end of his life, than by the fishing families themselves, who traded catch and net-twine from harbour to harbour and, riding along with them in the same creel, whatever a man had lately taken to believing. By the time Mànas was an old man it had reached Ros bheag down the coast and Cuan shean beyond it, both of them towns that had given their strand and their labour to the building of the fleet in the years before a' Scaradh and had never, in all the years since, quite stopped listening for word of anything to do with the sea beyond their own headlands; and it was at Cuan shean, among the rope-walks that had once measured cable enough for keels no one now living had seen launched, that the teaching took hold hardest and earliest of anywhere beyond Mànas's own quay.

An old rope-walker there named Tormod Ciar, who had walked the same length of ground backward twisting strand into cable since he was a boy too young to be paid a man's full wage for it, was among the first of Cuan shean to kneel, and he did it, by his own account, not for any word Mànas had ever spoken to him in person, for the two men never once met in this life, but because a travelling net-mender stopped under the eaves of the rope-shed one wet evening, waiting out a squall, and told the walkers gathered there what the preacher at Seann Skell had said of the mist and the fleet and the sea that must not be tried again. Tormod, who had spent the whole of his working life laying rope for ships that no longer sailed anywhere beyond sight of their own shore, and had never once, in all his years at the walk, been given a reason for it beyond that the fishing did not need longer cable than the fishing needed, found in the net-mender's telling the first account he had ever heard that made any sense of why his own trade had shrunk, year on year, without ever once, in his lifetime, growing back to what the old wrights' fellowship had once built it for. He swore Cupa na Fìrinne before his fellow rope-walkers on the walk itself the following morning, with no priest of the order nearer than Seann Skell to hear him, cupping harbour rain in his own two hands for want of a bowl, and told them afterward, more than once, that he had sworn it to the sea and not to any man standing on dry ground, and that the sea, unlike a man, had never yet broken an oath it was given honestly.

Mànas himself grew old at the harbour he had never left, and the house the order raised in those years, Taigh Mhanannain, stood not far from the harbour-court his father had sworn to, low and plain and built of the same grey stone as the quay, so that a stranger walking past it on a grey morning might have taken it, at first glance, for one more shed of nets and tar rather than the house of a growing order. He kept the rite the same each year he had strength left to stand for it, the bowl grown at last to a proper cup of plain silver that his own congregation had raised the silver for without his asking, and he is remembered by those who were young when he was old as a man who spoke less as the years went on rather than more, having said, he told one of his own who asked him plainly why an old teacher should fall so quiet, most of what he had ever had to say in the first years of his preaching, and seeing no good cause to say it twice over merely because he had lived long enough to be asked.

In the last winter of his life, when he could no longer stand the whole length of the blessing without a younger man's arm under his own, a woman of the order named Beathag nic Dhonnchaidh, who had kept his house those last ten years and would keep the order's house after him, asked him one evening by the fire whether he feared the mist would lift before the island had properly learned what Manannan had shut it in from. He answered, she told others afterward, that a fisherman who feared every squall before it rose would never once put out from the strand, and that a teacher who spent his last strength fearing a thing that had not yet come was a poor steward of the strength Manannan had given him to spend on the thing that had. He died soon after, at Seann Skell, in the house he had raised, within sound, his own people said, of the same water he had preached beside for six-and-thirty years, and was buried, at his own asking, under a plain slab, cut with no name, set facing the harbour mouth, so that the tide he had spent his whole life speaking of would be the last thing, and the first thing after, to pass over him. Those who came to Taigh Mhanannain in the years right after his death found it kept much as he had kept it, by men and women, Beathag nic Dhonnchaidh foremost among them, who had never once heard him preach with their own ears and knew his teaching only at second and third hand, the way the island, by then, knew most of what it believed.

## III. Of the Rule of the Headlands

Beathag nic Dhonnchaidh, who had kept Mànas's house and, after him, kept the order's, lived to see the teaching carried further than the old man had ever thought to carry it. The priests who rose up after him at Ros bheag, where the teaching had taken almost as deep a root as at Mànas's own quay, met through the better part of a winter to debate, by all the later order kept of it, not whether the sea beyond the headlands was Manannan's to forbid, which none of them doubted, but how far a boat might go before the forbidding took hold; and it was an old priestess of that house, one who had herself, as a girl, watched the last of the pilots die without finishing what he meant to teach, who argued the debate down at last to a single plain rule, that no boat of the faithful might go where the headland could no longer be seen from its own deck. In LE 694 it was laid down so, on pain of standing before Cupa na Fìrinne and answering for it, and the rule held on the west coast, once it was made, for longer than any one preacher's lifetime could have hoped to account for. It was not, those who kept it afterward always insisted, a fear of the sea itself, which Manannan's own faithful were taught to hold in a kind of grave and working affection rather than dread, but a fear of what the sea beyond sight of land had already once been made to carry away, and what it might, if the mist should ever thin, be asked to carry away again.

The rule was tested within its own first year, off Ros bheag, by a skipper named Coinneach mac Sheumais who had fished the same grounds for thirty years without troubling any priest's opinion of where his own boat might go, and who, on a clear still morning with the headland still just visible astern, no more than a low grey line, took his boat a little further out than he had ever taken it before, chasing a run of fish that seemed, that particular day, well worth the chasing. He was turned back before noon by two of the order's own boats, crewed by men he had drunk with his whole life, who came up on either side of him and told him plainly, not unkindly, that the rule made no exception for fish however plentiful, and stood off his bow, oars shipped, until he brought his own boat about and ran before the wind back the way he had come. "I could still see the headland," Coinneach is said to have told them, and the elder of the two boats' skippers is said to have answered only that the rule did not ask what a man could still see, only how far off the land he stood when he saw it, which silenced Coinneach more thoroughly than any longer citing of the rule could have done. He never fished that far out again, and told his own sons, afterward, that he had not minded the turning back nearly so much as he had minded finding out, in front of two men he had known since boyhood, that he had been wrong about how far a headland could still be seen once a man had already made up his mind to go past it.

What the rule cost the west coast, over the span of years it held, was harder to see in the turning back of a single boat than it was seen weighed whole, as those who came after had cause to weigh it. The steering of a course by the stars, already half lost on that shore since the pilots who had carried Seumas Reultach's own teaching west had sailed with the fleet and left behind them only what little they had passed to others in the years before, went out entirely where it had never before, in all the years since the fleet's building, had the chance to be forgotten so completely, for there was no longer any voyage sailed on the west coast long enough, or dark enough, or far enough from a known headland, to need it kept. A pilot's grandson at Ros bheag, a boy named Griogair, was asked one evening by a visiting priest of the order which star his grandfather, a man once counted among the last on that shore who could hold a course by night, had steered by. The boy, who had heard his grandfather's name spoken all his life with a kind of respect he had never fully understood the grounds of, only that the old man had once, before Griogair was born, gone further out on the water than any boat now went and had come home again, could not answer, and stood a while working at the question as though it might yield to being stared at hard enough before admitting, plainly, that he did not know. Nobody in his own house, it came out in the asking, had thought, while there was still anyone alive who remembered it, to write the star's name down or teach it onward, having had, each of them in turn, other and nearer things to teach a boy first.

At Àth shean, further inland and further still from any water Manannan's priests troubled themselves to bless, the royal granaries that had stood since before a' Scaradh, low buildings of timber and old stone that had weathered the tallies of a hundred harvests, were pulled down in LE 699 and built again from their own foundations, in dressed stone this time and on raised floors set well clear of the ground, against the rats that had for years been getting into the lower bins faster than any night-watch could keep them out. The tally-house went up new beside the granaries in the same stone, and the reeve who oversaw the rebuilding, an old man named Fearchar mac Phàdraig near the end of his own long service, walked the finished floors once with a lamp held low to the new stone and said only, when he was satisfied, that a granary built to outlast the rats might, with a little luck, outlast the reeve who had seen it built as well, and went back to his tallies without further comment on a labour that had taken the better part of three years and left the shire's grain, that first winter, dry from wall to wall without a single sack lost to damp or gnawing, a thing no man then living at Àth shean could remember having happened before.

It is told at Seann Skell, where the order kept its house and its rite long after the man who had begun both was laid under his plain slab facing the harbour mouth, that a keeper of Taigh Mhanannain in those same years was asked by a stranger passing through, a merchant of no particular faith who had heard the teaching only as one more curiosity of the west coast worth a traveller's idle question, whether the order held that the mist would lie over the eastern sea for ever. The keeper is said to have answered that Ceò Mhanannain had been drawn once, for a reason the order did not claim to know in full, and that it would lift, if it ever lifted, in its own time and by no persuasion of theirs, and that in the meanwhile Cupa na Fìrinne asked only truth of those who swore to it and left the sea's own intentions to the sea alone. The stranger asked nothing further and went on his way, and the keeper, watching him go, is said to have thought, though not to have said it aloud to anyone, that a boy at Ros bheag who could not name his own grandfather's star had already answered the merchant's question, without meaning to and without knowing he had done it, as well as any priest of the order ever could.

Rolla a' Chalaidh say nothing of the boy Griogair afterward, for a boy who does not follow the sea leaves no mark on a harbour board, and Manannan's own keepers, unlike the harbour scribes, wrote down oaths sworn and boats blessed and little else beside. It is told only, at Ros bheag among those who kept the priest's question and the boy's silence as a small cautionary tale of their own, that Griogair grew to a man who worked the land above the harbour rather than the water below it, and that when he had sons of his own he taught them, whatever else he judged worth a father's teaching, the names of every headland visible from the shore before he taught them anything of what lay beyond it, having decided, so far as anyone could later say for him, that a thing worth keeping was a thing a man ought to write down or speak aloud the first year he knew it, and not wait, as his own house had waited with his grandfather's star, for someone else's asking to prove the waiting had already cost him everything there was to lose.

# Chapter Twenty-seven: Of the Bargain of the Counts

*LE 700 – 769*

> *Cha do chuir mi cunntas air an fhìrinn, ach air an aonta.*
> I set no count upon the truth, only upon the agreement.
>
> — said to be Eòghann mac Pheadair's own saying, kept afterward at Muileann dhearg

## I. Of the Boy Set to the Tallies

Eòghann mac Pheadair was born in the shadow of the hill at Muileann dhearg, in one of the low stone houses the coal-breakers had raised at the hill's foot two generations before his own, and he grew up knowing the sound of Taigh na Fèithe's bell for opening and closing the galleries before he knew his letters. His father cut coal in the lower workings and never rose from it, and would have set his son to the same labour without a second thought, had the boy not shown, at seven or eight, a memory for numbers that the men about him came to think worth more than a strong back. It was the old scribe of Taigh na Fèithe, a stooped, dry man named Murchadh Beag who had kept the tallies of Na Seachd Taighean' galleries for thirty years and complained of his eyes every winter, who first noticed the boy reciting back a whole day's cartage, load for load, without once looking at the board where Murchadh had chalked it; and it was Murchadh who went to the boy's father and asked, not for the first time in his life, whether a household might spare a son from the coal-face for a scribe's stool.

He was set to it at seven, sweeping Taigh na Fèithe floor and mixing the ink before he was let touch a leaf, and Murchadh, who owned to no patience for a boy's questions during the day's proper work, would answer any question at all once the leaves were put away and the lamp burned only for the two of them: why a gallery's number changed when a house divided, why the same household might be entered twice in different years under different names, why the vein answered some galleries better than others though the custodians swore they worked them alike. Eòghann learned, by nine, to save his questions for that hour and no other, and Murchadh, who had buried a wife and outlived two apprentices before this one, came in time to keep the lamp burning a little longer than the work alone required.

By fourteen he could keep a day's tally as well as Murchadh himself, though not yet, the old man said, as fast, and it was that year, LE 714, that word came up from the coast to Taigh na Fèithe of a thing Eòghann was set to enter on the general leaf without at first understanding why it mattered to anyone away from the coast: that Cuan shean had taken up half its rope-walks and sown the ground with barley. Murchadh explained it to him plainly enough, once, and never again, for he was not a man who liked to say a thing twice: the rope had been laid for the fleet, and after the fleet for the fishing, and the fishing had never once, in all the years since, needed cable of the old length; so half the walks stood idle years on end, and idle ground, on an island that had grown to more mouths than it once fed, was a waste no reeve would suffer forever. The boy asked whether it did not grieve the rope-walkers, to break up ground their own fathers had walked, twisting strand, for a fleet none of them had ever seen sail; Murchadh said that grief was not a scribe's business to enter on a leaf, only the fact of the barley and the year it was sown, and that a scribe who let himself grieve every trade the island outgrew would have no ink left, by forty, for anything the living still needed written down.

Eòghann wrote it as he was told, a line among many, and thought no more of it for years, save that he had, without being asked to, begun to notice that every leaf he copied told the same story from some other angle: a trade shrinking here, a family moving there, all of it circling back, sooner or later, to the fleet that had sailed before any man now living was born. He asked Murchadh once more, the winter he turned sixteen, whether Taigh na Fèithe's own leaves said anything of where the fleet had gone, and Murchadh told him only that Leabhar a' Chùraim held what it held and no more, and that a boy who wanted the rest of that story would have to go looking for it in the harbour songs, which Eòghann never did, having by then more tallies of his own to keep than hours left over for songs.

## II. Of the Wave and the Market

He was four-and-twenty, and had Murchadh's old stool as good as his own though the old man had not yet the grace to die and leave it to him outright, when the report reached Muileann dhearg of the wave at Cnoc chaol on the south coast: a great swell that rose with no storm behind it to explain it, ran the drying racks off the beach, and carried off two children with them before any hand on the shore could reach them, 22 an Gearran, LE 724. Eòghann entered it on the general leaf as he entered every disaster that touched a household of the coal-right, cold and plain, the way Murchadh had taught him a scribe must enter grief if he meant to go on being of any use to the living: the names, the place, the day, and no word beyond what the day itself would bear. He asked Murchadh once, copying it fair, whether it did not seem a strange thing that a wave should rise from a flat sea with no wind in it, and Murchadh told him that the sea did what the sea did, and that a scribe who wanted an explanation for every strange thing the sea sent up would do better to find another trade, for there were more strange things in the tally-books of a coastal island than any one man's lifetime could account for. Cnoc chaol set its racks higher up the shore after, and Taigh na Fèithe's leaf recorded, the following season, that the household of one of the drowned children had struck itself from its old gallery and taken up a new one further from the water, which Eòghann understood, better than Murchadh's explanation had made him understand the wave, without needing to be told.

It was some years later, near his thirty-first year, that the master of Taigh na Fèithe sent him east on his own feet for the first time, to Baile Mòr dhìreach, the citadel on the straight eastern road, to stand witness for Na Seachd Taighean when the crown's grant of a market there was read out and the boundary stones of its ground were set, 11 an t-Samhain, LE 731. He had never before gone further from Muileann dhearg than a day's walk would carry him, and the road east, which took the better part of a week, showed him a coast he had only ever known as names on a leaf: the fish and sail-cloth of the shore towns coming up to meet the furs and hides and dyes of the hill country, the dyers of a neighbouring town selling colours he had never seen a colour merchant in the west carry, all of it converging on a market ground that had, the week before he arrived, been nothing but rough pasture with four stones sunk in it to mark its corners.

He slept the nights of that journey in road-houses he had never had cause to know by name, at tables set with strangers who asked him, once they had his trade out of him, what the vein answered these days for a household's handful, a question he had fielded a hundred times from custodians and never once, until that week, from a stranger who owned no gallery at all and only wanted, it seemed, to know that the thing still burned steady somewhere behind the hills he had never travelled to. Oddly, he found he did not mind the asking nearly so much as Murchadh had always claimed to; there was a kind of easiness, he thought, in a question that wanted nothing written down after it.

He stood at the reading with the other witnesses, said the words Taigh na Fèithe had sent him to say, and watched the first stalls go up the same afternoon, traders who had clearly been waiting only for the word to be spoken before they set their goods out, as though the market had existed in every mind but the law's for a year before the law caught up to it. A dyer of the hill towns spread lengths of cloth dyed a red Eòghann had no name for across a trestle not ten feet from where he stood, and told him, unasked, that the colour came from a root that grew nowhere lower than the high pastures and had never before had anywhere on the coast worth the carrying it to; and Eòghann, who wrote tallies all his working life and had rarely had cause to look twice at a colour, found himself standing longer at that trestle than his errand from Taigh na Fèithe had any need of him to stand.

He walked home slower than he had walked out, by his own account afterward; the weariness of the road was in it, but more of it was that he found, for the first time in his life away from a stool and a leaf, that he wanted to look at things a while before he wrote them down.

## III. Of the Scribe of the Red Hall

He was eight-and-thirty, keeper of Taigh na Fèithe's leaves in his own right by then, Murchadh eleven years in the ground and the stool unambiguously his own, when a rider came up from Cathair dhearg in 23 am Màrt, LE 739 to say that a scribe of the crown's own household was coming to Taigh na Fèithe on An Talla Dearg's business, and would the master of Taigh na Fèithe grant her Leabhar a' Chùraim for a day, or as many days as the matter took. The master, who had dealt with the crown's scribes before and found them, on the whole, no worse than any other visitor with a warrant, told Eòghann to give her whatever the book held and to mind his tongue about the rest of it, by which he meant Na Seachd Taighean' own accounts, which were not the crown's business and never had been.

The scribe was a woman not much past thirty herself, Mòrag nic Ìomhair, who arrived on a hired horse with a satchel of her own leaves and the particular brisk courtesy of someone who had ridden the thirty-nine miles from Cathair dhearg expecting Taigh na Fèithe to be difficult about its book and was pleasantly, visibly surprised to find it was not. She wanted, she told Eòghann plainly enough once the courtesies were done, to set the crown's reckoning of Bliadhnaichean an Diosail against Taigh na Fèithe's own, for An Talla Dearg's clerks had lately found, comparing an old grant to an old debt in the same year's business, that the two offices' counts did not agree, and nobody at Cathair dhearg could say with any certainty which of them, if either, was right.

She had brought her own bread and a small hard cheese wrapped in cloth, meaning, she said, to trouble Taigh na Fèithe's kitchen as little as its book, and ate it standing at the north window on her first evening, looking down the hill at the coal-breakers' town below, while Eòghann fetched Leabhar a' Chùraim from its chest and blew the dust from its cover in a way he had not troubled to do for a visitor in years. Watching him set it down, she asked him whether the book had ever left that room in all the years it had been kept, and when he told her it had not, not once, she said that a book which had never once been carried out into weather to be tested against another book's claim was a strange thing to call a record at all, and that she meant no offence by saying so, only that it was, in her trade, a kind of loneliness she had come some distance to end.

The two of them spent the better part of three days at the long table under Taigh na Fèithe's north window, each running a count forward from An Diosal by their own office's method, comparing tallies of burnings and gallery-openings and the ordinary business of years that each side had kept for its own purposes and never once, in all the years either count had been kept, set beside the other's. It was on the second evening, both of them ink-stained to the wrist and neither yet willing to say aloud what the columns had already told them, that Mòrag laid her leaf down next to his and said only that she counted An Diosal a year longer than his book did, and asked him plainly whether he could find the year in his own reckoning where the difference had crept in.

He could not, and told her so without pretending otherwise, which she said afterward was the thing that made her trust his count at all: that a scribe capable of admitting his own book might be wrong in a place he could not point to was worth more to her, in that hour, than one who would have sworn to every figure on the leaf sooner than own a gap in it. They went back through both counts a second time, by lamplight, the master of Taigh na Fèithe looking in once and going away again without a word when he saw how the evening stood, and found, near the end of it, that the fault lay nowhere either of them could finally lay a finger on: a year, somewhere in the first generation after the turn, entered twice by one office's habit or once by the other's, so far back and so quietly done that no leaf either of them had brought could say which office had erred, or whether either truly had.

## IV. Of the Agreement

They settled it, in the end, not by proof, for neither count could furnish proof the other would accept, but by agreement, which Mòrag said, and Eòghann came in time to agree with her, was worth as much to the living as proof would have been and a good deal easier to come by. In the end they took the crown's count for the reckoning that would go forward from that day, since the crown's business touched more households across more shires than Taigh na Fèithe's own and a single count serving the whole island was worth more than either office's pride in being first; and Eòghann wrote Taigh na Fèithe's agreement to it himself, in his own hand, on a fresh leaf, with the master of Taigh na Fèithe's mark set under his and Mòrag's own office's mark set under that, so that whoever read the leaf afterward would see two hands and two seals and no claim beyond what the leaf plainly said: that the offices had differed, and had agreed, and neither pretended the agreement was anything more than what it was.

The same days settled a second matter that had waited, unresolved, behind the first: the day of the year on which Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh should properly fall, which the two counts had also placed a little apart from each other for the same buried reason, and which every harbour from Seann Skell round the coast had until then kept each after its own custom, a day or two either side of its neighbours, without much troubling over the difference. Mòrag proposed, and Eòghann saw no cause to refuse her, that the same agreement that fixed the count should fix the day, so that a rite meant to be kept by the whole coast together might, from that year forward, at least be kept on the same day by all of it, whatever the coast might privately go on believing about which count had been the truer one before the two offices sat down together.

She rode back to Cathair dhearg with her copy of the leaf in the same satchel she had brought empty, and Eòghann kept his in Leabhar a' Chùraim, between two older leaves that had never expected to have a stranger's mark folded in among them. He said to the master of Taigh na Fèithe, when he was asked how the crown's scribe had been to deal with, that she was a hard woman to argue a figure past and an easy one to agree a figure with, which the master took, correctly, for the highest compliment Eòghann had it in him to pay another scribe. The two offices wrote to each other now and again in the years that followed, mostly on ordinary business, but Eòghann kept, folded inside his own working leaves for the rest of his working life, the short note Mòrag sent him the winter after, saying only that the coast had kept the rite on the agreed day without a single harbour writing to complain of it, which she counted, she said, a better proof than either of their books had managed to furnish on their own.

## V. Of the Year the World Went On Without Him

He was an old man by the time the question the two of them had settled with a leaf and two seals was taken up again, at Inis mhòr in the north, by younger minds who wanted more than agreement and asked, in a house of disputation the pupils of Dùn thais had founded there, whether the vein answered any true count of years at all or only the custom of counting it; the house's first master was remembered afterward, by those who studied under him, for refusing every answer he was offered rather than for giving one of his own, and word of it reached Taigh na Fèithe the way most northern news reached Eòghann in his last years, at second hand, by a rider glad of a fire and a cup and willing to talk while he warmed himself.

The rider, a young man who plainly relished the telling more than he understood the argument, said the pupils at Inis mhòr had gone so far as to ask whether a gallery worked faithfully by a house with no claim of blood to the crown answered any worse than a gallery worked by the oldest of the seven, and that their master had refused that question along with every other, saying only that the vein did not trouble to answer a question it had never once been asked. Eòghann heard it out, said that a house built to refuse every answer sounded a restless sort of house to keep, and went back to the leaf in front of him, for whatever the pupils of Inis mhòr chose to argue about the vein, the vein itself still wanted its tallies kept daily whether the argument was settled or not; though he owned to the rider, before the young man rode on the next morning, that he would not himself have minded hearing the master refuse a question or two in person, had his legs still been equal to a journey of that length.

That same year the crown at Cathair dhearg passed, without any disturbance that reached as far as Taigh na Fèithe's own hill, from the fifth ruler of the house of Catrìona, a woman Eòghann had never once in his life laid eyes on, to her granddaughter, a girl of eighteen crowned 10 an Gearran, LE 769, in the same hall her grandmother had held for near fifty years; Na Seachd Taighean sent their custodians down to Cathair dhearg to see the crowning done, as the compact required, though the master of Taigh na Fèithe went in Eòghann's stead, for by then a journey of thirty-nine miles was more than his legs would answer for in a single season, and he said so to the master plainly, without the shame a younger man might have felt owning it. He heard the crowning described to him afterward, the neck-rings of the seven heads catching the hall's lamplight, the new queen's voice, they told him, steadier than her years had any right to make it, and thought, hearing it, less of the girl herself than of the leaf he had once carried between two seals: that whoever sat in An Talla Dearg, the count the leaf had fixed would go on running under her reign exactly as it had run under her grandmother's, needing no crowning of its own to keep it true.

It was that same year, too, that the bath-house over Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh below Muileann ruadh was raised again in dressed stone by the house that kept it, and opened its doors one day in seven to the sick of any household, whoever they were sworn to; and it was to that bath-house, in the last cold turn of that same year, that Eòghann let himself be carried on a cart he would have refused, a few years before, as an old man's fussing, his chest gone tight in a way no winter before it had ever quite managed.

The physicians of the house that kept the springs asked him, before they would let him into the water, the ordinary questions they asked every stranger carried to them: his years, his trade, what house his gallery answered to; and Eòghann, giving the answers, found he could not keep himself from adding, as no physician had asked him to, that he had once made an agreement with a woman of the crown's own household over a difference of a single year, and that the difference had never once, in all the years since, been proven either of them wrong. The physician, a woman near his own age who had plainly heard a hundred old men's stray remembrances at that basin's edge and had long since stopped being surprised by any of them, told him only that a single year, set beside the water he was about to sit in, which had come up out of the same mountain warm since long before either count of years began, was a small thing to have carried folded in his working leaves for thirty winters, and helped him down the steps without further comment.

He sat in the warm water with men and women of houses he had spent his whole working life keeping separate on a leaf, coal-breakers and salt-carriers and a shepherd's widow from the hills, none of them minding, in that water, whose gallery any of the others answered to, and thought, before he let his eyes close a while against the steam, that it was a strange late lesson for a man who had given his whole life to counting differences to be taught, in a stone basin at the far end of it, how little the water troubled to keep them.

He kept, to the very end of that year, the leaf folded among his working leaves where he had kept it since the evening he and Mòrag nic Ìomhair had set their two counts down side by side and found neither of them equal to proving the other wrong; and it was that leaf, and not the crowning at Cathair dhearg nor the disputation at Inis mhòr nor even the warm water that had eased his chest a while, that he showed a young scribe he had lately taken to teaching his own trade, the way old Murchadh had once taught it to him, when the boy asked him, as boys will, what the finest thing was that he had done in a life spent mostly at a stool. Eòghann unfolded it for him without ceremony, the ink gone the brown of old peat-water and two seals still legible under it, and told him only that it was not the count itself the leaf was worth keeping for, since no leaf on the island could prove a count true past what its own scribe chose to believe, but the agreement written under it in two hands and sealed by two offices that had never, before that week, sat down at the same table; and that a boy who learned to write an honest agreement, he said, folding the leaf away again, would have learned more of the trade than any boy who only learned to write a stubborn count.

# Chapter Twenty-eight: Of the Sea-Thieves' Strand

*LE 775 – 835*

## I. Of the Boats Off the Small Islands

Coinneach mac Nèill had held the reeve's board at Baile chrom for eleven years before the first coaster came in short. It had been, until that summer, the post of a quiet man: he weighed the grain dues, he witnessed the marriages, he settled the small quarrels of a small town, and he went home each evening to a wife who teased him, gently, for the care he took over sums that would have troubled no one else in the shire. Baile chrom sat low on the north-west shore where the land ran out into a scatter of small islands, more rock than soil, and the town had lived the whole of its life off the strip of grey water between them: barley from its own thin fields, fish and grey seal-oil traded down the coast, and a peace so old that no one now living could have said when it began.

His father had held the same board before him, and his father's father before that, so far back as the town's own memory ran, and Coinneach had grown up under the low roof of the reeve's house believing, without ever having cause to examine the belief, that a reeve's chief labour was patience: patience with a fisherman who swore his catch had run smaller than it had, patience with a widow who could not pay her dues until the barley was in, patience with the slow turning of a year that asked, on that shore, little more of a man than that he keep faith with the tide and the season and not trouble himself overmuch with what lay beyond the small islands. He had taken a wife from a boat-building family two coves along, Beathag nic Artair, a woman with a dry tongue and a steadier hand at accounts than his own, and the two of them had settled into a life he expected, those first eleven years, to grow old and unremarkable in, much as his father had before him.

The town he kept that tally for was not large even in its best years, a few hundred souls strung along a single street above the strand, with a temple no bigger than a byre and a harbour that held, on a full market day, a dozen boats at most. It asked nothing grand of a reeve, and Coinneach had given it, in return, nothing grand: a fair weight on the scale, an honest word at the boundary disputes, and an ear that did not tire of hearing the same complaints season after season. He had thought, before the boats came, that this was the whole of what the office would ever ask of him.

It ended, so far as anyone in the town could afterward fix a beginning to it, on a still morning when the coaster out of Ros bheag came into the berth two days late and a third short in her hold, her skipper white about the mouth and unwilling, at first, to say why. She had been boarded off the small islands, he told Coinneach at last, sitting in the reeve's own kitchen with a cup of barley spirit he had not touched, by three boats that came out of a channel he had fished all his life and had never once thought to watch. The men who took her grain wore no mark and gave no name, and they had not troubled to hide their faces, which the skipper found, telling it, stranger and worse than any violence they had offered him, for it meant they did not fear being known.

The skipper's fright stayed with Coinneach longer than the loss did, which the town could and did absorb, a third of one coaster's hold being no great matter against a whole season's trade. He sat that night at his own table turning the strangeness of it over with his wife, who had heard the skipper's account through the kitchen wall and had her own reading of it ready before Coinneach had finished his. Men who hid their faces feared to be known, she said, setting down her needle; men who did not hide them had already reckoned that being known would cost them nothing, and a reeve who wanted to understand what he was dealing with would do better to ask himself why that reckoning might be a sound one on this particular stretch of coast, this particular year, than to ask who the men were. Coinneach had no ready answer for her that night either, and slept badly, turning the question over until the tide had gone out and come in again without his noticing either.

They were known, within the season. Rolla a' Chalaidh of the coast towns began, that year and the next, to set down names against the losses: not the names of strangers off some unmapped shore, as a body might have hoped, but names that half the reeves of the north-west could have matched, without much searching, to a face they had watched grow up. 24 am Faoilleach, LE 784, the first full count of the takings went up to Cathair dhearg, and it named among the sea-thieves a man of Baile chrom, a fisherman's son Coinneach had known since the boy was small enough to be carried on his father's shoulders down to the strand. His name was Aonghas mac Ruairidh, and his father Ruairidh had fished the same grounds as Coinneach's own father before either of them was born.

Coinneach went to the boy's mother himself, because he judged it a thing that ought to be done by the reeve and not left to Rolla a' Chalaidh to say for him, and found her at her door with the salt wind working at a strand of grey hair she had given up pinning back. She did not deny it. She said only that a young man who watches the fish thin out of his own home waters, season on season, for reasons no reeve and no priest has ever once explained to him, will in time go looking for a living where the living still is, and that if the living was to be found only in another man's hold, then another man's hold was where a hungry young man would go looking for it. Coinneach had no answer that satisfied either of them, and he walked back to his own house that evening turning over, more than the theft, the plainness with which she had said it, as though she had long since stopped expecting the world to be other than it plainly was.

He asked, that same week, at every house along the street where a young man had gone missing from his own boat without any word to his kin of where he had shipped instead, and found more such houses than he had let himself expect before he began asking. Some of the fathers would not speak to him at all, closing their doors on him with a civility colder than any rudeness could have been. One old fisherman, a man named Eachann who had fished beside Coinneach's own father, told him only that a reeve who came asking after another man's son should first go home and ask his own conscience how many seasons running he had watched the catch fall and done nothing but write it down smaller in his own book each year. Coinneach carried that home too, and found no more of an answer for it than he had found for Aonghas's mother.

## II. Of Half the Houses Standing Empty

The raiding did not slacken, and within a few years the town Coinneach had inherited a quiet post in was a town visibly thinning under his own eyes, the way a fire someone forgets to feed burns down slowly, house by house, to embers, never going out all at once. Families who had fished the same water for generations began, that stretch of years, to load a cart with what it would carry and go inland before the coast road closed for the winter mud, judging a hard life among strangers a smaller risk than a certain one on a shore the sea-thieves had made their own hunting ground. Coinneach counted the going as carefully as he had once counted grain, because it was, after all, the same board he kept the tally on, and by the time he made his report to the crown's own scribes, 26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 789, he could set down in his own hand that half the houses of Baile chrom stood empty, their thatch going to moss, their doors shut on rooms no one would sleep in again that year or any year he could then foresee.

He watched the going of one family in particular that stayed with him longer than the rest: a boat-wright named Murchadh and his wife and their three children, who loaded a single cart on a morning of thin rain with everything the cart would bear and stood a while at the edge of the street before they set off, looking back at a house Murchadh's own grandfather had raised. Coinneach walked down to see them off, as he judged a reeve owed at least that much to any household leaving his charge, and Murchadh, shaking his hand at the cart's tail, said only that a boat-wright with no boats left worth building for could build a cart instead, and had, and that he hoped Coinneach would forgive him for not staying to watch the town finish emptying around him. Coinneach told him there was nothing to forgive, and meant it, and watched the cart out of sight along the coast road before he turned back to a street that had, that morning, six fewer feet walking it than it had the evening before.

He wrote the report himself, sitting up two nights over it by a single lamp while his wife Beathag nic Artair sat opposite mending nets that fewer and fewer hands in the town still had any use for, and he wrote it plainly, without the flourishes a lesser reeve might have reached for to make his own trouble sound larger than his neighbour's, because he judged, rightly as it turned out, that the crown's scribes had trouble enough of their own to weigh without a reeve's vanity added to it. He asked only that the grain dues on the houses still standing be lightened, since a town paying dues reckoned for twice its present hands could not long keep bread in the houses that remained, and he sent the report south by the same rider who carried the coast road's other business, not troubling to send it apart, or to mark it urgent, judging that a true thing said plainly would carry its own weight without his help.

The answer came back before the winter closed the road, shorter than his own letter and written, he could tell from the hand, by a scribe who had many such letters that season to answer and little leisure to spend on any one of them: the grain dues of Baile chrom were remitted, from that year forward, to a sum reckoned by the households that stood, not the households that had once stood, and the reeve was thanked for a count taken, the letter said, with care. Coinneach read the letter twice through at his own table and then folded it away in the chest where he kept such leaves, and told his wife only that the town would not starve on the dues it could no longer pay, which was, he judged, as much as any reeve on that coast could honestly claim to have won that year.

## III. Of the Force Asked and the Force Sent

He did not ask for more, not at first, holding to the same plain reckoning that had served him with the dues: a town remitted of what it could not pay might yet feed itself, given time, on what its remaining hands could still bring in from the water. But the boats out of the small islands grew bolder as the coast grew emptier of eyes to watch them, and a season came when they no longer confined themselves to coasters caught alone on open water but put in, twice within the same moon, to strands within sight of Baile chrom's own harbour and took what stood in the drying-sheds before any hand in the town could be raised against them. It was after the second of these, in the same season the dues remission was scarcely settled in the crown's own ledger, that Coinneach sat down and wrote the letter he had put off writing as long as his own conscience would allow him to put it off, asking this time for a force outright, no longer for lightened dues alone, since a reeve with a tally-stick and a handful of fishermen too old or too young to have gone raiding themselves could no longer hold a coast that men of his own shire, grown desperate or grown greedy or grown both together, had made their hunting ground.

The letter went south in the last good weather of the year and the answer, this time, was slower in coming, for the crown had its own troubles to weigh, and a reeve's petition from a thinning shore on the far side of the island was not, Coinneach understood without needing to be told, the first leaf on any scribe's board that season. He waited through a winter and into the spring that followed, and he was still waiting, mending his own nets now beside his wife in the evenings for want of hands enough in the town to hire, when word came at last that a force under a captain named Iain mac Thormoid had been raised and was coming north by sea, sent, the letter said, on the queen's own word.

He read that line to his wife three times over before he set the letter down, less from any doubt of what it said than from a wish, he admitted to her, to hear it said aloud a third time and see whether it still sounded as unlikely to his own ears as it had the first. Beathag told him, not unkindly, that a man who had spent a whole winter fearing his letter had gone into a scribe's chest and been forgotten ought to allow himself an evening of believing it had not, before he went back to his habit of expecting the worst of every answer the capital sent him. He allowed himself the evening, and little more, for the spring brought planting before it brought ships, and a reeve with half his fields untended could not stand idle on the strand waiting for a sail that might yet be a season in coming.

Eilidh Bhàn had held the throne at Cathair dhearg two and thirty years by then, crowned a girl of eighteen and grown, in the reigning, into a woman the north-west knew mostly by the letters her scribes wrote in her name, for she had never once, in all those years, travelled so far from the capital as the coast her own force was now bound for. Iain mac Thormoid's ships put in at Baile chrom on a grey morning of driving rain, and Coinneach, standing on the strand to meet them with half the town's remaining hands at his back, found himself, for the first time in eight-and-twenty years as reeve, glad of a thing he had asked for that had actually arrived.

Iain mac Thormoid was a spare, weathered man who asked more questions in his first hour ashore than any capital officer Coinneach had dealt with before him, wanting to know the set of the tides among the small islands, which channels ran dry at the ebb, which coves a boat might lie hidden in through a whole daylight and never be seen from the open water. Coinneach answered what he could and sent for the town's own boat-men to answer the rest, and by the second evening the captain had a chart of the raiders' ground drawn out on the reeve's own table in charcoal, corrected twice over by men who had fished those waters since before Iain mac Thormoid was born.

They found the sea-thieves' own strand within the week, on Baile chrom's own fishermen leading the way, for there was not a man left in Baile chrom who did not, by then, know the channel among the small islands as well as he knew his own doorstep. 27 an t-Samhain, LE 801, the boats went in at first light on Eilean dhubh, and Coinneach, who had asked to go and been allowed to, on the plain ground that a reeve who knew the men by name might yet talk some of them down before it came to burning, found when the fighting was over that talking had bought him nothing at all. The landing was over faster than Coinneach had let himself expect, the sea-thieves having kept no proper watch on a shore they had held unchallenged for the better part of a decade, and most of the fighting, such as it was, went to Iain mac Thormoid's own men, better armed and readier for it than Coinneach's own fishermen, who had come along, most of them, to point out a channel and not to bear arms in earnest. Coinneach himself carried nothing heavier than the knife every man on that coast carried for gutting fish, and he used it for nothing that morning but cutting a length of rope from a burning hull's mooring, judging, once the fighting had truly begun, that an old reeve with a fish-knife had better make himself useful at some smaller task than stand about getting in a soldier's way.

Aonghas mac Ruairidh, thirty-one years old that spring and grown into a man Coinneach would have known nowhere except the strand where he had once been a boy, went down with a spear through him defending a hull he had likely never set foot in as an honest fisherman, and Coinneach, kneeling over him on the wet stones with the boats burning at his back, found he had no words ready for the mother he would have to tell of it, though he had had a full winter and spring to prepare some. He held the boy's hand a while, though he judged from the stillness of it that there was no longer anyone left inside it to feel the holding, and one of Iain mac Thormoid's own men, passing, asked him gently enough whether he had known the dead man. Coinneach answered that he had carried him on his own shoulder once, down to this same water, when the boy was too small to walk it himself, and the soldier, who had likely heard harder things said that morning, said nothing further and went on to the next of the fallen.

Uilleam Ruadh, who had led the sea-thieves for the better part of those years and was known, by then, up and down the whole north-west coast by name and by a red beard no disguise had ever troubled to hide, was taken alive off the strand and carried south to Cathair dhearg in irons, in the same ships that had burned his boats. He was six and thirty years old, and he was hanged there before the season turned, the crown's own scribes setting the day down without ornament in the rolls Coinneach afterward read at secondhand, a man's whole life closed in fewer words than Coinneach's own report on the emptied houses had run to. Coinneach felt no triumph in the reading of it that he could afterward account for, only a tiredness that sat in him, he told his wife, the way damp sits in a wall after a long wet season, never felt at any single hour, and never afterward quite gone.

## IV. Of the Harvests That Would Not Come

The raiding ended with Uilleam Ruadh's hanging, or near enough to ended that the coast road carried no further tidings of it, and for a handful of years Baile chrom's trouble was, at least, a trouble Coinneach recognised: the slow, ordinary work of a small town trying to fill again the houses a bad decade had emptied. It was not given the years to do it in. The harvests that should have carried that work began to fail, one on the heels of the last, in a run that the oldest hands in the town, asked, could not match to any dearth they themselves remembered, and by the ninth or tenth year of it the shared-meal custom that had always, in Coinneach's own lifetime, carried Baile chrom through a single bad season could no longer be stretched to carry a run of them.

He kept the custom himself as long as any grain remained to keep it with, standing at his own board each market day and dividing what the town's diminished fields had brought in as evenly as his own hand could manage it, and he told those who came to him, in the years the custom still held, that a shared hunger was at least a hunger a man need not carry alone. He remembered, of those market days, one old woman, Mairead, who had buried a husband and two sons to the sea before the dearth ever touched her, coming to his board with an empty basket and telling him, when he weighed out her share, that she had lived through three bad harvests in her own girlhood and had thought, until this one, that she had already learned everything a hungry year had to teach a body. She had not, she said, and neither, she suspected, had he, and she was proven right in that before either of them saw the end of it.

Coinneach kept his own account of the failing harvests the way he had once kept his account of the emptying houses, a column of numbers in the same chest of rolls, and he could have told, had anyone still cared to ask him, that the barley yield of his own charge had fallen by more than half across those years, and the fish catch with it, for the boats that remained had too few hands between them to work the grounds a full crew had once worked. He wrote no further letter south asking for relief, having learned, from the long wait over the force, that a plea for grain from a coast already known to the crown as thinly held and further thinning would travel no faster than the last one had, and judging, besides, that grain itself, unlike soldiers, was not a thing the capital could simply raise more of by the asking. But a hand, however fair, cannot divide what the ground has simply failed to give, and LE 819 the last of the households that had held on through the sea-thieves' years began, in ones and twos and then in whole families at once, to load their carts and go, as their neighbours had gone a generation before them, inland and east toward shires that still had bread to share. Coinneach's own wife Beathag died that same hard winter, of a chest complaint the town's one physician judged no different from a dozen such complaints she had seen through in better years, save that a body weakened by two thin harvests running had less in it to fight a fever with than a body fed as it ought to have been fed.
