Coinneach buried her on a morning with the ground half frozen and stood afterward at his own door a long while, by his own account to the few neighbours still near enough to hear him say it, working out for himself, he said, not whether he ought to follow the others east, which he judged by then past deciding, but only how long a man owed a post before the post no longer owed him anything in return. He held the board a further year, more from a settled habit of duty than from any hope left in him that the holding served a purpose the town still needed served, keeping the tally of a shire that had, by then, scarcely enough hands left in it to need a tally kept at all. Old Eachann, who had spoken hard to him once about a fallen catch and a reeve's slowness, came to him that year and told him, gentler than he had ever spoken to him before, that a man could grieve a wife and hold a board both at once for only so long before one or the other of them began to suffer for it, and that Eachann, for his own part, had watched enough men on that coast try to outlast a grief with work alone to know how the trying generally ended. Coinneach thanked him for the saying and did not, that year, act on it, telling himself there was still a use in him yet.

## V. Of the Roll Recopied and the Market at the Ford

The crown's own business went on, in those same years, at a distance the north-west shore had long since stopped expecting to feel. LE 829 the queen's scribes at Cathair dhearg took down the old Clàr nan Rìghrean from its resting place and copied it afresh onto new hide, adding to it, as the old roll had never troubled to, every ruler since the fleet had gone, and setting the new copy's beginning at An Roghnachadh rather than at the sailing, a small labour of a few scribes in a hall the width of the island away from any door a Baile chrom hand had ever knocked on. And some years after that a market grew up on the strand at Àth fhionn, where the coast road crossed the clear river, trading north-coast fish and the oil of stranded whales to a country that had, by then, stopped looking for either from the harbour Coinneach had spent his own working life keeping. Àth fhionn's strand grew loud with barter on market days in a way Baile chrom's own strand had not been loud in years, and the fishers of the north coast, Coinneach heard it said by a rider passing through, no longer troubled to carry their catch the longer road south to Inis mhòr at all, having found, in the new market, a nearer and readier hand to sell it into.

He heard both tidings the same way he had heard most tidings in his last years at the board, at secondhand, from travellers who stopped to water a horse and talked while it drank, and he set down neither of them in any report, judging, by then, that a reeve with fewer households under him than the roll now carried names for had little left worth reporting. It struck him, hearing of the market at Àth fhionn, that he had spent eleven good years and a score of hard ones keeping a harbour that a coast now further along than his own had simply grown past the need of, the way a man grows past the need of a coat that once fitted him, without any unkindness meant by the growing and none taken; and it struck him too, though he did not say this aloud to the rider who brought the tidings, that a market on a strand he had never once visited would go on trading fish and whale-oil for years after Baile chrom's own harbour stones had nothing left on them but gulls. He held the board through one further harvest, thinner than the one before it, and found, come the following spring, that he had at last worked out for himself the answer to the question he had stood at his own door asking on the morning he buried his wife: that a man owed a post exactly as long as the post still asked a true thing of him, and no longer.

He went from house to house that had a soul left in it, the morning he chose to go, and said what there was to say to each, which was little enough after so many years of saying it in smaller pieces across a market board. Old Eachann was among the last he called on, and told him only that he had been right, a full year late, and that being right late was still a kind of being right. Coinneach said he supposed it was, and left him with the last of the dried fish from his own stores, since a man who no longer had a household to feed had no further use for it and a man who still did might.

He set the reeve's own chest of rolls and tallies in order, for whoever might come after him, though he no longer much believed anyone would, setting the grain counts and the boundary leaves and the long, thinning column of households each in its own place, as though a careful ordering of a record no one would likely ever open again were still, somehow, worth a morning's labour. The hearth he swept clean himself, which his wife had always done before him, telling the one neighbour who watched him do it that a man ought to leave a room as he would wish to find one. Last of all he took down the strip of netting Beathag had left half mended in her own basket, and folded it, and set it on top of the chest, unable to bring himself either to finish it or to leave it lying loose upon the floor.

Then he shut his own door behind him, and set the road east under his feet, an old man by then in everything but the years any roll had ever troubled to count against his name, and did not look back at Baile chrom again before the road bent and the strand went out of sight behind him. It is told at the road-houses along that stretch of the eastern way that a grey-haired man walked in that year asking after no kin and no trade, only after a shire that would still have a use for a hand that had once kept a tally, and that when he was asked, as a stranger on that road is always asked, what town he came out of, he answered plainly, and then said nothing further about it that any who heard him thought worth carrying on.

# Chapter Twenty-nine: Of the Crown Joined to the Vein

*LE 841 – 939*

> *Is buan a' bheinn, is goirid an rìgh.*
> Lasting is the mountain, short is the king.
>
> — said at Muileann dhearg of every ruler since

## I. Of the Empty Hall

Queen Eilidh Bhàn died at Cathair dhearg at ninety years old, on 21 an Giblean, LE 841, in An Talla Dearg, where she had been crowned at eighteen, and with her the house of Catrìona, six rulers and near three hundred years, came to its end. She left no child living and had never named one to come after her; the clerks of An Talla Dearg, who had served her seventy-two years and thought they had prepared for every ordinary grief a crown could bring, found they had prepared for nothing at all for this one, and stood about the hall for the better part of a day not knowing whose office it now was to give an order. One of them, an old man who had cut her own coronation roll as a boy of twelve, was heard to say that he had buried five clerks under her and had never once thought to ask who would bury the queen herself, since he had somehow supposed, without ever putting the thought into words, that she would simply go on.

Riders went out that same evening to Na Seachd Taighean, as riders had gone out at every death of a ruler for two centuries, each carrying the same plain summons; and it is told that Na Seachd Taighean did not meet at Cathair dhearg to settle what should follow, as the custom of two hundred years might have led a stranger to expect, but rode instead to Muileann dhearg, up to Taigh na Fèithe above the mountain, and sat there among the galleries and Clachan a' Chrannchuir and the old smell of tallow and coal-dust rather than under An Talla Dearg's own roof. No one wrote why, and Leabhar a' Chùraim, when it came at last to enter the matter, entered only the fact and not the reason. A scribe of Taigh na Fèithe who was young that year and very old when she told it afterward said that the head of one house had proposed An Talla Dearg first, as custom asked, and that another had answered him, not unkindly, that a house with no ruler in it was no fit place to make one, and that the mountain, at least, had never once in all its years stood empty of an office worth the sitting in. Nobody argued the point a second time. It seemed to every head who rode up the hill, she said, a plainer thing to choose a king among Clachan a' Chrannchuir than among the tapestries the house of Catrìona had hung, and nobody thought to question it further because it felt, from the first hour, less like a choosing than like a homecoming.

They sat first nine days in the long room under Taigh na Fèithe's north window, the same table at which Eòghann mac Pheadair and the crown's own scribe had once laid two counts of years side by side and found neither able to prove the other wrong. The capital sent no word and asked for none; a runner rode down twice a week with grain prices and boundary pleas for the clerks to hold against whatever hand should next take them up, and rode back again each time having settled nothing, for there was nobody yet at Cathair dhearg with the standing to settle it, and the clerks learned to keep the pleas in a growing stack rather than pretend an office existed to answer them. The houses rode home from that first sitting with nothing settled, and rode up again at each season's turning for five years, while An Talla Dearg stood empty and the stack of pleas grew. The sittings are not told entire in any leaf that survives, save that they were quarrelsome for the first years and quiet for the last, that two heads left the table more than once vowing they would not return and returned each time before the evening meal, and that in the fifth year a name was spoken that had not been spoken among Na Seachd Taighean in living memory, and was not spoken down again once it had been raised.

## II. Of the Yard

Dòmhnall Ruadh was a man of Muileann dhearg in one sense and of the eastern hills in another, for his own household held its galleries and its house both at Muileann chrom, a morning's ride below the mountain, where snow still lay thick some winters on ground his own great-grandfather's father had once held before a battle changed whose it was. He was fifty-six that year, a quiet, careful man, heavier in the shoulders than in the face, who had spent most of his life managing three galleries of the coal-right and disputing boundary stones with neighbours who had long since stopped expecting to win an argument with him, for he kept his tallies as honestly as any custodian on the mountain and would give up a claim as readily as press one, if the measuring told against him. He had ridden up to Taigh na Fèithe at the second summons not because he thought the matter concerned him — he said as much, more than once, to the men who rode beside him — but because every head of every house that held so much as a gallery's worth of the right had been asked to come and be counted among the voices, and Dòmhnall Ruadh did not think it his place to be the one man absent from a table his own house had a lawful seat at.

The last morning of the last sitting found him standing in the yard among perhaps forty men and women who had ridden up for the same counting and had nothing else to do with the waiting but stand in the cold and talk of anything but the choosing itself, when word came down from the hall that the houses had settled on a name; some little while passed before he understood, from the way the men nearest him had gone quiet and turned to look at him rather than past him, that the name was his own. He said afterward, to the one clerk who thought to ask him plainly what he had felt in that moment, that he had felt mostly a kind of embarrassment, standing in a yard he knew as well as his own threshing floor, in his working clothes with mud still dried grey on his boots from the ride, being looked at as though he had done something remarkable, when he had done nothing that whole morning but come when he was asked and wait his turn like any other man of the coal-right.

It was an old man among the custodians, one of the last few alive who could remember his own father speaking of it, who took Dòmhnall Ruadh a little apart from the others and told him, plainly and without much ceremony, whose yard he was standing in: that it was the same stones, worn no smoother in nearly three hundred years, on which another man of his own house, Raghnall Ruadh, had once stood before a season of refused hearths and a war that killed him, and had taken a board of claimants' names from a shaking clerk's hands and said, of every name on it, *none of these*, and turned and gone in and shut the door with a sound the old man's own father had called, all his life, a very great deal too small a sound for what had just been done. Dòmhnall Ruadh had known the story his whole life, as every child of Clann Raghnaill knew it, half as a shame kept low at table and half as a thing nobody in the house had ever quite managed to be ashamed enough of to stop telling; he stood a while with his hand on the same stone gatepost the old man pointed to, and said only that he hoped he would prove a different sort of answer to the same question the mountain had once been asked, and the old man told him that hoping so, standing where he stood, was a better beginning than most men who had ever been offered a crown were given.

He sent that same afternoon for his wife and his two grown sons to come up from Muileann chrom, and it was his wife, by every account, who wept at the news and Dòmhnall Ruadh who did not, sitting up late that first night going over, aloud and to nobody in particular, which of his neighbours he could trust to keep his own galleries measured honestly in his absence, as though the crown of Dia-thìr were one more piece of land he had been handed to manage and nothing grander. He was crowned nine days later at Cathair dhearg, in the hall his own house had never once, in nearly three hundred years, been asked to enter as anything but petitioners with a board of names and a plea; and the crown sat, those who were there said, a little awkwardly on a man who had spent the whole ride down from the mountain more troubled about a boundary quarrel he had left half-settled at Muileann chrom than about who would keep the kingdom he was riding to receive.

## III. Of the Joining

Through the first years of his reign he kept two households running side by side and badly, the crown's business at Cathair dhearg and Taigh na Fèithe's business at the mountain, riding the thirty-nine miles between the two so often that the road's own keepers came to know his horse before they knew his face, and complained, in the way of men whose work has grown easier for a king's habits, that they had never in their lives shod one animal so many times in one man's service. The first winter he tried to hold court at Cathair dhearg for half the season and sit with the custodians at the mountain for the other half; by the second winter he had found that a boundary quarrel at the mountain waited no better on a king's absence than a grain plea at the capital, and that a man could not, in truth, be two rulers wearing one crown between two houses forty miles apart.

It was his reeves, not he, who first wrote the plain remedy into Leabhar a' Chùraim, on 6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859: that the ruler of Dia-thìr was, from that day, also master of Taigh na Fèithe, and that the two offices, which had grown up under different roofs since before any ruler now living remembered a time they were not separate, should from then on be kept under one seal and answered for by one hand. Dòmhnall Ruadh read the entry, when it was set before him for his own mark, a long while before he set it, and said to the reeve who had drafted it that it read less like a new law than like a plain account of a thing that had already, in practice, been true since the morning he stood in Taigh na Fèithe yard; the reeve answered that most of the best laws he had ever copied were exactly that, and Dòmhnall Ruadh laughed, which those who knew him said he did rarely enough that the reeve remembered it the rest of his own life.

The heads of Na Seachd Taighean, who had chosen him at the mountain and not at the hall, took their old office and carried it with them into the new arrangement without much debate, for it cost them, in the end, little that they had not already been doing in one form or another since the roll of the coal-right was first drawn. They sat thereafter as the king's own council at whichever of the two houses the business of the day required, and Leabhar a' Chùraim and the crown's rolls, kept apart for near three hundred years on separate shelves under separate roofs, were from that season copied by the same scribes onto the same shelves, a labour that took Taigh na Fèithe's clerks the better part of two years to finish and left, by the end of it, not one leaf of either record that a stranger could tell at a glance from the other.

The seal was cut that same year at Muileann dhearg, by a metalworker of the mountain town who had never before been asked to cut anything grander than a gallery-marker or a boundary stake, and who took, by his own telling afterward, near a season over the die where a marker would have cost him a morning. He complained, more than once, in the hearing of the custodians who came to watch him at it, that the gold would not sit as he wished it against the blue, and set the wax to the fire and cooled it and set it again more times than any of them cared to count; but what he cut, on 1 an t-Ògmhios, LE 865, was, when it was finished, judged by every custodian who saw it to be Taigh na Fèithe's own old device exactly, unaltered in its bones: the trellis of gold that the custodians read as the galleries of the mountain, laid on a field of blue, and over it the hollow stone, the mascle, for the slab that had covered the first break long before any ruler's name was written anywhere on the island. Across the whole of it, at the crown's own asking and at nothing more, he set a single band of white, thin as a finger's width, running the field from side to side. Dòmhnall Ruadh, looking at the finished die before it was ever set to wax, turned it over once in his hands and said that he could find nothing in it that was properly his to add, and the master of Taigh na Fèithe, an old woman who had buried three custodians and outlasted two kings before him, told him that a ruler who wished to add nothing to another man's seal was, in her own long memory of rulers, the rarest kind there was.

From that seal forward every letter the crown sent bore the mountain on it as plainly as it bore the crown's own arms, and no clerk at Cathair dhearg, writing out a grant or a summons in the years that followed, needed telling twice why a trellis and a hollow stone stood over the king's own name where once only a plainer mark of the house of Catrìona had stood.

## IV. Of the Mountain's Own King

He reigned five-and-twenty years, most of them, by his own account late in life, spent doing at An Talla Dearg exactly what he had once done at three galleries in Muileann chrom: walking boundaries, hearing disputes between neighbours who each believed the other had moved a stone, keeping a measure honest that others were forever tempted to lean on when they thought nobody was troubling to check. He never moved the seat of the crown to the mountain, though more than one of the seven heads pressed him to in the early years, saying plainly that a king who was also master of Taigh na Fèithe belonged among the galleries and not among the tapestries the house of Catrìona had left behind; he answered, each time he was asked, that a crown kept too near its own coal soon forgot it had ever been asked to answer for anything else besides the coal, and that he meant, so long as he held it, for it to go on being asked to answer for a great deal more.

A quarrel came before him in his ninth year that those who served him remembered longer than most: two households of Muileann chrom, his own old neighbours, disputing a boundary stone that had stood, by both sides' account, exactly where it now stood for four generations, until a spring flood shifted the stream beside it and left each side certain the water, and not the stone, had moved. Dòmhnall Ruadh rode down from the capital himself rather than send a reeve, walked the ground with both households at his heels arguing the whole way, and settled it at last by asking each household's oldest living member, separately and out of the other's hearing, where they remembered playing as children; both answers agreed, within a few paces, and Dòmhnall Ruadh set the boundary there and told the assembled households, a little dryly, that he had settled more quarrels in his life with an old woman's memory of where she had once chased a goat than with every measuring-rod Taigh na Fèithe owned.

He died at Cathair dhearg in his eighty-second year, on 10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871, the first man of his house in three centuries to be given, by the same seven heads who had once refused his ancestor to his face, every honour a dying king could be given: the lamps of An Talla Dearg kept lit three nights running, the roads from every shire seat sent a rider to carry the word, and Leabhar a' Chùraim, when it came to enter his death, gave him a longer leaf than it had given any ruler before him, though the leaf said little more, in the end, than that he had joined the crown to the vein and kept both honestly for five-and-twenty years. He was carried, at his own asking made long before he was ill, past the house of Catrìona's tombs at the capital and up to Muileann dhearg, to be buried under the mountain his family's name had once been driven from by a war and a refused board of claimants. The custodians dug the grave themselves rather than send for labourers, working through a night and half a day in a gallery no longer worked for coal, its walls still black with the old dust, and laid him with a single unlit lamp at his head, which Taigh na Fèithe's own rite asked for no other ruler before or since, the lamp's being unlit taken, by those who kept the rite, to mean that a man who had spent his whole reign making sure the measured handful reached every hearth honestly had no further need, in the ground, of a flame kept for him alone.

His son Raghnall Òg was crowned at Cathair dhearg a fortnight after, six-and-forty years old and already, from his father's long teaching, a good deal more at ease with a boundary dispute than with a court's ceremony, so that the clerks who had arranged his coronation found him asking, twice during the rehearsal of it, whether the whole business could not be shortened by an hour so that he might see a shire plea before dark. The crown and Taigh na Fèithe went on being one office under him without a word needing to be said about it, as though the joining his father had written into Leabhar a' Chùraim had already, in a single reign, stopped being a thing anyone thought to remark on at all.

It was in the years just after, while the mountain's own harbour of Seann Chwen finished its stone mole and the first barges of the coal-roads' carters began tying up where before they had only beached on shingle at low water, that a rider bringing the news south remarked, without much thinking about it, to a clerk at Cathair dhearg that he had ridden the whole way from the mole to An Talla Dearg under one seal the entire road, the mountain's trellis pressed into the wax of every letter he carried, and had not troubled, for the first time in his years of carrying such news between the two houses, to wonder for a moment which office he rode for.

## V. Of the Hawk that Split

It is told that Seabhag Acaill, whose priests had for six hundred years taught the vein as a bird fed a measured handful and never more, met in council at Cnoc bheag on 20 an t-Ògmhios, LE 889 and broke apart over a question its own founders had never thought to settle in all their teaching: whether the measure Mòd was fed could ever rightly be raised as the island's own numbers grew, or whether the handful fixed at the very first teaching, in a smaller age, must stand unchanged for as long as the order stood, whatever else changed around it. The council sat three days at Cnoc bheag, the elders on one side of the fire and the younger priests, most of them raised under teachers who had never questioned the measure at all, gathered on the other; and it is said that the argument turned at last on a single young priest rising to ask the elders, plainly, whether Mòd, could he be asked, would rather starve a flock that had outgrown his old handful than see the handful grown to meet it.

Those who held the older reading kept the name of An Seabhag Acrach, and kept the house at Cnoc bheag as it had always stood; those who held that a greater flock, grown these many generations past the numbers the first teaching had ever reckoned on, might rightly be fed a greater handful, were called from that council on An Seabhag Biadhte, and were asked, before the winter was out and not unkindly, to keep their teaching somewhere it would not be heard daily at Cnoc bheag's own hearth. They went north, most of them, to Seann Skell, the Seann Skell of the north coast and not the river port of the same name where Rolla a' Chalaidh had first been opened, and it was there, under a priestess named Beathag nic Sheumais, herself no more than a girl of nineteen at the schism and a woman near forty by the time she had built the house up from four families' worth of following to a proper school, that An Seabhag Biadhte raised their own house and kept their own teaching within sound of a sea that had never once, in six hundred years, given the island back so much as a word of what lay beyond it.

She rode south to Cathair dhearg herself, in her fiftieth year, to ask the king's council in person rather than trust the asking to a letter, and stood before the seven heads in An Talla Dearg, which Dòmhnall Ruadh's own house had once entered only as petitioners, and asked, on 25 an Lùnastal, LE 919, that the hearths of the north coast, which she said went colder in a hard winter than Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig had ever meant any hearth to go, be given a quarter more than the measured handful allowed them. She spoke, those who heard her said, without raising her voice once, laying out the north coast's winters as plainly as a scribe laying out a tally, and sat afterward while the council debated her plea across the length of a single short winter's afternoon; and the seven heads, with Raghnall Òg among them, heard her out in full and refused her, Leabhar a' Chùraim noting, at some length and for the first time in the whole record's history, every reason it gave for a refusal rather than the bare fact of one.

Beathag nic Sheumais rode back north with the refusal written out in her own satchel, as a leaf of another kind had once ridden south in another woman's satchel generations before her, and told her own house, when she reached it, only that the council had answered as councils answer, and that a hearth denied a quarter more was still a hearth, and would go on being kept whether Cathair dhearg agreed with the keeping of it or not. An Seabhag Biadhte's house at Seann Skell stood after that exactly as it had stood before, neither larger nor smaller for the asking, and its priests went on teaching, to any hawk-keeper of the north coast who cared to climb the hill and hear them, that Mòd's true hunger and the mountain's own measured hunger were not, whatever Cnoc bheag still held to the contrary, one and the same question at all.

## VI. Of the Fourteen Names and the Posts on the Road

A second tremor shook the hills above Cill ghlas on 14 an Dàmhair, LE 929, seventy years after the joining, and brought down a gallery that fourteen of the custodians' own labourers were working when the roof let go without warning in the small hours of the morning shift. Taigh na Fèithe closed the gallery for good rather than dig the dead free of it, judging, as the custodians of Cill ghlas had judged once before after an older fall, that the mountain had already taken what it meant to take and would give nothing more back for the digging; and it set, at the gallery's mouth that same season, a plain stone with the fourteen names cut into it in the order they had gone down, the youngest a boy of thirteen new to the coal-face and the oldest a woman who had worked that same gallery forty years without once being late to a shift. The custodians called the stone afterward Clach nan Ceithir Ainmean Deug and kept it swept of snow every winter that followed, whoever held the crown at Cathair dhearg, and it became the custom, among the mountain's own households, for a family that had lost someone to any gallery, in any year, to leave a small stone of their own at its foot on the day of the fall, so that within a generation the fourteen names lay half buried under stones that were not theirs, left by people the fourteen had never known.

It was in the ten years that followed, with the memory of the fourteen still fresh at every gallery-mouth on the mountain, that the king's council took a matter into its own keeping that had never before needed anyone's keeping at all: the roads that carried the measured coal down from the mountain to the coast towns and their temples, which any house with a grudge or a boundary quarrel might, until then, have closed for a season as easily as Raghnall Ruadh had once closed a granary to every hearth that had not declared for him. One of the heads of Na Seachd Taighean, laying the matter before the council, said plainly that fourteen names on a stone at a gallery's mouth were proof enough that the mountain gave up its coal at a real cost, and that a coal given up at such cost had no business being stopped on the road by any quarrel that was not the mountain's own; and none of the seven spoke against him.

On 12 an t-Samhain, LE 939, the council ordered every such road marked with the crown's own sign, that no house, whatever quarrel it carried, should ever again be free to stop the measured handful on its way to a hearth that had done that house no wrong: the carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, the road over the pass by Muileann fhada that the mountain folk called the northern way, the road south by Muileann chrom where Dòmhnall Ruadh's own people held their galleries, and the road down to Baile òg in the south. The posts went up through that whole autumn, a trellis and a hollow stone cut into each one at the joints where one shire's road gave over to the next, and the men who set them, coal-carters most of them, hired for the season and paid out of the tolls the new roads now raised, worked without much ceremony and without, so far as any leaf remembers, a single word said over the driving of the last one.

A carter named in no roll but his own household's, who had helped set posts on three of the four roads that autumn, was asked, the following spring, what the work had been like, and said only that a man could walk the whole length of any of them now, from the mountain to the sea, and never once lose the road for want of knowing whose it was; and it was that plain answer, more than any leaf Leabhar a' Chùraim kept of the council's own debate, that the mountain's households were still repeating to their children when the posts themselves had long since gone grey and lichened in the weather, the trellis and the hollow stone worn faint but never, in all the years that followed, unreadable.

# Chapter Thirty: Of the Stair under the Hill

*LE 944 – 1,015*

## I. Of the Road and the Empty Pastures

By LE 944 a rider going up from Cathair dhearg never rode the whole way on one horse. He changed at a road-house every few hours, wherever the coal-roads' own charter had set one, and the keeper of the house had a fresh animal saddled and standing before the old one had fully stopped, so that the word of the council could travel from An Talla Dearg to the mountain between one dawn and the next dark without once slowing to a walk. The stabling was paid, every quarter, out of the tolls the roads themselves raised, and a keeper who let a rider wait so much as the time it took to draw a bucket of water heard of it soon enough from the reeve who kept the charter.

A keeper of one such house, a widow named Mairead nic Aonghais who had held her stretch of the northern road for eleven years, kept a tally of her own beside the reeve's: a notch cut for every rider who came through wearing the crown's own badge, and a second, smaller notch for every one of them who thanked her by name rather than simply throwing the reins at her boy and swinging up onto the fresh horse before his feet were properly in the stirrups. She said, to the one traveller who ever thought to ask her about it, that the first tally kept the reeve satisfied and the second kept her own opinion of the office satisfied, and that the two tallies did not always run in step with one another. It became a boast repeated at every road-house table from the capital to the pass, all the same, that a rider of the crown's had never yet gone hungry, thirsty or afoot on a coal-road, whatever else might be said of the years, and Mairead's own notched stick, kept behind her door long after she was too old to saddle a horse herself, was shown to more than one grandchild as proof of it. She kept a third mark too, smaller still and cut with a different knife, for the riders who came through carrying nothing worth the council's own asking, grain prices and boundary pleas of no great weight, and she said once, to a reeve who pressed her on why she troubled to keep so fine a tally at all, that a woman who fed and mounted the crown's own business every day of her working life had earned the right to know, for her own satisfaction if nobody else's, how much of that business was worth the horse it rode on.

It was in LE 949 that the last shepherd families came down out of the high pastures of Doire uaine, in the hill country north of the mountain, and settled in the valley villages below. They gave the grazing as their reason, and the grazing was true enough; the grass up there had thinned with every dry summer for a generation, and a flock that once wintered fat on the high ground now came down each autumn with its ribs showing plainer than the year before. But every family that made the move, asked why now and not ten years before, spoke also of the Marbh-bheò, the dead-alive that was said to walk the empty shielings once the flocks had gone down, and not one of them could say exactly when they had first begun to feel that the high ground no longer wanted their company as much as their sheep still wanted its grass. An old woman of that country, the last to leave her own shieling, driving three goats and a lame ewe ahead of her down a track her own mother had walked before her, told the priest who met her at the valley's edge that a place could grow tired of being lived in alone by living things, and that she had felt the tiredness of it in her own bones a good while before her knees ever gave her a better reason to come down. The high shielings stood empty from that year, their turf roofs falling in one by one over the winters that followed, and no family of that country went up to winter a flock on that ground again. A drover passing that way some years on, driving cattle to the lowland market by the old high road because it was shorter than the coast way, said he had ridden the whole stretch of the empty pastures in half a day and had not once, in all that riding, heard a dog bark or seen so much as a wisp of hearth-smoke where a dozen shielings had once stood smoking every evening of his own boyhood. He said the silence of it troubled him more than any wolf or storm the road had ever given him, and that he pushed his cattle on rather than camp there the night, though the light was failing and a camp there would have cost him nothing but the asking of ground nobody was left to grant or refuse.

Ros fhionn kept its salt fair in LE 959 as it had kept it every year within living memory, the salters working the pans from before first light and the carters lining up their carts along the flats for a full mile before the gates opened. The reeve who counted heads that day, for no better reason than that the crowd looked larger to him than any he remembered counting, gave up somewhere past four thousand, lost among the press of carts and pack-mules and children darting between the pans to steal a pinch of the white crust before their mothers caught them at it. He wrote the figure down anyway, rounding it plainly rather than pretend to a precision the crowd itself had never held still for, and it stood, in the fair's own rolls, as the largest day the town's salt trade ever saw. Nobody standing on the flats that morning had any way of knowing it was the height the town would reach; the rolls that named it afterward the richest place in the north-east wrote no more, in truth, than what every salter and every carter on those flats had already believed of their own town without needing telling.

Further south, by LE 969, Cathair mhòr's market drew more carts off more roads than the capital's own, until a trader newly come to the island could stand in either market and know within a morning which town he was in by the noise of it alone. The capital kept the crown, and kept the name of the greater town in every old roll that still gave it so, but the weight of custom, such as there was in barter and salt and silver neck-rings, went where the goods went, and the goods went, season on season, more and more to Cathair mhòr. No council sat to write a law about it, for a town does not need a law to outgrow another; it needs only more roads meeting inside its own walls, and Cathair mhòr had those roads, and kept gaining them.

A carter of the southern road, asked once by a clerk of An Talla Dearg why he always sold his barley at Cathair mhòr's market and not the capital's, said only that a man carried his load to whichever gate opened first and paid best, and that the clerk's own question was the sort a man asked from a hall, not from a cart. The clerk wrote the answer down as given, without comment, and it is the plainest word that survives of how the one town came to outgrow the other: a thousand carters, each on his own morning, choosing the gate that opened first, with no single act any leaf remembers behind it.

## II. Of the Stair under the Hill

Calum Dubh mac Iain had cut stone on the quarry face north of the capital since he was old enough to hold a hammer without dropping it on his own foot, and by LE 979, the year the face gave way under him, he was nine-and-twenty, broad through the shoulders from the work and quieter than most men of his age, the kind of quarryman a foreman set to a stubborn seam because he would go on chipping at it a full day without once losing his temper over it. He had a wife at home and a boy not yet walking, and nothing about the morning the face opened marked it out, to him, from any other morning he had climbed the ladder to the working ledge with his lamp and his hammers slung over his shoulder.

The rock had been sounding wrong for the better part of a week, a hollowness under the ring of the tools that the older men on the ledge muttered about between themselves and the younger ones mostly let pass. On the morning it finally let go it did not fall so much as open: a slab the size of a door swung inward on nothing at all and left a black mouth in the rock where a solid seam had been standing a breath before. The men nearest it stepped back, as any man will step back from a hole where stone had just stood, and for a long moment nobody said a word, because the air that came up out of the opening was cold as well-water and carried no smell whatever, not damp earth nor old stone nor the tar-and-tallow reek of a worked gallery, and a nothing where a man's own nose looks for something is a stranger thing to stand near than any bad smell would have been.

One of the older men held his lamp in at arm's length, leaning as far over the black edge as he dared, and the light found steps: a stair cut into the living rock, tread below tread, each one worn to a shallow bowl at its middle as though feet beyond any counting had climbed it long before a single quarryman now living had drawn breath, going down and down past the point where the lamp's own light gave out entirely. It was Calum Dubh, standing a little behind the rest, who said the name before any other man on the ledge could get it past his own teeth: Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tellings that every quarryman's grandmother had used to frighten children quiet at the hearth, and that no living soul had ever set eyes on, since no living soul had ever known where the ground had hidden it. A boy who had come up that morning with the water-skins said afterward that the quiet on the ledge, once Calum Dubh had said the name, had a weight to it he had never once felt on a quarry face before, as though every man standing there had remembered, in the same breath, a thing they had agreed among themselves long ago, and never once out loud, not to look at too closely.

The foreman asked, in the flattest voice a man can manage when he is asking for something he does not want done, whether any of them would go down and look. Nobody answered him at once. Calum Dubh said afterward, to the one man who ever got more than a handful of words from him about that morning, that he could not rightly account for why it was his own hand and not another's that reached first for the second lamp; he had made no decision he could remember making, and found the lamp already lit and his own boot already on the top tread before the thought of volunteering had properly finished forming. Four men on the ledge drew straws for who should pay out the rope behind him, and every one of the four, by his own later telling, was glad past speaking of it to have lost.

His fellows watched the lamp go: a small light turning on the stair's own bends, dwindling fold by fold of the rock until it was no bigger than a star low on a winter sky, and then nothing at all, the dark of the shaft closing over it as complete as water closing over a dropped stone. They waited. Rope paid out and rope stood still; somebody counted his own heartbeats for a while and then gave it up, unable to say afterward how many he had reached. One of the men who kept that watch, an old quarryman near the end of his own working years, told his grandchildren once, and told no one else in his life besides, that they had waited long enough on that ledge to grow ashamed of how glad every one of them was, all at the same instant, when the light came back at last, small and rising, climbing the same bends it had gone down by.

Calum Dubh came up into the grey daylight of the ledge, sat himself down on the loose stone at the quarry's edge, and said nothing at all. He sat there long enough that the foreman sent the water-boy running for Taigh na Fèithe's own custodians rather than wait on a report from a man who plainly had none in him yet to give. When Calum Dubh did speak at last, to the foreman alone and out of the other men's hearing, he said nothing of what he had seen below. He said only, in a voice the foreman described afterward as tired past the ordinary run of tired and entirely steady besides, that the quarry face should be closed before any other man went near it, whatever word came back from the mountain.

The custodians rode down within the week, four of them, and stood a long while at the mouth of the opening without going in themselves, looking at the black of it the way a man looks at a dog he is not sure will bite. Their order, when it came, held fewer words than the morning seemed to want: the mouth of it was to be walled, stone set on stone and mortared and left, and no quarryman was to work that face again as long as Taigh na Fèithe had any say in the matter. It was done inside a month, a plain wall of dressed stone set flush into the face as though the stair had never once opened behind it, and the custodians took what little Calum Dubh gave them of his own account and entered it in Leabhar a' Chùraim exactly as he gave it, adding not one word of their own to fill out its silences.

He went on cutting stone for six-and-thirty years more, on other faces of the same quarry at first and later, as his own knees grew less willing, on quieter work nearer his house; and in all that time he never once told a living soul what he had seen on the stair below the last bend his fellows' watching had lost to the dark. His wife asked him, that first year and for some years after. His son asked him once, grown and thinking, perhaps, that a father might tell a grown son what he had never told a wife. Even Taigh na Fèithe's own scribe asked him, gently, of an evening when Leabhar a' Chùraim's entry on the matter seemed a good deal thinner than the occasion deserved. He gave every one of them the same answer, in the same tired, steady voice the foreman had first heard on the ledge: that a man who had gone down and come back owed the rock, if he owed it nothing else, the leaving of what he had found there exactly where he had found it. He died in his own house in his sixty-fifth year, an old man well liked in the quarry town for a quiet, careful kindness that carried in it nothing of a man weighed down by a fright he could not set aside; and whatever he had seen on the stair under the hill went into the ground beside him, unspoken to the end, first and last.

The walled face itself outlived him by no time at all worth remarking, for the quarry moved on to easier stone within a few years and the mortared stones grew a skin of moss no different from any other unworked rock on that hillside. But the quarry town kept, for as long as the town itself stood, a way of speaking of a close-mouthed man that named no stair and no shaft at all: to say of someone that he had *gone down and come up like Calum Dubh* was to say, plainly enough for anyone raised in that town to understand it, that here was a man who had seen something and judged, on his own authority and nobody else's, that it belonged kept rather than told. It was said of more than one quarryman, in the years that followed, who had seen a bad fall and would not speak of it, and of at least one custodian who kept his own counsel on a matter of Taigh na Fèithe's business that the coal-right households never did learn the whole of. None of them, so far as any leaf remembers, had gone anywhere near Toll-dubh at all; the saying had outgrown the man who first earned it, as sayings do, and stood on its own by then, needing no stair beneath it to be understood.

## III. Of the Ruins Ailean Measured

By LE 994 the copper-workers of Cathair mhòr had begun casting cooking pots for every hearth on the island that could spare a season's barter for one, each pot stamped on its underside with its own maker's mark, a leaf, a fish, or a plain letter worked into the mould before the metal was ever poured. They went out of that town on every road at once, north and along the coast and south to the market-towns, and a housewife of Ros fhionn or Cuan shean setting one over her own fire for the first time was, more often than she ever knew, cooking over the work of a hand she would never meet in a town she would never see. Some of those pots are still turned up by a plough or a ditcher's spade with the maker's mark worn thin on the underside, and no leaf that survives can say now which hand cast which.

It was in LE 999 that Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean at Dùn thais, walked north with a measuring cord and a set of wax tablets to the broken ring of standing stone the island called Làrach an Teampaill, the temple-ruin, which no living memory could say who had raised or to what purpose. He was nine-and-twenty that year, a careful, unhurried man his own teachers had marked out early as fitter for measuring stone than for arguing a bench, and he had asked the school's leave to spend a season doing nothing else at all but walk the old ruin's circuit with his cord and set down, plainly, whatever he found there. He laid his cord across the altar-stone at the ring's centre and found, when he had done, that it faced squarely toward the central mountains and turned its back on the sea; a plain fact, and one that no teller of the ruin's few surviving tales had ever thought worth the mentioning, since every teller before him had simply assumed, without once saying so aloud, that so old an altar must face the water as the schools' own shrines faced it now. Who had set the stone so, and to what end, Ailean would not guess. He said as much, in almost those words, to the two or three fellow scholars who pressed him for an opinion before his tables were even finished.

He went on, in the years after, to measure the other two ruins the island still argued over at its own hearths: Làrach an Dùin, the fortress-ruin whose fallen wall a farmer's own plough still turned up stone by stone at the edge of his nearest field, and Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, the watch-fort on its headland where a shepherd could still stand, on a clear day, and see three days' sail of coast running away in either direction. The farmer at Làrach an Dùin met Ailean at his own field boundary with a barrowload of the stones his plough had turned up that season and asked him, half in earnest, whether the school meant to pay a fair price for the ones his own field kept giving back every spring whether he wanted them or not. Ailean bought none of them, but he set every stone the farmer showed him into his tablets before it went back onto the boundary wall, the farmer standing over him the whole while with his arms crossed, plainly unconvinced that a stone worth measuring so carefully was not, by rights, a stone worth paying for. Each ruin he walked as he had walked the first, every standing wall and fallen stone measured with his own cord, every faced stone's bearing set into his tablets before he trusted himself to draw so much as a single conclusion from the whole of it. More than once a pupil pressed him to say what the numbers meant before he had checked them a second time against the first pass, and more than once he sent the pupil away unanswered until he had.

By LE 1,011, the year he judged the work finished, he had a set of tables giving the measure, the stone and the lie of all three ruins laid out side by side, set down more exactly than any single teller's account of any one of them had ever managed before him. He wrote, at the tables' close, that he could not himself say with any confidence whether one people had raised all three or three peoples each their own, for the stone of each ruin was cut in a manner none of the others quite matched, and the compass-bearings of their altars and gateways agreed with one another in no pattern he could find, however many ways he laid the figures side by side to look for one. He set the finished tables before the school at Dùn thais for its own judgment, and the school, after a winter's argument on its own benches, judged only that his measurements stood sound and his caution on the larger question stood sounder still.

No scholar who came after him, in all the years his tables were kept and copied out fresh for the school's own shelves, ever found in the numbers a pattern that Ailean himself had missed. His caution left the question no room to be answered more boldly than he had left it, and so the question the three old ruins had always asked of the island simply closed, from that year onward: measured as far as honest measuring could carry it, and no further, in the same plain hand as the rest of his own tables, which set down, alongside every figure he had taken, exactly how much of the matter must be left standing unmeasured.

# Chapter Thirty-one: Of the Thousandth Year

*LE 1,015 – 1,064*

## I. Of the Girl Who Kept the Tallies

Mòrag Ruadh was fifteen years old in LE 1,015, red-haired as her name said and quieter in a crowded hall than any of the old king's household thought a girl of her blood had need to be, and she had kept, since she was old enough to hold a stylus steady, a small wax-board tally of her own beside the steward's larger one: what her own chamber burned in candles through a winter month, what a new pair of boots cost against what the old pair had cost her two years before, what a horse ate in oats between one saddling and the next. She did this for no reason she could have given a questioner, only that the steward's own great ledger, kept for the whole of An Talla Dearg's household, swallowed every small thing into a sum too large to see the small thing inside it again, and she found she wanted, without knowing quite why she wanted it, to be able to lay a finger on one particular candle and say what it had cost.

The steward, an old man named Pàdraig mac Ìomhair who had kept the hall's own great ledger since before Mòrag Ruadh was born, found her at it one evening bent over her wax-board by a poor light, and asked her, not unkindly, why a girl who would never be asked to account for a single candle troubled herself so over sums a steward was paid to carry for her. She told him only that she had found, the week before, that her own tally of the winter's candles and his own great ledger's figure for the same month did not agree by some small measure, and that she meant to find, before she let the matter drop, which of the two of them had counted wrong. He laughed at her, gently, and went away to check his own figures against the chandler's own bill, and came back three days later, not laughing, to tell her that the fault had been his, a single tally-mark set down twice by a tired hand at the month's turning, and that he would be glad, from that evening forward, to have a second pair of eyes on his sums whatever the hall's own household thought of a girl who kept candle-counts for her own amusement. It is told that he never again, in all the years he served her afterward as queen, closed a month's reckoning without setting it first before her own eyes, whether she asked to see it or not.

The old king who sat An Talla Dearg in those years had sat it longer than any teller then living could put an exact number of winters to, and of the manner of his going, when it came, Leabhar a' Chùraim sets down no more than the year. What is told is that Na Seachd Taighean met at Taigh na Fèithe above Muileann dhearg in the same season, as they had met once before to name Dòmhnall Ruadh the better part of two centuries before her, and that they sent word to Cathair dhearg within the month that the crown would go, this time, to the girl of Clann Raghnaill who kept her own small tally beside the steward's, a choosing Leabhar a' Chùraim records in four lines and no more, giving no reason beyond her house and her blood, as though the reason had been plain enough to every house present that no house thought it needed writing down.

She was crowned at Cathair dhearg in LE 1,019, nineteen years old, in An Talla Dearg her own girlhood tally had been kept in under a steward's larger one, and it is told that the first order she gave as queen, before any grain ruling or any boundary plea, was to the same steward who had watched her keep her small board for four years without once asking him leave: that a proper ledger be bound for her, of good vellum and not wax, and that every measure spent on her own household, however small, be entered into it in her own hand from that day forward, so that a queen who could not say what her own candles cost had no business asking a shire to account for its grain. The steward bound the ledger before the month was out, a plain board-covered book with a clasp of iron rather than silver, at her own asking, and its first page, dated the day of her crowning, holds nothing but a single line: the cost of the feast the hall had kept that evening, set down to the last tally, with her own name signed beneath it as though she meant the entry to answer before any question was asked of it. It is the first household accounting of any ruler of Dia-thìr to survive whole from that day to its last page, and it survived, Taigh na Fèithe's own scribes noted afterward, for the plain reason that a queen who wrote so exactly of candles and horses had also, without troubling herself to say so, written exactly of a great deal else besides.

## II. Of the Letters No One Could Read

By LE 1,034 the moss on the old stone at Carragh Cnoc bheag, above Cnoc bheag, had grown thick enough over its carved face that a hawk-keeper's grandchild, sent up the hill on an errand, could no longer find the letters at all beneath the green of it, and it was a young priest of the house there, a careful man named Tòmas mac Aonghais who had kept the mews under Gormshuil's own teaching as a boy and turned, in his middle years, more to the shrine's old stones than to its birds, who asked the house's leave to clear it properly rather than let another generation grow up believing the carving had never held letters at all. He and two others of the house spent the better part of a month at it, working with wooden scrapers rather than iron for fear of the stone, and washing the face clean with water carried up from the shrine's own well a bucket at a time, until at last, on a grey morning with the whole house standing about him in a half-circle, Tòmas ran his own fingers over a face of stone as bare of moss as it had likely stood on the day it was first cut.

The letters were there, plainly enough, cut deep and old, but no man or woman of the house that morning, nor any scholar sent for afterward from Dùn thais, could put a single sound to a single one of them; they answered to no shape the schools' own tables of the letters had ever kept, and the oldest man of the house, who had climbed that hill since before Tòmas was born, said only that a stone could keep its own counsel as well as a man could, and that this one plainly meant to. Tòmas wrote the whole of it down anyway, in the shrine's own roll, tracing each letter as faithfully as his hand allowed and setting beside his tracing the plain words that no one at Cnoc bheag, that year or after, could read it; and it is told that word of the cleared stone and its unread letters reached An Talla Dearg before the season turned, carried down by the same wool-trade that had once carried Gormshuil's teaching up, and that Queen Mòrag Ruadh, hearing it read to her among the ordinary business of the hall, had the sum of Tòmas's own oil and vellum for the month's work entered into her own book without comment, and asked, of the messenger who brought the report, only whether the priests meant to try again. He answered that they did not know; that a letter which had kept its silence through however many years the moss alone could measure might, Tòmas himself had said, be owed the same silence back from those who could not answer it.

## III. Of the Nets that Broke the Salt

Caol shean's boats had fished the same stretch of the east coast, out from the mouth of the Abhainn chaol, for as long as the town's own rolls ran, taking a catch that varied, season to season, no more than any fisherman expected a catch to vary; and it was in LE 1,039 that the boats came in, three days running, so heavy in the water that the men rowing them swore afterward they had never once, in a working life apiece, seen a hull sit so low and still make its own harbour without shipping green water over the gunwale. The salters of the town, who kept pans enough for an ordinary season and a little over, ran through what salt they held by the second day and sent, within the hour, to every salt-town along that coast for more; but no cart could reach Caol shean before the catch began to turn, and a foreman of the salting-sheds, a broad, unhurried man named Ruairidh mac Neacail who had kept the sheds eleven years and never once in that time seen them idle in the height of a season, made the call, on his own head and without waiting on any word from the reeve, to hang what could not be salted out in the wind instead, strung on lines the length of every lane in the lower town, rather than let it go to waste on the strand.

It dried, after its fashion; the wind off that coast was salt-laden enough in its own right to help the drying along, and Caol shean's lanes stood hung, for the better part of two weeks, with more fish than any lane in that town had ever held at once, a sight that drew gulls from three parishes and children from every house to run beneath the lines and duck the drips. Ruairidh's own granddaughter, no more than six that year, was set by her mother to walk the lower lane twice a day with a long switch and drive the gulls off before they could strip a line bare, a labour she took to with more relish than any chore given her before or since, and she was fond of telling her own children that she remembered the smell of that fortnight before she remembered almost anything else of her own childhood, a smell the whole town carried on its clothes and in its hair until the last line was finally taken down.

But dried fish, however honestly dried, sold poorly against salted, the trading houses down the coast having long since built their custom around the one and not the other, and Ruairidh's own foreman's roll notes, in a hand plainer than most of its entries, that the greater part of that year's catch, the largest the town's own rolls had ever set down, fetched less at market than a middling season's salted catch had fetched the year before. The town went back to salting the next season and every season after, laying in salt enough, from that year forward, for a catch half again the size of any it had yet taken, a lesson Ruairidh is said to have summed up to his own daughter, when she came to keep the sheds after him, in a single sentence: that a good year could cost a town more than a bad one, if the town had made no ready place to hold it.

## IV. Of the Thousandth Year

Bliadhnaichean an Diosail, as Taigh na Fèithe kept them without a break of a single year since An Diosal, came in LE 1,039 to its thousandth year, a reckoning the custodians had watched approach for the better part of a decade and had argued over, in that time, more than any single number Mòrag Ruadh had yet heard argued in her own hall: whether the year deserved a feast, as some of Na Seachd Taighean held, or a fast, as others held, or nothing marked at all beyond the count's own turning of its page, as a few of the oldest custodians held, saying that a number was a number and owed no more ceremony at a thousand than it had owed at nine hundred and ninety-nine. It was the queen herself, hearing the three views laid before her in An Talla Dearg that autumn, who judged between them: one burning, she said, on the quay the count had begun from, no feast about it and no fast either, the measure and no more than the measure, so that the year would be marked as the count was kept, exactly and without excess on either side.

She rode down to Seann Skell herself for it, in the dark of the year, a journey of two short days over roads already hard with the season's first frosts, and stood, on the appointed evening, at the edge of Cidhe an Diosail among Taigh na Fèithe's own custodians and a crowd that had gathered along the whole length of the quay and back into the lanes behind it, more people than Seann Skell's own harbour-court had ever counted at one telling. The measure was brought down from Taigh na Fèithe in a plain iron scuttle, no more coal in it than any single hearth of the island might burn of an ordinary evening, and set alight on the stone where the harbour scribes had once cut the first tallies of the count, thirty generations of winters before. The flame that came up off it burned, by every telling that reached the hall afterward and by the queen's own account given to her scribe the next morning, the colour of the vein itself rather than any ordinary coal-fire's yellow, a deep, steady red that held its colour the whole while the scuttle burned down and gave off, the custodians said, no more smoke than a single hearth gives off in an evening, exactly as the measure had been meant to give.

A custodian of Taigh na Fèithe stood at the queen's own shoulder through the whole of the burning, an old woman of Na Seachd Taighean named Catrìona nic Fhearchair who had kept the count's own weights her whole working life, and it was she who leaned close, as the last of the coal in the scuttle settled to ash, to tell the queen, in a voice pitched under the crowd's own silence, that the count would go on the next morning exactly as it had the morning before, one more year added to the tally and nothing about the count's own keeping changed by the number it had just crossed. Mòrag Ruadh asked her, low enough that only the custodian and her own scribe standing near caught it, whether anyone now living understood why the count had been begun at all, on that quay, in that first year; and the old woman answered only that Leabhar a' Chùraim gave no reason beyond An Diosal, and that a keeping a thousand years old by then had needed no better reason than its own long habit to go on being kept.

The crowd that had come down every lane and cart-track of that shore to see a thousand years burn in one small fire watched it burn down to ash without, by every account that reached An Talla Dearg afterward, a single voice raised the whole while, neither in wonder nor in complaint, and went home in the same silence once the last of the flame had gone out, a silence the queen's own scribe, riding back up the coast road at her side, said afterward he had found harder to account for than any noise the crowd might have made instead. Mòrag Ruadh herself said little of it that night or after, to her scribe or to the hall she returned to; what she did say, more than once in the years that followed to those who asked her plainly what the burning had felt like to stand near, was only that a thousand years had gone into that scuttle and come out again as one evening's worth of an ordinary hearth's fire, and that she had stood close enough to feel the heat of it on her own face the whole while, and had thought, watching it, of nothing grander than how small a measure could be made to answer for so long a keeping.

## V. Of the Daughter Born at the Turn of the Year

Mòrag Ruadh's own daughter was born at Cathair dhearg the following spring, and named Beathag by her mother's own choosing before the child was a day old, for no reason the queen's book troubles to give beyond the name's own plainness; the book's entry for that week holds, beside the ordinary sums of candles and grain, one line set apart from the rest in a hand Taigh na Fèithe's own scribes afterward remarked was less steady than her usual, recording only the day and the name and nothing more of what a mother might have been expected to write of a first child. The hall kept a quieter feast for it than the thousandth year's burning had asked of Seann Skell, a single evening's ale and a fire built up higher than the season strictly needed, and Na Seachd Taighean sent, each in its own turn over the following month, a small gift to the cradle: a length of undyed wool from Clann Fhearchair, a carved horn spoon from Clann Mhuirich, small things a child could neither use nor remember receiving, given, Leabhar a' Chùraim notes, more for the houses' own satisfaction in the giving than for any need the cradle had of them.

## VI. Of the Market above the Mill-Race

The hill country above Baile ghorm, in the island's south-east, had traded its grain and its clay in small parcels along the roads for as long as any teller there could set a date to, each farm carrying its own cartload down to whichever town would take it that season; and it was the hill-lords of that country, in LE 1,051, who set a single market to gather the whole of that trade in one place rather than let it scatter, as it had always scattered, along a dozen separate roads. They set it at Cnoc bhàn, above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada, where the water ran fast enough the year round to turn three wheels at once and where a cart from any farm of that country could reach the flat ground beside the race in a single day's driving. It opened first as a small thing, a handful of carts and a morning's trading over grain and clay and honey, but it held one good beside the ordinary run of a market that no other market on the island could offer alongside it: pearls, taken by the shore-women of that same coast from the mussel beds in the shallows below the cliffs, sold nowhere else in whole parcels but at that one market above the mill-race.

A woman of the shore named Sìne nic Ruairidh, who had gathered mussels off that coast since she was a girl and had sold her pearls, before the market opened, one or two at a time to whatever trader passed near enough to ask after them, brought the whole of a season's gathering to the market's first opening rather than sell it piecemeal as she always had, and found, to her own plain surprise, that a buyer down from Cathair mhòr paid her more for the lot laid out together than she had ever been offered, in all her years of gathering, for the same pearls sold singly along the road. The buyer, a trader of Cathair mhòr who had come to that coast on other business and heard of the pearls only by chance from an innkeeper the night before, told her plainly, as he weighed the last of them into his own scale, that a buyer could judge the worth of a whole season's gathering laid out together in a way no single pearl handed across a cart-rail on a muddy road had ever let him judge it, and that she would do better, every season after, to make him wait for the market than to save him the ride by meeting him on the road herself. She told this to the other shore-women of her own stretch of coast before the season was out, and within a few years the whole of that coast's gathering came up to the mill-race market each season rather than trickle out along the roads a pearl or two at a time, so that a trader wanting pearls at all, from that year forward, learned to wait for the one market that held them rather than chase them down the coast in ones and twos. The queen's own book records, some years on, a single pearl bought at that same market and sent to the cradle at Cathair dhearg for her daughter's naming-day, its cost set down beside a cart-load of candles in the same plain hand as everything else the book ever held.

## VII. Of Baile Ghorm's Blue, and the Queen's Own Entry

The dyers of Baile ghorm had worked a common blue for their own wool since before living memory, a colour that held well enough through a season's wear but faded, every dyer of that town owned plainly, a full shade paler by the second washing than it had stood at the first; and it was in LE 1,064 that a dyer of that town, a patient woman named Oighrig nic Ailein who had spent the better part of ten years trying one mordant after another against the marsh plant her own mother had first shown her, found at last a mixing that held the colour fast through washing after washing without the fading her own mother's dye had always shown. She would not, by her own later telling, say exactly what turned the mixing from an ordinary blue into a fast one, only that she had changed one thing at a time across those ten years, keeping a careful board of her own beside her dye-vats much as the queen kept hers beside her household accounts, until one change at last held where every change before it had let the colour slip.

Cloth of that new blue was worn first at Taigh na Fèithe's own midwinter gathering the year it was made, and it is told that every house of custody present asked, before the evening was out, where cloth of that colour could be had, so that within a few years Baile ghorm's own blue had become the feast-day dress of Na Seachd Taighean entire, worn at every gathering of custody thereafter and known, wherever it travelled on a trader's cart, by the town that had first held the mixing that made it fast. Oighrig herself lived to see her own blue worn at three winters' gatherings running before she died, and taught her mixing, by hand and never by writing, to the two daughters who took up her vats when she could no longer stand at them.

Mòrag Ruadh's own book, in the same year, holds an entry for a length of that new blue bought for her own wear at Taigh na Fèithe's midwinter gathering, set down beside the ordinary sums of the season in the same plain hand the book had kept from its very first page; and it is that same book, turned back by a later hand to the page for the night of the thousandth year's burning, that gives the last word this telling has to give of that evening at Cidhe an Diosail. Against the date of the burning, where another queen's book might have set down a verse or a line of wonder at a thousand years made into one evening's fire, Mòrag Ruadh had written only the cost of the coal, reckoned to Taigh na Fèithe's own weights, and beneath it, in the same hand and no larger, five words and no more: one handful, nothing more.

# Chapter Thirty-two: Of the Swallowing Cough

*LE 1,075 – 1,159*

## I. Of the Cough at Muileann dhomhain

Beathag Fhionn was thirty-nine years old and had sat at her mother's right hand in An Talla Dearg for eleven of them, hearing boundary pleas and grain rulings and the slow ordinary business of a settled island, before she heard the word Muileann dhomhain spoken in a voice that made her set down the tally she was reading. The rider who brought it had ridden the eighteen miles from Muileann dhomhain without stopping to eat, and he stood in the hall's doorway swaying a little on his feet while he told it: that a sickness had come into the town that closed a man's throat until he could not swallow his own spit, still less bread or water, and that it had come quickly, house by house along the lower street first and then up into the hill lanes, and that the town's own healers, who had buried plagues before and thought they knew the shape of a hard season, had never seen a dying so fast nor a throat shut so tight against a cup held to it.

Her mother, Mòrag Ruadh, was seventy-nine years old that year and had worn the crown sixty years, since she was nineteen, and she heard the rider out in full before she said anything at all, which Beathag had long since learned was her mother's way with any tidings that frightened her, the silence buying her time to decide what a queen ought to feel before she let herself feel it. When she did speak it was only to ask how many, and the rider said he did not rightly know, that the healers had stopped counting somewhere past a hundred and had gone back to nursing rather than tallying, which was, he said, an answer of a kind. It is told at Cathair dhearg that the queen sent grain and dried fish south that same week, and priests of Òrd Mhacha to sit with the dying where the town's own could not, and that she sent nothing else, because there was nothing else on the island that a cough could be answered with.

Beathag rode south herself before the season was out, against her mother's own wish that she stay clear of the sickened town, and stood a morning at the edge of the lower street with a cloth held to her own mouth as the custodians had asked of her, watching two men carry a hurdle between them with a third man on it who could no longer swallow so much as the water they tried to give him. She did not go nearer than that edge of street, and she said afterward to no one but her own scribe that she had gone south chiefly to see with her own eyes what a rider's telling could only ever half give her, a thing she judged, looking back on it in her own age, to have been more for her own sake than the town's, since the town had no need of a queen's presence and every need of grain, fish, and priests, which had already been sent before she ever mounted a horse.

By the turn of the season the town had lost near a third of its people, the healers' own best count when the dying finally slowed enough to be counted, and the losing fell heaviest along the lower street where the houses stood close and shared a well, whole households going into the ground within a fortnight of one another, while houses two streets up, set apart on the hill with wells of their own, lost no one at all. Beathag heard this reckoning read aloud in the hall the following winter and thought, though she said it to no one, that the closeness of the houses, and not any fault in the blood, had done the killing, a thought she kept turning over long after the telling had moved on to other business, for she could see no way to prove it and no one in the hall who thought it worth the proving.

Two years on, the cough came down the coast to Seann Bhral, and Seann Bhral acted where Muileann dhomhain, taken by surprise, had had no chance to act at all: the town shut its own harbour before a single ship from the sickened towns could put in, and posted its own reeves at the gate to turn back any traveller on the coast road, and kept the shared meal, which had always been carried house to house by hand, by leaving baskets of bread and dried fish at the town gate instead, for whoever within needed them, so that no one from outside the walls need come near enough to catch a dying man's breath. It held. Seann Bhral lost fewer in that whole hard season than Muileann dhomhain had lost in a single fortnight, and the harbour towns down the coast, hearing how the shutting had been done, began that same year to talk among themselves, in a way they had not needed to before, about which of a town's own doors it might be wisest to close, and when, and who among their own people would have the stomach to keep a gate shut against a neighbour's own cart.

A reeve of Seann Bhral, an old woman who had kept the town's grain store for thirty years and was given the gate to keep as well once the shutting began, is said to have told a rider passing through, long after the sickness had gone by, that the hardest part of the whole season had not been the turning-away of strangers, who took a refusal at a strange gate as no more than the ill luck of the road, but the turning-away of the town's own folk who had gone out before the shutting to visit kin along the coast and came home to find the gate closed against them too, the rule allowing no house, however dear, an exception once the order was given. She had stood at that gate herself, she said, and told a fisherman she had known from childhood that he could leave food and word for his own wife within, but that his own body could not pass the gate until the season turned, and he had gone away up the road without answering her, and she had not slept easily for a week after, though she never once doubted the order had been the right one.

## II. Of the Reeve at the Ford

Beathag Fhionn was crowned in the same hall her mother had held for sixty-three years, forty-two years old that spring and grey already at the temples, and the first act her own scribes set down under her own seal, before a grain ruling, before a boundary plea, before anything the hall's ordinary business might have offered her instead, was the closing of the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain.
