It is told that she gave the order within the month of her crowning, before the cough had shown any sign of moving further west along that same road, judging, as her scribes later wrote it down, that a queen who waited for a sickness to prove itself before she acted against it had already waited too long to act at all.

The order she sent was plain enough for any reeve on that road to carry out without asking her leave a second time: that no traveller, cart, or beast was to pass between the two towns until the queen's own word released the road again, and that a reeve was to be set at every ford and every crossing of the coast road between them to see the order kept, day and night, through whatever weather the season sent. Six fords lay along that stretch of road, some no more than a stepping-place where the coast road crossed a stream too narrow to trouble naming, and to each of them the crown's scribes sent a reeve, chosen mostly from the towns nearest each crossing, men and women who knew the road, and were known on it, in turn.

To the ford nearest Muileann dhomhain, where the road ran closest to the sickened town and where, if the cough meant to travel west at all, it would first have to cross, the queen's scribes sent a young man of the town's own kin, Seumas mac Coinnich, thirty-two years old, who had held no office before that spring beyond keeping his own family's small herd of goats on the hill above the lower street where the dying had been thickest. He had lost, in the sickness's first passing, an aunt and two cousins and had watched, from his own high ground, smoke go up some mornings from more than one house on the lower street at once, and it was for that reason, the scribe who chose him is said to have written, and not for any skill the office required, that he was thought the surest hand to set at that particular crossing: a man who had already seen, at close hand, what the road behind him was closing against.

The other five reeves along that same stretch of road were of an ordinary sort, chosen for steadiness rather than for grief: a miller's widow at the ford above Caol dhearg, a shepherd who had never before left his own hill in a working life of forty years, a young clerk lent from the crown's own household at Cathair dhearg who found, within a week, that a ford asked patience of a kind no clerk's stool had ever asked of him. Between them the six held the whole of that road's crossing points, and it is told that not one of the six let a single traveller through in the three years the order stood, whatever the traveller's reason given, a plain and stubborn faithfulness the crown's own scribes remarked on afterward as owing less to any fear of the queen than to a thing harder to put a name to, which the scribes, wanting a word for it, called only the road's own discipline, as though the shutting itself had taught the six who kept it a single lesson none of them had known before that spring.

He held the ford through that first summer without much trouble, turning back carters who had not yet heard the order and travellers who had heard it and thought it need not apply to them, a labour that asked little more of him than a plain word said firmly and, once or twice, a hand kept near the staff he had been given, though he never once had to raise it. The travellers who came to his crossing in those first weeks were mostly strangers to him, or near enough, and a stranger turned back at a ford, however aggrieved, was a small enough thing to carry home at evening and set down.

It was near the season's end that his own brother came to the crossing, a cart behind him loaded with what looked, from the ford's near bank, like the whole of a household's goods, and called across the water before Seumas had properly seen who it was that their mother lay dying on the far side of the closed road, in a house two miles past the ford, and that he meant to go to her whatever any order said, closed road or no. Seumas knew the voice before he knew the face, and he is said to have stood a long moment at his own side of the ford with the staff loose in his hand, saying nothing, while his brother waited on the far bank for an answer that was, by both their own tellings ever after, longer in coming than either brother thought it ought to have been.

He turned him back. It is told, though Seumas never once spoke of that afternoon again in the whole of his life, that he said only that the order held for every traveller on the road or it held for none, and that a reeve who let his own kin through a ford he had sworn to keep shut had, by that one letting, already broken every other turning-back he had made or would make after it, whatever the reason given him. His brother called him hard names across the water, and then, when the names brought no answer either, turned the cart and went back the way he had come. It is told at Muileann dhomhain that their mother died within the week, and that the two brothers did not speak again for the better part of five years, until the road was long since opened and the cough forgotten by every household the sickness had not touched.

The road stayed closed the better part of three years, and the cough, whatever carried it, did not once cross west of the fords the reeves held; Muileann dhomhain buried its own dead and Seann Bhral kept its gate, and the rest of the coast, watching the two towns from a safe distance, learned a lesson it did not soon forget: that a shut door, held firmly enough and long enough, could hold back what no priest and no healer had found any other way to answer. It is told that Seumas mac Coinnich kept the crown's reeve-board at that same ford for the rest of his working life, near thirty years, until his own death in his sixtieth year, and that no other order he was ever given afterward asked so much of him again, nor was any other, in the town's own telling of it, ever kept so faithfully.

## III. Of the Houses Taken by Lot

Muileann dhomhain was slow to fill again. For twenty years and more after the road reopened the town stood at less than two in every three of the households it had held before the sickness, whole streets of the lower town given over to houses with no one left to claim them, their thatch going grey and their doors swinging on hinges no one troubled to mend, and the reeve who kept the town's own roll in those years, an old man who had lost a wife and a son to the cough, is said to have walked the lower street once a season and written down, without much comment, which roofs had fallen in since his last walking.

It was families from the hill country above the town, land too thin and too far from any market to hold a growing household easily, who came down in the end to take the empty houses, a handful each year rather than all at once, drawn by land already cleared and walls already standing, however far gone, and cheaper by far than the work of raising a new house from nothing on a hillside. Three brothers, sons of a hill farmer of Caol dhearg, walked down with their wives and children in a single autumn and drew, between the three of them, three houses standing side by side on the lower street where an entire family of the old blood had once kept a smithy, and it is told that the eldest of the three, Ruairidh mac Phàdraig, stood a long while before the middle house before he would go in, the smell of another family's hearth still on the walls after twenty years empty, before he said only that a house left standing was a house left standing, whoever had raised the roof-tree first.

The town's remaining custodians, judging that an empty house served no one and that a filled one, however filled, served the whole town better than a street of fallen roofs, opened the houses to lot rather than to purchase, a stone drawn from a bag for each household that asked, so that no family of the hill country could claim to have bought its way past a neighbour with a fuller purse, and no family of the town's own old blood could claim a house left standing by right of who its people had once been.

By the year the last lot was drawn, near thirty years after the sickness had first come down the lower street, the older families of the town, those few whose houses had never emptied at all, said afterward that they no longer knew, walking their own streets, half the faces they passed, and that a town which had once been able to name every household back three generations came, that generation, to name its own streets by house rather than by kin: the goat-herd's house, the old weaver's house, without much certainty any longer of whose hands had built them first. It is not told that this troubled the town greatly. The houses stood filled again, and the well that had carried the sickness fastest along the lower street was by then two wells, dug wider apart at the custodians' own asking, and Muileann dhomhain, by every measure a reeve's roll could set down, was once more a living town and not a street of empty roofs.

## IV. Of the Bridge Built Anew

Drochaid Ros fhionn had carried the salt carts of Ros fhionn across the Abhainn bheag for the better part of seven centuries by the year its own arches, worn thin by cart-wheel and flood alike, began to shed stone into the water below them faster than any mason thought safe to let pass unmended. A carter's mule went into the river with its whole load one wet spring when the road bed gave way beneath it, the mule drowned before anyone could cut it free of its traces and the carter left standing waist-deep in the current holding a dripping harness, and it was that one loss, small as it was against a season's whole trade, that the salt-masters afterward pointed to as the thing that had finally moved them to act rather than to wait another year on the crown's own masons.

The salt-masters of the flats, whose whole trade crossed that one bridge on its way to every market the island kept, met among themselves rather than wait any longer, and it is told that they raised, among their own number, the whole cost of the arches' rebuilding out of a season's trade, a thing no guild of salt-carriers had ever before been asked or offered to do for a bridge that was not, in any strict reckoning, theirs to keep.

The new arches, when they were finished, carried the salt-masters' own names cut into the keystones, each master's name set into the stone above the arch his own purse had paid for, a vanity the crown's reeve who came to see the work done is said to have remarked on, not unkindly, to the eldest of the masters present; and the old man answered him, the reeve's own letter to Cathair dhearg records, that a name cut in stone over running water would outlast any name set on a tally of silver, and that a salt-master who had spent his whole life watching his trade pass unremarked over another man's bridge might be forgiven, once, for wanting his own name to be the thing that held the road up.

Beathag Fhionn, by then in the thirty-seventh year of her reign and growing heavier in the years than she liked to feel herself grow, sent word that the crown would meet whatever the salt-masters' purses could not, and that the bridge, however it was paid for, remained the road's own bridge and not any one guild's to close or open as it pleased; but it is told that no crown's silver was in the end asked for, the salt-masters' own trade having carried the whole cost between them before her letter reached the flats, and that she let the matter stand as it had settled itself, judging, her own scribes later wrote, that a bridge mended without her silver was no less mended for the lacking of it.

## V. Of the Queen's Death

She died at Cathair dhearg at nine-and-eighty years old, in An Talla Dearg, where she had sat at her own mother's right hand and closed a road against a sickness within the month of her crowning, and it is told that she was clear in her mind to the last day, dictating a grain ruling to her scribes on the same morning she took to her bed and did not rise from it again. The scribe who took down that last ruling, a young woman new to the hall's service, said afterward that the queen had asked her, once the ruling was finished and set aside, whether the road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain still stood open, a question the scribe had no ready answer for, the road having been open more than forty years by then and given no cause to be spoken of in the hall in all that time; the queen, told that it did, said only that she was glad of it, and closed her eyes, and did not open them again to speak of any other matter.

Her son Ailean was crowned within the season, fifty-nine years old himself and no longer a young man by any measure the hall could offer, the first king of that name in Sliochd Raghnaill, and it is told that he wept once, briefly and without shame, at his own crowning, and that no one in the hall thought the less of him for it, his mother's reign having been long enough that half the hall had known no other queen in the whole of their own working lives.

## VI. Of the Fading Things

It is told at Baile ghorm that the last dyer who knew the true mixing of Baile ghorm's own blue died in those same years without ever having taught it whole to either of the two apprentices she had quarrelled with and sent from her house in turn, so that the blue the town's weavers dyed thereafter, though it answered to the same old name, was in truth no more than the common blue any dyer on the island could mix, and it is said that the older weavers of the town, holding a length of the new cloth up against a length kept from before the old woman's death, could tell the two apart at a glance and never once, in the whole of their own lives after, stopped mourning the difference aloud to anyone who would listen.

Lightning found the ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal on a summer night some twenty years after the queen's death, and burned them to their footings before the keepers could carry so much as a bucket from the well, and it is told that the keepers, setting new posts in the old ground the following season, cut the names again as best their own memory and Leabhar a' Chùraim together could recover them, and owned plainly, in the roll they kept of the cutting, that a handful of the names so cut were guesses only, the old carving too far gone in the years before the burning for even the oldest keeper living to swear to every letter of them. No one is told to have thought the less of the new posts for the owning. A name guessed at in good faith and cut with the same care as a name known outright, the keepers held, honoured the dead it stood for no less than certainty would have, and the roll's own plain admission of the guessing was kept alongside the new posts, for any who came after to read and judge as they pleased.

The Abhainn bheag silted at Ros fhionn in the years that followed, a shifting bar building itself below the salt flats faster than any dredging the salt-masters could set their own hands to clear it, until the loaded barges that had once run the river to the sea on every tide found themselves grounding, one after another, a bowshot short of open water, their pilots standing in the shallows and cursing a bar that moved a little further out with every season's flood, no two years' soundings ever quite matching the last. The salt-masters, whose own fathers had cut their names into Drochaid Ros fhionn's keystones not forty years before, took their trade at last to Caol gharbh's own harbour along the coast, where deeper water asked no such patience of a laden barge, and it is told that the flats above Ros fhionn went on making salt as they always had, the brine springs caring nothing for a river's silting, but that the barges that had once carried it out grew fewer year on year, until a pilot standing at the old bar on a still morning might watch a whole tide turn and go out again without a single loaded hull crossing it, and count himself, by then, not much surprised.

# Chapter Thirty-three: Of the Table of Years

*LE 1,165 – 1,266*

> *Druim fon aisne, aisne fon chlàr,*
> *clàr ri clàr is an cuan fodhpa.*
> Keel under rib, rib under plank,
> plank to plank and the sea beneath them.

## I. Of the Narrows and the New Harbour

The salt of Ros fhionn had gone out by cart for as long as anyone at the market-court could remember, over Drochaid Ros fhionn and down the coast road to whatever harbour would take it, and for as long as anyone could remember the carters had grumbled at the bridge's toll and paid it anyway, because there was no other way to the sea that did not cost a full day more on the road. The salt-masters had moved their loading down to a landing at the river-mouth ten years before, when the river silted below the flats and the barges could no longer be trusted to clear the bar; but the landing was shallow too, and open to every gale that came up from the south, and more than one master had said, standing on its strand with a ruined cargo at his feet, that a harbour chosen in haste answered a haste and nothing more.

It was the masters themselves, in LE 1,169, who put their money together and sent it north to Caol gharbh, a fishing village on a deep inlet that had never held more than a few dozen boats and a smokehouse. They walled the inlet's mouth against the sea and dug the mud from its bed until a laden barge could lie there at any tide, and within three years Caol gharbh was posting its own harbour dues and calling its own quay, without much argument from anyone, the salt port of the north-east. The village that had smoked herring for its own tables now weighed and shipped more salt in a season than Ros fhionn's flats had once sent out in three, and the men who had cut turf for the smokehouse fires found themselves instead loading barges and learning a trade none of their fathers had known.

Not every cargo that left the new harbour came safely to open water. A season after the walls were finished, a barge heavy with the first full loading struck the reef at the narrows below the inlet, in the narrows off the neck of land between Caol gharbh and Caol chrom, where the tide off the point meets the river's own current and neither gives way to the other. Those who had grown up on that shore knew the place by the standing wave it threw up at the ebb, a ridge of broken water that never lay flat even on the stillest day, and every fisher's child was taught early to keep well clear of it in anything smaller than a laden hull. The barge's own steersman had crossed it a dozen times before without harm and misjudged the tide by less than the turn of a glass; the hull struck, held a moment, and broke her back on the rock, going down with half her salt still in her before the two men aboard could do more than throw themselves clear. They swam ashore in water cold enough that neither worked a hand rightly for a fortnight after, and the elder of the two, asked afterward whether he meant to go back to the loading, said only that a man who had felt that water close over his head once did not need telling twice what it could do. The harbour-masters set a withy at the rock the following spring, the first mark Caol gharbh's channel had ever needed, and it stood there the rest of the age, renewed each year by whichever household the harbour-court named to the duty. On that same neck, at a standing stone above the narrows, the headmen of Caol gharbh and Caol chrom met that year to settle what dues the salt-boats should pay each harbour; they met there again over every quarrel of the strait that followed, and the stone came to be called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich.

Drochaid Ros fhionn, meanwhile, fell quiet in LE 1,179. The salt no longer crossed it, and within a few years neither did much else, for the road it carried had been built for the salt trade and little besides. The office of bridge-keeper, which had passed from father to daughter and back again for longer than Leabhar a' Chùraim troubled to record, was done away with when the last keeper died and no one came forward to ask for it in his place; the crown's reeve at Ros fhionn simply let the post lapse; and travellers who still crossed the old stone, a few carters, a few pilgrims bound for the coast shrines, found the toll-gate standing open and unmanned and did not trouble to ask why.

Yet the market-court did not move. It had sat at Ros fhionn since before the bridge was built, judging boundary pleas and grain disputes for the whole of that shire, and though more than one voice argued in those years that the court's business had followed the salt to Caol gharbh and ought to follow it in body too, the court's own clerks answered, when the question was put to them formally, that a court sat where the shire's disputes were brought to it and not where its trade happened to lie that season, and that moving a bench built of oak two centuries old to chase a harbour wall built in three years struck them as a poor exchange. The court stayed. Caol gharbh grew rich on salt and never once, in all the years that followed, gained so much as a single clerk of its own to hear a plea.

The channel that had swallowed the barge was marked properly at last a few years on, Seòlaid Ros fhionn laid out with withies from the old bar to the deep water beyond the flats, so that a pilot new to the trade might learn it in a season rather than in the ten years the old salt-masters had needed. It answered well enough while the withies were tended. In the years the harbour-court grew careless of the duty, the marks drifted and the channel with them, and more than one barge found the bar again the hard way before a fresh set of withies put it right.

## II. Of the Millers and the Watcher in the Sea

At Muileann shean, some way inland of the salt trade's noise, the millers cut a new gearing for their wheels in LE 1,189, oak toothed against oak so that one wheel now turned two stones where it had once turned one. The first winter it ran, half the town came to watch it work and went away arguing whether the flour it ground was finer or coarser than the old way's, a question no two households ever answered alike; within a generation the gearing had spread to every mill of consequence in the north, and the millers of Muileann shean, who had cut it first, kept a carved model of it hung over their own door as a kind of boast, though the boast grew quieter with each mill that copied it without asking leave.

Off the thinned coast of the north-west, in the same years, the fishers of the small boats still working those waters began to speak again of the thing they called Uilebheist na Mara, seen close enough in LE 1,199 to foul a net and leave it in ribbons on the strand the following morning. Whether it was one beast or the name given to whatever the sea chose to show a frightened crew, no two tellings agreed, but the boats of that coast drew further in after that season and stayed nearer the headlands than their grandfathers had ever needed to, so that the last few miles of open water off the north-west cape went, within a lifetime, from a fishing ground to a stretch the boats no longer troubled to cross.

It was into a household of that same north-west coast, at a farm two days' walk from the thinned water, that Raghnall mac Chaluim had been born, six years after the salt-masters first walled Caol gharbh's inlet. His father kept sheep on ground too poor for much else, and his mother's people had once fished the same water Uilebheist na Mara now kept for its own, a trade her own father had given up before Raghnall could remember him at it. The boy showed no gift for either sheep or nets. What he showed, from an age his mother could never afterward fix exactly, was a habit of counting: stones in a wall, sheep through a gate, the notches on a tally-stick left over from some dispute of his father's, and asking, of anyone patient enough to answer him, whether the count came out the same the second time. His mother said once, late in her own life, that she had known him for a strange child the evening he came in from the fold in tears, six years old and furious, because he had counted the flock at the gate twice and got two different numbers, and would not be comforted until his father had gone back out with a lamp and counted a third time to settle which of the boy's two counts had been right. It was the sheep that were wrong, as it happened, one having slipped a hurdle and gone back to graze; the boy remembered only that a thing could be counted carefully and still come out crooked, and it troubled him, his mother said, far past the age when it ought to have stopped troubling a child at all.

A priest of the schools of the stag, passing that way on his own circuit the year the millers' new gearing was still news even on that coast, heard the boy through a whole afternoon of it and told his father, not unkindly, that a mind so set on counting things twice belonged at a house of disputation and not on a hillside among the sheep. His father, who had four other sons for the sheep and could spare the one, sent him south the following spring, a boy of fourteen, to Dùn thais, where Taigh na Deasbaid had stood since before any hand now living could say who first raised it, and where scholars of every rite came to argue questions the rest of the island had no leisure to ask.

## III. Of the Table of Years

Raghnall spent the better part of twenty years at Dùn thais before he wrote the thing that would carry his name past his own death. He came to Taigh na Deasbaid as a boy who counted sheep through gates and left it, in the eyes of the scholars who taught him, a man who counted people the same plain way, without flinching from what the count showed him.

The question that took hold of him was one he said, later in his life, had first occurred to him watching his own uncles: that his mother's brothers, who had fished the thinned water until Uilebheist na Mara drove them off it, had died younger, every one of them, than the custodians' kin he came to know at Dùn thais, whose galleries fed them well in every season the vein answered at all. It was an unremarkable thing to notice and say aloud over a meal. It was another thing to test it.

He began, in his twenty-fifth year, going through every roll of births and deaths Taigh na Deasbaid would let him copy: Leabhar a' Chùraim's own entries where they touched Na Seachd Taighean, the shire seats' tallies of their dead, the death-rolls the priests of every rite kept for their own dead alone. He set the heads of the custodian houses beside the tenants who worked their galleries and their land, house against house, generation against generation, and totted the years each had lived before Leabhar a' Chùraim or a priest's roll marked them gone. It took him the better part of nine years, most of it done by lamplight after Taigh na Deasbaid's own business was finished for the day, and more than one scholar who shared his table said afterward that they had thought him, for years together, a man chasing a private grief that any ordinary grief ought to have worn thin.

On 29 an t-Samhain, LE 1,209, he laid the finished table before Taigh na Deasbaid entire, called together in its own hall on a morning of hard frost, the scholars sitting in their winter cloaks because the fires had not yet been lit that far into the season and no one had thought, until the doors were shut, to send for wood. Clàr nam Bliadhnachan was a single broad sheet ruled into columns, house against tenant, generation against generation, the years each had lived set down in a hand grown small and cramped from nine years of the same close work; Raghnall had had it copied fair the week before onto a hide large enough that two scholars were needed to hold it up before the hall could read it whole. The heads of Na Seachd Taighean lived, on the whole, some years longer than the tenants of their own lands lived, and the gap did not close, house by house, no matter how the sums were run again. He read the table aloud himself rather than let another scholar do it for him, his voice, those present said, steadier than his hands, and he asked, when he had finished, the one question the sums could not answer for him: whether the vein answered the hand that held it, and answered it more kindly than it answered the hand that only worked it.

No one at Taigh na Deasbaid that day gave him an answer either. Some scholars called it a fair piece of counting and nothing more, the kind of pattern a mind will find in any sufficiently large pile of numbers if it looks for one hard enough. One rose before the hall had properly settled and said as much aloud, that a man might set any two rolls of the dead side by side and find some difference or other between them if he wished hard enough to find it, and that a wish dressed in columns was still a wish. Raghnall answered him only that he had run the sums four times over four winters and would gladly run them a fifth in the scholar's own presence, on rolls the scholar chose himself, and the scholar, after a silence the hall remembered longer than the exchange itself, sat down without taking up the offer.

Others left the hall without speaking to him at all, and one old scholar, a custodian's own son by birth, is said to have told him afterward, in private, that a table was a poor vessel for a question that could unmake every house on the mountain if it were ever answered wrongly, and that he would do better to burn the sheet and keep the question, if he must keep it, in his own head.

Raghnall did not burn it. He sent a fair copy to Taigh na Fèithe, addressed to no one custodian in particular, and kept his own working copy at Dùn thais, and for a few years the table passed from hand to hand among scholars of every house, argued over, copied badly, copied well, until word of it reached the king's council at Cathair dhearg by a route no one afterward could trace to its first carrier.

On 29 an Giblean, LE 1,219, the council forbade the table's copying. Taigh na Deasbaid was shut for a generation by the same order, its scholars sent back to their own shires and its hall given over, for a time, to the storing of grain against a lean year that never came. Raghnall himself was neither punished nor praised; the council's order named the table, not the man who had made it, and Raghnall, forty-four years old that year and past the age when a scholar without a school might easily start again elsewhere, went home to the north-west coast and kept sheep, badly, for the rest of that season, before a custodian of Taigh na Fèithe he had never met sent word asking whether his own working copy still existed and might be sent to the mountain for safekeeping.

He sent it. It was entered in Taigh na Fèithe's own inventory that same year, one line among the galleries and Clachan a' Chrannchuir and the old tallies of coal owed and coal burned, Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, forbidden to be copied, kept. No custodian who read the entry after him is recorded to have asked that it be destroyed, and none is recorded to have asked that the forbidding be lifted either. It stayed on the shelf Taigh na Fèithe had made for it, read by whoever came to the inventory with leave to read it and closed again by whoever came after, a question kept rather than answered, which is not, Raghnall is said to have told the custodian who took the copy from his own hands, quite the same thing as a question forgotten.

## IV. Of the Gale, the Boundary and the Pilgrims

Raghnall lived one-and-twenty years past the forbidding, most of them quietly, at a small house near Dùn thais that the shut school let him keep for the asking, and it is told that he went on counting things to the end of his life, though what he counted in those last years no leaf that survives says plainly.

In LE 1,229, before the grain fleet had sailed for the season, a gale drove up the river at Inis mhòr higher than any then living had seen. It came in the night out of the north-east with no warning any watcher on the strand could afterward point to, and the harbour's own people woke to a wind that laid the reed thatch flat on the landward side of every roof and a river running backward with the sea's own push behind it. Boats moored two deep along the strand were crushed against one another faster than a lantern could be got down to them, and by the grey of morning the strand was heaped with broken plank from stem to stern of the harbour, timbers that had been whole hulls the evening before now fit for nothing but a boat-builder's fire. The fleet that should have carried that year's grain south did not sail until the following spring. Inis mhòr rebuilt what the gale had taken through that whole winter, every hand in the town given some part of the work whether it had ever held an adze before or not, and when the spring fleet finally went out a season late, the harbour counted itself no worse off in the end than a hard winter might have left it regardless.

Raghnall mac Chaluim died at Dùn thais in his sixty-fifth year, in the small house the shut school had let him keep, and the scholars who had once argued his table over a shared table of their own carried him to the burying ground the school no longer had the standing to consecrate, and buried him there anyway, judging that a house shut by a king's council was not thereby unmade in every other sense that mattered to the dead. No stone was cut for him. A tally-stick was, notched once for every year the making of the table had cost him, and set at the head of the grave, where it stood until the weather took it, as weather takes most things left standing in the open on Dia-thìr.

In LE 1,246, in the far north-east, Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh went to law over the grazing on the hills between them, a quarrel old enough that neither shire seat's own clerks could say, when the case was first brought, how many times it had already been argued and settled and argued again by their grandparents. Each side came to Cathair dhearg with its own boundary stones to point to and its own old herders to swear where the line had always run, and each old herder swore a different line from every other, so that the council's clerks, hearing the third day of testimony, are said to have privately agreed among themselves that no one now living had ever known the true boundary and that both sides believed, with equal honesty, in a line neither could produce a single stone to prove. It came before the king's council three times before it was settled at last by dividing the disputed ground along a stream that ran, conveniently for the judgment though not, the council's own clerk noted dryly, for either party's satisfaction, almost exactly down its middle. Both shire seats grazed their flocks to the water's edge from that year on, and the herders on each bank, meeting at the ford in ordinary weather, were said within a generation to have forgotten there had ever been a quarrel at all, though the stones each side had carried to Cathair dhearg and carried home again unused stood afterward in both towns' own boundary walls, still pointing, for whoever troubled to walk out and look at them, to a line the water had long since made no matter of.

The keepers of Na Seann Spioradan renewed, in LE 1,259, the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, where a stream ran clear as glass and was said, by every rite that had ever sent a pilgrim to it, never once to have failed those who drank of it at the right turning of the moon. A guest-house was built beside the water that same year for those who walked from every shire to drink there, timber and thatch enough for a dozen travellers at a time, with a hearth kept lit through every season by whichever keeper held the turn of duty. Its own book of names, kept from the first season, showed within a few years pilgrims of every rite on the island entered side by side on the same leaf, dawn-hawk beside an Fhianna, Manannan's sworn beside Òrd Mhacha of Macha, a mixing the keepers of the stream had not expected and, once it had happened, did not trouble to prevent, for the water itself, they said, had never once asked a pilgrim which rite had sent him before it answered him.

## V. Of the Two Sons

King Ailean mac Raghnaill died at Cathair dhearg on 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,266, sixty-six years old, having reigned long enough that few at An Talla Dearg that year could remember another king's seal on a letter. He left two sons by different mothers, and it was known, before the year was out, that each of the two had been told plainly, by whichever parent had raised him, that he and not the other was the one meant to wear the crown after their father. Neither had been told this as a secret; both households had said it openly for years, at hearths and hall-tables where a saying travels whether it is meant to or not, and An Talla Dearg's own clerks, drawing up the king's burial roll, are said to have left a blank space where the name of the heir should have stood, unable to agree between themselves which of the two names to write and unwilling, in the king's own house and so soon after his death, to write neither. The council that had once forbidden a scholar's Clàr nam Bliadhnachan met that winter to consider a harder sum than any Raghnall mac Chaluim had ever set before it, and found, by the time the snow came, that it had no answer ready either.

At Taigh na Fèithe above Muileann dhearg the inventory was read out that same winter, as it was read every winter, gallery by gallery, tally by tally, down to the single line a custodian long dead had entered nearly fifty years before: Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, forbidden to be copied, kept. The custodian reading it that year paused over the line a moment longer than the others, as the custodians before her had done and the custodians after her would go on doing, and then read on to the next line, for the inventory did not wait on any one entry, however long a shadow it had cast, and there was a great deal more of it still to be read before the reckoning of that year's coal could be closed.

# Chapter Thirty-four: Of the Brothers' Peace

*LE 1,266 – 1,319*

## I. Of the Two Courts

The council that had failed to fill the blank space on the burial roll did not try again the following year, nor the year after that, and in the space where an heir's name should have stood a kind of silence settled over Cathair dhearg that everyone at An Talla Dearg understood and no one troubled to name aloud. Iain Ciar, the elder by two years, kept his own following at An Talla Dearg, in the wing his mother's kin had held since before his birth; Alasdair Bàn kept his in the south country, where his mother's people had given him land and men enough that he need ask leave of no one to sit at his own table. For four years the two households traded no worse than cold courtesy, gifts sent at Na Ceithir Fèilltean, messengers who ate at one hall and rode to the other without any word carried between them that either brother could afterward be blamed for.

The keeping of a house that was not quite a court and not quite a private hall had fallen, some years before the war broke, to a woman of the mining road with no part in either brother's quarrel: Mairead nic Mhurchaidh, who took up An Taigh-seinnse Mòr from her own father, the last of a long line of keepers descended, the road said, from Iain mac Mhurchaidh, who had built the house its second byre and begun, in a careful hand, the book of the ox-teams that lodged there through the mountain snows; she kept both after her father without changing so much as the ruling of the ledger's columns, and travellers on the central road who had known her father's keeping said, more than once, that they could not have told the two hands apart on the page had the years not told them which was which. Nothing in those years marked the road-house as a place either brother's fortunes would ever turn on. It was simply the halfway stage, the byre, the book, the fires kept through the worst of the snow for whichever ox-team the weather had caught between one shire and the next.

It could not hold, and everyone at both tables, if asked plainly, would have said so from the first winter. Iain Ciar was thirty years old when it broke and Alasdair Bàn twenty-eight, both of an age to have stopped waiting on their fathers' word and begun to trust their own, and each had spent four years hearing, from men who wanted a lord's favour more than they wanted peace between brothers, that the other meant to move first if he was given time enough to gather the strength for it. A messenger of Alasdair Bàn's, riding to An Talla Dearg with the ordinary gift at the feast of Bealltach, was turned back at the gate that fourth year on some pretext of the season's business too full to receive him, the first courtesy either household had refused the other in four years of careful giving, and it is told that Alasdair took the refusal, small as the matter was on its own account, as the answer he had been waiting four years to hear. Alasdair moved first. In LE 1,270 his men took Cnoc naomh in a night, a small holding worth little on its own account but sitting square on the road between the two households' lands, and held it eleven days before Iain Ciar's own riders came up and took it back with less blood than either side afterward claimed. Na Seachd Taighean, who had watched the four years of cold courtesy without committing themselves to either table, could no longer sit apart once blood had been drawn on ground both brothers claimed. Four declared for Iain Ciar and three for Alasdair Bàn, and it was from that first taking and retaking of a holding no one had thought worth a war that the fighting which followed took its name: Cogadh nam Bràithrean.

What the two brothers said to one another in those first weeks, if they said anything at all beyond what their messengers carried, no leaf that survives records. It is told only that neither sent to the other any word of grief for what four years of cold courtesy had come to, and that both, within the same season, called up every man their own three or four houses owed them, and set every road between the two halves of the island under one following's watch or the other, so that a carter who had crossed freely from west to east his whole life found, that first winter of the war, that he must now say plainly at every second crossing which brother's peace he travelled under.

## II. Of the Burning of Ceann mhin and the Fall Below Muileann ghlas

Alasdair Bàn's ships came down the coast to Ceann mhin in LE 1,272, which had declared for his brother, and burned its waterfront before the town's own bell had finished ringing the alarm. The fire took the rope stores first, where the tarred cordage went up faster than any hand could carry water to it, and then the granary beside them, so that by the second morning Ceann mhin had lost in one night both what it needed to put its boats back to sea and what it needed to feed itself until the next harvest came in. Men who had spent the day hauling water from the harbour to a blaze no bucket-line could master were found by dawn simply sitting on the strand among the salvaged nets, too spent even to grieve aloud over the char that had been the granary. The town sent to Cathair mhòr, which had taken no side in the quarrel and could afford to be asked, and Cathair mhòr sent grain enough that no household at Ceann mhin went hungry that winter, though the debt of it, one way and another, was still being spoken of at the two towns' markets a generation later, a favour neither given nor asked for lightly and neither forgotten easily either.

Iain Ciar heard of the burning three days after it happened, at An Talla Dearg, from a rider who had changed horses twice to bring the word faster than any single beast could carry it the whole way. He is said to have asked the rider only two questions, how many had died and whether the granary had burned before or after the rope stores, and to have given no answer of his own to either the rider or the hall until he had heard both answers in full. What he did afterward needed no further asking. He called up Na Ceithir Taighean sworn to him and marched west through a season of hard rain that turned the mining road to a mire under every cart and every marching foot, and in LE 1,274, below Muileann ghlas where the road narrows between the river and the hill, he brought Alasdair Bàn's own men to a stand at last and broke them.

Little of the fighting is remembered in any particular that survives; what is told is mostly the outcome. Alasdair Bàn was taken alive on the field, and his captains were let go home unransomed and unpunished on Iain Ciar's own order, given only his word that the war their lord had made was ended so far as they themselves were concerned. It was a mercy some at Iain Ciar's own table thought unwise, arguing that a captain sent home free was a captain free to be called up again if Alasdair's cause ever found new strength; Iain Ciar is said to have answered that a war fought to its bitter last man on both sides left nothing behind it but sons who would fight the next one for their own dead fathers, and that he had rather end this one clean than begin the next one already owed. Alasdair was carried east under guard to a house of his brother's own choosing, kept comfortably and watched closely, while the two households that had traded cold courtesy for four years and then blood for four seasons more waited to learn what their two lords would make of what was left between them. Word of the victory reached An Taigh-seinnse Mòr within the week, carried by an ox-driver who had turned back from the mountain road rather than push his team through country still unsettled by the fighting, and Mairead nic Mhurchaidh, hearing it at her own hearth, is said to have asked the driver only where the two brothers now stood to one another, and to have got, in answer, a shrug and the plain word that no one yet knew.

## III. Of the Keeper's Day

The peace, when it came on 12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276, was made on ground that belonged to neither brother: An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, the great road-house at the halfway stage of the central mining road, where the ox-teams of the mountain waited out the snow every winter of the year and had done since before either brother's grandfather was born. Mairead nic Mhurchaidh was given, by whichever messenger carried the choosing of the ground to both households at once, a single day's warning that the two brothers and their two followings were riding for her hall, there to settle, one way or another, what four years of cold courtesy and four seasons of war had left unsettled.

She spent the day scrubbing. It is the one particular of that day that every telling of it agrees on, whatever else each teller adds or leaves out: that Mairead nic Mhurchaidh, keeper of a house that answered to no lord but the road, took a single day's warning of two kings' followings arriving at her door and used the better part of it on her knees with a bucket and a brush, scouring a floor that had taken the boots of ox-drivers and reeves and pilgrims for longer than her own father could remember, because she had heard it said, by travellers who had seen greater houses than hers, that great men will quarrel over the length of a bench sooner than they will quarrel over the matter that brought them to the table, and she meant to give neither brother the smallest excuse. She set the long board in the common room with a bench to either side, and measured the two benches against one another with her own hands until neither ran so much as a finger's breadth longer than its match, and she set at each end of the board the same loaf, baked from the same batch of the same flour, and the same jug of the same ale, so that no clerk of either household, however he wished to find a slight in it afterward, could find one in the setting of the table.

Both followings drew up in the yard outside a little before noon, the two bodies of armed men keeping a careful distance from one another across the frozen mud, and it was into that silence, thick enough already that Mairead nic Mhurchaidh heard every hoof-fall on the yard's stones from inside her own kitchen, that Iain Ciar came in first, on foot from the yard where his own men had halted a bowshot short of the door, and sat at the end nearest the fire without waiting to be shown to it. Alasdair Bàn came after him under guard that fell back at the threshold and did not follow him in, walking stiffly in the way of a man not long out of the custody of another man's house, and sat down across the board from his brother without a word of greeting passing between them that the keeper, standing by the fire and trying to look as though she were not listening, could afterward report to anyone who asked her. For a long while neither brother spoke at all. What she remembered longest of that silence, she told those who came after her at the house, was the sound of the oxen shifting in the byre behind the common room, a sound so ordinary on any other day that she had never once, in all the years of her keeping, troubled to notice it before that afternoon, and that grew, the longer the two men sat without a word, to fill the whole of the room in her own hearing until she could have named which beast had shifted its weight by the particular creak of the timber under it.

What passed between the two brothers in the time that followed, she never told, whether because she never fully heard it over the fire's own noise or because she judged, once the telling of it had been asked of her a hundred times by a hundred different travellers over the years that followed, that a thing two brothers had settled between themselves belonged to the two of them and not to a keeper's fireside story. Asked by an old reeve of Cathair mhòr, years afterward, whether the two men had raised their voices at any point in the long silence, she answered only that she had heard nothing through the door she had not already heard from her own oxen, and would say no more of it however the reeve pressed her. The end of it she would tell, and told the same way every time she was asked: that Alasdair Bàn gave up whatever claim he had carried into the room and was granted, for the whole of his own life, the lordship of Seann Chwen and nothing more; that Iain Ciar, thirty-six years old that year, was acknowledged crowned by the brother who might otherwise have contested it to both their deaths; and that when the two men rose at last from the board, each loaf at each end had been broken by the hand nearest it and neither had been eaten, as though the breaking of the bread had stood in that room for something neither brother had needed nor wished to put into plainer words. Mairead nic Mhurchaidh swept the crumbs from the board herself that evening, after both followings had ridden their separate ways, and is said to have kept, for the rest of her own keeping of the house, a horror of seeing any loaf served whole and any loaf served broken set down together on the same table, a small superstition her own daughters after her never quite understood and never quite gave up either.

## IV. Of the Years the Road Kept Its Peace

Alasdair Bàn kept the peace he had made for the whole of his own life, and it was said of him at Seann Chwen, where he held his lordship without complaint to the end of his days, that a man who has once sat across a board from his own brother with nothing between them but two whole loaves learns something about the keeping of a promise that no amount of being told can teach a man who has never sat there. He is remembered to have gone up to An Talla Dearg himself twice in those years, once at the birth of a nephew he would never rule after and once at the burying of an old captain of his own who had asked, dying, only that Alasdair carry the news of it to the king with his own mouth rather than send it by a rider; Iain Ciar received him both times without ceremony and sent him home again with a following no larger than the one he had come with, a small courtesy that satisfied neither brother's clerks, who would have preferred either a grander welcome or none at all, but seems to have satisfied the two brothers themselves well enough. He died at Seann Chwen in LE 1,291, a man of forty-nine, in the house his brother had let him keep, and no word of any quarrel renewed in his name is told of the years between the peace and his death. His lordship, on his dying, returned to the crown, as the peace had settled it should, and Iain Ciar is said to have kept, for the rest of his own reign, the lordship vacant rather than grant it to any other man, a small stubbornness An Talla Dearg's own clerks never once asked him to explain.

It was the burning of Ceann mhin, more than the battle that avenged it, that Iain Ciar is said to have carried longest in his own reckoning of the war. Having seen one shire seat beg its bread of another for the whole of a hard winter, he commanded, once his throne stood settled enough for such commands to be kept, that every shire seat of the island hold in store against the next war a full year's grain, measured and counted by the crown's own reeves at each autumn's close. The law, made LE 1,299 and called after him Lagh an Stòir, was kept faithfully while he himself sat An Talla Dearg to see that it was kept, and every granary on the island filled and emptied and filled again each year exactly as he had ordered.

The road below the road-house, in the years between, carried a new trade the two brothers' war had never touched. Masons of Ceann leathan, building a new front for their own temple, sent north in LE 1,295 for a stone none of their own quarries could match, a veined white marble found in the hills above Baile Mòr dhomhain, and from the year the first cart of it came south the road below An Taigh-seinnse Mòr carried a traffic that had never passed that way before: carriers who smelled of stone dust rather than coal or grain, and who paid, more often than not in cut stone itself rather than in silver or salt, for whatever fodder and shelter the road-house could offer their teams. Mairead nic Mhurchaidh kept a slab of it, unworked and no bigger than a hand, on the mantel above her own hearth for the rest of her keeping, a small vanity she never fully explained even to those who asked her outright why a road-house keeper should want a piece of stone bound for someone else's temple.

Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, a clerk of the king's own household, came to An Taigh-seinnse Mòr himself in those years, sent by no one but his own wish to set the war down properly before those who remembered it firsthand had all died out of the telling of it. He arrived on a wet evening with a satchel of wax tablets and a servant to carry them, and stayed three nights under the road-house's roof at his own expense rather than the crown's, working each evening by the same fire the two brothers had sat beside on the day of the peace, and asking, of every ox-driver who came in from the road, whether they had heard the tale told any way but the one the keeper herself told it. He sat with Mairead nic Mhurchaidh at the same board, by then scarred with the ordinary use of years rather than scrubbed for a single afternoon, and asked her plainly what had passed between the two brothers on the day of the peace. She told him, as she had told every asker before him, only the setting of the table and the silence and the two loaves broken and left; whatever words the two brothers had exchanged across that board she either had not heard or would not repeat, and Pàdraig, for all his asking, came away from her hearth with no more of it than anyone else who had asked her the same question over the years. He is said to have thanked her for her patience all the same, and to have left, before he rode on, a small silver ring of no great value pressed into her hand for the fire and the bed, which she kept afterward on the same mantel as the mason's slab of white stone, two keepsakes of two very different visitors set side by side without any comment from her that either was worth more than the other.

## V. Of the Book, and the Meeting at the Far-Off House

The account Pàdraig mac Ruairidh finished at last, LE 1,304, praised the king at every turn it could find a turn to praise him on, and it is the only account of Cogadh nam Bràithrean that survives whole to be read by anyone who asks after it, a fact that has vexed more than one later reader who would have liked a fuller word from the losing side of the table. Of the keeper's day it says only that the peace was made at a road-house between the brothers' lands and that both loaves set upon the board were left uneaten, which is not quite the whole of what Mairead nic Mhurchaidh herself had told him and is, all the same, the only part of her telling that Pàdraig's book chose to keep.

Mairead nic Mhurchaidh died at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr in her own bed, in the sixty-ninth year of her life, on a night an ox-team lodged in the byre below her window as ox-teams had lodged there every winter of her own keeping and her father's before her, so that the last sound the household afterward remembered her waking to was the same shifting of hooves on straw that she had once told a hundred askers she remembered above every other sound of the brothers' peace. The keeping of the house passed from her to a sister's daughter who had grown up under the same roof and learned the same careful measure of a bench and a loaf that her aunt had never once, in all the years since the brothers' peace, allowed to slip; the ledger her forebear had begun and her aunt had kept without altering so much as its ruling passed with the house, and the niece continued it in a hand the ox-drivers who had known both women said they could not tell from either.

It was this niece who stood at the door of An Sligeanach Fad' às on the eastern road, in LE 1,319, when the crown at last chartered the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit and made their keepers answerable, each for the stretch of road nearest their own hearth, to one another rather than to any single lord. Six other keepers stood there with her that same day, from six other houses of the circuit she had never before had cause to set eyes on, each carrying the same charter in the same crown hand, and it was a strange thing to her, she said afterward, to find that six strangers already knew the shape of her own work as well as she did, down to the particular trouble of a byre in a hard winter and the particular trick of stretching one season's stores through an unlooked-for extra month of snowbound travellers. The seven keepers met there for the first time that same winter to settle their accounts, a meeting the charter itself commanded be held once every year from that one onward, and it was at that first gathering, among keepers who had never before had cause to sit at one table together, that the new keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr was asked, more than once, whether the road-house tale of the two brothers and the two loaves broken and left uneaten was truly as her aunt had always told it.

She answered, each time she was asked, exactly as her aunt had answered every asker before her: the table set, the benches measured to a finger's breadth, the silence, the sound of the oxen in the byre, and the two loaves broken and left, and nothing more, for a thing two brothers had settled between themselves at her aunt's own hearth was not hers to finish telling, whatever the charter now asked of the keepers who had inherited the roads their fathers and mothers had kept before them. One of the six other keepers, an old woman of a road-house on the bare northern stretch who had kept her own house through worse winters than any of the others at that table could match, said only, when the answer was given, that a peace kept quiet by the one who made the table for it was worth more than a peace any keeper cared to dress up for a stranger's asking, and the seven of them, meeting for the first time under a charter none of them had sought, drank to that and to nothing grander before the account-books were opened and the year's long business of the roads began.

# Chapter Thirty-five: Of the Keel-Song

*LE 1,320 – 1,439*

> *Druim fon aisne, aisne fon chlàr,*
> *clàr ri clàr is an cuan fodhpa.*
> Keel under rib, rib under plank,
> plank to plank and the sea beneath them.
>
> — the rope-makers' song of Cuan shean, as Iseabail nic Lachlainn set it down

## I. Of the Law That Lapsed

King Iain Ciar died at Cathair dhearg in LE 1,326, eighty-six years old and the longest-reigning of Raghnall's line since the peace at the road-house had made him king over his brother. He had kept his own grain law by will more than by love; the shire seats had grumbled at the cost of a full year's store set aside against a war that did not come again in his lifetime, and more than one reeve had let the measure slip a bushel or two in a lean season and been made to answer for it before the old king's own steward. Within a few years of his death the law went the way he had foretold in the note his clerk found among his leaves. No one troubled to repeal it; it simply fell away, store by store, seat by seat, until the granaries held what each town's own harvest gave them and no more. Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, who had written Leabhar nam Bràithrean in the old king's praise, had died some years before him, and no one came after to keep the granaries' tale as he had kept the war's.

The road-houses he had chartered stood, though, for a charter is a harder thing to let slip than a habit of storing grain, and the keepers went on meeting once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts and complain, in the words the charter-roll had grown used to, of the price of everything and the honesty of no one. It was at two of those houses, in the years just after the old king's death, that the circuit's record set down the small things that were all it had left to tell.

## II. Of the Houses on the Circuit

An Taigh-seinnse Òir, at the eastern end of the mining road, was written into the charter-roll in LE 1,339 for a dish of beef cooked slow in its own fat and a syrup the house kept secret, served to the custodians' reeves on their winter rounds when nothing else on the road stayed warm past the second hour of riding. The entry that follows it in the roll is a complaint, in a reeve's own hand, that the house had raised the price of the dish three years running without raising anything else about it, and that a man who had eaten it twice a winter for a decade had come, in his own words, to resent it a little more each time even as he asked for a second helping. The keeper's answer, set down beneath the complaint by whichever clerk thought it worth the ink, was that a secret cost what it cost, and that the reeve was welcome to eat elsewhere on the bare northern road if he found one.

He was not, as it happened, for the bare northern road offered him only An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, and it was there, a few winters later, that the charter-roll gained its longer entry. A party of reeves bound for the last shire seat before the pass was caught by a fall of snow that closed the road behind them and did not open it again for the better part of a season. They lived, by their own account written afterward at length and in a hand that grew steadily worse as the winter wore on, on pickled spinach and the keeper's own fire milk, a spirit distilled from whatever grain the house could spare and named, not kindly, for the way it burned going down. The keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Reòta kept them fed and kept her own accounts through it besides, and when the road opened she sent the reeves on their way and sent after them, by the first cart through, a bill for every jar of spinach and every cup of the fire milk, itemised. It was paid in full. The reeves' complaint about the season stands in the charter-roll beside her bill, the two together, and neither party comes off the better in the telling.

## III. Of the Hull That Filled

At Seann Skell, in LE 1,359, a boat-builder named Seumas mac Iain set himself to raise a deep-keeled hull from what the strand still remembered of Comann nan Saor-luinge's craft: the shape of a rib, the run of a plank, a keel laid true along its whole length rather than built up in the short sections the island's boats had used for generations since the last shipwrights of that lore died without apprentices. He had no drawing to work from, only what the old men of the harbour could still tell him and what he could reason out for himself from a wreck's ribs that a storm had once turned up on the strand at Ceann mhòr and that no one had thought, until Seumas came asking, to measure properly before the tide took it back. He worked at her through two winters, in a shed by the harbour that the town let him have rent-free on the strength of his father's name, and the harbour watched him do it the way a harbour watches anything that costs it nothing and might yet come to something.

She went into the water on a morning bright enough that half the town came down to see her float, and floated she did, for the length of time it takes to walk from the shed to the end of the quay and back. Then she took water at a seam along her new keel that no one, not even Seumas, could afterward say they had watched open, and settled by the stern, and went down in water shallow enough that her mast still showed above it an hour after. She went down slowly, by degrees, and the crowd that had come to cheer her stood the whole while and watched the mast go over, which some said afterward was the cruellest part of the whole business.

Manannan's priests at Taigh Mhanannain preached on her for a year after, from the same text each time, that the god had unmade the fleet's craft once with reason and did not mean it remade by a boat-builder's guesswork. Seumas mac Iain did not build again. He kept the shed a few years longer, mending ordinary boats for ordinary fares, and when he died the harbour-court noted only that he had once tried something no one else had tried in living memory and that the town was neither richer nor poorer for it, which was as near as the record ever came to kindness about him.

## IV. Of the Fishers Who Went East, and the Lane to the South

The harbour at Caol ìseal had been silting for longer than any one season could be blamed for it, and by LE 1,369 the fishing families who had worked it for generations gave the last of it up and moved east along the coast to Caol bheag, where the water still ran clean enough to float a boat at any tide. They did not go emptyhanded. They carried their nets, their smoking-racks, and the small shrine at the harbour's edge that had stood as long as the harbour had, stone by stone, and set it up again at Caol bheag exactly as it had stood, so that a stranger coming to the new place might have thought, from the shrine alone, that nothing at all had changed. Caol ìseal itself did not empty. The houses nearest the silted water turned to farming the ground behind them, and within two generations the town that had once smelled of fish and tar smelled, on most days, of turned earth instead.

Further south, the fishers of Caol fhiadhaich had for as long as anyone could remember kept their boats inside the wild strait that gave the town its name, never venturing past its own two capes into open water. In LE 1,389 a handful of the younger men, restless with a strait that gave up less each season than it had the season before, took their boats round the southern capes instead, into water none of their fathers had fished, and found it ran the whole length of the south coast without a harbour worth the name until the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, where they came at last to the landing of Cidhe Beag, below the busy river-town of Baile thais. The dried fish they had carried down that coast for want of anywhere nearer to sell it fetched grain at a price better than their own market had offered in years, and they came home with full holds and a lane behind them that the charter-roll named, plainly enough, for the men who had first sailed it: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich. The older harbours further along that coast, which had never in living memory put a boat past their own headlands, took a season or two to believe the story and then, one after another, began to follow the same lane south.

## V. Of Iseabail nic Lachlainn

Iseabail nic Lachlainn was born into the royal household at Cathair dhearg the winter the reeves lay snowed in on the bare northern road, the daughter of a woman who kept the king's linen and a father no one at court troubled to name. She grew up under the stairs and along the kitchen passages of a house that had more songs in it than most, for every servant who came to the king's hall from every shire brought a handful of her own along with her box and her letter of service, and Iseabail, who was quicker with her ears than with her hands, learned to sit still in a corner of the kitchen and take them all in without being sent off to some more useful work.

By the time she was grown she had a name in the household for knowing more songs than the harpers who were paid to know them, and it was the king's own steward, more from wanting the girl out from under his feet at the linen-presses than from any great faith in the work, who first sent her out on Rathad na Banrighinn with a mule and a letter asking any shire seat's reeve to give her lodging, to see what she could bring back from the towns that no one at court had thought to ask before. She was thirty-four years old the first time she set out, and she did not come back to Cathair dhearg for good until she was past sixty, having in the years between walked or ridden the length of every road on the island that a mule could manage, and a fair number that one could not, taking down in her own hand whatever the island's kitchens and rope-walks and byres still sang while they worked.

## VI. Of the Rope-Walk at Cuan shean

She came to Cuan shean in her middle years, in LE 1,389, for no better reason than that she had heard, from a carter on the road above it, that the rope-makers there sang while they walked their strands, and that she had not yet taken down a rope-maker's song from that stretch of coast. The rope-walk ran the length of a field behind the harbour, half of it given over that year to barley for want of enough hemp to fill it, and the men worked backward along it in a line, twisting the strands as they went, each keeping pace with the man ahead of him by the beat of a song rather than by any word passed between them.

Tormod Ròpaire led them, a big, slow-spoken man who had walked that same field since he was a boy carrying spinning-tops for his father's crew, and it was his voice she heard first from the harbour road, keeping the others in step with the ordinary stuff of a working song: a line about a girl in the next town, a line about the price of hemp, the kind of thing every rope-walk on the island sang and no two walks sang quite alike. It was a cold, bright morning, the tide well out and the mud of the harbour showing its whole grey breadth below the field, and half the walk's length that year stood in barley rather than hemp, so that the men worked backward through green stalks for the first thirty paces and only came onto bare turned earth past the low wall where the true crop began. She stood at the field's edge with her tablets out, taking down what she could of it as she had taken down a hundred like it before, and might have gone on to the next town with nothing more than that, had Tormod not, without any word of warning to the men behind him, struck into a different tune altogether.

The others fell in behind him at once, as a crew that has sung together for years falls into a tune it knows without needing to be told it is coming. Iseabail caught two words of it clear across the field, *druim* and *aisne*, keel and rib, and put her tablet down and went nearer, and stood at the very edge of the walk with the strand-dust settling on her skirts, writing as fast as her hand would go while the men kept time with their feet and never once looked round at her.

When the song ended and the men stopped for their meal, she asked Tormod what it was about. He said it was about rope, the way every song on the walk was about rope, whatever else it seemed to be about. She asked him what the words further on meant, the ones after *druim* and *aisne*, and he looked at the men beside him, and they looked back at him, and none of them could tell her. It was, he said at last, the song his own father had taught him, who had it from his father before him, back further than any of them could put a name to, and none of them had ever thought to ask what the words meant, only to keep the tune and the count right, for a rope walked out of step is a rope with a bad lay in it, and a bad lay is a rope that parts when a hull most needs it not to.

They were, all of that crew, sworn to Òrd Mhanannain, as most of the rope-walks on that coast had been for longer than anyone could say, wearing the god's grey knot at the collar the way every sworn rope-maker did; and when she asked whether the god's own priests might know the words, since the song plainly spoke of a hull's own bones, Tormod said only that the priests knew what Manannan wished them to know, and that a rope-maker's song was not, in his experience, high on that list. He sang it because his father had sung it and his father's father before him, and he saw no reason a man needed to understand a thing in order to keep it. One of the younger men, a stripling not yet trusted with the lead, said he had always supposed the odd words were simply older speech, worn down past hearing by however many hundred years of mouths, the way a stone step wears smooth under feet that never mean to wear it at all; and Tormod told him that might well be so, and that it changed nothing about how the strand was to be walked.

Iseabail stayed at Cuan shean the better part of a month, taking the song down whole across a dozen hearings, matching one man's memory of a line against another's where they differed, until she had as much of it as the rope-walk itself could give her. Two lines she could set beside island words she knew and be certain of: keel under rib, rib under plank, plank to plank and the sea beneath them. The rest ran on in sounds she could shape with her pen well enough but could not turn into sense in any tongue she had ever gathered a song in, on that coast or any other.

## VII. Of the Reading at Court

Two years after, when the whole of that circuit's gathering was written fair, she brought it back to Cathair dhearg and set it before the king's court, in the hall where such things were read when a gatherer came home from a long round of the shires: the harpers first, to hear whether anything she had taken down was worth the setting to their own strings, and after them whoever else at court cared to listen, which on the day she read Òran na Druime was near enough the whole hall, for word of it had gone round in advance and a song no one could explain draws more of a crowd than one everybody already half knows.

She read the ordinary verses first, the girl in the next town and the price of hemp, and got the laugh from the hall that such verses are meant to get. Then she read the rest of it, keel under rib and the words that followed it, in the plain voice she had trained herself to read in, without dressing it up as more than it was.

The hall went quiet in a way it had not gone quiet for the rest of her reading. Even the king's own hounds, that had been shifting and scratching under the benches through the ordinary verses, lay still while she read the rest of it through. An old harper, who had been at court longer than most of the household could remember and had heard every song brought back from every shire in that time, asked her to read the strange lines again, and she did, twice more, and he shook his head each time and said he knew no tongue on the island that fit them, not the plain speech, not the priests' own forms, not the oldest words the harpers kept for the oldest songs. A clerk of Taigh na Fèithe, who was there for some other business and had stayed to listen, said that the shape of the words put him in mind of Leabhar a' Chùraim's oldest entries, the ones copied so many times over that no one now living could say for certain they had ever been read straight through rather than copied blind, letter by letter, by clerks who trusted the hand before theirs to have got it right. He did not say the two things were the same. He said only that neither of them made sense to him, and that this was, in his long experience of old writings, not nothing.

The king himself, who had sat through the reading with the same patience he gave any other business of the hall, asked at the end of it whether the song might be sung as well as read, since a tune sometimes carried a meaning that plain speech let drop. Iseabail said she had no voice for singing it as Tormod Ròpaire and his crew had sung it, walking the strand in step, but she gave the court what she could of the tune all the same, and the hall listened to that too, and was no wiser after it than before.

No one in the hall that day could tell Iseabail what the words of Òran na Druime meant, any more than Tormod Ròpaire and his crew had been able to at their own rope-walk, and she wrote as much into her own account of the reading, plainly, without trying to make more of the not-knowing than the not-knowing was.

## VIII. Of the Schism, the Storm, and the New Harbour

While she was still on the road gathering the last of what would go into that reading, the temple of Òrd na Cloiche at Inis thais split over a question that had lain under its floor for longer than either side liked to admit: whether the dead, who belonged to Donn, might rightly be prayed for by name at Clach, or whether such prayer trespassed on ground that was not Òrd na Cloiche's to offer. Those who said no kept the old temple. Those who said the dead might be named there built a second house at Baile gheal, finished within ten years of the first quarrel, and the two congregations went their own ways from that day, neither troubling the other much and neither, in all the years that followed, giving ground.

A storm the coast called Gailleann Ghlas came in out of the east within a few years and tore the harbour apart at Seann Tarr, leaving the village standing but its quay in pieces past any mending worth the cost. The boats that had worked out of it went to Cuan ruadh instead, which built a second harbour arm within the decade to take them, and throve on the fishing of both towns' waters for the rest of the age, while Seann Tarr kept its houses and its shrine and let its harbour go, and became, in the charter-roll's own dry word for such places, a village again.

Tormod Ròpaire died at Cuan shean within a few years of it, seventy years old, still walking the same field he had walked as a boy, though by his last years he let a younger man keep the count and the lead while he sang along behind. His crew kept Òran na Druime after him as they had kept it before him, word for word as he had given it to them, understanding no more of it than he had, and no less either.

## IX. Of the Queen Small and the Grey Glaze
