Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill was crowned at Cathair dhearg in LE 1,429, twenty-nine years old, the first queen the island had raised in more than three centuries. The record, in the plain way it keeps to for such things, notes that she was small, and that no one at her own court said so twice.

At Muileann gheal, in the last years the record has to tell of this stretch, the potters of one household found a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island could match for its colour or its wear, and the custodian houses bought their table-ware from that one family and no other. The secret of it stayed within Clann Mhic Phàil, mother to daughter, and was not written down, for a thing kept in the hand and the eye, they said, needs no writing to be kept; which was true of it, as it was true of Òran na Druime, until the day it was not.

## X. Of the Song Unexplained

It is remembered of Iseabail nic Lachlainn, in the household she served the rest of her life, that she was asked more than once, in her last years at court, whether she had ever learned what Òran na Druime's strange words meant, and that she answered every time in nearly the same way: that she had asked every scholar the household could bring before her, and every priest of Manannan who would speak with a woman on such a matter at all, and had been told, by all of them together, less than the rope-makers of Cuan shean had told her standing in their own field with the strand-dust on her hem.

She kept the tablets herself until she died, and left them to Taigh na Fèithe with the rest of her collection, where the clerks who took them in wrote, in the plain hand of an inventory and not of a song, that the gathering held one item they could not describe by its meaning, only by its sound and its keeping: a rope-maker's work-song out of Cuan shean, sung by Manannan's own people, who did not know what they sang and sang it anyway, that spoke, as far as anyone could tell, of a keel, and a rib, and a plank, and the sea beneath them, and of nothing that any hall at Cathair dhearg, that day or any day after, could put into plainer words than its own.

# Chapter Thirty-six: Of the Queen Who Went Round

*LE 1,440 – 1,629*

## I. Of the Oath of the Seven

Queen Catrìona Bheag called the heads of Na Seachd Taighean to Cathair dhearg in LE 1,449 to swear again to Riaghailt an Teallaich, as no queen had asked of them since Catrìona Bhuadhach set the ruling down. None of the seven had ever refused it; none of them, either, had been asked to swear it again in three generations, and there is a difference, An Talla Dearg's own clerk noted at the foot of his roll, between a promise a house keeps because it was never tested and a promise a house is called to make a second time before witnesses. Clann Mhuirich swore first, as their custom was from the founding of the seven, and Clann Fhearchair and Clann Ìomhair and Clann Raghnaill and Clann Thormoid after them each in turn, a hand laid flat on Taigh na Fèithe's own hollow stone that a rider had carried down from Muileann dhearg for the day and would carry back again before the moon was out.

Clann Choinnich swore last. The head of that house, an old woman who had held it thirty years and buried two husbands in the holding of it, stood the better part of an hour at the foot of the hall while the other six spoke their oath and sat again, and when her turn came at last she stood a while with her hand still at her side and asked the queen plainly, before the whole hall, whether the swearing changed the measure her house held or only the manner of swearing to it. Catrìona Bheag answered that it changed nothing but the manner, and the old woman said that a manner asked twice in three generations was worth asking after, and swore then, her hand flat on the stone the same as the other six had laid theirs, no louder and no softer. The clerk who kept An Talla Dearg's roll wrote that all seven had sworn and that one had asked a question first, and thought it worth the extra line, though he could not himself have said what he expected any reader after him to make of it.

The stone had come down from Muileann dhearg two days before under a rider's own care, wrapped against the weather in the same hide it had travelled in the last time Mionnan nan Seachd was sworn, and it went back up the same road the morning after, carried by a different rider on a different horse, so that no single house of the seven could ever afterward claim to have held it longer under its own roof than any other house had. The custodians who kept it at Taigh na Fèithe between such swearings let no one handle it but the rider charged with the carrying, and are said to have counted, on its return each time, the small chips at its edge against a tally kept for that purpose alone, a caution against nothing anyone could name and against everything, at once, that fourteen centuries of careful custody had taught Taigh na Fèithe to guard.

At Cathair mhòr that same decade the priests of Macha finished the floor of their great house, black and white stone laid in a pattern none of the masons who set the last of it had themselves begun, for the floor had been eleven years in the laying and every hand that had cut the first courses was long dead or long retired by LE 1,459. It stood, when it was done, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr, and the priests who walked it barefoot on the day of its consecration said afterward that the black and the white ran so true underfoot that a man could close his eyes on it and still tell, by the cold of the stone alone, which colour he stood on.

## II. Of the Stair Found Again, and the Dry Years

Charcoal-burners working the eastern woods in LE 1,469 broke through into a cut stair going down under the hill, the same shape and the same worked stone as the stair the quarrymen of the west had walled up five centuries before and never spoken of again. Word of it reached Taigh na Fèithe within the season, and the custodians who came to look at it did what their fathers' fathers had done at the first one: they had it walled, the new stone set flush with the old rock so that a stranger walking the wood afterward would find nothing but a hillside grown over with bramble. The scribe who kept Leabhar a' Chùraim bound the two entries to one another with a line in the margin of each, the eastern find to the western, though he wrote nothing of what either stair went down to, for nothing had ever been written of the first and no one saw reason to begin with the second.

The shires about Achadh shean had the worse of it in those same years. Three seasons running, from LE 1,479, the rain that the eastern hills had always caught for the wells below them failed to come, and the wells themselves ran low and then dry, one after another, until the reeves of the shire sent word to Cathair dhearg that the shared meal alone would not carry them through a fourth dry summer. The crown carted grain in from the south by the mining road, ox-team after ox-team through a country too parched even for the carts to raise the dust they usually raised, and the shire held, though it held thin. When the rain came back the reeves did not trust it to stay, and in LE 1,489 they set down on a board at the well-head how the deep wells would be shared among the households by lot and by turn, so that no single dry year again could be answered only by whichever family reached the water first. The board was cut new each generation as the old one wore, the names on it changed with the households that held the shares, but the lots themselves were never drawn again; the first sharing held, by habit more than by law, for as long as the shire kept any memory of the dry years at all.

It was at Àth shean, not many years after, that a young clerk newly set over the granary's accounts found, going back through the ledgers for a reason he could no longer afterward name, that the firlot the granary measured its grain by had worn smaller than the standard kept at Cathair dhearg, and had been worn so, by the plainest reckoning he could make of the old entries, for longer than any single reeve's term of office could account for. He carried the matter up rather than let it stand, and in LE 1,499 the reeve had every account the granary held corrected as far back as the ledgers would allow the reckoning to run, a labour of a whole winter's evenings that satisfied no one so much as it satisfied the clerk himself, who is remembered to have kept, for the rest of his own service, a private habit of weighing his own hand's firlot against the standard each Samhnas whether any question had been raised against it or not.

## III. Of the Last of Clann Mhic Phàil

Muileann gheal had been known the length of the eastern road for the grey-green glaze its potters set on the custodian houses' own tables, a colour no other kiln on the island had ever matched and no potter of the town had ever fully explained even to the sons and daughters who grew up firing the same kilns. The secret, so far as it was a secret and not simply a knowledge no one outside one family had troubled to learn, had stayed inside Clann Mhic Phàil for as long as the town's own memory ran, passed from a potter to whichever child of the house showed the surest hand at the wheel and the wet clay, and by the time Iain Mac Phàil came to the kilns as a young man there was no one left in the family but himself to pass it on to and no child of his own yet born to take it.

He tried, in the last years of his life, to set the glaze's making down in some form another hand might follow, and failed at it in a way that seemed to surprise him more than it surprised anyone who watched him try: the mixing he could describe well enough, the grinding of the stone and the ash and the water measured against each dish's own weight of clay, but the firing, the moment at which the kiln's heat had to be let fall rather than pushed higher, was a thing his own hands knew and his own words could not carry over to another man's hands however carefully he chose them. Two apprentices he took in those last years, both quick enough at the wheel, and both came away from their years under him able to throw a passable dish and unable to glaze it grey-green rather than the ordinary brown every other kiln on the island already knew. He died in LE 1,509 with neither apprentice yet trusted to try the firing alone, and for a generation after him the potters of Muileann gheal tried, by every method any of them could reason out or borrow, to find the measure of heat and the moment of its falling that Iain Mac Phàil had carried out of the world with him, and none of them came near it. The custodian houses kept the dishes they already held, and are said to have prized a chipped one, thereafter, above a whole dish of any other glaze the island's kilns could offer.

Baile Mòr ruadh, in the same decade, found a smaller kind of fortune in a cattle fair its own market had held for years without any particular note being taken of it, until drovers from as far as Àth chiar and the eastern hills began, in LE 1,519, to bring their beasts down for it every autumn rather than sell nearer home. It became, within a few more years, the greatest fair in the east, and the town's reeve, who had inherited a market of modest size and modest reputation, is remembered chiefly for having done nothing at all to bring the fair's new fortune about beyond widening the ground it was held on, a plain honesty he himself is said to have insisted on whenever anyone tried to praise him for foresight he had never claimed.

## IV. Of the Queen Who Went Round

Sìleas Òg was crowned at Cathair dhearg in LE 1,529, twenty-four years old and the first of her line in three reigns to come to the throne with both her parents still living to see it, though neither lived to see much of what she made of it. She had grown up, by her own account given years later to a clerk who asked her plainly what had put the notion in her head, hearing the shire seats named at her father's own table as places on a map and nowhere else, a string of names a reeve's report might carry to An Talla Dearg once a year and no oftener, and she had thought, young enough still to say so aloud without anyone troubling to correct her, that a queen who had never set foot in Achadh shean or Baile Mòr ruadh or Doire fhionn knew those places the way a child knows a story told at the hearth: well enough to repeat it, not well enough to have stood in the rain there.

She began her round within two years of her crowning and kept at it, a shire seat or two each season as the roads and the weather allowed, until in LE 1,535 her circuit had carried her, by Taigh na Fèithe's own reckoning of her comings and goings, to every seat the island's shires held, the first ruler of Dia-thìr of whom that could be said. It cost her nothing so grand as the reeves at each seat feared it might when word of the coming visit reached them first: she asked for no feast beyond what the house already kept, sat at the ordinary board rather than any board raised for her, and asked, at every seat alike, the same plain question of whoever the town set before her, what the shire lacked that the crown might supply and what the crown asked of the shire that the shire could not in truth give. She reached the last seat of her round at last, on the bare northern stretch few queens before her had troubled to visit at all, some half-dozen years into her reign, and is remembered to have said, of the whole labour of it, only that she had at last stopped repeating a story and started remembering a place, a distinction she never explained further to the clerk who wrote it down and that he never asked her to.

At Achadh shean, on the leg of her round that carried her furthest east, she stood at the well-head and had the reeve read her the board where the shares were cut, name by name, and asked him why the lots had never been drawn a second time in all the years since the dry seasons. The reeve, an old man who had held the office longer than the queen herself had been alive, answered that no one had ever wanted to be the household that asked for the lots to be drawn again, for the asking would have said, to every other household on the board, that the first sharing had been unfair, and no shire wanted that said of it over a matter of water it had, in the end, survived. Sìleas Òg is remembered to have looked at the board a long while before she answered him, and to have said only that a shire that would rather keep an old unfairness than name it was a shire she understood better for having stood at its well than she ever could have from a reeve's yearly report, and she rode on the next morning without asking the reeve to change anything at all.

It was on the strength of what her round had shown her, more than any single report a reeve had ever carried to An Talla Dearg unasked, that she commanded, once home again, a new count of every household holding the right to the coal. The count came back in LE 1,539 smaller than any before it, the right narrowed by two centuries of house joining to house and holding swallowing holding until fewer families held more of it between them than had ever held any part of it before, and Sìleas Òg, reading the figure Taigh na Fèithe's scribes laid before her, had it entered in Leabhar a' Chùraim without a word of comment either way, a silence the scribes themselves are said to have found harder to read than any word she might have spoken over it.

Ceann mhin burned a second time in LE 1,549, and this time no war stood behind the fire for anyone to blame it on; a spark from an ordinary hearth, in an ordinary wind off the water, was all the town's own reeve could afterward find to set against the loss of half its waterfront a second time in living memory. He gave the order himself, before the ash had cooled, that the town be rebuilt with gable walls of stone standing between each house and its neighbour, so that whatever caught next would have to cross stone rather than thatch to reach the house beside it, and Ceann mhin was rebuilt that way within the decade, the only town on the coast, for a generation after, that a stranger could tell from its own neighbours by the stone standing plain between one roof and the next.

## V. Of the Silver Refused and the Steel Lost

Clann Choinnich brought a petition to the queen's council at Muileann dhearg, drafted by the house's own clerk after three winters of the head's own arguing at her own table that the coal, burning hotter than any charcoal the smiths of the east could otherwise buy, might be spared beyond the measured handful to smelt the silver of the seam at Muileann chiar. It was the first such asking Leabhar a' Chùraim had ever recorded, for the coal until that year had been burned only for worship, the small hearth-measure of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig and no more, and the council that heard the petition in LE 1,559 sat the better part of a day over it before it refused, by what the clerk's own record calls a narrow voice and does not further number. Sìleas Òg, presiding, is said to have given no ruling of her own beyond confirming the council's, and to have told Clann Choinnich's head, privately and afterward, that a law kept since before the fleet sailed for one reason was not easily bent to a second reason however sound the second reason was, a courtesy the old woman is said to have accepted without being in any way persuaded by it.

The clerk who had drafted the petition, a younger kinsman of the house who had spent the better part of a year weighing the coal's heat against the charcoal it would spare and setting the figures down in a hand as careful as any Taigh na Fèithe's own scribes kept, is remembered to have asked, once the council's refusal was final, whether the figures themselves had been wrong. He was told they had not; the council had refused the asking and not the arithmetic, and the distinction, small as it sounds set down plainly, was one the young clerk is said to have carried with him the rest of his working life, keeping thereafter, in every leaf he drew up for his house, a line at the foot of it noting which of his figures the council had never in fact disputed.

The smiths of Dùn dhearg, who had made the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses since the walls of that town first stood, lost in LE 1,569 the last man among them who knew how the fellowship's layered steel was folded, a craft that had passed master to apprentice within four families for longer than the oldest leaves of Leabhar a' Chùraim could account for and that died, when the last of those four families' last trained hand died with no apprentice yet far enough along to have learned the whole of it, as completely and as suddenly as Muileann gheal's glaze had died sixty years before. The blades of Dùn dhearg were ordinary blades after him, well enough made and no better than any other smith's on the island, and the houses that had once prized a Dùn dhearg blade above any other kept the ones they already held the way the custodian tables kept their chipped grey-green dishes, a possession valued now for what it had once been rather than for anything the town's own forge could still produce.

The houses themselves, in LE 1,579, began burying their own heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name still legible on them, a custom the council settled on for reasons Leabhar a' Chùraim gives only as fitting the dignity of the houses and no further. The tenants of the land about Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, who had buried their own dead where their own families had always buried them, called the new custom unwise to bury the great among graves no one living could any longer read the names of, and went on burying their own kin where they always had, a small disagreement between the houses and the land they held that neither side pressed the other to settle.

Of Sìleas Òg's own last years less is told than of her round or her count, and Clàr nan Rìghrean passes from her long reign to that of a kinsman of her own house, Ailean mac Raghnaill, with no note of grief or of gladness set between the one reign and the next, the plainest kind of ending An Talla Dearg's own clerks ever gave a ruler who had done as much as she had to be known by name in every shire seat on the island.

## VI. Of the Short King and the Shut Sea

Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth king of that name, was crowned at Cathair dhearg in LE 1,589 at nine and thirty years old, and is remembered in Clàr nan Rìghrean for nothing else at all, for within the year he was dead at forty, the shortest reign the list had ever set down. What ailed him Leabhar a' Chùraim does not say, only that his sister Mòrag nic Raghnaill, four and thirty years old herself, was crowned in his place before the same season had turned, and that she went on to reign some forty years more, Clàr nan Rìghrean's longest run of entries recording, in all that time, nothing graver than good harvests and the keeping of the rite. A clerk who served her the whole of those forty years is said to have remarked, near the end of his own service, that he had written more entries under her reign than under any three reigns before it and had, in all of them, set down no death by war, no famine and no quarrel between Na Seachd Taighean worth the ink to record it, a run of quiet years An Talla Dearg's own roll had not seen the like of since before the sundering fleet had ever gone down the river. Mòrag nic Raghnaill herself is remembered to have kept, of her brother's short reign, one habit only: she had the year of his crowning and the year of his death cut on the same stone rather than on two, a small economy of grief that her own clerks never asked her to explain and that stood, long after her own reign had ended, as the plainest record Clàr nan Rìghrean gave of the brother she had outlived by forty years.

It was in the first year of her reign, LE 1,590, that the priests of Manannan gathered in synod at Seann Skell and restated, before the assembled orders of their own house, the rule of sight-of-land that Manannan's priests at Ros bheag had first laid down nine centuries before: that no boat of the faithful was to go beyond sight of the headlands, on Manannan's own word that the mist behind the fleet was shut once and would not be opened a second time for any pilot bold enough or foolish enough to look for it. To the old rule the synod added a new prayer, to be said by the priests at the foot of the river pool where the fleet had once turned sunwise and gone, words the synod itself is said to have argued over through two full days before agreeing on the shortest form of them: *A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.* Manannan, keep the sea shut.

Further down the eastern road, in years quieter than any the priests' synod troubled itself with, a ferry family settled at Cidhe Beag on the Abhainn uaine in LE 1,619 and took up the crossing there by canoe, carrying folk and their goods across water that no bridge had ever been thrown over and none, in that stretch of the river, was ever likely to be; they held the landing, father to daughter and daughter to son, for the rest of the age, and travellers on that road came to speak of the crossing the way they spoke of any other fixed thing on the road, a ford, a road-house, a ferry that had simply always been there. And on the slopes above Àth shean, growers who had pressed blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine for their own tables since no one could say when began, in LE 1,626, to sell the pressing along the eastern road in casks that kept a full year without souring, and the road-houses of that stretch took to serving it as black wine to travellers who had never before had anything darker than ale set before them at a road-house table, a small trade that outlasted, as small trades sometimes do, a good deal that the age's own reeves and councils had thought far more likely to last.

The priests of Manannan said their new prayer at the foot of the river pool that same year and every year after, at every tide the rite required of them, long after the ferry at Cidhe Beag and the black wine of Àth shean had settled into the ordinary business of the roads and no longer seemed, to anyone who used them, like anything new at all: keep the sea shut, said at the water's edge where the fleet had gone, the one part of that whole age's business with the sea that the island's own priests were still, after so many centuries, careful to say aloud.

# Chapter Thirty-seven: Of the Loft over the Mill

*LE 1,630 – 1,749*

## I. Of the Barge Kept on the Strand

By the seventeenth century of the count the island had grown better roads than it had ever had reason to build ships, and the coasting trade that had once gone by water from Ros chiar to Caol mhin, the cold way along the north coast, went by cart instead, year on year, until the last barge that had worked that water was laid up for good at Inis mhòr in LE 1,634. The men of Inis mhòr did not break her up for her timbers, as they would have done with any hull too old to caulk. They hauled her above the tide-line, chocked her level, and left her there, and told their children she was the last of the boats that had gone the cold way, though none of the children, and precious few of the fathers, could have said any longer what the cold way had been the cold way from, or to.

It was the temper of those years, on the whole island and not only at Inis mhòr: to keep the last of a thing on a strand or a shelf once there was no more need to use it, rather than let it go the way of the thing before it, which no one had troubled to keep at all. Fifteen years on an earthquake shook Dùn ìseal and cracked the wall of the spirit-house there, and the keepers took the crack for a warning and set a lamp before it, and could not agree among themselves, that year or any year after, of what the warning had been. A shudder of ground that had done no man any harm was made, by the very fact of nobody being harmed, into a thing that had to mean something; it is the way of an age that keeps more than it uses and asks more of what it keeps than the keeping can answer.

## II. Of the Widow of Muileann chaol

At Muileann chaol, on the millrace above the ford, Beathag nic Thòmais had kept the mill alone since her husband Artair mac Dhòmhnaill died of a fever four years into their marriage, leaving her a widow at thirty with the wheel, the stones, and the ledger of who owed the mill grain and who the mill owed nothing. She kept it well, better by most accounts than Artair himself had kept it, for she had the kind of head for a ledger that does not let a debt run past the season it was struck in, and the millers up and down the ford came to her before they came to their own kin when an account needed settling without ill will on either side.

It was not the ledger that filled her loft, in the years after. She had grown, somewhere in the quiet of a house with no children in it, a taste for old writings that had nothing to do with the mill's business at all: a taste her neighbours found harmless enough, if a little strange in a woman with a trade to mind, and one that cost her, at the start, no more than the odd measure of meal for a board of accounts some dead reeve's grandson was glad to be rid of. She began, in LE 1,659, to ask about the ford and the market at Muileann chaol, and then further, by rider and by the carters who came through with grain, whether any house that no longer troubled to read them had an old copy of Leabhar a' Chùraim lying in a chest, or a page or two of Rolla a' Chalaidh of Seann Skell that some great-grandfather had kept for reasons nobody living now remembered. Houses that had such things, more often than not, were glad enough to sell them. A page nobody reads is worth less to the house that holds it than the meal a miller's widow will give for it, and Beathag paid a fair measure and never once haggled a seller down, which is why, within a few years, word of what she wanted travelled further than her own riders ever went.

She stacked what she bought in the loft over the mill, above the grain floor, where the heat of the stones kept the damp off better than any chest at ground level could. Her neighbours called it, at first, the widow's rubbish, and said so to her face more than once, in the way a small town says a true unkindness and calls it a joke so that no one need answer for it. Beathag answered nothing to it either way. She went on buying, and stacking, and in a year or two the loft held more pages of the island's own past than any single chest in any single hall from Cathair dhearg to Seann Skell, though not a soul beyond her own ford knew it yet.

A carter out of Cathair mhòr brought her, one wet Faolach, a board no bigger than a serving-tray, black with age at the edges, that a house on the Cathair mhòr road had been using to weight down a cheese-press for as long as any living man there could remember. He had noticed, only because the light happened to fall across it while he waited for his own cheese to be wrapped, that the underside of the board carried a hand of writing, and had thought of the widow at Muileann chaol who paid a fair measure of meal for such things and asked no questions past the price. Beathag scraped the mould from the board's grain with the flat of a bone comb before she would let herself read it, and found a tally, three generations old, of what one house's coal-right had paid out at four winter burnings running, and nothing in it that mattered to anyone alive. She paid the carter his meal all the same, set the board on the shelf with the others, and told him, when he asked why she troubled over so small a thing, that a board a house had forgotten it owned was worth exactly as much to her as one it still prized, since neither house could tell her, any longer, which of its old writings would matter and which would not, and she had long since stopped trying to guess in their place.

It became, in that way, less a taste than a trade of its own, though she never asked a price of anyone for what she kept and would not, when asked, put a name to what she was doing beyond "keeping what's going begging." A vein-house clerk riding through on the crown's business, hearing of the loft from an innkeeper who thought it a curiosity worth a traveller's amusement, climbed the mill stair one afternoon out of nothing better than idleness, and came down some three hours later a good deal less idle than he had gone up, having found among her boards a copy of a custodians' ruling his own office at Muileann dhearg had lost the only other copy of in a fire two generations back. He asked her, before he rode on, whether she meant the loft for the crown's use, or Taigh na Fèithe's, or her own. Beathag said she had not decided, and did not think it was hers to decide alone in any case, and the clerk, who had ridden in expecting a curiosity and was riding out with a ruling his own custodians badly wanted back, allowed that this was, on the whole, a wiser answer than most he had been given that year.

## III. Of the Rag Paper

A neighbour of hers at the same ford, a woman a full twenty years her junior named Anna nic Coinnich, had a trade Beathag's own custom had unwittingly fed: Anna's father had kept a fulling-mill on the same race, beating cloth clean of its grease in wooden troughs, and Anna, who had grown up among the rags that trade threw off and never burned, for a good rag burns badly and smells worse, took to soaking the worst of them down to a pulp and pressing the pulp thin and letting it dry, the way her father's cloth dried on the tenter-frames, until in LE 1,674 she had a sheet that would take ink from a reed pen without tearing and without drinking the ink into a blot the way old skin sometimes did in a damp season. It was the first such sheet made on Dia-thìr, though Anna herself, standing over her troughs with her sleeves wet to the elbow, would have said only that it was a way of not wasting a rag, and thought no further of it than that.

Beathag was the first customer she had for it who wanted more than a single sheet to try. She had watched Anna work the pulp for a season before she ever asked to buy any of it, standing at the trough's edge with her sleeves pinned back the same as Anna's own, asking why this batch pressed thinner than that one and whether a rag of wool behaved as a rag of linen did, until Anna, more amused than put out by a widow twenty years her elder learning her trade at her elbow, told her plainly that she might as well take a hand at the frame herself if she meant to stand there asking questions a whole afternoon. Beathag did, and pressed a sheet with her own hands that came out uneven at one corner and perfectly good at the other three, and kept that first sheet of her own pressing, uneven corner and all, on a shelf of the loft apart from the rest for as long as she lived, though she never said, even to Anna, quite why.

Leabhar a' Chùraim of Taigh na Fèithe, which had been kept on hide since Fionnlagh Dall's own day and passed hand to hand at every winter burning until its oldest leaves were soft as cloth themselves, was copied that same generation onto Anna's paper for the first time, a leaf a week through one whole winter, by a clerk of Taigh na Fèithe who complained, at first, that the new stuff took the ink strangely and gave it up, by spring, that it took the ink better than hide ever had once a hand grew used to it. It was Beathag who carried the proposal to Taigh na Fèithe in the first place, riding the sixty miles herself rather than trusting it to a rider, for she judged, rightly as it turned out, that a custodian would sooner hear a strange notion from a widow with a mill's ledger behind her name than from anyone he could take for a huckster with a rag-heap to sell. The custodian who heard her out asked only whether the new stuff would hold the ink another sixteen centuries as the hide had; Beathag said she could not promise him that, since no one had yet had sixteen centuries to try it in, and the custodian, who had spent a long career answering harder questions with less certain answers than that, said it would do, and let the copying go ahead. Beathag bought reams of it herself for her own copying after, and it is from that winter that the loft's papers begin to run, in among the older hides and boards, on the paper of the same ford that made them.

## IV. Of the Three Copies

Among the things that came to her loft, in the ordinary way of a house up the coast selling off what a dead grandfather had kept, was a leaf that gave the tidings of the fleet as they had first reached Seann Skell, sixteen centuries before: two coasts found, not one, and the fleet parted between them on the far side of the sea. Beathag read it once and thought little of it, for every child on the island had heard as much at a hearth in one telling or another. It was only when a second copy came to her, some years later, from a different house entirely, that she noticed the two did not agree: one gave the northern coast first and the southern second, and the other gave it the other way about, and where one said nineteen hulls reached a shore the other said one-and-twenty.

She went looking, after that, the way she had never gone looking for anything else in the loft, and within two more years had a third copy, from a house at Cathair dhearg that had kept it folded inside the cover of an older book entirely, as though whoever put it there had wanted it kept and not read. The third agreed with neither of the first two, not in the order of the coasts nor in the count of the hulls, and in LE 1,679 Beathag laid all three out on the boards of the loft floor, side by side in the low afternoon light that came through the one window, and read them through again from the beginning, each in turn, looking for the seam where one could be shown to be the copy and the others the truth it had been copied wrong from.

There was no such seam to find. Each of the three was written in a hand that meant to be believed, none troubled to say where its own figures had come from, and all three, read close, agreed on the one thing that mattered most, that two coasts had been found and the fleet parted upon them, and disagreed on everything a court might have wanted settled beyond it. Anna, who had come up the mill stair with a fresh ream under her arm and found Beathag still on her knees over the three leaves at dusk with a cold supper untouched at her elbow, asked her outright which of the three she believed. Beathag said she believed all three of them, in the sense that she thought none of the three writers had set down a single figure he did not himself hold to be true; and she believed none of the three, in the sense that three men equally certain and equally honest had between them given the island three different pasts, and a woman with no better claim on the truth than any of the three dead hands that had written it down had no business choosing one of their certainties over the other two merely for the comfort of having chosen.

Beathag wrote out a fair copy of each, in her own hand, on Anna's paper, laid the three fair copies together in the loft where the originals had lain, and chose none of them. It was not laziness in her, nor a want of nerve; she had settled harder questions than this one for lesser men over her own mill's ledger without blinking, and more than one debtor at the ford had learned that a mild manner in a widow was no sign at all of a soft one underneath it. She judged, and said as much to the one or two who ever asked her outright, that a woman who had not been on the quay that grey morning had no business making three uncertain tellings into one false certainty merely because a false certainty reads easier than three that will not agree. A niece of hers, hearing the tale told at the fireside years after, asked why she had not simply burned the two that were wrong and kept the one that was right, since three could not all be true together. Beathag, by then an old woman, said that this was precisely the question the whole loft existed to refuse an answer to, and that the girl would understand it better the day she found she could not tell, of two things equally well attested and wholly at odds, which one to burn.

## V. Of the North-West Counted

The crown, in the same years, sent a reeve down the empty roads of the north-west to list what households still stood between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr, for the tallies that fed the winter burning had not been walked that coast in a long while and Taigh na Fèithe wanted a true count before another season's measure was cut. He rode it alone, with a boy to lead the pack-horse and carry the tally-sticks, and found, at more than one landing along that coast, a row of berths cut square into the old harbour stone with no boat standing in any of them and no house behind them with a fire lit, the roof gone in on some and the door simply left standing open on others, as though whoever had gone out last had not troubled to shut it behind them and no one since had troubled to notice it stood open. He counted the berths at each landing before he counted the households, from a habit of a careful man doing the easier reckoning first, and by the time he came to the households themselves he already half knew, from the berths alone, what shape his answer would take.

The reeve came back, in LE 1,694, with a figure smaller than the one the old rolls gave him to expect, and smaller by more than the ordinary slow drift of the years could account for: fewer households, by his own careful count, than there were berths cut into the old harbour stone at any one of the three towns he walked through. He wrote his figure into the crown's own book, in the plain hand a reeve is taught to keep for such things, and rode home, and no one at Cathair dhearg asked him to walk the coast a second time to be sure of it, for a second count, by then, was a thing the island had learned long since not to want too badly. The boy who had led his pack-horse, grown to a man himself, told it afterward that his master had said only one thing to him the whole ride back that was not business: that a berth cut in stone outlasts the hand that cut it and the household it was cut for both, and that a coast can go on looking, from the sea, exactly as it always looked, for a long while after there is no one left on it to look back.

## VI. Of the Loft Left to the Town

Beathag died at Muileann chaol in LE 1,699, seventy-four years old, in the same room above the mill she had slept in since her wedding night, with Anna nic Coinnich, by then a woman of middle years herself, sitting by her through the last of it. In her last days she asked twice to be carried up the mill stair to see the loft once more, and was twice refused by Anna, who told her plainly that a woman of seventy-four with a fever on her had no business on a ladder-steep stair for the sake of looking at boards she had looked at every week for forty years and knew, by then, better than she knew her own hands. Beathag did not ask a third time. She asked instead that the shelf holding her own first, uneven sheet of Anna's paper be brought down to her, and held it a while, and gave it back, and said nothing more about the loft until the day she died.

She left the mill to a nephew who had no interest in old paper and a great deal in grain, and the loft, with everything in it, to the town, on the one condition that nothing kept there should ever be burned, for whatever reason and by whatever hand. The nephew, reading the will aloud to the assembled kin the day after her burying, stumbled over that one clause twice, as a man will stumble over words he privately thinks foolish and would rather not be the one caught reading aloud, and more than one of the kin present said afterward that they had marked the stumble and thought the less of him for it, though none said so to his face while there was grain business still to be settled between them.

The town of Muileann chaol kept that condition, and did rather less well by the rest of her wishes, which had run, in the fuller will her nephew read out and then quietly set aside, to a hope that some clerk might be found each generation to keep the loft in order and add to it what the age still produced. No such clerk was ever paid to do it. The loft stood, its door latched but never locked, and townsfolk who had a paper they no longer wanted burned took to bringing it up the mill stair rather than to the hearth, more from habit than from any oath sworn over Beathag's grave, until the habit itself became the nearest thing the town had to a keeper. A reeve of a later generation, passing through on the crown's business and finding the loft kept by no one office and no one name, asked the miller who had it in charge by then what right the town had to hold papers that plainly belonged, by their matter, to Taigh na Fèithe or the crown or both. The miller, who was Beathag's own great-nephew and had never in his life climbed the stair for any purpose but to fetch down a paper some other traveller had come asking after, said only that the town had held them fifty years without Taigh na Fèithe or the crown ever once asking for them back, and that he took a fifty years' silence, in such a matter, for an answer of a kind.

## VII. Of the Roads, the Beasts, and the Empty Harbour Kept Thin

The crown that Beathag never once wrote of, though she must have heard its business talked over at every ford she rode, passed in these same years by a road of its own that the loft's papers do not trouble to follow closely. Tormod mac Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill was crowned at Cathair dhearg in LE 1,709, nine-and-twenty years old, and held the throne longer than any king before him in Leabhar a' Chùraim's own count, though the record keeps of that long reign chiefly its roads and little else. Within a few years the priests of Manannan at Seann Skell, who had restated their rule of sight-of-land at their last synod, took to saying their own prayer for the shut sea on the very day of Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh, so that the two were kept together on Seann Skell's old quay ever after; and neither the empty-harbour keepers nor Manannan's own priests were pleased to find the other's rite standing on the stones beside theirs, though neither would give an inch of the day to the other either.

Tormod spent the better part of two decades building stone bridges over the fords his own riders had once had to swim their horses through in spate, one of them at Cnoc ìseal, and gave land in amends to the ferry-keepers whose living the bridges took from them, which the ferry-keepers, on the whole, judged fair dealing and said so. One ferryman of that ford, offered his choice of two parcels in amends, is said to have asked the king's own reeve which of the two had the better crossing to it, meaning the crossing of a road and not of water, and been told, with no more of a smile than the question deserved, that a man who had spent thirty years reading a river's moods might do worse than spend his last years reading a market's instead; he took the parcel nearer the market and did well enough by it that his sons never went back to the water at all.

A few years into his bridges the panthers of the southern roads crossed in numbers beyond any herder's memory, and for a whole season the days of the panthers' crossing ran into one another without a clear morning between them, so that flocks from Muileann dhomhain's hills to the coast were kept folded far longer than any shepherd liked and lambed thin that year for it. Old men of that country, telling it after, said they had never known the beasts run so many nor so long, and disagreed among themselves, as old men telling such a thing will, on whether it was the worst crossing within memory or only the worst any of them happened to have lived through, which is not, they allowed on being pressed, quite the same claim.

The salt pans of Caol gharbh failed within the same reign, the sea having risen over them by degrees no one pan-keeper's lifetime was long enough to notice until it was done, and the trade that had once fed the north-east from that coast went south instead, to a town that grew fat on it while Caol gharbh itself grew, as the record's own dry word has it, poorer than the coast it had once undersold ever was. A south-westerly storm, not many years after, put the low town of Baile ghorm under water to more than a man's height and drowned three-and-twenty of its people before the water turned, and the town that survived it raised its own sea-wall the height of a man higher than before, and has not since let the sea in a second time.

It is told, of Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh in those same years, that fewer families kept it each turn than had kept it the turn before, until at the last only the harbour priests of Cidhe an Diosail and a handful of the oldest houses of Seann Skell still stood on the stones for it at all. A scribe out of Cathair dhearg, sent down the coast on some other errand of the crown's and told by his own masters to note the rite while he was there for the crown's own book, stood among that handful one grey Là an Diosail near the reign's end and asked, first one old woman and then another, on what day, in the true telling, the fleet had gone down the river all those centuries before. Each gave him an answer, and no two of the answers he was given agreed, any more than the three copies that had once lain on Beathag nic Thòmais's loft floor had agreed with one another; and he wrote as much into the crown's own book, in a hand that meant to be believed as much as any of the three had, and could no more say which of his own answers was the true one than Beathag, fifty years dead by then, had ever been able to say of hers.

# Chapter Thirty-eight: Of the Queen's Progress

*LE 1,750 – 1,799*

## I. Of the Sea-Wall of Cuan dhearg

At Cuan dhearg the sea had come twice now over the same low street, and the second time, 23 an Giblean, LE 1,754, it had put the water to the thresholds of An Gàire Dubh and left a rime of salt on the door-boards that no scrubbing got out before the next tide freshened it again. The first flood the town had answered by moving the street back a length of two houses and calling the matter closed; the second it answered otherwise. The harbour was a small one, fifty households at the most generous count, drying nets and curing fish and sending a little salt fish inland by cart, and a town that size does not build in stone for the pleasure of it. But the elders who had watched two floods in one lifetime, when their own fathers had watched none, judged that the sea was not moving the street back a second time, and set the whole harbour, from the oldest hand to the youngest able to carry a basket, to hauling stone up from the point for a wall.

Gormshuil nic Thormoid, then nine-and-thirty years old and no more than her father's daughter in the eyes of most who did not sit at his board, rode down to see it in its second summer of building, for her father the king no longer rode so far and had asked her to carry his eye where his own legs would not take him. The wall rose in courses no higher than a man's shoulder that summer, dressed stone laid dry at the base and mortared above, and the whole harbour worked it in shifts between the tides, so that the masons and the net-menders and the children set to carrying water for the mortar all learned, before the season was out, exactly how many hours the ebb gave them and no more. She stood on the half-built wall with the harbour-master, a woman with salt worked so deep into the creases of her hands that no washing showed them clean, and asked her plainly whether the wall would hold the third flood if a third flood came. The harbour-master said that no one living could promise her that, since the sea had never troubled to explain either of the first two floods to anyone. A wall a man could stand behind was worth more than a street he could only run from, she said, and the harbour meant to stand behind this one. She added, when Gormshuil pressed her further, that the town had buried the old boundary stones of the moved street rather than break them up, on the chance that some later hand might want to know how far the water had once come; Gormshuil thought this a harbour-master's own kind of custody-book, kept in stone instead of hide, and said so. The harbour-master allowed that she had never thought of it in those words, but did not deny them either. Gormshuil found she had no better answer to bring her father than the wall's own building, and rode home and gave him the whole of it, word for word, and the king, who by then answered most things that reached him more slowly than the shires liked, laughed once, short and dry, and said that it was the soundest counsel to come up from the coast in a year.

## II. Of the House Reopened at Dùn thais

Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais had stood shut behind its own wall for the better part of a generation, since the last argument to be heard in it had turned, as such arguments in that house always turned in the end, toward the question Clàr nam Bliadhnachan had first set and no one since had been let ask again in the open: why the heads of Na Seachd Taighean lived out their years a little longer than the tenants who worked their coal-right for them. It was reopened, 20 an Giblean, LE 1,759, on the one condition that had closed it, restated and accepted afresh: the question of longer lives would not be raised inside its walls, this time or any time after. The druids of the schools who had petitioned longest for the doors to be unbarred agreed to the condition without a murmur that reached the crown's own ears, and once inside took up instead the argument of the vein, whether Leabhar a' Chùraim's measure of the handful answered rightly to what the coal gave out, a question with edges sharp enough to fill a house of disputation for as long as anyone cared to keep arguing it and answer nothing that touched the older, forbidden one.

Gormshuil, riding to Dùn thais for the reopening at her father's side, asked the eldest of the schools' druids, an old man leaning on a stick cut from the school's own holy wood, whether he thought the coal question would satisfy the house as long as the other one had. He said that a house built to argue will always find something to argue, and that the schools had never once, in all the generations the record kept of them, run short of a subject; it was answers, not subjects, that a house of disputation was built to go without. Gormshuil thought this a strange thing to hear said with such evident contentment, and said so. The old druid told her that a woman who had not yet sat a lifetime in an argument that could not be closed had no cause yet to find it strange, and that she might ask him again when she had.

## III. Of the Death of the King

Tormod mac Ruairidh had held An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg for more than fifty years by the time his own legs failed him past riding even the short road to Taigh na Fèithe, and in the last of those years he governed from a chair set by the hearth, hearing what the shires sent up and answering it in a voice that had grown no less certain for growing quieter. He died 9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766, six-and-eighty years old, the longest-lived king Leabhar a' Chùraim had entered since Clàr nam Bliadhnachan first began to measure such things and find them wanting less than they once had. Gormshuil sat with him the last night, in a room kept warmer than the rest of the hall by a fire built up past what the season strictly wanted, and he spoke to her in the broken way of a man saving his strength between sentences rather than spending it on any one of them whole. He told her, near the end and with no great weight laid on the words, that he had built bridges over every ford he had ever had reason to be afraid of and had never once, in fifty years, found the courage to ask Taigh na Fèithe's own custodians a question Taigh na Deasbaid was forbidden to ask on his behalf. She asked him what the question was. He said that she would find it herself soon enough, being his daughter, and that finding it was the easier half of the trouble in any case; the harder half, he said, closing his eyes on it, was living long enough afterward to be satisfied with whatever answer she was given, and that he did not know, of the whole fifty years behind him, a single custodian who had managed that.

She was crowned in An Talla Dearg a fortnight after, one-and-fifty years old herself. The custodians of Na Seachd Taighean stood for her in the order Clachan a' Chrannchuir had long since fixed for such standings, and the priest of Macha who made the crowning said the same words over her that had been said over her father and his mother before him, word for word as Leabhar a' Chùraim kept them, so that no one in the hall that day could have named the year the words were first spoken without going to Leabhar a' Chùraim to be sure of it.

## IV. Of the Progress and the Book of Grievances

Where her father had governed from a chair by his own hearth, Gormshuil began, the year after her crowning, 12 an Giblean, LE 1,771, to do what no ruler of the island had done since Sìleas Òg's own round two centuries and more before her: she rode out from Cathair dhearg to every shire seat in turn, and kept riding it, season on season, until the shires came to expect her the way they expected the winter burning, a thing that returned. At each seat her clerks opened Leabhar nan Gearan and wrote down, in the shire's own words as near as a clerk's hand could catch them, whatever grievance the seat's own reeve or a plain householder chose to bring before the queen in person: a boundary stone moved in the night, a firlot short-measured, a bridge toll raised past its charter, a coal-right disputed between two houses of the same blood. Gormshuil heard every one of them out, asked her own questions where a question seemed wanted, and answered none of them in writing before she rode on to the next seat.

A householder of Baile chrom, at one of the earliest seats of that first round, brought before the queen a boundary stone she said her neighbour had shifted a full arm's length into her own barley in the dark of the same Samhnas night three years running, always shifted back before any reeve could be fetched to see it moved. The neighbour, standing his own ground not ten feet off, said the stone had never once moved under his own hand and that a woman who watched her boundary by moonlight three Samhnas nights running had more reason to doubt her own eyes than his honesty. Gormshuil's clerk set both accounts down as each had given them, word for word, and Gormshuil herself measured the disputed ground with her own stride before she rode on, and told the two of them plainly that she came to write the ground down, not to judge it, so that the next time either side troubled to look, the writing would at least know exactly how far an arm's length of barley actually ran.

It became, over the years of her riding, the one thing every shire agreed to say of her, whether they judged it praise or plain complaint: that the queen wrote everything down and settled nothing on the page. A reeve of one of the smaller seats, more plain-spoken than most, asked her outright, the third or fourth year of her round, what the writing was for if no answer ever followed it. Gormshuil told him that a grievance written down in the shire's own words was at least a true grievance, and that an answer written down too quickly, before the queen had ridden the whole round and heard how the same trouble sounded in six other shires' mouths, was more often a false ease than a true one. The reeve said that this might satisfy a queen who meant to ride the round again next year, and asked, not quite as a question, whether she did. Gormshuil said that she did, and rode on, and kept riding it for as long as her own legs would carry her, which turned out to be longer than most at that first seat had wagered.

Fifteen years into the round, in a summer when her company had grown large enough that a single road-house strained to feed it, she came to An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the eastern road, and its keeper, a woman named Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, 25 am Màrt, LE 1,786, set pan-fried spinach and black wine before the queen's whole train and fed every rider and every horse-boy besides, though her own charter allowed her stores for nothing near so great a company. Gormshuil, hearing after the meal what it had cost the house to feed her round unwarned, forgave Peigi her road dues for the year that followed, and told her, when Peigi tried to protest that she had asked for no such thing, that a house which fed the crown's whole progress without being asked to had earned more than a year's dues forgiven and would have to be content with what the crown could actually give her. Peigi's black wine was spoken of at every road-house between there and Cathair dhearg for longer than the dues she was spared, though Leabhar a' Chùraim, being a custody-book, kept the dues and let the wine go untold beyond that.

## V. Of the Silver Petition Refused

Clann Choinnich had asked once before, in the reign of a queen long before her, for leave to burn the coal beyond the handful's own measure to feed the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, and had been refused by custodians who judged the vein's own long custom worth more than one house's silver. They asked a second time in Gormshuil's reign, 5 an Gearran, LE 1,776, and this time three of Na Seachd Taighean stood behind them at Taigh na Fèithe board, more than had ever stood behind the asking before, so that the matter came, for the first time in Leabhar a' Chùraim's memory of it, within a single voice of passing.

The voice that held it back was Aonghas mac Lachlainn's, of Clann Lachlainn, who had ridden to Taigh na Fèithe that season, by every account that reached Gormshuil afterward, meaning to vote with the three houses and not against them. He changed his vote at the board itself, between the asking read aloud and the custodians' hands raised to answer it, and gave no reason for the changing beyond the bare word that he had changed his mind. Leabhar a' Chùraim's clerk wrote his name down as the voice that refused the petition, plainly, as the book required; he did not write, because Aonghas would not tell him, what had turned the vote in the short space between the reading and the raising of the hands.

Gormshuil, who sat the board that day as she sat every board Taigh na Fèithe held, asked Aonghas afterward, in a quieter corner of the hall than the board itself, whether he meant to say why he had turned. He told her, with a courtesy that gave nothing away under it, that a man's reason for a single hand raised at a single board was his own to keep, the same as any other man's, and that a queen who pressed every custodian for the private reason behind every private vote would find herself, before long, with a board full of men who voted as she wished rather than as they judged, which he did not think she wanted of him any more than he wanted it of himself. Gormshuil found she could not fault the answer, though it left her no wiser than she had been before the asking, and she let the matter lie, as Leabhar a' Chùraim let it lie, with his name written and his reason not.

## VI. Of the Last Count of Hands

Taigh na Fèithe counted, 27 an Gearran, LE 1,791, the households across the whole island that still held the right to the coal, as it had counted them at long intervals since the first count made before the fleet sailed, and it was the last such count the age would keep. The tally came in fewer than any count before it, households having failed into other households or into no households at all across the generations since the last reckoning, and yet larger than any count before it too, for the households that remained held, between them, a greater weight of the coal-right than households of that number had ever held; Leabhar a' Chùraim's own clerk noted, in the dry hand the book had kept since Donnchadh's day, that three of Na Seachd Taighean now held more than half the whole right among themselves.

One house of the four smaller ones, hearing its own share of the right read out lower than it had stood at the count before, asked whether a house that held too little coal-right to keep its own hearth measure through a hard winter might be granted its neighbour's unused share rather than buy it, as Leabhar a' Chùraim allowed in years Taigh na Fèithe judged hard enough to warrant it. The custodians debated the asking a full afternoon and granted it in the end, though more than one voice at the board noted, in words the clerk set down as spoken and not softened, that a house asking such a grant twice running was a house whose trouble Taigh na Fèithe could ease once but not mend for good.

Gormshuil read the count at Taigh na Fèithe board with the custodians ranged along it as they had been ranged for Athchuingean an Airgid, and asked the clerk who had cast it up whether the coal had grown scarcer to account for so much of it falling into so few hands. The clerk said that the vein gave out what it had always given out, no more scarce and no less, and that it was the households, not the coal, that had grown fewer; three houses holding half the right meant only that the other four had, between them, less than half a right to hold, which was a different kind of scarcity than the coal's own, and one Taigh na Fèithe's count could show her plainly enough without being able to say what ought to be done about it. Gormshuil thanked him for the plainness and let the count stand in the book as it was cast, unaltered and unanswered, the way her own progress left every shire's grievance.

## VII. Of the Timber Out of the Mist

In the last years of her reign the fishers of Ceann mhòr, working the empty water off their own headland where Faire a' Chinn had lapsed seventeen centuries before, found a worked timber cast up on the strand, 22 an Cèitean, LE 1,794, longer by half again than any tree that had ever grown on the island and fastened along its length with nails of a make no smith on Dia-thìr had ever forged or seen forged. The fishers who found it stood over it a long while before any of them would put a hand to it, and it was the eldest among them, a woman who had fished that water sixty years, who said at last that a thing so plainly worked by hands could not have grown in the sea any more than a boat could, and that hands which forged nails unlike any island nail had not, in all likelihood, forged them on the island.

They carried it, by cart and then by boat the last stretch of the way, to Seann Skell and laid it before Manannan's priests on the same quay where Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh was kept each year, for if any order on the island could say what a worked thing out of the eastern mist might be, the priests who prayed the sea shut at every tide were judged the likeliest to know. The priests looked at it a long while too, turned it over, ran their hands along the nails, and said among themselves, in words the fishers standing by did not catch all of, that a timber which came from beyond the mist was better answered by fire than by argument. They burned it on the quay before the fishers' own eyes, the flames running strange colours along the metal of the nails before the nails themselves melted and were lost in the ash, and gave the fishers no clearer word than that of what it had been or where, exactly, beyond the mist, it had come from.

## VIII. Of the Winter Burning She Did Not Come Down From

Gormshuil went up to Taigh na Fèithe at Muileann dhearg for the winter burning, as she had gone up for every winter burning of her reign since her crowning thirty years before, riding the road herself rather than sending a custodian in her place, for she had told more than one custodian over those thirty years that a queen who never climbed the coal-road herself had no business asking Taigh na Fèithe to answer to her. She was eighty years old that winter, the oldest ruler Leabhar a' Chùraim had entered crowned and still reigning since long before Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, and the riders who went up with her noted nothing in her that winter that they had not noted in a dozen winters before it: a queen a little slower on the stair than she had been, taking the custodians' hands more readily than she once had to steady her climb, but asking the same plain questions of the same counted galleries she had always asked. The road up was iced that year past what the coal-carts liked, and the riders walked their horses the last steep mile rather than trust them at a trot, Gormshuil walking her own the same as the rest of them though more than one rider offered to lead it for her; she told them, as she had told them most winters, that a queen who let another hand lead her horse up the one road she still rode every year might as well let another hand rule from the chair at the bottom of it too.

She did not come down to Cathair dhearg again. Leabhar a' Chùraim records the winter burning kept, the coal measured, the handful cut as the law required; of the queen who had gone up with the riders and did not ride back down the same road she had climbed, nothing more is told. The custodians of Na Seachd Taighean, meeting at An Talla Dearg the following year in the place the crown's own chair had always stood empty for her progress and never before for any other cause, sent their word up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe by the same riders who had carried the crown's business all Gormshuil's reign, and Taigh na Fèithe sent back no word that unsettled the custodians' sitting, and the custodians sat on.

They wrote their letters that year and the year after in the crown's own hand, sealed with Taigh na Fèithe's own trellis and hollow stone as every crown letter had been sealed since Dòmhnall Ruadh joined the two, and above the seal, where a queen's name had stood on every such letter since Leabhar a' Chùraim's oldest leaves, they set no name at all, neither Gormshuil's own nor any other's, and no clerk of Taigh na Fèithe or An Talla Dearg was ever asked, in writing or otherwise, to explain the blank space where a name should have stood.

## IX. Of the Last Lamp at Seann Skell

Oidhche nan Lòchran at Seann Skell had been kept, in Gormshuil's own girlhood, by every house along the waterfront that could spare a rush-light and a window to set it in; by the last years of her reign it was kept by fewer houses each year that the harbour scribe troubled to count, until at last, 24 an Dàmhair, LE 1,799, none of the waterfront's own households set a lamp at all. It was an old woman of the town, Ealasaid nic Iain, who had kept the custom in her own family's window since before her husband died and saw no reason the town's own forgetting should end her keeping it, who set the one lamp that burned on the waterfront that year, in the harbour-house window where Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh was kept each Là an Diosail on the stones below. The harbour scribe who noted it in Rolla a' Chalaidh, the same office that had once counted every lamp along the whole quay, wrote plainly that the lamp burning that year was Ealasaid's own and not the town's, and let the sentence stand without further word, the way the crown's own letters had learned, across these same years, to let a blank space stand where a fuller one no longer had anything true to fill it with.

# Chapter Thirty-nine: Of the Eleven and the Thinning Mist

*LE 1,800 – 1,819*

## I. Of the Eleven at Cidhe an Diosail

The book Eòghann mac Nèill kept at Cidhe an Diosail was not Leabhar a' Chùraim, and no vein-house clerk had ever asked to read it, but it had passed from scribe to scribe at that quay for longer than any man living could reckon without a rod and a rule, and Eòghann, who had held it eleven years by the winter of LE 1,803, had long since stopped wondering whether the hand before his own had felt, on a grey Là an Diosail, anything like what he felt now, setting the board on his knee and wetting the reed.

The stones of the old quay ran green at the foot, where the river had worked at them since the fleet went down it, and the green did not wash off in any season, wet or dry; Eòghann had asked an old woman once whether it had always been so, and she had said only that the stone remembered the water better than the water remembered the stone. He stood a little back from the rite that year, as the scribe's place required, and counted the people on the quay the way he counted anything that mattered to Taigh na Fèithe's own reckoning: once by eye, and again by touch, a thumb moved along the tally-notches cut into the board's edge so that the eye could not lie to itself twice running. Both counts came to the same number. Eleven.

It was not so few as it had been the winter before, when a wet Gearras had kept half of Seann Skell indoors and only nine had stood the rite; nor was it so many as the year Eòghann had first held the book, when a full score had come down to the water, most of them the harbour priests of the old order and their households and a handful of the town's oldest families who kept the rite the way a house keeps a debt long unpaid to anyone living, since a debt let lapse has a way of being called in unlooked for. He wrote the number first, as the custom of the book required, and then the weather, a grey morning with no wind off the water and the tide at half ebb, and then, because Manannan's own priest had said the prayer that year at the same stones and at the same hour as the rite, as had become the way of it these ninety years, Eòghann noted that too, in the same hand and the same ink, though the two rites had never once, in his own years at the quay, agreed to be called one thing.

He sat a while after the last of the eleven had gone up from the water, the reed still wet in his hand, and thought, as he had thought more than one year running now, that there was more he might have written and did not: that the old woman who had told him the stone remembered the water was not among the eleven that year, having kept her bed since Samhnas with a cough that would not leave her chest; that the priest's prayer, said each tide now and not only on the rite's own day, had begun to sound in the ears of Seann Skell less like an asking and more like a habit a town keeps going out of fear of what silence might mean if the asking stopped; that no one under thirty years old had stood on the quay stones that morning at all, of the eleven or of anyone else. None of it went into the book. The book was for the number, the weather, and the tide, and had been for as long as it had been kept, and Eòghann mac Nèill, who had never in eleven years added a line the book did not ask of him, was not the man to begin the year the count came to eleven.

Eòghann closed the board and carried it back up the harbour-house stair, past the window where a lamp had stood every dark of the year since before he held the office, and did not need to look at the sill to know the lamp was not lit; it had not been lit in three winters, since the old woman who had kept it, Ealasaid nic Iain, took to her own bed at the far end of the same street and never rose from it again. He had gone to her burying himself, one of a bare dozen who did, and had heard it said over her grave, by a niece who had never once climbed the harbour-house stair in her own life, that Ealasaid had kept the lamp because the town would not, and that the town, now she was gone, would have to find some new reason to keep it or else own that it had none. No new reason had been found. The window stood dark that winter and every winter after, and Eòghann, passing it each Là an Diosail with the board under his arm, had come to think of the dark glass less as an absence than as a kind of company: the one other thing on that street, besides himself, that had gone on doing its office to the end without once being thanked for it.

He had not always meant to keep the harbour scribe's book so long, nor so close to the letter of it. He had come to the office at nine-and-twenty, a fisherman's son with a fair hand and no kin among the old harbour families, taken on because the man before him had died of a fall on the very stair Eòghann now climbed and left no son of his own trained to the work; and Eòghann, in his first winters at the board, had thought the office a thin thing to give a life to, a count and a weather-note and a tide, set down for no one he could name and read by no one he had ever met. It was only slowly, and never all at once, that he had come to feel what the scribes before him must also have felt, standing where he stood: that a book kept faithfully once no one still troubled to ask what was in it becomes, by the keeping alone, a kind of company of its own, and that a man who breaks that faith to say something truer than the book allows has broken the one thing the office was ever for.

## II. Of the Petition Laid Aside

Word reached Seann Skell late, as word from Cathair dhearg mostly did, that Aonghas mac Lachlainn had died in his own bed in the spring after the rite of the eleven, four-and-eighty years old and the last of the council that had sat when Athchuingean an Airgid was refused. He had turned his own vote against the smelt at Muileann chiar by a single voice, eight-and-twenty years before, and Leabhar a' Chùraim had written down his name and nothing of his reason, and in all the years since, at every fair and every ford where the tale was told, someone had always claimed to know at last why a man of Clann Lachlainn, whose own kin stood to gain by the silver as much as any house on the coal-right, had turned against his own house's asking. No two of the tellings agreed. A kinsman of his, sitting by him in the last week, is said to have asked him plainly whether he would not, now that it could cost him nothing, say what had turned his hand that day; Aonghas is said to have looked at the kinsman a while, and to have answered that a man who explained a thing he had done for good reason usually did it because the reason had stopped seeming good to him, and that his own had not, and he saw no cause to give it up now for the asking. He died within the week, and whatever he knew of his own vote went into the ground at Cathair dhearg with him.

Aonghas was carried to Cathair dhearg's own burying-ground under the ordinary rite of his house, with no more said over him than was said over any man of four-and-eighty years who had held no crown and started no war, and Leabhar a' Chùraim's clerk who entered his death wrote his name, his age, and the year, and nothing further, having no more to go on than the town did. A rider from Muileann chiar came down for the burying, sent by the silver guild there on the strength of an old courtesy and no closer tie, and stood at the back of the small crowd through the whole of it without once being asked, by anyone present, why a silversmith's rider had troubled to come so far for a man who had cost his own guild a fortune it never got to make. If he had an answer ready, no one at Cathair dhearg thought to want it.

Clann Choinnich, who had brought the petition twice and been refused twice, did not bring it a third time. The house had no want to test a new council on a question the old one had settled by so slight a margin, with the one man who had settled it now beyond any second asking, and Leabhar a' Chùraim's own note on the matter, written some years after by a clerk with no memory of the day, says only that the petition lay unbrought and unanswered, and that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, which had measured the hearth's own handful since Fionnlagh Dall's day, was kept as it had always been kept. No house is known to have grieved the silver it might have made. Muileann chiar's smelters went on working the ore they had always worked, at the heat charcoal gives and no more, and if any among them thought the coal beneath their own hills might have served them better, Leabhar a' Chùraim does not trouble to say so, and neither, in all the years Eòghann kept his own book at Seann Skell, did anyone who came through the harbour say it to him either.

Of the queen, in these same years, there was less and less to write, and at last nothing. She had gone up to Taigh na Fèithe eight winters before the rite of the eleven and had not come down to An Talla Dearg again, and no rider came from Muileann dhearg to say why, nor any word at all beyond the plain fact of her absence, which the council at Cathair dhearg kept from growing into a question by the simple means of never once asking it aloud in any hall where a clerk might be minded to write the asking down. Eòghann, at his own remove on the coast, heard of it the way he heard of most things from the capital: late, and thin, and by the mouth of a carter who had it from a carter who had it from someone nearer An Talla Dearg than either of them had ever been.
