He entered none of it in his own book, telling himself it was no business of the harbour scribe's what the council at Cathair dhearg chose to leave unsaid, though he noted, privately and only to himself, that a crown gone quiet in that particular way asked a great deal more of the men who kept the record after it than a crown that had simply died and been buried in the ordinary manner, with a date and a name and an heir to write down after both.

## III. Of the Chair Left Empty

Na Seachd Taighean had sat at Cathair dhearg in the queen's place since the winter after she went up to the burning, and it was in the seventeenth winter after her going that they came to the matter of a name; no one of them had called that sitting first, but each had by then sent its own rider up the same road on its own business, and the riders, finding one another at the same door on the same day, had gone in together rather than wait apart for a summons that no one left at Cathair dhearg had the standing to send. An Talla Dearg in those years held perhaps five hundred souls in all its lanes and closes, fewer than a single one of Na Seachd Taighean' own tenants counted in a good year, and the board where the seven sat was the same board Catrìona Bheag had sworn them to Riaghailt an Teallaich over, twelve generations before, its grain gone dark with the hands that had rested on it since.

No new crown was proposed. Clann Raghnaill's own head, an old woman by then and no friend to haste, said first what more than one of the seven had thought and none had yet spoken: that a crown with no one to wear it was no crown at all, whatever Taigh na Fèithe's rolls might go on calling it, and that Na Seachd Taighean sitting at one board with no voice among them answerable for what the board decided was a slower kind of ruin than any war the record kept. She proposed no new crown. She proposed only that the seven, sitting as they now sat, should call themselves by some plain name for what they in fact were, custodians of the coal-right and, in the queen's long silence, of a good deal more besides, and that one among them should speak for the seven when a single voice was wanted, at Taigh na Fèithe or on the road or before any stranger who came asking who ruled at Cathair dhearg now.

They named themselves, that same sitting, Comhairle a' Chùraim, a name near enough to Leabhar a' Chùraim that no clerk in any hall would need the thing explained to him twice. For the one voice, they turned to Tormod mac Ailein, eight-and-thirty years old and the youngest man at the board by a full generation, a custodian's son of no house among the seven who had kept Taigh na Fèithe's own accounts at Muileann dhearg since he was a boy and was trusted, by every house there for reasons each gave differently, to want nothing for himself that the other six had not already agreed he might have. They called him Ceann a' Chùraim, and he took the name the way a man takes a coat handed him against weather he had not himself chosen to walk out in, gravely, and without much show of being glad of it.

Clann Choinnich alone, of the seven, asked whether a council so newly named might not also, in the same sitting, be asked again about the silver; the head of that house put the question mildly, and mildly it was set aside, the board's temper being for settling one uncertainty at a time and no more, and the silver, as every house at the board well knew, being the one uncertainty the last council had settled by a single voice now in the ground. Nothing more was said of it that winter, nor at the sitting after.

The chair at the head of the board, the queen's own chair, they left standing empty. No one proposed that Tormod sit in it, and Tormod himself, asked once by a clerk which chair he meant to take at the next sitting, said only that his own place at the board's foot had served him well enough thus far and he saw no cause to move up it now. The chair stood empty at every sitting after, and moving it would have wanted an explaining nobody at the board was minded to give. The council's own letters, from that first winter on, went out from Cathair dhearg sealed with Taigh na Fèithe's own trellis and hollow stone and no name written above the seal, a custom An Talla Dearg's clerks had already begun in the queen's last silent years and saw no reason, now, to give up merely because the silence had at last been given a name of its own.

## IV. Of the Fisher of Ceann mhòr

At Ceann mhòr, twenty miles up the coast from Seann Skell where the fishing was thin and the houses fewer with every count the crown's reeves had ever troubled to make, a fisher named Oighrig nic Eachainn kept her father's boat after him, one of perhaps a dozen boats still put out from that shore at all, the rest laid up above the tide-line the way the last barge of Inis mhòr had been laid up long before, less because anyone had decided the sea was done with than because there was no longer hand enough left on that coast to man them. Oighrig went out before first light most mornings the winter after Na Seachd Taighean named themselves at Cathair dhearg, though word of it did not reach her for the better part of a year; a fisher of Ceann mhòr had small cause to trouble herself with what An Talla Dearg called its own council, so long as the fish still ran and the priests at Seann Skell kept their own rule of sight-of-land, which was the only rule of the crown's that had ever reached so far up the coast in any form a fisher needed to remember.

That rule she had known from a child, the way she had known to reef a sail before her father ever let her hold the tiller: a boat went out as far as the eye could keep the headland, and no further, for beyond the headland lay Manannan's own mist, and no boat that had ever gone into it, in all the tellings the coast still told, had come back to say what lay past it. Mànas mac Dhùghaill, the priest who kept Manannan's rite at Seann Skell those years, had taken, on 27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813, to writing into his own book of the rite a thing the older priests before him had said only at the hearth and never on paper, that the grey out past the headlands stood thinner each year than the year before, so that a morning that would once have shown a fisher nothing beyond an arm's length of grey water now sometimes showed her the grey itself, thin as a held breath, with something beyond it that was not mist at all. He said the prayer at every tide by then, not only at the rite's own day, the same words the synod had given the priests two centuries back, Manannan, keep the sea shut, and he wrote in his own book that he did not know whether the saying of it more often was holding anything back or merely making plainer, each time it was said, how little the saying now held back.

Oighrig rested on her oars one still morning that same winter, further out than the rule strictly allowed but not so far that any priest watching from the shore could have called it a true crossing of the line, and looked north into the grey the way she had looked at it every morning of her life without ever once, before that morning, seeing anything in it but grey. The water lay flat and dark under her hull, and the mist stood off the bow the way it always stood, a wall with no far side that the eye could find. Then, for the space of a few breaths only, before the grey closed again the way it always closed, she saw a line beyond it, hard and dark and level, ruled clean across the edge of the world where the water met the sky and went on past where any headland could account for it. It was there and it was gone, and she could not afterward have sworn, put to it plainly, that she had not simply willed herself into seeing what every fisher on that coast had half hoped and half dreaded to see since the priests began saying the prayer at every tide instead of once a year.

Her father had drowned off that same headland eleven years before, in weather no worse than a dozen he had come through safely in his own life, and Oighrig had grown up hearing the coast agree, without ever quite saying so to her face, that the sea took a man in the end for no better reason than that it had waited long enough; she troubled little enough with the thought on an ordinary morning; that morning, with the hard line still standing before her eyes though the mist had long since closed over it again, she found herself wondering, for the first time in eleven years, whether her father had ever, on some grey dawn like this one, rested on his own oars a moment past where the rule allowed and seen the same thing she had seen, and said nothing of it either, for the same plain reasons she meant to say nothing of hers.

She turned for home as the rule said a fisher must, and did not speak of it at the shore, not that morning nor for some while after, telling herself there was little enough good that came of a fisher's tale believed too readily and a good deal of harm that came of one believed and then found false. When she did speak of it, months on, it was to no priest and no reeve but to her own mother, mending a net by the one lamp their house still burned after dark, and her mother heard her out and said only that a woman who had seen a true thing and kept it to herself a season had already shown better sense over it than most who saw such things at all, and that she might do worse than go on keeping it a while longer yet. Oighrig did. It went into no book at Seann Skell and no roll at Cathair dhearg, and the only record that she ever spoke of it stands in her own mother's memory and, after that, in no record at all.

## V. Of the Last Winter

By the fifteenth winter after the rite of the eleven, the harbour-house at Seann Skell had stood so long with its lamp-window dark that a stranger asking after the custom of Oidhche nan Lòchran would have found no one on the waterfront under sixty years old able to say from their own memory what the night had once looked like, lit. Eòghann mac Nèill, who had kept the harbour scribe's book at Cidhe an Diosail for six-and-twenty years by then, still walked down to the stones each Là an Diosail with the same board under his arm, and still counted, and still wrote the number and the weather and the tide in the same plain hand the book had always asked of him, though the number by then had not risen above a dozen in longer than he cared to reckon, and one bitter year had come down, by his own careful count, to seven.

That last winter the record tells of, the count is not written, for the book, if Eòghann kept it to the end, does not survive to say what he wrote in it; what is told of that season comes from elsewhere; from Mànas mac Dhùghaill's own book of the rite at Seann Skell, which does survive, and which sets down, in a hand grown old and careful by then, that the priests said the prayer at every tide that winter as they had said it every winter for thirty years, and that on more than one still morning the line beyond the mist stood plain enough from the harbour wall that a man need not put out in any boat at all to see it. And from Leabhar a' Chùraim, which notes, in the same dry hand that had entered every winter burning since Fionnlagh Dall's day, that the council of the custody sat at its board in An Talla Dearg through the dark of that year as it had sat through every year since the seven had named it, and sent its letters out sealed as it had always sent them, with no name above the seal, and no word in any of them of the chair that stood empty at the board's head, which by then no clerk living had ever seen anyone sit in at all.

On a still morning near the year's dark heart, with no wind on the water and the tide at the ebb it kept at that season, the priests of Manannan said their prayer at Seann Skell as the sun came up grey behind the mist, and further up the coast at Ceann mhòr the few boats still fishing that shore put out before light as they always had, and one or two of the older hands among them, resting a while on their oars past where the rule strictly allowed, looked north a moment longer than the rule strictly asked of them either, before they turned, every one, for home. At Cathair dhearg the council sat at its board in An Talla Dearg with the chair at its head standing empty as it had stood three-and-twenty years, and wrote its letters, and sealed them, and sent them out by riders down roads Taigh na Fèithe had kept in good repair since before any house now sitting at that board had held the custody at all. And on the waterfront at Seann Skell, where a lamp had once stood in every window on Oidhche nan Lòchran, the one window that had kept a lamp longest of all stood dark, as it had stood every winter since the woman who kept it went into the ground, and no one that year, nor any year after within this record's telling, set a light there in her place.

The mist stood on the water as it had stood since the fleet went down the river into it eighteen centuries before, and it stood, that winter, thinner than any priest at Seann Skell could remember it standing, and no boat put out to try it. The prayer was said at every tide. The council kept its board. Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measured the hearth's own handful, hearth by hearth, as it had measured it since Fionnlagh Dall first laid down the rule, and three houses of the seven held between them more of the right than the other four together, and the petition that might once have changed it lay where it had lain twelve years, unbrought and unanswered, in Taigh na Fèithe's own inventory. Of the crown, nothing further was written. The lamp-window stood dark on the waterfront through that winter and the winters after it, and the mist, each morning the tide allowed a boat to look, lay a little thinner on the water than the morning before.

# The Annals of the Age

## The Years LE 1 – 100

- <a id="ev-III-0001"></a>**6 am Faoilleach, LE 1** — *Land is found*. Word comes of a land across the open water, where no people like the Dia-thìrich dwell. Who first found it is not told.
- <a id="ev-III-0002"></a>**9 an t-Samhain, LE 1** — *The tidings at Cathair dhearg* (Cathair dhearg). Three crews from the western harbours bring word of the far land to the hall of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich, at Cathair dhearg. None claims to have been first. The queen's scribe takes down all three tellings; they agree on the coast and on nothing else.
- <a id="ev-III-0003"></a>**8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The Choosing*. A vote, or what the later chroniclers call a vote, settles who will go. Only the willing go; no lots are drawn and none are pressed.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1001"></a>**12 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The tale on the quays of Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). In the moon of Faolach the word of a far coast is on the quay at Cuan shean, told in the lee of the rope-sheds and at the crews' fire. No one says he saw the coast, and every telling leads back to another. By the moon's end it is told at Ros bheag, Inis àrsaidh and Ceann mhòr.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0001"><em>Land is found</em>, 6 am Faoilleach, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1002"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The pilot of Ros bheag* (Ros bheag). A pilot of Ros bheag, blown off the land in the autumn gales, comes home after nine days with his water gone. The coast shows up in the talk as his, but he swears he saw nothing but grey water, too loudly.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0001"><em>Land is found</em>, 6 am Faoilleach, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1003"></a>**14 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The Cuan shean crew heard in An Talla Dearg* (Cathair dhearg). Eachann mac Lachlainn, skipper of Cuan shean, tells the queen of a low dark coast west and north of west, with smoke on it and no hall. Asked if he was first to hear it, he says he was about the last.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0002"><em>The tidings at Cathair dhearg</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1004"></a>**19 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The Ros bheag crew heard in An Talla Dearg* (Cathair dhearg). Oighrig nic Raghnaill, skipper of Ros bheag, tells the queen that the coast lies north past the north cape, high and forested, with a white river, and that the pilot who saw it swore on the cup at Seann Skell.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0002"><em>The tidings at Cathair dhearg</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1005"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The Ceann mhòr crew heard in An Talla Dearg* (Cathair dhearg). Tòmas mac Uilleim of Ceann mhòr tells the queen that the land lies east behind the mist, and can be smelt on some mornings; the old men of the north-west have always said so.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0002"><em>The tidings at Cathair dhearg</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1006"></a>**22 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *Murchadh's leaf of the three tellings* (Cathair dhearg). The queen's scribe Murchadh mac Eòghainn writes the three tellings on one leaf and adds at its foot that they agree on the coast and on nothing else. The leaf is kept in the chest of An Talla Dearg.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0002"><em>The tidings at Cathair dhearg</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1007"></a>**24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *How many days' water* (Cathair dhearg). At the lower board of An Talla Dearg the queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill asks the Cuan shean skipper how many days' water a boat would need. He answers that no boat of the island could make the crossing, and that none has ever been built that could.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0002"><em>The tidings at Cathair dhearg</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1008"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The question at the hearths*. Through the moon of Dubhlas the question 'Would we go?' is asked at hearths from Baile chrom to Seann Vell, most of all on the west coast. No lots are drawn and no lord or priest gives a word.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0003"><em>The Choosing</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1009"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *Two households of Inis àrsaidh* (Inis àrsaidh). In the drying-shed at Inis àrsaidh two households say before the whole town that they will go if a boat is ever made that can make the crossing. The town laughs, then stops laughing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0003"><em>The Choosing</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1010"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *A custodian asks for the three tellings* (Cathair dhearg). Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a young custodian of the western diggings, comes down to Cathair dhearg on an errand of Taigh na Fèithe and asks to hear the three tellings from the queen's scribe.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0003"><em>The Choosing</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1011"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *Mòrag at Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill rides alone to Cuan shean and questions Eachann mac Lachlainn on seams, winds and wood. He tells her a hull that needs no sewing would want great oak and a keel, and that no one alive knows how to set one.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0003"><em>The Choosing</em>, 8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1012"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The queen keeps the journey from the roll* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag watches her sister walk the Cuan shean skipper to the gate of An Talla Dearg and look down the river road west. She bids Murchadh write nothing of it, since it is no matter for the roll yet.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1013"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *The ninth year of Queen Beathag* (Cathair dhearg). An Talla Dearg's rolls enter the first year of the age as the ninth year of Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill, crowned at fifteen and now three-and-twenty: a good year for barley and a middling one for fish, with no child yet born to her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0002"><em>The tidings at Cathair dhearg</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1014"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1** — *Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill at nineteen* (Cathair dhearg). The queen's sister Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, nineteen years old and two years married to a man of the western shore she chose herself, comes up to the capital for the winter and sits at the lower board when the crews are heard.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0002"><em>The tidings at Cathair dhearg</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0004"></a>**12 an t-Sultain, LE 2** — *The roll of the willing* (Seann Skell). The harbour scribes of Seann Skell open a roll of those who mean to go, written by household and not by name, on boards in the harbour-house. A later hand notes that names were struck out as often as they were added.
- <a id="ev-III-0005"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, LE 2** — *The queen neither commands nor forbids* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag declares that the crown will send no one across the water and keep no one back. Within the season her younger sister, Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, enters her own household on the roll at Seann Skell.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1012"><em>The queen keeps the journey from the roll</em>, 30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1015"></a>**15 an Dàmhair, LE 2** — *The first household asks to be written* (Seann Skell). In the moon of Pailteach a fisher of Inis àrsaidh and his wife come into Taigh a' Chalaidh and ask to be written down as meaning to go. The harbour scribe Calum mac Nèill planes a new board and heads it: Those who mean to go.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0004"><em>The roll of the willing</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1016"></a>**16 an Dàmhair, LE 2** — *The rule of the whole household* (Seann Skell). Calum mac Nèill will write a household whole or not at all, since Taigh na Fèithe measures the handful to the hearth and not to a single man or woman. The roll is kept by household from its first board.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0004"><em>The roll of the willing</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1017"></a>**23 an Dàmhair, LE 2** — *The first striking-out* (Seann Skell). Iain, a net-maker of Seann Skell, strikes his household from the roll before the moon is out, having woken at night unable to breathe for thought of the open sea. He enters again in spring and strikes out again by midsummer.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0004"><em>The roll of the willing</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1018"></a>**24 an Dàmhair, LE 2** — *A struck name is cut through* (Seann Skell). Asked to scrape a struck name from the board, the harbour scribe refuses and cuts it through with one stroke, so that the roll shows both the meaning to go and the change of mind. The custom holds for every board of the roll.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0004"><em>The roll of the willing</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1019"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, LE 2** — *The widow of the strand* (Seann Skell). A boat-wright's widow of the Seann Skell strand is entered alone and struck three times over the first year, her name standing on the board three times like a ladder. She does not come back.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0004"><em>The roll of the willing</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1020"></a>**8 an t-Samhain, LE 2** — *The late lamp in the harbour-house* (Seann Skell). For those who cannot say it by day, Calum mac Nèill keeps a lamp burning in the harbour-house late into the night and pays for the oil himself. The harbour-house becomes a place between a court and a shrine.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0004"><em>The roll of the willing</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1021"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, LE 2** — *Taigh na Fèithe sends to read the roll* (Seann Skell). A custodian's servant comes by night to read Rolla nan Deònach and ask how many households on it hold the right to the coal. From then on the harbour scribe marks each hearth that takes the handful with a notch like a flame.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1022"></a>**17 an t-Samhain, LE 2** — *Dòmhnall mac Chaluim asks that the boards be closed* (Seann Skell). The harbour scribe's son and clerk asks his father to close the roll and send the people to the queen. Calum will not close what the queen has not closed.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0005"><em>The queen neither commands nor forbids</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1023"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, LE 2** — *Alasdair mac Iain reads the roll* (Seann Skell). A boat-wright of the strand, Alasdair mac Iain, reads every board of the roll and says there is not a boat on the island that could carry the half of them, and that somebody had better build one.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1024"></a>**25 an t-Samhain, LE 2** — *Seonag asks the harbour scribe whether he would go* (Seann Skell). Lying in the box-bed with the wind over the roof, Calum mac Nèill's wife Seonag, who keeps geese and sells their eggs on the quay, asks him whether he would go. He answers that the boards need a keeper.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0004"><em>The roll of the willing</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1025"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, LE 2** — *The sisters in the bower* (Cathair dhearg). Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill rides to Cathair dhearg and asks her sister to command or forbid the crossing. The queen answers that the crown has never sent anyone anywhere, nor kept back anyone free, and will not begin with her sister.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0005"><em>The queen neither commands nor forbids</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1026"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 2** — *The queen's word sent to the harbours* (Cathair dhearg). The queen's word, written by Murchadh mac Eòghainn and sealed, goes by rider to Seann Skell and every harbour of the west and to Taigh na Fèithe: the crown will send no one and keep no one back, and will judge any quarrel of the venture by the old law.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0005"><em>The queen neither commands nor forbids</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1027"></a>**11 an Dùbhlachd, LE 2** — *The word read at the harbour-house door* (Seann Skell). Calum mac Nèill reads the queen's word twice from the harbour-house door to the town standing in the rain. Few cheer; most had wanted the crown to choose for them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0005"><em>The queen neither commands nor forbids</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1028"></a>**18 an Dùbhlachd, LE 2** — *The queen's word made a song* (Seann Skell). On the quay at Seann Skell the fishers say the queen's word over until it becomes a line of song: I will send no one over, and I will keep no one back. The harbour songs keep it so.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0005"><em>The queen neither commands nor forbids</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1029"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, LE 2** — *Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh says yes* (Inis àrsaidh). At Inis àrsaidh Mòrag's husband, Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh, a farmer of the land up the river, agrees that their household will go before she has finished asking.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0005"><em>The queen neither commands nor forbids</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1030"></a>**28 am Faoilleach, LE 3** — *The custodians dispute the right of those who go* (Muileann dhearg). Through the winter the custodians at Taigh na Fèithe argue whether the right to the coal goes with a hearth that crosses the sea or is struck on the day it sails. Fearchar mac Ruairidh holds that the right lives in the hands.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1031"></a>**13 am Màrt, LE 3** — *The roll copied for Taigh na Fèithe* (Seann Skell). The harbour scribe's son copies Rolla nan Deònach onto skin, with a flame-mark beside each household that holds the right to the coal, and sends it up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1032"></a>**14 an t-Ògmhios, LE 3** — *Fearchar mac Ruairidh's household on the roll* (Muileann dhearg). Fearchar mac Ruairidh tells the custodians, after the second count, that he entered his own household on the roll at Seann Skell in the moon of Samhnas and ticked his own name twice.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1033"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, LE 3** — *Nine days at the long table* (Muileann dhearg). In the moon of Lùghnas the custodians of Taigh na Fèithe sit at the long table with the copied roll on one side and Leabhar a' Chùraim on the other, and count hearth by hearth, name against name, for nine days.
- <a id="ev-III-0006"></a>**14 an Lùnastal, LE 3** — *The custodians count the cost* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house above Muileann dhearg, keeper of Crom's stone and heir to the Keepers' Hall at Dùn ìseal where Brìde's flame was first bound, counts the households of the coal-right that have entered the roll. The custody-book makes it nearly one in five, and says the count was made twice, for the first figure was not believed.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1021"><em>Taigh na Fèithe sends to read the roll</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, LE 2</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1031"><em>The roll copied for Taigh na Fèithe</em>, 13 am Màrt, LE 3</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-1032"><em>Fearchar mac Ruairidh's household on the roll</em>, 14 an t-Ògmhios, LE 3</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-1033"><em>Nine days at the long table</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, LE 3</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1501"></a>**5 am Faoilleach, LE 4** — *Alasdair's small hulls* (Seann Skell). On the strand below Seann Skell the boat-wright Alasdair mac Iain builds hulls no longer than his arm on spines of oak and floats them in the river pool and the river mouth, to learn what a keel does. He finds that a keel makes a hull stiff and lets it be built bigger.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1502"></a>**3 an Gearran, LE 4** — *Mòrag undertakes to pay for the oaks* (Inis àrsaidh). At Inis àrsaidh Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh hear Alasdair out and send him to look at the grove of Doire fhionn. Mòrag undertakes to pay for the felling and hauling out of her own silver.
- <a id="ev-III-0007"></a>**16 an t-Iuchar, LE 5** — *The ships are built*. The shipwrights of the island, used to small coasting craft, build ships to keep the open sea, the first in the memory of Dia-thìr.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1501"><em>Alasdair's small hulls</em>, 5 am Faoilleach, LE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0008"></a>**14 an Lùnastal, LE 5** — *Alasdair Saor lays the first keel* (Seann Skell). On the river strand below Seann Skell the shipwright Alasdair mac Iain, called Alasdair Saor, lays down the first deep-keeled hull built on Dia-thìr. Until then the island's boats were sewn-plank coasters that never lay a night out of sight of land.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1023"><em>Alasdair mac Iain reads the roll</em>, 24 an t-Samhain, LE 2</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0009"></a>**26 an Lùnastal, LE 5** — *The oaks of Doire fhionn* (Doire fhionn). The oak grove that named Doire fhionn is felled for the keels of the fleet and drawn to the coast on ox-sleds. It never grew again, and the village kept a name it had no more cause for.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1502"><em>Mòrag undertakes to pay for the oaks</em>, 3 an Gearran, LE 4</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0010"></a>**24 an t-Sultain, LE 5** — *The shipwrights' fellowship* (Seann Skell). Alasdair Saor gathers the wrights of the Seann Skell strand into one fellowship, and binds each apprentice for seven years after the manner of the vein custodians. The custody-book names it Comann nan Saor-luinge, the fellowship of the ship-wrights.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1503"></a>**25 an t-Sultain, LE 5** — *The naming of the trees* (Doire fhionn). Eilidh nic Ruairidh, keeper of the grove of Doire fhionn, makes Alasdair choose each oak he will take and hear its name. He chooses fifty-four and leaves one young tree, the Child, standing alone.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0009"><em>The oaks of Doire fhionn</em>, 26 an Lùnastal, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1504"></a>**12 an Dàmhair, LE 5** — *The felling of the Queen* (Doire fhionn). Eighty men of the households of the roll fell the grove of Doire fhionn through the summer, each tree onto a bed of brush. The greatest, called the Queen, takes two days to bring down.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0009"><em>The oaks of Doire fhionn</em>, 26 an Lùnastal, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1505"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, LE 5** — *The ox-sleds on the north road* (Doire fhionn). The keel-timbers are dragged forty-two miles south to the sea on sleds of oak shod with ash, six yoke to a sled. The road is widened at every bend and a causeway built over the stream below Doire fhionn.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0009"><em>The oaks of Doire fhionn</em>, 26 an Lùnastal, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1506"></a>**2 an t-Samhain, LE 5** — *Woodcutters' huts at Doire fhiadhaich* (Doire fhiadhaich). Woodcutters of the roll build huts at the edge of a wild oak wood on the shore of Loch chrom to fell crooked oak for the fleet's frames and knees. They go home when the felling is done and the huts fall in; the wood keeps its name.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0007"><em>The ships are built</em>, 16 an t-Iuchar, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1507"></a>**21 an t-Samhain, LE 5** — *The bed of the first keel* (Seann Skell). Alasdair levels a line of oak blocks on the strand above the high-water mark and digs a saw-pit beside it. The Queen oak is rolled onto the blocks and hewn to a keel with a ridge along its underside.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0008"><em>Alasdair Saor lays the first keel</em>, 14 an Lùnastal, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1508"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, LE 5** — *Coinneach mac Fhearghais sworn* (Seann Skell). At the feast of Lugh the wrights of the strand bind themselves into one fellowship. A custodian of Taigh na Fèithe swears their apprentices over a coal, and the first sworn is Coinneach mac Fhearghais, a coaster-wright's son of fourteen.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0010"><em>The shipwrights' fellowship</em>, 24 an t-Sultain, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1509"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 5** — *The first frames stand on the strand* (Seann Skell). By the moon of Pailteach the first frames rise from the keel in pairs, pegged with heart-oak. The harbour scribe writes that the hull looks like the ribs of a great beast picked clean on the shore.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1510"></a>**19 an Dùbhlachd, LE 5** — *The Child walled* (Doire fhionn). The village of Doire fhionn builds a low wall of stones round the one young oak left on the grove hill, and its old keeper sits beside it every evening until dark.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0009"><em>The oaks of Doire fhionn</em>, 26 an Lùnastal, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1511"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 5** — *Alasdair walks north with a knotted line* (Seann Skell). In the moon of Gearras, after Là Fhèill Brìde, Alasdair mac Iain sets out alone on the north road with a pack, a staff and a line knotted every arm's length for measuring, making fifteen miles the first day and sleeping in a byre.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0009"><em>The oaks of Doire fhionn</em>, 26 an Lùnastal, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0011"></a>**12 an t-Sultain, LE 6** — *The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh* (Inis àrsaidh). The first finished hull is taken down the Abhainn naomh and out past Ros àrsaidh, where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put to sea, for trial in open water. It founders in a following sea and eleven are drowned. Alasdair Saor alters the setting of the keel, and every later hull of the fleet is built to the new pattern.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1509"><em>The first frames stand on the strand</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 5</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1512"></a>**20 an t-Sultain, LE 6** — *An Fhaoileag launched* (Seann Skell). The first deep-keeled hull, planked and rigged, is floated off the blocks below Seann Skell with a coal from Taigh na Fèithe set at her step. The town calls her An Fhaoileag, the gull, for the way she rides the water.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0011"><em>The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1513"></a>**6 an Dàmhair, LE 6** — *The nine named at Inis àrsaidh* (Inis àrsaidh). The roll-keeper of Inis àrsaidh cuts eleven names into the village's board on the night of the drowning, the village sitting up with her as the custom asks. Alasdair's sister's son Tormod Beag is among the eight bodies brought back; three more are never found.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0011"><em>The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1514"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, LE 6** — *The keening at Inis àrsaidh* (Inis àrsaidh). The eight recovered dead are keened on the shingle under sailcloth and a lamp at each head; for the three never found a single lamp is lit and burns down unwatched. Alasdair stays three days doing whatever the village asks of him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0011"><em>The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1515"></a>**27 an Dàmhair, LE 6** — *Households struck and households entered* (Seann Skell). Eleven households strike themselves from the Seann Skell roll after word of the drowning, and eleven others enter in the same weeks, among them kin of a survivor and a widow of Ros bheag who gives her daughters' names. Calum mac Nèill records both counts without comment.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0011"><em>The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1516"></a>**27 an t-Sultain, LE 7** — *The second keel laid to the changed pattern* (Seann Skell). Alasdair Saor lays a second keel on the strand below Seann Skell, built to the fuller, hollow-bowed run he redrew by a driftwood fire after the drowning. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill sends silver again to see her built.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0011"><em>The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0012"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, LE 8** — *The rope-walks of Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). Cuan shean lays out long rope-walks along its harbour front and gives all its hemp fields to cordage for the fleet. Its rope trade lasts some centuries beyond the Sundering.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1517"></a>**9 an t-Samhain, LE 8** — *The rope-walks learn the names of a keel* (Cuan shean). After shroud-lines sent west from Cuan shean fail within a season, the wrights walk the rope-walks and name the parts of a hull to the spinners and walkers. Iain Ròpaire, master of the walks, takes to walking one himself to learn the words in his own hands.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0012"><em>The rope-walks of Cuan shean</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 8</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1518"></a>**18 an t-Samhain, LE 8** — *Birth of Raghnall mac Uilleim* (Cathair dhearg). A son, Raghnall, is born at Cathair dhearg to Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill and her consort Uilleam mac Iain, in the queen's sixteenth year crowned and her own thirtieth year of life.
- <a id="ev-III-0013"></a>**9 an t-Samhain, LE 9** — *The sail-cloth levy* (Baile àrsaidh). Every weaving household in Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh owes a set length of close-woven sail-cloth, scored on tally-sticks at the shire seat. The tallies survive; how many paid is not known.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1519"></a>**28 an t-Samhain, LE 9** — *The sail-cloth tallies at Baile àrsaidh* (Baile àrsaidh). The shire seat's tally-keeper cuts notches for close-woven lengths from households across Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh, far more than expected, some sent by weavers with no kin on the roll and no thought of sailing. The sticks fill a chest that wants a second lid.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0013"><em>The sail-cloth levy</em>, 9 an t-Samhain, LE 9</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1520"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 9** — *An Dara Fhaoileag planked* (Seann Skell). An Dara Fhaoileag stands planked from keel to sheer and steps her mast on the strand below Seann Skell. The wrights name her An Dara Fhaoileag, the second gull, and the doubt among the older wrights over her fuller, hollow-bowed lines goes quiet.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0011"><em>The trial hull lost off Ros àrsaidh</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 6</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1521"></a>**19 an Gearran, LE 11** — *Six pilots sent east to Cuan ruadh* (Ros bheag). Fearchar mac Ruairidh finds that no pilot of the west coast has ever held a course by night, and six are chosen to walk the hundred miles to the old steersmen of Cuan ruadh: two of Ceann mhòr, two of Ros bheag, one of Cuan shean, and Catrìona nic Iain, who asks to be sent before she is asked.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1522"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, LE 12** — *The six pilots reach Cuan ruadh* (Cuan ruadh). After seven days on foot over the mountain country the six pilots come down to Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast and are given lodging without question. They are sent, the next morning, to the steersman Seumas Reultach.
- <a id="ev-EIV-1523"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, LE 12** — *Seumas Reultach begins the teaching* (Cuan ruadh). On the headland above Cuan ruadh the old steersman Seumas Reultach begins teaching the six pilots the wheel of the sky and Reul na Stiùire, by which it is held. Most of what he gives them is spoken, night after night, and set down nowhere.
- <a id="ev-III-0014"></a>**20 an Giblean, LE 13** — *The star-lore of Cuan ruadh* (Cuan ruadh). The old steersmen of Cuan ruadh on the eastern coast, the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night, teach the pilots of the fleet to steer by the stars. Their lore was written down only in part, and that part is lost.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1521"><em>Six pilots sent east to Cuan ruadh</em>, 19 an Gearran, LE 11</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-1522"><em>The six pilots reach Cuan ruadh</em>, 24 an t-Samhain, LE 12</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-1523"><em>Seumas Reultach begins the teaching</em>, 23 an Dùbhlachd, LE 12</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1524"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, LE 13** — *Part of the star-lore set on hide* (Cuan ruadh). At Taigh na Fèithe's asking, Seumas Reultach has his granddaughter cut onto a scraped hide the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the four turning marks of the year. He keeps back the swell-reading and the wind-smell, saying some things a hide can hold and some things only a life can.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0014"><em>The star-lore of Cuan ruadh</em>, 20 an Giblean, LE 13</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1525"></a>**31 an t-Iuchar, LE 14** — *Death of Seumas Reultach* (Cuan ruadh). In the moon of Faolach the old steersman of Cuan ruadh dies on the cliff path above the town where he taught the six pilots the stars, and is buried there among his own people. His granddaughter gives the hide of star-marks into Catrìona nic Iain's keeping to carry west.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0014"><em>The star-lore of Cuan ruadh</em>, 20 an Giblean, LE 13</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1526"></a>**29 an Lùnastal, LE 14** — *The pilots return west* (Cuan ruadh). The six pilots cross the mountain country again to the west coast, carrying the hide of star-marks and what they have learned of the wheel of the sky, Reul na Stiùire and the smell of the dark before a change of wind.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0014"><em>The star-lore of Cuan ruadh</em>, 20 an Giblean, LE 13</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1527"></a>**26 an Dàmhair, LE 14** — *The first night-steering trial off Ros àrsaidh* (Ros àrsaidh). Off Ros àrsaidh two boats go out after dark, one steered close along the shore by lantern, the other by Catrìona nic Iain alone by Reul na Stiùire with every lantern doused. She brings her boat home first, exactly where and when she had said she would.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0014"><em>The star-lore of Cuan ruadh</em>, 20 an Giblean, LE 13</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-1528"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 18** — *Catrìona nic Iain made pilot of An Ròn Glas* (Seann Skell). Catrìona nic Iain reaches Seann Skell after the households of the roll have chosen Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and Fearchar mac Ruairidh to lead them. On the west quay Mòrag asks her to be pilot of her hull, An Ròn Glas, and Catrìona names her Reul na Stiùire.
- <a id="ev-III-0015"></a>**19 an Cèitean, LE 18** — *The willing choose their leaders* (Seann Skell). The households of the roll meet at Seann Skell and choose Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill, the queen's sister, and Fearchar mac Ruairidh, a custodian of the vein, to lead them. The custody-book records the choice; how it was made is not told.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1032"><em>Fearchar mac Ruairidh's household on the roll</em>, 14 an t-Ògmhios, LE 3</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EIV-1528"><em>Catrìona nic Iain made pilot of An Ròn Glas</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 18</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2001"></a>**28 an t-Ògmhios, LE 19** — *Fearchar's petition for the coal* (Muileann dhearg). Fearchar mac Ruairidh comes to Taigh na Fèithe and asks that each hull found fit to sail be allowed to carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household's season under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig. The custodians send him down the hill with a promise only to put the matter to the board.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2002"></a>**27 an t-Iuchar, LE 23** — *Donnchadh mac Thormoid given to Taigh na Fèithe* (Muileann dhearg). Tormod, a turf-cutter of the moor above Muileann dhearg, walks his son Donnchadh, nine years old, up the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe and leaves him there sworn to the vein's service for seven years, and does not look back.
- <a id="ev-III-0016"></a>**17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25** — *The handful for the new hearth* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house rules that each departing ship may carry one sealed measure of the coal, no more than a single household may burn in a season under the Small-Burning Law. It is the only writing in the custody-book addressed to those who were leaving.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-1030"><em>The custodians dispute the right of those who go</em>, 28 am Faoilleach, LE 3</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2001"><em>Fearchar's petition for the coal</em>, 28 an t-Ògmhios, LE 19</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2002"><em>Donnchadh mac Thormoid given to Taigh na Fèithe</em>, 27 an t-Iuchar, LE 23</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2003"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, LE 25** — *The custodians' debate at the winter burning* (Muileann dhearg). After six winters of argument Taigh na Fèithe's board finally votes on Fearchar's petition. Cailean and others hold that the coal has never crossed water and should not; Fearchar answers that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig measures a hearth wherever a hearth chooses to stand. Leabhar a' Chùraim is opened and the question is put to writing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0016"><em>The handful for the new hearth</em>, 17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2004"></a>**3 an Gearran, LE 26** — *The sealed measures made* (Muileann dhearg). The first measures of coal are weighed and sealed at Taigh na Fèithe, each against the words "for each hull that shall be ready", with no count kept against any known number of hulls. Fearchar mac Ruairidh stands by in silence to see the first one made.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0016"><em>The handful for the new hearth</em>, 17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2005"></a>**4 am Màrt, LE 28** — *The queen lends masons for the quay* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill sends a gang of masons from the capital, under Ailean mac Nèill, down to Seann Skell to lengthen the west quay with dressed stone "for the harbour's trade", the crown's word for it and no other named.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2006"></a>**17 am Faoilleach, LE 29** — *The fair copy of the ruling, Donnchadh's first entry* (Muileann dhearg). Donnchadh mac Thormoid, the boy-clerk, is set at fifteen to render the ruling clean for Leabhar a' Chùraim, after it has lain four years in rough marks: one sealed measure a ship, a single household's season, Taigh na Fèithe's own mark. He copies it exactly as given, though he notices it carries no blessing, as other entries do.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0016"><em>The handful for the new hearth</em>, 17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 25</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2007"></a>**2 an Giblean, LE 29** — *The queen at Seann Skell to see the stones laid* (Seann Skell). Beathag rides the twenty-four miles to Seann Skell and stands on the new-laid stone of the west quay in the evening light, the only time she is known to have come to see the fleet's building with her own eyes. Her sister Mòrag joins her there, and the two speak of small things, not of the roll.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2008"></a>**1 an Cèitean, LE 29** — *Death of Uilleam mac Iain, the queen's consort* (Cathair dhearg). Uilleam mac Iain, husband to Queen Beathag and father of her son, dies after a summer's illness. The queen keeps the funeral small, a single day at Cathair dhearg with the household and a few custodian heads, and no great muster of the shires.
- <a id="ev-III-0017"></a>**16 an t-Iuchar, LE 30** — *The west quay lengthened* (Seann Skell). Masons from the capital lengthen the west quay at Seann Skell with dressed stone, so that the deep hulls may lie alongside at low water. On these stones the later rite was held.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2005"><em>The queen lends masons for the quay</em>, 4 am Màrt, LE 28</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2007"><em>The queen at Seann Skell to see the stones laid</em>, 2 an Giblean, LE 29</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2009"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, LE 30** — *Death of Eòghann mac Mhuirich* (Muileann dhearg). The master of Taigh na Fèithe, who wrote the first count of the departing households in LE 3, dies at Taigh na Fèithe grown very old, soon after seeing the ruling of the coal for the departing set down and its first measures sealed.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2010"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 30** — *The iron cramp of the last stone* (Seann Skell). Ailean mac Nèill's gang sets the last stone of the lengthened quay at the seaward end, where the new masonry meets the old timber staging, and Ailean drives home the iron cramp that binds them with three blows and no more.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0017"><em>The west quay lengthened</em>, 16 an t-Iuchar, LE 30</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2011"></a>**28 an t-Ògmhios, LE 37** — *Tormod mac Coinnich remembers the dearth of his boyhood* (Àth shean). As the council weighs how much grain the fleet may take, the reeve of the granaries at Àth shean turns over an old memory: a reeve before him who smiled and gave no grain, and a store-house that stood swept and empty a whole hungry spring. He resolves that his own stores will not be opened on a smile.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2012"></a>**27 an t-Iuchar, LE 37** — *A lean harvest in the south shires* (Àth shean). The barley comes in thin across the shires south of the mountain, the fourth-poorest harvest in eleven years by the granary reeve's own tallies. The stores at Àth shean, well kept, would see the country through to spring, but word soon comes that the fleet's crossing must be fed from them too.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2013"></a>**25 an Lùnastal, LE 37** — *The council of An Talla Dearg divided on the grain* (Cathair dhearg). Through the autumn the queen's council argues over how much stored grain the departing may carry, some holding that no household should cross open water without bread enough, others that Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig was never meant to measure a granary. The queen gives no opinion any rider carries south.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2014"></a>**23 an t-Sultain, LE 37** — *Petitioners come to the barred granary* (Àth shean). With no ruling yet come from the capital, petitioners for the fleet's stores gather at Tormod mac Coinnich's door at Àth shean on no authority he can name. He bars the store-house doors and sets a watch of four, and turns away captain's steward and quiet petitioner alike until the council's own seal comes down.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2015"></a>**22 an Dàmhair, LE 37** — *The watch stands through the winter* (Àth shean). Four men keep the granary doors at Àth shean through Samhnas and Dubhlas and the black months after, relieved every third day, while riders come from the capital with sealed leaves that settle nothing. Tormod mac Coinnich walks the round with them most nights, unable to say when, or whether, the matter will be settled.
- <a id="ev-III-0018"></a>**20 an Gearran, LE 38** — *The strife over the grain*. Strife over how much of the island's stored grain the ships may take all but ends the venture. Within a season it is settled; how is not recorded.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2012"><em>A lean harvest in the south shires</em>, 27 an t-Iuchar, LE 37</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2013"><em>The council of An Talla Dearg divided on the grain</em>, 25 an Lùnastal, LE 37</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0019"></a>**21 am Màrt, LE 38** — *Àth shean shuts its granaries* (Àth shean). In the strife over the fleet's grain Tormod mac Coinnich, reeve of the granaries at Àth shean, bars the store-houses and sets a watch on them until the matter is settled. He holds no office afterward.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2011"><em>Tormod mac Coinnich remembers the dearth of his boyhood</em>, 28 an t-Ògmhios, LE 37</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2014"><em>Petitioners come to the barred granary</em>, 23 an t-Sultain, LE 37</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2015"><em>The watch stands through the winter</em>, 22 an Dàmhair, LE 37</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0020"></a>**3 an Giblean, LE 38** — *Grain down Abhainn dhomhain* (Abhainn dhomhain). The strife settled, grain barges go down Abhainn dhomhain to the capital, on by the coast to Ros àrsaidh, and up the Abhainn naomh to Seann Skell. A tally-keeper at Drochaid Cathair dhearg counts forty-one barges passing.
- <a id="ev-III-0021"></a>**2 an Cèitean, LE 38** — *The fleet assembled* (Seann Skell). The fleet lies complete at Seann Skell. The custody-book gives nineteen hulls; a later hand in the margin makes it twenty-one. Which is right has never been settled.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2016"></a>**19 an t-Ògmhios, LE 38** — *The granary doors reopened* (Àth shean). A single rider comes to Àth shean with no sealed leaf, only a word that the grain may move at a fixed measure. Tormod mac Coinnich takes the bar down himself and calls off the watch; how the strife was settled, and by whom, he is never told. He holds no office after, and walks home to his father's farm.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0019"><em>Àth shean shuts its granaries</em>, 21 am Màrt, LE 38</a>; → Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0020"><em>Grain down Abhainn dhomhain</em>, 3 an Giblean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2017"></a>**30 an t-Sultain, LE 38** — *Mairead nic Iain's tally of the barges* (Drochaid Cathair dhearg). On Drochaid Cathair dhearg the tally-keeper Mairead nic Iain cuts a notch in a hazel stick for every laden barge that passes beneath, going down Abhainn dhomhain toward the coast. When the season's grain has all gone by she makes the count forty-one, and writes it down with no more comment than that.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0020"><em>Grain down Abhainn dhomhain</em>, 3 an Giblean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2018"></a>**17 an Dàmhair, LE 38** — *Calum's daughter's household entered* (Seann Skell). At Taigh a' Chalaidh, Calum mac Nèill cuts his own daughter's household onto Rolla nan Deònach: Mairead nic Chaluim, her husband Dùghall mac Iain, a fisher of Inis àrsaidh, and their two small children. His son Dòmhnall sets the cup of ale in his sister's hands, and Calum's hand shakes only once the harbour-house stands empty again.<span class="fn fl">○ Same place <a href="#ev-III-0021"><em>The fleet assembled</em>, 2 an Cèitean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2019"></a>**6 an Dùbhlachd, LE 38** — *The fleet's stores laid in at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The grain that came down Abhainn dhomhain and up the Abhainn naomh is measured out and sealed aboard the hulls at Seann Skell against the fleet's crossing, one measure to a household under Taigh na Fèithe's own ruling. By spring the quay stands full of hulls that had not existed when the first tale of a far shore reached the river road.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0021"><em>The fleet assembled</em>, 2 an Cèitean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2020"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, LE 38** — *Niall mac Dhòmhnaill counts the hulls and loses count* (Seann Skell). Calum's grandson Niall, nine years old, runs the length of the new quay after his lessons, touching each hull's timbers as he passes and trying, unasked, to count the whole fleet. He never once brings the count out even, and a wright who helped lay four of the hulls tells him he could not have done better himself.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0021"><em>The fleet assembled</em>, 2 an Cèitean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2021"></a>**16 am Màrt, LE 39** — *The queen walks the new quay at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). In the moon of Sìolach, Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill comes down to Seann Skell with a small household and walks the whole length of the new stone quay at the harbour scribe's side, saying little, before finding her sister on the strand below.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0021"><em>The fleet assembled</em>, 2 an Cèitean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2022"></a>**14 an Giblean, LE 39** — *The queen and her sister on the stones* (Seann Skell). Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill comes up from the rope-maker's gear to meet her sister on the new stones. What passes between them is not told; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives only that the queen was seen upon the quay with her sister, and went home again before the sailing, as her own word bound her to do.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0021"><em>The fleet assembled</em>, 2 an Cèitean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2023"></a>**11 an t-Ògmhios, LE 39** — *The queen rides home before the sailing* (Seann Skell). Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill leaves Seann Skell the same evening she comes to it, telling the harbour scribe she will not be at the quay for the sailing itself, for a queen who has sworn to send no one over and keep no one back has no cause to watch her own sister taken by that same promise.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0021"><em>The fleet assembled</em>, 2 an Cèitean, LE 38</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0022"></a>**18 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The night of lamps* (Seann Skell). On the last night before the sailing every house on the Seann Skell waterfront sets a lamp on its sill and keeps it burning till morning. It is the first custom of the Sundering written down as a custom, and the town kept it long after its cause had become a tale.
- <a id="ev-III-0023"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The Setting-Out*. The willing sail out past the north cape. The chronicles of the island fall silent on them as the ships clear the harbour; the Dia-thìrich tell that the fleet sailed into Manannan's mist, toward the Otherworld.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2031"><em>The queen hears a boundary plea on the morning of the sailing</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2024"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *Niall given the counting-stick* (Seann Skell). On the eve of the sailing Calum mac Nèill gives his grandson Niall, eleven years old, a shaved hazel stick and a knife, and sets him on the wall of the west quay to cut one notch for every hull that passes in the morning, with the single instruction to keep his eyes on the count and not on the faces.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0022"><em>The night of lamps</em>, 18 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2025"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The lamps lit unasked along the strand* (Seann Skell). Beginning at one widow's window by the fish-stones, a lamp is set on every sill along the Seann Skell waterfront the evening before the sailing, and kept burning until morning, though no one has told the town to do it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0022"><em>The night of lamps</em>, 18 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2026"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *Mairead nic Chaluim's household goes aboard* (Seann Skell). Calum mac Nèill's daughter Mairead, her husband Dùghall mac Iain and their two children take their places aboard their hull on the eve of the sailing, their stores lashed under oiled hide; Mairead asks a deep notch cut for her hull, whichever number it falls at.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0022"><em>The night of lamps</em>, 18 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2027"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *Mòrag walks the waterfront alone* (Seann Skell). On the last night Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill walks the length of the Seann Skell strand twice over, naming to herself the household behind every lit window, a leave-taking asked of no one and told to no one beforehand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0022"><em>The night of lamps</em>, 18 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2028"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *Catrìona takes the steering oar of An Ròn Glas* (Seann Skell). Aboard An Ròn Glas on the eve of the sailing, the pilot Catrìona nic Iain tells Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill that the oar answers well and the ship rides true, whatever else the morning brings.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0022"><em>The night of lamps</em>, 18 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2029"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *Fionnlagh stands by his cart and does not go* (Seann Skell). A carter of Seann Skell named Fionnlagh, who has brought loads down to the quay for departing households all that season without putting his own name to the boards, stands by his empty cart through Oidhche nan Lòchran and through the sailing itself, and does not go aboard any hull.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0022"><em>The night of lamps</em>, 18 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2030"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *Niall's tally of An Diosal* (Seann Skell). On the morning of the sailing Niall mac Dhòmhnaill cuts one notch on his hazel stick for every hull that passes the west quay wall going round the river pool sunwise, and keeps the finished stick inside his shirt afterward; no one ever asks him for it back.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0024"><em>The sunwise turn</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2031"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The queen hears a boundary plea on the morning of the sailing* (Cathair dhearg). At Cathair dhearg, on the same morning the fleet turns out of Seann Skell, Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill hears an ordinary dispute between two farmers over a shifted boundary ditch and rules it with the same care she gives any such matter, no rider from the coast yet able to have reached her.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0023"><em>The Setting-Out</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2032"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The empty berths walked that evening* (Seann Skell). That evening Calum mac Nèill walks the whole length of the west quay and finds the berths standing empty for the first time in three years, and tells his son Dòmhnall that a harbour built for nothing but to be full is a strange thing to walk when it stands empty.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0024"><em>The sunwise turn</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0024"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 40** — *The sunwise turn* (Seann Skell). Before going down the Abhainn naomh to the open sea the fleet goes once round the river pool of Seann Skell sunwise, diosal, for luck, and the watchers on the quay count the hulls as they pass. The harbour scribe's account ends at the foot of the pool.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2030"><em>Niall's tally of An Diosal</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 40</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2032"><em>The empty berths walked that evening</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2501"></a>**6 an t-Samhain, LE 40** — *Leabhar a' Chùraim's entry of the turn* (Muileann dhearg). At Taigh na Fèithe Donnchadh mac Thormoid enters the turn of the fleet into Leabhar a' Chùraim under a day after Samhain, a full turning of the moon and more after every other account sets the sailing itself. The gap between the two dates is copied faithfully and explained by no word in the leaf that reaches him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0024"><em>The sunwise turn</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 40</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0025"></a>**22 am Faoilleach, LE 44** — *The years counted from the turn* (Muileann dhearg). Donnchadh mac Thormoid, scribe of the vein-house, begins to number the years from the sunwise turn at Seann Skell, and calls them the years of the Diosal. The count is his; the crown's scribes take it up a generation later.
- <a id="ev-III-0026"></a>**27 an Dàmhair, LE 44** — *Tidings reach Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). Tidings of the fleet reach Seann Skell, by what road or whose mouth is not told. The harbour scribe copies them in a shaking hand; the copy came down to later keepers water-stained and lacking its end.
- <a id="ev-III-0027"></a>**24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44** — *Two landfalls*. Such broken tidings as come back tell of two coasts reached, not one. In this telling lies the seed of the two peoples that came after.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2502"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44** — *Donnchadh begins Bliadhnaichean an Diosail* (Muileann dhearg). For his own ledger's convenience, and for no reason he offers anyone, Taigh na Fèithe clerk Donnchadh mac Thormoid begins to number years from An Diosal rather than from a reign, working the count backward through his private book to the turn itself. No one above him asks him to keep it, and he tells no one that he does.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0025"><em>The years counted from the turn</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, LE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2503"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44** — *Broken tidings come to the harbour-house* (Seann Skell). Word of the fleet reaches Seann Skell by a boat that does not stay to be questioned. Calum mac Nèill copies the telling that same night in a shaking hand; the letters run smaller toward the leaf's foot, and the copy stops without warning where the telling itself stopped.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0026"><em>Tidings reach Seann Skell</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2504"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44** — *Two shores, not one* (Seann Skell). Calum's leaf tells of two separate landfalls reached by hulls that had not held together the whole crossing, whether by storm, purpose, or a quarrel the telling does not say. It gives no word of which households reached which shore, and its torn end settles nothing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0027"><em>Two landfalls</em>, 24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2505"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44** — *The tidings copied to An Talla Dearg and Taigh na Fèithe* (Seann Skell). A fair copy of Calum's leaf goes by rider to Cathair dhearg for the queen's own council; a second copy, made by his son Dòmhnall, goes east to Taigh na Fèithe, where Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets it beside his own four-year-old entry of the turn and finds the silence between them unexplained by either leaf.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0026"><em>Tidings reach Seann Skell</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2506"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44** — *The council divided over the two shores* (Cathair dhearg). At An Talla Dearg the custodians argue whether two landfalls mean the fleet prospered or was scattered, and which of the nineteen or one-and-twenty hulls reached which coast. Queen Beathag hears the whole of it and says nothing, and the council lets the matter drop for the day's ordinary business.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0027"><em>Two landfalls</em>, 24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2507"></a>**25 an t-Iuchar, LE 45** — *The tale kept two ways at once at Inis àrsaidh* (Inis àrsaidh). The broken telling of two shores reaches the fishing hearths of Inis àrsaidh, which gave more households to the roll than any other place. With no way to know which shore holds which kin, the town keeps both halves of the tale alive together, grieving toward one and hoping toward the other by turns.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0026"><em>Tidings reach Seann Skell</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 44</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2508"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, LE 45** — *Birth of Raghnall mac Raghnaill* (Cathair dhearg). A son, named for his father, is born at Cathair dhearg to Raghnall mac Uilleim, the queen's heir, then seven-and-thirty years old. The boy is Beathag's first grandson and the third of her line under An Talla Dearg's roof.
- <a id="ev-III-0028"></a>**1 an Lùnastal, LE 46** — *Mòrag's line struck* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag strikes her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the succession, as no longer on Dia-thìr. The act stands without comment between a grain ruling and the mending of a bridge.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2509"></a>**30 an Lùnastal, LE 46** — *The grain ruling settled* (Cathair dhearg). A long dispute over grain owed the crown's granaries by the upland shires is settled in the queen's favour, the reeves agreeing at last to a measure put to them in her own hand rather than a steward's.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2510"></a>**21 an t-Sultain, LE 46** — *The bridge at Àth shean mended in stone* (Àth shean). The cracked middle pier of the bridge at Àth shean, shored with timber since a flood two winters before, is rebuilt in stone by masons from the capital, the last props pulled clear on a morning cold enough to break the river's ice.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2511"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, LE 46** — *Mòrag's line struck in the ordinary hand* (Cathair dhearg). Between the grain ruling and the bridge, in the same plain hand as either, the queen has Murchadh mac Eòghainn enter that Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and her children are struck from the succession, as persons no longer on Dia-thìr. Only the old scribe's pen slows at the shaping of the name.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0028"><em>Mòrag's line struck</em>, 1 an Lùnastal, LE 46</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2512"></a>**8 an Dùbhlachd, LE 46** — *Murchadh sands the leaf* (Cathair dhearg). Alone in the near-emptied hall, old Murchadh mac Eòghainn sands the leaf that struck the queen's sister from the roll, the same practised motion he has closed every entry with for forty years, giving away nothing of what lies written beneath the sand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0028"><em>Mòrag's line struck</em>, 1 an Lùnastal, LE 46</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2513"></a>**28 an Cèitean, LE 50** — *The taproom tales of An Tanachadh at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). A coal-carrier's widow tells at the harbour-house that the children born to the departed on the far shore carry less in their hands than their parents did, and less again by the third generation. A custodian down from Taigh na Fèithe answers her over a jug that the coal was never carried in the blood at all, only left behind at Muileann dhearg like a tool in an unvisited shed. Neither tale is tried against anything Seann Skell holds.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2514"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, LE 50** — *A third telling that silences a room* (Seann Skell). A telling heard less often than the other two at Seann Skell holds that nothing thins at all: the far shore never had the coal to answer to, so its children are unremarked only for want of anything to remark them against. It is told least of the three, though it silences a hearth where the others merely fill one.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2515"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, LE 52** — *The rite named an Tùrsa Geal* (Cathair dhearg). The court names the queen's mourning an Tùrsa Geal, and within a generation any household on the island that gave someone to the fleet keeps some form of the same rite unasked, undyed wool and an empty place laid with cup, trencher and straight knife, needing no crown or law behind it.
- <a id="ev-III-0029"></a>**3 an t-Iuchar, LE 53** — *The thinning*. Cut off from the vein, the strength the crossing asked of them fades in the children of those who went. By the third generation over the water nothing is left that Dia-thìr would know.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2513"><em>The taproom tales of An Tanachadh at Seann Skell</em>, 28 an Cèitean, LE 50</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EIV-2514"><em>A third telling that silences a room</em>, 23 an Lùnastal, LE 50</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0030"></a>**28 an t-Sultain, LE 53** — *The custodians' second count* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house counts again the households of the coal-right and sets the loss at one hand in five. Beside it Donnchadh mac Thormoid writes that the vein answers no differently for those who stayed.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2516"></a>**7 an Dàmhair, LE 53** — *Taigh na Fèithe's second count made* (Muileann dhearg). Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now nine-and-thirty, carries the greater share of Taigh na Fèithe's second tallying, checking Rolla nan Deònach against the coal-right's remaining hearths column by column. The count stands where the first count of the roll had stood: one hearth in five gone from the coal-right, no more and no fewer than had sailed.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0030"><em>The custodians' second count</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, LE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2517"></a>**22 an Dàmhair, LE 53** — *Donnchadh's note that the vein answers no differently* (Muileann dhearg). Beneath the count Donnchadh mac Thormoid sets a second line unasked: that the vein answers no differently now to the hands of those who stayed than it answered before the turn, and that whatever thins in the departed's children thins on their own shore, not on this side of the water. It is carried up to Cathair dhearg with the season's reckoning.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0030"><em>The custodians' second count</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, LE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2518"></a>**5 an t-Samhain, LE 53** — *Beathag reads the second count twice* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill reads Taigh na Fèithe's figure of one hand in five, a number she has carried unwritten in her own reckoning since the fleet sailed, and reads Donnchadh's note beneath it a second time more slowly than the first. She sets the leaf down in its place among the season's ordinary business and says no more of it that day.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0030"><em>The custodians' second count</em>, 28 an t-Sultain, LE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2519"></a>**6 an t-Samhain, LE 53** — *The queen first wears the undyed wool* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill comes into An Talla Dearg in plain undyed wool for the first time in more than fifty years of reigning in the deep blue of the house of Dòmhnall, and takes up the day's first petition as though nothing were changed, giving the court no word for it.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2520"></a>**5 an Dùbhlachd, LE 53** — *The empty place first laid at the queen's table* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag lays a cup, a trencher and a straight knife at the foot of her own table each evening she dines in hall, mourning her sister Mòrag with no grave to stand at and no body to wash. The court, told by the queen's steward that she mourns a sister ten years and more beyond any word reaching Cathair dhearg, does not know at first whether to speak of the place or pass it in silence.
- <a id="ev-III-0031"></a>**1 an Lùnastal, LE 54** — *The Mourning Custom*. Dia-thìr sets in order a rite of mourning for the departed, neither wholly grief nor wholly feast. In a far later age it was used again, uneasily, for a very different leaving.
- <a id="ev-III-0032"></a>**27 an Dàmhair, LE 54** — *The white sorrow first kept at court* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag mourns her sister in undyed wool, with one place left empty at a meal that is neither feast nor fast. The court calls it an Tùrsa Geal, the white sorrow, and within a generation it is kept in every harbour town of the island.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2515"><em>The rite named an Tùrsa Geal</em>, 26 an t-Ògmhios, LE 52</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2519"><em>The queen first wears the undyed wool</em>, 6 an t-Samhain, LE 53</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2520"><em>The empty place first laid at the queen's table</em>, 5 an Dùbhlachd, LE 53</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-2521"></a>**13 an t-Samhain, LE 54** — *Donnchadh speaks of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's limit* (Muileann dhearg). At a sitting of Taigh na Fèithe called for another matter, Donnchadh mac Thormoid, now its senior clerk, says plainly that the old apprenticeship built for the numbers before the turn has gone as far as the older custodians' own stretching can carry it, and that Taigh na Fèithe owes itself an honest look at what remains.
- <a id="ev-EIV-2522"></a>**27 an t-Samhain, LE 54** — *The sitting on the seven kindreds argued two days* (Muileann dhearg). A custodian of a small old name that kept a single gallery for three generations speaks bitterly against folding his household's right into a larger kindred. An old woman of Clann Thormoid, who has buried a brother and two nephews to the roll, answers that she would sooner see her right folded into a house that can still walk its galleries than stand alone over ones it cannot serve, and the sitting turns on her answer.
- <a id="ev-III-0033"></a>**7 am Faoilleach, LE 55** — *The custodians fewer*. With part of the coal-bound folk gone, the Dia-thìrich order themselves anew about a smaller and closer class of custodians. From this shape every later nobility descends.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-2521"><em>Donnchadh speaks of Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig's limit</em>, 13 an t-Samhain, LE 54</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-2522"><em>The sitting on the seven kindreds argued two days</em>, 27 an t-Samhain, LE 54</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0034"></a>**4 an t-Iuchar, LE 55** — *The seven houses of custody* (Muileann dhearg).
