Uilleam Ruadh, leader of the sea-thieves for the better part of a decade, is taken alive off Eilean dhubh's strand and carried south in irons to Cathair dhearg, where he is hanged before the season turns, six and thirty years old.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0133"><em>The raid on Eilean dhubh</em>, 27 an t-Samhain, LE 801</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5043"></a>**8 an Giblean, LE 815** — *The dearth on the north-west shore* (Baile chrom). A run of failed harvests along the north-west shore grows more than the shared-meal custom can carry. Coinneach mac Nèill keeps the custom at his own board as long as grain remains to keep it with, dividing what the diminished fields bring in as evenly as his hand can manage.
- <a id="ev-III-0134"></a>**19 an Giblean, LE 819** — *The dearth on the north-west shore* (Gorta Baile chrom). Harvest after harvest fails along the north-west shore, and the dearth is more than the shared meal can bear. Families leave the coast for the inland shires and the east, and the north-west is thinly held from this time to the end of the age.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-5043"><em>The dearth on the north-west shore</em>, 8 an Giblean, LE 815</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5044"></a>**29 an Lùnastal, LE 819** — *Beathag nic Artair dies of the winter's sickness* (Baile chrom). In the hard winter of the dearth, Beathag nic Artair, wife of the reeve of Baile chrom, dies of a chest complaint her body, weakened by two thin harvests running, has no strength left to fight. The last of the town's households load their carts and go inland and east the same season.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0134"><em>The dearth on the north-west shore</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 819</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5045"></a>**4 an Lùnastal, LE 821** — *Coinneach mac Nèill leaves Baile chrom* (Baile chrom). Coinneach mac Nèill, reeve of Baile chrom for eight-and-forty years, sets the reeve's chest of rolls and tallies in order for a successor he no longer believes will come, shuts his own door behind him, and sets the coast road east under his feet.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0134"><em>The dearth on the north-west shore</em>, 19 an Giblean, LE 819</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5046"></a>**30 an Dàmhair, LE 825** — *Birth of Raghnall Òg*. A son, Raghnall, is born at Muileann chrom to Dòmhnall Ruadh, then five-and-thirty years old and keeper of his house's three galleries.
- <a id="ev-III-0135"></a>**20 an Cèitean, LE 829** — *The king-list recopied* (Cathair dhearg). The scribes of Queen Eilidh Bhàn copy the king-list of Dia-thìr afresh from its oldest surviving roll, adding the rulers since the Sundering. The new copy begins the present age with the Choosing and not with the fleet.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5047"></a>**5 an Dùbhlachd, LE 829** — *Clàr nan Rìghrean recopied* (Cathair dhearg). The queen's scribes at Cathair dhearg take down the old Clàr nan Rìghrean from its resting place and copy it afresh onto new hide, adding every ruler since the fleet had gone and setting the new copy's beginning at An Roghnachadh rather than at the sailing.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0135"><em>The king-list recopied</em>, 20 an Cèitean, LE 829</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5048"></a>**10 an Gearran, LE 835** — *The strand-market at Àth fhionn* (Àth fhionn). A market grows up on the strand at Àth fhionn, where the coast road crosses the clear river, trading north-coast fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of the north coast no longer carry their catch the longer road south to Inis mhòr.
- <a id="ev-III-0135a"></a>**19 an Gearran, LE 835** — *The strand-market at Àth fhionn* (Àth fhionn). Àth fhionn, the ford town where the coast road crosses the clear river, holds a market on the strand for the north coast, of fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of the north coast no longer carry their catch to Inis mhòr.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-5048"><em>The strand-market at Àth fhionn</em>, 10 an Gearran, LE 835</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0136"></a>**21 an Giblean, LE 841** — *Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Eilidh Bhàn dies at Cathair dhearg without a child, and the house of Catrìona ends with her. The seven houses meet at the vein-house and not at the capital.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5501"></a>**20 an t-Sultain, LE 841** — *Na Seachd Taighean ride to Taigh na Fèithe rather than An Talla Dearg* (Muileann dhearg). On the queen's death Na Seachd Taighean' messengers pass over the empty capital and ride straight to Taigh na Fèithe above the mountain, choosing to settle the succession among the galleries and Clachan a' Chrannchuir rather than under the house of Catrìona's own roof. No leaf gives the reason; a young scribe of Taigh na Fèithe later says it felt from the first hour less like a choosing than a homecoming.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0136"><em>Eilidh Bhàn dies without an heir</em>, 21 an Giblean, LE 841</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5502"></a>**5 an Cèitean, LE 842** — *Nine days at the long table* (Muileann dhearg). The heads of Na Seachd Taighean sit first nine days at the table under Taigh na Fèithe's north window, and ride up again at every season's turning for five years, while the capital's clerks hold grain prices and boundary pleas unanswered for want of anyone with standing to settle them. At the last sitting the name of Dòmhnall Ruadh of Muileann chrom is spoken and not spoken down again.
- <a id="ev-III-0137"></a>**23 am Màrt, LE 846** — *Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned* (Cathair dhearg). The houses name Dòmhnall Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill, of the line of the claimant slain at Muileann chrom. He is crowned at Cathair dhearg and keeps the mastery of the vein-house with the crown.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-5037"><em>Birth of Dòmhnall Ruadh</em>, 5 an Gearran, LE 790</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5502"><em>Nine days at the long table</em>, 5 an Cèitean, LE 842</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5503"></a>**4 an t-Iuchar, LE 846** — *Dòmhnall Ruadh told whose yard he stands in* (Muileann dhearg). An old custodian takes the newly named Dòmhnall Ruadh aside in Taigh na Fèithe yard and tells him it is the same ground on which Raghnall Ruadh, of his own house, once refused every claimant offered him and shut the door on a season of refused hearths. Dòmhnall Ruadh says only that he hopes to prove a different answer to the same question.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0137"><em>Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned</em>, 23 am Màrt, LE 846</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5504"></a>**9 an Lùnastal, LE 846** — *Dòmhnall Ruadh's household summoned from Muileann chrom*. Riders carry word to Muileann chrom for Dòmhnall Ruadh's wife and two grown sons to come up to Cathair dhearg; he spends his first night as king naming aloud which of his neighbours he trusts to keep his own galleries honestly measured in his absence, troubled more by that than by the crown awaiting him.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0137"><em>Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned</em>, 23 am Màrt, LE 846</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5505"></a>**9 an t-Sultain, LE 846** — *Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned at six-and-fifty* (Cathair dhearg). Dòmhnall Ruadh is crowned at Cathair dhearg nine days after the houses name him, six-and-fifty years old, in a hall his house had never in nearly three hundred years entered as anything but petitioner.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0137"><em>Dòmhnall Ruadh crowned</em>, 23 am Màrt, LE 846</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5506"></a>**9 am Faoilleach, LE 850** — *The king's horse known on the mountain road* (Muileann dhearg). Riding the thirty-nine miles between Cathair dhearg and Taigh na Fèithe so often in the first years of his reign, Dòmhnall Ruadh is known by his horse before his face, and the road's keepers complain that they never shod one animal so often in one man's service.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5507"></a>**6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 855** — *The boundary stone of the shifted stream*. Dòmhnall Ruadh rides down from the capital to Muileann chrom himself to settle a boundary dispute between two households of his own old neighbours, and fixes the stone's place by asking each household's oldest member, separately, where they remember playing as children, rather than by any measuring Taigh na Fèithe owns.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5508"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, LE 855** — *The king keeps his seat at An Talla Dearg* (Cathair dhearg). Pressed by more than one of the seven heads to move the crown's seat to the mountain, since a king who is master of Taigh na Fèithe belongs among the galleries, Dòmhnall Ruadh keeps it at Cathair dhearg for the whole of his five-and-twenty years.
- <a id="ev-III-0138"></a>**6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859** — *The crown and the custody joined* (Muileann dhearg). Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeves write into the custody-book that the ruler of Dia-thìr is also master of the vein-house. Thereafter the heads of the seven houses sit as the king's council, and the custodians and the court are one body.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5506"><em>The king's horse known on the mountain road</em>, 9 am Faoilleach, LE 850</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5508"><em>The king keeps his seat at An Talla Dearg</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, LE 855</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5509"></a>**18 an t-Sultain, LE 859** — *The reeve's entry read out to the king* (Muileann dhearg). Dòmhnall Ruadh's reeve reads him the fair copy of the entry joining the crown to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe before it is set to the king's own mark; Dòmhnall Ruadh says it reads less like a new law than a plain account of what has already been true since the morning in the yard, and the reeve agrees.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0138"><em>The crown and the custody joined</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5510"></a>**21 an Gearran, LE 860** — *Leabhar a' Chùraim and the crown's rolls copied onto one shelf* (Muileann dhearg). Taigh na Fèithe's clerks spend the better part of two years copying Leabhar a' Chùraim and the crown's rolls, kept apart under separate roofs for near three hundred years, onto the same shelves in the same hands, until no leaf of either record can be told from the other at a glance.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0138"><em>The crown and the custody joined</em>, 6 an t-Ògmhios, LE 859</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5511"></a>**23 am Faoilleach, LE 864** — *The metalworker who cuts the seal* (Muileann dhearg). A metalworker of Muileann dhearg who has never before been asked to cut more than a gallery-marker spends near a season on the new seal's die, complaining that the gold will not sit against the blue as he wishes. Dòmhnall Ruadh, seeing it finished, says he can find nothing in it that is properly his to add.
- <a id="ev-III-0138a"></a>**1 an t-Ògmhios, LE 865** — *The custody's seal on the king's letters* (Muileann dhearg). From the joining of the crown and the custody the king's letters bear the vein-house's own seal: a trellis of gold on blue, which the custodians read as the galleries of the mountain, and over it a hollow lozenge for Crom's slab, laid on the first break. The crown adds a white band across the field and nothing more. From this time the seal is the arms of the kingdom.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5511"><em>The metalworker who cuts the seal</em>, 23 am Faoilleach, LE 864</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0139"></a>**10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871** — *Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Dòmhnall Ruadh, the first to hold both the crown and the vein-house, dies at Cathair dhearg and is buried at Muileann dhearg. His son Raghnall Òg is crowned.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-5046"><em>Birth of Raghnall Òg</em>, 30 an Dàmhair, LE 825</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5512"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871** — *Dòmhnall Ruadh buried under the mountain* (Muileann dhearg). Dòmhnall Ruadh is carried, by his own long-standing wish, not to the house of Catrìona's tombs at Cathair dhearg but up to Taigh na Fèithe, where the custodians dig his grave themselves in a worked-out gallery and lay him with a single unlit lamp at his head, a rite kept for no other ruler before or since.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0139"><em>Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5513"></a>**22 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871** — *Raghnall Òg asks to shorten his own coronation* (Cathair dhearg). At the rehearsal of his coronation Raghnall Òg twice asks the clerks whether the ceremony might be shortened by an hour so that he can see a shire plea before dark, more at ease already with a boundary dispute than with a court's ceremony.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0139"><em>Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5514"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871** — *Raghnall Òg crowned at six-and-forty* (Cathair dhearg). Raghnall Òg is crowned at Cathair dhearg after his father's burial under the mountain, six-and-forty years old, keeper already of the crown's shire pleas.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0139"><em>Death of Dòmhnall Ruadh</em>, 10 an Dùbhlachd, LE 871</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0140"></a>**20 an t-Ògmhios, LE 889** — *The schism of the Hawk* (Cnoc bheag). A council of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag divides over whether Mòd's measure may ever be raised. Those who hold it fixed for ever keep the name of the Hungry Hawk and the house at Cnoc bheag; those who hold that a greater flock may be fed a greater handful are called the Fed Hawk.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5515"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, LE 889** — *The young priest's question at Cnoc bheag* (Cnoc bheag). At the council of Òrd an t-Seabhaig a young priest rises to ask the elders whether Mòd himself would rather starve a grown flock than see his old handful grown to meet it. The council turns on the question, and An Seabhag Biadhte is named from that day.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0140"><em>The schism of the Hawk</em>, 20 an t-Ògmhios, LE 889</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0141"></a>**17 an Lùnastal, LE 899** — *The harbour of Seann Chwen* (Seann Chwen). Seann Chwen builds its harbour mole and becomes the port of the coal-carts coming down from the mountain to the coast towns of the south.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5516"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, LE 900** — *The first barges tie up at Seann Chwen's new mole* (Seann Chwen). The first coal-barges of the mountain roads tie up at Seann Chwen's finished stone mole where before they only beached on shingle at low water; a rider carrying the news south remarks that he rode the whole way under one seal without troubling to wonder which office he rode for.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0141"><em>The harbour of Seann Chwen</em>, 17 an Lùnastal, LE 899</a>.</span>

## The Years LE 901 – 1,000

- <a id="ev-III-0142"></a>**23 an Giblean, LE 909** — *The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). The priests of the Fed Hawk, driven from Cnoc bheag, settle at Seann Skell on the north coast, not the western river port of that name. The custody-book writes their teaching down as an error, and at length.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5517"></a>**2 an Lùnastal, LE 910** — *Beathag nic Sheumais builds An Seabhag Biadhte's house* (Seann Skell). Beathag nic Sheumais, nineteen at the schism, builds An Seabhag Biadhte's following at Seann Skell on the north coast from four families to a proper school over two decades, within sound of a sea that has never given the island a word of what lies beyond it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0142"><em>The Fed Hawk at Seann Skell</em>, 23 an Giblean, LE 909</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0143"></a>**25 an Lùnastal, LE 919** — *The Fed Hawk's petition* (Seann Skell). From Seann Skell the Fed Hawk asks the king's council to raise the measured handful by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast. The council refuses. It is the first plea on record to alter the Small-Burning Law.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5518"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 919** — *Beathag nic Sheumais rides south to petition in person* (Cathair dhearg). Rather than trust the asking to a letter, Beathag nic Sheumais rides to Cathair dhearg herself in her fiftieth year and lays the north coast's cold winters before the seven heads without once raising her voice; the council refuses her at length, and she carries the refusal home in her own satchel.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0143"><em>The Fed Hawk's petition</em>, 25 an Lùnastal, LE 919</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0144"></a>**14 an Dàmhair, LE 929** — *The gallery at Cill ghlas* (Cill ghlas). A second tremor in the hills of Cill ghlas brings down a gallery of the vein and kills fourteen labourers of the custodians. The vein-house closes the gallery and sets at its mouth a stone with the fourteen names.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5519"></a>**24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 929** — *The fourteen named at the gallery's mouth* (Cill ghlas). Taigh na Fèithe sets a stone with the fourteen names of Cill ghlas cut in the order they went down, the youngest a boy of thirteen, the oldest a woman forty years at the same gallery. Households of the mountain take up the custom of leaving their own small stones at its foot on the day of the fall.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0144"><em>The gallery at Cill ghlas</em>, 14 an Dàmhair, LE 929</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5520"></a>**14 an Lùnastal, LE 938** — *A head of the seven names the fourteen before the council* (Cathair dhearg). Laying the matter of the coal-roads before the king's council, one of the seven heads says plainly that fourteen names on a stone at a gallery's mouth are proof enough the mountain's coal is given up at a real cost, and that no house's quarrel has business stopping it on the road. None of the seven speaks against him.
- <a id="ev-III-0145"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, LE 939** — *The coal-roads kept by the crown* (Cathair dhearg). The king's council takes the roads from the mountain to the coast into the crown's keeping, that no house may stop the carts bearing the measured coal to the temples. The roads are marked with posts bearing the crown's sign: the carriers' road down to Cathair dhearg, An Rathad Tuath over the pass by Muileann fhada, Slighe Muileann dhearg south from the hills by Muileann chrom, and Slighe Baile òg down to the southern Seann Skell.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5520"><em>A head of the seven names the fourteen before the council</em>, 14 an Lùnastal, LE 938</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5521"></a>**21 an t-Samhain, LE 939** — *The posts driven along the coal-roads* (Muileann dhearg). Coal-carters hired for the season and paid from the roads' own tolls drive posts the length of all four coal-roads through a single autumn, a trellis and a hollow stone cut at every shire joint, without ceremony or a word said over the last post.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0145"><em>The coal-roads kept by the crown</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, LE 939</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5522"></a>**29 an t-Samhain, LE 939** — *A carter's answer, remembered afterward*. A carter who helped set posts on three of the four coal-roads is asked the next spring what the work was like, and says only that a man can now walk any of them from the mountain to the sea and never lose the road for want of knowing whose it is; his answer outlives the council's own leaf of the debate.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0145"><em>The coal-roads kept by the crown</em>, 12 an t-Samhain, LE 939</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0145a"></a>**17 an Gearran, LE 944** — *The crown's riders* (Cathair dhearg). Fresh horses are kept for the crown's riders at the waypoint houses on the coal-roads, and a rider changing at every house carries the council's word from Cathair dhearg to the mountain between dawn and dark. The stabling is paid out of the coal-road tolls.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5523"></a>**23 am Màrt, LE 944** — *Mairead nic Aonghais's three tallies* (Cathair dhearg). The keeper of a road-house on the northern coal-road keeps three notched sticks beside the reeve's own tally of the crown's riders: one for every rider through, one for those who thank her by name, and one for those carrying business she judges not worth the horse it rode on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0145a"><em>The crown's riders</em>, 17 an Gearran, LE 944</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0146"></a>**17 an Lùnastal, LE 949** — *The high pastures of Doire uaine forsaken* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). The last shepherd families leave the high pastures of the Doire uaine hills for the valley villages. They give the grazing as the reason; every one of them speaks also of the Marbh-bheò.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5524"></a>**7 an Dàmhair, LE 949** — *The last shieling of Doire uaine* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). An old woman drives her last three goats and a lame ewe down from her own shieling in the high pastures of Doire uaine, the last of her country to come down, and tells the priest who meets her at the valley's edge that a place can grow tired of being lived in alone by living things.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0146"><em>The high pastures of Doire uaine forsaken</em>, 17 an Lùnastal, LE 949</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5525"></a>**6 am Faoilleach, LE 953** — *A drover crosses the empty pastures* (Marbh-bheò Doire uaine). A drover taking cattle to the lowland market by the old high road finds the whole stretch of the forsaken shielings of Doire uaine silent from end to end, not a dog barking nor a hearth smoking, and pushes his herd on rather than camp the night on ground nobody is left to grant or refuse.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0146"><em>The high pastures of Doire uaine forsaken</em>, 17 an Lùnastal, LE 949</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0147"></a>**9 an Lùnastal, LE 959** — *The salt fair at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). Ros fhionn holds its great salt fair, and the reeve counts some four thousand people on the flats in a single day. It is the height of the town, and the chronicle calls it the richest place in the north-east.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5526"></a>**30 an Lùnastal, LE 959** — *Four thousand counted on the salt flats* (Ros fhionn). The reeve of Ros fhionn's salt fair loses his own count somewhere past four thousand among the carts, pack-mules and children on the flats, and writes the figure down rounded rather than pretend to a precision the crowd never held still for.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0147"><em>The salt fair at Ros fhionn</em>, 9 an Lùnastal, LE 959</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0148"></a>**31 an Dàmhair, LE 969** — *Cathair mhòr the largest town* (Cathair mhòr). Cathair mhòr, its market drawing the trade of all the south, grows greater than the capital. The capital remains the seat of the crown, and the lesser town.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5527"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 969** — *A carter's plain answer* (Cathair mhòr). Asked by a clerk of An Talla Dearg why he sells his barley at Cathair mhòr and not the capital, a carter of the southern road answers that a man carries his load to whichever gate opens first and pays best; the clerk enters the answer as given.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0148"><em>Cathair mhòr the largest town</em>, 31 an Dàmhair, LE 969</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0149"></a>**18 an t-Sultain, LE 979** — *The stair at Toll-dubh* (Toll-dubh). Quarrymen north of the capital break into Toll-dubh, the shaft of the old tales, long lost, and find a stair cut in the rock going down beyond their lamps. The custodians of the vein-house wall up the entrance. The one quarryman who went down never tells what he saw.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5528"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, LE 979** — *The quarry face opens on Toll-dubh* (Toll-dubh). A stubborn seam on the quarry face north of the capital swings inward on nothing and opens on a cold, scentless dark; the quarryman Calum Dubh mac Iain names the shaft Toll-dubh before any other man on the ledge can, and the whole crew falls silent.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0149"><em>The stair at Toll-dubh</em>, 18 an t-Sultain, LE 979</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5529"></a>**12 an Dàmhair, LE 979** — *Calum Dubh climbs the stair* (Toll-dubh). Calum Dubh mac Iain goes down the stair of Toll-dubh alone with a lamp and a paid-out rope while his fellows watch the light dwindle and vanish; he climbs out again, sits a long while on the loose stone, and tells the foreman only that the face must be closed.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0149"><em>The stair at Toll-dubh</em>, 18 an t-Sultain, LE 979</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5530"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, LE 979** — *Leabhar a' Chùraim takes Calum Dubh's silence as given* (Toll-dubh). Taigh na Fèithe's custodians wall the mouth of Toll-dubh within a month and enter Calum Dubh mac Iain's own brief account of the walling exactly as he gives it, adding nothing to fill out what he leaves unsaid.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0149"><em>The stair at Toll-dubh</em>, 18 an t-Sultain, LE 979</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0150"></a>**11 an Gearran, LE 994** — *The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr begin to make cooking pots, which are sold on every road of the island. Each bears its maker's sign, and some are still found in the ground.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5531"></a>**18 an Gearran, LE 994** — *The copper-workers' maker's marks* (Cathair mhòr). The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr stamp every cooking pot with its own maker's mark, a leaf, a fish or a plain letter, and the pots go out on every road at once, carried by hands their makers will never meet.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0150"><em>The copper-workers of Cathair mhòr</em>, 11 an Gearran, LE 994</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5532"></a>**4 an t-Sultain, LE 995** — *A saying born of a silent man* (Cathair dhearg). The quarry town takes up a way of speaking of any close-mouthed man, that he has gone down and come up like Calum Dubh, and the saying outgrows him within a generation, applied to men who never went near Toll-dubh at all.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0149"><em>The stair at Toll-dubh</em>, 18 an t-Sultain, LE 979</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0151"></a>**31 am Faoilleach, LE 999** — *Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill* (Làrach an Teampaill). Ailean mac Dhùghaill, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, measures the ruin of Làrach an Teampaill and writes that its altar faces the central mountains and not the sea. Who set it so he will not guess.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5533"></a>**9 an Gearran, LE 999** — *Ailean measures the temple-ruin's altar* (Làrach an Teampaill). Ailean mac Dhùghaill lays his cord across the altar-stone of Làrach an Teampaill and finds it faces the central mountains, its back to the sea, a plain fact no teller of the ruin's tales had ever thought worth the mentioning; he says only that he will not guess who set the stone so.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0151"><em>Ailean measures Làrach an Teampaill</em>, 31 am Faoilleach, LE 999</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5534"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, LE 1,000** — *Birth of Mòrag Ruadh*. A daughter, Mòrag, red-haired and called Mòrag Ruadh, is born into Clann Raghnaill; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives the house and the year, for no one yet has cause to write more.

## The Years LE 1,001 – 1,100

- <a id="ev-EIV-5535"></a>**12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,004** — *The farmer's barrowload of stone*. A farmer whose plough turns up stone every spring at the edge of his field meets Ailean mac Dhùghaill at Làrach an Dùin with a barrowload of it, half in earnest asking whether the school will pay for what his own ground keeps giving back; Ailean measures every stone and buys none of them.
- <a id="ev-III-0152"></a>**20 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,011** — *Ailean's tables of the old ruins* (Làrach an Dùin-fhaire). Ailean mac Dhùghaill finishes his tables of Làrach an Dùin-fhaire, Làrach an Dùin and Làrach an Teampaill, with the measure, stone and lie of each. He cannot say whether one people built all three, and because of his tables no scholar after him could say either.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5535"><em>The farmer's barrowload of stone</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,004</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5536"></a>**26 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,011** — *The school judges Ailean's tables*. The school at Dùn thais argues a winter over Ailean mac Dhùghaill's finished tables of the three old ruins and judges only that his measurements stand sound and his caution on their makers sounder still, closing the question no scholar after him could reopen.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0152"><em>Ailean's tables of the old ruins</em>, 20 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,011</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5537"></a>**25 am Màrt, LE 1,015** — *Death of Calum Dubh mac Iain, still silent* (Toll-dubh). Calum Dubh mac Iain dies in his own house in his sixty-fifth year, well liked in the quarry town for a quiet kindness, having told no living soul, wife, son or scribe, what he saw on the stair under the hill.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0149"><em>The stair at Toll-dubh</em>, 18 an t-Sultain, LE 979</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5538"></a>**17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,017** — *The steward's mistaken tally* (Cathair dhearg). The girl Mòrag Ruadh finds her own small wax-board tally of the hall's candles does not agree with the steward Pàdraig mac Ìomhair's great ledger; he finds the fault his own, a tally-mark set down twice, and sets his sums before her eyes from that evening forward.
- <a id="ev-III-0153"></a>**23 am Faoilleach, LE 1,019** — *Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Mòrag Ruadh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. Hers are the first household accounts of a ruler that survive whole.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-5534"><em>Birth of Mòrag Ruadh</em>, 11 an Dàmhair, LE 1,000</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5538"><em>The steward's mistaken tally</em>, 17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,017</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5539"></a>**21 an Lùnastal, LE 1,019** — *Na Seachd Taighean name Mòrag Ruadh* (Muileann dhearg). Na Seachd Taighean, meeting at Taigh na Fèithe on the death of the old king, send word to Cathair dhearg within the month that the crown will go to the girl of Clann Raghnaill who keeps her own small tally beside the steward's; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives four lines and no reason beyond her house and her blood.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0153"><em>Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned</em>, 23 am Faoilleach, LE 1,019</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5540"></a>**11 an t-Sultain, LE 1,019** — *The queen's own book bound* (Cathair dhearg). Mòrag Ruadh has a vellum ledger bound within the month of her crowning, clasped in iron rather than silver at her own asking, and enters the cost of her own coronation feast on its first page, signed under her own name.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0153"><em>Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned</em>, 23 am Faoilleach, LE 1,019</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5541"></a>**16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,019** — *Mòrag Ruadh crowned at nineteen* (Cathair dhearg). Mòrag Ruadh is crowned at Cathair dhearg at nineteen, the youngest ruler An Talla Dearg has seen since Eilidh Bhàn, and keeps her own small tally beside the steward's from the first day.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0153"><em>Queen Mòrag Ruadh crowned</em>, 23 am Faoilleach, LE 1,019</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0154"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,034** — *The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). The priests of the Hawk at Cnoc bheag clear the moss from the obelisk of Carragh Cnoc bheag and try to read the old letters on it. They cannot, and they write down that they tried.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5542"></a>**12 an t-Samhain, LE 1,034** — *Tòmas clears the moss from Carragh Cnoc bheag* (Carragh Cnoc bheag). The priest Tòmas mac Aonghais spends a month clearing moss from Carragh Cnoc bheag with wooden scrapers rather than iron, and finds, once the stone stands bare, letters cut deep and old that answer to no shape the schools' own tables keep.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0154"><em>The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned</em>, 18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,034</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5543"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,034** — *The queen asks after the unread stone* (Cathair dhearg). Hearing the report of Carragh Cnoc bheag cleared read to her hall, Mòrag Ruadh enters the cost of Tòmas mac Aonghais's oil and vellum into her own book without comment, and asks only whether the priests mean to try the letters again; the answer she is given is that they do not know.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0154"><em>The obelisk at Carragh Cnoc bheag cleaned</em>, 18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,034</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0155"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, LE 1,039** — *Caol shean's fishing year* (Caol shean). Caol shean, whose boats fish the east coast from the mouth of the Abhainn chaol, lands the greatest catch in its rolls, so great that the salt runs short and half is dried in the wind. The dried fish sells poorly, and the town goes back to salting.
- <a id="ev-III-0156"></a>**15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039** — *The thousandth year* (Seann Skell). The vein-house marks the thousandth year of its count with a single measured burning of the coal on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell, and Queen Mòrag Ruadh is there. It is told that the flame burned the colour of the vein, and that the crowd went home without a word.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5544"></a>**20 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039** — *Ruairidh mac Neacail hangs the catch in the wind* (Caol shean). When Caol shean's salt runs out on the second day of its greatest catch, the shed-foreman Ruairidh mac Neacail hangs what cannot be salted on lines strung the length of the lower town's lanes rather than let it spoil on the strand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0155"><em>Caol shean's fishing year</em>, 19 an t-Sultain, LE 1,039</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5545"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039** — *The queen judges the thousandth year a measure and no more* (Cathair dhearg). Asked by Na Seachd Taighean whether Taigh na Fèithe's thousandth year deserves a feast or a fast, Mòrag Ruadh judges between them: one burning on the quay the count began from, no more coal in it than an ordinary hearth burns of an evening.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0156"><em>The thousandth year</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5546"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039** — *The queen's journey to Seann Skell* (Seann Skell). Mòrag Ruadh rides down to Seann Skell over roads already hard with the season's first frosts to stand at Cidhe an Diosail for the thousandth year's burning, a week's journey she makes to see the measure kept rather than take a scribe's report of it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0156"><em>The thousandth year</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5547"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039** — *The queen's entry for the burning* (Seann Skell). Where another ruler's book might have set down a verse for a thousand years made into one evening's fire, Mòrag Ruadh's own book gives the cost of the coal reckoned to Taigh na Fèithe's weights, and beneath it five words: one handful, nothing more.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0156"><em>The thousandth year</em>, 15 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,039</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5548"></a>**5 am Faoilleach, LE 1,040** — *Caol shean returns to salting* (Caol shean). The dried catch sells poorly against salted fish, fetching less at market than a middling salted season the year before; Caol shean lays in salt from that year for a catch half again the size of any it has yet taken.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0155"><em>Caol shean's fishing year</em>, 19 an t-Sultain, LE 1,039</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5549"></a>**3 an Gearran, LE 1,040** — *Birth of Beathag Fhionn* (Cathair dhearg). Mòrag Ruadh's daughter is born at Cathair dhearg and named Beathag before the child is a day old; the queen's book holds one line for the day and the name, set apart from the ordinary sums in a hand less steady than usual.
- <a id="ev-III-0156a"></a>**28 an Giblean, LE 1,051** — *The market above the mill-race* (Cnoc bhàn). The hill-lords of Baile ghorm hold a market for the farms of the south-east at Cnoc bhàn, above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada. Its common goods are grain, clay and honey. Its rare good is pearls, which the women of the shore take from the mussel beds in the shallows, and which no other market sells.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5550"></a>**3 an Lùnastal, LE 1,051** — *The mill-race market opened above Muileann fhada* (Cnoc bhàn). The hill-lords of Baile ghorm set a single market at Cnoc bhàn above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada to gather the south-east's scattered trade in one place, its rare good the pearls no other market sells in whole parcels.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0156a"><em>The market above the mill-race</em>, 28 an Giblean, LE 1,051</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5551"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,051** — *Sìne nic Ruairidh sells a season's pearls whole* (Cnoc bhàn). The shore-woman Sìne nic Ruairidh brings a whole season's gathering to the mill-race market's first opening rather than sell it a pearl or two at a time along the road, and a trader of Cathair mhòr pays her more for the lot than she has ever been offered piecemeal.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0156a"><em>The market above the mill-race</em>, 28 an Giblean, LE 1,051</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0157"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, LE 1,064** — *The blue dyers of Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). The dyers of Baile ghorm in the south-east make a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own. Cloth of Baile ghorm blue becomes the feast-day dress of the seven houses.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5552"></a>**4 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,064** — *Oighrig nic Ailein fixes Baile ghorm's blue* (Baile ghorm). After ten years changing one thing at a time in her own mordant, the dyer Oighrig nic Ailein finds a mixing that holds Baile ghorm's blue fast through washing after washing; cloth of it is worn within the year at Taigh na Fèithe's midwinter gathering.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0157"><em>The blue dyers of Baile ghorm</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, LE 1,064</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5553"></a>**20 an t-Samhain, LE 1,070** — *Birth of Ailean, son of Beathag Fhionn* (Cathair dhearg). A son, Ailean, is born at Cathair dhearg to Beathag Fhionn, the queen's daughter, then thirty years old, in the one-and-fiftieth year of Mòrag Ruadh's reign.
- <a id="ev-III-0158"></a>**29 an Lùnastal, LE 1,079** — *The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain* (Muileann dhomhain). A sickness that closes the throat breaks out at Muileann dhomhain and moves along the coast road. The town loses near a third of its people.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5554"></a>**22 an Dàmhair, LE 1,079** — *Word of the cough reaches An Talla Dearg* (Cathair dhearg). A rider who has ridden the eighteen miles from Muileann dhomhain without stopping to eat brings word of a sickness that closes the throat. Beathag Fhionn, thirty-nine and eleven years at her mother's right hand, sets down the tally she is reading.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0158"><em>The swallowing cough at Muileann dhomhain</em>, 29 an Lùnastal, LE 1,079</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0159"></a>**26 an Cèitean, LE 1,081** — *The cough at Seann Bhral* (Seann Bhral). The swallowing cough comes to the port of Seann Bhral. The townsfolk themselves close the harbour, and keep the shared meal by leaving food at the town gate.
- <a id="ev-III-0160"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,082** — *Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Fhionn, crowned after her mother Mòrag, closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets reeves at the fords to turn travellers back. The cough goes no further west.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5555"></a>**25 an Lùnastal, LE 1,082** — *Reeves set at the fords against the cough* (Cathair dhearg). Newly crowned, Beathag Fhionn closes the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain and sets a reeve at each of the road's six fords with orders to turn back every traveller until the road is released. Chosen mostly from the towns nearest their own crossing, the six hold the road shut for three years, and the cough never crosses west of them.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0160"><em>Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,082</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5556"></a>**14 an t-Sultain, LE 1,082** — *The ford-reeve turns back his own brother* (Muileann dhomhain). At the crossing nearest Muileann dhomhain, the reeve Seumas mac Coinnich turns back his own brother, who has come to the closed road to reach their dying mother on its far side. He tells him the order holds for every traveller or for none. Their mother dies within the week, and the brothers do not speak again for five years.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0160"><em>Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,082</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5557"></a>**28 an t-Sultain, LE 1,082** — *Death of Queen Mòrag Ruadh* (Cathair dhearg). Mòrag Ruadh dies at Cathair dhearg at two-and-eighty, sixty-three years crowned, the longest reign An Talla Dearg has yet entered. Her own ledger, clasped in iron, is closed on its last sum.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0160"><em>Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,082</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5558"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, LE 1,082** — *Beathag Fhionn crowned at two-and-forty* (Cathair dhearg). Beathag Fhionn is crowned in the hall her mother held sixty-three years, forty-two years old and grey already at the temples; the first act set down under her own seal is the closing of the coast road.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0160"><em>Queen Beathag Fhionn closes the roads</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,082</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5559"></a>**25 am Faoilleach, LE 1,095** — *The reeve of Muileann dhomhain walks the lower street* (Muileann dhomhain). The old reeve of Muileann dhomhain, who lost a wife and a son to the cough, walks the lower street once a season and writes down which roofs have fallen in since his last walking; the town stands at less than two households in three.

## The Years LE 1,101 – 1,200

- <a id="ev-III-0161"></a>**5 an Lùnastal, LE 1,104** — *Muileann dhomhain resettled* (Muileann dhomhain). Families from the hills about Muileann dhomhain settle the town that the swallowing cough emptied, and take the empty houses by lot. The older families of the town say they never again knew half their neighbours.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5559"><em>The reeve of Muileann dhomhain walks the lower street</em>, 25 am Faoilleach, LE 1,095</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5560"></a>**23 an Dàmhair, LE 1,104** — *Three brothers from Caol dhearg come down* (Muileann dhomhain). Three brothers, sons of a hill farmer of Caol dhearg, walk down to Muileann dhomhain and take empty houses on the lower street, land already cleared and walls already standing being cheaper than any new house on a hillside.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0161"><em>Muileann dhomhain resettled</em>, 5 an Lùnastal, LE 1,104</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5561"></a>**7 an t-Samhain, LE 1,118** — *A carter's mule lost at Drochaid Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The road bed of Drochaid Ros fhionn gives way under a salt-carter's mule one wet spring; the mule drowns in its traces and the carter is left standing waist-deep in the Abhainn bheag holding a dripping harness.
- <a id="ev-III-0162"></a>**13 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,119** — *Drochaid Ros fhionn repaired* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). The arches of Drochaid Ros fhionn, worn by seven centuries of salt carts, are built anew at the cost of the salt-masters of Ros fhionn, whose names are cut on the keystones.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-5561"><em>A carter's mule lost at Drochaid Ros fhionn</em>, 7 an t-Samhain, LE 1,118</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0163"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,129** — *Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag Fhionn, who closed the coast road against the cough, dies at Cathair dhearg. Her son Ailean is crowned, first of four kings of that name in the house of Raghnall.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-5553"><em>Birth of Ailean, son of Beathag Fhionn</em>, 20 an t-Samhain, LE 1,070</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5562"></a>**10 an Dàmhair, LE 1,129** — *Beathag Fhionn's last question* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Beathag Fhionn dies at Cathair dhearg at eighty-nine, dictating a grain ruling the morning she takes to her bed; her last question to the young scribe beside her is whether the road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain still stands open.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0163"><em>Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn</em>, 2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,129</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-5563"></a>**11 an Dàmhair, LE 1,129** — *Ailean crowned at nine-and-fifty* (Cathair dhearg). Ailean, son of Beathag Fhionn, is crowned at Cathair dhearg within the season of his mother's death, nine-and-fifty years old and no longer a young man by any measure the hall can offer.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0163"><em>Death of Queen Beathag Fhionn</em>, 2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,129</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0164"></a>**13 am Màrt, LE 1,139** — *The Baile ghorm blue fades* (Baile ghorm). The last dyer who knew the Baile ghorm mordant dies without apprentices, having quarrelled with both of hers. The blue that follows is the common blue of the rest of the island.
- <a id="ev-III-0165"></a>**11 an Giblean, LE 1,149** — *The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned* (Dùn ìseal). Lightning fires the ancestor-posts at Dùn ìseal. The keepers cut the names again from memory and from the custody-book, and own in their roll that some are guesses.
- <a id="ev-EIV-5564"></a>**15 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,150** — *The names cut again at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). Setting new ancestor-posts in the old ground the season after lightning burns the old ones to their footings, the keepers of Dùn ìseal cut the names again as best their own memories and their neighbours' can give them back.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0165"><em>The ancestor-posts of Dùn ìseal burned</em>, 11 an Giblean, LE 1,149</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0166"></a>**29 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,159** — *The silting of Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). A shifting bar below Ros fhionn silts up the Abhainn bheag, and the salt barges can no longer reach the quays. The salt-masters take their trade to Caol gharbh on the coast.
- <a id="ev-III-0167"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,169** — *Caol gharbh takes the salt* (Caol gharbh). Caol gharbh, a fishing village, becomes the salt port of the north-east, and its harbour is dug out and walled with the money of the Ros fhionn masters.
- <a id="ev-III-0167a"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,169** — *The stone on the neck* (Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich). Caol gharbh and Caol chrom, the two harbours of the strait, send their headmen to a stone on the neck of land between them, and there settle the dues the salt-boats pay to each. Thereafter they meet at that stone over every quarrel of the strait, and it is called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich, the meeting of the neck.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6001"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, LE 1,170** — *A barge broken at Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich* (Caol gharbh). A laden barge out of the new harbour at Caol gharbh misjudges the tide at the narrows called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich and strikes the reef, going down with half her salt still aboard. Both crewmen swim ashore alive. The harbour-masters set the channel's first withy at the rock the following spring.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0167"><em>Caol gharbh takes the salt</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,169</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6002"></a>**29 an t-Sultain, LE 1,172** — *The last bridge-keeper of Drochaid Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The keeper of Drochaid Ros fhionn dies with no daughter or kinsman willing to take up the toll, and the crown's reeve at Ros fhionn lets the office lapse rather than name a stranger to it. The toll-gate stands open thereafter, and no crossing is ever again refused for want of a toll.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6003"></a>**28 an Dàmhair, LE 1,173** — *The market-court's answer* (Ros fhionn). Asked whether Ros fhionn's market-court should follow its trade to Caol gharbh, the court's own clerks answer that a court sits where disputes are brought to it, not where the season's cargo happens to lie, and the bench of two-hundred-year oak is not moved.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6004"></a>**26 an t-Samhain, LE 1,176** — *Seòlaid Ros fhionn withied* (Ros fhionn). The channel above the flats where the barge was lost is marked from the old bar to open water with a line of withies, Seòlaid Ros fhionn, so that a new pilot may learn the crossing in a season rather than the ten years the old salt-masters once needed.
- <a id="ev-III-0168"></a>**20 an Cèitean, LE 1,179** — *Drochaid Ros fhionn falls quiet* (Drochaid Ros fhionn). The salt going by sea from Caol gharbh, the carts no longer cross Drochaid Ros fhionn. The office of bridge-keeper is done away with, and from this time the bridge is little used.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6002"><em>The last bridge-keeper of Drochaid Ros fhionn</em>, 29 an t-Sultain, LE 1,172</a>; ⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-EIV-6003"><em>The market-court's answer</em>, 28 an Dàmhair, LE 1,173</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-6004"><em>Seòlaid Ros fhionn withied</em>, 26 an t-Samhain, LE 1,176</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0168a"></a>**16 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,184** — *The market-court stays at Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The salt-masters take their ships to Caol gharbh but leave their market-court on the headland at Ros fhionn, where the weights and tally-sticks are kept. The farms and forges of the north-eastern hills still bring their goods there, and the town keeps its market after it has lost its harbour.
- <a id="ev-III-0168b"></a>**25 am Màrt, LE 1,189** — *Seòlaid Ros fhionn* (Ros fhionn). The salt of Ros fhionn now goes by sea: its boats run down the river past Caol gharbh, round the north-east cape, south along the eastern shore past Seann Tarr and Àth bheag, and west again into the bay below Caol shean, where the salt goes inland. The lane is called Seòlaid Ros fhionn after the town whose salt made it, and the eastern boats keep it long after the salt-pans fail.
- <a id="ev-III-0169"></a>**15 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,189** — *The millers of Muileann shean* (Muileann shean). The mills of Muileann shean are fitted with a new gearing, cut in oak, that turns two stones from one wheel. Within a lifetime it spreads to the mills of the north.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6005"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,189** — *Raghnall mac Chaluim sent to Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). A priest of the schools of the stag, hearing a shepherd's son of the north-west coast count and recount a flock through an afternoon, tells the boy's father the child belongs at a house of disputation. Raghnall mac Chaluim, fourteen years old, is sent south to Dùn thais the following spring.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6006"></a>**25 am Faoilleach, LE 1,195** — *The gearing model hung over the millers' door*. The millers of Muileann shean, who first cut the gearing that lets one wheel turn two stones, hang a carved model of it over their own door, a boast that grows quieter with every mill in the north that copies it without asking leave.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0169"><em>The millers of Muileann shean</em>, 15 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,189</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0170"></a>**21 an Giblean, LE 1,199** — *The Sea-Watcher off the north-west* (Uilebheist na Mara). Fishers of the thinned north-west coast see the Sea-Watcher, Uilebheist na Mara, near enough to foul their nets. The few boats still working those waters draw further in.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6007"></a>**21 an Gearran, LE 1,200** — *Birth of Ailean mac Raghnaill* (Cathair dhearg). A son, Ailean, is born in Sliochd Raghnaill, the crown's own house since the reign of Mòrag Ruadh; Leabhar a' Chùraim gives the year and the house and no more.

## The Years LE 1,201 – 1,300

- <a id="ev-EIV-6008"></a>**13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,205** — *Raghnall begins the count of years* (Dùn thais). Raghnall mac Chaluim, thirty years old, begins setting the birth and death rolls of the custodian houses beside those of their tenants at Dùn thais, a labour that will occupy his lamplit evenings for nine years before he brings any finding before Taigh na Deasbaid.
- <a id="ev-III-0171"></a>**29 an t-Samhain, LE 1,209** — *The table of years at Dùn thais* (Dùn thais). Raghnall mac Chaluim, a scholar of the druid school at Dùn thais, sets out a table showing that the heads of the custodian houses live some years longer, on the whole, than the tenants of their lands. He asks whether the vein answers the hand that holds it. The finding is set down with unease, and no answer.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6008"><em>Raghnall begins the count of years</em>, 13 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,205</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6009"></a>**19 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,209** — *A scholar answered at the reading* (Dùn thais). When a scholar of Taigh na Deasbaid calls Raghnall's table a wish dressed in columns, Raghnall offers to run the sums a fifth time on rolls the scholar himself chooses. The scholar sits down without taking up the offer, and the hall remembers the silence longer than the exchange.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0171"><em>The table of years at Dùn thais</em>, 29 an t-Samhain, LE 1,209</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0172"></a>**29 an Giblean, LE 1,219** — *The table forbidden* (Muileann dhearg). The king's council forbids the copying of Raghnall mac Chaluim's table of years, and the house of disputation at Dùn thais is shut for a generation. Raghnall's own copy is kept in the vein-house and entered in its inventory.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6010"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,219** — *Raghnall's copy entered in Taigh na Fèithe inventory* (Muileann dhearg). A custodian who has never met Raghnall mac Chaluim writes to ask whether his working copy of Clàr nam Bliadhnachan still exists and might be sent to the mountain for safekeeping. It is sent, and entered that year in Taigh na Fèithe's own inventory, one line among the galleries and Clachan a' Chrannchuir.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0172"><em>The table forbidden</em>, 29 an Giblean, LE 1,219</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0173"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,229** — *The great gale at Inis mhòr* (Inis mhòr). Before the autumn grain fleet has sailed, a gale out of the north-east drives the sea up the river at Inis mhòr higher than any then living had seen. Boats are crushed at their moorings, and the grain fleet does not sail until spring.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6011"></a>**27 am Faoilleach, LE 1,240** — *Death of Raghnall mac Chaluim* (Dùn thais). Raghnall mac Chaluim dies at Dùn thais in his sixty-sixth year, in the small house the shut school let him keep. The scholars who once argued his table carry him to the school's own burying ground and set a tally-stick at his grave's head, notched once for every year the making of the table cost him.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0172"><em>The table forbidden</em>, 29 an Giblean, LE 1,219</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6012"></a>**25 an Gearran, LE 1,240** — *Birth of Iain Ciar* (Cathair dhearg). A son, dark-browed and called Iain Ciar, is born to Ailean mac Raghnaill, then forty years old, the elder of two sons he has by different mothers.
- <a id="ev-III-0174"></a>**3 an t-Sultain, LE 1,246** — *Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh* (Baile ruadh). Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh in the far north-east go to law over the grazing on the hills between them. The case is heard three times at Cathair dhearg, and settled by dividing the hills along a stream.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6013"></a>**25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,246** — *The boundary stones carried home unused* (Baile ruadh). After the king's council divides the disputed grazing between Baile ruadh and Achadh naomh along a stream, both shire seats carry home the boundary stones they had brought to argue their claim and set them, unused, into their own walls, where they stand for the rest of the age pointing to a line the water has already made no matter of.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0174"><em>Baile ruadh's quarrel with Achadh naomh</em>, 3 an t-Sultain, LE 1,246</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0175"></a>**10 an t-Samhain, LE 1,259** — *Pilgrims at Allt an Àigh* (Allt an Àigh). The keepers of the Old Spirits renew the pilgrimage to Allt an Àigh, and a guest-house is built beside the stream for those who come to drink at the right phase of the moon. Its book names pilgrims from every shire.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6014"></a>**20 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,264** — *The keeping of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr passes to Mairead nic Mhurchaidh* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). The last keeper of a long line descended from Iain mac Mhurchaidh, who built the road-house its second byre and began the book of the ox-teams that lodged there, gives over the keeping to his daughter Mairead. She continues the ledger in a hand the ox-drivers of the mining road cannot tell from her father's.
- <a id="ev-III-0176"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,266** — *Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill* (Cathair dhearg). King Ailean mac Raghnaill dies at Cathair dhearg, leaving two sons by different mothers, Iain Ciar and Alasdair Bàn, and each has been told he is the heir.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6007"><em>Birth of Ailean mac Raghnaill</em>, 21 an Gearran, LE 1,200</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6015"></a>**16 an Lùnastal, LE 1,266** — *The blank space on the burial roll* (Cathair dhearg). Drawing up King Ailean mac Raghnaill's burial roll, An Talla Dearg's clerks leave a blank space where the heir's name should stand, unable to agree between themselves which of his two sons to write and unwilling to write neither.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0176"><em>Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,266</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6016"></a>**19 an t-Sultain, LE 1,266** — *The inventory read past the forbidden line* (Muileann dhearg). At the winter reading of Taigh na Fèithe's inventory, the custodian pauses a moment longer than usual over the line entered nearly fifty years before, Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, forbidden to be copied, kept, and then reads on, for the reckoning of that year's coal still has a great deal more of the shelf left to answer for.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0172"><em>The table forbidden</em>, 29 an Giblean, LE 1,219</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6017"></a>**24 an Giblean, LE 1,269** — *A refused gift at the feast of Bealltach* (Cathair dhearg). A messenger of Alasdair Bàn's, riding to An Talla Dearg with the household's ordinary feast-gift, is turned back at the gate on a pretext of business too full to receive him, the first courtesy either brother's household has refused the other in four years of careful giving.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0176"><em>Death of King Ailean mac Raghnaill</em>, 7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,266</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0177"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270** — *The battle of Cnoc naomh* (Cnoc naomh). Alasdair Bàn's men seize Cnoc naomh and Iain Ciar takes it back. The houses divide four to three, and from this battle Cogadh nam Bràithrean, the Brothers' War, takes its name.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6017"><em>A refused gift at the feast of Bealltach</em>, 24 an Giblean, LE 1,269</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6018"></a>**4 an t-Sultain, LE 1,270** — *The roads set under one following's watch or the other*. With both households calling up every man their houses owe them, the two brothers set every road between the two halves of the island under one following's watch or the other, so that carters who have crossed freely their whole lives must now say plainly which brother's peace they travel under.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0177"><em>The battle of Cnoc naomh</em>, 8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,270</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0178"></a>**17 an Lùnastal, LE 1,272** — *The fire at Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the waterfront of Ceann mhin, which held for his brother. The fire takes the rope stores and the granary, and the town begs its bread of Cathair mhòr.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6019"></a>**25 an t-Sultain, LE 1,272** — *Cathair mhòr feeds Ceann mhin* (Cathair mhòr). After Alasdair Bàn's ships burn the rope stores and the granary of Ceann mhin in one night, the town sends to Cathair mhòr, which has taken no side, and Cathair mhòr sends grain enough that no household at Ceann mhin goes hungry that winter.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0178"><em>The fire at Ceann mhin</em>, 17 an Lùnastal, LE 1,272</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0179"></a>**19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,274** — *The battle of Muileann ghlas* (Muileann ghlas). Iain Ciar defeats Alasdair Bàn below Muileann ghlas. Alasdair is taken alive; his captains are let go home.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6020"></a>**11 an t-Sultain, LE 1,274** — *Word of Muileann ghlas reaches the road-house* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). An ox-driver who turns back from the mountain road rather than push his team through unsettled country brings word of Iain Ciar's victory to An Taigh-seinnse Mòr within the week. Asked where the two brothers now stand to one another, he can only shrug: no one yet knows.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0179"><em>The battle of Muileann ghlas</em>, 19 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,274</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0180"></a>**12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276** — *The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). The brothers make peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, on neutral ground between their lands. Alasdair Bàn gives up his claim and has the lordship of Seann Chwen for life. Iain Ciar is crowned.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6021"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,276** — *The keeper warned a day before* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). A messenger carries word to An Taigh-seinnse Mòr that the two brothers and their followings are riding for the road-house to make their peace there. Mairead nic Mhurchaidh is given a single day's warning and spends the better part of it scrubbing the common-room floor.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0180"><em>The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6022"></a>**23 an Dàmhair, LE 1,276** — *The benches measured to a finger's breadth* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). Before the brothers arrive, Mairead nic Mhurchaidh measures the two benches of the common-room board against one another with her own hands until neither runs longer than its match, and sets the same loaf and the same jug of ale at either end, giving neither man the smallest excuse to find a slight in the setting of the table.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0180"><em>The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6023"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,276** — *Iain Ciar crowned at six-and-thirty* (Cathair dhearg). With the brothers' peace made at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr, Iain Ciar is crowned at Cathair dhearg, six-and-thirty years old, ten years after his father's burial roll was drawn with a blank where the heir's name should stand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0180"><em>The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6024"></a>**23 an Cèitean, LE 1,282** — *A reeve of Cathair mhòr presses the keeper for more* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). Years after the peace, an old reeve of Cathair mhòr asks Mairead nic Mhurchaidh whether the two brothers raised their voices in the long silence at her board. She answers only that she heard nothing through the door she had not already heard from her own oxen, and will say no more of it.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0180"><em>The brothers' peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr</em>, 12 an t-Sultain, LE 1,276</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6025"></a>**7 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,283** — *Alasdair Bàn rides up with a dead captain's news* (Cathair dhearg). Alasdair Bàn goes up to An Talla Dearg himself to carry word of an old captain's death to the king with his own mouth, as the captain asked dying; Iain Ciar receives him without ceremony and sends him home with no larger following than he came with.
- <a id="ev-III-0181"></a>**8 an Dàmhair, LE 1,291** — *Death of Alasdair Bàn* (Seann Chwen). Alasdair Bàn dies at Seann Chwen, having kept the peace he made. His lordship returns to the crown.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6025"><em>Alasdair Bàn rides up with a dead captain's news</em>, 7 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,283</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6026"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,291** — *Iain Ciar keeps his brother's lordship vacant* (Seann Chwen). On Alasdair Bàn's death the lordship of Seann Chwen returns to the crown as the brothers' peace had settled it should. Iain Ciar keeps the lordship vacant for the rest of his own reign rather than grant it to another man, a stubbornness An Talla Dearg's clerks never once ask him to explain.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0181"><em>Death of Alasdair Bàn</em>, 8 an Dàmhair, LE 1,291</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0181a"></a>**29 an Dàmhair, LE 1,295** — *White stone from Baile Mòr dhomhain* (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Masons of Ceann leathan buy a veined white stone from the hills above Baile Mòr dhomhain for the new front of their temple. From this time the quarry is worked, and its marble goes south by the carriers' road to every town that can pay for it.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6027"></a>**24 an Giblean, LE 1,296** — *A mason's slab kept on the road-house mantel* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). With the first carts of white marble passing south from the quarries above Baile Mòr dhomhain, Mairead nic Mhurchaidh keeps an unworked slab of the stone, no bigger than a hand, on the mantel above her own hearth, a small vanity she never fully explains to those who ask her why a road-house keeper should want a piece of stone bound for someone else's temple.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0181a"><em>White stone from Baile Mòr dhomhain</em>, 29 an Dàmhair, LE 1,295</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6028"></a>**27 am Faoilleach, LE 1,298** — *Pàdraig mac Ruairidh lodges three nights at the road-house* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). Gathering material for Leabhar nam Bràithrean, the king's clerk Pàdraig mac Ruairidh stays three nights at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr at his own expense, working each evening by the fire the two brothers once sat beside, and asks the keeper and every passing ox-driver for the tale of the peace. He leaves her a measure of meal for the fire and the bed before he rides on.
- <a id="ev-III-0182"></a>**20 an Giblean, LE 1,299** — *Iain Ciar's grain law* (Cathair dhearg). Having seen Ceann mhin beg its bread, King Iain Ciar commands that every shire seat keep a year's grain in store against the next war. The law is kept as long as he lives.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6029"></a>**21 an Giblean, LE 1,299** — *Death of Mairead nic Mhurchaidh* (An Taigh-seinnse Mòr). Mairead nic Mhurchaidh dies at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr in her own bed, at sixty-nine years old, on a night an ox-team lodges in the byre below her window. The keeping of the house passes to a sister's daughter raised under the same roof.

## The Years LE 1,301 – 1,400

- <a id="ev-III-0183"></a>**14 an Lùnastal, LE 1,304** — *The account of the Brothers' War* (Cathair dhearg). Pàdraig mac Ruairidh, a clerk of King Iain Ciar, writes the story of the Brothers' War. It praises the king at every turn, and it is the only account that survives, to the vexation of later readers.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6028"><em>Pàdraig mac Ruairidh lodges three nights at the road-house</em>, 27 am Faoilleach, LE 1,298</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0184"></a>**28 an Giblean, LE 1,319** — *The inns of the mining roads chartered* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The crown grants a charter to the seven great road-houses of the mining circuit, An Sligeanach Fad' às among them, and makes their keepers answerable for the roads between them. The keepers meet once a year at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6030"></a>**25 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,320** — *The keepers' first yearly meeting* (An Sligeanach Fad' às). The seven keepers of the newly chartered road-houses meet for the first time at An Sligeanach Fad' às to settle their accounts, as the charter now commands once every year. Asked whether the tale of the brothers' peace is as her aunt always told it, the new keeper of An Taigh-seinnse Mòr gives the same answer, word for word.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0184"><em>The inns of the mining roads chartered</em>, 28 an Giblean, LE 1,319</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6031"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, LE 1,320** — *Pàdraig mac Ruairidh's death* (Cathair dhearg). The clerk who wrote Leabhar nam Bràithrean in King Iain Ciar's praise dies some years before his king, and no scribe comes after him to keep the tale of the grain law's slow lapsing as he had kept the tale of the war itself.
- <a id="ev-III-0185"></a>**17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,326** — *Death of Iain Ciar* (Cathair dhearg). King Iain Ciar dies at Cathair dhearg. His grain law lapses within a few years, as he had foreseen in a note in his own hand.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6012"><em>Birth of Iain Ciar</em>, 25 an Gearran, LE 1,240</a>; ← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-6031"><em>Pàdraig mac Ruairidh's death</em>, 23 an Lùnastal, LE 1,320</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0186"></a>**22 am Màrt, LE 1,339** — *An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef* (An Taigh-seinnse Òir). An Taigh-seinnse Òir, at the eastern end of the circuit, is written into the charter-roll as keeping syrupped beef for the custodians' reeves on their rounds. It is the first dish of that house on record; the rest of the entry is a complaint about the price.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6032"></a>**25 an Giblean, LE 1,339** — *The reeve's price complaint at An Taigh-seinnse Òir* (An Taigh-seinnse Òir). A custodians' reeve who has eaten the house's secret syrupped beef twice a winter for a decade writes into the charter-roll that the price has risen three years running with nothing else about the dish improved, and asks for a second helping in the same breath.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0186"><em>An Taigh-seinnse Òir's beef</em>, 22 am Màrt, LE 1,339</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0187"></a>**20 an Giblean, LE 1,349** — *An Taigh-seinnse Reòta* (An Taigh-seinnse Reòta). An Taigh-seinnse Reòta, the road-house on the bare northern road, is snowed in for a whole season with a party of custodians' reeves within. They live on its pickled spinach and fire milk, and their complaint stands in full in the charter-roll.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6033"></a>**13 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,349** — *The keeper's itemised bill* (An Taigh-seinnse Reòta). When the snow that trapped a party of reeves at An Taigh-seinnse Reòta finally lifts, the house's keeper sends after them, by the first cart through, a bill for every jar of pickled spinach and every cup of fire milk they took, itemised, and it is paid in full.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0187"><em>An Taigh-seinnse Reòta</em>, 20 an Giblean, LE 1,349</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0188"></a>**11 am Màrt, LE 1,359** — *The hull that sank at launch* (Seann Skell). Seumas mac Iain, a boat-builder of Seann Skell, tries to build a deep-keeled hull again from the scraps of the Sundering fellowship's lore still remembered on the strand. At its launch it fills and sinks, and Manannan's priests preach on it for a year.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6034"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,362** — *Seumas mac Iain gives up the deep keel* (Seann Skell). After a year of Manannan's priests preaching against his sunken hull, the boat-builder of Seann Skell builds no more deep keels, and keeps his harbour shed mending ordinary boats for ordinary fares until his death.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0188"><em>The hull that sank at launch</em>, 11 am Màrt, LE 1,359</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0189"></a>**31 an Cèitean, LE 1,369** — *The Caol ìseal fishers go east* (Caol ìseal). Their own harbour silted, the fishing families of Caol ìseal on the north coast move east to Caol bheag. Caol ìseal becomes a farming town.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6035"></a>**13 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,369** — *The shrine carried whole to Caol bheag* (Caol bheag). The fishers who leave Caol ìseal's silted harbour carry their nets, their smoking-racks and the small shrine from the harbour's edge, and set the shrine up again at Caol bheag stone by stone in the same order, so that it stands as it always stood.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0189"><em>The Caol ìseal fishers go east</em>, 31 an Cèitean, LE 1,369</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6036"></a>**13 an Gearran, LE 1,380** — *Caol ìseal turns to the plough*. The houses of Caol ìseal nearest the silted water turn to farming the ground behind them after the fishers go east, and within two generations the town that smelled of fish and tar smells, most days, of turned earth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0189"><em>The Caol ìseal fishers go east</em>, 31 an Cèitean, LE 1,369</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0189a"></a>**4 an Gearran, LE 1,389** — *The southern lane* (Caol fhiadhaich). The fishers of Caol fhiadhaich, on the wild strait of the west coast, take their boats round into the southern sea, along the whole south coast to the mouth of the Abhainn uaine, and up it to the landing of Cidhe Beag below Baile thais, where they sell dried fish for grain. The older harbours of the south coast, which had never sailed beyond their own capes, begin to follow. The lane is named for its first sailors: Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.
- <a id="ev-III-0190"></a>**5 am Màrt, LE 1,389** — *The keel-song of Cuan shean* (Cuan shean). Iseabail nic Lachlainn, a gatherer of songs for the royal household, takes down a work-song of the rope-makers of Cuan shean that names the parts of a deep keel. Half its words mean nothing to those who sing it. It is all that survives, in any form, of the craft of the Sundering fleet.
- <a id="ev-III-0191"></a>**25 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,389** — *The Stone's schism at Inis thais* (Inis thais). The Stone's congregation at Inis thais divides over whether the dead may be prayed for at Clach. Those who say no keep the temple; the others build a second house at Baile gheal.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6037"></a>**27 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,389** — *Iseabail nic Lachlainn sent out on the king's road* (Cathair dhearg). The steward of the royal household at Cathair dhearg, wanting a linen-maid's quick-eared daughter out from under his feet, sends her out with a mule and a letter of lodging to gather what the shires' kitchens and rope-walks still sing at their work.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0190"><em>The keel-song of Cuan shean</em>, 5 am Màrt, LE 1,389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6038"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,389** — *A rope-maker's guess at the old words* (Cuan shean). A young man of Tormod Ròpaire's crew, not yet trusted with the lead, tells the gatherer Iseabail that Òran na Druime's strange words are likely only older speech worn smooth by centuries of mouths that never meant to wear it; Tormod answers that it changes nothing about how the strand is walked.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0190"><em>The keel-song of Cuan shean</em>, 5 am Màrt, LE 1,389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6039"></a>**3 am Faoilleach, LE 1,391** — *Òran na Druime read at the king's court* (Cathair dhearg). Iseabail nic Lachlainn reads her whole gathering before the king's hall at Cathair dhearg, and Òran na Druime's strange lines silence a room grown used to songs it half knows already; an old harper and a clerk of Taigh na Fèithe each say the words fit no tongue or hand they know, and neither can say more than that.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0190"><em>The keel-song of Cuan shean</em>, 5 am Màrt, LE 1,389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6040"></a>**11 an t-Sultain, LE 1,391** — *The older southern harbours follow the new lane* (Baile thais). A season or two after Caol fhiadhaich's boats are first believed, the older harbours of the south coast, which had never in memory put a boat past their own headlands, begin one after another to follow Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich down to the landing at Cidhe Beag.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0189a"><em>The southern lane</em>, 4 an Gearran, LE 1,389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0192"></a>**3 an Gearran, LE 1,399** — *The grey storm at Seann Tarr* (Seann Tarr). A storm named Gailleann Ghlas comes out of the east and destroys the harbour of Seann Tarr. The village is rebuilt and the harbour is not; its boats go to Cuan ruadh.
- <a id="ev-III-0193"></a>**8 an Lùnastal, LE 1,399** — *The second wolf-house at Baile gheal* (Baile gheal). The dissenters from Inis thais raise their house at Baile gheal and pray there for the dead by name. The two houses of the Stone are not reconciled in this age.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6041"></a>**6 an t-Sultain, LE 1,400** — *Death of Tormod Ròpaire* (Cuan shean). The rope-maker who led the walk that sang Òran na Druime dies at Cuan shean, seventy years old, having in his last years let a younger man keep the count while he sang on behind him; his crew keeps the song after him exactly as he gave it, no better understood than before.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-III-0190"><em>The keel-song of Cuan shean</em>, 5 am Màrt, LE 1,389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6042"></a>**5 an Dàmhair, LE 1,400** — *Birth of Catrìona Bheag*. A daughter, Catrìona, is born into Clann Raghnaill, the crown's own house; she is small from the cradle, and the house calls her Catrìona Bheag.

## The Years LE 1,401 – 1,500

- <a id="ev-EIV-6043"></a>**3 an t-Samhain, LE 1,405** — *Seann Tarr becomes a village again* (Seann Tarr). With its harbour broken past mending and its boats gone to Cuan ruadh, Seann Tarr keeps its houses and its shrine but is entered in the charter-roll, in the roll's own dry word for such places, as a village once more rather than a harbour town.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0192"><em>The grey storm at Seann Tarr</em>, 3 an Gearran, LE 1,399</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0194"></a>**29 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,409** — *Cuan ruadh's new harbour* (Cuan ruadh). Cuan ruadh builds a second harbour arm for the boats from Seann Tarr, and thrives on the east-coast fishing for the rest of the age.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6044"></a>**14 an Giblean, LE 1,420** — *Iseabail's tablets entered in Taigh na Fèithe* (Muileann dhearg).
