On Iseabail nic Lachlainn's death the household she served the rest of her life sends her whole collection to Taigh na Fèithe, where the clerks write into the inventory that it holds one item they can describe only by its sound and its keeping, not its meaning.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0190"><em>The keel-song of Cuan shean</em>, 5 am Màrt, LE 1,389</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0195"></a>**31 an Cèitean, LE 1,429** — *Queen Catrìona Bheag crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Catrìona Bheag of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg, the first queen in more than three centuries. It is written that she was small, and that no one said so twice.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6042"><em>Birth of Catrìona Bheag</em>, 5 an Dàmhair, LE 1,400</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0196"></a>**26 an Lùnastal, LE 1,439** — *The grey glaze of Muileann gheal* (Muileann gheal). The potters of Muileann gheal make a grey-green glaze that no other kiln on the island can match, and the custodian houses buy it for their tables. The secret is kept within one family, Clann Mhic Phàil.
- <a id="ev-III-0197"></a>**28 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,449** — *The oath of the seven* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Catrìona Bheag has the heads of the seven houses swear to the ruling of the hearth before her, the first renewal of the oath since Catrìona Bhuadhach. Clann Choinnich swears last.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6501"></a>**29 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,449** — *Clann Choinnich's head asks the manner of the oath* (Cathair dhearg). Before swearing last to Riaghailt an Teallaich, the head of Clann Choinnich asks Queen Catrìona Bheag plainly whether the renewed oath changes the measure her house holds or only the manner of swearing to it. The queen answers that it changes only the manner, and the old woman swears.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0197"><em>The oath of the seven</em>, 28 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,449</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0198"></a>**14 am Màrt, LE 1,459** — *Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr* (Cathair mhòr). The priests of Macha raise their great house at Cathair mhòr, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr in this age. Its floor of black and white was eleven years in the laying.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6502"></a>**23 an Lùnastal, LE 1,459** — *The last stone laid in Macha's floor* (Cathair mhòr). The black and white floor of Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr is finished, eleven years in the laying, by masons none of whom cut its first courses. It stands the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0198"><em>Macha's great house at Cathair mhòr</em>, 14 am Màrt, LE 1,459</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0199"></a>**17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,469** — *The eastern Toll-dubh* (Toll-dubh). Charcoal-burners in the east find again the eastern Toll-dubh of the old tales, with the same cut stair as the one walled up in the west. The custodians wall this one too, and the scribe binds the two entries of the custody-book each to the other.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6503"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,469** — *Leabhar a' Chùraim binds the two stairs* (Toll-dubh). When charcoal-burners break into the eastern Toll-dubh, the scribe of Leabhar a' Chùraim binds its entry to the western stair's with a line in each margin, though nothing is written of what either stair goes down to.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0199"><em>The eastern Toll-dubh</em>, 17 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,469</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0200"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,479** — *The dry years at Achadh shean* (Tiormachd Achadh shean). Three dry seasons one after another empty the wells of the eastern shires about Achadh shean. The shared meal holds, and the crown carts grain in from the south.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6504"></a>**10 am Màrt, LE 1,483** — *The well-head board first cut* (Achadh shean). As the crown's grain carts still reach Achadh shean by the mining road against a second dry season, the reeves cut a board at the well-head setting down how the deep wells will be shared among the households by lot and by turn. The board is renewed each generation; the lots themselves are never drawn again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0200"><em>The dry years at Achadh shean</em>, 2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,479</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0201"></a>**2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,489** — *The water-rights of Achadh shean* (Achadh shean). The reeves of Achadh shean share the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn, and write the sharing on a board at the well-head. The board is renewed each generation; the lots are never drawn again.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-6504"><em>The well-head board first cut</em>, 10 am Màrt, LE 1,483</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6505"></a>**27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,498** — *A clerk finds the worn firlot* (Àth shean). A young clerk newly set over the granary accounts at Àth shean finds, going back through the ledgers, that the firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for longer than any one reeve's term could account for. He carries the matter up rather than let it stand.
- <a id="ev-III-0202"></a>**24 an t-Sultain, LE 1,499** — *The firlot of Àth shean* (Àth shean). The granary of Àth shean finds that its firlot has worn smaller than the standard of Cathair dhearg, and has been so for generations. The reeve's accounts are put right as far back as anyone can reckon.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6505"><em>A clerk finds the worn firlot</em>, 27 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,498</a>.</span>

## The Years LE 1,501 – 1,600

- <a id="ev-EIV-6506"></a>**24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,505** — *Birth of Sìleas Òg* (Cathair dhearg). A daughter, Sìleas, is born in the house of the crown in the seventy-seventh year of Queen Catrìona Bheag's reign, and called Sìleas Òg after the queen who first measured the island's baskets.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6507"></a>**22 an t-Sultain, LE 1,505** — *Iain Mac Phàil tries to write the glaze down*. In the last years of his life Iain Mac Phàil, the last of Clann Mhic Phàil at Muileann gheal, tries to set the grey-green glaze's making down in some form a stranger might follow, and finds the moment of the kiln's cooling will not go into words.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6508"></a>**22 am Faoilleach, LE 1,507** — *Two apprentices fail the grey-green firing* (Muileann gheal). Iain Mac Phàil takes two apprentices in his last years and teaches them the mixing of the grey-green glaze, but neither learns to judge the moment the kiln's heat must be let fall. Both come away able to throw a passable dish and unable to glaze it.
- <a id="ev-III-0203"></a>**30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,509** — *The grey glaze lost* (Muileann gheal). The last of Clann Mhic Phàil dies at Muileann gheal without passing on the glaze. For a generation the potters of the town try to match it, and fail.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6507"><em>Iain Mac Phàil tries to write the glaze down</em>, 22 an t-Sultain, LE 1,505</a>; → Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6508"><em>Two apprentices fail the grey-green firing</em>, 22 am Faoilleach, LE 1,507</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6509"></a>**10 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,518** — *Drovers of Àth chiar bring their beasts to Baile Mòr ruadh* (Baile Mòr ruadh). Drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills begin bringing their cattle down to Baile Mòr ruadh's autumn fair rather than selling nearer home, and within a few years it is the greatest fair in the east.
- <a id="ev-III-0204"></a>**18 an Dàmhair, LE 1,519** — *Baile Mòr ruadh's fair* (Baile Mòr ruadh). Baile Mòr ruadh in the east holds a cattle fair that draws drovers from Àth chiar and the eastern hills. It becomes yearly, and the greatest fair in the east.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6509"><em>Drovers of Àth chiar bring their beasts to Baile Mòr ruadh</em>, 10 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,518</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0205"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,529** — *Queen Sìleas Òg crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Sìleas Òg of Clann Raghnaill, named for the queen of the firlot, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. She is the first ruler known to have visited every shire seat.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6506"><em>Birth of Sìleas Òg</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,505</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6510"></a>**13 am Faoilleach, LE 1,531** — *Sìleas Òg questioned on her purpose* (Cathair dhearg). Asked years later what put the notion of a round of every shire seat in her head, Queen Sìleas Òg says she had grown up hearing the seats named at her father's table like places in a story, and wished to know them as a place stood in rather than a tale repeated.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0205"><em>Queen Sìleas Òg crowned</em>, 9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,529</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6511"></a>**2 am Faoilleach, LE 1,534** — *The reeve of Achadh shean questioned at the well-head* (Achadh shean). On her round, Sìleas Òg stands at the well-head of Achadh shean and asks the reeve why the lots for the deep wells were never drawn a second time. He answers that no household wished to be the one that named the first sharing unfair. She rides on the next morning without asking him to change it.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0201"><em>The water-rights of Achadh shean</em>, 2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,489</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6512"></a>**21 am Faoilleach, LE 1,535** — *Sìleas Òg reaches the last shire seat of her round*. Queen Sìleas Òg's circuit carries her at last to the bare northern stretch few rulers before her had visited, the first ruler of Dia-thìr known to have stood in every shire seat the island holds.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0205"><em>Queen Sìleas Òg crowned</em>, 9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,529</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0206"></a>**4 an Dàmhair, LE 1,539** — *Sìleas Òg's count of hands* (Muileann dhearg). Queen Sìleas Òg commands a new count of every household holding the right to the coal. It is smaller than any before, for the right has narrowed into fewer and larger households, and the queen has it entered without comment.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6513"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, LE 1,539** — *The queen enters the count without comment* (Muileann dhearg). Reading the new, smaller count of households holding the right to the coal, Sìleas Òg has it entered in Leabhar a' Chùraim without a word either way, a silence her own scribes find harder to read than any word she might have spoken.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0206"><em>Sìleas Òg's count of hands</em>, 4 an Dàmhair, LE 1,539</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0207"></a>**5 an t-Sultain, LE 1,549** — *The fire of Ceann mhin* (Ceann mhin). A second great fire burns Ceann mhin, and this time there is no war to blame. By order of its reeve the town is rebuilt with gable walls of stone between the houses.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6514"></a>**29 an t-Sultain, LE 1,549** — *Ceann mhin's reeve orders the gable walls* (Ceann mhin). Before the ash of the second fire has cooled, the reeve of Ceann mhin orders the town rebuilt with gable walls of stone standing between each house and the next, so that a fire must cross stone to spread.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0207"><em>The fire of Ceann mhin</em>, 5 an t-Sultain, LE 1,549</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6515"></a>**28 an Giblean, LE 1,550** — *Birth of Ailean the Fourth* (Cathair dhearg). A son, named Ailean mac Raghnaill after the kings of that name before him, is born into the crown's house in the two-and-twentieth year of Queen Sìleas Òg's reign.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6516"></a>**31 am Faoilleach, LE 1,556** — *Birth of Mòrag nic Raghnaill* (Cathair dhearg). A daughter, Mòrag, is born to the same house, six years younger than her brother Ailean.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6517"></a>**1 am Màrt, LE 1,558** — *Clann Choinnich's clerk drafts Athchuingean an Airgid* (Muileann dhearg). After three winters of the head of Clann Choinnich arguing that the coal might be spared beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, a younger kinsman of the house drafts the petition the council will hear, the first written asking to burn the coal for work rather than worship.
- <a id="ev-III-0208"></a>**31 an Lùnastal, LE 1,559** — *The silver smelt refused* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). Clann Choinnich asks leave to burn the coal beyond the measured handful to smelt silver at Muileann chiar, since the coal burns hotter than charcoal. The council refuses. It is the first asking to burn the coal for work and not for worship.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6517"><em>Clann Choinnich's clerk drafts Athchuingean an Airgid</em>, 1 am Màrt, LE 1,558</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6518"></a>**12 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,559** — *The queen's word to Clann Choinnich's head* (Muileann dhearg). Once the council's refusal is final, Sìleas Òg tells Clann Choinnich's head privately that a law kept since before the fleet sailed for one reason is not easily bent to a second, however sound. The old woman accepts the courtesy without being persuaded.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0208"><em>The silver smelt refused</em>, 31 an Lùnastal, LE 1,559</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6519"></a>**22 an Lùnastal, LE 1,568** — *The last blade of the old folding* (Dùn dhearg). The fellowship of Dùn dhearg loses the last smith trained far enough in the layered steel's folding to finish it alone. The blades made after him are ordinary work, prized now only for what the craft once was.
- <a id="ev-III-0209"></a>**22 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,569** — *The lost smithing at Dùn dhearg* (Dùn dhearg). The smiths of Dùn dhearg, makers of the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses since the walls were built, lose the last man who knew how their layered steel was folded. After him the blades of Dùn dhearg are ordinary.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6519"><em>The last blade of the old folding</em>, 22 an Lùnastal, LE 1,568</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0210"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,579** — *The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). The custodian houses begin to bury their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, among graves older than any name on them. The tenants of the land about call it unwise, and go on burying their own dead elsewhere.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6520"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,580** — *The tenants of Tuam Cnoc dhìreach keep their own ground* (Tuam Cnoc dhìreach). When Na Seachd Taighean begin burying their heads at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach, the tenants of the land about it call the custom unwise and go on burying their own dead where their own families always have, a disagreement neither side presses to settle.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0210"><em>The houses bury at Tuam Cnoc dhìreach</em>, 2 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,579</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0211"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,589** — *King Ailean the Fourth crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Ailean mac Raghnaill, fourth king of that name, is crowned at Cathair dhearg. He is remembered only for the shortest reign in the king-list.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6515"><em>Birth of Ailean the Fourth</em>, 28 an Giblean, LE 1,550</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0212"></a>**13 an Giblean, LE 1,590** — *The synod of Manannan's order* (Seann Skell). The priests of Manannan meet at Seann Skell and lay down again the rule of sight-of-land. To it they add a prayer, said at the foot of the river pool, that Manannan keep the sea shut: A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte.
- <a id="ev-III-0213"></a>**12 an Cèitean, LE 1,590** — *Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Ailean's sister Mòrag nic Raghnaill is crowned after him. She reigns forty years, and the king-list has for her its longest run of entries telling of nothing but good harvests and the rite.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6516"><em>Birth of Mòrag nic Raghnaill</em>, 31 am Faoilleach, LE 1,556</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6521"></a>**17 an Cèitean, LE 1,590** — *One stone cut for two reigns* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill has the years of her brother Ailean the Fourth's crowning and death cut on a single stone rather than two, the plainest record Clàr nan Rìghrean gives of the short reign she outlives by forty years.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0211"><em>King Ailean the Fourth crowned</em>, 9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,589</a>; → Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0213"><em>Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned</em>, 12 an Cèitean, LE 1,590</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6522"></a>**12 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,590** — *The synod argues two days over the prayer's words* (Seann Skell). The priests of Manannan in synod at Seann Skell spend two full days over the wording of a new prayer before agreeing on its shortest form, to be said at the foot of the river pool where the fleet once turned.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0212"><em>The synod of Manannan's order</em>, 13 an Giblean, LE 1,590</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6523"></a>**24 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,590** — *Death of Ailean the Fourth at forty* (Cathair dhearg). King Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth of the name, dies at Cathair dhearg within the year of his crowning, forty years old; Leabhar a' Chùraim does not say what ailed him, and his sister Mòrag, four-and-thirty, is crowned before the season turns.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0213"><em>Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned</em>, 12 an Cèitean, LE 1,590</a>.</span>

## The Years LE 1,601 – 1,700

- <a id="ev-III-0214"></a>**16 an t-Samhain, LE 1,619** — *The ferry at Cidhe Beag* (Cidhe Beag). A ferry family settles at Cidhe Beag on Abhainn uaine and carries folk and goods down the river by canoe. They hold the landing for the rest of the age.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6524"></a>**2 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,619** — *The ferry family holds the landing father to daughter* (Cidhe Beag). The family that settles the ferry crossing at Cidhe Beag holds the landing from father to daughter and daughter to son for the rest of the age, a fixed thing on the eastern road like any ford or road-house.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0214"><em>The ferry at Cidhe Beag</em>, 16 an t-Samhain, LE 1,619</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0214a"></a>**1 an Dàmhair, LE 1,626** — *The dark wine of Àth shean* (Àth shean). The growers on the slopes above Àth shean press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that keeps a year in the cask. It is sold along the eastern road, and the road-houses serve it as black wine.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6525"></a>**24 an t-Samhain, LE 1,626** — *The road-houses take up the black wine* (Àth shean). The road-houses of the eastern stretch above Àth shean take to serving the growers' dark blaeberry and bramble pressing as black wine, a trade that outlasts a good deal the age's councils thought more likely to last.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0214a"><em>The dark wine of Àth shean</em>, 1 an Dàmhair, LE 1,626</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6526"></a>**7 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,628** — *A clerk reckons forty quiet years* (Cathair dhearg). A clerk who has served Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill the whole of her reign remarks, near the end of his service, that he has written more entries under her than under any three reigns before and set down in all of them no death by war, no famine and no quarrel of Na Seachd Taighean.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0213"><em>Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned</em>, 12 an Cèitean, LE 1,590</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6527"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,630** — *The reign of Mòrag nic Raghnaill ends* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill's reign ends in her four-and-seventieth year, after forty years crowned; Clàr nan Rìghrean sets down the end of it and little else, as it has set down little else of all her quiet years.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0213"><em>Queen Mòrag nic Raghnaill crowned</em>, 12 an Cèitean, LE 1,590</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0215"></a>**2 an t-Samhain, LE 1,634** — *Inis mhòr's grain fleet laid up* (Inis mhòr). The coasting grain barges of Inis mhòr, which had sailed Slighe-uisce fhuar, the cold way along the north coast from Ros chiar to Caol mhin, since the early years of the Sundering, are laid up for good as the roads grow better. The last is kept on the strand as a wonder.
- <a id="ev-III-0216"></a>**7 an Lùnastal, LE 1,649** — *Earthquake at Dùn ìseal* (Dùn ìseal). An earthquake shakes Dùn ìseal and cracks the spirit-house. No one is killed. The keepers take it for a warning, but cannot agree of what.
- <a id="ev-III-0217"></a>**21 an Cèitean, LE 1,659** — *Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies* (Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Thòmais, widow of a mill-owner of Muileann chaol, begins to buy old copies of the custody-book and the harbour rolls from houses that no longer read them. She keeps them in a loft over her mill.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6528"></a>**10 an Cèitean, LE 1,662** — *A cheese-press board sold to the widow of Muileann chaol* (Cathair mhòr). A carter brings Beathag nic Thòmais a blackened board a Cathair mhòr road house has used for years to weight a cheese-press, having noticed writing on its underside: a coal-right tally three generations old. She pays a fair measure of meal for it, telling the carter that a house's own forgetting is no measure of what a board is worth.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0217"><em>Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies</em>, 21 an Cèitean, LE 1,659</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6529"></a>**11 an Giblean, LE 1,665** — *A clerk of Taigh na Fèithe finds a lost ruling in the loft* (Muileann chaol). A clerk riding through Muileann chaol on the crown's business climbs the mill stair out of idleness and finds, among Beathag nic Thòmais's boards, the only surviving copy of a custodians' ruling Taigh na Fèithe had lost to fire two generations before. He asks whether she means the loft for the crown's use or her own; she says the question is not hers to answer alone.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0217"><em>Beathag nic Thòmais gathers the old copies</em>, 21 an Cèitean, LE 1,659</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0218"></a>**28 am Faoilleach, LE 1,674** — *The paper mill at Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). A mill at Muileann chaol begins to make paper from rags, the first on Dia-thìr. In this generation the custody-book is first copied onto paper.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6530"></a>**29 am Faoilleach, LE 1,674** — *Beathag nic Thòmais presses her own sheet of rag paper* (Muileann chaol). Having watched Anna nic Coinnich work her pulp-troughs a season, Beathag presses a sheet with her own hands, uneven at one corner, and keeps it apart from the loft's other papers for the rest of her life without ever saying why.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0218"><em>The paper mill at Muileann chaol</em>, 28 am Faoilleach, LE 1,674</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6531"></a>**13 an Giblean, LE 1,674** — *Beathag carries the proposal of paper to Taigh na Fèithe* (Muileann dhearg). Beathag nic Thòmais rides the sixty miles to Taigh na Fèithe herself to put Anna's rag paper before a custodian, judging a widow's word better heard than a stranger's. Asked whether the new stuff will hold ink sixteen centuries as hide has, she says she cannot promise it, and the custodian lets the copying go ahead.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0218"><em>The paper mill at Muileann chaol</em>, 28 am Faoilleach, LE 1,674</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0219"></a>**27 an Giblean, LE 1,679** — *Three copies of the landfall tidings* (Muileann chaol). Among her papers Beathag nic Thòmais finds three copies of the tidings of the two landfalls. They differ in the order of the coasts and the number of hulls. She writes out all three side by side and does not choose between them.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6532"></a>**12 an Lùnastal, LE 1,679** — *Beathag answers Anna on the three copies* (Muileann chaol). Found still kneeling over the three tellings of the landfall at dusk, Beathag tells Anna nic Coinnich that she believes all three writers honest and none of their three pasts more true than the others, and that choosing one for comfort's sake would be a falsehood of her own making.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0219"><em>Three copies of the landfall tidings</em>, 27 an Giblean, LE 1,679</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6533"></a>**2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,680** — *Birth of Tormod mac Ruairidh*. A son, Tormod, is born to Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill, the crown's own house, in the years Beathag nic Thòmais is filling her loft at Muileann chaol.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6534"></a>**23 am Faoilleach, LE 1,691** — *A niece asks why the wrong copies were not burned* (Muileann chaol). Hearing the tale of the three copies at the fireside, Beathag's niece asks why the two that disagreed with the truth were not simply burned. Beathag, by then old, tells her this is the very question the loft exists to leave unanswered.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0219"><em>Three copies of the landfall tidings</em>, 27 an Giblean, LE 1,679</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0220"></a>**3 an Cèitean, LE 1,694** — *The north-west coast counted* (Baile chrom). The crown sends a reeve to list the households of the thinned north-west coast between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. He counts fewer households than there are harbour berths.
- <a id="ev-III-0221"></a>**24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,699** — *The loft at Muileann chaol* (Muileann chaol). Beathag nic Thòmais dies, and leaves her loft of papers to the town of Muileann chaol on condition that nothing in it be burned. The town keeps that condition and very little else of her wishes.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6535"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, LE 1,699** — *The nephew stumbles reading the loft's condition* (Muileann chaol). Reading Beathag nic Thòmais's will aloud to the assembled kin, her nephew stumbles over the clause forbidding any burning of the loft's papers, and more than one kinsman marks the stumble and thinks the less of him for it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0221"><em>The loft at Muileann chaol</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,699</a>.</span>

## The Years LE 1,701 – 1,800

- <a id="ev-III-0222"></a>**6 am Màrt, LE 1,709** — *King Tormod mac Ruairidh crowned* (Cathair dhearg). Tormod mac Ruairidh of Clann Raghnaill is crowned at Cathair dhearg. His reign is remembered for its roads and its length.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6533"><em>Birth of Tormod mac Ruairidh</em>, 2 an Dàmhair, LE 1,680</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0223"></a>**5 an Gearran, LE 1,714** — *Manannan's harbour prayer* (Seann Skell). The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell begin to say their prayer for the shut sea on the day of the rite of the empty harbour, so that both are kept together on Cidhe an Diosail. Neither side is pleased.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6536"></a>**15 am Faoilleach, LE 1,715** — *Birth of Gormshuil nic Thormoid* (Cathair dhearg). A daughter, Gormshuil, is born at Cathair dhearg to King Tormod mac Ruairidh, five-and-thirty years old and six years crowned.
- <a id="ev-III-0224"></a>**6 am Màrt, LE 1,719** — *Tormod's bridges* (Cnoc ìseal). King Tormod builds stone bridges over the fords of the south-central shires, one of them at Cnoc ìseal. Ferry-keepers who lose their living are given land in amends.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6537"></a>**8 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,721** — *A ferryman chooses the market road over the water* (Cnoc ìseal). Given his choice of two parcels in amends for the bridge that ends his crossing, a ferryman of Cnoc ìseal asks the king's reeve which has the better crossing to the market road, and takes it; his sons never return to the water.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0224"><em>Tormod's bridges</em>, 6 am Màrt, LE 1,719</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0225"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,729** — *The panther year* (Imrich nam Pantar). The panthers cross the southern roads in numbers beyond any herder's memory, and for a whole season the crossing days run into one another. Flocks are kept in folds from Cnoc àrsaidh to the coast.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6538"></a>**8 an Gearran, LE 1,731** — *A miller answers a reeve on the town's right to the loft* (Muileann chaol). A crown reeve asks Beathag nic Thòmais's great-nephew, by then the loft's unpaid keeper, what right the town has to papers that belong by their matter to Taigh na Fèithe or the crown. He answers that fifty years of neither office asking for them back is itself an answer.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0221"><em>The loft at Muileann chaol</em>, 24 an Lùnastal, LE 1,699</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0226"></a>**10 an t-Samhain, LE 1,734** — *Caol gharbh loses the salt* (Caol gharbh). The sea rises over the salt pans of Caol gharbh and they fail, and salt comes to the north-east from the south instead. The town that took the trade of Ros fhionn is poorer than Ros fhionn had been.
- <a id="ev-III-0227"></a>**12 an Dàmhair, LE 1,739** — *Storm at Baile ghorm* (Baile ghorm). A south-westerly storm floods the low town of Baile ghorm and drowns twenty-three. The town raises its sea-wall by the height of a man.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6539"></a>**16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,748** — *A scribe questions the last keepers of the rite* (Seann Skell). Sent to note Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh for the crown's book, a scribe asks the last old women of Seann Skell on what day the fleet truly sailed. No two answers agree, and he writes as much into the crown's own book, unable to choose among them any more than Beathag nic Thòmais once could among her three copies.
- <a id="ev-III-0228"></a>**22 an Cèitean, LE 1,749** — *The rite kept by few* (Seann Skell). The rite of the empty harbour on Cidhe an Diosail at Seann Skell is kept by the harbour priests and a few old families. A visiting scribe writes that none there could say on what day the fleet had in truth sailed.<span class="fn fl">← Leads to <a href="#ev-EIV-6539"><em>A scribe questions the last keepers of the rite</em>, 16 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,748</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0229"></a>**23 an Giblean, LE 1,754** — *Cuan dhearg flooded again* (Cuan dhearg). The sea comes over the waterfront of Cuan dhearg a second time, and the street moved back after An Gàire Dubh is flooded to the thresholds. The town builds a sea-wall and does not move again.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6540"></a>**26 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,754** — *Gormshuil carries the harbour-master's counsel to the king* (Cuan dhearg). Sent by her father to see the sea-wall building at Cuan dhearg, Gormshuil nic Thormoid hears the harbour-master say a wall a man can stand behind is worth more than a street he can only run from, and rides home to give the king the counsel word for word.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0229"><em>Cuan dhearg flooded again</em>, 23 an Giblean, LE 1,754</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6541"></a>**2 an Lùnastal, LE 1,754** — *Cuan dhearg buries its own boundary stones* (Cuan dhearg). Rather than break up the boundary stones of the street the sea first moved, Cuan dhearg buries them on the chance a later hand may want to know how far the water once came.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0229"><em>Cuan dhearg flooded again</em>, 23 an Giblean, LE 1,754</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0230"></a>**20 an Giblean, LE 1,759** — *The house at Dùn thais reopened* (Dùn thais). The house of disputation at Dùn thais, shut and opened more than once since the table of years, is opened again on condition that the question of longer lives is not raised. The druids of the schools accept it and argue about the vein instead.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6542"></a>**9 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,759** — *The schools take up the question of the vein instead* (Dùn thais). Reopened on condition that the question of longer lives is never raised again, Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais turns instead to whether Leabhar a' Chùraim's measure of the handful answers rightly to what the coal gives out.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0230"><em>The house at Dùn thais reopened</em>, 20 an Giblean, LE 1,759</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0231"></a>**9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766** — *Death of King Tormod* (Cathair dhearg). King Tormod mac Ruairidh dies at Cathair dhearg after a reign of more than fifty years. His daughter Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned.<span class="fn fl">◇ Same person <a href="#ev-EIV-6536"><em>Birth of Gormshuil nic Thormoid</em>, 15 am Faoilleach, LE 1,715</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6543"></a>**26 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766** — *The king's last night* (Cathair dhearg). Tormod mac Ruairidh tells his daughter Gormshuil, on the last night of his seven-and-fifty-year reign, that he never once found courage to ask Taigh na Fèithe a question Taigh na Deasbaid was forbidden to ask on his behalf, and that finding it will be the easier half of her trouble.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0231"><em>Death of King Tormod</em>, 9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6544"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766** — *Gormshuil crowned at one-and-fifty* (Cathair dhearg). Gormshuil nic Thormoid is crowned in An Talla Dearg a fortnight after her father's death, the same age he had been when the sea-wall of Cuan dhearg was still only a plan on a tally-stick.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0231"><em>Death of King Tormod</em>, 9 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,766</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0232"></a>**12 an Giblean, LE 1,771** — *Queen Gormshuil's progress* (Cathair dhearg). Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid rides round every shire seat of the island, the first ruler to do so since Sìleas Òg. Her clerks write down the grievances of each shire; the queen answers none of them in writing.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6545"></a>**8 an Gearran, LE 1,772** — *A boundary measured and not judged* (Baile chrom). At the first seat of her progress a householder accuses her neighbour of shifting a boundary stone by moonlight three years running; Gormshuil measures the disputed ground herself and has it written down, so that the writing, not the queen, will settle it.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0232"><em>Queen Gormshuil's progress</em>, 12 an Giblean, LE 1,771</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6546"></a>**6 an Cèitean, LE 1,772** — *Leabhar nan Gearan opened at every seat*. At every shire seat of Queen Gormshuil's progress, in the sixth year of her reign and her seven-and-fiftieth of life, her clerks open Leabhar nan Gearan and write down each seat's grievance in the shire's own words.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0232"><em>Queen Gormshuil's progress</em>, 12 an Giblean, LE 1,771</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6547"></a>**11 am Faoilleach, LE 1,775** — *A reeve asks the queen what the writing is for*. A plain-spoken reeve asks Gormshuil why she writes down every shire's grievance and answers none of them; she tells him a hasty answer given before hearing the whole round is a false ease, and rides on.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0232"><em>Queen Gormshuil's progress</em>, 12 an Giblean, LE 1,771</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0233"></a>**5 an Gearran, LE 1,776** — *The second silver petition* (Muileann dhearg). Clann Choinnich asks again to burn the coal beyond the measure for the silver smelt at Muileann chiar, now with three of the seven houses behind it. Queen Gormshuil's council refuses by one voice. The name of the member who changed his vote is written down; his reason is not.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6548"></a>**14 an t-Ògmhios, LE 1,776** — *Aonghas mac Lachlainn turns his vote* (Muileann dhearg). Meaning by every account to vote with the three houses behind Athchuingean an Airgid, Aonghas mac Lachlainn changes his vote at the board itself and gives no reason beyond the bare word that he has changed his mind.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0233"><em>The second silver petition</em>, 5 an Gearran, LE 1,776</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6549"></a>**18 an Lùnastal, LE 1,776** — *Gormshuil asks Aonghas his reason and is refused* (Muileann dhearg). Gormshuil asks Aonghas mac Lachlainn privately why he turned his vote; he answers that a man's reason for his own hand at the board is his to keep, and she lets the matter lie as Leabhar a' Chùraim lets it lie.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0233"><em>The second silver petition</em>, 5 an Gearran, LE 1,776</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0234"></a>**25 am Màrt, LE 1,786** — *An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). An Taigh-òsta Grianach on the eastern road feeds the queen's progress with pan-fried spinach and black wine, as the charter-roll records. Its keeper, Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, is spared her road dues for a year.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6550"></a>**21 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,786** — *Peigi feeds the queen's whole progress unwarned* (An Taigh-òsta Grianach). Peigi nic Dhonnchaidh, keeper of An Taigh-òsta Grianach, feeds Gormshuil's whole company on pan-fried spinach and black wine though her charter allows stores for far less; the queen forgives her a year's road dues.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0234"><em>An Taigh-òsta Grianach's spinach</em>, 25 am Màrt, LE 1,786</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0235"></a>**27 an Gearran, LE 1,791** — *The last count of hands* (Muileann dhearg). The vein-house counts for the last time in this age the households holding the right to the coal. They are fewer than at any count before, and greater; the custody-book notes that three of the seven houses now hold more than half the right between them.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6551"></a>**26 an Lùnastal, LE 1,791** — *A smaller house is granted its neighbour's unused right* (Muileann dhearg). At the last Cunntas nan Làmh the custodians grant a house whose share has fallen too low to keep its hearth measure a neighbour's unused coal-right, though more than one voice warns that a house asking twice can be eased once but not mended for good.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0235"><em>The last count of hands</em>, 27 an Gearran, LE 1,791</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6552"></a>**17 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,791** — *Three houses hold more than half the right* (Muileann dhearg). Leabhar a' Chùraim's clerk notes under the last Cunntas nan Làmh, in the dry hand kept since Donnchadh's day, that three of Na Seachd Taighean now hold more than half the whole right to the coal among themselves.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0235"><em>The last count of hands</em>, 27 an Gearran, LE 1,791</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0236"></a>**22 an Cèitean, LE 1,794** — *Timber out of the mist* (Ceann mhòr). A worked timber, longer than any tree on the island and fastened with nails of a make no smith of Dia-thìr knows, comes ashore at Ceann mhòr on the north-west coast, from beyond Manannan's mist, as the fishers say. It is carried to Seann Skell, shown to Manannan's priests, and burned.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6553"></a>**21 an Dàmhair, LE 1,794** — *The fishers of Ceann mhòr find the timber* (Ceann mhòr). Fishers working the empty water off Ceann mhòr, where Faire a' Chinn has long lapsed, find a worked timber cast up, longer than any island tree and fastened with nails no smith on Dia-thìr forged; the eldest among them says hands that made such nails did not make them on the island.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0236"><em>Timber out of the mist</em>, 22 an Cèitean, LE 1,794</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6554"></a>**13 an Giblean, LE 1,795** — *The queen goes up to Taigh na Fèithe for the winter burning* (Muileann dhearg). Eighty years old, Gormshuil nic Thormoid rides the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe for the winter burning as she has every year of her reign, and walks her own horse up the last, iced mile rather than let another hand lead it.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6555"></a>**17 an Dàmhair, LE 1,795** — *The oldest crowned ruler since Clàr nam Bliadhnachan* (Muileann dhearg). Riding up to the winter burning at eighty, Queen Gormshuil nic Thormoid is the oldest ruler Leabhar a' Chùraim has entered crowned and still reigning since long before Clàr nam Bliadhnachan, nine-and-twenty years crowned.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0236"><em>Timber out of the mist</em>, 22 an Cèitean, LE 1,794</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6556"></a>**30 an t-Samhain, LE 1,796** — *The council sits in the queen's empty place* (Cathair dhearg). With no word of Gormshuil since the winter burning, the custodians of Na Seachd Taighean meet at An Talla Dearg in the place the crown's own chair has always stood empty for her progress, and send their word up the coal-road by the same riders who carried the crown's business all her reign.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6557"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,798** — *A crown letter sealed with no name above the seal* (Cathair dhearg). The custodians seal their letters with Taigh na Fèithe's trellis and hollow stone as every crown letter has been sealed since Dòmhnall Ruadh joined the two, but set no name above the seal, and no clerk is ever asked to explain the blank space.
- <a id="ev-III-0237"></a>**24 an Dàmhair, LE 1,799** — *The lamps at Seann Skell go out* (Seann Skell). Fewer houses at Seann Skell keep the night of lamps each year, and at last none on the waterfront. An old woman sets a lamp in a window of the harbour-house, and the scribe writes that it was she and not the town.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6558"></a>**28 an t-Samhain, LE 1,799** — *Ealasaid nic Iain keeps the last lamp* (Seann Skell). With no household left on the Seann Skell waterfront still keeping Oidhche nan Lòchran, an old woman, Ealasaid nic Iain, sets the one lamp that burns in the harbour-house window; the scribe writes that the lamp was hers and not the town's.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0237"><em>The lamps at Seann Skell go out</em>, 24 an Dàmhair, LE 1,799</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6559"></a>**8 an Gearran, LE 1,800** — *Ealasaid nic Iain's lamp goes dark* (Seann Skell). Ealasaid nic Iain, who alone had kept a lamp burning in the harbour-house window at Seann Skell after the rest of the waterfront let the custom lapse, dies in her own bed, and no one after her sets a light there again.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0237"><em>The lamps at Seann Skell go out</em>, 24 an Dàmhair, LE 1,799</a>.</span>

## The Years LE 1,801 – 1,819

- <a id="ev-III-0238"></a>**25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803** — *The last rite of the empty harbour in this age* (Seann Skell). Eleven people keep the rite of the empty harbour at Seann Skell. The harbour scribe enters their number, the weather and the state of the tide, and nothing more.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6560"></a>**1 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,803** — *Eòghann mac Nèill counts the rite of the eleven* (Seann Skell). At Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh on Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill, eleven years the quay's scribe, stands back as the scribe's place requires and counts the people on the stones twice, once by eye and once by name: eleven.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0238"><em>The last rite of the empty harbour in this age</em>, 25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6561"></a>**3 an Dàmhair, LE 1,804** — *Death of Aonghas mac Lachlainn* (Cathair dhearg). Aonghas mac Lachlainn dies at Cathair dhearg, four-and-eighty years old, the last of the council that had refused Clann Choinnich's Athchuingean an Airgid; asked once more on his deathbed why he had turned his own vote, he answers only that his reason had not stopped seeming good to him, and says no more.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0233"><em>The second silver petition</em>, 5 an Gearran, LE 1,776</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6562"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, LE 1,804** — *A rider of Muileann chiar attends the burying he was never asked to* (Cathair dhearg). A rider sent down by the silver guild of Muileann chiar on the strength of an old courtesy stands at the back of Aonghas mac Lachlainn's small burying at Cathair dhearg, and no one there asks him why a guild his vote had cost a fortune troubled to send anyone at all.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0233"><em>The second silver petition</em>, 5 an Gearran, LE 1,776</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0239"></a>**28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806** — *The silver petition laid aside* (Muileann chiar — baile mèinne airgid). The member who had turned the vote being dead, Clann Choinnich does not bring its silver petition to the council again. It lies unanswered in the vein-house, and the age ends with the Small-Burning Law still kept.<span class="fn fl">→ Caused by <a href="#ev-EIV-6561"><em>Death of Aonghas mac Lachlainn</em>, 3 an Dàmhair, LE 1,804</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6563"></a>**31 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806** — *Eòghann mac Nèill keeps the book with the window dark* (Seann Skell). Eòghann mac Nèill, harbour scribe of Seann Skell, passes the harbour-house window each rite-day and finds no reason offered for a light to be set there again; he enters nothing of it in his own book, which is kept for the number, the weather and the tide alone.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0237"><em>The lamps at Seann Skell go out</em>, 24 an Dàmhair, LE 1,799</a>; ← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0238"><em>The last rite of the empty harbour in this age</em>, 25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6564"></a>**27 am Faoilleach, LE 1,812** — *Na Seachd Taighean name themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim* (Cathair dhearg). Meeting at Cathair dhearg by chance of their riders' errands rather than by any summons, the heads of Na Seachd Taighean call themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim, the council of the custody, and name Tormod mac Ailein, eight-and-thirty years old and a custodian's son of no house among the seven, Ceann a' Chùraim to speak for them with one voice.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0239"><em>The silver petition laid aside</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6565"></a>**25 an Gearran, LE 1,812** — *Clann Choinnich's question is set aside at the first sitting* (Cathair dhearg). At the same sitting that names the council of the custody, Clann Choinnich alone asks whether the silver might be raised again; the board sets the question aside mildly, unwilling to test a new council on the one asking that had already cost the last one a member's death.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0239"><em>The silver petition laid aside</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6566"></a>**26 am Màrt, LE 1,812** — *The queen's chair is left standing empty* (Cathair dhearg). Na Seachd Taighean leave the chair at the head of the board, the queen's own, standing empty at every sitting after her name is no longer spoken; Tormod mac Ailein, offered it, keeps his place at the board's foot instead, and in time no clerk living can say with certainty whose absence the chair still marks.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0239"><em>The silver petition laid aside</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6567"></a>**20 an t-Iuchar, LE 1,812** — *The council's letters keep no name above the seal* (Cathair dhearg). The newly named council of the custody sends out its letters from Cathair dhearg sealed with Taigh na Fèithe's own trellis and hollow stone and no name written above the seal, continuing without comment a custom An Talla Dearg's clerks had already begun in the queen's last silent years.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0239"><em>The silver petition laid aside</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6568"></a>**29 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,812** — *An Talla Dearg holds five hundred souls* (Cathair dhearg). In the year Na Seachd Taighean name their council, An Talla Dearg at Cathair dhearg holds perhaps five hundred souls in all its lanes and closes, fewer than the tenants of a single one of Na Seachd Taighean in a good year.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0239"><em>The silver petition laid aside</em>, 28 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,806</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-III-0239a"></a>**27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813** — *The mist thins* (Seann Skell). The priests of Manannan at Seann Skell write that the mist on the eastern sea, which has hidden Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it since the fleet of the Sundering sailed into it, lies thinner each winter. They say their prayer, A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte, at every tide, and on still mornings the fishers of the north-west coast begin to see the line of the open sea beyond the headlands.
- <a id="ev-EIV-6569"></a>**1 an t-Samhain, LE 1,813** — *Mànas mac Dhùghaill writes that the mist lies thinner* (Seann Skell). Mànas mac Dhùghaill, priest of Manannan's rite at Seann Skell, sets down for the first time in his own book a thing the older priests had only ever said at the hearth: that the grey past the headlands stands thinner each year, and that he cannot say whether saying the prayer at every tide holds anything back at all.<span class="fn fl">→ Leads to <a href="#ev-III-0239a"><em>The mist thins</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6570"></a>**15 an t-Samhain, LE 1,813** — *Oighrig nic Eachainn sees the line of the open sea* (Ceann mhòr). A fisher of Ceann mhòr, Oighrig nic Eachainn, rests on her oars past where the rule of sight-of-land strictly allows and sees, for a few breaths before the grey closes again, a hard dark line beyond the mist, ruled clean across the edge of the world.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0239a"><em>The mist thins</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6571"></a>**23 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,813** — *Oighrig keeps what she saw to her own mother* (Ceann mhòr). Oighrig nic Eachainn turns for home as the rule says and tells no priest and no reeve what she saw beyond the mist, speaking of it months after only to her own mother, who tells her she has already shown better sense in the keeping of it than most who see such things at all.<span class="fn fl">⇄ At the same time <a href="#ev-III-0239a"><em>The mist thins</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6572"></a>**6 an Lùnastal, LE 1,818** — *The last winter of the age* (Seann Skell). On a still morning near the year's dark heart, the priests of Manannan pray at every tide at Seann Skell, the boats of Ceann mhòr turn for home before the rule strictly asks it of them, and the council keeps its board at Cathair dhearg with the chair at its head still empty, while the harbour-house lamp-window that once marked Oidhche nan Lòchran stands dark for another winter.<span class="fn fl">⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0239a"><em>The mist thins</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813</a>; ⇝ Legacy <a href="#ev-III-0238"><em>The last rite of the empty harbour in this age</em>, 25 an t-Samhain, LE 1,803</a>.</span>
- <a id="ev-EIV-6573"></a>**4 an t-Sultain, LE 1,818** — *Eòghann mac Nèill at the last winter* (Seann Skell). Six-and-twenty years the scribe of Cidhe an Diosail, Eòghann mac Nèill walks down to the stones each Là an Diosail with the same board under his arm and writes the number, the weather and the tide in the same plain hand.<span class="fn fl">← Follows from <a href="#ev-III-0239a"><em>The mist thins</em>, 27 an Dàmhair, LE 1,813</a>.</span>

# A Gazetteer of the Age

#### A

**Achadh naomh** (Achadh naomh). Founded 28 an t-Sultain, FE 2,324. The shire seat of Achadh naomh was the other party to the grazing quarrel with Baile ruadh that the king's council settled along the stream in LE 1,246. Like its neighbour it carried home the stones it had brought and set them into its own walls unused. Known for the grazing quarrel settled by the stream.

**Achadh shean** (Achadh shean). Founded 21 an Giblean, GE 3,125. The farming country of the far east caught the rain the eastern hills always had until three seasons ran dry from LE 1,479, and the crown's grain carts reached it by the mining road. Its reeves shared the deep wells among the households by lot and by turn and cut the sharing on a board at the well-head. The board was renewed each generation; the lots were never drawn again. When Queen Sìleas Òg stood at the well-head on her round and asked why, the reeve answered that no household wished to be the one to call the first sharing unfair, and she rode on without asking him to change it. Known for the board at the well-head.

**Àth chiar** (Àth chiar). Founded 18 an Giblean, FE 2,769. The citadel town in the eastern hills sends its drovers over the hills each year with cattle for the mining towns; from LE 484 they marked their road with a cairn at every day's stage, the first roads on the island so marked, so that a beast lost in mist or a driver new to the trade might find the way again. A boundary dispute at Àth chiar was still unsettled after three seasons when Tormod Bàn lay dying, and his last clear order gave it to the custodians to finish. In the sixteenth century its drovers took their beasts to the fair at Baile Mòr ruadh instead of selling nearer home. Known for the drovers' cairns.

**Àth dhomhain** (Àth dhomhain). Founded 19 an Lùnastal, LE 1,611. The deep ford on the northern river could be crossed safely only on horseback and by one path, and in LE 1,611 Raghnall Àthach and his kin, who knew that path, settled on the near bank and took a toll of every rider they led over. The ford-keepers' households grew into a town that held the one safe crossing of that country, and the family that owned the path came to be spoken of as lords of it before the age was out. Known for the horseman's ford.

**Àth fhiadhaich** (Doire chaol). Founded 14 an t-Sultain, FE 995. The fishing town kept its boats and nets shared among the households of a fellowship, and in the third century of the count King Fearchar mac Lachlainn, old and curious, kept one of its fishermen a full hour answering questions on how the sharing was done. Having lost catch to poor curing, it began in LE 394 to send carts north for Ros fhionn salt, and from then the mining shires ate their salt fish cured with salt carried over Drochaid Ros fhionn. Known for its fishers' fellowship and its salt fish.

**Àth fhionn** (Muileann shean). Founded 30 an Dùbhlachd, LE 697. Fishers of the north coast settled in the eighth century of the count at the ford where the coast road crosses a clear stream, and by LE 835 a market had grown up on their strand trading north-coast fish, the flesh and oil of stranded whales, wool and barley. The fishers of that coast no longer carried their catch the longer road south to Inis mhòr, and the ford town became the market of the north coast. Known for the strand-market of the north coast.

**Àth shean** (Àth shean). Founded 9 an t-Iuchar, GE 2,361. The walled ford town on the river above the granaries keeps the old crossing of the eastern road. In LE 554 Dùghall Garbh, guided by drovers who had used a hidden ford above the town for forty years to move cattle untolled, crossed his host in the dark and broke Raghnall Ruadh's camp at the ford; Leabhar a' Chùraim counts some three hundred dead, most of them drowned, and one old soldier swore to Seònaid nic Coinnich that the fighting took two days, not one. In the seventeenth century the growers on the slopes above the ford began to press blaeberry and bramble into a dark wine that kept a year in the cask, and the road-houses of the eastern stretch took to serving it as black wine. Known for the ford of Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean, and the black wine.

**Àth shean** (Àth shean). Founded 15 an Dàmhair, FE 1,963. The granary town south of the mountain kept the crown's stores. In the grain strife of LE 37 its reeve, Tormod mac Coinnich, who remembered a store-house swept empty behind a smiling reeve when he was seven, barred the granary doors and set a watch of four on them through Samhnas, Dubhlas and the black months, turning away every petitioner until a single rider came in Sìolach with a word that the grain might move; how the strife was settled he was never told. The middle pier of its bridge was rebuilt in stone in LE 46. Sìleas's firlot settled its first quarrel here, a carter and a miller measured true before the crowd their shouting drew. In LE 699 the granaries, standing since before a' Scaradh, were pulled down and built again in dressed stone on raised floors against the rats, under the reeve Fearchar mac Phàdraig. Eight centuries after that a young clerk found the town's firlot worn smaller than the capital's standard, and had been for generations. Known for the barred granary, and the worn firlot.

#### B

**Baile àrsaidh** (Baile àrsaidh). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, FE 879. The shire seat a little north of Cuan shean raised the sail-cloth for the fleet. Its tally-keeper cut a notch on his sticks for every close-woven length delivered from the households of Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh, owed once and reckoned against nothing, and by the ninth year he had cut more notches than he had thought the shire held households, some from weavers with no kin on the roll and no thought of sailing. The sticks filled a chest that wanted a second lid. After the sailing the shire went back to weaving for its own backs and the coasting trade, and the levy-chest is remembered in the shire as the one thing it ever gave that it did not count the cost of. Known for the sail-cloth levy for the fleet.

**Baile chrom** (Baile chrom). Founded 2 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,464. The north-west coast town was a quiet reeve's post until the sea-thieves of the small islands began boarding the coasters off its shore in the eighth century of the count. Its reeve Coinneach mac Nèill counted the going as carefully as he had counted grain, and in LE 789 reported half the houses empty, their thatch going to moss; the crown reckoned his town's dues by the households that stood. When the thieves put in twice in a moon within sight of his harbour he asked the crown for a force, and Eilidh Bhàn sent Iain mac Thormoid by sea; the town's own fishermen led the boats through the channel to Eilean dhubh, where the thieves' hulls were burned, one of the town's own sons, Aonghas mac Ruairidh, was killed on the strand, and Uilleam Ruadh was taken. Then the harvests failed one on the heels of the last. The reeve's wife Beathag nic Artair died in the hard winter of LE 819, the last households loaded their carts and went inland, and Coinneach, reeve eight-and-forty years, shut his door and took the coast road east. A reeve sent down the empty coast in LE 1,694 counted more berths than households between Baile chrom and Ceann mhòr. Known for the sea-thieves, and the reeve who stayed until the last cart.

**Baile gharbh** (Baile gharbh). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, GE 2,662. The weavers of the north-eastern town make a heavy undyed cloth that sheds rain, and in the fourth century of the count it became the common cloak of the north-east. In LE 361 the district took it as its cloth of mourning, worn plain through a household's season of loss as the whole island had once worn an Tùrsa Geal, and an Tùrsa Geal was kept in it in that country from then on. Known for the undyed rain-cloth worn for mourning.

**Baile gheal** (Baile gheal). Founded 27 an Giblean, GE 4,347. The old town of the south-west coast near Inis thais took Òrd na Cloiche's second house. When the congregation at Inis thais divided in LE 1,389 over whether the dead might be prayed for by name at Clach, those who said they might built their own temple of Òrd na Cloiche here, finished within ten years of the first quarrel, and the two congregations went their own ways, neither troubling the other much and neither giving ground. Known for the second temple of Òrd na Cloiche.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 7 an t-Ògmhios, GE 622. The low harbour town of the far south kept its citadel and its fishing through the age. In LE 1,739 a south-westerly storm flooded the low town and drowned twenty-three, and the town raised its sea-wall by the height of a man. Known for its sea-wall.

**Baile ghorm** (Baile ghorm). Founded 22 an Gearran, FE 837. The south-eastern town's dyers made a fast blue from a marsh plant and a mordant of their own, and in LE 1,064 the dyer Oighrig nic Ailein, after ten years changing one thing at a time, found the mixing that held the blue through washing after washing; cloth of it was worn at Taigh na Fèithe's midwinter gathering within the year and became the feast-day dress of the custodian houses. The last dyer who knew the mordant quarrelled with both her apprentices and died without teaching either, and the blue that followed, though it kept the old name, was the common blue of the rest of the island; the old weavers held the two lengths side by side and mourned the difference aloud for the rest of their lives. Known for the Baile ghorm blue, and its losing.

**Baile Mòr dhìreach** (Baile chaol). Founded 7 an Gearran, FE 2,051. The citadel on the straight eastern road, raised by custodians of the road in An Aois Naomh, was granted a market for the east coast in LE 731, and its boundary stones were set the day the grant was read, with a young vein-house scribe, Eòghann mac Pheadair, standing witness for Na Seachd Taighean. The fish and sail-cloth of the coast towns met the grain of the inland farms there, and the first stalls went up the same afternoon. Known for the market of the eastern road.

**Baile Mòr dhomhain** (Baile Mòr dhomhain). Founded 24 an t-Samhain, FE 101. The walled town near Taigh na Fèithe is the hall of Clann Fhearchair. Fearchar mac Lachlainn was born here, the elder son, and bound as a boy to a custodian's household for seven years while his younger brother Iain was kept at home to learn the hall; when the houses chose Fearchar king in LE 182, he kept his court part of each year here that he might take counsel of Taigh na Fèithe without a journey, and Iain kept Clann Fhearchair's hall when the court was at the capital. The brothers' letters across every season of the double court were gathered here into one leaf-book, boundary disputes beside a long complaint about the capital's cooking. Dùghall Garbh held his following here in the years before Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean, and died here of the wound he took at Muileann chrom, his last words asking whether Taigh na Fèithe gates stood open. In the thirteenth century masons of Ceann leathan began to buy the veined white stone of the hills above the town, and its quarries were worked from then on. Known for the double court, and the hall of Clann Fhearchair.

**Baile Mòr mhòr** (Baile Mòr mhòr). Founded 13 an t-Sultain, GE 2,616. The upland town took in so many families from the failing hill farms after a run of poor seasons in the fourth century of the count that it all but doubled, and in LE 324 its reeve marked out shares of the common grazing for households that had never held a share of it before. Known for the grazing shared anew.

**Baile Mòr ruadh** (Seann Tarr). Founded 15 an Lùnastal, GE 3,311. The walled town of the east by Seann Tarr held an autumn cattle fair that in LE 1,519 began to draw the drovers of Àth chiar and the eastern hills, who brought their beasts down to it rather than sell nearer home. It became yearly, and within a few years the greatest fair in the east. Known for the cattle fair of the east.

**Baile ruadh** (Inis mhin). Founded 9 an t-Iuchar, FE 957. The shire seat of Baile ruadh quarrelled with Achadh naomh over grazing along a stream that had shifted its bed, and in LE 1,246 the king's council divided the ground along the stream as it then ran. Both shire seats carried home the boundary stones they had brought to argue their claims and set them unused into their own walls, where they stood for the rest of the age pointing at a line the water had already drawn. Known for the boundary stones set into its walls.

#### C

**Caol bheag** (Caol bheag). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 2,414. The coastal town at the mouth of the Abhainn ghorm received the grain barges of Inis mhòr from the second century of the count. Its fishers' sons walked three days to sit the benches at Dùn thais, and one of them, Aonghas mac Nèill, stayed to keep the house's register. In LE 1,369 the fishers of silted Caol ìseal came to it and set up their shrine again stone by stone in the same order, so that it stood as it always had. Known for the shrine carried whole from Caol ìseal.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Caol fhiadhaich). Founded 12 an t-Iuchar, GE 1,547. The old harbour town of the south-west coast took the coughing sickness in LE 156, and it reached the reeve's own household. His wife would not let their door be barred against the shared board, holding that a household which eats apart out of fear will go on eating apart after the fear has passed; she lived, and the custom of the shared meal outlasted the sickness in that country. Known for the shared meal kept through the cough.

**Caol fhiadhaich** (Inis thais). Founded 13 an t-Iuchar, LE 739. The fishing town on the wild strait near Inis thais was founded in LE 739. Its fishers had always kept their boats inside the strait that gave the town its name, never past their own headlands, until in LE 1,389 some of them went out and found a safe lane south to the landing at Cidhe Beag. Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich was not believed at first; within a season or two of its being believed, the older harbours of the south coast followed it one after another. Known for Slighe-mhara Caol fhiadhaich.

**Caol gharbh** (Caol gharbh). Founded 10 am Màrt, GE 4,128. The fishing village on the rough strait of the north-east became the salt port of the north-east in LE 1,169, when the Ros fhionn masters dug out and walled its harbour with their own money after their river silted. A laden barge out of the new harbour struck the reef in the narrows called Coinneachadh na h-Amhaich in its first year and went down with half her salt, both crewmen swimming ashore; the harbour-masters set the channel's first withy at the rock the next spring. The trade held for five and a half centuries, until the sea rose over the salt-pans in LE 1,734 and they failed, and the salt of the north-east came from the south instead. Known for the salt harbour, and the narrows.

**Caol ìseal** (Caol ìseal). Founded 21 am Màrt, FE 1,450. The harbour on the north coast had been silting longer than any one season could be blamed for, and in LE 1,369 its fishing families gave the last of it up and moved east to Caol bheag, carrying their nets, their smoking-racks and the small shrine from the harbour's edge, stone by stone. The town did not empty; the houses nearest the silted water turned to farming the ground behind them, and within two generations it smelled of turned earth rather than fish and tar. Known for the harbour given up to the plough.

**Caol leathan** (Caol leathan). Founded 12 am Faoilleach, GE 1,560. The small walled harbour on the south-west coast beside Inis thais kept a harbour shrine that the priests of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and an Fhianna both came to claim in LE 427, their feast mornings falling on the same day. The king's reeve, Murchadh mac Ailpein, halved the shrine's hours between them, as the sacred woods of an older age had once been divided, and nailed the division on a strip of hide to the shrine door. The division held, and neither order was pleased with it. Known for the shrine with two orders' hours.

**Caol shean** (Caol shean). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 4,196. The fishing town took the greatest catch of its memory in LE 1,039 and ran out of salt on the second day. The shed-foreman Ruairidh mac Neacail hung what could not be salted on lines strung the length of the lower town's lanes rather than let it spoil on the strand; the dried fish sold poorly against salted, and from that year the town laid in salt for a catch half again the size of any it had taken. Known for the year the lanes were hung with fish.

**Cathair dhearg** (Cathair dhearg). Founded 6 an Dàmhair, GE 18. The kings and queens of the age kept their hall on An Cnoc Ruadh above the Abhainn dhomhain, and every crowning of the age was made there. Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill heard the three crews in An Talla Dearg in the first year, gave her word that the crown would send no one and keep no one back, and wore undyed wool for her sister from the thirteenth year of the count until she died in the fifty-fifth. The houses first chose a king here when Ìomhar's line failed, in a cold yard where seven neck-rings caught the sun and nobody spoke for a morning. Sìleas set the standard firlot here and widened the bridge for two carts abreast; Catrìona Bhuadhach laid her stone road south from it to Inis thais. The crown was joined to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe in Dòmhnall Ruadh's reign, and from then An Talla Dearg's letters carried the custody's seal. The capital grew slowly and Cathair mhòr passed it in the tenth century of the count; in the age's last years the hall held perhaps five hundred souls. After Queen Gormshuil went up to the winter burning in LE 1,795 and nothing more is told, Na Seachd Taighean sat at her board with her chair left empty, and named themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim there in LE 1,812. Known for An Talla Dearg, the queen's empty chair, and the board of Na Seachd Taighean.

**Cathair dhomhain** (Cathair dhomhain). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, FE 634. The walled harbour city above the river mouth, with its citadel of An Aois Naomh and granaries deep enough for two winters, declared for Dùghall Garbh in the second year of Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean, chiefly because its harbour-master had once carried grain for him. Catrìona nic Aonghais came against it in the autumn of LE 556; borrowed fishing coasters shut its water gate by night while her lines held the land gate. With no ground beyond the walls for burying, the dead were laid near the well-heads, and a sickness of the gut went through the streets and the garrison. On the fortieth day Niall Mòr mac Leòid surrendered, and Catrìona let his garrison march out between her silent lines on his sworn word, carrying its dead and wounded by name. It was in her camp before this city that Dùghall Garbh came with six men and no herald to offer her his host against Raghnall Ruadh. Known for the siege of forty days and the garrison freed on oath.

**Cathair fhada** (Cathair fhada). Founded 13 an Cèitean, GE 2,523. The long walled city on its ridge south of the capital was granted a market at every full moon by Queen Sìleas in LE 287, with a tally-house for the south, the first market right cut on paired sticks. At its first full-moon market traders came from three days' walk in every direction and carried honey, hemp, wax and pottery north as one company, and a trader of the long city asked the capital's clerk what stopped a false notch being cut after a bargain, and was shown how the grain of a split stick runs true only when its two halves are laid together. Known for the full-moon market and the paired tallies.

**Cathair mhòr** (Cathair mhòr). Founded 9 an Dùbhlachd, GE 2,847. The walled market city of the south took in forty-one burnt-out households of Doire mhin in LE 555 at the temple of Macha and fed them through the winter on the temple's grain without asking whose claim they had favoured. In the winter of the refusal its temple fire went out in Dubhlas, on a morning so still the smoke of the last coals stood upright, and when a carrier's basket brought coal again it was the first of the cold shires' hearths to burn. Its market drew the trade of all the south, and a carter asked why he sold his barley here and not at the capital said a man carries his load to whichever gate opens first and pays best; by LE 969 it was greater than the capital. Its copper-workers stamped every cooking pot with a maker's mark and sent them out on every road. It fed Ceann mhin after the burning of Cogadh nam Bràithrean, and in the fifteenth century the priests of Macha finished their great house here, its floor of black and white eleven years in the laying, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr. Known for Macha's great house, and the copper pots of every hearth.

**Ceann mhin** (Ceann mhin). Founded 18 an Lùnastal, FE 745. The walled harbour city declared for Iain Ciar in Cogadh nam Bràithrean, and in LE 1,272 Alasdair Bàn's ships came down the coast and burned its waterfront before the town's own bell had finished ringing the alarm. The fire took the tarred rope stores and then the granary; by the second morning the town had lost both what it needed to put to sea and what it needed to eat until harvest. Cathair mhòr, which had taken no side, sent grain enough that no household went hungry that winter. In LE 1,549 a second great fire burned it with no war to blame, and before the ash had cooled its reeve ordered it rebuilt with gable walls of stone between each house and the next, so that a fire must cross stone to spread. Known for its two fires, and the gable walls.

**Ceann mhòr** (Ceann mhòr). Founded 6 an Cèitean, FE 163. The fishing town twenty miles up the coast from Seann Skell sent Tòmas mac Uilleim to An Talla Dearg in the first year with the telling that the far land lay behind the mist and could be smelt on some mornings. After the sailing Seonag nic Dhùghaill climbed its headland at first light in LE 66 and kept it through the day, and household after household took a turn after her; the custom was called Faire a' Chinn, and Seonag kept her own turns for forty years. The watch lapsed long before the age was out, and the fishing thinned with the rest of the north-west, until perhaps a dozen boats still put out from its shore. In LE 1,794 its fishers found a worked timber cast up, longer than any tree of the island and fastened with nails no smith of Dia-thìr had forged. In the last years of the age a fisher of the town, Oighrig nic Eachainn, rested on her oars past where the rule of sight-of-land allowed, saw a hard dark line beyond the grey for a few breaths, and turned for home and told only her mother. Known for Faire a' Chinn, and the timber out of the mist.

**Cill ghlas** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 4 am Faoilleach, FE 1,814. The small village in the hills a short way from Muileann dhearg sits over the galleries of the vein. An earth tremor in LE 379 cracked three of its wells and brought down a byre; the custodians sent men into the galleries below and found the deep workings untouched, and gave the village stone from their own surplus to raise the byre again, a kindness it did not forget. A second tremor in LE 929 brought down a gallery on fourteen of the custodians' own labourers in the small hours of the morning shift. Taigh na Fèithe closed the gallery rather than dig the dead free, and set a stone at its mouth with the fourteen names cut in the order they went down, the youngest a boy of thirteen, the oldest a woman forty years at the same gallery; households of the mountain leave small stones at its foot on the day of the fall. Known for Clach nan Ceithir Ainmean Deug.

**Cnoc bhàn** (Baile ghorm). Founded 23 an Dùbhlachd, LE 250. The hill-lords of Baile ghorm walled a pale hill above the long mill-race of Muileann fhada in the third century of the count, and in LE 1,051 set a single market there to gather the south-east's scattered trade into one place. Its rare good was the pearls of the south-eastern shallows, sold in whole parcels as at no other market; at the first opening the shore-woman Sìne nic Ruairidh brought a whole season's gathering rather than sell it a pearl at a time along the road, and a trader of Cathair mhòr paid her more for the lot than she had ever been offered piecemeal. Known for the market above the mill-race, and its pearls.

**Cnoc bheag** (Cnoc bheag). Founded 5 an t-Sultain, GE 3,908. The walled town above Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag kept the dawn-hawk rite of An Aois Naomh, and in the third century of the count the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair taught there that the hawk of the rite was Mòd himself, and that the vein under Muileann dhearg was a hawk of his kind, to be fed the measured handful and never glutted past it. Her father Artair kept the mews before her; she first called the hawk down alone at three-and-thirty. Her watchers raised Taigh an t-Seabhaig below the mews block in LE 232, and after her death Ùisdean mac Pàdraig wrote her sayings as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig. By royal grant in LE 471 Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag passed to the priests of Macha alone. At the council of Òrd an t-Seabhaig here in LE 889 a young priest asked whether Mòd would rather starve a grown flock than see his handful grown to meet it, and those who held he would not were named An Seabhag Biadhte and asked to keep their teaching elsewhere. In the eleventh century the priest Tòmas mac Aonghais cleared the moss from Carragh Cnoc bheag above the town with wooden scrapers and found letters no table of the schools could read. Known for the house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig and Leabhar an t-Seabhaig.

**Cnoc chaol** (Seann Vell). Founded 23 am Faoilleach, LE 167. The village of Cnoc chaol on the south coast lost two children in LE 724 to a great swell that rose with no storm behind it and ran the drying-racks off the beach. The household of one of the drowned struck itself from its old gallery-claim and took up a claim further from the water, and Taigh na Fèithe's young scribe Eòghann mac Pheadair entered the removal the next season, cold and plain, as he had been taught. Known for the wave with no storm behind it.

**Cnoc naomh** (Cnoc naomh). Founded 10 an t-Samhain, GE 2,894. The walled temple town in the middle country was seized by Alasdair Bàn's men in LE 1,270 and taken back by Iain Ciar. Na Seachd Taighean divided four to three over the brothers, and Cogadh nam Bràithrean is counted from this fight. Both households set every road between the two halves of the island under one following's watch or the other, and carters who had crossed freely all their lives had to say plainly whose peace they travelled under. Known for the first battle of Cogadh nam Bràithrean.

**Cuan dhearg** (Seann Vell). Founded 31 am Faoilleach, FE 1,384. The harbour town under the red cliffs of the south, the other Cuan dhearg, lost its waterfront in LE 519 to the storm the south-coast rolls call An Gàire Dubh, which drove the sea over it in a single night and spoiled the season's salt fish on the racks. King Tormod Bàn sent grain south before any asking came, and the town rebuilt a full street back from the old shore, on ground no telling said the sea had reached; the king rode down to see it, the one journey of his reign made for a storm's sake. In LE 1,754 the sea came over the waterfront a second time and flooded the moved street to its thresholds, and the town built a sea-wall; Gormshuil nic Thormoid, sent by her father to see it building, carried home the harbour-master's word that a wall a man can stand behind is worth more than a street he can only run from. The town buried the boundary stones of the first street rather than break them up. Known for the street moved back from the sea, and the sea-wall.

**Cuan ruadh** (Cuan ruadh). Founded 1 an t-Sultain, GE 2,387. The eastern harbour, a hundred miles from the west coast over the mountain country, kept the only sailors of the island who had ever held a course by night. Six pilots of the west walked to it in LE 11 and were sent to the old steersman Seumas Reultach, who taught them on the headland above the town the wheel of the sky and Reul na Stiùire, and had his granddaughter cut part of it on a hide; he died on the cliff path in LE 14 and is buried among his own people. After the pilots went west nobody at Cuan ruadh sailed by night any longer. In the fifteenth century it built a second harbour arm to take the boats of Seann Tarr when that harbour broke, and throve on the fishing of both towns' waters for the rest of the age.
