Known for the star-steersmen, and its second harbour arm.

**Cuan shean** (Cuan shean). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 2,755. The harbour a dozen miles down the coast from Seann Skell heard the first tale of a far shore on its quays in the moon of Faolach of the first year, and its skipper Eachann mac Lachlainn told the queen of a low dark coast west and north of west. For the fleet it gave its hemp fields to cordage, and by the sixth year its waterfront was three rope-walks end to end, where Iain Ròpaire and his walkers learned the names of a keel so that the shroud-lines would stop failing. The walks turned off hands when the harbour trade halved after the sailing, and were shortened in the eighth century of the count, half the ground sown with barley. The rope-walker Tormod Ciar swore Cupa na Fìrinne on the walk itself, cupping rainwater in his hands. In the fourteenth century Tormod Ròpaire's crew still walked their strands to a work-song whose strange words named the parts of a deep keel, and Iseabail nic Lachlainn took it down there; the crew kept singing it exactly as he gave it, no better understood. Known for its rope-walks, and Òran na Druime.

#### D

**Doire chiar** (Doire chiar). Founded 8 an Giblean, GE 4,183. The village in the north-eastern hills is where Eilidh nic Iain, Eilidh Dhubh, taught at the well from LE 460, at thirty years old, the teaching her grandmother had taught her in secret: that the vein answers labour and not birth. She wrote it down in a hand her mother taught her, and pupils copied her tracts for households too far to hear her. When Taigh na Fèithe burned some hundred of them in its yard in LE 484 she walked there to see it done and said nothing. One hide in her mother's hand stayed whole in a hollow beam of her house. She died here in LE 505, teaching within the hour of her death, and was buried behind her own house; Coinneach Odhar read the tracts at her grave from the copy he had carried thirty years. Known for Eilidh Dhubh and her tracts.

**Doire fhiadhaich** (Ros dhomhain). Founded 18 an Dùbhlachd, LE 1,506. A wood of wild oak, crooked and never anyone's grove, stood on the shore of Loch chrom below the capital, and in the fifth year woodcutters of the roll built huts at its edge to fell crooked oak for the fleet's frames and knees. The huts did not outlast the felling. The wood kept its name, and the tellers of that shore say that timber for the fleet was felled there. Fifteen centuries on, other woodcutters came to what was left of the wood and stayed, and their huts became the village of Doire fhiadhaich, a fishing and cutting place on the capital shore that remembered the fleet chiefly as a reason for its name. Known for its oaks, said to have built a' Scaradh fleet.

**Doire fhionn** (Doire fhionn). Founded 4 an t-Samhain, FE 1,149. The village in the north took its name from the oak grove on the hill above it, and in the fifth year Alasdair Saor came up the north road to fell it for the keels of the fleet. Its keeper, Eilidh nic Ruairidh, made him choose each tree he would take and hear its name; he chose fifty-four and left one young oak, the Child. Eighty men of the roll felled the grove through the summer, the greatest tree, the Queen, taking two days to bring down, and the keel-timbers went forty-two miles south to the sea on sleds of oak shod with ash, six yoke to a sled, over a causeway built across the stream below the village. The grove never grew again. The village built a low wall of stones round the Child, and its old keeper sat beside it every evening until dark. In LE 109 Taigh na Fèithe set down the coppice law of Doire fhionn, and the village lived thereafter by cutting coppice rather than oak, some of the fellowship's released journeymen among its cutters. Known for the oaks felled for the fleet, and the Child walled on the hill.

**Doire mhin** (Doire mhin). Founded 10 an t-Ògmhios, FE 2,260. The granary village on the road south of the ford had given carts and coal to Taigh na Fèithe without complaint for as long as anyone remembered, and did nothing to deserve what it got in LE 555, save stand on the road Raghnall Ruadh's broken host had to pass. The retreating men took what grain the granary held, fired it and a dozen houses about it, and went on. Coinneach mac Ailein carried his daughter Seònaid and the year's seed-corn out of the fire. Forty-one households walked six days south and wintered at Cathair mhòr on the charity of Macha's temple, where the fire went out in the winter of the refusal; Seònaid grew up to write Leabhar nan Trì Tagraichean. The village was rebuilt, and its people kept the tale of Na Teallaichean Fuara longer than any other in the island. Known for the burning of LE 555, and the child who wrote its history.

**Doire shean** (Doire shean). Founded 14 an Lùnastal, GE 695. The village on the southern shore laid out oyster beds in its shallow bay in the seventh century of the count and sent oysters by cart to the capital, a trade that made it rich enough to keep its temple. The old road-house Am Buabhall Fortanach stands by it on the road south, rebuilt in stone by Eilidh nic Chaluim after it burned to its footings in LE 164, where a boy of Clann Fhearchair was given a bowl of the jugged buffalo before the roof was on; Catrìona Bhuadhach's stone road went past it to Inis thais. Known for its oysters, and Am Buabhall Fortanach.

**Dùn dhearg** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 9 an Gearran, GE 4,274. Clann Ìomhair, who hold the land about the city in the eastern hills, walled it in stone in LE 261 without the crown's leave, the first walls on the island raised by a custodian house. Queen Sìleas summoned their head to a cold supper at An Talla Dearg; neither spoke of the walls, both understood, and the walls stood. The smiths of the city made the ceremonial blades of the custodian houses from the layered steel of their fellowship, folded and refolded, until in LE 1,568 the fellowship lost the last smith who knew the folding well enough to finish a blade alone; the blades made after him were ordinary work. Known for the walls of Clann Ìomhair, and the layered steel lost.

**Dùn ìseal** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 9 an Lùnastal, GE 1. The old hall at Dùn ìseal, where Brìde's flame burns in Talla na Lasrach and the stone cup stands on the threshold, was the heir of the custody before Taigh na Fèithe took it; in this age it is the seat of Na Seann Spioradan of the eastern shires. In LE 179 their keepers raised a house for the ancestors there and cut the names of the eastern dead on wooden posts, renewed each generation; a young man of Clann Fhearchair, reading them, said a shire that trusted wood to hold its dead must trust its memory further than he would. Lightning burned the posts to their footings in LE 1,149, and the keepers cut the names again from memory and from Leabhar a' Chùraim, owning in their roll that some were guesses. An earthquake cracked the spirit-house in LE 1,649 and killed no one; the keepers took it for a warning and could not agree of what. Known for the ancestor-posts and Brìde's flame.

**Dùn thais** (Dùn thais). Founded 28 am Màrt, GE 2,473. The walled temple city in the north-east is the seat of Taigh na Deasbaid. Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn, a druid of the schools of Flidais who had walked the carters' roads for forty years, raised Taigh na Deasbaid here in LE 314 and had the schools' old question, Carson an làmh seo?, cut into its lintel before the roof was on; a question once put was argued a full year before any answer came from the master's chair. Pupils walked three days from Caol bheag to sit its benches. In LE 324 Coinneach asked there whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, and each of Na Seachd Taighean forbade the question at its own table. Ailean mac Dhùghaill's tables of the three old ruins were judged here, and in the thirteenth century Raghnall mac Chaluim set out here Clàr nam Bliadhnachan that showed the heads of the houses living longer than their tenants; the table was forbidden and the house shut. It was opened and shut more than once, and last reopened in LE 1,759 on condition that the question of longer lives never be raised; its schools turned instead to whether Leabhar a' Chùraim's handful answered to what the coal gave out. Known for Taigh na Deasbaid, and the questions it was forbidden.

#### I

**Inis àrsaidh** (Seann Skell). Founded 28 am Faoilleach, FE 76. The fishing village a little below Seann Skell gave more households to Rolla nan Deònach than any other place on the island. Two of its households said in the drying-shed, in the first year, that they would go if a boat were ever built that could make the crossing, and the village laughed and then stopped laughing. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and her husband Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh farmed the land above it, and it was at their board that Alasdair Saor was sent north to the oaks of Doire fhionn. When An Fhaoileag An Fhaoileag lay down off Ros àrsaidh in the sixth year, its boats brought back three living and eight dead; the roll-keeper cut eleven names on the village's board in one night, and a lamp burned on the shingle for the three the sea kept. When the broken tidings of two landfalls came, the village kept both halves of the tale at once. Ruairidh mac Artair had a deep hull built here in the fourth century of the count; it listed at launch and was broken up within a fortnight, for no wright still living held the old scarfing of the keel. Known for the eleven names on its board, and the households it gave to the fleet.

**Inis chrom** (Inis chrom). Founded 25 an Giblean, FE 1,601. The walled harbour town on the south-west coast took a spotted fever among its fisher households in LE 624 that killed some forty. An Fhianna nursed the sick, and many of them died of it, and the town followed Òrd na Cloiche from then on. Known for the fever an Fhianna nursed.

**Inis mhòr** (Inis mhòr). Founded 16 an Dàmhair, GE 4,328. The river town of the north built barges in the second century of the count to carry grain down the Abhainn ghorm and west along the cold way of the north coast, and a boy of the town watching the first one loaded asked his father why it should not simply cross open water by the shorter way, and got a look and no answer. Pupils of Dùn thais founded a house of disputation here in LE 769, the question of the vein argued in the north for the first time. The great gale of LE 1,229 drove the sea up the river higher than anyone living had seen and heaped the strand with broken plank. As the roads improved the coasting trade went by cart, and in LE 1,634 the last barge that had worked the cold way was hauled above the tide-line and chocked level, kept rather than broken up, though few of the town's fathers could say any longer what the cold way had been the way from. Known for the grain barges of the cold way, and the last one kept on the strand.

**Inis thais** (Inis thais). Founded 21 an Lùnastal, GE 2,408. The walled harbour city of the south-west coast kept an old wolf-stone called Clach, watched for generations by families who had forgotten why. In LE 405 a net-maker of the strand, Dòmhnall mac Ailein, thirty-five years old, began telling the men who mended nets beside him that the stone was Lia Fàil and its watchers an Fhianna, sworn to keep the island as a wolf keeps its range, and his hearers became Òrd na Cloiche. They raised the first temple on the island to Lia Fàil by name, roofed with northern slate the shipmaster Beathag nic Raoghnaill fetched by sea, and blew a horn at every turn of the tide. Dòmhnall taught on the strand five-and-thirty years and never took an office. Catrìona nic Aonghais was born here in LE 526 to the king's brother, and her mother kept her here rather than raise her at An Talla Dearg; as queen she laid Rathad na Banrighinn in stone from the capital to her own gate. In LE 1,389 Òrd na Cloiche's congregation divided over whether the dead might be prayed for at Clach; those who said no kept the temple. Known for the wolf-stone Clach and Òrd na Cloiche.

#### M

**Muileann chaol** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 18 an t-Ògmhios, GE 3,218. The mill town on the hill road of the east had a widow's loft by the seventeenth century of the count. Beathag nic Thòmais, whose husband had owned its mill, began in LE 1,659 to buy old copies of Leabhar a' Chùraim and Rolla a' Chalaidh from houses that no longer read them, and in her loft a crown clerk found the only surviving copy of a custodians' ruling Taigh na Fèithe had lost to fire. In LE 1,674 Anna nic Coinnich began to make paper from rags at the town's ford, the first on Dia-thìr; Beathag carried it sixty miles to Taigh na Fèithe herself, and Leabhar a' Chùraim was copied onto it for the first time. Among her papers she found three copies of the tidings of the two landfalls that did not agree, copied all three fair, and chose none. She left the loft to the town when she died in LE 1,699, on condition that nothing in it be burned, and the town kept the condition; its unpaid keeper told a crown reeve that fifty years of neither office asking for the papers back was itself an answer. Known for the paper mill and the loft of Beathag nic Thòmais.

**Muileann chiar** (Dùn ìseal). Founded 10 an Lùnastal, FE 7. The hill town of the silver seam keeps the sacred wood of Flidais, where the elder teachers of Scoiltean nan Draoidhean met, and its smiths beat the silver neck-rings that the heads of Na Seachd Taighean first wore in LE 149, so that a stranger might know a custodian by the collar before a word was said. Beathag nic Ruairidh taught in its grove when Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn came to it with the question he had carried on the roads, and told him the schools wanted a fixed ground where it might be argued whole. From LE 479 the schools kept the wood and walked its bounds each year in a procession open to anyone who would walk with them. Twice in the age Clann Choinnich asked that the coal be burned beyond the handful to smelt the silver here, in LE 1,559 and in LE 1,776, and twice the council refused; the second time by a single turned vote. Known for the silver collars, the wood of Flidais, and the smelt refused.

**Muileann chrom** (Muileann chrom). Founded 11 an Gearran, FE 1,556. The town eight miles from Muileann dhearg below the mountain was a custodians' town of Clann Raghnaill, whose households kept galleries there. The hosts of Catrìona nic Aonghais and Dùghall Garbh, joined for the purpose, met Raghnall Ruadh below it in LE 560, and Raghnall fell on the field; the next morning his own custodians struck the seal from Taigh na Fèithe store without waiting to be told who now held the mountain. Dùghall took a cut below the arm there that he hid from his physicians and died of it. Three centuries later the heads of Na Seachd Taighean, sitting five years at Taigh na Fèithe to choose a king, spoke the name of Dòmhnall Ruadh of Muileann chrom, who kept three galleries there, and he spent his first night as king naming which of his neighbours he trusted to measure them honestly in his absence. He came back as king to settle a boundary between two households by asking each one's oldest member where they had played as children. Known for the battle that ended Raghnall Ruadh's refusal, and the mountain's own king.

**Muileann dhearg** (Muileann dhearg). Founded 30 an t-Sultain, LE 2. Coal-breakers of the central diggings settled below the gate of Taigh na Fèithe, in the first years of the age, and Taigh na Fèithe above them kept Leabhar a' Chùraim, Crom's stone in its inner room, and the lamp in the niche that was never let go out. The custodians counted Rolla nan Deònach against the book here in the third year, nine days at the long table, and found one hearth in five of the coal-right meant to go; here they ruled one sealed measure of coal to each hull that should be ready, and the boy-clerk Donnchadh mac Thormoid made the fair copy at fifteen and began, at thirty, the count of years from An Diosal that the crown took up after him. Na Seachd Taighean were sworn before Crom's stone in LE 55 and drew their galleries by lot in the hall in LE 109. Eachann Briseadair's household built the first stone house below the gate, and the row became a town with its own well, smith and reeve in his lifetime. Eilidh Dhubh's tracts were burned in Taigh na Fèithe yard in LE 484; Raghnall Ruadh refused the handful to the shires that stood against him from its store in LE 558, and Riaghailt an Teallaich was drafted in the same yard seven years later. Dòmhnall Ruadh joined the crown to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe, and was buried at his own wish in a worked-out gallery with an unlit lamp at his head. Queen Gormshuil rode up to the winter burning here in LE 1,795, as she had every winter of her reign, and nothing more is told. Known for Taigh na Fèithe and Leabhar a' Chùraim.

**Muileann dhomhain** (Muileann dhomhain). Founded 9 an t-Samhain, FE 1,417. The south-eastern mill town took the swallowing cough in LE 1,079, a sickness that closed the throat until a man could not swallow his own spit; it went house by house along the lower street and up into the hill lanes, and the town lost near a third of its people. Beathag Fhionn, crowned in LE 1,082, shut the coast road between Seann Bhral and Muileann dhomhain within the month and set a reeve at each of its six fords, and the road stayed shut three years; the cough never crossed west of them. The town stood at less than two households in three for twenty years and more, its old reeve walking the lower street once a season to write down which roofs had fallen, until families from the hill country above came down a handful a year and took the empty houses by lot. Known for the swallowing cough, and the houses taken by lot.

**Muileann gheal** (Dùn dhearg). Founded 7 an Dàmhair, LE 1,082. White-stone millers raised the mill town in the south-east in LE 1,082 to grind for the city of Dùn dhearg. Its potters of Clann Mhic Phàil made a grey-green glaze that no other kiln could match, and the custodian houses bought their table-ware from that one family; the secret went mother to daughter unwritten. The last of the family, Iain Mac Phàil, took two apprentices in his last years, and neither learned to judge the moment the kiln's heat must be let fall. He died without passing it on in LE 1,509, and for a generation the town's potters tried to match it and failed. Known for the grey-green glaze, and its losing.

**Muileann ghlas** (Dùn chrom). Founded 16 an t-Samhain, FE 748. The small mill town under Dùn chrom saw the last battle of Cogadh nam Bràithrean in LE 1,274, when Iain Ciar defeated his brother Alasdair Bàn below it, took him alive and let his captains go home. An ox-driver who turned back from the mountain road rather than push his team through unsettled country carried word of it to An Taigh-seinnse Mòr within the week, and could not say where the brothers now stood to one another; the peace was made two years later at the road-house. Known for the battle that ended Cogadh nam Bràithrean.

**Muileann naomh** (Muileann naomh). Founded 24 am Faoilleach, GE 2,986. The southern mill town became the southernmost house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in the sixth century of the count. Its bell-founders cast the first bronze bell on Dia-thìr to hang in a hawk-house in LE 514, with King Tormod Bàn standing at the casting; it cracked in its first frost, and the second, thicker at the waist, held, and rang at every measured burning. There Òrd an t-Seabhaig's teaching was still given whole and unsoftened when it faded elsewhere, and pilgrims came to it from further south than any hawk-house had drawn from before. Known for the first bell of a hawk-house.

**Muileann ruadh** (Cnoc leathan). Founded 15 am Faoilleach, LE 190. The town where warm water rises from the ground in the east country was founded in LE 190, and in LE 769 its bath-house was rebuilt below it. Coal-breakers, salt-carriers and shepherds sat in the warm water together without minding whose gallery the others answered to, and the old vein-house scribe Eòghann mac Pheadair was carried there by cart in his last cold season. Known for its bath-house over Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh.

**Muileann shean** (Muileann shean). Founded 1 an t-Samhain, FE 1,093. The millers of the northern mill town cut a new gearing for their wheels in LE 1,189, oak toothed against oak, so that one wheel turned two stones where it had turned one. Half the town came to watch it the first winter and went away arguing whether the flour was finer or coarser. Within a generation every mill of consequence in the north had it, and the millers hung a carved model of it over their own door as a boast that grew quieter with every mill that copied it without asking leave. Known for the gearing that turned two stones.

#### R

**Ros àrsaidh** (Ros bheag). Founded 16 an t-Ògmhios, FE 1,221. The small walled harbour on the point below Ros bheag is where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put out to sea. The first finished hull, An Fhaoileag, was taken past it for her trial in the sixth year and lay down in a following sea off its headland with fourteen aboard. Eight years later its strand was the ground of the first night-steering trial, when Catrìona nic Iain, home from the steersmen of Cuan ruadh, took one boat out past the headland with every lantern doused and brought her in by Reul na Stiùire before the lantern-boat that hugged the shore. Half the town came down to see it fail. After the fleet sailed the point went back to the coasting trade and the fishing, and nobody out of it is recorded to have sailed by night again. Known for the loss of An Fhaoileag, and the first night steered by a star.

**Ros bheag** (Ros bheag). Founded 2 an Dàmhair, GE 1,274. The walled harbour town of the Ros bheag cape sent its skipper Oighrig nic Raghnaill to An Talla Dearg in the first year with a telling of a high forested coast past the north cape, and two of the six pilots who walked east to learn the stars at Cuan ruadh were its own, Catrìona nic Iain among them. After the sailing it was a fishing and coasting town like its neighbours. Manannan's teaching came to it down the coast with the fishing families, and in LE 694 the priests of the order at Ros bheag laid down that no boat of the faithful might go out of sight of the headlands; within the year two of the order's boats turned back its own skipper Coinneach mac Sheumais when he chased a run of fish too far. Four years later a priest there asked a pilot's grandson, Griogair, which star his grandfather had steered by, and the boy could not say. The rule of the headlands was kept on the west coast for the rest of the age. Known for the rule of sight-of-land, and the pilot who forgot his star.

**Ros fhionn** (Inis bheag). Founded 29 an Lùnastal, FE 41. The small walled river town of the north-east found its fortune in LE 350, when a farmer digging a ditch above it struck warm water that tasted of salt. Pans were laid out on the flats within the season, and the salt went inland over Drochaid Ros fhionn, whose keeper Iain mac Ùisdein took a handful from every load for his toll and filled an iron-bound salt-box faster than any box on that road. Ros fhionn salted the fish of the mining shires, and at the height of its fair in LE 959 the reeve lost his count past four thousand people on the flats. The salt-masters rebuilt the bridge's arches at their own cost in the twelfth century after a carter's mule went into the river through the road bed. Then a shifting bar silted the Abhainn bheag, the barges could no longer reach the quays, and the salt went by sea through Caol gharbh; the market-court stayed on its headland with its bench of old oak, the bridge's last keeper died with no one to take the toll, and the channel was withied from the bar to open water. Known for its salt, its bridge and its market-court.

**Ros gheal** (Ros gheal). Founded 29 an Dùbhlachd, FE 1,009. The harbour town on the north coast took the dawn rite of Òrd an t-Seabhaig in LE 239, when two of Gormshuil nic Artair's pupils, a brother and sister of a coastal household, carried it down from Cnoc bheag so that the fishing families need not walk two days inland for it; Gormshuil came down herself to judge whether the teaching had travelled whole. Its hawk-house took charge of the measured burning for the country between the coast and the hills, and was eight years old when Gormshuil died. Ùisdean mac Pàdraig came here to gather what her pupils remembered for Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, and marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth. Known for the second house of Òrd an t-Seabhaig.

#### S

**Seann Bhral** (Seann Bhral). Founded 30 an Lùnastal, VE 1,005. The walled port of the south-east was the second town the swallowing cough reached, in LE 1,081. Its townsfolk closed the harbour themselves before any order came, and kept the shared meal by leaving food at the town gate for the households that could no longer come to the board. The coast road from it to Muileann dhomhain was shut by the queen's reeves for three years after. Known for the harbour shut against the cough, and the meal at the gate.

**Seann Chwen** (Seann Chwen). Founded 19 an Giblean, VE 32. The harbour town on the south coast below the mountain finished its stone mole in LE 899, and the coal-barges of the mountain roads tied up there where before they had beached on shingle at low water; it became the port of the coal-carts coming down to the coast towns of the south. After Cogadh nam Bràithrean Alasdair Bàn held its lordship for life under the peace, kept the peace he had made to the end of his days, and died here in LE 1,291. The lordship returned to the crown, and Iain Ciar left it vacant for the rest of his reign. Known for the coal mole, and the lordship left vacant.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 19 an t-Samhain, VE 1,833. The northern Seann Skell, on the bay the hawk-keepers call their own, is not the river port of the west. In the fifth century of the count it put up a wall around its streets for the first time, and the crown granted a market inside the new landward gate where the amber of that coast was sold beside whale-oil, honey and the wool of the northern moors; the amber-workers swore to sell no rough stone outside the walls, and one of them, Ailig an Òir, forfeited a season's gathering to his own guild for breaking the oath within the year. After the schism of Òrd an t-Seabhaig the priests of An Seabhag Biadhte settled here, and under Beathag nic Sheumais built a following of four families into a school. From here in LE 919 she rode to Cathair dhearg to ask that the measured handful be raised by a quarter for the hearths of the north coast, and carried the refusal home in her own satchel; the house stood after exactly as it had before. Known for the amber market inside the gate, and the house of An Seabhag Biadhte.

**Seann Skell** (Seann Skell). Founded 6 an Gearran, VE 173. The river port at the mouth of the Abhainn naomh was the town a' Scaradh was made in. In its harbour-house, Taigh a' Chalaidh, Calum mac Nèill opened Rolla nan Deònach in the second year and wrote every household whole or not at all, cutting a struck name through with one stroke rather than scraping it. Alasdair Saor laid the first deep keel on the strand below the town, the fellowship of the strand swore its apprentices over a coal, and the queen's masons lengthened the west quay in dressed stone for what the crown called the harbour's trade. On the night before the sailing a lamp stood in every window along the waterfront, and in the morning Calum's grandson Niall cut one notch on a hazel stick for every hull that went round the river pool sunwise and down to the sea. The quay was called Cidhe an Diosail after that, and its old name passed to a fish-wharf. The harbour carried half its old trade within a generation. Mànas mac Ruairidh preached Manannan on its stones in the seventh century of the count, and Taigh Mhanannain was raised beside the harbour-court. Its synod set the prayer for the shut sea at the foot of the river pool. Oidhche nan Lòchran thinned household by household until one old woman, Ealasaid nic Iain, kept the last lamp; eleven people stood on the quay at the last Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh the age records, and the harbour scribe Eòghann mac Nèill counted them. Known for Rolla nan Deònach, Cidhe an Diosail and Oidhche nan Lòchran.

**Seann Tarr** (Seann Tarr). Founded 25 an Giblean, VE 1,212. The old harbour of the east coast below Cuan ruadh was torn apart in LE 1,399 by the storm the coast called Gailleann Ghlas, which came in out of the east and left the village standing but its quay in pieces past any mending worth the cost. Its boats went to Cuan ruadh, which built a second harbour arm to take them. Seann Tarr kept its houses and its shrine, let its harbour go, and was entered in the charter-roll, in the roll's own dry word for such places, as a village again. Known for the harbour given up after Gailleann Ghlas.

**Seann Tarr** (Muileann bheag). Founded 30 an Cèitean, VE 884. The small citadel harbour of the east kept an ancestor shrine of Na Seann Spioradan, and from LE 644 the crowds that came to it for the great feasts held a market on the three feast days, chiefly of honey, beeswax for the shrine's lights and the wool of the hill farms. The market outgrew the feasts in time and was held whether the shrine had a feast or not. Known for the feast-market at the shrine.

**Seann Toll** (Seann Toll). Founded 8 an t-Samhain, VE 1,033. The harbour town of the north coast lost its old harbour wall in one night in LE 259, in the storm its fishers call Am Fuath Mòr, and with it forty boats at their moorings and eighteen men and women who had gone down in the dark to save them. Its young reeve, Raghnall mac Nèill, thirty-four and four years in office, stood knee-deep hauling on a rope to bring in a boat with two children lashed inside, and afterward lost his count twice burying the dead in a single row on the headland. The town built its wall again higher and with a hooked end, to a plan the reeve had from the capital's masons, and the hooked wall stood through every storm of the age after. Known for the hooked harbour wall.

**Seann Vell** (Seann Vell). Founded 4 an t-Ògmhios, VE 396. The small citadel port far off on the south-east coast keeps its mills on its river. In a wet spring in LE 244 the river broke its banks and carried away the lower mills, and the mill-wrights built them again on the higher ground; a pupil of Òrd an t-Seabhaig house at Ros gheal who saw it called the flood a kind of overfed hawk, and Gormshuil nic Artair told him a river was a river, and sent him back to watch the mills rebuilt before he judged further. At the end of the age's first year the question whether anyone would go with the fleet was asked at hearths from Baile chrom in the north-west as far as Seann Vell. Known for its mills, and the flood of LE 244.

**Seann Warr** (Seann Warr). Founded 27 am Màrt, VE 725. The walled port nearest the capital on the west keeps salt-pans and brine springs behind its walls, and they fed it through Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean. Its reeve Mairead nic Ruairidh gave the heralds of all three claimants the same answer at the western gate: the town would open to trade and shut to hosts until the houses agreed which claim to answer. Dùghall Garbh sat before it a fortnight in LE 553, and Mairead sold his host bread at the market rate until his carters cost him more than the town was worth; he came back better provisioned three years later and sat a month, and marched away when Catrìona closed the gates of Cathair dhomhain. In LE 594 Catrìona Bhuadhach granted Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls, and the grant was cut in stone letters over the landward gate. Known for the gate shut against all three claimants, and the grant cut over it.

#### T

**Tobar dhearg** (Tobar dhearg). Founded 12 an Dàmhair, GE 2,947. The quarry village of the south-east burned in LE 446 when fire ran through its thatch, and most of it went. King Aonghas sent what the crown's granaries could spare before the winter closed the roads. A quarryman's household was the first to roof again in slate, judging that a man who cut the stone had less excuse than his neighbours to sleep under straw, and the village was rebuilt in slate from the quarries nearby and known for its slate roofs from then on. Known for its slate roofs.

**Tobar dhìreach** (Cnoc bhàn). Founded 25 an t-Iuchar, VE 42. The village among the wells of the eastern hill country keeps the naming rites of the old reciters. At a naming there in LE 525, for a steward's son of Tormod Bàn's household, the reciter Muireach mac Ailein of Clann na Ceiste said the line of An Clachair over the child instead of the long line of Rìghrean na Cloiche that royal namings there had called on for generations. Known for its namings at the wells.

# Appendix A — The Kings, the Queens and the Houses

For the eighteen centuries of a' Scaradh Dia-thìr kept one crown at Cathair dhearg, one vein-house above Muileann dhearg, and between them Na Seachd Taighean that answered to both and were, for most of the age, the stronger. This appendix gives the crowned rulers as Clàr nan Rìghrean recopied in LE 829 and Leabhar a' Chùraim give them, with their years and their ages; Na Seachd Taighean and those of their heads the record names; the masters of Taigh na Fèithe; the scribes who kept the harbour-house at Seann Skell; and the end of the crown. Years are counted from the first year of the age, as the rolls counted them after the crown took up Donnchadh's count; ages are given at the crowning and at the death, as Leabhar a' Chùraim sets them down. Na Bliadhnachan Fada of the old blood had thinned to an ordinary span by An Aois Naomh, and in this age no one, crowned or not, is entered as living past five-and-ninety.

## The crowned rulers

**Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill**, of the house of Dòmhnall, daughter of Mòr nic Coinnich. Crowned at fifteen in FE 2,953, eight years before the first year of the age; she was three-and-twenty when the three crews came to An Talla Dearg. She gave the word that the crown would send no one over and keep no one back, struck her sister Mòrag and Mòrag's children from the succession in the ordinary hand in LE 46, and wore undyed wool for her sister from the thirteenth year of the count. She died at Cathair dhearg in LE 55, at seventy-six, after one-and-sixty years crowned, holding a boundary petition to its end the morning she took to her bed. Her consort Uilleam mac Iain died in LE 29.

**Raghnall mac Uilleim**, her son, born LE 8. Crowned in LE 55 at seven-and-forty, with a strip of undyed wool at his wrist beneath the crowning colours. He died in LE 92 in his eighty-fifth year, four-and-eighty years old, after seven-and-thirty years crowned.

**Raghnall mac Raghnaill**, his son, born LE 45. Crowned in LE 92 at seven-and-forty, grey already at the temples. He died in LE 125 at eighty, three-and-thirty years crowned.

**Ìomhar mac Raghnaill**, his son, born LE 92. Crowned in LE 125 at three-and-thirty with the same cup and the same oath as his father. His only son, Raghnall Beag, died of a fever in LE 170. Ìomhar died in LE 180 at eight-and-eighty, five-and-fifty years crowned and without an heir, and the line of Beathag ended with him.

**Fearchar mac Lachlainn**, of Clann Fhearchair, born LE 157 at Baile Mòr dhomhain, the elder son, bound seven years to the galleries as a boy. Chosen by the heads of Na Seachd Taighean in the yard of An Talla Dearg in LE 182, when his younger brother Iain, head of the house, turned the choosing aside and named him; he drank his first oath from the cup of Clann Mhuirich, the crown having none ready. Crowned at five-and-twenty. He kept his court part of each year at Baile Mòr dhomhain. He died in LE 211 at four-and-fifty, nine-and-twenty years crowned, and asked that no more coal be burned for him than the ordinary handful.

**Fearchar Donn**, his son, born LE 188. Crowned in LE 211 at three-and-twenty. He died in LE 256 at eight-and-sixty, five-and-forty years crowned; the heads of Na Seachd Taighean held the hall in his daughter's name for two years.

**Sìleas nic Fhearchair**, his daughter, born LE 243. Crowned in LE 258 at fifteen. She married Dùghall mac Ìomhair of Clann Ìomhair, set the firlot of Cathair dhearg as the one measure of the island, put a tally-house in every royal granary, chartered the full-moon market of Cathair fhada and widened the bridge of the capital. She died in LE 324 at one-and-eighty, six-and-sixty years crowned, the longest reign An Talla Dearg had then seen.

**Uisdean mac Dhùghaill**, her son, born LE 270 in the twelfth year of her reign. Crowned in LE 324 at four-and-fifty. He died in LE 352 at two-and-eighty, eight-and-twenty years crowned.

**Uisdean mac Uisdein**, his son, born LE 322. Crowned in LE 352 at thirty. He had his son taught his letters by a tutor, Mòr nic Nèill, the first heir so taught. He died in LE 394 at two-and-seventy, two-and-forty years crowned.

**Aonghas mac Uisdein**, his son, born LE 372. Crowned in LE 394 at two-and-twenty, with less dispute than any crowning in living memory. He took up Òrd Mhacha' rite of Macha and made it the crown's custom, and half his household took it up after him. He died in LE 450 at eight-and-seventy, six-and-fifty years crowned.

**Aonghas Òg mac Aonghais**, his son, born LE 400. Crowned in LE 450 at fifty. He died in the winter of LE 484 at four-and-eighty, four-and-thirty years crowned, the first king carried to his grave by the rite of Macha.

**Iain mac Aonghais**, his son, born LE 435. Crowned in LE 484 at nine-and-forty. He had three sons, the youngest, Dùghall, by a second wife. He died in LE 496 at one-and-sixty, twelve years crowned: the third king the hall had buried in a single generation.

**Tormod mac Iain, Tormod Bàn**, his eldest son, born LE 460. Crowned in LE 496 at six-and-thirty. His two sons were drowned together when the ferry on the Abhainn fhionn overturned in LE 534, and his brother Aonghas mac Iain had died four years before. He named no heir. He died in LE 547 at seven-and-eighty, one-and-fifty years crowned, and Na Seachd Taighean held the hall in common while three claims stood unanswered.

**Catrìona nic Aonghais, Catrìona Bhuadhach**, daughter of Aonghas mac Iain and Mairead nic Ailein, niece of Tormod Bàn, born LE 526 at Inis thais. She won Cogadh nan Trì Tagraichean and was crowned in LE 562 at six-and-thirty. She bound every claimant, house and king by Riaghailt an Teallaich, laid Rathad na Banrighinn in stone to her own gate, and honoured Seann Warr's gates. Her husband Iain mac Eachainn died in LE 594. She died in LE 604 at eight-and-seventy, two-and-forty years crowned, the last ruler who had fought in the war.

**Lachlann mac Iain**, her son, born LE 565. Crowned in LE 604 at nine-and-thirty; the seven heads swore to him within a single day of his mother's burial. He had Leabhar nan Trì Tagraichean read into the record and forbade that any copy of it be made shorter than the one before. He died in LE 654 at nine-and-eighty, fifty years crowned.

**Anna**, his daughter, born LE 600. Crowned in LE 654 at four-and-fifty. She died in LE 685 at five-and-eighty, one-and-thirty years crowned.

**The fourth of the house of Catrìona**, Anna's child, born LE 635. Crowned in LE 685 at fifty; died in LE 722 at seven-and-eighty, seven-and-thirty years crowned. Clàr nan Rìghrean as recopied keeps the years and has lost the name.

**The fifth of the house of Catrìona**, child of the fourth, born LE 680. Crowned in LE 722 at two-and-forty; died in LE 769 at nine-and-eighty, seven-and-forty years crowned. The name is likewise lost.

**Eilidh Bhàn**, granddaughter of the fifth, born LE 751. Crowned in LE 769 at eighteen. She sent Iain mac Thormoid against the sea-thieves of the small islands and had Clàr nan Rìghrean recopied onto new hide in LE 829. She died in LE 841 at ninety, two-and-seventy years crowned, the oldest ruler of the age, and without an heir.

**Dòmhnall Ruadh**, of Clann Raghnaill, a custodian of three galleries at Muileann chrom, born LE 790. Named by Na Seachd Taighean after five years of sittings at Taigh na Fèithe, and crowned at Cathair dhearg in LE 846 at six-and-fifty. In LE 859 the crown was joined to the mastery of Taigh na Fèithe, and from LE 865 the custody's seal, the trellis and the hollow stone, went on the crown's letters. He died in LE 871 at one-and-eighty, five-and-twenty years crowned, and was buried at his own wish in a worked-out gallery under the mountain with an unlit lamp at his head.

**Raghnall Òg**, his son, born LE 825. Crowned in LE 871 at six-and-forty, more at ease with a boundary plea than with his own coronation. The record gives no year for his death, and Clàr nan Rìghrean for the century and a half after him keeps reigns that this record does not number.

**Mòrag Ruadh**, a girl of Clann Raghnaill, born LE 1,000. Named by Na Seachd Taighean on the death of the old king and crowned in LE 1,019 at nineteen. She kept her own ledger, clasped in iron at her own asking, from the first month; she judged that the thousandth year of the count deserved one handful burned on Cidhe an Diosail and no more, and rode down to see it burned. Her daughter was born in LE 1,040. She reigned sixty-three years; the ledger's last sum is of LE 1,082.

**Beathag Fhionn**, her daughter, born LE 1,040. Sat at her mother's right hand for years before she was crowned in LE 1,082 at two-and-forty, and closed the coast road against the swallowing cough within the month. She died in LE 1,129 at nine-and-eighty, seven-and-forty years crowned, asking whether the road stood open.

**Ailean**, her son, born LE 1,070. Crowned in LE 1,129 at nine-and-fifty. The record gives no year for his death.

**Ailean mac Raghnaill**, born LE 1,200. The record gives no year for his crowning. He reigned long enough that few at the hall could remember another king's seal, and died in LE 1,266 at six-and-sixty, leaving two sons by different mothers and a burial roll with a blank where the heir's name should stand.

**Iain Ciar**, his son, born LE 1,240. He won Cogadh nam Bràithrean against his half-brother Alasdair Bàn and made the peace at An Taigh-seinnse Mòr with two loaves left uneaten on the board. Crowned in LE 1,276 at six-and-thirty. He kept his brother's lordship of Seann Chwen vacant after Alasdair's death in LE 1,291, made the grain law of LE 1,299, and chartered the road-houses of the mining roads in LE 1,319. He died in LE 1,326 at six-and-eighty, fifty years crowned.

**Catrìona Bheag**, of Clann Raghnaill, born LE 1,400. Crowned in LE 1,429 at nine-and-twenty, the first queen in more than three centuries; the record notes she was small, and that no one at her court said so twice. She had the seven heads swear Riaghailt an Teallaich afresh in LE 1,449.

**Sìleas Òg**, born LE 1,505. Crowned in LE 1,529 at four-and-twenty. She rode a round of every shire seat on the island, the first ruler to stand in all of them, entered the smaller Cunntas nan Làmh of LE 1,539 without a word, and presided when the council refused the first of Athchuingean an Airgid in LE 1,559.

**Ailean mac Raghnaill, the fourth of the name**, born LE 1,550. Crowned in LE 1,589 at nine-and-thirty; dead within the year at forty, the shortest reign Clàr nan Rìghrean sets down. Leabhar a' Chùraim does not say what ailed him. His sister had the years of his crowning and death cut on one stone.

**Mòrag nic Raghnaill**, his sister, born LE 1,556. Crowned in LE 1,590 at four-and-thirty. She reigned forty years, to LE 1,630, and her clerk set down under her no death by war, no famine and no quarrel of Na Seachd Taighean.

**Tormod mac Ruairidh**, of Clann Raghnaill, born LE 1,680. Crowned in LE 1,709 at nine-and-twenty. The record keeps of his reign chiefly its roads and its bridges. He governed his last years from a chair by the hearth and died in LE 1,766 at six-and-eighty, seven-and-fifty years crowned, the longest-lived king Leabhar a' Chùraim had entered since Clàr nam Bliadhnachan; he told his daughter the last night that he had never found the courage to ask Taigh na Fèithe the forbidden question.

**Gormshuil nic Thormoid**, his daughter, born LE 1,715. Crowned in LE 1,766 at one-and-fifty. She rode a progress of every shire seat from LE 1,771 and had Leabhar nan Gearan written at each. In LE 1,795, eighty years old and nine-and-twenty years crowned, she rode the coal-road to Taigh na Fèithe for the winter burning, as she had every winter of her reign, and walked her own horse up the last iced mile. Nothing more is told.

## The empty chair

From the winter after the queen went up, the custodians of Na Seachd Taighean sat at An Talla Dearg in her place, sending their word up the coal-road by the riders who had carried the crown's business, and from LE 1,798 they sealed their letters with the custody's trellis and hollow stone and no name above the seal. No clerk was asked to explain the blank. In the seventeenth winter, LE 1,812, the heads, meeting at Cathair dhearg by the chance of their riders' errands, called themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim, the council of the custody, and named Tormod mac Ailein, eight-and-thirty, a custodian's son of no house among the seven, Ceann a' Chùraim to speak for them with one voice. He was offered the queen's chair at the head of the board and kept his place at its foot. The chair stood empty at every sitting after, and by the last winter of the age no clerk living could say with certainty whose absence it marked.

## Na Seachd Taighean

The houses were made at Taigh na Fèithe in LE 55, when a fifth of the coal-right's households had gone with the fleet and the old apprenticeship could no longer serve the galleries. The remaining custodian households were gathered into seven kindreds, their heads sworn before Crom's stone, and from that year the right to the coal passed by house: Clann Mhuirich, Clann Fhearchair, Clann Ìomhair, Clann Raghnaill, Clann Thormoid, Clann Choinnich and Clann Lachlainn. In LE 109 each head drew a marked stone from a covered bag for the galleries, and the bag hung on its peg in Taigh na Fèithe hall for the rest of the age. From LE 149 the heads wore the silver neck-rings of Muileann chiar.

**Clann Mhuirich.** Its head, a woman, lent the house's own cup for Fearchar mac Lachlainn's first oath in LE 182. The record names no other head of it.

**Clann Fhearchair**, of Baile Mòr dhomhain. It gave the crown Fearchar mac Lachlainn and his line, and its head **Iain mac Lachlainn**, born LE 160, head from LE 179, kept the house's hall while his brother reigned, and died in LE 219.

**Clann Ìomhair**, of the eastern hills about Dùn dhearg. It walled Dùn dhearg in LE 261 without the crown's leave and gave Queen Sìleas her consort, Dùghall mac Ìomhair. **Beathag nic Uisdein**, its head, set her mark last and longest to Riaghailt an Teallaich in LE 565 and knelt first to Lachlann mac Iain in LE 604.

**Clann Raghnaill.** Its head **Raghnall Ruadh**, born LE 505, was chosen master of Taigh na Fèithe in LE 540 over two men of longer service, claimed the crown after Tormod Bàn, refused the measured handful to the shires that stood against him in LE 558, and fell below Muileann chrom in LE 560. The house gave the crown Dòmhnall Ruadh and, from Mòrag Ruadh on, most of the rulers of the age's second half.

**Clann Thormoid.** An old woman of the house, who had given a brother and two nephews to the roll, turned the sitting of LE 54 by saying she would sooner see her right folded into a house that could walk its galleries than stand alone over ones it could not serve.

**Clann Choinnich.** Its head, a woman, argued three winters that the coal be burned beyond the handful to smelt the silver of Muileann chiar, and the house brought the first of Athchuingean an Airgid in LE 1,558 and the second in LE 1,776; both were refused, and the house asked a third time at the first sitting of Comhairle a' Chùraim and was set aside. At the renewed oath of LE 1,449 its head asked whether the oath changed the measure or only the manner.

**Clann Lachlainn.** **Aonghas mac Lachlainn**, born LE 1,720, sat on the council that refused Athchuingean an Airgid and turned his own vote against it at the board without a reason; he died at Cathair dhearg in LE 1,804 at four-and-eighty, the last of that council, and kept his reason.

By the last Cunntas nan Làmh in LE 1,791 three of the seven held more than half the whole right between them, and one of the four smaller houses was eased with a neighbour's unused right.

## The masters of Taigh na Fèithe

**Eòghann mac Mhuirich**, master at the opening of the age, who made the first count of the departing households in LE 3 and saw the measures for the fleet sealed; he died in LE 30, very old. The custody-book leaves the masters after him unnamed until the war. **Raghnall Ruadh** of Clann Raghnaill was chosen in LE 540 and held the mastery until he fell in LE 560. From LE 859 the king was master of Taigh na Fèithe, and the crown and the custody kept their records on one shelf.

The scribes of Leabhar a' Chùraim the record names are **Donnchadh mac Thormoid**, born LE 14, given to Taigh na Fèithe at nine, maker of the fair copy of the ruling of the coal at fifteen and of the count from An Diosal at thirty, who died at Muileann dhearg in LE 109 at five-and-ninety; **Murchadh Beag**, who took a coal-breaker's son from the face for a scribe's stool and died about LE 728; and **Eòghann mac Pheadair**, born LE 700, who settled the two counts of An Diosal with the crown's scribe **Mòrag nic Ìomhair** in LE 739 and died about LE 770. Under them **Eòghann mac Dhùghaill**, master of the store in the war, kept Raghnall Ruadh's list of refused hearths face to the wall and never scraped it, and his son **Dòmhnall mac Eòghainn** let Seònaid nic Coinnich copy it.

## The harbour scribes of Seann Skell

**Calum mac Nèill**, born FE 2,930, opened Rolla nan Deònach in LE 2 and kept the boards six-and-fifty years; he died in the room above the harbour-house in LE 58. **Niall mac Dhòmhnaill**, his grandson, born LE 29, who counted the hulls with a hazel stick at eleven, kept the boards from LE 58 to his death in LE 104 and was buried with the stick in his hand; his father **Dòmhnall mac Chaluim** kept the trade rolls beside him and died in LE 66. **Murchadh mac Raghnaill** was harbour-master in Niall's time and made the count of half trade. **Ailean mac Mhurchaidh** kept the harbour-house when Seònaid nic Coinnich came to read the old boards in LE 612, and **Donnchadh mac Ailein**, scribe of the harbour-court, would not enter Manannan's blessings beside the tallies of hulls. **Eòghann mac Nèill**, born LE 1,763, kept the book at Cidhe an Diosail from LE 1,792 to the end of the age, counted the eleven at the last Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh, and wrote the number, the weather and the tide in the same plain hand every Là an Diosail after.

## The queen's scribes

**Murchadh mac Eòghainn**, born FE 2,925, wrote the three tellings on one leaf in the first year, sealed the queen's word, and entered Mòrag's line struck in LE 46, sanding the leaf as he had sanded every entry for forty years; he died in LE 49. **Seònaid nic Coinnich**, born LE 549, came to An Talla Dearg at seventeen from the charity of Cathair mhòr, served Catrìona Bhuadhach and Lachlann, and wrote Leabhar nan Trì Tagraichean, finished in LE 624; she died in LE 631 at two-and-eighty. **Pàdraig mac Ruairidh** wrote Leabhar nam Bràithrean in Iain Ciar's praise and died about LE 1,320. **Pàdraig mac Ìomhair**, steward, set his sums before the girl Mòrag Ruadh from the evening she found his tally wrong.

# Appendix B — The Orders and the Rites

An Creideamh Sean that the island kept at the opening of a' Scaradh had no orders in it. There were the dawn-hawk rite at Cnoc bheag, the sacred woods kept in common by whoever kept them, Scoiltean nan Draoidhean with no ground of their own, the wolf-stone at Inis thais watched by families who had forgotten why, the old spirits of the hearths with their keepers in the east, and the handful of coal burned at every lawful hearth under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig. By the end of the age the same faith had five orders with their own houses, books and quarrels, and the island had made for itself a set of rites for the departed that no order owned. This appendix gives each as the record gives it: when it began, where it held, and what it quarrelled over.

## The coal and Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig

Under all the orders lay the custody of the vein. Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig, measured to every hearth that held the right a handful of the coal, burned at the winter burning and at the rites of the household, and no more. The custodians of Taigh na Fèithe above Muileann dhearg kept the law in Leabhar a' Chùraim and kept Crom's stone in the inner room, with a lamp before it that was never let go out. The law was bent three times in the age and broken once. It was bent when the custodians ruled in LE 25, after six winters of argument, that each hull of the fleet found ready might carry one sealed measure, a single household's season; when Na Seachd Taighean were made in LE 55 and the right passed by house rather than by apprenticeship; and when a smaller house was granted a neighbour's unused right at the last Cunntas nan Làmh. It was broken in LE 558, when Raghnall Ruadh refused the handful to every hearth and temple of the shires that stood against him, and Riaghailt an Teallaich of LE 565 bound every claimant, house and king never to withhold it again. The first asking to burn the coal for work rather than worship, Athchuingean an Airgid of Clann Choinnich, was refused in LE 1,559, and the second in LE 1,776.

## Òrd an t-Seabhaig

The dawn-hawk rite of An Aois Naomh was kept at Cnoc bheag by a single family of hawk-keepers. In the third century of the count the priestess Gormshuil nic Artair, who took the mews from her father Artair, taught that the hawk of the rite was Mòd himself, Seabhag Acaill, and that the vein under Muileann dhearg was a hawk of his kind: a hungry hawk, to be fed the measured handful and never glutted past it, since a bird fed past its measure is as useless as one starved of it. Her watchers called themselves a house and raised Taigh an t-Seabhaig below the mews block in LE 232; her pupils raised a second house at Ros gheal in LE 239, which took charge of the measured burning for the coast country. Ùisdean mac Pàdraig wrote her sayings after her death as Leabhar an t-Seabhaig, and marked every saying he had not heard from her own mouth; the marked sayings outnumber the rest. Òrd an t-Seabhaig reached the south when the bell-founders of Muileann naomh hung a bronze bell in a hawk-house there, and at Muileann naomh the teaching held whole when it softened elsewhere.

At the council of Òrd an t-Seabhaig at Cnoc bheag in LE 889 a young priest asked whether Mòd would rather starve a grown flock than see his handful grown to meet it. Those who held that a greater household might rightly be fed a greater handful were named An Seabhag Biadhte, and asked to keep their teaching somewhere it would not be heard daily at Cnoc bheag. They settled at the northern Seann Skell on Bàgh an t-Seabhaig, where the priestess Beathag nic Sheumais built them from four families into a school; her petition of LE 919 to raise the handful by a quarter for the north coast was refused, and the house went on as before.

## The schools of the druids

Scoiltean nan Draoidhean of Flidais, lady of the deer, taught Feallsanachd an Fhèidh, the stag's teaching: that the vein answers a hand for some measure in it, which the schools never agreed how to name. They had no ground of their own until LE 479, when they took up the yearly walk of Coille Naomh Muileann chiar at Muileann chiar, a procession open to anyone who would walk it. Their elder teacher there, Beathag nic Ruairidh, told the travelling druid Coinneach mac Mhàrtainn that the schools wanted a fixed ground where the old question might be argued whole, and he raised Taigh na Deasbaid at Dùn thais in LE 314 with Carson an làmh seo?, why this hand?, cut on the lintel. The rule of the house was that a question once put was argued a full year before any answer came from the master's chair. Coinneach's own question in LE 324, whether the hands that went with the fleet were those the vein answered best, was forbidden at every one of Na Seachd Taighean' tables, the first time the houses forbade a question rather than a deed. Pupils of Dùn thais founded a second house of disputation at Inis mhòr in LE 769. Raghnall mac Chaluim's Clàr nam Bliadhnachan at Dùn thais was forbidden in LE 1,219 and the house shut; it was opened and shut more than once and last reopened in LE 1,759 on condition that the question of longer lives never be raised.

The rival teaching of An Aois Naomh, that the vein answers labour and not birth, was woken at Doire chiar by Eilidh Dhubh from LE 460. Taigh na Fèithe had some hundred of her tracts burned in its yard in LE 484, and the teaching went on in copies and in her pupil Coinneach Odhar's readings, without an order and without a house.

## Òrd Mhacha, Macha of the two horses

Macha's rite was Òrd Mhacha' rite of the moors, which keeps the two horses of one chariot, foaled on one night, Liath Macha the grey and Dubh Sainglenn the black: light and dark, two powers in balance, and the vein belonging to both. At the rite the horses were brought up together to the yoke-poles and the worshipper stood with a hand on each pole, since one horse pulling alone draws a chariot only in a circle. King Aonghas mac Uisdein took it up in his own old age in LE 441 against his councillors' warning, and within a year half An Talla Dearg's household had taken it up with him, so that Òrd Mhacha became the order of Cathair dhearg without a quarrel fought over it. Coille Naomh Cnoc bheag, held in common since An Aois Naomh, passed to Macha's priests alone by royal grant in LE 471. King Aonghas Òg was the first king carried to his grave by the rite in LE 484. Macha's temple at Cathair mhòr fed the burnt-out households of Doire mhin through the winter of LE 555 without asking whose claim they had favoured, and its fire was the first of the cold shires' hearths relit in LE 560. In the fifteenth century the priests raised their great house at Cathair mhòr, with a floor of black and white stone eleven years in the laying, the largest roofed building on Dia-thìr.

## Òrd na Cloiche

At Inis thais the wolf-stone Clach had been watched for generations by families who kept the watch without a name for it. In LE 405 the net-maker Dòmhnall mac Ailein began to say on the strand that the stone was Lia Fàil, which cries out under the rightful, and its watchers an Fhianna, sworn to keep the whole island as a wolf keeps its range. His hearers became an Fhianna and raised the wolf-house, the first temple on the island to Lia Fàil by name, roofed with northern slate, and blew a horn at every turn of the tide. Dòmhnall taught on the strand five-and-thirty years and never took an office in the order named after his teaching. Òrd na Cloiche and Òrd an t-Seabhaig both claimed the harbour shrine at Caol leathan in LE 427; the king's reeve divided its hours between them. An Fhianna nursed the sick of Inis chrom through the spotted fever of LE 624, many of them dying of it. In LE 1,389 the congregation at Inis thais divided over whether the dead, who belong to Donn, might be prayed for by name at Clach; those who said no kept the temple, and the others raised a second house at Baile gheal.

## Òrd Mhanannain, Manannan of the mist

Òrd Mhanannain began on the quay of Seann Skell in LE 654, when Mànas mac Ruairidh, son of a sworn-man of the harbour-court, preached that the one power was Manannan mac Lir, lord of the sea, whose cup, Cupa na Fìrinne, bears the yellow scorpion; that Manannan had shut the eastern sea behind the fleet with his mist, which hides Dia-thìr from every ship beyond it; and that the crossing must not be tried again. His own father knelt first. He blessed boats at Cidhe an Diosail by passing a plain wooden bowl of harbour water over each hull, and his congregation later raised the silver for a proper cup of plain silver without his asking. Taigh Mhanannain was raised beside the harbour-court. The teaching went down the coast with the fishing families to Ros bheag and Cuan shean, where the old rope-walker Tormod Ciar swore Cupa na Fìrinne on the rope-walk in rainwater cupped in his hands. In LE 694 the priests at Ros bheag laid down that no boat of the faithful might go out of sight of the headlands, and the rule of sight-of-land was kept on the west coast for the rest of the age. The synod of the order at Seann Skell in LE 1,590 laid down the rule of sight-of-land again and argued two days over a new prayer before agreeing its shortest form, to be said at the foot of the river pool: A Mhanannain, cùm a' mhuir dùinte. From LE 1,714 the priests said it on the day of Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh as well, on the same stones, and neither the keepers of the rite nor the priests were pleased; by the end of the age they said it at every tide. In the age's last years the priest Mànas mac Dhùghaill wrote that the grey beyond the headlands stood thinner each year, and that he could not say whether the prayer held anything back at all.

## The old spirits

The keepers of Na Seann Spioradan, the faith of the hearths, kept the ancestors in the east. In LE 179 they raised a spirit-house at Dùn ìseal and cut the names of the eastern dead on wooden posts, renewed each generation. Lightning burned the posts in LE 1,149 and the keepers cut the names again from memory and from Leabhar a' Chùraim, owning in their roll that some were guesses. The shepherds of the Doire uaine hills lit no fire on the high pastures after dark, for fear of Marbh-bheò of the old carvings, and a reeve sent to argue them out of it came down before dark and never went back. The shrine at Seann Tarr held its feast-market from LE 644.

## The rites of the departed

No order made these, and every order kept them.

**Oidhche nan Lòchran.** On the evening before the sailing, beginning at one widow's window by the fish-stones, a lamp was set on every sill along the Seann Skell waterfront and kept burning till morning, though no one had told the town to do it. It was kept each year on the eve nearest the day of the turn, household by household, and thinned over the centuries until one old woman, Ealasaid nic Iain, kept the one lamp in the harbour-house window; she died in LE 1,800 and no one set a light there again.

**An Tùrsa Geal.** Queen Beathag put on undyed wool for her sister in LE 53, with no grave to stand at and no body to wash, and laid a cup, a trencher and a straight knife at the foot of her table each evening. Within a generation any household that had given someone to the fleet kept the same rite unasked. In the north-east it was kept in the undyed rain-cloth of Baile gharbh.

**Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh.** On the eve nearest the day of the turn the households of Seann Skell brought small lights down to the west quay and set them along the stones the fleet sailed from. The harbours kept it on different days until the bargain of LE 739 fixed one day for all of them, Là an Diosail. It was kept by fewer each generation; eleven people stood on Cidhe an Diosail at the last rite this record tells of, in LE 1,803.

**Faire a' Chinn.** Faire a' Chinn was kept at Ceann mhòr from LE 66, household by household in turn, for returning sails that never came, and lapsed long before the end of the age.

**Roghnaich.** The rolls came to use the word roghnaich, to choose, standing alone to mean one who chose the crossing, and the harbour scribes let it stand.

# Appendix C — The Reckoning of An Diosal

In An Aois Scaraidh the island first numbered its years from a single day, and the day it chose was the day its kin went away. This appendix tells how the count was begun, how two offices came to keep it a year apart and settled the difference by agreement rather than by proof, how the moons were reckoned beneath the years, and how a year was written in the rolls of the age. The years of this record are counted from the first year of the age, the year the tidings of a far coast came to the quays; An Diosal fell in its fortieth year.

## Before the count

At the opening of the age no one on Dia-thìr numbered the years from any day at all. An Talla Dearg counted by reigns and by harvests, and the first year of the age went into its rolls as the ninth year of Queen Beathag, a good year for barley and a middling one for fish. Leabhar a' Chùraim at Taigh na Fèithe counted by burnings: a year was the year in which the handful was measured and burned at every lawful hearth, and it was named, when it had to be named, by the master of Taigh na Fèithe and the winter it fell in. The harbour-house at Seann Skell counted by the scribe's own keeping, the sixth or seventh year of Niall's boards. Clàr nan Rìghrean gave the names of the kings in order and the length of no reign. A debt within living memory could be reckoned so. The distance between two reigns could not, and no one had yet needed it.

## Donnchadh's count

The count was not made at the time of the turn. Donnchadh mac Thormoid, a clerk of Taigh na Fèithe, had entered the turn of the fleet in Leabhar a' Chùraim at six-and-twenty, under a day after Samhain, a full turning of the moon and more after every other account set the sailing itself; the leaf that reached him did not explain the gap, and he copied it faithfully. Four years later, at thirty, in LE 44, for his own ledger's convenience and for no reason he offered anyone, he began to number the years from the turn as Leabhar a' Chùraim entered it, and called them Bliadhnaichean an Diosail. The word means, in the island's speech, a turning sunwise: the way a hand moves, a boat rounds a point or a procession goes about a cairn, with the right shoulder toward the centre and the course following the sun. He worked the count backward through his private book to the turn itself. There was no year nought; the years before the turn were counted backward, as years before the turn. No one above him asked him to keep it, and he told no one that he did.

The crown's own scribes at An Talla Dearg took up the count about a generation later, in the seventies of the age, setting aside the reckoning by a king's reign for the turning Donnchadh had first set his own hand to as a clerk of thirty. From that time the rolls of An Talla Dearg, Leabhar a' Chùraim and the harbour boards dated their entries by An Diosal, and the old reckoning by reigns survived in Clàr nan Rìghrean alone.

## The two counts

The harbour scribe at Seann Skell had set Am Falbh and An Diosal on one morning. Leabhar a' Chùraim set the turn after the next Samhain. The crown's scribes, taking up the count when the court remembered the departure as a single thing, counted from the year the ships sailed; Taigh na Fèithe, following Donnchadh, counted from the turn as its own book entered it. Both began each year at Samhain, by the moon, as Talla na Lasrach had done before Taigh na Fèithe; so the sailing and the turn lay in different years of the old year, and the two counts stood a year apart. Nobody noticed for the better part of seven centuries, for the two offices seldom had cause to set a date of one beside a date of the other.

In LE 738 they found that their counts did not agree. Mòrag nic Ìomhair, a scribe of An Talla Dearg's own household, rode the thirty-nine miles to Taigh na Fèithe with the crown's leaves, and the master granted her Leabhar a' Chùraim for as many days as the matter took. She and Taigh na Fèithe scribe Eòghann mac Pheadair worked three days by lamplight and traced the difference back to a single year early after the turn, entered twice by one office's habit or once by the other's. Neither leaf either scribe had brought could say which office had erred, or whether either had. In LE 739 Taigh na Fèithe took the crown's count for the one that would go forward, since it touched more households than Taigh na Fèithe's own, and Eòghann wrote Taigh na Fèithe's agreement to it in his own hand, the master's mark under his and the crown scribe's office mark under that. A later hand in Leabhar a' Chùraim adds that the scribes afterward ceased to pretend it had been fixed by proof. The same agreement fixed, for the first time, one day on which every harbour of the coast should keep Deas-ghnàth a' Chalaidh Fhalaimh, which the two counts had placed differently; not one harbour wrote to complain of it. From that year there was one count of An Diosal on Dia-thìr, and it followed the harbour scribe, setting the sailing and the turn both in its first year.

## The thousandth year

By the settled count the thousandth year of An Diosal fell in LE 1,039. Na Seachd Taighean asked Queen Mòrag Ruadh whether it deserved a feast or a fast, and she judged between them: one burning on the quay the count began from, no more coal in it than an ordinary hearth burns of an evening. She rode a week over frost-hard roads to stand on Cidhe an Diosail for it, and her own book gives the cost of the coal reckoned to Taigh na Fèithe's weights and, beneath it, five words: one handful, nothing more.

## The night-count and the moons

Beneath the years the island reckoned by the moon, and it counted time by nights and not by days. The night went before its day, as the dark half of the year went before the bright: a feast began at dusk on its eve, and a debt of ten nights fell due at the tenth dusk. Leabhar a' Chùraim calls this reckoning cunntas nan oidhcheannan, the count of the nights.

The year began at Samhain, with the dark half of the year. It held twelve moons of thirty nights and twenty-nine in turn, each begun on the night of the full moon: waning through its dark half to the dark of the moon, then waxing through its bright half to the next full. Below the moon the island had the half-moon, fourteen nights or fifteen as the moon ran, and no week. A debt, a sentence or a turn in the galleries was set by the half-moon; the markets met at the full, as Queen Sìleas's charter to Cathair fhada granted; the night of the full and the night of the dark were rest-nights, on which no coal was cut and no net set.

Twelve moons make some eleven nights fewer than the sun's year, so about every thirtieth moon a thirteenth, Eadrach, the between-moon, was put in at the year's end, after Damhrach and before Samhnas, so that Samhain should not come before the summer was out. In An Aois Naomh Talla na Lasrach declared the between-moon; in this age Taigh na Fèithe declared it, and entered the years in which it was put in beside the burnings. Harbour scribes dated deaths to it like any other moon: Calum mac Nèill died in the between-moon of LE 58.

The moons, in their order from Samhain:

| No. | Moon | Nights | The rolls of the age remember it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Samhnas | 30 | Samhain on its first night; the granary barred at Àth shean in LE 37 |
| 2 | Dubhlas | 29 | the black moon; the temple fires of the cold shires going out in LE 558 |
| 3 | Faolach | 30 | the wolf-moon; the first tale of a far coast on the quay at Cuan shean; Seumas Reultach's death |
| 4 | Gearras | 29 | Là Fhèill Brìde on its first night; Alasdair Saor setting out on the north road |
| 5 | Sìolach | 30 | the seed-time; the granary doors reopened; An Gàire Dubh |
| 6 | Bearnach | 29 | the gap between the last of the stores and the first green; Queen Sìleas at the widened bridge |
| 7 | Bealltach | 30 | Bealltainn on its first night; Fearchar Donn's death |

| 9 | Teasach | 30 | the hot moon; the launching of the last coaster Alasdair built |
